FALLING LEAVES
The True Story of an Unwanted
Chinese Daughter.
By Adeline Yen Mah.
Illustrated. 278 pp. 
New York:
John Wiley & Sons. 
$22.95.
ADELINE Yen Mah's "Falling Leaves: The True Story of an Unwanted Chinese Daughter" opens with the reading of the first page of her father's will in the opulent office of a Hong Kong attorney. 
Joseph Yen's entire estate is left to his second wife, Jeanne, who declares that since there is nothing left -- without explanation, her husband's two tons of gold bullion, stocks and shares, and worldwide real estate holdings have disappeared -- the rest of the will is meaningless. 
With that, the siblings are instructed to hand over their copies, which, because they have been bullied by this woman their entire lives long, they do.
Mah alludes to a traditional Chinese aphorism -- "falling leaves return to their roots" -- to describe her narrative journey back in time to the roots of her Shanghai family. 
Although the early stories are inspiring and even heartwarming -- Mah's great-aunt defies tradition by resolutely refusing to have her feet bound and founds the Shanghai Women's Bank; another aunt exudes unconditional love -- "Falling Leaves" is nothing if not a traditional memoir of a bad childhood.
These early memories are soon supplanted by a litany of abuses. 
The family irrationally blames Mah for the death of her mother, who died in childbirth. 
Her father, Joseph Yen, soon takes up with Jeanne Prosperi, the 17-year-old daughter of a French father and a Chinese mother. 
With her European ancestry, great beauty and convent education, she is seen as the ultimate trophy wife. 
By the age of 23, Jeanne has two children of her own in addition to her five stepchildren, whose Chinese names she immediately bans. 
Overnight they become Lydia, Gregory, Edgar, James and Adeline, and are subjected to verbal degradation. 
"I do think Adeline is getting uglier and uglier as she grows older and taller," Jeanne observes at one point. 
This Mommy Dearest beats her own baby daughter, and Adeline, a plucky first grader, is the only person to object. 
"I shall never forget or forgive your insolence," Jeanne announces. 
"Never!
Never!
Never!"
She keeps her word. 
Just as the Japanese invade, Adeline is sent away to boarding school, where she is abandoned for years. 
So beguiled is Joseph by his luscious and headstrong wife that he never intervenes on his children's behalf.
To be fair, this entire family seems almost psychotically cruel. 
Adeline's brothers urinate into her orange juice. 
When one of those brothers writes that he'd like to become a professional bridge player, his father sends a telegram: "Why don't you become a pimp instead?"
The elder Yens repeatedly pit one child against the other. 
Those who dare to protest are disowned and disinherited. 
Through it all, Adeline never stops longing for her family's love and acceptance. 
But with the exceptions of Adeline and her half sister Susan (herself married to a Hong Kong billionaire), these are people who plot and scheme to the very end for their father's long hidden and greatly depleted fortune of $30 million.
Mah's story is almost a casebook study of the effects of long-term abuse, but she doesn't seem to have the self-awareness to place it in this context. 
So when her first love affair is with someone emotionally abusive, or her first husband is a batterer, she sees these interludes, which so clearly follow the pattern of victimization, as just two more bad things that happen to her. 
Only rarely does she offer a glimpse into her sex's historical plight, even though abortion, infanticide and abandonment of female children occur routinely in Chinese culture even now. 
Still, in many ways the turbulence of Mah's family life mirrors the great conflicts of China during the last century. 
"Bear many sons. 
Sublimate your own desires. 
Become the willing . . . spittoon of the Yens and we will be proud of you," Mah's grandmother was told on the eve of her wedding. 
Even her radically independent aunts are eventually stripped of power and position, condemned and persecuted. 
Humbled, they eke out their last days without protest.
Like so many memoirists, Mah finally triumphs over adversity. 
While never winning the Yens' love, she becomes a respected physician, marries a fine man and starts her own family. 
It's hard not to admire her persistence and perseverance, or to think of those siblings scattered around the world, spending their inheritances and maybe taking a peek at their sister's scorching and vivid account.

text:
ï»¿
Not long ago, Tsingtao Brewery looked unbeatable.
With a high quality product, a well established name, a booming beer market and ambitious plans to quadruple production in five years, Tsingtao seemed perfectly positioned to ride China's locomotive-like economic growth. 
In 1993, when the Government allowed China's top companies to list shares on Hong Kong's stock exchange, Tsingtao was chosen to go first, and its stock was one of the hottest issues of the year.
Yet Tsingtao (pronounced ching-dow) is going nowhere. 
Its profits are sagging, its stock is near an all-time low, and its expansion plans have stalled. 
Tsingtao managers have been reluctant to explain why the $190 million they raised in 1993 has not been invested in expansion.
Tsingtao's story straddles a central paradox in China today. 
In this nation's wrenching shift from a planned to a market economy, explosive growth has been accompanied by bumbling financial operations mired in a hopelessly inefficient system run by the Communist Party. 
The heralded entry of Chinese stocks into securities markets in Hong Kong and Shanghai has been a dud.
"Even by the year 2000 China could become an economic giant but remain a financial pygmy," Timothy Beardson, chairman of Crosby Securities in Hong Kong, said at a recent conference in Beijing.
The contradiction is striking: China has emerged as a magnet for international investment, as manufacturers like Motorola, Coca-Cola and General Motors pour in. 
Economic growth has averaged a sparkling 12 percent annually for four years, and an awakening demand for consumer goods and services is likely to continue for decades.
Yet the financial system envisioned by China's leaders is stuck in its infancy. 
China's stock markets remain tiny and lackluster: in the past six months, as the Dow Jones industrial average kept racking up new highs, Chinese shares on the Hong Kong and Shanghai markets have drifted lower and lower.
Unforeseen difficulties are inevitable, of course, when capital markets are being built from scratch. 
In China, though, such problems are compounded by a situation that most Western investors have a hard time fathoming: companies that say they want to make money are still run by Communist Party bureaucrats who care more about meetings and Government policy than revenues or profit margins.
Many businesses survive on Government subsidies and loans that banks are ordered to give them, and those selected to issue shares are picked as much for political reasons as for financial ones.
Tsingtao's difficulties are especially striking because the opportunity is so great. 
China's beer market is now about 118 million barrels annually, roughly 15 times as big as it was in 1980 and growing so fast it has overtaken Germany to become the world's second largest, after the United States.
But Tsingtao, unused to entertaining questions from anyone but Government officials, is almost completely indifferent to investors and analysts, offering them little information.
Of the 17 China-based companies now listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, only one, Shanghai Petrochemical, trades at more than its original listing price. 
And Brilliance China Automotive Holdings, a Bermuda-registered company that promoted itself as China's first listing on the New York Stock Exchange, shot up to $30 shortly after its debut in 1992, but now trades at around $4.
American investment banks like Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and Smith Barney, after big expansions into China in 1993, now have little business here.
Any analyst can list a number of reasons Chinese stocks are down this year: Many have suffered from Beijing's tight-credit policy, others were hit by unexpected tax increases, still others were simply priced badly. 
But the main problem is that it has gradually dawned on investors that they understand little about how Chinese companies are run. 
When they do get a peek inside, they don't like what they see.
Tsingtao is a prime example. 
It has been making beer here since the Germans opened the brewery in 1903, when they colonized a section of the Shandong peninsula in northeast China. 
As it earned a reputation for making the best beer in China, Tsingtao gained a robust 70 percent of China's beer exports.
When they announced plans to list shares as the first of many "red chip," or mainland Chinese, stocks in Hong Kong, Tsingtao executives boldly proclaimed plans to dominate China's fragmented beer market, in which more than 800 breweries compete.
Response was overwhelming, and the initial offering was so oversubscribed -- more than 100 times -- that few investors could get in.
After Tsingtao was listed at 36 cents a share, it climbed to $1.40, a towering 98 times earnings, in 1994. 
The Anheuser-Busch Companies, the American beer giant, bought a 5 percent stake.
But bad news began emerging about Tsingtao in the middle of this year.
Profit in the first half fell 49 percent, as prices of raw materials rose sharply but competition prevented Tsingtao from charging more for its beer. 
More troubling, analysts looking over the company's puzzlingly vague annual report discovered that Tsingtao's managers had taken nearly half of the $190 million from their share issue and, rather than investing it in plant expansion -- as had been promised in a prospectus -- lent it to other Chinese companies that Tsingtao will not identify.
With its new capital thus mysteriously tied up, Tsingtao had to scale back expansion plans and cut projected growth in beer production, which is now at about three million barrels a year, by half. 
Worse, it remains unclear how much of Tsingtao's loans will be repaid: China's state-owned enterprises are famous for losing money and remaining immune to demands for repayment.
"When we called with questions, they wouldn't come to the phone," said Lim Cheang Yee, an analyst for H. G. Asia in Hong Kong. 
"They screwed around with minority shareholders' money, but wouldn't explain anything."
Ms. Lim said that Tsingtao had apparently recovered much of its loan money in recent months, and had even become more responsive to questions. 
But she said that it would still take a long time to repair the damage done to its credibility.
Talks between Anheuser-Busch and Tsingtao about expanding the American company's stake to 15 percent or more went sour. 
Anheuser-Busch executives have told colleagues at other beer companies that the deeper they looked into Tsingtao, the more pessimistic they became about the company's ability to expand its share of this fragmented market.
While Tsingtao is one of China's largest breweries and clearly its best known, it has just 2.2 percent of the market. 
And though its 70 percent share of China's beer exports sounds good, that accounts for just 10 percent of Tsingtao's sales over all. 
Moreover, those sales are blurred by the complex set of distribution rights, which vary from market to market, that the company agreed to when first entering international markets several years ago.
"They're amazingly arrogant," said a distributor who works with Tsingtao managers. 
"They say, 'We're Tsingtao, we don't need to advertise.'
It's so ridiculous. 
Even Coca-Cola has to advertise."
The markets have judged Tsingtao harshly as well, with the stock now trading at less than $2 and its American depository receipts selling for pennies. 
[On Tuesday, the company's shares closed at 1.82 Hong Kong dollars, and its A.D.R.'s closed at 23 cents.]
Tsingtao executives brush away questions about their unorthodox lending.
"I don't see what the fuss is about," said Qiao Qijian, a senior executive at Tsingtao, in an interview at company headquarters here during which he downed three glasses of Tsingtao draft. 
"Many investors from Hong Kong are concerned. 
But when they come to visit, they can see that everything is going fine."
Mr. Qiao said Tsingtao had been unable to invest its newly raised capital immediately because of shifting policy in Beijing, and had to delay its planning throughout 1994 until a meeting was held in February 1995. 
At that time, Beijing officials informed company executives about the need to shift China's alcoholic consumption away from the traditional favorite, grain alcohol, because of a growing shortage of grain.
That means beer and wine production is to be encouraged, which sounds good for Tsingtao. 
Yet the fact that a leading beer company's expansion was dictated by a Government meeting, itself most concerned with the politics of grain production, was an indication of how the emphasis remains on Government planning rather than on market demand.
Moreover, Mr. Qiao conceded that the financing of increased beer production was not even discussed at the meeting.
That seems short-sighted. 
China's beer market is entering an intensely competitive stage, with foreign breweries marching into China every day. 
Asahi and Kirin of Japan and Foster's of Australia recently announced plans to expand, and Beck's of Germany and Pabst of Milwaukee are already making beer in China.
With prospects for Tsingtao bleak, Anheuser-Busch went ahead with a joint venture to produce Budweiser with a different brewery in the central Chinese city of Wuhan.
"Our greatest concern with the company has always been that competition will force Tsingtao to cap price growth," Ms. Lim of H. G. Asia wrote in an analysis of the brewery, recommending that shareholders sell. 
"Profit growth will therefore have to depend on volume growth."
On paper, Tsingtao's expansion plans call for a fourfold production increase by the year 2000, which would come to 10 percent of today's domestic market. 
But Mr. Qiao, the Tsingtao executive, conceded that with all the delays it has encountered, the company would be pleased to achieve half as much.
Even with scaled-back plans, it is unclear where additional financing will come from, since China is in the midst of a tight credit policy that shows no signs of easing.
Mr. Qiao leaned back in a puffy chair and took a deep breath when asked about this.
"We have three options: bank loans, Government subsidies or another share issue," he said.
Unfortunately, he added, none of those look feasible anytime soon.

text:
ï»¿
Asia's largest investment bank outside Japan, Peregrine Investments Holdings, was forced to shut down today, the first major casualty of the economic and currency crisis that has swept through the region since summer.
Moreover, Peregrine's collapse is the first major bankruptcy in Hong Kong since the territory reverted to Chinese rule last July.
News of Peregrine's failure shook Hong Kong's stock market, which was already rattled by the growing financial difficulties in Indonesia. 
Stock prices plunged today, with the Hang Seng market index falling985.51 points, or 11.1 percent, to 7,909.13, by the midday trading break.
The shutdown of Peregrine came after a weekend of frenzied negotiations with potential rescuers.
"It looks like liquidation this afternoon," said Tom Grimmer, a Peregrine spokesman. 
"Bankers didn't go for any sort of rescue operation last night. 
There are no alternatives left."
Founded a decade ago by a former British race car driver and a local investment banker with support from an array of Hong Kong's leading tycoons, Peregrine quickly emerged as the principal underwriter for Chinese companies listing in Hong Kong and the largest brokerage firm here.
Peregrine earned a reputation for daring and rapid decision-making, and for a formidable network of connections with Hong Kong and China's most powerful financial figures.
But as rapidly as the bank soared, it was pulled down as quickly by mounting economic turmoil in Asia, especially in Indonesia, where Peregrine had committed one-third of its capital as a loan to a Jakarta taxi and bus company.
Last summer, Peregrine decided to back Jopie Widjaya, the owner of Steady Safe, a taxi company listed on the Jakarta stock exchange. 
Mr. Widjaya sought financing to expand into ferries and toll roads, plans apparently supported by the daughter of President Suharto. 
Like many of Peregrine's deals, Mr. Widjaya's connections seem to have played a key role in the decision to loan Steady Safe $270 million.
Since the loan, however, the Indonesian rupiah began a swift decline from 2,400 rupiah to the dollar to nearly 10,000 rupiah to the dollar last week. 
Steady Safe found itself unable to meet its obligations and over the weekend its doors in Jakarta were shuttered and locked. 
Peregrine was left with a gaping hole in its balance sheet.
In November, Peregrine announced that it had reached a deal with the Zurich Group of Switzerland to take a 24.1 percent stake in the bank, in what would have amounted to a bailout. 
That deal fell apart as the rupiah continued its slide and the depths of Peregrine's problems became apparent.
As a last-ditch effort, Peregrine approached the Bank of China, but according to a Bank of China executive, senior officials in Beijing ruled out the possibility of taking a stake in the troubled bank.
Over the weekend, Hong Kong's senior civil servants sought to calm the waters as anxieties over the economy mounted, but Donald Tsang, Hong Kong's financial secretary, said the Government would not intervene to save Peregrine.
Zurich Group's withdrawal sent Peregrine's co-founders, Philip Tose and Francis P. T. Leung, into a frenetic search for a savior for their bank. 
Apart from the Bank of China, Deutsche Bank A.G. glanced briefly at Peregrine before shying away.
In Beijing, there was some consternation that Peregrine had even dared to approach the Bank of China, a move that some Chinese bankers saw as running counter to the deliberate policy of insuring Hong Kong's virtual autonomy from Beijing.
And none of Peregrine's original backers, some of the most high-profile tycoons in Hong Kong, appeared willing to come to the rescue of the bank.
As one banker put it this morning: "No one really knows what Peregrine's liabilities are or what it's exposure to Southeast Asia is. 
How could you step in at the last minute?"
About 700 Peregrine employees are expected to be laid off in Hong Kong, with another 1,000 losing their jobs elsewhere in Asia.

text:
ï»¿
Stepping through grass, mud and clods of dirt, Ding Shilong ran his hands across a new wire fence and beamed at the thought of what a mini-Hong Kong might look like on this huge chunk of barren land.
After nearly five years of internal wrangling, the central Government has finally allowed foreign developers to begin construction of an 11.6-square-mile port and manufacturing center here, in the southern island province of Hainan. 
The project, which is expected to cost $1.3 billion for the initial stages, is one of the boldest economic experiments the Chinese authorities have begun.
For the first time, a foreign consortium is being allowed to transform an empty patch of dirt into a small planned city. 
If all goes well, the giant town will have a mixture of shops, offices, factories, warehouses, gardens and apartments for 250,000 residents, all separated by a fence from the rest of the island and the rest of China.
The interest in the project from Chinese officials and company executives is enormous, with high-ranking Government employees frequently coming down to assess the prospects in Yangpu. 
In Chinese, officials formally refer to Yangpu as a development zone, but in a sign of how they really view Yangpu, they often switch to English in the middle of their Chinese conversations and call it the "free port" project.
Yangpu has not yet been given permission to be a free port like Hong Kong, where almost all goods imported would be available duty-free to the population. 
But it has received a wide variety of privileges, including one of the country's most relaxed policies toward duties on industrial and consumer goods. 
And Hainan officials say that if Yangpu is successful they hope its privileges may be extended to the entire island.
"This is an experiment," said Fan Yueqin, a senior manager at the Pearl River Enterprise Company, a real estate company in the island's provincial capital of Haikou. 
"If Yangpu is successful, Hainan can use Yangpu as a model. 
If we want to become a Hong Kong, then Yangpu is a trial."
But for now, all this is still on paper.
"My biggest worry now is that there's no special development zone yet -- it's just a piece of bare land," said Mr. Ding, a Chinese official who has spent the last three years on the project, as he rode in a car down the narrow two-lane road from the provincial capital to Yangpu. 
The scenery was of hills, eucalyptus trees and peasants with pointed straw hats -- a great contrast from his dream city.
The project at Yangpu (YAHNG-poo) is a victory for Kumagai Gumi (H.K.) Ltd., which is partly owned by the Japanese construction company. 
Kumagai Gumi will have land-use rights on the property for 70 years and will then sell those rights to other companies that want to build factories or offices.
In the three months since Kumagai began selling plots from its Hong Kong office, the company says it has sold about 8 percent of the zone's space. 
In a sign of the economic frenzy that pervades the nation, mainland Chinese companies have been the quickest to sign up, some apparently buying land simply in the hope of reselling at a profit.
Â 
Holding Down Speculation
"There's bound to be speculation in any project like this," said Frederick S. Ma, executive director at Kumagai Gumi (H.K.) Ltd. in Hong Kong. 
"The key is that we don't have so much speculation that the place becomes a ghost town."
China began experimenting more than a decade ago with special economic zones, inspired by the booming achievements of similar endeavors in Taiwan and Hong Kong, and to some extent in Malaysia and Singapore. 
These days, the greatest influence on Yangpu comes from Shenzhen, once a patch of countryside on the border with Hong Kong, which was allowed certain economic freedoms by the central Government.
Today, it is the most successful of China's experiments.
Yangpu expects to have a freer hand in foreign currency transactions than the rest of China, with its banks possibly able to change the local currency, or renminbi, into foreign currencies at their counters. 
Currently, the renminbi can be traded only into United States dollars or Hong Kong dollars at special foreign currency swap centers.
Kumagai, which has a 30 percent stake in the project, has been organizing the consortium and negotiating the terms, which included the purchase of the 70-year land-use rights at $350 an acre. 
It also had to pay to relocate a small population of peasants.
Â 
Power, Roads and Water
It recently began construction on a $200 million power station and is laying the groundwork for $1.1 billion more in roads, water supplies and residential areas that will be ready in one year for certain parts of the zone.
The Yangpu project emerged in 1988, when it was a favorite plan of the Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang. 
He envisioned it as a free port and the centerpiece of the national development strategy.
Mr. Zhao was never able to get approval for the project, however, in part because it reminded hard-liners of the foreign enclaves that existed in China in the first half of this century. 
The Communists have always denounced those foreign concessions, which were most famous in Shanghai, and so the idea that foreigners would have a major role in developing enclaves struck some nationalists as a threat to sovereignty.
Then Mr. Zhao was purged in 1989, after the Tiananmen democracy movement, and for several years the proposal was put on hold. 
It was finally approved by the State Council, China's cabinet, in the fall, but it gets little attention in the Chinese press and the leadership seems uncertain about whether it should be proud of what it has done -- or embarrassed.
For now, Mr. Ding is elated at the construction of the wire fence, which will stretch 5.4 miles and separate the industrial zone from the rest of the island.
Â 
'A Big Political Risk'
"China is taking a big political risk in Yangpu," Mr. Ding said, glancing around at the expanse of land. 
"Some officials are saying that with Yangpu, we are betraying the country. 
In 10 years, we should be like a small Hong Kong, and if we aren't at least better than Shenzhen is now, then we won't be completely successful."
Shenzhen is a special economic zone on the Chinese side of the border near Hong Kong. 
In the last 12 years it has been transformed from a region of rice paddies to an urban center with plush hotels, a huge manufacturing base and a stock exchange.
Kumagai says that it is not sure how much it will ultimately invest in the project. 
But so far, it has been able to keep the actual amount of its investment relatively low by financing the construction with bank loans -- three of the seven partners in the consortium are local Chinese banks. 
Cash is also coming in from land sales.
"The major advantage is that foreign investors only need to deal with Kumagai and the consortium, and not with Chinese officials," said Carl K. B. Wong, a senior analyst at Wardley James Capel (Far East) Ltd. in Hong Kong. 
"But this advantage may no longer be solely available at Yangpu in the future. 
Other parts of China may get increasingly decentralized so they can provide lenient terms to foreign investors."
Kumagai is trying to attract investors from Taiwan and Southeast Asia, but China's coastal areas are all competing for foreign investment, and the central Government itself has invested a great deal of capital in a virtually barren region of Shanghai called Pudong.
Pudong has been given numerous special privileges, but the difference is that Pudong is run by the Chinese, whereas Yangpu will be run by a foreign developer.
Â 
'It's Like Hong Kong'
"There will be periods when the whole thing slows down a lot, and then they'll be periods when it picks up," said Mr. Ma of Kumagai. 
"How do you define when the project is finished?
It's like Hong Kong. 
It's like a city. 
It may take seven years to sell all the land. 
But maybe we don't want to sell it all."
The advantage of Yangpu is that it is in a relatively undeveloped part of China, so land and labor are fairly cheap. 
It is also close enough to Hong Kong that shipping and air routes could eventually become convenient.
For now, many foreign investors are cautious, noting that the work force is essentially unskilled, that many local factories are losing money and that transportation links are backward.
Compared with Guangdong Province, which is linked by land to Hong Kong, Yangpu is far away and less convenient for Hong Kong and Taiwan business executives. 
There is no airport yet at Yangpu, and no decision has been made about whether to build one, so for now business executives must take the two-and-a-half-hour car ride from the small airport at the provincial capital of Haikou.
"You need to get a pioneer to go and build a factory out there in Yangpu,"
said Gillian Y. S. Kong, a real estate analyst at Sun Hung Kai Securities Ltd. in Hong Kong.

file: A Perfect Madness of Plants.txt
text:
ï»¿
The architecture of Dan Hinkley's garden on the Kitsap Peninsula in Washington State is native, shaped by old Douglas firs and a seeping bog. 
But in the cultivated understory, he has convened plants from all around the globe, reuniting the tribes of the botanical diaspora. 
More than 50 kinds of arisaemas -- called jack-in-the-pulpit in North America -- rocket from the soil, and one, Arisaema nepenthoides, stands fully erect, a single cobralike spathe beside a rotting stump crowned with ferns. 
Thirty-five varieties of Solomon's seals, or polygonatums, from China, Japan, Taiwan, Nepal and Sikkim unspiral from their early growth, and dozens of types of hellebore have just passed their prime. 
Throughout the garden, hydrangeas and viburnums are beginning to dispense their leaves; Stachyurus and Edgeworthia, winter-flowering shrubs from Asia, are leafing out. 
On some loops of the garden trail, where a Cardiocrinum giganteum thrusts its antediluvian seedpod six feet into the air, you almost expect to see a dinosaur wander past. 
Bud-break has stirred among an orderly chaos of growth-forms.
The man behind this collection of plants is Daniel Hinkley, a 45-year-old native of northern Michigan who has come to be regarded as one of the pre-eminent plant explorers in the world. 
Hinkley is the co-owner and chief plantsman of Heronswood Nursery, started in 1987, which lies within the visual domain of the Olympic Mountains across Puget Sound from Seattle. 
Heronswood is Hinkley's personal garden, his trial garden and a two-and-a-half-acre commercial nursery rolled in one. 
It's also Hinkley's home, which he shares with his partner, Robert Jones, an architect who is to the mailing list, the account books and the commercial operations at Heronswood what Hinkley is to the plants.
Here are more than 9,500 plants sprung from seed gathered all over the world. 
Most are numbered and listed in a loose-leaf binder that Hinkley calls the Big Bang, a compilation of plants already for sale and those that someday will be. 
The binder listing current inventory is called the Grand Mal. 
To most gardeners, the plants on these lists would be unfamiliar. 
Instead of the classic Hosta "Frances Williams," for instance, there is Hosta kiyosumiensis, which Hinkley collected from Mount Kiyosume in Japan's Chiba Prefecture in 1995. 
Instead of hybridized Asiatic and Oriental lilies, there is Lilium nanum, collected by Hinkley during a joint expedition to the Himalayas in 1995. 
Instead of a Norway maple or a David Austin rose, there is Acer rufinerve, a striped-bark maple he gathered in central Japan in 1997, and a rose of as yet undetermined species collected from an altitude of 10,800 feet in China's Yunnan province in 1996.
From this garden each year also comes the Heronswood catalogue, a major literary artifact in the world of gardening ephemera. 
Printed solidly in small type, it begins with Hinkley's wry musings on the imperfect art of running a mail-order nursery and ends 300 pages and some 2,500 plants later. 
The catalogue is a saga of botanical excitement and a chronicle of adjectival fatigue, the fate of a man driven to travel the world searching for remarkable plants and then doomed to write a terse, descriptive paragraph about one $6 or $8 clone after another, beginning with Abies balsamea "Nana" in the "Conifers" section and ending with the New Zealand sedge Uncinia unciniata, the final plant in the section on grasses.
Though it advertises nowhere and admits visitors only by appointment, Heronswood Nursery mailed 35,000 copies of the 1999 catalogue, and subscription requests are currently arriving at the rate of 100 a week. 
At $8 for a two-year subscription, the catalogue just pays for itself, unless you count the cost of Hinkley's writing time, in which case it is grossly underpriced. 
Subscribers pleasantly lost among Hinkley's paragraphs can be forgiven for wondering whether the nursery exists to justify the catalogue, or vice versa. 
Still, appealing to a newly adventurous generation of gardeners, Heronswood was an almost instant success. 
In 1993, the year after it incorporated, it had a gross income of $220,000. 
In 1998, it was five times larger, $1,100,000. 
These days, as Robert Jones says, he and Hinkley are trying to choose their limits, trying to let Hinkley's interests, rather than mere economic growth, continue to shape their offerings.
Plant introduction has traditionally been one of the reasons public agencies, public gardens and university arboretums -- like the United States Department of Agriculture, the New York Botanical Garden and the Arnold Arboretum at Harvard University -- have mounted collecting expeditions. 
But such institutions, as even they sometimes admit, usually do a far better job of collecting and studying plants than they do releasing them to the public. 
There is a historic rivalry between the public gardens and commercial nurseries like Heronswood, which dates to well before the days when the legendary plant hunter Ernest Henry Wilson combed turn-of-the-century China first for Veitch's nursery and then for the Arnold Arboretum. 
It's a rivalry, as the academics would put it, between science and mere trade or, as the tradesmen might put it, between exclusivity and openness. 
But these days, in fact, many public gardens and arboretums buy directly from Hinkley, sometimes taking a share in his plant-collecting expeditions, which entitles them to a portion of the seeds Hinkley gathers. 
"They're some of my best customers," he says.
Mid-April is the peak of the spring plant-shipping season at Heronswood, where overworked staff members try to meet the florid expectations of gardeners by selling them plants that are not only garden-worthy but that also carry, for many customers, an echo of the exotic places where Hinkley has collected -- Nepal, Sikkim, China, Japan, Korea, Tasmania, Mexico and Chile. 
The nursery office, an attractive prairie farmhouse of sorts, is surrounded by open shade-canopies sheltering tables crowded with flats, each marked with a customer's name and shipping date.
Hinkley's Michigan drawl crackles over a walkie-talkie clipped to a plant-packer's belt. 
Concealed somewhere in the woodland garden, he is the ghost in this botanic machine, enjoying a 10-day respite from a busy spring speaking schedule and preparing for a collecting trip to Japan. 
A path leads into the benign enveloping shade characteristic of the Northwest woods. 
The light falling on the mounded garden beds seems detached from its source, and what it illuminates has a freshness that is an attribute of the early season and of the vegetation itself. 
A hundred yards down the path, Hinkley works in mottled shade helping a new crew member shovel steer manure from a garden cart onto a planting site. 
No matter how exotic his expeditions may be, this is the end point of every collecting trip -- making a hole in the ground, sprinkling a little 20-20-20 fertilizer in it and grubbing the earth back into place by hand around the stem of a newly propagated plant.
Hinkley speaks quietly, slowly, but there is a sense of haste about him, the result of living in what he calls "a perfect madness of plants," a garden that needs to be brought into peak condition within the next few weeks. 
"At this point it feels like it's moving day," he says. 
"But as long as I keep bringing new plants into trial, it's always going to be like this. 
I get tired of one plant, or it's just not doing for me, so I get rid of it and start over again. 
But every time you do that you want to rejuvenate the soil, and to do that you've got to move another plant."
Hinkley kneels on the ground, chopping at the soil with a border spade and looking up from time to time as he talks. 
He is direct and delicate at the same time, handling plants with none of the hesitation of the amateur gardener. 
He overflows with affection for the garden he has made, and yet his criticism of each individual plant-form -- a kind of veiled self-criticism in fact -- is unsparing.
Hinkley is bearded and balding, and he wears wide suspenders over a T-shirt from the J.C. 
Raulston Arboretum at North Carolina State University. 
Raulston, who died at 56 in a car accident three years ago, was one of Hinkley's mentors and a widely respected emblem of intellectual and horticultural generosity. 
Hinkley has dedicated his next book, "The Explorer's Garden," which Timber Press will publish in the fall, to Raulston and to Gerald Straley of the University of British Columbia, another gardening mentor who died in his 50's. 
"J.C.'s everywhere in this garden," Hinkley said. 
"Every day, I could take out a plant that he gave me, and I would never run out of plants. 
He knew, he sensed what a good plant was."
To sense what a good plant is -- to recognize it in the wild and then confirm it in his own garden -- is the essence of Hinkley's work. 
At Heronswood, there are really three different kinds of garden and, hence, of garden-worthiness. 
Among the greenhouses, for instance, there is the denatured, rationalized garden, which consists of plants grouped by size and species -- garden-worthy, in Hinkley's judgment, but also able to withstand shipping. 
In the woodland garden, tested and marketed varieties of plants compete with untested kin. 
The search here is for better form, greater hardiness, a distinctive virtue -- variegation or a more upright or prostrate habit -- or simply for the illumination, vital to Hinkley's task, that comes from growing many related species in proximity to each other. 
"For me," Hinkley says, "it makes a more complete, more understandable portrait of plants if I get the opportunity to grow many different relatives together."
And then there is the private garden surrounding the house, which is set at the back of the property. 
This is a place where Hinkley has tried to set aside at least some of the cultural limitations that frame our sense of what makes a garden. 
It is a subject he understands very well. 
"We have all this Lutheran guilt," he says. 
"We all moved west from the Midwest where we couldn't have winter gardens, and so our gardens in Seattle and Portland and Vancouver are amazingly timid as far as what our climate can actually do."
But there is no timidity in this garden. 
What takes it beyond timidity isn't massed plantings or vibrant color or expansive scale or even mere exoticism. 
It is Hinkley's subtle reliance on the globally diverse forms of individual plants. 
Each plant, grown well, reveals itself and reveals something, too, about its neighbor. 
What creeps grows next to what climbs. 
The fastigiate and the pendulous conspire. 
Bark peels, thorns protrude, vines finger their way across an arbor, and what unites it all, what makes these plants garden-worthy, is the interest they bestow upon each other.
There are few explicit canons for deciding what makes a plant garden-worthy, but one of them -- a base line below the realm of the esthetic -- is lack of ecological invasiveness. 
Most gardeners are familiar with species that tend to be invasive in the garden, like Ajuga reptans, sometimes called carpet bugle. 
But what haunts Hinkley is the thought of plants that can break loose from cultivation and run rampant across the landscape -- purple loosestrife, kudzu, tamarisk, honeysuckle. 
"My greatest concern," he says, "is the introduction of a bad plant."
To help prevent that, Hinkley has hired Sarah Reichard as a consultant. 
Reichard, an ecologist at the University of Washington's Center for Urban Horticulture and a founder of Washington's Native Plant Society, began to wonder while collecting seed in South America as a graduate student whether any of those plants would prove invasive in the Pacific Northwest. 
She has constructed a model -- a decision tree, based on a plant's observed characteristics, which asks questions about how quickly the species reproduces and whether it belongs to a family or genus already strongly invasive in North America -- that indicates whether a plant is likely to become invasive.
On the burn pile at Heronswood lay one of the results of Reichard's work. 
There, atop other horticultural debris, was Ligustrum delavayanum, a species of privet named after the French priest and botanist Jean Marie Delavay, who collected plants in China in the late 19th century. 
This ligustrum bore fruit in Hinkley's garden for the first time in October, and it caught the attention of Roy Lancaster, the English dean of plant explorers, who was visiting Heronswood at the time. 
"He said he'd never seen a more beautiful form of it," Hinkley told me. 
"But it's a broad-leafed evergreen, and those do really well in the Northwest. 
I looked at it all winter long and battled with it in my conscience. 
You've probably seen what Ligustrum sinense has done in the Southeast. 
It's everywhere. 
Finally we had Sarah run it through her model, and she said, Reject."
Invasiveness is a hot issue, and it inspires a botanical xenophobia, a fear that just because a plant is exotic -- i.e., non-native -- it's inevitably invasive or otherwise harmful to the suite of native plants, changing the balance of nitrogen in the soil, for instance, or causing the water table to dip below the roots of native plants. 
But in horticulture, as in agriculture, the distinction between exotic and native has been blurred by the ancient, extensive exchange of plants for their economic or ornamental value. 
Because plant material -- seeds, cuttings, fruits -- moves as readily as humans do, human plant collecting, like the invention of agriculture, predates history itself. 
Gardening may be a way of enclosing a distinctive botanical world -- separating the cultivated from the uncultivated -- but few gardeners have ever restricted themselves to growing only native plants. 
The literature of gardening is underwritten by the literature of plant trafficking -- Robert Fortune, Joseph Hooker, Joseph Banks, Armand David, Ernest Henry Wilson and a host of predecessors traversed temperate Asia searching for plants of botanical and horticultural interest. 
Their motto, and Hinkley's as well, might be the words of William Bartram, who explored America in the late 18th century, when it was still the gardening world's China. 
"Let us advance to the spot in which nature has seated them," Bartram wrote of the plants he sought.
If there's an ecological argument to be made against plant collecting, there are many to be made for it. 
The term itself is a misnomer. 
Hinkley does not collect plants. 
As he notes in the Heronswood catalogue, "Our wild collections are primarily of seed, which we collect in a very conservative manner."
This means collecting only when there is abundant seed, adhering to the terms of local permits and customs and making sure the seed is carefully prepared to meet U.S.D.A. restrictions (free of any potentially contaminating soil, insects and so on). 
The image of ship decks full of Wardian cases -- the enclosed, portable greenhouses that made the 19th-century boom in plant hunting possible -- has been replaced by the image of tired botanists cleaning seeds for U.S.D.A. inspection under less-than-ideal conditions. 
"It isn't necessarily a fun thing to do," Hinkley says, remembering a trip to Nepal, "especially when you're doing it in a tent at night and it's raining cats and dogs outside and the only light is a headlamp."
Gathering seed from wild plant populations is also a means of preserving genetic diversity in the face of widespread environmental degradation. 
In Nepal, for instance, a grazing yak-cow hybrid, the dzo, has had a grave impact on alpine plant communities. 
In China, deforestation is proceeding at a rate that far outstrips the ability of Chinese and foreign botanists to inventory and collect seeds from endangered plants. 
Even in a gardening culture as traditional as Japan's, there's a tendency to overlook native species in favor of the exotic -- which in the case of Japan means American species. 
After searching Shikoku Island in 1997 for a wild Japanese hydrangea called Hydrangea sikokiana, Hinkley began scouting Japanese nurseries, hoping to find the plant in cultivation. 
"We thought we'd see it from a distance in every single nursery, and we'd go up to it and it was our native Hydrangea quercifolia. 
No one we talked to had even heard of sikokiana. 
They had no interest in growing it because they had this very exotic, much, much more exciting hydrangea from America."
The exotic sikokiana is now growing at Heronswood, not far up the woodland path from the native quercifolia.
But the ultimate rationale for Hinkley's work is the garden itself. 
He shapes his expeditions by looking for climates similar to that of the Pacific Northwest, traveling to places where plants show similar hardiness because of elevation or latitude, and are accustomed to similar rainfall patterns. 
Sometimes a collecting trip broadens the gene pool for a plant that has already been collected, like Paris polyphylla, a Nepalese trillium relative Hinkley had grown at Heronswood for a decade but was the only clone in North America. 
Often a trip leads to a new understanding of how, as Hinkley puts it, a plant "wants" to grow. 
It can also be a means of expanding the idea of the garden philosophically and esthetically by allowing Hinkley to see cultivated species and their wild near kin in their native habitat. 
Perhaps, Hinkley says, re-collecting seed "will bring additional hardiness or additional insect or disease resistance, so I never pass up a plant if it's in seed, if indeed I think it's a plant that deserves to be in cultivation."
Hinkley's garden feels like a glimpse of another creation, a place where the monoculture of the mind is disturbed by a willingness to push beyond the familiar botanical forms into a realm of pleasing visual discomfort. 
Walking along the woodland trails at Heronswood, Hinkley points out some of the plants he admires -- like Podophyllum delavayi, a May apple from Sichuan, which, he says, "deserves to be worshiped" -- and some of the plants he thinks will become important to American gardeners in the years ahead, not only among "plant nerds," as he puts it, but also among gardeners generally. 
He points out a group called the woodland lilies -- Smilacinas, Polygonatums, Uvularias, Disporums and Disporopsis.
But above all he points out Hepatica -- Hepatica acutiloba, an American native and Hepatica maxima, which grows only on one island in the Japan Sea, Hepatica in a single clone, in many clones, in enough clones one day to sell. 
To a casual visitor, these are perplexing plants, modest, growing in low mounds with rather formal, old-fashioned leaves and small flowers, not half as striking as the arisaemas and trilliums that are rioting in the woodland. 
But besides being a "simply good" plant, Hepatica maxima, for one, is also very rare in cultivation, which makes its goodness no longer simple. 
It goes about its business in a quiet corner of the garden, reaffirming a strange premise of life itself, for being there at all is part of its beauty.

file: A Savory Guide To the Exotica Of Chinatown_s Food Vendors.txt
text:
ï»¿
A THOUSAND years ago, in the villages of China at the beginning of the Sung dynasty, before there were restaurants, and before peasants had ovens, food vendors roamed mud streets.
From morning to night, the vendors hawked fried puffy breads, sweet sticky rice and plump barbecued chickens. 
They brought the food from larger, nearby towns where the chickens were roasted in ovens, then tucked into tiered bamboo baskets that hung on poles slung across their shoulders. 
The food was humble, but tasty -- tasty enough that the tradition is alive today on the streets of Beijing, Hong Kong and Manhattan.
In Manhattan's Chinatown, there are six or seven vendors along the south side of Canal Street, starting at Centre Street and heading east five short blocks to the Bowery, and several more vendors are located on the Bowery, south one block to Bayard Street.
To operate legally, each vendor must pass an inspection to receive a license and permit from New York City's Department of Health. 
As proof, the vendor numbers are prominently displayed on the front of each cart. 
The vendors offer the foods of 1,000 years ago, and people queue up to buy fried scallion pancakes, braised honeycomb tripe, barbecued duck and the snacks of both northern and southern China.
Very little has changed.
Gone are the bamboo baskets, and in their place are stainless steel carts equipped with steam tables, griddles and plastic take-out containers. 
White plastic forks and spoons have replaced chopsticks.
An informal tasting of the foods offered by these street vendors was conducted in three visits in the last three weeks. 
The vendors stake their claim to particular spots on the sidewalk and work six days a week, usually from 9 A.M. to 6 P.M. Kee Lim, a vendor who sets up in front of 226 Canal Street, was a street vendor in Hong Kong for six years before moving to New York.
Some vendors, like Mr. Lim, were chatty in Cantonese. 
A few spoke minimal English, enough to understand that a customer wanted one pancake, or four dumplings. 
The provenance of the food was a mystery. 
A few, like Mr. Lim, bought from restaurants, but they wouldn't say which ones. 
Still others said nothing. 
They cooked, they sold, but they did not reveal sources.
To find the best food, go where the crowds are, and assume that in dishes like dumplings or braised meats, there will be a bit of monosodium glutamate.
People clustered and gawked at the Hong Kee Food Corporation's street stall -- an extension of the take-out food store -- that sells traditional Chinese snacks at 234 Canal Street (Centre Street). 
Working on a griddle, Shirley Kong took a roll of silky white rice noodle and wrapped it around crisp-on-the-outside, chewy-on-the-inside fried dough, a breakfast food that was both soothing and was filling ($1). 
To warm the roll up, she lightly sauteed it on the griddle, and to offset its bland flavor, she drizzled it with thinned-out soy sauce that had been simmered with sugar, scallions, ginger, garlic and broth.
On the other side of the griddle, rectangles of turnip pudding were sizzling. 
Made of grated white Chinese turnips seasoned with ginger and garlic, the pudding was steamed, sliced and pan-fried until crisp and golden on both sides (three slices for $1). 
It slithered down the throat, slippery and savory. 
It is best eaten with a sprinkle of oyster sauce. 
If the cook doesn't offer the oyster sauce, ask for it. 
Hong Kee's vendor number is 19863.
Where street food stands apart from homemade or high-quality restaurant food is usually in the degree of refinement or luxuriousness of ingredients. 
At a good dim sum parlor, the turnip pudding is sometimes studded with bits of dried shrimp and Chinese sausage. 
At Hong Kee, the turnip pudding lacked the shrimp and sausage. 
But who complained?
Judging from the crowds, the answer was no one.
About three steps to the east of Hong Kee, Shu Chen, No. 16592, was one of two vendors on Canal Street selling deep-fried scallion pancakes, a Shanghai specialty. 
Filled with freshly chopped scallions, the perfect pancake is crisp on the outside, greaseless, slightly salty, with the scallions adding a sweet flavor. 
Here, the pancake (50 cents) was imperfect -- somewhat tough, and scanty on the scallions. 
But the fried chicken wings, which tasted like they were marinated briefly in soy sauce and a splash of wine, were warm, crisp and greaseless (two for 50 cents).
The other purveyor of scallion pancakes was Sung M. Wong, No. 19890, who operated in front of 228 Canal Street. 
His pancakes looked like the others, were priced the same (50 cents each), but were much closer to the ideal of crisp outside and tender within.
He also sold one of the most ancient of Chinese snacks, the dumpling or jiao tze, a pleated pouch traditionally filled with minced cabbage and pork, and seasoned with ginger, soy sauce and sesame oil. 
The historical importance of the dumpling was discovered in the 1960's when the Chinese unearthed a pair of preserved dumplings that dated from the eighth or ninth century, the time of the Tang dynasty, which lasted from 618 to 907 A.D. More than 1,000 years later, the crescent shape of the jiao tze, and the number of pleats, is unchanged.
Here, the dough was thick, somewhat crude and chewy, but the filling of minced Chinese chives and pork, along with the highly familiar dash of MSG, was both pungent and tasty (four for $1).
Farther east down Canal Street is Mr. Lim, one of the friendlier vendors. 
He hovered over a stainless steel cart that is divided into compartments, each holding a different hot dish, none of which he had cooked. 
Instead, like the food vendors of the Sung dynasty, he bought the food from different restaurants or suppliers.
He offered rice gruel, also called jook; slippery rolled sheets of rice noodle; curried squid, and braised beef tripe cooked with turnip. 
The tripe, made into a honeycomb with chunks of white turnip, was cooked in a rich, aromatic broth of soy sauce, rice wine, garlic, ginger, soy sauce, water, sugar, salt and star anise. 
The tripe was tender, the turnip soft ($1.25 for a container). 
The food "is Hong Kong style," Mr. Lim said. 
To spot him, look for No. 16872.
Culinary treasures like roast ducks, soy sauce chickens, roast pork and braised barbecued pork are sold at bargain prices by Ying Chun Hui, whose cart, No. 16982, is usually in front of 208 Canal Street. 
But, surrounded by crowds, it's not hard to find.
One recent weekend, a woman waited in line to buy a duck to be presented as an offering at a temple. 
Another woman was struck by the prices, and said, "The duck is cheaper than Ollie's!"
She was referring to the popular chain of restaurants with three locations on the west side of Manhattan, where a whole roast duck sells for $17.50. 
At Kam Man, a Chinese grocery store at 200 Canal Street, the roast duck was $13. 
Mr. Hui sold ducks for $10 apiece -- and they were flawless. 
Each day, he said, he sells at least 20 ducks.
The skin was burnished and crisp, the tender meat subtly flavored by the marinade of scallions, garlic, bean sauce, soy sauce, chicken stock and sugar that filled the cavity of the duck as it roasted. 
(The same sauce is traditionally retained to be poured over the duck at serving time.)
The roast pork (not to be confused with the red-tinged strips of barbecued pork) had crisp, golden blistered skin -- like cracklings. 
When served, the pork is considered perfectly cooked when there are three distinct layers: the thick crunchy skin, a slender layer of sweet fat, and a thicker layer of lean yet moist meat ($5 a pound.) Mr. Hui's pork was perfect.
Who cooked these meats?
And where?
Mr. Hui would say only that the cook was a professional who moved from Hong Kong to New York and once worked in a local restaurant.
Scattered along Canal and the Bowery are vendors who sell egg-shaped cookies made from a batter of egg, flour, sugar and milk. 
They pour the batter into an iron griddle that has egg-shaped indentations and resembles a waffle iron. 
The cookies tasted like warm sponge cakes. 
Whenever an adult stood in line to buy the cookies (20 for $1), there was often a child hovering nearby, seeming to salivate.
At the corner of the Bowery and Bayard Street, in front of the National Westminster Bank, a husband and wife sold their specialty -- tripe and turnips -- which drew a steady line of customers, often six deep. 
The man, Chuck Au, said, "This is the best tripe."
Mr. Au was not a braggart; he spoke a humble gastronomic truth. 
The tripe almost melted in the mouth but still had a little crunch. 
The turnips were tender. 
But it was the flavor -- the classic combination of soy sauce, star anise and sugar -- that ran deep.
One customer bought four containers of tripe at $1.25 each. 
Others bought the rice gruel, which was subtly flavored with dried fish and blanched peanuts ($1). 
The cart is No. 16816.
When asked how their popular tripe was prepared, Mrs. Au, who did not want to give her first name, said, "Buy it, boil it and let it dry before you season it."
She paused, poured some water into the steam table, and said, "It's hard work."
But the results are delicious.

file: A Specialist In Esthetics Of Offbeat Violence.txt
text:
ï»¿
His films are notable for cascading glass, falling bodies and enough bullets to touch off a war. 
But John Woo, Hong Kong's most celebrated filmmaker, whose movies are almost operatic in their excess, insisted that the flamboyant violence stamping his work resembles a ballet, almost ethereal, even otherworldly.
"It's like dancing," the 51-year-old director remarked the other day as he nervously awaited the opening of "Face/Off," his most ambitious American film, starring John Travolta and Nicolas Cage, which opened No. 1 at the box office this weekend. 
"My actors are amusing and exciting. 
I grew up on films like 'Singin' in the Rain' and 'Seven Brides for Seven Brothers.'
That's what I want!
It's like a cartoon."
And the anarchic violence in his films?
The BBC once called Mr. Woo "the Mozart of mayhem."
"Violence in real life is horrid, frightening," Mr. Woo said. 
"The news on television is scary, not movies. 
Movies are fake, not real. 
People know the movies are not real."
Mr. Woo, who moved to Los Angeles five years ago to flee what he termed the creative constraints of Hong Kong, is now poised to become an American success story after a 1993 misstep with "Hard Target," starring Jean-Claude Van Damme, and the far more successful 1996 movie "Broken Arrow," with Mr. Travolta and Christian Slater.
Thus far, however, Mr. Woo's fame rests on Hong Kong movies that have been lauded by directors like Martin Scorsese and Quentin Tarantino. 
Films like "A Better Tomorrow" (1986), "The Killer" (1988) and "Hard Boiled" (1992) transformed the traditionally low-budget king-fu action genre into bizarrely over-the-top fantasies inevitably involving two men inextricably linked and hurtling toward a fatal collision.
"Face/Off," a film released by Paramount, which received the best reviews of Mr. Woo's career, is a weird saga involving a law enforcement officer, played by Mr. Travolta, who undergoes radical surgery to "borrow" the face of Mr. Cage, a psychopath bent on destroying Los Angeles. 
Mr. Travolta wants to find the site of a poison gas bomb. 
Of course, things go awry. 
Mr. Cage awakens from a coma with the face of Mr. Travolta. The film has Mr. Woo's trademarks: a dizzy plot, hypercharged editing, blunt religious symbolism, offbeat humor and unimaginably creepy villains. 
Subtlety is not Mr. Woo's strong point.
In its opening as No. 1 this weekend, the film grossed $22.7 million, said the Exhibitor Relations Company, which tracks ticket sales. 
It outflanked Disney's "Hercules" as well as "Batman and Robin," which was No. 3 at the box office and dropped off so sharply in its second week that it looms as a major disappointment.
Referring to the movie, Mr. Woo said the duality of good and evil is central to the film and to his work. 
"It's my usual theme, always good and evil mirroring each other," he said, in an office near the 20th Century Fox studios in West Los Angeles, where he is starting work on a new film. 
"I like imperfect characters. 
Perfect heroes bore me."
Mr. Woo's films, with their choreographed and often slow-motion violence, seem surprisingly funny and bloodless, as if all that killing were not horrific. 
His sources, he said, are rooted in films by directors of the 1950's and 60's: Sam Peckinpah, Stanley Kubrick, Akira Kurosawa, Alfred Hitchcock and Arthur Penn.
As Peter Rainer, chairman of the National Board of Film Critics, wrote last week in the newspaper New Times: "Woo openly courts -- and satisfies -- our primal desire to see people pulverized. 
Even five years ago his brand of mayhem might have seemed too way out for American audiences, but because of the increasingly heightened violence in our movies -- and especially because of the Hong Kong movie influence in the films of Quentin Tarantino -- Woo may soon be anointed as Hollywood's new crown prince of estheticized gore."
Mr. Woo said he moved to Los Angeles in 1992 partly because he felt stymied in Hong Kong -- "The Government in Hong Kong, the police, treat filmmakers like beggars" -- and partly to spend more time with his family. 
"I worked seven days a week in Hong Kong. 
My children hardly saw my face, they never really had a father and there were misunderstandings, difficulties," said Mr. Woo, a compact man with a wide smile and an open, engaging manner. 
"I was guilty, very guilty."
"Now I stay home after work," said Mr. Woo, who lives with his wife, 15-year-old son and two daughters, 17 and 20. 
"I try to be a good father. 
I cook for them."
Mr. Woo himself is part of a vanguard of Hong Kong filmmakers working increasingly in Los Angeles and clearly a bit uneasy about the end of colonial rule after 156 years when Britain hands the colony back to China on Tuesday. 
.
"Some people say it will be tough on the film business at first," he said. 
"There will be censorship, but perhaps this will be temporary. 
I don't see many problems."
Mike Simpson, senior vice president of the William Morris agency, which represents many of Hong Kong's top filmmakers, agreed that there was some nervousness within the movie business there -- as well as anticipation.
Among the filmmakers the agency represents are Mr. Woo; Jackie Chan, the action star of "Rumble in the Bronx" and "Supercop"; Chow Yun-Fat, a frequent star of Mr. Woo's films who is making his Hollywood debut early next year opposite Mira Sorvino in "The Replacement Killers"; Stanley Tong, director of "Rumble in the Bronx," who is now making "Mr. 
Magoo" for Disney, and Michelle Yeoh, one of Hong Kong's top female movie stars, who appears in the new James Bond film, "Tomorrow Never Dies."
"There is some feeling of apprehension or wariness, of uncertainty," Mr. Simpson said. 
"There's also a sense of excitement."
Mr. Simpson said the migration of Chinese talent to Los Angeles had little to do with the handover. 
"The level and quality of films made there just began to go down and down," he said. 
"They were remaking bad versions of good films they made earlier."
He also noted that American action films had simply usurped many Chinese-language films in the Asian marketplace in recent years, leading to a deteriorating financial base for Hong Kong films and a decline in quality.
As for Mr. Woo, he said his next movie, called "King's Ransom," which is set to start filming later in the year, is a comedy.
A John Woo comedy?
Mr. Woo smiled. 
"It's like the 1960's heist movies, like 'To Catch a Thief' or 'The Thomas Crown Affair,' " he said. 
"It will, I hope, be funny and charming and elegant. 
Only a little bit of shooting."

file: A Top Dissident Flees China And Is Admitted to the U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
A dissident who ranked third on the Chinese Government's list of "most wanted" student protesters after the 1989 Tiananmen Square demonstrations has been admitted to the United States after fleeing China, the White House confirmed today.
The dissident, Liu Gang, 35, was arrested in June 1989 and sentenced to six years in prison and two years' deprivation of political rights. 
From remote Lingyuan Labor-Reform Camp in Liaoning Province, he smuggled out a letter accusing the authorities of torturing him, and he staged several hunger strikes.
After his release in June 1995, he was kept in isolation in his remote hometown of Liaoyan, with his phone cut off. 
He said he was unable to find a job or to live with his family. 
He violated his parole last month to go to Beijing, and from there he was smuggled to the United States.
In a telephone interview from Cambridge, Mass., where he is staying, Mr. Liu said he arrived in Boston on Thursday. 
But he refused to describe his route, saying he does not want to jeopardize the safety of his relatives in China and Hong Kong.
He said he expected to stay in the United States and attend school.
"I've just applied to go to school now, to some universities in Boston and other places," said Mr. Liu, who has a master's degree in physics.
He has not applied for political asylum, officials said. 
He was allowed into the United States under a provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act allowing entry "temporarily for immediate emergency reasons or the public interest."
The United States and China are sparring over the spread of nuclear weapons, intellectual piracy, Taiwan and human rights, with the expectation that Washington will soon impose billions of dollars in sanctions on the weapons and piracy issues.
The White House spokesman, Michael D. McCurry, said the Liu case should not further damage relations with China. 
"We are confident we can maintain the broad constructive engagement with China which reflects the status of our current bilateral relations," he said.
Regarding Taiwan, the State Department spokesman, Nicholas Burns, confirmed a report in The Washington Post that senior American officials met with Taiwan's national security adviser, Ting Mou-Shih, on March 11 in New York, to urge Taiwan to avoid provocative actions during China's military exercises at that time.
The American officials were Under Secretary of State Peter Tarnoff and Samuel R. Berger, deputy national security adviser. 
The meeting was one of the highest-level contacts since 1979, when Washington broke off diplomatic relations with Taipei.
Mr. Burns said he was unaware of any formal Chinese expression of unhappiness about the meeting. 
"In light of the tensions in the Taiwan Strait," he said, "the U.S. 
Government believed it was important to communicate directly and at a high level with both the People's Republic of China and with Taiwan."
