file: Air Safety Seeks to Keep Up With Growth_China Sends Controllers to U.S. To Improve English Proficien.txt
text:
ï»¿
The task for the student air traffic controller was routine: tell the pilot to maintain level flight and pass over a specific point before proceeding to a landing at Orlando International Airport.
But in this drill, the controller was Chinese, as was the man in the role of the pilot. 
They were among 15 controllers who spent the last eight weeks here learning to speak and understand an unfamiliar language in which the fate of hundreds of lives can turn on a single phrase.
"TWA 754, Orlando approach," said the controller, Shu Xiaobin, identifying himself to the plane as he had been drilled. 
"Maintain 6,000 feet."
He continued, "Proceed direct to ----," then paused and said something the pilot did not understand, possibly because it sounded nothing like the destinations Mr. Shu announces in Jiangxi Province or the ones heard around Beijing by the man playing pilot, Li Jianming. 
"What?"
Mr. Li said over his headset. 
"Proceed direct to what?"
This was just an exercise, at an air traffic control laboratory at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University here. 
But starting in just over a year, Chinese controllers are to begin talking in English to all pilots, both Chinese and foreign, in all parts of China with international traffic.
Including the 15 Chinese controllers, Embry-Riddle has trained 75 such students from China in a rare international program that teaches veteran controllers to work in another language at a time when English-speaking air traffic is rapidly growing in their country. 
Officials at the school say the controllers arrive here with varying levels of training in English and leave here with skills that are better, but still uneven.
Proficiency in English among air traffic controllers and pilots is a problem around the world, and has been blamed for several recent crashes. 
Some airlines put an interpreter in the cockpit, and at critical moments, some pilots whose English is not adequate have been known to obtain language help from flight attendants whose English is better.
But with airplanes moving at hundreds of miles an hour in often crowded airspace, American safety experts worry about such practices. 
They say that nothing can substitute for the language abilities of the pilots and controllers themselves. 
After an American Airlines jet crashed in Colombia a year ago, the National Transportation Safety Board recommended that the Federal Aviation Administration do more to help improve the language proficiency of foreign controllers worldwide.
"It's certainly an issue that needs vigilance," said Barry M. Sweedler, the director of the office of safety recommendations at the board.
As the world grows smaller, Mr. Sweedler and others say they think that the language gap may grow larger because, he said, "air traffic will be expanding to nations that haven't had as great a need to have controllers proficient in English."
That description fits China. 
In early 1995, Delta Air Lines asked the Chinese authorities for permission to fly a new route into Beijing. 
Because the route would take the planes over Heilongjian, Jilin and Liaoning, three northeastern provinces where few controllers spoke English, the Civil Aviation Authority of China set a price: Delta would have to arrange to train controllers in English.
Delta sent them to Embry-Riddle, a 70-year-old institution that is the world's largest and oldest institution of higher learning dedicated to aviation. 
United Air Lines and Federal Express, which also want to expand their routes in China, have also sponsored such courses. 
Financing for Mr. Shu's group was provided by Federal Express. 
The airlines pay about $100,000 for each group of 15 students.
China will need hundreds more because the central Government has set Jan. 
1, 1998, as the date when controllers and pilots are to speak English to one another in all sectors with international traffic. 
This is a safety measure used all over the world, so that all pilots in a sector can listen in on all conversations and know the locations of all other planes.
Some of those listening are native speakers of English, but others are not. 
In the case of China, there are pilots of planes from Germany, Italy and other countries who are expecting the conversations to be intelligible in English.
Chen Yawen, the deputy director of the air traffic control department in the Chinese Civil Aviation Authority, who arrived here today for the graduation ceremonies, said in an interview that the change would have to be phased in gradually. 
Mr. Chen did not offer a timetable and said some controllers would learn English in China.
The program at Embry-Riddle is the largest language-training effort for foreign controllers in the United States. 
The Federal Aviation Administration enrolls some students, primarily from the Middle East and parts of Asia outside China, at the agency's academy in Oklahoma City, but it teaches them air traffic control, not English.
The Center for Aerospace Science, at the University of North Dakota, trained 120 Russian controllers in English in the early 1990's, and conducted one class of 21 Chinese in 1993, but such instruction has not been continued there. 
The students appear to prefer Florida to North Dakota.
Students from China face special problems, because their language has no common roots with English. 
But to be understood over radio links to pilots, they must master all its sounds. 
The teachers here simulated operations at Vero Beach, Fla., but the V and R sounds are both very difficult for Chinese speakers, and they tend to drop the last syllable. 
As a result, at first most of the students from China could not pronounce the name of the airport, said Graham R. Elliott, the director of language training at Embry-Riddle.
But working in "simulated airspace" designed by Embry-Riddle -- the Orlando area, with some distant airports squeezed in closer and a few mountains thrown in, to make the traffic patterns more challenging -- the students mastered the basics, including checking that they had been understood.
For example, Wang Qiang practiced directing the crew of an Air China flight to take off from a small airport near Orlando (an unlikely event but a part of the training exercise). 
Mr. Wang told the Air China flight to climb to 6,000 feet, proceed to a radio beacon some miles distant and make contact with another controller on a different frequency. 
Mr. Wang had trouble getting through to the crew in his airspace but, as trained, he used the officially approved phraseology to address the situation.
"American Flight 254, state your intentions," he said in a command that roughly translates as "Hey, captain, wake up!"
If the controllers' communication was not often grammatical, its meaning was clear. 
One could be heard telling a flight crew over his headset, "Speak louderly."
An outsider would have found the conversations difficult to follow, but that was a matter of content as well as accent. 
When spoken by an American controller, standard air traffic phraseology "sounds like a foreign language to English speakers," said Paul E. McDuffee, a university vice president who helped set up the program with the Civil Aviation Authority of China.
The training laboratory here reverberates with phrases like "Climb and maintain 5,000 feet proceed direct webs" or "Descend and maintain 2000 report airport in sight," all in heavy Chinese accents.
Air traffic control language is highly structured and clipped, a corpus of about 500 words and phrases meant to convey precise meanings covering everything that can happen in a routine flight, for rapid communication over busy radio frequencies. 
But communicating precisely is a big task even if the pilot or controller's first language is English and sometimes plain English words are needed. 
At Embry-Riddle, which primarily teaches aviation, not English, instructors tell horror stories about misunderstandings.
Mr. Elliott said in one training flight, a controller told a foreign pilot to cross the river and turn right, and then he would see the airport. 
The pilot asked what "cross the river" meant.
A foreign student pilot recently put his training plane in danger by following the instructor's orders too literally, Mr. Elliott said. 
He said the instructor knew that the pilot was flying too slowly as his plane approached the runway for landing, and told the student to "put the power back in."
The pilot pulled back on the throttle, slowing the engine, and then pushed it in, speeding it up. 
The instructor has sworn off that phrase, Mr. Elliott said, and will say "increase power" or "decrease power."
To improve the students' general knowledge of English, the teachers have been immersing them in the language by taking them to such places as a nearby shopping mall. 
On Thursday, in a late stop in preparation for their departure today, Li Jianming showed that his general command of English was up to the challenge of shaking off a saleswoman at the cosmetics counter.
The saleswoman was pushing a $17.95 vanilla musk cologne set, with talcum powder and body lotion. 
In response, Mr. Li said, "But my suitcase hasn't any empty area."
Yet for the 15 Chinese air controllers, their command of English was not sufficient to understand American movies. 
Along with the 4,500 regular students here, the Chinese were offered a movie every Thursday night. 
They liked "Independence Day," "Courage Under Fire" and "Phenomenon," but said the dialogue was too much and too fast. 
"The Rock" was easier, some said.

file: Amendment Killed, Way Is Cleared for China Trade Bill.txt
text:
ï»¿
With surprising and decisive ease, the Senate cleared the last major hurdle today to passing a trade bill with China and handing President Clinton one of his top remaining foreign policy goals.
Senators rejected a contentious amendment to impose sanctions on Chinese companies that export sophisticated weapons to hostile nations, setting the stage to vote in a few days on legislation to give China permanent normal trading privileges.
The amendment was defeated on a bipartisan vote, 65 to 32, after a furious last-minute lobbying campaign this week by pro-trade business leaders and several of Mr. Clinton's cabinet officers, who argued that the measure was redundant and could scuttle the bill.
The vote virtually assures that the Senate will join the House in ending the annual Congressional review of China's trade status, a ritual for 20 years that Beijing considers humiliating but that opponents argue is a lever for improving human rights. 
More than 70 senators are generally expected to vote for the overall bill.
"This is the big enchilada," said Senator Max Baucus of Montana, a pro-trade Democrat who led the fight against the amendment. 
"We've got it now."
Unlike the situation in the House, where the trade bill survived intense opposition from a coalition of labor and religious groups, final passage in the Senate was never been in doubt, only the course to get there.
Supporters of the legislation have pressed for a bill free of amendments because they say there is not enough time before Election Day to reconcile an amended Senate bill with the version that the House passed in May.
One after another, amendments to improve human rights, religious freedom and labor standards in China have fallen by lopsided votes this week, not because senators opposed them on merit but because of their potential harm to the underlying bill.
But the amendment sponsored by Fred Thompson, Republican of Tennessee, and Robert G. Torricelli, Democrat of New Jersey, to penalize Chinese companies that traffic in nuclear, chemical and biological weapons, as well as long-range missiles, struck a strong chord with lawmakers who are increasingly alarmed by intelligence reports of Chinese arms exports.
Under the amendment, the president would have been required to conduct an annual review of China's proliferation activities. 
If Chinese companies trafficked in the prohibited weapons, Mr. Clinton could have cut off sensitive technology exports and United States government loans or credits. 
The president could have waived the sanctions if it was in the national security interest of the United States.
"Senator Thompson is asking us to put national security ahead of greed," said Senator Robert C. Byrd, a West Virginia Democrat who supported the amendment. 
"What's wrong with that?"
Senator Mike DeWine, Republican of Ohio, added: "This amendment is not just about holding other nations accountable as proliferators. 
It is also about holding our President accountable as the world's principle proliferation enforcer."
But other senators, including Phil Gramm, Republican of Texas, voiced support for the overall bill and its trade benefits and objected to any amendments that could imperil them.
Mr. Thompson mocked Mr. Gramm for naively believing that trade could help reverse Beijing's penchant for selling missiles and missile technology to countries like North Korea and Pakistan.
"His response is trade with them, and one day we will magically wake up and they will be dismantling their armaments," said Mr. Thompson, who has clashed with Mr. Gramm in recent months over a bill to govern export controls. 
"When that happens, I will present the tooth fairy on the floor of this body."
Even after Mr. Thompson had watered down his amendment to address administration complaints that it focused too narrowly on China and that its sanctions would hurt American farmers, the Clinton administration strongly objected.
This week, several cabinet members, including Defense Secretary William S. Cohen and the national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, telephoned senators who were wavering on the amendment, warning that it overlapped existing law and hindered the president's ability to compel China to curb proliferation.
In the end, 35 Democrats and 30 Republicans voted against Mr. Thompson's measure, while 23 Republicans and 9 Democrats voted for it. 
Several Republicans, who favored the amendment as a separate bill, including Thad Cochran of Mississippi, Connie Mack of Florida and Don Nickles of Oklahoma, voted against it as an amendment.
"This is it, it's settled, it's all over but for the shouting," said Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a New York Democrat who has championed the trade bill.
After the vote, Mr. Thompson's aides said he had not ruled out bringing up the measure again before the Senate adjourns.
The United States and China reached agreement last fall on a deal to help pave China's eventual entry into the World Trade Organization, the 135-member trade group that sets the rules for global commerce. 
China will enter the W.T.O. no matter how the Senate votes. 
But without Congress's blessing, Beijing could withhold some of the trade benefits, including lower tariffs, from the American farmers and companies that it will extend to other members of the trade group.
Business leaders hailed the surprisingly wide margin of the vote and predicted speedy passage of the overall bill, perhaps as early as Thursday.

file: American Deported From China Kept Secret Diary of Life in Jail.txt
text:
ï»¿
"I lied to them," said the human rights campaigner Harry Wu, leaning forward in his study today as he recounted his two months of imprisonment in China, "and so what?"
"I said that if they released me I would stay away from politics and have a good life with my wife," he said in an interview just hours after his expulsion from China and return to his home here, 30 miles south of San Francisco.
Mr. Wu, whose arrest had become an irritant in United States-Chinese relations, declined to say whether he would continue his secret forays into China investigating forced labor camps. 
But he said would continue his human rights work.
"Why should I be honest with them?" he said. 
"I deal with men as men deal with me, and they lied to me from the very beginning."
And then he turned to politics, and the decision by Hillary Rodham Clinton to attend a women's conference in Beijing next month.
"She had to judge by herself to go or not to go," he said. 
"But if my release is part of a deal, if this is a condition for Mrs. Clinton to go to China, I will be angry about it."
He added: "The release of Harry Wu does not mean the Chinese human rights record has improved. 
The police told me, 'You are lucky you are an American citizen.'
This made me very sad."
In a detailed account of his ordeal, Mr. Wu said he was keenly aware of the special treatment he received as an American. 
He was kept in an air-conditioned room in a medical building, was fed the same food as his guards and was told to shave before the monthly visits of an American consular official.
Mr. Wu, 58, who spent 19 years in Chinese camps as a young man before coming to the United States in 1985 and becoming a citizen, has made a career of publicizing abuses in the labor camp system, returning in secret to China four times to compile his reports.
It was during his most recent visit, on June 19, that he was seized at the border. 
This week he was convicted of spying and stealing state secrets and sentenced to 15 years of imprisonment and expulsion. 
Immediately after his sentence was read, he said, the judge smiled, patted him on the arm, and told him he could go home.
Today was Mr. Wu's chance to tell the story of his most recent stint in a Chinese prison, in the first person, and his words began flowing before he had even taken his seat -- about the cell he was forced to share with three guards, the duel he played with his interrogators, and the secret diary he kept, in tiny Chinese characters, in the inner margins of a fat Chinese-English dictionary.
An expert on the tricks prisoners play, Mr. Wu made a thin glue from rice and water and sealed the inner edges of the pages together to hide his journal entries. 
As he gingerly pulled them apart today, his hidden chronicle of pressures and interrogation sprang to light.
The page numbers denoted the month and day of the entry. 
On page 704, July 4, two weeks after his arrest, the entry reads: "Got fresh air for the first time."
Page 710, July 10, reads: "They take away my ring and my watch. 
I request medicine. 
I protest that I wrote a letter to my wife and they did not send it."
July 11: "Talked to them about my back pain."
July 18: "Two doctors from the medical university examined me. 
Talked about my counter-revolutionary crimes from 10 to 12 o'clock. 
Afternoon interrogation about my activities in China in 1994."
Mr. Wu said he broke his back in a coal mine accident while serving in a labor camp 20 years ago. 
As a result, he said, without medication his left leg was in constant pain.
At the start of his two months of interrogations, Mr. Wu said, "I played it tough because I didn't know what they wanted. 
They said, 'Do you know what is your problem?
You have caused us big trouble. 
We have wanted you for a long time.'
"I said, 'Here I am, like meat on the chopping block for you. 
Whatever you want, you can chop."'
Later, he said, he asked his interrogators, "Why are you doing this?
You are making me a hero. 
Are you crazy?
Maybe my books will sell well again."
The interrogations focused on television documentaries he had made about conditions in Chinese labor camps, Mr. Wu said, and he won some points and lost some points.
"I admitted violating the law," he said. 
"It is true. 
If America has a speed limit of 55 and China has a speed limit of 40 and you go 55 in China, then you break the law. 
If a watchtower is a secret and you film the watchtower, what can I say?"
Last night, with the time change and the exhilaration of his release, Mr. Wu said, he could hardly sleep. 
Only hours before, he had expected to spend the next 15 years in prison.
"But something funny happened," Mr. Wu said today. 
"After the sentence was read, they did not put handcuffs on me. 
The police very kindly said, 'Now we can go.'
"
Within two days, Mr. Wu said, he was put on a Chinese commercial flight from Shanghai to San Francisco.
"As soon as I boarded, the door closed, and an hour later the American consul was informed of my departure," Mr. Wu said. 
"Everything was prearranged. 
A pretty good show."

Americans Enjoy 70 Healthy Years, Behind Europe, U.N. Says.txt
text:
ï»¿
The United States falls behind almost every country in Europe as well as Canada, Australia and Israel in what the World Health Organization calls "healthy life expectancy," according to a report released today.
With the report, the organization joins a trend toward measuring life expectancy in a new way, for the first time factoring in the diseases and disabilities that are likely to rob people of a lifetime of good health.
By this adjusted measure, Japan leads the world in healthy life expectancy, according to W.H.O., which is part of the United Nations system. 
A Japanese citizen can expect to lead a life of 74.5 healthy years, it said. 
At the very bottom of the scale is battered Sierra Leone, where a child born in 1999 can expect to live a healthy life of fewer than 26 years.
Almost every country with a healthy life expectancy below 40 is in Africa, where AIDS and warfare are lowering life spans significantly. 
The group estimates that H.I.V.-AIDS has cut 15 to 20 years off life expectancy in southern Africa, and 5 to 10 years in other parts of the continent.
As in other measures of well-being, the study found, the United States loses ground against other industrial nations because it has its own "third worlds" within its population. 
Not surprisingly, the health agency says, years lost to disease, injury and other disabilities are substantially higher in poorer countries, and poorer communities in richer nations.
The new study lists poor health among American minorities, the effects of AIDS, tobacco-related cancers, heart disease and violence as factors in reducing a healthy life expectancy in the United States.
At the Population Reference Bureau, a private demographic research organization in Washington, Carl Haub, who compiles annual statistics on world population, said the American ranking is not particularly surprising.
"We have a 25 percent minority population that has lower life expectancies," he said, adding that even by traditional measures of mortality, the United States does not rank among the nations with the highest levels of longevity. 
"If you look at the U.S. by ethnic group, you see a somewhat different result. 
African-Americans in the U.S. have a much lower life expectancy, particularly males."
Using traditional methods, the United States had a life expectancy of 76.7 years in 1998, Mr. Haub said, with men at 73.9 years and women at 79.4.
The World Health Organization table of healthy life expectancy lowers the level to 70 years for Americans overall, with 67.5 years for men and 72.6 years for women.
Nicholas Eberstadt, who follows demographic surveys at the American Enterprise Institute in Washington, said there has been a trend, beginning in Europe, to add new dimensions to the study of longevity. 
"There has been an enormous amount of work done on healthy life expectancy," he said. 
"Some of these efforts have been inventive, but none have been particularly compelling."
Mr. Eberstadt said that a number of surveys have factored in perceptions about health and well-being among populations, which can vary dramatically from one country or region to another despite the statistical similarities.
The World Health Organization survey does not deal with perceptions, but does include projections based on what is known about major health factors like heart disease or lung cancer related to smoking. 
In Japan, for example, the new survey says that lung cancer rates for men "are expected to jump in coming years as the long-term effects of the post-World War II smoking popularity begin to hit."
China, the world's most populous nation, with one-fifth of the world's people, was found to have a healthy life expectancy of 62.3, well ahead of the second-largest country, India, at 53.2. 
The Chinese figure is considered particularly impressive, given the country's income level, W.H.O. says. 
China outranks not only India in a healthier life but also Russia and many nations in Central Asia, the Middle East and North Africa.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: Ancient Chinese Craft Shifts Building Designs in the U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
After six months of tough negotiations with a group of Taiwanese investors, Barry Lewen, a real-estate broker, thought he was just days from completing the $14 million sale of a building at 366 Madison Avenue when he was unexpectedly told there was one last detail.
The investors insisted that before anything more was done, a Chinese mystic had to be flown from Taiwan to determine if the building's qi, or life force, was acceptable. 
"I thought they were joking," said Mr. Lewen, an executive managing director of The Galbreath Company, a Manhattan real-estate company.
A few days later, however, he anxiously watched as a practitioner of the ancient Chinese craft of feng shui paced the site for 30 minutes before giving his approval.
"I wasn't sure if he was a witch doctor or what," Mr. Lewen said. 
"I can tell you there were a lot of sweaty palms."
Long a tradition in the Far East, the millennia-old craft of feng shui (pronounced fung shway) has begun to exert a subtle influence on the hard-edged world of real estate in America. 
Feng shui, which means "wind" and "water" in Chinese, is a blend of astrology, design and Eastern philosophy aimed at harmonizing the placement of man-made structures in nature.
Driven by the influx of investors from Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan and China, the use of feng shui has surfaced in the design and marketing of projects from mini-malls in Los Angeles to skyscrapers in Manhattan.
Its influence is more apparent in West Coast cities with large Chinese populations, like Los Angeles and San Francisco. 
Its impact on New York City's skyline is still barely perceptible: a rounded corner on a building, mirrors in hallways, oddly placed offices and blocked-off doorways -- measures taken to manipulate the flow of qi (pronounced chee).
But as more Chinese investors have come to the New York area, feng shui has become an increasingly familiar term to developers and designers. 
The former Gulf and Western Building on Columbus Circle, 40 Wall Street and the China Trust Bank in Flushing, Queens, are among projects in which developers called in feng shui experts to review the sites.
In West Orange, N.J., the developers of the Eagle Ridge residential development touted their project with full-page advertisements in Chinese newspapers featuring a Chinatown feng shui master, Tin Sun, who declared: "Its feng shui is unassailable!"
Even the $2.5 billion Riverside South project on the Upper West Side could include some elements of feng shui because of the entry of a group of Hong Kong investors as Donald J. Trump's new partners in developing the site. 
"It's just another element in which you can have the advantage over your competitors," Mr. Trump said. 
"Asians are becoming a big part of our market and this is something we can't ignore."
The theory behind feng shui is that a life force flows through all things -- buildings, hills, rivers, power lines, people -- and the manipulation of the force through the proper orientation of physical structures can enhance a person's luck, wealth and good health.
In the Far East, buildings with good feng shui can draw mobs of buyers eager to enhance their fortunes. 
Bad feng shui, in the opinion of a practitioner, can break a deal in a moment.
Although the craft, known as geomancy in English, originated at a time of rural villages and crude structures, feng shui masters say that analyzing the effect of modern phenomena, like elevator shafts, car traffic and air-conditioning ducts, follows the same principles.
In the basement of the Wing Fat Mansion in Chinatown is the office of Master Tin Sun and his daughter Master Pun Yin, a Hunter College graduate in film production who has worked with her father since she was a teen-ager.
They both practice a traditional form of feng shui that relies on analysis of the physical attributes of a site using the luopan, or feng shui compass, and the astrology of the client to determine the most auspicious arrangement.
Master Tin Sun said that feng shui had nothing to do with superstition, but rather drew on common-sense rules of design that enhance sunlight and air flow through a building. 
But he added there was also a mystical component of sensing the flow that required a trained practitioner.
"It is metaphysics," said the master, who has his own weekly radio show on feng shui on a Cantonese-language station. 
"The rules are only the mechanics. 
The rest you must feel through meditation."
Each master has a different way of looking at a structure's feng shui. 
Lin Yun, a well-known West Coast practitioner who has lectured at the Library of Congress and Harvard University, said he had no use for the luopan and relied instead on his intuition to determine the flow of qi. 
Some use mirrors and crystals to alter the flow of qi; others reject the method as a silly gimmick.
For believers, feng shui can influence every aspects of their lives, from the selection of a grave to the orientation of their desk and bed.
But even nonbelievers say that using feng shui has become a business necessity in some cases because the practice is so important to some Chinese.
Edmund Yu, president of Kinson Properties, which is renovating the 1.1-million-square-foot office building at 40 Wall Street, said that even though he was an avowed nonbeliever, he still commissioned the construction of a $300,000 pool in the building's lobby on the advice of a feng shui master.
"It's like killing two birds with one stone," he said. 
"Other people will just see it as an attractive addition. 
But for the Chinese, when they see it, they will know."
Before embarking on a $230 million renovation of the Trump International Tower and Hotel, formerly the Gulf and Western Building, on Columbus Circle, Scott Coopchik, an executive managing director of the Galbreath Company, decided to call in Master Tin Sun for advice after hearing that many potential tenants could come from the Far East.
Whether architects will heed the master's advice to move the main entrance to the north and sheath the building in an earth-toned glass is still under discussion, but Mr. Coopchik added that developers may take advantage of the master's feeling that the northwest corner of the buildings had the best feng shui, opening the possibility of marketing the normally less popular spaces at premium prices.
"If the marketing people are correct that 20 to 30 percent of our buyers will come from the Pacific Rim, we might as well respect their customs," Mr. Coopchik said.
Joseph S. Tarella, an architect with Greenfield, Sawiki, Tarella, was two months into the design of the $15 million China Trust Bank in Flushing when he was told that a feng shui master had advised moving the elevator shafts to a different side of the building and installing a two-foot-high water fountain in the cash-machine vestibule.
"We've never installed a fountain in an A.T.M. vestibule before," Mr. Tarella said. 
"But you have to be flexible if you want to work. 
Besides, I like it."
While many non-Chinese developers see feng shui only as a business necessity, its focus on harmonizing man-made structures with nature has attracted a growing number of architects and interior designers intrigued with its Eastern philosophy.
"It's one of those hot, buzzword fads right now," said Joseph Pryweller, senior editor of the American Society of Interior Designers Report. 
"Everyone wants to know at least how to pronounce it correctly."
Sarah Rossbach, who has written three books on feng shui, likes to describe the craft as "environmental psychology."
She has dropped the more superstitious aspects of feng shui, and instead focuses on the spiritual approach to design.
"It's really a manipulation of your environment to manipulate your life," said Ms. Rossbach, who learned the craft from Mr. Lin.
The increasing interest in feng shui has even prompted one designer, Ronald D. Chin, a third-generation Chinese-American architect, to open a company that specifically markets itself as using feng shui.
"Americans are really acknowledging there are other ways of looking at a space," he said. 
"I think they realize there should be a greater recognition of that intangible part of a space that deal with feelings and emotions."
But as feng shui becomes more popular, it also raises the possibility of creating new problems.
In Hong Kong, the Bank of China's 70-story tower has caused unease among the colony's feng shui believers, who say the building's sharp angles have caused bad feng shui for the area. 
Some residents have placed mirrors in their windows to deflect the evil energy supposedly coming from the building.
In some parts of Hong Kong, feng shui duels have emerged, with residents aiming mirrors at each other to reflect evil influences from buildings -- a decidedly unharmonious development.
"You can be driving down a street and you see your headlights reflected all over the place," Ms. Rossbach said. 
"It can get very dangerous."
The ancient Chinese craft of feng shui (pronounced fung shway) is the practice of arranging surroundings to promote prosperity and harmony. 
Here are basic guidelines from Tin Sun, a feng shui master, for assessing the feng shui of an urban apartment.
Â 
EXTERIOR
Â 
A building should not have its front door facing oncoming traffic. 
Cars and lights create negative forces that disturb the peace.
Â 
There should not be any sharp objects or corners facing a doorwya of a building or apartment. 
The corners are like arrowheads, shooting negative e4nergy toward the building and its tenants.
Â 
One should avoid facing glass buildings. 
The buildings would absorb the negative energies of their surroundings and reflect them back.
Â 
If a building is on a hill, the back of the building should not be on the lower part of the slope. 
It would be like a chair without back support - the energy would roll down the hill.
Â 
It is not advisable to have bridges in close proximity. 
They create tension and negative forces.
Â 
INTERIOR
Â 
An apartment should not be next to or facing an elevator, especially if one hears the mechanics of it. 
The humming of the elevator machinery disrupts the flow of qi, or life force.
Â 
When one enters an apartment, the stove should not be visible. 
It can turn happiness into sorrow because of its concentration of fire, which disturbs the peace of the space. 
This is a common cause of family problems.
Â 
An apartment should not be next to or facing a garbage disposal chute, which draws away energy from the apartment. 
Heavy traffic around the chute also disrupts peace.
Â

Archeologists have found remains of a sacrificial site near the tomb of China's first emperor and said the discovery was as significant as the famed terracotta warriors who guard it, the New China News Agency said today.
Offerings of food were placed four times a day and a grand rite held once a month at the sacrificial building that is part of the sprawling mausoleum of Qin Shi Huangdi, historical records showed.
The emperor, credited with unifying China in 221 B.C., ruled with an iron fist until his death 11 years later. 
China has said it lacks the resources to excavate his tomb, which according to legend is filled with booby traps to deter robbers.

file: ANNUAL U.N. RITUAL CONDEMNING CHINA LOSES U.S. SUPPORT.txt
text:
ï»¿
Only days after deciding to move up a Presidential trip to Beijing, the Administration has given China another important boost by dropping American sponsorship of an annual United Nations resolution condemning China's record on human rights.
The move, which effectively kills a resolution before the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva, was described by senior officials today as a response to Beijing's recent efforts to improve its rights record, including its decision this week to sign an important international human rights treaty.
"China still has an enormous way to go, and we intend to press them at every opportunity," a senior Administration official said. 
"But in light of these steps, we have decided not to sponsor the resolution. 
It's certainly not a reward. 
It is being done as a calculation. 
It is being done because we believe it is the way to make progress in the future."
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, hinted strongly that China had agreed to release a number of prominent political prisoners if the United States dropped its sponsorship of the resolution. 
"I believe there will be further releases," he said, declining further comment. 
"Lives are at stake."
The Administration's decision was denounced by human rights groups, which said the Administration was abandoning one of its best tools to press Beijing to end what the Administration agrees are widespread human rights violations.
The annual resolution, first introduced at the commission in 1990 after the massacre of unarmed civilians at Tiananmen Square the year before, has infuriated China, even though it has never been adopted by the 53-member commission. 
The commission is to open its annual meeting in Geneva next week.
"If the President visits China without clear human rights preconditions and also drops any resolution at the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva, what leverage will the United States use to press for concrete progress?" asked Mike Jendrzejczyk, Washington director of Human Rights Watch Asia. 
"They've caved."
The White House announced this week that Mr. Clinton, who would be the first President to visit China since the 1989 crackdown on the democracy advocates, had moved up his trip to June from November in order to build on progress made during the visit by President Jiang Zemin of China to the United States last fall.
Chinese officials leapt at the proposal for an earlier meeting.
The Administration's steps to improve relations with China came as President Clinton sought to play down the importance of new evidence that China had tried to sell nuclear technology and equipment to Iran.
The President told reporters at the White House that the sale, first disclosed by the State Department in testimony before Congress on Thursday, was halted in response to an American protest last month.
"The Chinese followed through on it and kept their agreement to the letter," the President said. 
"I am well pleased, actually, with the way that issue came out."
Administration officials said that soon after President Jiang agreed during last year's summit talks to halt nuclear cooperation with Iran, the United States learned about negotiations concerning the sale to Iran of tons of chemicals that could enrich uranium for nuclear weapons.
Far from seeing the incident as a violation of the American-Chinese pact, Administration officials said today that only low-level Chinese officials had negotiated with the Iranians and that senior Chinese Government leaders had blocked the sale as soon as it was brought to their attention by the United States.
"Chinese authorities investigated the matter and promptly informed us that a transaction like that had not been agreed to and that China had no intention of making such a transaction," said James P. Rubin, the State Department spokesman. 
"This is a case that demonstrates how nonproliferation works."
The Administration's critics on Capitol Hill, however, viewed the incident as fresh evidence that China's commitment to its nuclear agreement with the United States was still in question.
Senator John Ashcroft, a Missouri Republican who is a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, described the potential deal as troubling and said President Clinton had a "policy of blind engagement" toward Beijing.
The committee chairman, Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina, said through a spokesman, "We now have the spectacle of the Clinton Administration questioning China on whether it is continuing to provide nuclear weapons assistance to various countries even while, at the same time, a Presidential certification to the contrary is pending before the Senate."
Administration officials said -- and human rights groups agreed -- that the decision to drop sponsorship of the human rights resolution probably meant that no resolution against China would be offered this year.
Last year the resolution, sponsored by the United States and Denmark, was defeated, 27 to 17, after a vigorous lobbying campaign by the Chinese Government, which labeled the resolution "an outrageous distortion of China's reality."
A senior Administration official said Washington decided not to seek a new resolution because of recent actions taken by China at the request of the United States and other nations. 
These included the release of several prominent political prisoners and this week's announcement by China that it would sign the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.
The covenant, a United Nations treaty, is intended to provide guarantees of freedom of expression, religion, assembly and movement, and equality before the law. 
By signing the treaty, China would be required to file periodic reports on its human rights record that would be subject to review by international human rights experts.

file: ANTIQUES_Tang Horses Are Out In Full Force.txt
text:
ï»¿
According to the Chinese zodiac, this is not the Year of the Horse. 
But it should be. 
Ancient Chinese horse sculptures are showing up all over.
There are four life-size terra-cotta chariot horses from the Qin dynasty (221-207 B.C.) in "The Golden Age of Chinese Archeology," a show at the National Gallery of Art in Washington that opened on Sept. 
19 and runs through Jan. 
2. These horses, with ears forward and nostrils dilated, are part of a group of 500 horses and soldiers excavated from tombs in Shaanxi province in 1976.
Ten horses from the Tang dynasty (618-906 A.D.) are among the works in "Abstraction and Reality: Chinese Art From the Warring States to the Liao," which opened two days ago at the Chinese Porcelain Company, a gallery at Park Avenue and 58th Street. 
Some of the horses are glazed, in glorious blue, green, amber and cream, with tasseled bridles and elaborate saddle blankets. 
Others are unglazed, which makes them look modern to Western sensibilities.
One unglazed pale taupe horse has its head raised, neighing. 
Another twists its neck to catch a fly. 
Still another has its muzzle to the ground. 
They are subtly modeled to catch the light and create shadows.
"These are very rare models," said Jim Lally, who runs J. J. Lally, at 41 East 57th Street, and specializes in ancient Chinese art. 
"The Tang was a moment in Chinese art when there was a strong move toward realism and a strong decorative impulse. 
Horses imported from the Near East were precious. 
In Tang China, the horse was the emblem of wealth and power. 
They are meant to embody rank and speed."
Mr. Lally, who sells Tang horse sculptures, currently has a classic example in pale green glaze with an amber saddle cloth, for $100,000.
In addition, there is a herd of nine Tang horses for sale at E. & J. Frankel Oriental Art, 1040 Madison Avenue, at 79th Street, and there are a few more at the Alvin Lo Gallery, 5 East 57th Street.
China's love affair with the horse probably began in the Shang dynasty (circa 1600 to 1100 B.C.), when real horses and human charioteers were interred with Shang emperors. 
Initially, the Chinese had only small, sturdy horses they used as draft animals. 
After the Chinese were attacked by enemies riding larger, stronger horses, they began importing horses from the Middle East, breeding them and training them for warfare and sport.
This all came together in the Tang dynasty. 
Mario Prodan wrote in "The Art of the Tang Potter" (Viking, 1961), "This is China's moment of greatness, artistic, political, military and cultural."
He continued, "Whenever the Chinese dream of imitating nature, of achieving the unbroken line, may have begun, it is certain that it is at last fulfilled in the art of the Tang potter."
The horse was a favorite subject of these artists, but the horse has always been a source of inspiration in China. 
Chinese composers and poets wrote songs and poems about horses, and artists painted them, carved their portraits in stone and created pottery sculptures.
Today, Tang pottery pieces are the most valued of Chinese horse sculptures. 
They range in price from a few thousand dollars to millions. 
Unlike jade, a Tang horse offers a buyer a certain comfort level because thermoluminescence tests can prove its age and fakes can be detected.
The popularity of these works was proved again in Christie's New York sale of Chinese sculpture on Sept. 
16. One horse, which was estimated to sell for $60,000 to $80,000, went for $266,500.
Unglazed, it had its head lowered toward its left foreleg, which was slightly raised. 
There was a grooved channel running the length of the arched neck, where a real horsehair mane would have been inserted, and there was a hole for a horsehair tail.
An amber glazed horse with a textured fur saddle blanket glazed green went for $310,000. 
It was not unlike one that Sotheby's London sold in 1989 for the British Rail Pension Fund for $6.1 million, the world record for a Chinese work of art.
"Tang horses are the most widely popular image of Chinese art," Mr. Lally said, "because they are immediately accessible to everyone. 
You don't have to read a book on Chinese art to love a Tang horse."
Among the horses in the Chinese Porcelain Company show is a cream-colored, glazed one decorated with splashes of cobalt blue. 
Khalil Rizk, co-owner of the gallery, said: "Only 5 percent of Tang horses have blue glaze. 
Cobalt was put on during the last firing. 
Cobalt was a treasured commodity imported from the Middle East; it was more valuable than gold. 
Its use means the horse was for someone of the highest rank."
This horse is 15 inches tall and turns its head to the left. 
It has an ornamental harness and bridle. 
Originally, Mr. Rizk said, it would have had bronze decorations as well.
"Generally speaking, glazed horses used to be more sought after, especially in Japan," Mr. Rizk said. 
"But some horses were so well sculpted they may have been deliberately left unglazed."
One unglazed horse at the show has bent its head back toward its left shoulder in a natural pose. 
It would be considered a fine work of art in any culture.
The show continues through Oct. 
28. Prices for the horses are $35,000 to $2 million.

Chairs With Curves
American antique chairs can have more curves than Marilyn Monroe.
As the American furniture sale at Christie's New York, set for Thursday, approaches, Christie's experts are touting the virtues of a high-style, finely carved Philadelphia mahogany side chair commissioned by Gen. John Cadwalader about 1769. 
It is magnificent, but the star of the sale may be Lot 185, a Queen Anne carved walnut armchair that has been on display in the Diplomatic Reception Rooms of the State Department for the last 20 years.
The chair, circa 1740-1760, belongs to George G. Meade Easby, a descendant of its original owner, Robert Waln, a Quaker merchant in Philadelphia. 
And it is a study in well-executed, bold S-curves.
The arms have knuckle grips that look like fiddlehead ferns. 
The cabriole legs have shells carved on the knees. 
The crest has double scrolls, and the elbow rests are rounded and concave. 
The estimate is $600,000 to $900,000.
The chair is marked No. 1, and thought to be part of a set that is already represented in the Chipstone Foundation and the Kaufman collection, two important American furniture repositories.
The Queen Anne chair could be paired with a handsome Queen Anne carved walnut games table, circa 1740, in Sotheby's sale of American furniture next Friday. 
The table has rounded "turret" corners, carved shells on its knees, and claw and ball feet. 
The estimate is $30,000 to $50,000. 
This pair could really make a statement in the right environment.

file: AOL Merger Is Unlikely to Reshape AsianInternet Business.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was hardly Paris, but Shanghai played a part in the brief, intense courtship between America Online and Time Warner.
America Online's chairman, Stephen M. Case, attended a Fortune magazine conference there in October, during which he mingled with Time Warner's top executives, including Gerald M. Levin and Ted Turner. 
Later, the executives traveled to Beijing for the 50th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China. 
A Time Warner executive who was there recalls a teasing exchange between Mr. Case and Mr. Turner, when the two found themselves stranded in the rain outside the Great Hall of the People.
"Ted, your big, merged company isn't getting you off the steps," Mr. Case shouted to Mr. Turner.
"Steve," he replied, "your billions ain't getting you anywhere either."
It is not clear, even after America Online's extraordinary bid for Time Warner, that this huge merged company will be able to get off the steps in China -- or elsewhere in Asia. 
In contrast to Europe, where America Online has built a valuable regional franchise through its partnership with Bertelsmann A.G., the Internet in Asia remains a fractured business with few large competitors and virtually none that cross national boundaries.
"AOL and Time Warner have tremendous critical mass in the United States and, through AOL and Compuserve, in Europe as well," said Michael J. Wolf, the partner in charge of the media practice at Booz, Allen & Hamilton, the New York-based consultancy. 
"But to a large extent, Asia is up for grabs."
America Online operates an on-line service in Japan, and recently started one in Hong Kong. 
But it has yet to enter the Chinese mainland, where Yahoo, the Internet portal service, is one of the few major American Internet companies to have established a foothold. 
Time Warner distributes movies and music in China -- as well as CNN and Time magazine, when they are not being banned by the Chinese government. 
But like most other American media companies, Time Warner has not been able to make deep inroads in the country because of hazards ranging from piracy to onerous regulations and political pressure. 
The proposed merger will not eliminate those.
Some analysts said that America Online would benefit more from a deal than Time Warner because its credibility will be burnished in the eyes of the Chinese government. 
Although Beijing, after months of equivocation, recently indicated that it would allow foreign companies to invest in the Internet, officials seem likely to pick and choose among potential entrants. 
Analysts said America Online's odds of receiving favorable treatment would be higher if it tied up with a media giant like Time Warner.
"CNN and Ted Turner will open doors for this company politically, allowing it to do things that other companies may not be able to," Mr. Wolf of Booz, Allen & Hamilton said.
Brian C. Lippey, chief executive of Tokai Asia, a hedge fund based in Hong Kong, added: "The merger gives AOL international credibility. 
Time Warner is a good old-fashioned multinational."
And although a combined company's prospects in Asia are uncertain, news of the huge deal reverberated through the region, prompting talk of more mergers and strategic alliances involving Asian companies. 
Shares of local media companies and Internet access providers soared on Tuesday, though most fell back as the initial giddiness over the announcement subsided.
This may reflect some basic truths about Asia. 
Lehman Brothers noted in a report that the ownership of many Asian media companies is concentrated in the hands of one or two big investors. 
That would make huge, widely held combinations like AOL-Time Warner unlikely, at least in the short term.
Cultural, linguistic and regulatory differences among Asian countries also militate against the creation of pan-Asian companies. 
Two decades after CNN was founded in the United States, Star TV, a satellite television unit of the News Corporation, remains the only genuinely regional media service based in Asia.
"If you look at Japan, there are some wonderful media companies, but very little of their material sees the light of day outside Japan," said Alexander A. Arena, the group managing director of Pacific Century Cyberworks, a Hong Kong company that is designing a satellite-delivered Internet service.
Still, analysts and stock pickers were quick to draw up lists of Asian companies they contended would benefit from the changes suggested by a merger of America Online and Time Warner. 
Leading the list are obvious candidates like Sony, the Japanese electronics giant, and less obvious ones like TVB, a Hong Kong television broadcaster that owns the world's largest library of Chinese-language programming.
Analysts said that Pacific Century Cyberworks and other companies that aspire to deliver information and entertainment to subscribers over high-capacity wires would also benefit. 
Hong Kong's dominant local phone company, Cable and Wireless HKT, may also come into favor because of its recent alliance with Star TV, in which the two plan to offer television programming to the phone company's customers.
For all the excitement, Asian reactions to the AOL-Time Warner deal have had an unfocused quality. 
Experts said that reflects the Internet's relative lack of development here, which makes picking winners and predicting the future even chancier than in the United States.
"It's a simple question of supply and demand," Mr. Lippey said. 
"There aren't that many quality Internet companies in Asia."

file: Approaches To Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
THERE are three ways of entering Tibet legally, and on each of three trips I have made there as a budget traveler, I have used a different route.
In 1992, on my first trip, I entered from Nepal, joining a tour because of Chinese regulations. 
I chose the Arniko Travel Agency in Katmandu and acquired a week's visa extension in Tibet beyond the departure of the tour. 
We traveled by hired bus from Katmandu to the unpaved climb to Zhangmu across the border in China. 
The next day we ascended the perilous gorge filled with trees, ferns and tumbling water. 
We stopped at mud slides to help local people heave rocks into the road so we could continue on our way. 
Cresting the pass, we left the green, water-drenched gorge and entered the Himalayan rain shadow of brown, beige and taupe.
On this route, which took 10 days from Katmandu to Lhasa, the traveler can visit Sakya Monastery and the former monastery city of Tashilhunpo outside Shigatse, once a pretty Tibetan town but now just another Chinese shambles of stained concrete and cracked blue glass. 
Gyangtse, my favorite Tibetan town, half a day's journey farther southeast on this route, has not yet met that fate. 
A stroll down the main street between Tibetan houses topped by rippling prayer flags takes one to the monastery and the Kumbum, a white wedding-cake structure honeycombed with chapels whose walls are bright with 15th-century murals. 
It is the Ste.-Chapelle of Asia.
I lost count of the passes we crossed bumping along over the potholes, but all were spectacular. 
We also drove along the shores of Lake Yamdrok, 40 miles southeast of Lhasa, a flawless turquoise set among jagged white mountains.
When my tour left Tibet, I moved from the Holiday Inn in Lhasa to the Yak Hotel, one of a handful of hotels run by Tibetans that cater to budget travelers. 
I spent the week learning the ropes -- where to eat (at Tashi's), where to shop (the Barkhor), where else to stay (the Banok Shul, the Snowlands or the Kirey). 
On the flight back to Katmandu on Southwest China Air, I was served a meal consisting of a bag of cashews, digestive biscuits, a boiled duck egg, an apple and cough drops. 
Because there was no regulation of carry-on luggage, baggage obstructed the aisle. 
The Lhasa airport was filthy, crowded and inefficient, but the views of the Himalayas during the flight were superb.
Â 
Chengdu
In 1995, on my second journey to Tibet, I flew from Hong Kong to Chengdu, capital of Sichuan Province, in the northeastern corner of China, where, as part of the needlessly expensive package I bought in Hong Kong, I was picked up by a guide with driver and car.
Chengdu, a heavily polluted town, has a number of interesting, rundown Chinese monasteries, such as the Wenshu and the Quingyang, where people worship by lighting joss sticks and prostrating themselves. 
There is also the "cottage" of the famous eighth-century poet Du Fu, where you can rent a fishing pole and fish in the stocked pond that smells of drains.
I waited four days for the Tibetan permit I'd arranged for in Hong Kong. 
At the end of my two-day package at the $100-a-night Chengdu Hotel, where electric wires snake in and out of holes in the walls and a dingy, feltlike carpeting covered the floors, I transferred to the Traffic Hotel by the bus station, a Spartan, clean place where I shared a triple with two other women for $5.45. 
I shared the bathroom, which was down the hall and also clean, with innumerable people.
Finally my visa and ticket arrived, and at 5:30 A.M. I was picked up at the Traffic by my guide, who funneled me efficiently through all the formalities onto Southwest China Air. 
Food and restrictions concerning carry-on luggage had improved 100 percent since my last flight. 
The new airport outside Lhasa was also an improvement.
I was very careful when I picked up my backpack because I could feel an altitude headache lurking. 
I knew from previous trips that bending over would make the top of my head explode. 
By flying in, I had come up too fast to an altitude of 12,000 feet.
On this trip I had organized, with two other Americans I met in Lhasa, an exhausting, adventurous and fascinating month's journey to Mount Kailas -- the holy mountain, considered the navel of the world by Hindus, Jains and Buddhists -- Lake Manasarowar and the Guge Kingdom. 
We traveled in the back of a baby-blue Chinese truck with a motley group of nine Europeans and Americans. 
Flying in meant that I had time to arrange the Mount Kailas trip before my three-month visa expired. 
Again, I flew out to Katmandu, to see Mount Everest up close.
Â 
Lhasa
In October 1996 I made my third trip, coming in overland from China, starting again in Chengdu. 
One cannot yet go by bus from Chengdu to Lhasa, which would be scenically thrilling, if difficult. 
The roads are bad and the Chinese worry about losing foreigners to accidents. 
One can, however, travel from Chengdu to Lhasa in hops, using different forms of transportation. 
Again I started in Hong Kong, this time booking through Time Travel Agency, which got me a flight and a two-month visa in a record eight hours. 
I would at some point have to get a Tibetan permit as well. 
After my previous experience, I knew that in Chengdu, at the Traffic Hotel's agency, I could get a flight to Xining (pronounced syee-neeng), the capital of Qinghai province, the next stop on the way to Lhasa. 
I spent two days in Chengdu arranging ticket, flight and permit.
During the short flight to Xining on Southwest China air, I munched a spicy potato-chip-like snack while looking down on mountains at first partly forested, then drier mountains terraced top to bottom like layers of phyllo dough.
I shared a taxi into town with Cendi and Hay, a Dutch couple I'd met at the Traffic Hotel. 
Xining has a mixed population of Muslims, Chinese and Tibetans. 
The Muslim men wear white crocheted caps; the women cover their hair with flocked black scarves. 
We thought we'd sighted a mosque on the river but it was our hotel. 
The endless stairs passed a floor housing a roller skating rink. 
On the floor that housed the hotel, we were led to a room for three where orange imitation-taffeta curtains sagged askew on a broken rod but the sheets appeared to be clean. 
With no lock on the door, I didn't mind being three in a room. 
The view across the river was of bluffs striated in yellow and red reminiscent of the landscape of Utah.
CENDI, pronounced "Sandy," asked the reception clerk for the name of a good Muslim restaurant. 
We piled into a taxi and for $1.35 were taken to a largely empty restaurant, clean and swagged with red velvet hangings. 
With the help of my Chinese conversation book, we ordered "sheep meat," eggplant, mixed vegetables, steamed bread and rice. 
The "sheep meat," flakes of lamb on toothpicks, was superb.
The next morning Hay, pronounced "Hi," toted my backpack to the train station for me. 
For $22.50 I had a bottom bunk with two blankets in a hard sleeper, Chinese second class. 
Because it was a local, it was relatively empty. 
At first we passed villages of small, flat-roofed brick houses with carved wooden arches and protruding wooden rafters. 
There was piped-in music, nasal American rock and saccharine Chinese pop.
The land became parched, fields disappeared into sloping sand dunes as we passed Quinghai Lake (Koko Nor), the largest lake in China, which contains an island breeding ground for birds. 
Other passengers bought food at the stations through the windows or from a cart that came down the aisle selling snacks. 
Not trusting Chinese dining cars, I had gone to a supermarket in Hong Kong and bought Laughing Cow cheese, Danish camembert, canned tuna, tea bags and a tin of duck with orange rind.
After probably three hours, we entered an area of grasslands where yak grazed. 
Two men sat on the bunk opposite me playing a game akin to checkers, but they had really come to stare at the only Westerner on board. 
The dining car chef came by to have a phrase-book conversation with me. 
Everyone smoked. 
I forbade it in my area, how ever, by pointing at the appropriate phrase in my book. 
My companions were mildly surprised, but willing to go along for the pleasure of staring at me.
We arrived in Golmud, formerly Tibetan, now a Chinese town, a small oasis in a barren area, at about 7 A.M. The Golmud Hotel dorm ($5) housed only a young Japanese man who had worked as a cook's assistant in Milan. 
He was going home to Tokyo to open an Italian restaurant. 
I went over to the office of CITS, the Chinese equivalent of the old Russian Intourist, and booked the last leg of my trip, from Golmud to Lhasa by bus, for $160, including a three-day tour, a low-end hotel and the necessary Tibetan permit. 
One could not just buy a bus ticket. 
My total was an outrageous price, since locals pay $9.50 for the bus.
When I returned to the dormitory, my Japanese friend had been replaced by a young American, Brian, from Oakland on his first foreign trip. 
We went out to the market, where we inspected plastic pails and garish-colored yarns and had an excellent dinner of shredded pork, cloud ears and red tofu at a place around the corner from the hotel.
At 10:30 the next morning we took a van to the bus station, where we were issued bits of paper by female bureaucrats. 
Our fellow passengers were a mixed lot -- four Japanese, Brian, myself, two Tibetan nomad men with long swords in silver scabbards and gold caps on their teeth, and a number of bearded Muslims wearing straw hats over white caps, which made them look Amish. 
One Tibetan, unsheathing his sword, peeled an apple in one long corkscrew.
There were flimsy curtains on the windows and the seats were covered in electric-blue plush. 
The bus started out clean but accumulated cookie wrappers, orange and apple peels, cigarette butts and other garbage. 
Rest stops were rare, so it was advisable to get out for every one of them, and we did, with women going to one side and men to the other (there were no toilets). 
Everybody chain-smoked except the Muslims.
We drove through sand dunes and jagged rock for two hours. 
At 4 P.M. we came to a row of restaurants on one side of the road and a row of white-topped mountains on the other. 
Brian and I watched a man blast a heap of goats' heads with a blow torch, then smash them open for their brains. 
In one restaurant, where the owner's wife fed her baby spoonfuls of soup, we motioned to have our bowls of dried noodles, bought in the Golmud market, filled with boiling water. 
Brian opened the can of stewed duck with orange peel and we feasted.
After dinner, climbing through barren rock, we came round a bend almost hitting a herd of horses. 
By nightfall the road was unpaved and terrible. 
Chinese Army convoys streamed by all the way to Lhasa. 
I slept a little but the road was like corduroy. 
Awakened by a bump, I gazed into a snowstorm thickly covering road and countryside. 
I was cold despite long underwear, sweaters and a down jacket because I had to keep the window open to thin out the smoke.
In the morning it was snowing lightly. 
I took two of Brian's aspirins for my altitude headache, which I wouldn't have had if I'd drunk enough water, but I was worried by the infrequency of the rest stops.
We were surrounded by big hills of velvety green. 
Large black birds with rufous bibs on their chests roosted on electric poles beside the road. 
A herd of antelope burst from a hill, racing us. 
The antelope were replaced by sheep and goats with twisted horns, yaks with babies trotting beside them, and black-and-gray nomad tents.
PASSING a battalion of snowy mountains we saw men and women making prostrations along the road. 
It would be weeks before they prostrated themselves all the way to the Jokhang in Lhasa, whereas we arrived late that afternoon, 28 hours after starting from Golmud, coming in along the ugly new strip of Chinese office buildings. 
I spent a month trekking around Lhasa, visiting temples and monasteries there and in the Yarlung Valley, a day's trip southeast, before flying to Katmandu.
This last is the most rewarding route I've taken into Tibet, since I was able to see countryside while avoiding a tour. 
If it were possible to take a bus from Katmandu to Lhasa without being in a group, I might find that the best way. 
But the next time I go, I will go via Golmud.
Â 
Places to bunk down
The best time for a trip to Tibet is late August through November.
Â 
Where to Stay
CHENGDU, CHINA: The Traffic Hotel: an inexpensive travelers' hotel, charges about $4 for an immaculately clean bed in a triple with bath.
XINING: The Young Fu Hotel: $3.40 will get you a bed in a triple with bath and hot water.
GOLMUD: The Golmud Hotel: There are two hotels next to each other but under one name -- the only place you can stay in Golmud. 
One is cheap, about $2.75 for a bed in the dorm with slept-in sheets and a nasty bathroom down the hall. 
The other is about $8 with cleaner sheets and private bath.
LHASA, TIBET: The Chinese-owned Holiday Inn is about $100 a day. 
The Yak, the Kirey, the Banok Shul and the Snowlands are all around $4.75 for a dorm room. 
Private rooms, single or double with bath are about $22. 
These are Tibetan-run ventures.
Â 
Travel Agents
HONG KONG: Time Travel, 16th floor, Block A, Chungking Mansions, 40 Nathan Road, Kowloon; (852) 2723-9993. 
They can get you a flight to Chengdu within eight hours.
KATMANDU, NEPAL: Arniko Travel, Nag Pokhari, Naxal, Post Office Box 4695, Katmandu; (977-1) 414-594; fax (977-1) 411-878. 
A two-week tour, all inclusive, by bus to Lhasa is around $1,000.

text:
