file: As North Korea Defector Hides in China, Another Is Shot in Seoul.txt
text:
ï»¿
With one high-ranking North Korean official still holed up in the South Korean mission in Beijing, two gunmen today shot and critically wounded another North Korean defector here in an attack apparently ordered by the Communist country.
A senior police official said North Korean agents were suspected in the shooting of Li Il Nam, known in South Korea as Lee Han Yong, a 36-year-old nephew of the girlfriend of North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Il.
Mr. Li was the first North Korean defector to be shot in South Korea since an armistice ended the Korean War in 1953, said the official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Mr. Li was shot outside his home in Bundang, just south of the capital, Seoul, late this evening, the official said. 
A nurse at a nearby hospital said Mr. Li later underwent surgery, but she gave no details of his condition. 
The gunmen escaped and were being sought by the police.
The police official said he suspected that the gunmen were North Korean agents and that the shooting was intended as a warning to South Korea after the defection this week of the highest-ranking official ever to flee North Korea.
The latest North Korean defector, Hwang Jang Yop, one of 11 members of the secretariat of the ruling Workers' Party, has been holed up in the South Korean mission in Beijing since Wednesday, when South Korean officials said he arrived in a taxi and asked for political asylum in South Korea.
North Korea insists Mr. Hwang, who is ranked 25th in the country's hierarchy, was kidnapped by South Korea and has said it would retaliate if he was not returned, without specifying how.
Mr. Hwang's apparent defection has caused a huge loss of face for a North Korean Government, and Seoul has taken the threat seriously, ordering tighter security at all its overseas missions.
The defection of Mr. Hwang, 72, a thin, bespectacled man who served as an ideological theorist for the North, could potentially be the most damaging ever to North Korea, where the Government is already reeling from severe food shortages and economic disaster brought on in part by floods last year.
Mr. Hwang, who was once a tutor to the North Korean leader, would have had access to much of the inner workings of the secretive Pyongyang Government, which rules one of the world's most isolated states.
If he is willing to talk, he could provide a bonanza of information to Western intelligence officials, analysts said this week.
The Chinese Government must now decide on Mr. Hwang's future -- whether to allow him to be flown to Seoul, where he could be expected to reveal crucial secrets about North Korea, or to send him back to Pyongyang.
South Korea suggested today that it was prepared to go along with China's decision to take its time in finding a way to resolve the diplomatic crisis.
"I think we have started a good discussion with China and we have to wait and see," Foreign Minister Yoo Chong Ha told reporters. 
"I don't think that its right now to make any judgment on this."
A North Korean delegation arrived in Beijing today, but it was unclear if the group was there to discuss Mr. Hwang's case. 
The identities of the North Koreans were not known, and the North Korean Embassy in Beijing declined to comment.
Although recent signs indicated that North Korea might be seeking to ease its isolation, tensions between the two Koreas remain high.
Late last year, in an unusually conciliatory gesture, the Pyongyang Government apologized after a submarine incursion along the South Korean coast in September.

file: As Taiwan Votes in Close 3-Way Race Today, a Weak Government Is the Likeliest Outcome.txt
text:
ï»¿
No matter who wins the hotly contested presidential election on Saturday, the outcome will almost certainly be the weakest, most divided government since Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists fled to the island in 1949.
At fervent rallies tonight that brought hundreds of thousands of flag-waving citizens into the capital's streets, the three main candidates made their final appeals in a race that appeared too close to call.
Polling has not been allowed in the final 10 days, adding to the suspense of an election that has been fought with all the exuberance of a young democracy facing profound choices.
The contenders are Vice President Lien Chan from the governing Nationalist Party; James Soong, a former Nationalist official who is running as an independent; and Chen Shui-bian of the Democratic Progressives, the main opposition party.
Hanging over the campaign were heavy-handed warnings from Beijing, which considers Taiwan a region separated from the mainland since the civil war of the 1940's and threatened war if the island indefinitely delayed reunification talks.
But a more immediate problem for the Nationalists, who have firmly governed Taiwan through 51 years of dictatorship and then a democracy that they ushered in, is that this election represents a wrenching turning point, transforming the island's politics.
The Nationalist candidate, Mr. Lien, is in serious danger of losing in a three-way, winner-take-all race that has disastrously divided the party's traditional majority. 
Even if he wins, the prospect is for debilitating internal clashes.
"Everyone is focusing so much on the cross-straits problem," said Steven M. Goldstein, an expert on Taiwan politics at Smith College, in Massachusetts. 
"But no matter who gets elected, there's going to be a constitutional crisis."
The once impregnable Nationalists have been seriously weakened by charges of corruption and by an internal rift that produced Mr. Soong's breakaway candidacy and improves the chances of victory for Mr. Chen.
However, in an unusual prospect of a divided government here, either Mr. Chen or Mr. Soong, if elected, would have to contend with a Nationalist majority in the legislature, which is not up for re-election.
Even if Vice President Lien gains a plurality, allowing the Nationalists to hold on the presidency, the party will face new challenges to its vast business holdings and freewheeling political deals.
Both Mr. Chen and Mr. Soong have gained from their campaigning against "black gold" in politics, the term here for the business manipulations, alliances with mobsters and vote buying that have plagued Taiwanese politics. 
Many supporters of Mr. Chen and Mr. Soong are united in disgust at what they call the continued corruption of the Nationalists under the departing president, Lee Teng-hui.
"We have to get rid of the corruption and organized crime and vote buying," said Lu Chiu-chien, 42, a social worker from Keelung City who furiously waved a Chen flag here tonight.
Mr. Soong's credibility was hurt by evidence, released by the Nationalists, that he diverted party money to personal accounts in the past. 
But supporters like Mary Lu, 45, a homemaker who was out cheering for Mr. Soong, say he has been persecuted by a vindictive Mr. Lee.
Also, although he is stepping down as president, Mr. Lee has said he wants to serve out his remaining one and a half years as chairman of the Nationalist Party, a position that has arguably been more powerful than the presidency.
"Suddenly, the same person will no longer be both president and chairman of the party," said John Hsieh, the Taiwan-born director of the Center for Asian Studies at the University of South Carolina. 
"A serious confrontation is likely."
But attitudes toward Taiwan's independence remain the fundamental cleavage in the electorate, said Mr. Hsieh, an expert on public opinion here. 
The campaign has not only brought out festering animosities within the Nationalist Party, but also between those who basically favor independence and the majority, who want to leave well enough alone.
Cheng Yin-fu, 41, a furniture seller who was wildly waving a Chen Shui-bian flag at the stadium tonight, expressed the attitude that China -- and some worried Taiwanese -- dread to hear. 
"Spiritually and morally I support independence," he said. 
"But as for the actual action, we can wait for a while."
President Lee has outraged Chinese officials with his insistence on Taiwan's equal status with the mainland, a position that is widely shared here. 
But in recent days, Beijing has pointedly attacked Mr. Chen, the opposition party challenger, warning that his victory would be dangerous.
Alone among the candidates, Mr. Chen long championed a Taiwanese declaration of independence. 
But in this campaign, he moderated his position, saying a formal declaration would be unnecessary because Taiwan was effectively sovereign.
Although he has tried to press the anticorruption theme, he has had to spend much of his campaign trying to assure voters that he will not act recklessly and will seek peace.
Given China's deep suspicions, his election would open a period of serious tension, anxiously watched in Washington, because the United States has pledged to help defend Taiwan and would be drawn into a cross-strait war.
With a wide sense that Mr. Chen was gaining ground, Vice President Lien started trying to scare voters with warnings that electing Mr. Chen would court a military attack. 
Tonight he told cheering supporters that Mr. Chen and his party represented "chaos, disaster, war!"
Holding high Mr. Lien's hand at tonight's rally, President Lee continued this line of attack, shouting that Mr. Chen "is inexperienced, and everything he says will give jitters to everyone!"
But Mr. Chen's generally ardent supporters, including many younger people who yearn for a fresh and cleaner government, as well as an independent Taiwanese identity, have not been deterred.
"Taiwan, stand up!" was a loud chant at the Chen rally tonight, the largest and most frenzied of the three, which spilled far into the streets from a packed football stadium.
Considered by many to be a weak candidate, Mr. Lien, who has an American doctorate in political science and has held several top government posts, has offered little more in his campaign than appeals to experience and stabilityI.
After having been pushed aside by his former mentor, President Lee, Mr. Soong, a onetime Nationalist stalwart, has driven his independent run by attacking the corruption of the party that he had long served and by billing himself as a more competent leader than Mr. Lien.
At the same time, Mr. Soong, who also has an American doctorate in politics, is more willing to discuss the mainland's core principle of "one China."
He says he would be best able to negotiate with the mainland. 
But the independence-leaning supporters of Mr. Chen fear that he would sell out Taiwan's interests.
All three candidates say they will seek to broaden economic ties with the mainland. 
But whether any of them can meet Beijing's demands for unity talks is unclear, because the vast majority of voters prefer their current status of undeclared independence. 
And political experts wonder how the island will cope with pressures from Beijing if its government is seriously divided.
At the Hsingtien Buddhist temple here today, hundreds of people attended daily services. 
Most were older women. 
"At the beginning of the prayers, everybody here made a wish for peace and stabilityI," said one, Zhang Pai-tsai. 
She was worried by China's threats and said she would vote for Mr. Lien.
Outside the temple, Lin Tsai-cheng, 32, an electrician, said he was leaning toward Mr. Soong. "It's time for a change, but since Soong comes out of the KMT, it won't be too drastic a change," said Mr. Lin, using the initials for the Nationalists.
Mr. Chen's supporters tend to shrug off the mainland warnings.
"I don't give a damn about the threats from the mainland," Li Jing-huang, 50, a guide for Japanese tourists, said. 
"I was in the Taiwanese marines in Vietnam and I saw real war. 
But I don't think they'll attack. 
China can't afford a war."

file: ASIA-PACIFIC ISSUE_A WORLD OF CHOICES_ Taipei.txt
text:
ï»¿
Taipei lacks both charm and beauty, a rather damning assessment on the face of it. 
But beneath the gray, polluted skies, the monotonous low-rise buildings and the mad scooter drivers who swarm the roads, it remains the most vital and vibrant city in the Chinese-speaking world. 
The back lanes of every neighborhood (just walk behind whatever hotel you stay in) are crammed with cafes, tea houses, restaurants, herbal medicine stalls and pocket temples. 
The city is changing daily, adding buildings, restaurants, shopping centers. 
Nonetheless, visitors tend to come to Taiwan primarily for what is older, enduring, traditional.
The newest piece of Taipei is an overhead light rail system, a project that has been riddled with corruption, cracking cement pillars and balky French-made rail cars. 
After years of frustration, certainly among the Taipei citizens who endure horrendous traffic conditions, the placing of steel corsets around doubtful pillars and endless test runs of the rubber-wheeled driverless cars is finished and the train is open for business. 
It scoots passengers through the city a bit bouncily, but efficiently. 
Fares depend on how far you're going.
April is perhaps the best month to visit Yangmingshan Park, a 30-minute drive from Taipei. 
Set in the hills, the park's cornucopia of flower gardens, particularly its azaleas and the endless cherry blossoms -- now in bloom -- are a major attraction for Taipei's residents. 
In addition, the park has waterfalls, hot springs and a profusion of hiking trails that snake through the hills.
By far the most significant attraction in Taipei is the National Palace Museum, which while not new, still surprises visitors. 
The building, constructed in Ching dynasty palace style by the defeated Kuomintang Government of China after its retreat to Taiwan, houses the spectacular collection of Chinese paintings, ceramics, bronzes and antiquities, some of which is currently on view at the Metropolitan Museum in New York. 
After a political uproar, some of the rarest treasures scheduled for the American exhibit stayed at home, the only place one will be able to view them.

file: ASIA-PACIFIC ISSUE_Dancing and Skiing With the Yaks.txt
text:
ï»¿
BEFORE the Yellow River turns yellow, before it is even much of a river, its blue-green waters meander gently through the sandstone crags of China's Qinghai Province. 
A one-lane road, rutted and unpaved, winds alongside. 
Last spring, two friends and I hired a guide and a car and traveled this road for three days, until we reached its terminus high in the Anyemaqen Mountains.
Then we drove back.
This is not a common tourist excursion. 
Qinghai (pronounced ching-high) is in the very center of China, on the northeastern flanks of the Tibetan plateau. 
Much of the province sits over 10,000 feet above sea level; for visitors, a low-grade headache is likely to be a continual accompaniment.
Beyond Qinghai's main city, Xining, there are few tourist facilities. 
Only the most basic of accommodations are available, often without plumbing or electricity. 
In many places, yak meat and bread are the sole obtainable foods. 
No one speaks a word of English.
One of my travel partners, Kyle Westgard, lived on mainland China for eight years and still does business there. 
He is fluent in Mandarin. 
I had been introduced to Kyle through a mutual acquaintance. 
We exchanged E-mail, and I agreed to hire him as interpreter and facilitator. 
Within days of meeting him in Beijing, we became fast friends. 
Despite Kyle's language skills, he could communicate with few people in Qinghai -- on the route we followed, Tibetan is the primary tongue. 
Inconveniences aside, Qinghai is where I wanted to go. 
Cities in China are often crowded and polluted. 
Qinghai, I'd heard, was empty and pristine.
It is rich with Tibetan culture; until the 1700's, Qinghai was part of Tibet, and is still often referred to as Lower Tibet. 
But in the province, one faces neither the permit hassles necessitated by a trip to Tibet nor any chance of stumbling upon a Hollywood star in the lotus position.
Further, Qinghai, like Tibet, is endowed with dramatic mountains. 
I am attracted to all things alpine -- the expansive vistas, the rugged peoples, the challenging weather -- and have devoted many of my travels to visiting the great ranges of the world. 
The second of my travel partners, Chris Anderson, feels the same. 
All three of us are avid skiers, and we hauled ski equipment along, in hopes that we could make a pioneering descent.
Kyle had mentioned a mountain in southern Qinghai called Anyemaqen Mountain (also known as Maqen Gangri). 
The mountain, 20,610 feet high, is sacred to Tibetans, a sight of great pilgrimages in which supplicants circle the peak, clockwise, on weeklong treks filled with chanting and prayer. 
We made the mountain our destination.
Flights into Xining are erratically scheduled, so we flew from Beijing to Lanzhou, capital of Gansu Province, just east of Qinghai. 
We then took a four-hour ride on a modern, comfortable and uncrowded train to Xining, rolling through eroded, badlands-like countryside while munching on dried squid flakes and steamed chicken feet, specialties of the train's snack cart.
Qinghai is a province of minorities. 
Besides Tibetans, there are sizable populations of Kazakhs, Mongols and Hui. 
The few ethnic Chinese -- Han Chinese -- live primarily in and around Xining. 
The city is neither enchanting nor off-putting, just rows of squat buildings fronting wide avenues, the traffic equal parts bicycle and auto.
Kyle made a few phone calls from Beijing and hired a guide, Wang Wan, of the Government-run China Qinghai Tourist Corporation. 
Mr. Wang, a Han Chinese in his mid-50's, speaks both Mandarin and Tibetan. 
It was for this skill that we hired him. 
We spent much of our first evening in Qinghai haggling about the price of our tour. 
Eventually, we settled on the equivalent of $55 a day, including use of a car and a driver, Mr. Xie. We left Xining the next day.
The Anyemaqen Mountains, of which Anyemaqen Mountain is the centerpiece, are about 500 miles southwest of Xining. 
Between the city and the peak are a half-dozen lesser ranges; between each of these are vast stretches of open prairie. 
We drove over mountain passes 11,000 and 12,000 feet high, vermilion cliffs tight against the twisting road.
Mr. Xie, our professional driver, exhibited an unorthodox style, upshifting when a lower gear was called for, fishtailing on the icy spots. 
(He also seemed to harbor a serious aversion to using headlights, ostensibly to save gasoline.) Then we'd plunge down into the broad valleys, sometimes with the engine off and the car in neutral, another of Mr. Xie's gas-saving ideas.
In the valleys, young women in pink head scarves were bent over hoes, working the potato fields. 
Men guided wooden plows pulled by burros. 
Mud-brick homes were tucked against the hills. 
The only trees were scrubby, corkscrewed pinyon pines. 
There were herds of yaks, slow-moving and hairy, like hippie cows.
Most of the road traffic was on foot, or burro, or yak. 
One woman, carrying her infant son, wore a backplate ornamented with a mosaiclike pattern of turquoise and orange stones that extended from her shoulders to the backs of her knees. 
At her hip hung a silver scabbard.
Several men, on their way to market with a mule-drawn cart, modeled head wear of the most baroque styling, an explosion of fur radiating a foot in every direction. 
Everyone appeared to own a long, thick yak-hair coat, brown or black -- in late March, it's still winter at such high elevations -- which was worn in a curious manner, left arm in the left sleeve, the right sleeve traditionally wrapped around the waist.
We spent the night in the village of Guide (pronouced guai-duh), a few dozen homes pressed together along the dusty road. 
Our hotel room, three dirty cots and a broken sink, pit toilet down the hall, cost 10 renminbi (or yuan) -- about $1.25. 
We played pool at an outdoor billiards hall, 7 cents a game, while a crowd gathered to scrutinize the foreigners. 
At the sole restaurant, where a pair of saddled yaks were tied to the hitching post out front, we had our choice of pig ear, pig stomach, pig brain, pig heart or pig tongue with noodles.
That evening, we went to the disco. 
It was a narrow room, crowded, with a modest stereo and a Christmas tree's worth of blinking lights. 
The music was Chinese techno. 
Kyle had a long conversation with a Mandarin-speaking man, who informed him of the proper rules of comportment. 
Kyle relayed the rules to us.
At first, Kyle said, we should dance only with members of the same sex. 
And so we did. 
Several of my male partners danced as though they were being administered electric shocks. 
There was a long stretch during which the dance floor emptied and everyone milled around eating sunflower seeds, spitting the shells on the floor. 
Then dancing disco style with the opposite sex was allowed, but only with partners considerably older or younger. 
Finally, after I'd shuffled beneath the lights with several of the town's elders, it was acceptable for me to ask a woman closer to my own age to dance.
IN the morning, a few miles outside of Guide, we spotted a woman who was weaving dark wool on what appeared to be a giant loom. 
"She's making a yak-hair tent," Mr. Wang said. 
Most families who raise yaks live in tents during the summer, when their stock are moved to higher pastures.
We pulled over. 
Mr. Wang introduced us as tourists from America. 
The woman invited us into her one-room home, where we met her husband and son and were served yak-butter tea, the water heated on a stove fueled by yak dung. 
We sat cross-legged on blankets laid over the dirt floor. 
The husband said we were the first foreigners he had ever seen, except once, in town, on television.
"On TV, the Westerners all looked scary," he said, speaking Tibetan. 
"Big and blond and with blue eyes. 
You do not look scary at all."
We had a long conversation about yaks, my questions translated into Mandarin by Kyle and then into Tibetan by Mr. Wang.
The next village we came to, Lajia Si, is the site of the area's largest monastery. 
The road was crowded with monks, swaddled head to toe in magenta robes. 
There were prayer wheels everywhere, hundreds of them, painted with joyous kaleidoscopic flower patterns and inscribed with intricate Tibetan script. 
Some were barrel shaped and as big as water towers, at least 20 feet in diameter. 
Each time a monk walked by a wheel he'd give it a spin; their chattery clicking sounds pulsed through the street, every rotation of every wheel releasing yet another prayer into the cool spring air.
By this point the Yellow River, our faithful companion for nearly 400 miles, had grown as wide as an interstate, though its waters remained Caribbean clear. 
We finally parted ways just before the city of Dawu, the water taking the path of least resistance around the mountains, Kyle, Chris and I heading directly for Anyemaqen.
We spent the night in Dawu, a comparatively cosmopolitan place, brick buildings three- and four-stories high, with bicycle taxis plying the streets, electricity for all, and even a mile or two of paved road, covered with a thin coat of snow. 
The markets were stocked with imported vegetables from other Asian countries; the hats were even more expressive than those I'd seen in the road to Guide.
Our hotel room had real beds and warm water, and set us back $8. 
The city is more than 11,000 feet above sea level but the view south from town is all upward, the Anyemaqen Mountains, huge and white, serrating the skyline.
It was in Dawu that we encountered problems. 
Mr. Wang, out of the blue, told us he could no longer take us to Anyemaqen. 
Past Dawu, he said, we'd be in a national park where he did not have the authority to guide us. 
We asked why he didn't mention this earlier. 
He was unable to provide a reasonable answer.
Kyle scoured town and discovered a business called the Anyemaqen Area Travel Service. 
Anyemaqen Mountain, Kyle confirmed, is indeed in a national park. 
The park is free for Chinese citizens. 
For foreigners, the entrance fee is an absurd $100 a person a day. 
Our agreed-upon price with Mr. Wang had included a trip into the park. 
Now, in a part of the world where credit cards are useless, we would have to deplete our cash reserves for even the briefest of visits.
We stayed up all night sorting out the mess. 
By dawn, we had dismissed Mr. Wang, hired a guide from the Anyemaqen Area Travel Service, and received enough of a discount on the entrance fee to allow us to remain in the park for two days. 
In all, it cost about $200 a day for the three of us.
We also learned why the fee was so high: there is a pervasive perception in Qinghai that all tourists are rich. 
When I asked Suo Ba, the general manager of the Anyemaqen Travel Service, to guess how much our plane tickets from New York to Beijing cost, he estimated $40,000. 
He was astounded to learn that the round trip was under $1,000.
Our new guide was Tai Shu, an insightful, energetic 27-year-old Tibetan. 
He dispensed with the formalities used by the Chinese, and asked us to call him Tai. 
He spoke both Tibetan and Mandarin.
We drove out of Dawu and deep into the mountains. 
It began to snow. 
At a small Buddhist temple, Tai instructed the driver to pull over. 
We followed Tai up a hill behind the temple, where thousands of prayer flags were snapping in the wind. 
This, said Tai, is a Tibetan cemetery. 
There were no signs of any headstones.
TAI pointed to two bed-sized slabs of rock. 
He explained that when a Tibetan dies, he or she is brought to these rocks -- one used for men, one for women -- whereupon a monk cuts the body into small pieces, and the pieces are carried away by eagles and eaten. 
The ground was strewn with knives; a new knife must be used for each ceremony. 
In front of the women's rock was a pile of braids.
Traditionally, a Tibetan woman never cuts her hair during her life; only in death are her braids removed. 
Then, Tai motioned skyward. 
High overhead were dozens of eagles, soaring and circling and riding the updrafts.
We stayed that evening at the home of Shenja Gehreh, a friend of Tai's. 
Shenja, 49, introduced us to his wife, his daughter, his two sons, his daughter-in-law, his yaks, his horses, his sheep and his cat. 
His home, made of brick, had glass windows and several rooms, signs of a successful family.
He owned a solar panel, and if the day was sunny a single light bulb illuminated the main room. 
We ate yak ribs for dinner, washed down with yak milk, and swapped stories late into the night. 
Kyle, Chris, Tai and I all slept in the same wide bed.
The morning skies were perfect and blue, and the three of us, Tai and Shenja's sons all hiked into the mountains, our ski equipment in tow. 
We worked our way through the snow up a rounded mountain called Gong Bao Lari, with a plaque at the top inscribed with a portrait of Buddha, and a steep, skiable gully plunging back down.
It was there that we finally beheld the whole of Anyemaqen Mountain, the wind shearing a snow-cloud off its pyramidal summit, the sun refracting off its glaciers, snow melt trickling down the valleys, gradually working its way to the Yellow River. 
And then we pushed off, the three of us skiing down the gully, the others hiking down. 
We met at Shenja's house, where we were greeted with steaming cups of yak milk.
Â 
If you go
A trip to the rural outposts of Qinghai Province requires a fair amount of planning. 
Getting to Xi ning, the province's largest city, is relatively easy -- there are occasional flights direct from Beijing, and daily flights from Beijing to Lan zhou, a four-hour train ride away.
Once in Qinghai, though, English is not spoken, and it is strongly recommended that at least one person in the group speak either Tibetan or Mandarin. 
Though I visited in early spring, the best time to go is from May through October, when even the highest elevations receive pleasant weather, the chances of joining a Western tour group are good (though the area gets few tourists over all) and the weather in other areas of China is also enjoyable.
Flexibility and a willingness to rough it are essential in Qinghai. 
Hotels are extremely basic; bathroom facilities usually consist of an outhouse. 
Food is always available, though there may not be much of a choice: yak meat is ubiquitous. 
There's no bottled water. 
I drank well water with no ill effects, and tea is served everywhere.
A good place to start planning is the recorded information from the China National Tourist Office, in New York, (212) 760-9700, or in Los Angeles, (818) 545-7505, which can provide visa applications and a list of outfitters offering tours to China.
Lonely Planet publishes a guide to China ($29.95), which includes some information on Qinghai and a lot on China in general. 
Call (510) 893-8555 or see www.lonelyplanet.com.
Kyle Westgard, one of the people I traveled with, is the president of the China Ski Corporation, a company devoted to developing ski resorts in China, but was not traveling to Qinghai in any official capacity. 
He is also available to organize tours off the beaten path in Qinghai. 
Call (303) 277-0500 or see www.chinaski.com.MICHAEL FINKEL

text:
ï»¿
ALTHOUGH Mount Kailas, at 22,028 feet, is not one of the highest Himalayan peaks, it is among the world's most beautiful mountains. 
A delicately curved pyramid with a rounded top, its most striking feature is concentric bands of dark rock on which snow accumulates, forming stripes of black and white.
But it is something beyond physical beauty that, for more than a thousand years, has drawn pilgrims, who perform a kora -- a 32-mile walk around the mountain, ascending almost 5,000 feet along the way -- to pay homage to the gods. 
Kailas, the most sacred mountain in mainland Asia, is considered the home of gods of three faiths: Hinduism, Buddhism and Bon, the ancient religion predating Buddhism in Tibet.
Last May, my husband, Philip, and I drove across western Tibet to Mount Kailas (also known as Kailash) and nearby Lake Manasarovar, and to the splendid murals in the monasteries of Tholing and Tsaparang, capitals of the medieval kingdoms of Guge. 
Accompanied by three Sherpas provided by a trekking agency in Nepal, we rode from Katmandu to Zhangmu on the Tibetan border, a trip of seven hours. 
There we met our Tibetan crew and transferred our gear onto a large truck that also carried 10 55-gallon drums of gasoline, since there are no service stations in western Tibet. 
From there, we rode in a Land Cruiser (the terrain makes it essential to travel in vehicles with high ground clearance) with our Tibetan guide and driver.
Upon arriving in Tibet one is catapulted within a few hours to high altitudes. 
Our route lay across the Changtang, the wild, desolate plateau of northwestern Tibet, where on average we traveled and slept at altitudes equal to the more than 14,000-foot height of the Matterhorn.
As we drove across the Changtang I suddenly remembered a line of Pascal from my college French class, about the terrifying immensity of enormous spaces. 
Scoured by fierce winds, under a sky glowing from one horizon to the other with golden light, and set between snowy mountains that seem to float in the blue, the Changtang is an immense space made for the deities with which the Tibetans have populated it through religious beliefs. 
Nearly empty, inhabited mainly by nomads (and, these days, by clusters of Chinese soldiers and officials), the Changtang is alive with spirits.
In May its color was golden, but our guide said that during the summer rains its thin, sparse grass would turn green. 
Wildlife was abundant: kiang (wild asses) ranged in the distance, small, slender gazelles darted across our track and woolly hares bounded away from our vehicle. 
An eagle stood on the ground -- no trees to perch on here. 
Although the land is barren, we saw numerous lakes, each a slash of vivid turquoise, the color so bright it seemed to burn against the golden land.
Across the huge, empty space and in the clear, dry air even a solitary creature, however distant or small -- yak, horse or person -- is startlingly visible, a black shape against the yellow plain, arousing anticipation and excitement. 
At long intervals we would see a nomad in Tibetan dress -- sheepskin cloak, felt boots, fur cap (one man wore a wolfskin cap), perhaps alone on horseback, more often herding yak or sheep. 
We saw one man herding his yaks on a bicycle. 
A herd of the massive, shaggy creatures on the move was an impressive sight.
Occasionally we saw a single nomad's tent or a cluster of two or three, and stopped several times to follow our guide into one, where he would sit cross-legged on a rug on the ground, smoking, offering cigarettes and accepting cups of Tibetan tea (a brew made in a churn with salt and butter). 
The tents, some woven of coarse black yak wool, were held up by wooden poles, with a slit overhead to let out smoke from the open hearth.
In one tent we found only a child and his gaunt, bent grandmother, tending a metal pot steaming on the fire. 
A little portable shelf served as an altar, on which were laid the yak-butter lamps Tibetans use for worship, and an object covered with a white cloth. 
Glancing at her for permission, I raised a corner of the cloth and saw photographs of monks: I then clasped my hands and made the worship gesture of touching head, mouth and heart, evoking a smile from the old woman. 
At another encampment we saw women in spectacular jewelry: silver amulets, necklaces of turquoise and coral and long earrings. 
One had silver coins worked into her braided hair.
We averaged about 18 miles an hour and 156 miles a day, following traces of tire marks considered to be roads. 
We jounced, bounced, pitched and churned in the Land Cruiser; I sat on my down jacket to cushion the shocks, and sometimes posted as if riding a horse. 
Our Sherpas took turns in the extra car seat, otherwise riding in the open back of the truck. 
At day's end their bones hurt, and they were covered with dust.
The austere beauty and silence of the landscape are interrupted at intervals by clusters of square, squat concrete buildings sprouting antennas and satellite dishes -- Chinese Army and Government posts that our guide called "administrative centers."
Sometimes we camped, sometimes we stopped in an administrative center at a guesthouse, a kind of rough Tibetan motel. 
Rooms held a few cots, a little iron stove and a bucket of sheep-dung pellets for fuel; some had an outdoor latrine, some not even that.
The only town along our entire route was Gar (called Ali by the Chinese), with grandiose buildings lining a wide main street. 
We stopped at a large hotel with an imposing facade and a huge, cavernous lobby, where we had some difficulty finding a light bulb for our room. 
None of the toilets were functioning and guests had to use the latrine. 
Guests (who were mainly traveling government functionaries) often use a blowtorch to cook in their rooms, as did our Tibetan guide's cook.
A LONG, tough ride to the western edge of Tibet brought us to the monasteries of Tholing and Tsaparang, where despite severe damage during the Cultural Revolution, there are important murals from the 15th through 17th centuries in relatively good condition; the statues had fared worse. 
The murals depict deities and high lamas and scenes of court life, showing foreign emissaries in Islamic and central Asian dress paying respect to Tibetan royalty.
From there we turned southeast to reach Darchen, the small settlement at the base of Mount Kailas and the starting point for the kora. 
Here for the first time we met other groups of Westerners at the guesthouse, which offered camp beds in narrow concrete rooms and an unroofed latrine outside the gate. 
Strolling through Darchen, carrying a rock or two to ward off the fierce Tibetan mastiffs guarding the houses, we watched a group of nomads separating a large flock; the women, heads and mouths wrapped in huge shawls against the relentless wind and dust, swung ropes to drive the sheep.
Our guide hired a few Tibetan pilgrims to carry our gear for the kora and we started the next morning. 
On the first day we walked about six and a half hours through a long, deep valley between walls of sheer red rock. 
Along the kora route are numerous sites associated with spiritual masters and supernatural beings, where pilgrims perform devotions. 
The east face of Kailas loomed above: a forbidding, serious place, desolate, silent, swept by the wind -- a fit home for the gods.
We followed the orthodox Buddhists, who circumambulate in a clockwise direction, but occasionally we saw Bon pilgrims, who walk counterclockwise. 
In late afternoon we stopped at a little six-room guesthouse belonging to a small monastery, with walls and floors of dried mud and rough wooden planks for a bed, upon which some men in sheepskin cloaks and turquoise earrings, their hair in wild, tangled braids, laid out dirty cotton mattresses and covers for our crew. 
With intense cold and a wind that did not stop buffeting us until early in the morning, my husband and I slept in our tent.
The next morning we rose before 5 to make an early start for the pass one must cross to circle the mountain. 
In late May the pass was still covered with snow and icy patches. 
As we climbed, we passed a woman who was prostrating her way around the mountain, an act of the highest devotion, which can take 13 days or more. 
Making the prayerful gesture of touching clasped hands to head, mouth and heart, and then raising her arms high, she flung herself upon the frozen, rocky ground, then rose, walked the few steps to the place her fingertips last touched, and prostrated herself again. 
She wore a thick apron and canvas shoes on her hands to keep them from being scraped raw.
AFTER nearly four hours, reaching the pass at 18,600 feet, where prayer flags placed by pilgrims and monks fluttered atop a cairn, we shouted "Lha Gyalo!"
(Victory to the Gods!) like all pilgrims. 
The snow and pile of rocks were strewn with colorful scraps of clothing left by the faithful as marks of devotion.
From the pass we descended to another long valley and after nine exhausting hours stopped to camp outside a shelter of mud rooms; we completed the kora at noon the next day. 
We took the standard two and a half days to walk the 32 miles, with an ascent of 4,920 feet, but some Tibetans can do the kora in one.
The weather cleared as we drove southward for 90 minutes to Lake Manasarovar, where we first visited Chiu Gomba, a little monastery (recently rebuilt) perched on a craggy knoll above the plain. 
A group of nomads about to start a circumambulation of the sacred lake were worshiping here, eyes bright with reverence. 
The women wore brightly colored cloaks on which were sewn applique in bold geometric patterns and contrasting colors, such as red and gold on a green background, and many necklaces, amulets and earrings.
From a ridge behind the gomba, we had a splendid view of the lake and of Kailas, rising high above the nearby mountains, an image of utter purity -- inviolate, unclimbed because it is sacred. 
There are no buildings, no hotels or guesthouses, no promenade walk along the lake shore to spoil the prospect, the integrity of this holy place. 
We had spent 16 days in Tibet, driving 1,380 miles. 
We continued on foot with our Sherpas for five and a half days, over 65 miles on some of the roughest trails in Nepal, to the airstrip at Simikot and a flight to Katmandu.
Three colors -- blue, gold and white -- linger in my image of Tibet: the blue of the sky and the unearthly azure of the lakes, the golden plain and golden light, the snowy mountains. 
Silent, often empty. 
Cleaned to the bone by the winds. 
A beautiful, wild place, where the human spirit feels it can stretch without limit. 
And where the Tibetans still believe in their beloved gods and in spirits that cling to the mountains and ride on the wind.
Â 
Arranging for the trek and getting equipped
Â 
Planning a Journey
Our trip for two was organized by Himalayan Explorers, Post Office Box 1737, Sanu Gaucharan, Katmandu, Nepal; telephone (977 1) 422-656, fax (977 1) 471-529, a trekking agency in Nepal that obtained our visas for Tibet and made all arrangements. 
The agency provided our food and sent three Sherpas who cooked, managed our camping and led our return trek through northwestern Nepal. 
We brought our own camping gear, but the agency will supply it if necessary for about $50 a person.
Above the Clouds Trekking, Post Office Box 398, Worcester, Mass. 
01602-0398, (800) 233-4499, is also reported to be another good organizer of similar trekking tours.
Our trip took 25 days (16 spent in Tibet) and cost $4,980 a person, including visas. 
The Simikot-Nepalgang-Katmandu flight at the end cost $180 a person extra. 
We spent about $400 on incidentals, including tips (about $50 for each Sherpa, more for the lead guide). 
Travelers should bring United States currency because traveler's checks are not accepted in Chinese banks in western Tibet.
Â 
Weather and Altitude
In May, the Tibetan plateau was mainly sunny and cool during the day, ranging from the upper 40's to the 60's. 
Temperatures at night were in the 20's or 30's.
Because of high altitude, sunglasses and sunblock for skin and lips are essential; ski goggles or industrial safety goggles and bandannas are helpful against wind and dust, as are eyedrops for irritation. 
The Mount Kailas region can be severely cold and windy. 
Travelers should take warm sleeping bags. 
To walk around the mountain, take warm, windproof clothing and good boots.
Medical care is not available, so a medical kit, including antibiotics, is necessary.
From Kailas you can return to Zhangmu by a four-wheel-drive vehicle. 
If you plan to trek out through Nepal, altitudes will decrease and temperatures will be warmer. 
The exceedingly rough and occasionally dangerous trails of the Humla district make a pair of collapsible trekking poles useful. 
M. R. L.

text:
ï»¿
WHILE most of the glitzy soirees being planned for the handover are private affairs, there is still much for the visitor to see and do that opens doors to Hong Kong past and Hong Kong future. 
Crowded in among the mirror-slabbed office towers that are sprouting like stands of bamboo are small lanes and quiet byways through which the visitor can amble, reflecting on the Hong Kong that was even as the territory's metamorphosis looms nearby.
A two- to three-hour excursion, not particularly strenuous despite some steps, covers the highlights. 
It begins with the tram, a glorious double-decker throwback to the first years of the century that trundles along narrow-gauge tracks through cars, trucks and people, to the end of the line in Sheung Wan. 
Pay HK$1.60 (about 20 cents) as you get off and walk across the tracks to the red brick Edwardian-style Western Market.
With its louvered shutters and great stone arches, it began life as a food market, a role it played for 83 years until it was renovated in 1989 and converted into a small shopping center filled with stalls selling antique cameras, cloth merchants in tiny shops packed with bolts of silk, organza, velvet and cotton prints, tourist shops selling T-shirts and a kiosk with old photographs of Hong Kong.
Leaving the market on the east side, walk south on Morrison Street. 
Across the street from the Western Market is the Starite Book Company, mostly a stationery store now, but on the tables along the sidewalk, piles of string-bound fortune-telling guides are for sale. 
For HK$14 (about $1.80), you can buy a guide, called Tong Sing in Cantonese, which, while a jumble of obscure Chinese numerology and stargazing, is one of those garish items worth collecting.
Wander up Morrison Street and turn left on Bonham Strand, a crooked lane walled by shops dealing in the exotic and plain. 
On your right, the first store sells handmade brooms, grass mats, low wooden stools used by old women huddling in circles to gossip and old men to smoke, and the huge, circular woven-grass peasant hats that rise to a peak for only HK$20 (about $2.60). 
Along the street, there are shops with immense sacks of a dozen varieties of dried mushrooms, dried orchid petals and bags of nuts. 
And farther on is Dai Fat Swallow's Nest Company, one of several such establishments selling the fragile and jarringly expensive swallows' nests used in special -- very special -- soups. 
A plastic box the size of a butter cookie tin will set you back HK$17,500, or about $2,273. 
Across the street, at the Lam Kie Yuen Tea Company, bins of tea, from Pu-erh to plain green, are surrounded by shelves of tiny blue-clay teapots, considered best for steeping Chinese teas. 
Pots are priced from HK$30 (about $3.90) to HK$350 ($45).
At Cleverly Street, turn right and about five doors up find Kau Kee Birds Shop, an open-air market of birds, delicate red cages and bags of crickets. 
Everywhere in Hong Kong you will find people walking their birds, in exquisite cages, through parks and along lanes; at building sites, construction workers take their birds and hang the cages on nearby trees or scaffolding.
A few doors up from the bird store is Tai Hing, a small craft shop where a carpenter makes the red lacquer and gold-tinted devotional cabinets that many people keep in their homes as shrines to one god or another. 
A few more doors down is Hop Lee, a storefront selling bundles of incense, or joss sticks, and stacks of paper money -- the brand name here is Hell Bank Note -- in $50 million denominations, papier-mache cars and telephones and television sets and cardboard stacks of gold bullion, all of which is burned on funerary occasions to send the departed into the next world with all the basics and some pocket money.
Walking up Cleverly, across Queen's Road Central, you will come to the steps of Ladder Street, which lead up to Upper Lascar Row and the Cat Street antique market. 
Here, along a narrow lane hemmed in by tables and kiosks of antique and knickknack dealers, can be found much of the detritus of Chinese culture -- bad ceramic vases, imitation Tang dynasty horses and clunky bronze Buddhas -- along with the occasional treasure: a fine Yixing teapot or nice ivory mah-jongg set. 
Here you can find a white porcelain history of Communism: busts of Marx and Engels, Lenin, Stalin and Mao.
Turn left at the end of Lascar Row and walk up a small flight of steps, across Hollywood Road and up Sai Street to Tai Ping Shan Street. 
On the right, in what amounts to a cul-de-sac, is a small temple to the god Kwan Yin. 
Often there is a huddle of ancient neighborhood women sitting in front of the temple discussing their families and their neighbors. 
A tabby cat with a crooked tail hangs around as well.
Make a U-turn and head east on Tai Ping Shan, down a typically old-style Hong Kong street, a jumble of low-rise apartments over storefronts, all the apartments with garden boxes and clothing drying from bamboo poles slung over the street. 
As you walk, on the downhill side small lanes squirt downhill and often there are tiny temples tucked away in shaded corners, wisps of incense betraying their presence. 
Work your way along the street, turning with it left and then right, past the coffin makers', and wind up at the Man Mo Temple, containing two separate but abutting halls of stone with deep red beams and soaring roof peaks. 
On the corner is one of Hong Kong's oldest mailboxes, a red, round cylinder stamped with the seal of King Edward VII.
The Man Mo Temple, dedicated to the gods of literature, Man, and war, Mo, is believed to date from 1842. 
Its large temple bell was cast in bronze in Guangzhou in 1847, while several teak sedan chairs inside glass cases date from the mid-19th century. 
The air of the temple swirls thickly with incense as neighborhood people and visitors perform prayers in the temple.
Beyond the heart of Hong Kong, there are still the remnants of colonial rule, the remaining edifices of more than 150 years of British suzerainty. 
In the Central district, amid the clumsy and elegant office towers, huddles the Legislative Council building, a granite structure with an Ionic colonnade that was opened in 1912 as the Supreme Court Building. 
One of the few old buildings to survive the wrecker's ball, it now houses Hong Kong's elected legislature, a body that will be ousted on July 1 and replaced by a legislature appointed by Beijing.
Up the hill, in the lower reaches of Hong Kong Park, is the territory's oldest surviving colonial-era structure, Flagstaff House. 
A graceful two-story house surrounded by thin columns and a second-floor verandah, the house is now the Museum of Tea Ware. 
Currently under renovation until June 23, the house was occupied in 1846 by Maj. Gen. George Charles D'Aguilar, who was the commander of Britain's land forces in China. 
In those days, the house offered a breathtaking view of Hong Kong's harbor and the mountains of Kowloon; now, the towers of international commerce hem the white house in on all sides, its view but a sliver of a harbor fast vanishing under developers' landfill. 
The new K.S. 
Lo Gallery has been recently opened exhibiting a collection of ceramics and Chinese seals.
Farther uphill, on Upper Albert Road, is the home of Britain's last Governor, Chris Patten. 
By the time it was completed in 1855, Hong Kong was on its fourth governor. 
Set amid spendid formal gardens, the ivory house is a sober, neo-classical example of colonial architecture, modified during World War II by the Japanese, who added a central tower hinting at Japanese architectural style. 
Mr. Patten will leave this house on June 30, but his successor, the shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, has decided not to move in, claiming that the house is possessed of inauspicious feng-shui, the traditional Chinese belief in harmonizing the placement of manmade structures in nature.
But as much as Hong Kong remains redolent of British colonialism -- many of the territory's streets are named after governors, prime ministers, harbormasters, assorted British royals and even a ship -- the future lies northward, toward China and Beijing. 
Already, of course, there are dramatic examples of China's presence.
Perhaps none is more startling than the origami-like I. M. Pei tower of the Bank of China, a mirror-walled, knife-edged building slicing skyward from Hong Kong's Central Business District. 
And perhaps no building in Hong Kong provokes more heated opinion, with students of architecture often rapturous and Hong Kongers usually fiercely hostile, an attitude that stems not from any distaste for Mr. Pei, but a firmly held view that the building reeks of bad feng-shui: its sharp angles are seen as daggers and the two antennas at the top are reminiscent of chopsticks shoved into a bowl of rice, a distinctly ominous sign. 
Indeed, many offices in sight of the building are hung with small convex feng-shui mirrors intended to ward off the bank's bad aura.
Along the seafront, the new Hong Kong is rising as well. 
In Wan Chai, jutting into the harbor by the Grand Hyatt Hotel, is a convention and exhibition center designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, a glass-walled building covered with an undulating, overlapping roof intended to emulate the wings of a gull. 
The center, still unfinished, is scheduled to be the setting for the handover ceremony. 
There, on July 1, China will formally assert its sovereignty over Hong Kong.

text:
