Southeast Asian foreign ministers weighed into the China-Taiwan dispute today, giving support to Beijing's "one China" policy in a communique that also warned that rising tensions could harm economic growth.
Tensions between China and Taiwan will be the backdrop for a meeting between Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright and the Chinese Foreign Minister, Tang Jiaxuan, on Sunday. 
It will be the highest level diplomatic meeting between China and the United States since the NATO bombing of Beijing's embassy in Belgrade in May.
The two will hold talks on the sidelines of the annual meeting of foreign ministers from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which runs until Wednesday.
The foreign ministers at the meeting said they hope for a peaceful resolution to the conflict between China and Taiwan, which was renewed when President Lee Teng-hui of Taiwan said on July 9 that it was ending the "one China" policy, which had kept the peace in the Taiwan Strait for decades.
Negotiations with China would take place on a state-to-state basis, Mr. Lee said.
China continues to consider Taiwan a renegade province. 
The notion of "one China" stems from the civil war that ended in 1949, when Taipei and Beijing both claimed to be the one legitimate government of all of China.
"We expressed our concern over the tension that arose in the Taiwan Strait after July, 9, 1999, which could seriously affect regional peace and stabilityI and prospects for economic recovery," the communique said.
"We hoped for a quick and peaceful return to normalcy. 
We reaffirmed our commitment to our 'One China Policy.'
"
The organization includes Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Brunei and Myanmar.
The communique also included a reference to a code of conduct for the Spratly Islands, a contested cluster of potentially oil- and gas-rich islands that are claimed by China, the Philippines, Brunei, Taiwan, Malaysia and Vietnam.

file: Asian Nations Wary on Free Trade.txt
text:
ï»¿
The nations of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, which represent more than half the world's economic output, all say they agree in principle with President Clinton that the path to further prosperity is to lower ever more barriers to trade and investment.
But as leaders from the United States and the other 17 member countries gather here for a summit meeting, the notion of achieving even a vague commitment for a giant Pacific free-trade zone from Chile to China, even far in the future, has led to apprehension as well as expectation.
The Pacific zone was pressed vigorously by President Clinton a year ago, when he spoke in Seattle of an Asian Pacific "community."
The leaders are gathering here to decide whether to begin turning that concept into reality by setting a target date for free trade.
Foreign ministers and trade officials will meet on Friday and Saturday here in the capital. 
On Tuesday heads of state, including President Clinton, will assemble in Bogor, a scenic area just outside Jakarta. 
In between, the leaders will pair off for bilateral meetings.
To be sure, any declaration that emerges from Bogor will be vague and nonbinding. 
Exactly how to achieve free trade will be left to future meetings. 
And the deadlines being contemplated, 2020 for developing nations and perhaps 10 years earlier for some other countries, are far enough away so that it will not have much immediate impact.
But in an organization that spans four continents and levels of wealth ranging from Japan's per-capita output of more than $30,000 a year to China's $400, there are certain to be conflicting agendas.
Initially there were fears that the West wanted to create a model of the European Union, an idea that raised fears of an integrated association that could threaten the sovereignty of member nations.
And many of the Asian nations with closed markets have suspicions that despite Washington's talk of community, it is merely interested in using the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation group, known as APEC, to break down trade barriers that prevent American companies from selling more products to the fast-growing markets of the East.
"Asia is an area where there is potential economic opportunity for the United States, and that is as far as it goes," said Derek da Cunha, senior fellow at the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies in Singapore, describing his view of Washington's priorities.
It is too soon to tell whether Mr. Clinton's ability to influence events here will be weakened by the triumph of Republicans in mid-term elections this week. 
But the Republican sweep has raised some doubts about whether the Democratic-controlled, lame-duck 103d Congress will approve the GATT agreement at a special session after Thanksgiving. 
Most nations at the conference are counting on GATT to spur their economies.
The first skirmish of the meeting in Jakarta has already broken out. 
In preparatory talks this week, the United States objected to a proposed voluntary code aimed at liberalizing foreign investment in member countries, saying it did not go far enough.
China has expressed reservations about a timetable for free trade. 
"In view of the diversity of the Asia Pacific countries, this timetable should be very flexible," President Jiang Zemin said before leaving Beijing earlier this week.
Even more firm in his opposition is Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad of Malaysia, who fears APEC will diminish the importance of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or Asean, six countries that are already moving to form a trading bloc. 
Mr. Mahathir has also championed an East Asian Economic Caucus, which would include Japan but exclude the United States, Australia and other Western members of the larger group.
Rafidah Aziz, Malaysia's Minister of International Trade and Industry, said this week that an effort to establish a trade timetable was a meaningless exercise because the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum has no means of enforcement.
Still, many analysts say the prospects for movement forward are probably better now than they were a year ago.
"There is discussion and debate about whether there should be a target or not, but nobody disagrees on trade liberalization," said Ippei Yamazawa, a professor of economics at Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo and a member of the so-called Eminent Persons Group, a committee of private citizens that drafted proposals for APEC trade liberalization.
Last year, Asian nations were also fearful that linking up in a big community would subject them to more pressure from Washington on human rights, although those fears were eased somewhat by the decision to detach human rights concerns from China's trade status.
Moreover, this year the free trade agenda is being pushed most strongly by Indonesia, the host country. 
It is harder for developing nations to resist the appeals of one of their own.
Indonesia last year resisted the United States trade proposals. 
Some experts say Indonesia's about-face this year reflects the desire of President Suharto to leave an international legacy by making the Bogor declaration something to remember.
Even without the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation group, the Asian region is moving toward economic integration. 
The member nations' economies are becoming too big to grow simply by exporting to the United States and Europe. 
Now, they must sell to to one another.
Japan's exports to Asia now exceed its exports to the United States, in part because Japanese companies have built a network of factories in Southeast Asia that must be supplied with components and machinery. 
Some of the biggest investors in China are ethnic Chinese entrepreneurs from Hong Kong, Taiwan and Southeast Asia.
The six Asean nations -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand -- recently accelerated plans to lower tariffs among themselves.
Even some of those who favor free trade, however, wonder whether APEC should be the organization to bring it about. 
The group was started in 1989 as a forum for discussion. 
The fact that its name, Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation, does not end with "organization," "association" or a similar noun attests to the reluctance of its founders to make it an institution. 
It operates by consensus, without any mechanism for voting, and many members would prefer to see it stay that way.
"At this stage, making it rigid might not be the right emphasis," said Rizalino Navarro, secretary of trade and industry of the Philippines. 
"The emphasis should be on the direction, not the timetable or the institution."
But APEC is rapidly growing more institutional. 
Two years ago members decided to create a permanent secretariat based in Singapore, and this year there is talk of expanding it. 
More committees have been formed. 
The number of members has grown. 
And Chile's enrollment at this year's meeting extends the forum into South America.
A big step toward increasing the group's importance came at last year's meeting in Seattle, when the heads of state were invited for the first time.
Another question is whether an APEC free-trade plan is needed and whether it would conflict with or complement the global trading system under GATT or the smaller, more tightly integrated trade zones like the North American Free Trade Agreement and the new Asean Free Trade Area.
"With progress made in the GATT and with progress made in unilateral liberalization, the need for regional arrangements weakens a great deal," said Djisman Simandjuntak, a member of the board of the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Jakarta.

file: Asian-American Politician in Washington State Looks to Blaze New Trails.txt
text:
ï»¿
The invitation to the fund-raising event for Gary Locke, a Democrat who wants to be Washington State's next Governor, makes no mention of party affiliation or wedge issues. 
Instead, it says, "Help us make history."
Mr. Locke, one generation removed from China, is campaigning on a personal story as old as America, with a Pacific Rim twist: an immigrant's son whose supporters believe that he is likely to become the highest-ranking Asian-American political figure in the continental United States.
"This is beyond people's wildest dreams," said Assunta Ng, who publishes The Northwest Asian Weekly, a newspaper based in Seattle.
If the early polls are to be believed, it may be more than a wild dream for Mr. Locke, who, if elected, would be the first Asian-American governor in the mainland United States. 
Polls show that Mr. Locke is leading throughout the state among a wide field of candidates seeking to replace Gov. Mike Lowry, a Democrat who is not seeking a second term.
Mr. Locke's parents were born in China. 
He grew up in a household where Mandarin Chinese was the main language, and nobody ever talked about politics, he said.
After emigrating to Seattle, his father, James Locke, fought with the 10th Armored Division under Gen. George S. Patton against the Germans in World War II. 
The younger Mr. Locke was reared in a housing project for returning soldiers, worked in his father's restaurant at an early age, became a Boy Scout and fell in love with the great outdoors of the Pacific Northwest, then went to Yale University and Boston University Law School.
At 46, Mr. Locke is the King County Executive, leading a county of 1.6 million people. 
From his office in downtown Seattle, he overlooks a site where Chinese-Americans were routed out of their beds and marched at gunpoint aboard ships nearly 100 years ago.
The event, recalled every year in a solemn ceremony, ended at the dock's edge after a judge ordered the mob to cease. 
The people were angry at the Chinese, who had been brought to America to help build the railroads, because they were thought to be taking jobs from others.
"A lot of people support him not because he is Gary Locke but because this is something to hold up to their children and grandchildren," Ms. Ng said.
The primary election in Washington State -- the second most populous state in the Far West, after California -- is not until September, so Mr. Locke's candidacy has attracted little attention in other regions in this busy political year, with one big exception. 
Among Asian-Americans on both the West Coast and the East Coast, Mr. Locke is the main attraction at fund-raising events and political gatherings.
At least three such events have been sponsored by the Asian-American community in Seattle this month, and the campaign is also raising money in San Francisco, New York and Washington.
"You have to remember that Gary Locke is as American as somebody named Wilson or a fellow named Clinton," said Henry Tang, the New York co-chairman of the Committee of 100, a nonprofit group of Chinese-Americans who are active in public affairs. 
"But just as the Irish-American community was excited about John F. Kennedy, there is that great interest among Chinese-Americans for Gary Locke."
People of Asian descent make up 3.7 percent of the population of the United States and are the nation's fastest growing ethnic group. 
In 1994, more than a third of all the nation's immigrants came from Asia. 
Roused by Congressional proposals to limit immigration, Asians-Americans have vowed to take a more active political stance this year.
"In general, people say that Asian-American political fortunes have regressed, which is one reason why people are so excited about Gary Locke," said J. D. Hokoyama, executive direction of LEAP, a nonprofit Asian-American education and leadership group in Los Angeles.
Mr. Locke can raise money from Asian-American communities far removed from Washington State, Mr. Hokoyama said, because "in many ways he will represent all of us."
There have long been a handful of Asian-American members of Congress, and a few Asians have been big-city mayors; Representative Norman Y. Mineta, Democrat of California, was Mayor of San Jose in the early 1970's. 
But outside Hawaii, no Asian-American has ever been governor of a state.
With a politician's touch for remembering the names of his constituents, Mr. Locke was a powerful member of the Washington Legislature before he was elected King County Executive. 
He is perhaps best known locally as the person who helped broker a new baseball stadium for the Seattle Mariners and for going into battle with the owner of the Seattle Seahawks when an attempt was made to move the football team to Southern California.
When asked about his early life, Mr. Locke recalled a trip to visit his grandmother in Hong Kong, then a city on the cusp of the modern age, when he was 10 years old. 
"I remember open sewage in the streets, people sleeping in doorsteps, and there was my grandmother living in this tiny hut, 8 foot by 8 foot," he said. 
"She had one front tooth and was very sick. 
That image remains."
Mr. Locke says he never experienced racism as a child and did not feel poor. 
His father ran a small Chinese-American restaurant, called Sadie's Cafe, in the Pike Place Market section of Seattle. 
The most persistent value he learned at home was hard work, he said.
"My mother worked at a sewing factory, and my father at his restaurant, seven days a week," Mr. Locke said. 
"All of us kids started working with him starting at age 12."
He is the second of five children.
Mr. Hokoyama said Mr. Locke helped to dispel a stereotype of Asian-Americans as a "model minority" enamored primarily of math and science. 
"Asian-Americans have not always been very active in politics," Mr Hokoyama said. 
"To do that, you have to excel in people skills, not just the things that make up the old model-minority myth."
A governor, Mr. Locke said, can expand Americans' understanding of Asian-American issues.
"This is a state that is so dependent on trade, and also a state where everybody, except the Native Americans, came from somewhere else," he said. 
"So it is incumbent on the Governor to speak out on these issues."
The Asian-American vote, of course, is not monolithic. 
Nor in Washington State is it unusually large -- about 4.5 percent of the total electorate. 
One of Mr. Locke's main rivals for the Democratic nomination here is Mayor Norm Rice of Seattle, the first black to be Mayor of this city. 
About 3 percent of the state's residents are black, and Mayor Rice has long had strong support from Asian-Americans.
"You're going to see Asian-Americans supporting Rice and African-Americans supporting Locke," said Martha Choe, a member of the Seattle City Council who is a Korean-American. 
"But there is a real sense of urgency among Asian-Americans this year, of getting out the vote and getting people registered."
Republicans say Mr. Locke has a record of supporting too many tax increases while in the Legislature. 
If he is the nominee, Republicans say, he will be attacked for his view of a government much bigger than most people favor.
To the surprise of some political experts, Mr. Locke is running strong in the polls in rural eastern Washington, where it is generally thought that being a member of a minority from Seattle is political poison. 
An eastern Washington legislator, Dale Foreman of Wenatchee, is running for the Republican nomination for Governor.
To Mr. Locke, it is no mystery why he has support beyond his immediate base. 
With unblinking optimism, he says he does not expect there will be a racial overtone to the vote.
"I don't expect anybody to vote for me because I'm Asian-American," he said. 
"Nor should anyone vote against me because of that. 
I'm running simply as a guy who gets things done."

file: Astute Collector of Big Money and Powerful Friends.txt
text:
ï»¿
Charles Yah Lin Trie, the Chinese-American restaurateur and businessman who raised hundreds of thousands of dollars in questionable contributions for President Clinton's legal defense fund, has always been a hard worker and a quick learner, say those here who have known him. 
And the lesson he learned most astutely, they say, is the importance of knowing people in high places.
"Charlie learned in America not only how to work hard but how to get in with people and get what he wanted out of life," said Julia Hughes Jones, who learned to like and admire Mr. Trie while serving as Arkansas state auditor from 1981 to 1995. 
"He knew who was important, and he made a point of making over them."
Jim Dailey, the Mayor of Little Rock, had similar impressions. 
"He sort of is one of these collectors of people," Mr. Dailey said. 
"When I was in Washington once I went to his place and there were people from all different departments of government and Chinese officials. 
It just amazed me."
Now Mr. Trie, who has lived for most of the last 20 years in Little Rock but now spends most of his time working in Washington and China, has become the latest in a series of businessmen of Asian origin whose fund-raising practices for Mr. Clinton and the Democratic National Committee have come under scrutiny.
Mr. Trie, who could not be reached for comment today, has acknowledged to reporters that a $15,000 gift from one of his companies to the Democratic National Committee in 1994 came from foreign funds, an apparent violation of Federal law. 
He has said he was unaware that the law prohibited United States companies from donating money generated outside the country.
Shortly after Mr. Trie delivered $460,000 to the defense fund, on March 21, his proposed appointment to a 16-member advisory panel on Asian trade was approved by the White House. 
Jim Farris, a former Arkansas business associate of Mr. Trie, said Mr. Trie had long asserted that he would parlay Mr. Clinton's election into a Federal appointment. 
"He bragged for years that he would get an appointment once Clinton was elected," Mr. Farris said.
Mr. Trie, who is said to be in his 40's, came to the United States in the mid-1970's from Taiwan, where his family had moved from China in 1949. 
Ms. Jones said Mr. Trie had told her that his father, a member of the Chinese Air Force, had commandeered an Air Force plane and flown his family to Taiwan while Mr. Trie's mother was pregnant with him. 
Mr. Trie could not be reached for comment today.
Beginning as a busboy in Chinese restaurants, Mr. Trie worked his way up to the ownership of a series of restaurants in Little Rock, one of which was only a few blocks from the Capitol, where Bill Clinton served as Governor. 
Mr. Clinton apparently was an occasional diner at the restaurant, Fu Lin, and like many of the government officials who frequented the restaurant, he was warmly received by Mr. Trie.
"The food was excellent," said Mr. Dailey. "But the place had its ambiance because Charlie circulated and knew everybody and always had that big smile on his face."
Mr. Trie was considered a benevolent employer within Little Rock's small Asian community, said Ruey Wang, who worked for Mr. Trie as a cook and now owns his own Chinese restaurant. 
"He treated his employees very well, a really nice guy," Mr. Wang said. 
Mr. Wang's son, Jay, who was translating for his father, said, "When my father had a quadruple bypass and was laid up in the hospital, he told him, 'Don't worry about it, you come back when you feel better.'
"
Over the years, Mr. Trie opened and then sold a number of Chinese restaurants in Little Rock. 
He apparently does not have financial interests in restaurants now, having spent most of the 1990's running a number of export-import and real estate companies, most of them with Chinese connections.
On numerous occasions, Mr. Trie took delegations of Arkansans, including Mr. Dailey and Ms. Jones, on trade and good-will missions to China that he organized and apparently financed. 
"We were on his credit card," Ms. Jones recalled.
Neither Mr. Dailey nor Ms. Jones said they knew how or why Mr. Trie had managed to raise so much money for Mr. Clinton and the Democrats. 
"Everything I've seen is that he does it with the best of intentions," Mr. Dailey said. 
"But he does love to be known as somebody who knows people in the right places."
Ms. Jones added that she quickly fell out of Mr. Trie's circle after switching from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party in 1993. 
"Charlie came by and said goodbye," she said. 
"He wanted to be in with Clinton and he knew I could only do him harm. 
As I recall, his statement was that his business was dependent on the Democrats and he was sorry. 
I understood."

file: Asylum Plea by Chinese Sect_s Leader Perplexes the U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
A request for political asylum in the United States by the leader of one of China's largest spiritual movements has put Washington in the difficult position of harboring a possible criminal or handing over to Beijing a man hunted for his beliefs.
After trying to keep the case quiet for months, the United States delayed a decision on the request by Zhang Hongbao, the founder of a meditative discipline popularly known as Zhong Gong, at a court hearing in Guam on Friday.
Granting him asylum would amount to the United States telling China that it does not believe the country's criminal charges against him and reinforce China's perception that Washington acts as an agent for domestic groups that Beijing believes are intent on eroding the power of the Communist Party.
The case comes during a widespread crackdown on spiritual groups in China that began with the banning of the larger Falun Gong movement a year ago. 
Like Falun Gong, Zhong Gong is based on qi gong, traditional Chinese breathing and meditation exercises that seek to channel the vital energy of body and the universe to various ends.
Last year, the United States declined China's request for help in returning Falun Gong's founder, Li Hongzhi, who now lives in New York.The United States aid that Mr. Li was a permanent resident and that it regarded China's charges against him as politically motivated.
But Mr. Zhang's case is more nettlesome because he arrived in Guam in February without a visa and, if he is to stay, the United States must play an active role in keeping him on American soil.
And China's claims that Mr. Zhang is wanted for criminal activity have a more complex history than the charges against Mr. Li, which were related primarily to his role in organizing a protest against the Beijing government.
By the mid-1990's, rumors of a dark side to Zhong Gong began to circulate. 
A close disciple defected from the group and wrote a scathing expose alleging that Mr. Zhang was a fraud and had illicit sex with followers.
Those rumors were amplified by self-appointed "cult buster," Sima Nan, who has made a career of exposing fraudulent claims by qi gong masters. 
He alleges that Mr. Zhang is guilty of rape and may even be responsible for the murder of some former followers.
Chinese officials have repeated the rape allegation to United States officials, though they have not presented any evidence or documentation of formal charges.
Mr. Zhang disappeared from public view in 1995 as criticism of his group grew. 
It operated a nationwide network of schools and healing centers based on his particular brand of qi gong before China outlawed it earlier this year.
While his followers insisted for years that he had simply retired from the world to seek further enlightenment, the group's Web site (www.zgzg.net) now says the police have been trying to arrest him since he disappeared.
The United States has no extradition treaty with China, but last month the two countries signed a mutual legal assistance pact that was intended to provide a framework for the return of criminals by either side.
The United States has asked China for the return of two men wanted in the slaying of five men in a gambling den in Boston's Chinatown nearly 10 years ago. 
China, in turn, has asked the United States for help in finding Mr. Zhang, saying he is wanted on criminal charges.
Mr. Zhang's request for asylum now complicates any proposed law enforcement cooperation, which in any case has long been plagued by a lack of trust on both sides.
Earlier this month, United States officials said they had not informed China of Mr. Zhang's whereabouts, hoping to keep the case quiet until the Boston extradition request had been resolved.
But on Friday, an immigration court judge in Guam said at a hearing for Mr. Zhang that China had formally requested that the United States return the spiritual leader. 
As a result, the judge delayed a decision on his asylum request.
Another Zhong Gong member was granted political asylum in Guam on Friday, said Frank Lu, a human rights advocate in Hong Kong.
Mr. Zhang was born in the northeastern Chinese city of Harbin in 1954. 
He spent 10 years working on a state farm before studying metallurgy and working at a succession of northeastern gold mines. 
He later went to study in Beijing, where he learned qi gong in his spare time. 
He started Zhong Gong, his own school of qi gong, in 1987.
The group, whose full name translates as the China Life Preservation and Intellect Improvement Discipline, was one of dozens of schools started by self-styled masters during the period of loose social controls that led to the pro-democracy demonstrations of 1989.
After the violent suppression of the democracy movement by military force, millions of people flocked to the qi gong movement for spiritual solace, a sort of mass recoil from the perils of political engagement and the soulless materialism then sweeping the country.
During the early 1990's, Zhong Gong became the most popular of the various schools, but as controversy gathered around Mr. Zhang and his group, the rival Falun Gong group gained in popularity, eventually superseding Zhong Gong as the largest movement of its kind. 
In the book that Falun Gong followers regard as their bible, its founder, Mr. Li, makes veiled criticisms of Mr. Zhang, calling him a "sham qi gong master."
China's growing unease with the spreading qi gong movement eventually forced Mr. Li to leave the country in 1998. 
And a mass demonstration by Falun Gong followers at the central government compound in Beijing last year set off a crackdown on it and other groups.
Falun Gong, Zhong Gong and a handful of other qi gong schools have since been outlawed and hundreds of their senior members have been arrested. 
Before the crackdown, Zhong Gong claimed 38 million followers, though that number, as with Falun Gong's claim of 100 million adherents, is certainly grossly inflated.
Despite its widely broadcast propaganda campaign against Falun Gong, China has moved quietly in its ban of Zhong Gong, charging that the group has misguided people and closing dozens of Zhong Gong schools around the country.
The movement's hospital near Qingcheng Shan, a mountain in Sichuan Province sacred to Taoists, has been shut down for practicing unlicensed medicine. 
Only last year it was in full operation, with dozens of patients.
There, one young doctor in a white lab coat demonstrated Zhong Gong's method of treatment to a visiting reporter by waving two fingers ray-gun-like at the head of an 8-year-old girl with a large brain tumor that had penetrated her scalp, leaving her head a misshapen mass of scabs and sores.
The doctors asserted that the girl had regained the ability to walk thanks to their treatment, and several people at the hospital said they had been cured of serious illness by Zhong Gong.
Many others said Zhong Gong had given them paranormal powers, including the ability to go without food for months at a time.
Much of the hospital and school were like a shrine to Mr. Zhang, who was depicted in paintings with an improbably high pompadour and a German shepherd by his side. 
Even Mr. Zhang's old Russian car, the tires flat, sat unmoved from where he had last parked it.

file: At 27, a Talk Star Sets Out To Transform Chinese TV.txt
text:
ï»¿
Yang Lan traveled from Shanghai to New York City to attend graduate school because, she said, her fans back home in China would not have left her alone to study. 
Oprah Winfrey could sympathize.
Like Ms. Winfrey here, Ms. Yang has been one of her country's most popular television talk-show hosts. 
Her weekly program, "Zheng Da Variety Show," was the top-rated talk show in China from 1990 to 1993. 
Unlike Ms. Winfrey, Ms. Yang quit her gig in 1994 to enroll at Columbia University, where she is about to earn a master's degree in international relations.
Two weeks shy of her 28th birthday, Ms. Yang is plotting a return to the small screen when she goes home in June. 
She is developing a weekly syndicated series, "Yang Lan Horizon," which will be devoted to Western popular culture and the influence that people like Steven Spielberg and Sir Andrew Lloyd Webber exert on Chinese culture.
With her polished manner, telegenic looks, and razor-sharp grasp of the economics of show business, Ms. Yang is emblematic of a new generation of Chinese who are taking the first steps toward transforming Chinese television from a creaky, Government-controlled public utility into a more entrepreneurial American-style business.
With the support of her new husband, Bruno Z. Wu, a Shanghai television entrepreneur, and a little help from a well-financed former music executive, Robert J. Morgado, Ms. Yang even hopes to develop and star in programs that would be broadcast in the United States -- reversing, if only slightly, the tide of American television that flows into Asia.
"I'm only getting started," Ms. Yang said over lunch recently at Tang Pavilion, a Shanghai-style restaurant in Manhattan, "but I want to start early."
As a television personality, Ms. Yang has already shown her ability to appeal to a mass audience. 
Now, she and her husband are using Western-style business practices in an effort to make Ms. Yang a one-woman television franchise in China.
By Hollywood standards, Ms. Yang is already a major star. 
She was selected to host "Zheng Da" in an open audition at the age of 22, while still a senior at the Beijing Foreign Studies University.
The program, which Ms. Yang described as a cross between "Good Morning America" and "Donahue," became an instant sensation: Its frothy mix of interviews with Chinese celebrities and games involving a studio audience routinely drew the highest ratings of any program on Chinese Central Television, the Government-owned national network.
Ms. Yang, who carried on a spirited repartee with her older, male co-host, Zhao Zhong-Xian, also became a favorite of Chinese Government officials, who asked her to act as a host at various events, including the United Nations women's conference in Beijing last September.
By the age of 25, though, she felt burned out. 
Ms. Yang, who is a native of Beijing and whose father is a professor of linguistics at her old university, said she wanted to attend graduate school to gain the intellectual resources to tackle more serious topics on television.
At Columbia, Ms. Yang has been in the International Media Communications program, which is part of the School of Public and International Affairs. 
To hone her skills as a journalist, Ms. Yang also took classes in reporting and writing at the Graduate School of Journalism.
Donald H. Johnston, a Columbia professor and the director of the media communications program, recalls the day that Ms. Yang came as a prospective student for an interview. 
"She knocked me over because she was dressed like someone from Fifth Avenue, and she was as poised as anyone who ever came out of American television," he said.
Ms. Yang's academic pursuits faithfully reflect her professional interests. 
She said, for example, that she was researching a term paper about American talk shows.
"These shows seem to be very liberal and progressive on the surface," she said in flawless English, "but when you listen to the hosts talking, they are actually reinforcing stereotypes about people."
For all her criticism of American talk shows, Ms. Yang studiously avoids controversial issues as they apply to her country. 
She describes herself as basically apolitical and said that in her new series she would eschew politics for coverage of cultural issues.
"I'm in a position to do something beyond ideology," she said.
Ms. Yang met Mr. Wu at a lunch with friends in New York last year. 
They were married in October in a lavish ceremony at the Plaza Hotel -- and have forged a partnership that may prove as important to her professional future as anything she learned in graduate school.
Mr. Wu, who is 29, owns a syndication company that distributes American and Australian programs to Chinese stations. 
His big break came in late 1993 when Time Warner's music division signed a deal with his company, Youban Entertainment Group, to distribute a music-video program called "Warner Music Stars" on Chinese television.
Mr. Morgado, who was then the chairman of Warner Music Group, played a key role in negotiating the deal. 
And when Mr. Morgado started a firm this year to invest in small overseas media companies, his first move was to acquire Warner's minority stake in Mr. Wu's company. 
Mr. Morgado has pledged to invest further in Youban, and Youban is helping to finance Ms. Yang's series.
Mr. Wu said his company had syndicated "Yang Lan Horizon" to 51 regional and municipal television channels in China, which reach about 80 percent of the nation's 200 million television households.
For now, China is still dominated by Government-controlled broadcasters: Chinese Central Television, with its five channels; 30 regional networks based in the provinces; and more than 700 local channels operated by the major cities.
But experts on Asian media said that emergence of cable and satellite television would inexorably expand that market -- and create a keen desire for programs like Ms. Yang's. "Once the change in leadership stabilizes and the Government liberalizes, there will be tremendous new demand," said S.K. 
Fung, the president of NBC Asia.
Those are big uncertainties, of course. 
But Ms. Yang means to be ready in any event. 
She has returned to China during each break in classes to tape specials. 
"I keep appearing on the TV so they won't forget me," she said with an easy laugh, sounding for all the world like Oprah.

file: At a Beijing Aquarium, Dolphins Are Hostages.txt
text:
ï»¿
When it opened last June to huge crowds, the Beijing Aquarium seemed destined for success: a high-tech blue glass dome housing a rain forest, shark pools, fish and corals galore and -- as its centerpiece -- a serene island habitat complete with caves and bridges, the stage for its dolphin, sea lion and whale show.
In a common business arrangement here, a Chinese company built the aquarium, with a Western partner providing technical expertise. 
JV China Inc. of Lompoc, Calif., acquired and trained the marine mammals, cared for them and oversaw the life support systems that created their delicate ecosystem.
But less than a year later, the partners are involved in a contract dispute so vicious that the United States Embassy has intervened. 
And the animals, who just months ago waved fins and jumped through hoops to delight children, are now effectively on strike, with their ownership and safety hotly contested.
"My Chinese partners have endangered my animals and failed to meet contractual agreements," said Tim Desmond, JV China's president, producing stacks of angry memos he has sent. 
"I would have walked if there wasn't an ethical dilemma with the animals."
And so, on Feb. 
29, JV China suspended its shows, saying the aquarium was months behind in payments and had skimped on promised life support systems. 
The aquarium, denying the danger, in turn tried to evict JV China, turned off chlorine to the pools and then claimed ownership of the animals for themselves.
At one level it is "an ordinary commercial dispute," as it was called last week by Wei Hongying, the aquarium's executive director. 
But with China trying to enter the World Trade Organization, it is also a cautionary tale about the perils of business in this booming country where the rule of law and standard business practices have not fully taken hold.
And then there are dolphins held hostage.
"In the U.S. and Western Europe, the law is more closely interwoven with business," said Stanley Lubman, a California lawyer who has represented many companies in business disputes here. 
"In China you're dealing with a much looser texture of rules. 
And when things go wrong, there's a more fragile legal system for resolving them."
The executives of JV China anticipated that they could handle China's rough-and-tumble business world, having trained animals for zoos and aquariums and for movies including "Free Willy."
The contract, signed in September 1998, says that JV China "shall provide the criteria for and shall be solely responsible for the standards for the operation of the facility, including the life support system and other equipment and facility and specifications of the quality of the water at the facility."
Ms. Wei refused to discuss the specific terms before the outcome of legal action. 
But Chiu Man, a Hong Kong-based businessman who identified himself as a founder, major investor and board member of the aquarium, said the aquarium was justified in all of its actions toward JV China according to his interpretation of the document.
"We all agree that contractually the animals belong to them," he said in a phone interview. 
But he added that now "we have the right to buy the animals -- sorry, that word isn't 'buy' -- we have the right to keep the animals. 
And that's because JV China owes us a great deal of money, since their performance has not been up to fulfilling the agreement."
Mr. Chiu conceded that the aquarium had never complained about JV China's work previously but said that "there wasn't a need to rake them over the coals."
From the start the contract did little to resolve tensions in a troubled partnership. 
At an inspection visit before JV China delivered 9 dolphins, 10 sea lions and 6 whales early last year, Mr. Desmond found that only half of the chlorine jets worked, filters had been filled with a cheap, ineffective sand and workers had not been properly trained.
In a memo from February 1999, JV China said that one of the three sets of pumps in the sea lion pen was broken and that its chlorine level was more than 10 times the acceptable limit, enough to cause blindness.
In July another memo listed high bacteria levels in the water from "repeated failure of the system," as well as hazardous sharp gratings in the pools.
Just one month after the show opened, JV China was threatening to leave. 
And the aquarium was already behind on payments to the company specified in the $11 million contract.
By September payments had stopped.
Ms. Wei said the differences had arisen from legitimate "technical debates" over animal care. 
Both Ms. Wei and Mr. Chiu said a Chinese company call General Oceanic Environmental Engineering Consultants, partly owned by Mr. Chiu, now controled the life support system, essentially overriding the contract.
They defended the new company's decisions, including turning off the chlorine, used as a backup disinfectant, a move that JV China insists is hazardous because primary life support systems are not functioning properly.
"JV China are not water quality experts," Mr. Chiu said. 
"They know about animals. 
I think they've been very dumb and don't use common sense."
He said the water now fell within the standard ranges that JV China had stipulated for things like acidity and bacteria counts and therefore was adequate to meet contractual obligations -- two points that JV China disputes.
In January an independent scientist from Idea Inc. in Cambridge, Mass., was hired by both sides to inspect the aquarium, whose regular exhibits remain open to the public, and serious problems were discovered:
*Pool water contained oxygen levels that were four times normal because of problems with the ozone system, leading to a dangerous overgrowth of bacteria.
*Fine filters had never been installed in the aquarium's air system, forcing the marine mammals to breath Beijing's air pollution. 
The whales have had persistent respiratory problems.
*Water chemistry was beginning to drift out of balance, and the aquarium did not have a "supply of the dry chemicals" required to correct the problem.
But Mr. Chiu said: "All of our measures of water quality show that there are no problems, and if JVC has concerns, they need to produce numbers and to make reasonable suggestions. 
As for the air, Beijing is a heavily polluted city -- everyone knows that -- and that is not something we or JVC can solve."
Mr. Chiu said JV China had not been paid for six months because its performance was "far too poor."
Pressed for examples, he cited two: JV China had changed specifications for a tiny steel doorway, and the animals "were not performing as expected."
The contract lists 18 skills -- from tail walks to object retrieval -- for a whale and dolphin show. 
Mr. Chiu complained that while the animals together could perform the tasks, no one creature could do them all.
After JV China said in late February that it was canceling its shows, simmering tension turned to war. 
Aquarium board members and security guards ordered the company's employees out of the building, and when they resisted, citing contractual obligations, aquarium officials called the contract "a piece of paper," a JV China employee said. 
After a standoff, JV China's employees agreed to leave, with guarantees that they could continue to take care of their animals.
In a memo dated March 1, Ms. Wei said JV China's failure to possess proper permits for its animals had "necessitated the eviction," although that charge has since been dropped.
The American Embassy has written letters to Chinese officials expressing concern about the business practices and the animals' welfare. 
Two of the sea lions were imported from the United States and under American law must be kept in facilities that meet or exceed United States requirements.
"Most disputes are resolved amicably," an American diplomat here said. 
"But there are a large number of contract disputes in China that involve inappropriate action by Chinese."
Other experts place some blame for the current standoff, which seems headed for arbitration in the Chinese government arbitration system, on naive investors. 
"Foreigners come in without knowing what happened to their predecessors," said Mr. Lubman, the lawyer who has worked on business disputes here. 
"They are dazzled by the size of the market."

ATLANTA_ DAY 11 -- SOFTBALL_One More Victory to Nail U.S. Gold.txt
text:
ï»¿
The United States is one victory away from winning a gold medal in softball.
But what a battle to get there. 
It took a typical pitching performance by Lisa Fernandez (a three-hitter and 13 strikeouts) and a 10th-inning bases-loaded single by Sheila Cornell tonight to beat a stubborn Chinese team, 1-0.
The victory sent the United States into the championship game Tuesday night against Australia or China. 
Australia beat Japan, 2-0, in tonight's second game, on home runs by Kerry Dienelt and Haylee Petrie and Tanya Harding's two-hit pitching. 
Australia will play China at 4:30 P.M. Tuesday, and that winner moves on to the 7 P.M. final against the United States.
International softball officials created the peculiar setup to reward the team with the best record in the round-robin preliminary round, in this case the United States (6-1).
After the game, the Americans were drained, and not just from the 87-degree temperature and 51 percent humidity.
"When you miss so many opportunities," said Dot Richardson, the American shortstop, "it drains you. 
This has been a very emotional tournament for us because of so many close games."
The doubleheader at downtown Golden Park drew a sellout crowd of 8,729, including Juan Antonio Samaranch, the president of the International Olympic Committee. 
Scalpers were asking $200 for $32 tickets.
Fernandez is a 25-year-old California-bred right-hander with a fastball that reaches 66 miles an hour, a huge problem for batters only 40 feet away.
For six innings, she pitched a perfect game, and the Chinese could not even hit the ball out of the infield.
The perfect game ended when Zhang Chunfang led off the Chinese seventh with a single. 
The only hits Fernandez allowed were chipped singles that fell in front of outfielders.
But for nine innings, her teammates could not get a run. 
In the third, Julie Smith, trying to score from second base on a single to right field, was thrown out. 
In the sixth, with two Americans on base, Zhang, the Chinese center fielder, misjudged Danielle Tyler's long fly before grabbing it just in front of the fence.
Softball games usually last seven innings. 
If the game is tied after seven, the eighth and (if necessary) ninth innings are played under normal rules.
If the score is still tied after nine, international rules dictate that each half-inning start with a runner on second base.
In the 10th, Richardson was that gift runner. 
Julie Smith, the leadoff batter, was hit in the right thigh by a pitch, putting Americans on first and second. 
Then Dionna Harris grounded to shortstop. 
The throw to third base to force Richardson hit her in the back, and the bases were loaded.
"I purposely didn't slide," Richardson said, "because I was trying to get hit. 
Luckily for me, it worked. 
I've never been so happy to get hit by a ball."
So now the bases were loaded with none out. 
China's relief pitcher, Wang Lihong, struck out the next batter, Kim Maher.
Up came Cornell, a 5-foot-8-inch, 178-pound first baseman and, like Richardson, a 34-year-old veteran of the Americans' 10-year climb to the top.
"When I stepped to the plate," Cornell said, "I said to myself, 'This is where I want to be.'
I love being able to make or break the game. 
I wasn't trying to hit a home run because we just needed one run."
Cornell ran the count to 3-0, then took a called strike. 
On the next pitch, she hit a sharp grounder between second base and the diving Chinese second baseman, Yan Fang. 
Before Cornell left the batter's box, she was grinning and pumping her arms because she knew the ball would get through the infield. 
It did, Richardson scored and the Americans won.
For Fernandez, the victory was revenge of sorts. 
Because she has a tender ankle, this was only her second appearance in these Olympics. 
The first was last Friday, when she struck out 15, retired 29 straight batters and pitched a perfect game against Australia until there were two out in the 10th. 
Then, with the United States leading by 1-0 and an 0-2 count against Joanne Brown, a rising pitch by Fernandez hung over the center of the plate, Brown knocked it over the fence and Australia won, 2-1, the only American loss here.
"In the top of the 10th tonight," Fernandez said, "China had a runner on second and I kept saying, 'Not again, not again, not again.'
I reached for something extra. 
I found my energy from my teammates."

file: ATLANTA_ DAY 14 -- SOCCER_Women_s Soccer_ 76,481 Fans, 1 U.S. Gold.txt
text:
ï»¿
They have been together a long time close to a decade for some of them -- and tonight the American women won a prize they could not have imagined when they began assembling. 
By beating a spirited and talented China, 2-1, they won a gold medal in the first women's soccer tournament in Summer Games history.
Tiffeny Milbrett scored the historic goal in the 68th minute at the end of a fast break begun by Mia Hamm on the right side, who pushed the ball to Joy Fawcett in the middle, who set up Milbrett racing in from the left.
The attendance was 76,481, apparently the largest crowd to watch a women's game anywhere in the world. 
Last Sunday's crowd of 64,196 was the largest to see the women's team in this country, just shy of the 65,000 that saw them play the World Cup final in Guangzhou, China, in 1991. 
Team officials said there is no record of any women's team -- in any sport, in any country -- playing before a larger crowd.
However, almost nothing of the game was shown on NBC, and afterward, Hank Steinbrecher, the executive director of the United States Soccer Federation, blasted the network, saying, "NBC must think the world is full of divers."
In renovated Sanford Stadium at the University of Georgia, where the fabled hedges were cut back to allow for more seating, the public-address announcer called the sport "football," the way most of the world does.
This jittery championship, after the United States had been outhustled during the middle of the match, is the second world victory for the United States. 
The women won the first women's World Cup in 1991 in China, finished third in the second World Cup in Sweden in 1995 and paved the way for the 1999 World Cup to be held in the United States.
And they had played together long enough to be a real team, like the New York Islanders used to be, like the old Boston Celtics.
You could read it in the "caps," the soccer term for international appearances: Kristine Lilly with 121, the sore-legged Hamm with 120, Carin Gabarra, who replaced Hamm in the closing minutes, earned her 117th, and Michelle Akers would have had more than 109 caps but for her struggle with the debilitating Epstein-Barr virus in recent years.
Fawcett made her 101st appearance tonight. 
Fawcett celebrated the victory by holding her 2-year-old daughter, Katelyn Rose, in her arms as she waved to the fans after the semifinal victory over Norway.
Tonight, Carla Overbeck, the star defender, played her 100th game and received the traditional engraved watch, Julie Foudy reached 96 caps, Tisha Venturini 71, Milbrett 65, Tiffany Roberts came on late for Milbrett and played in her 54th, goalkeeper Briana Scurry reached 46 and Brandi Chastain toughed it out with her right leg heavily taped and reached 40.
And Shannon MacMillan, in the starting lineup tonight, reached 28 caps and scored the first goal in the 18th minute, a goal involving 378 games of international experience. 
The weary but wise Akers trapped a loose ball at midfield and sent it wide to the left for Lilly, who dribbled downfield and turned the corner, firing the ball left-footed. 
It ricocheted out to Hamm, who shot on goal, and the rebound went to MacMillan, who put the ball into the net.
Then the Americans went into a shell, apparently trying to contain the Chinese rather than attack. 
Akers was hobbling, apparently with leg cramps, and the Americans seemed listless. 
They paid for it in the 32d minute when Sun Wen got past Overbeck and chipped the ball over Scurry, who had left the goalmouth.
Some aggressive work by Hamm woke the United States from its lethargy. 
Women's soccer does not have the booming power or the intricate negative defenses of world-level men's soccer. 
The way to go in women's soccer is full speed ahead.
Hamm chases the ball obsessively, the way Pete Rose used to pursue base hits. 
She tore up her ankle in the second game of this tournament. 
Coach Tony DiCicco has been complaining about the rules allowing only 16 players a team for a five-game schedule in 12 days. 
The women had just enough left to produce the burst of energy for the gold medal.
China did not lack for support, with three separate clusters of yellow-and-red-clad fans waving bright red banners and flags and dancing to the halftime tunes like "Y.M.C.A." by the Village People.
Norway, which lost a heartbreaking semifinal to the United States on Sunday, won the bronze medal tonight with a 2-0 victory over Brazil. 
Linda Medalen deliberately set up a goal in front by Ann Aarones in the 21st minute and Aarones boomed an untouchable rocket in the 25th minute.
Soccer or football, it is now an Olympic sport for women, and it fills stadiums. 
And the first champion is a team that stuck together for a decade for this night, when the players would run around an American football field in front of 76,481 fans.

file: ATLANTA_ DAY 15 -- DIVING_For First Time in 84 Years, Americans Miss Out on Gold.txt
text:
ï»¿
Greg Louganis stopped by the Georgia Tech Aquatic Center earlier this week. 
He was working as a television reporter, and his presence was a nagging reminder of how much American divers have slipped since he wrung out his chamois for the last time after winning two more gold medals at the 1988 Summer Olympics.
The Americans ended up winning no golds in Atlanta, and the last time that happened in an Olympics in which Americans competed was 1912 in Stockholm.
They could not manage a medal of any color in tonight's final event: the men's 10-meter platform, in which Dmitri Sautin of Russia put an end to China's hopes of an Olympic sweep.
Sautin, the reigning world champion, did it with a superb, steady performance, receiving no score lower than a 7.5 on any of his six dives and consistently receiving scores of 9.0 or higher.
On his final effort -- a back one-and-a-half somersault with three-and-a-half twists -- he received the only perfect 10 awarded during the men's competition (the other six judges settled for 9.0's and 9.5's).
"I was very mad at myself," said Sautin of his surprisingly low fifth-place finish in the men's springboard competition. 
"So I came out and managed to accomplish what I needed to accomplish on platform."
Sautin, the first Russian or Soviet to win the Olympic platform title, finished sixth in this event in 1992. 
That was less than a year after he was stabbed in the stomach several times during a fight. 
He nearly died from loss of blood and spent two months in a Russian hospital. 
Since then, he has reasserted his imposing, if not always graceful, presence.
"Sautin's not a style diver," said American Coach Ron O'Brien. 
"He's a power, acrobatic, good-entry diver."
He took the lead from Jan Hempel of Germany after the first round in tonight's final and never relinquished it, scoring no lower than 76.50 on any of his six dives and winning by a comfortable 29.07 points. 
Hempel settled for the silver; Xiao Hailiang of China for the bronze, which means that China won 5 of the 12 diving medals awarded in Atlanta.
David Pichler of the United States was sixth; Patrick Jeffrey was ninth, which means that the United States won only two medals in Atlanta: a bronze from Mary Ellen Clark on women's platform and another bronze from Mark Lenzi on men's springboard.
That is hardly a major surprise. 
The Americans won no golds in the 1994 world championships in Rome. 
Nor did they win any in the four Olympic events contested at the 1995 Pan American Games.
The trend continued here despite the support of a large and unabashedly partisan crowd. 
The Americans were far from abysmal. 
All eight United States divers qualified for the finals, something no other delegation accomplished, not even the Chinese. 
But they could not rise (or better yet, fall) to the highest level.
"We need to take another look at our program," O'Brien said. 
"We have done it to some degree, but we were late reacting. 
It's not that our guys have gotten worse. 
It's just that others have made great improvements."
Today's finals were a case in point. 
Neither Pichler nor Jeffrey made a major error, and yet when the last dive had been completed, they were well off the pace. 
At 31, Jeffrey is the oldest male diver in Atlanta. 
He competed in the 1988 Olympics, where he contracted a virus and finished 12th.
"I'm a little disappointed, but I'm not upset," he said. 
"I'm walking out with my head up."
While Jeffrey was waxing sanguine, his competitors were dividing the spoils. 
The Chinese had won the first three events in Atlanta, with Fu Mingxia winning on both the women's platform and springboard and Xiong Ni winning on the men's springboard. 
But Xiao and the 16-year-old Tian Liang -- both competing in their first Olympics -- would be unable to complete the first Olympic sweep in 44 years.
"We were new divers; this was our first time in a competition like this," said the 19-year-old Xiao. 
"We wanted to win the fourth gold for our country, but we were not under any pressure to win it."
Sautin was simply too good, his scores too consistently high. 
They were the kinds of scores that once were the rule for a man named Louganis. 
But Louganis is now reporting for television, and the Americans are no longer dominant.
