file: Bad Timing for Some Epic Projects_Asia_s Financial Crisis Leaves New Airports Scrambling for Passeng.txt
text:
ï»¿
When President Jiang Zemin of China leaves here on Thursday after celebrating the first anniversary of Hong Kong's handover, he will be the first passenger to take off from the new $20 billion Hong Kong International Airport. 
Unfortunately for Hong Kong, there will be nowhere near as many people following him as originally planned.
The airport, the last and grandest monument here to British colonial rule, was pushed through at a time when Asia was riding high. 
Second in cost only to Kansai International Airport in Osaka, Japan, it also includes -- beyond its two runways and a 45-acre terminal building that is the world's largest -- a vast network of highways, bridges, tunnels and railways to transport people the 21 miles into town.
For several years, the airport project was the world's largest, employing 20,000 laborers and more than half the world's dredging fleet to create a man-made island in the waters off Hong Kong.
"They built this airport at the wrong time," said Jim Eckes, an aviation consultant at Indoswiss Ltd. in Hong Kong. 
"It should have been built when Hong Kong's economy was suffering and opened when it was strong."
Predicting economic cycles is a fool's game, of course. 
And in the fullness of time, Hong Kong's airport may come to be seen as a wise investment in the future. 
But for now, it is coinciding with a bust in air travel. 
The number of tourists visiting Hong Kong fell 24 percent in the first quarter, and the airport seems likely to fall far short of its capacity of 35 million passengers a year.
Hong Kong is only one of several Asian cities that are investing heavily in new airports. 
Malaysia opened its $2.5 billion Kuala Lumpur International Airport on Tuesday. 
Over the next six years, Seoul, and Guangzhou in China, plan to open huge new airports, while Singapore, Taipei, and Manila are adding terminals to their existing airfields. 
Bangkok may also build a new airport.
The trouble is, overall passenger traffic declined in Thailand and Korea in 1997, while it slowed dramatically in Hong Kong and Singapore. 
The International Air Transport Association, in an highly unusual move, cut its five-year forecast of the annual growth in traffic for the region to 3.7 percent from 7.7 percent. 
As with so many other industries here, Asia's airports are entering an era of potentially severe overcapacity.
"This really couldn't be happening at a worse time, but that's the breaks," said Tony Tyler, director of corporate development at Cathay Pacific Airlines, the flagship carrier at Hong Kong's airport, which has invested $1 billion in a new headquarters, staff hotel and flight-training center.
While airport planners in Kuala Lumpur and Hong Kong insist that their projects will pay off in coming decades, they acknowledge they will fall well short of their passenger targets for the first few years. 
And that will put a pinch on everyone from the airlines, freight carriers, and shop owners to the governments, which took on billions in debt to pay for the projects.
The Malaysian Government will have to stretch out the repayment of loans to banks, according to Clifford F. Herbert, the executive chairman of the Kuala Lumpur International Airport.
Analysts said Hong Kong's Airport Authority should have no trouble repaying its first set of bank loans, which come due in 2001. 
But the steep cost of the project has forced the airport to demand high prices for everything from the landing fees it charges to the rent for duty-free shops.
"It is certainly the most expensive airport I'm aware of in Asia and it is more expensive than any airport in Europe," said Ross Allen, the operations director of DHL Worldwide Express in Hong Kong.
Airports are potent symbols of civic pride, and Hong Kong and Kuala Lumpur spared no expense to create glittering gateways. 
Though brand new, these projects are symbols of an era in which Asia's economic growth and the ambitions of its political leaders knew no bounds.
On a lush site 45 miles from Kuala Lumpur, the Malaysian Government built a futuristic terminal with sweeping glass walls and an atrium with a tropical rain forest. 
It also installed a modern computer system that integrates every function of the airport, from baggage carousels to elevators. 
With the capacity to handle 25 million passengers a year, the new airport is palatial compared with the cramped, somewhat shabby quarters of its predecessor, which will remain in only limited service.
Mr. Herbert believes Malaysia, which began planning the airport in 1992, will eventually use every inch of the new facility. 
But he conceded that "if the recession had set in," when the airport was being planned, "we would have had to scale it down, and the architecture would have been different."
Kenneth C. Brown, the president of GE Southeast Asia in Singapore, defended the airport's size, noting: "Asia has always been chasing the curve in terms of infrastructure. 
Building this airport ahead of demand is not a bad idea."
Still, experts said Kuala Lumpur's airport had a glaring weakness in that it opened without a high-speed rail link to the city. 
That could mean two-hour trips to Kuala Lumpur on traffic-clogged roads. 
The train will not be ready for two years, and the Government will not allow municipal taxis to take passengers into the city because it has signed a contract with an airport taxi service.
Hong Kong's new airport, complete with railway, was conceived by the British Government in 1989 as a statement of confidence in Hong Kong's future after the Tiananmen Square massacre. 
Britain chose a site off Lantau Island, west of Hong Kong. 
That required chopping the hills off two small islands and filling in the water between them to create a giant platform.
As Phillip Bruce, a spokesman for the Airport Authority, likes to put it, "We built something the size of Heathrow out of the sea."
Rearranging the topography was expensive: Mr. Bruce said the airport itself cost $6.3 billion, while the roads, bridges, and tunnels cost another $13.7 billion. 
As an airport alone, Kansai was more expensive, at $14 billion. 
Most analysts treat Hong Kong's related projects as part of the airport.
The epic scale of the airport caused a rift between the British and the Chinese, who were already feuding over the terms of the handover. 
China accused Britain of depleting Hong Kong's reserves to build a project that enriched British design and engineering firms. 
When the invitations went out for Thursday's dedication ceremony, Hong Kong's last British Governor, Chris Patten, was left off the list -- as he was for other anniversary events -- even though he had championed the project.
Like any huge investment in infrastructure, the airport pumped money into Hong Kong's economy. 
But Ian K. Perkin, the chief economist at the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce, said Hong Kong's economy would have run full tilt with or without the project. 
In fact, he said the airport might have squeezed out some private-sector development because so much of Hong Kong's construction resources were being soaked up by the project.
Today, Hong Kong could use an economic jolt. 
But most of the main spending is finished. 
The man-made island has room for a satellite terminal, which would expand capacity to 87 million passengers a year from 35 million. 
But given that the airport will be lucky to draw the 29 million people that passed through close-in Kai Tak Airport last year, Hong Kong is unlikely to break ground soon.
These days, people involved in the project find themselves on the defensive. 
Sir Norman Foster, the renowned British architect who designed the terminal, said the building, which has an undulating roof-line and swooping wings that resemble a giant pterodactyl, came in on budget. 
It was even cheaper per square foot than other terminals, he said, because it used prefabricated materials.
Sir Norman said he was frustrated that economic concerns were overshadowing what he called an extraordinary engineering achievement.
When money begins flowing again here, Hong Kong International will scoop up as much of it as it can. 
The terminal has a vast shopping center, called Sky Mart, with 143 stores, including a Chinese tea shop and an Irish bar. 
Clinton Leeks, the corporate development director, said the airport hoped to generate 63 percent of its revenue from nonairline activities -- an unusually high percentage for an airport outside the United States.
The airport's large hotel and shopping mall also give it the chance to serve as a regional hub within Asia so that, say, a passenger traveling from Bangkok to New York could change planes in Hong Kong. 
The hub market has been dominated by Singapore's Changi Airport, which has amenities such as a hotel within the terminal complex. 
But Hong Kong is better situated geographically than Singapore, since it can be reached from most European and North American cities with a nonstop flight.
Hong Kong, though, may be in danger of pricing itself out of the market. 
Landing fees, depending on the size of the plane, will be anywhere from 20 percent to 60 percent higher than at Kai Tak, which will be shut down this weekend when the new airport opens for normal traffic. 
The one-time fee to land a 747 is set at more than $3,000. 
And since Cathay Pacific uses a lot of 747's, Mr. Tyler said it would be unprofitable to add many extra flights unless the fees came down.
Mr. Leeks said the airport would re-evaluate its landing fees after a year. 
But it is holding the line against retailers, who have tried to renegotiate rich multiyear leases now that it is clear that traffic will fall far short of the forecasts.
With the spate of new airports in the region, Asia may soon see a dogfight between airports not unlike that waged between airlines. 
Kuala Lumpur has set its landing fees below those of neighboring Singapore. 
And in a direct challenge to Hong Kong, the nearby Portuguese colony of Macao cut fees in half for late evening flights at its new airport.
The battle for passengers in southern China will only intensify further when Guangzhou, which operates the third-busiest airport in China, opens a new field sometime after 2001.
"I would view this as the first step in severe airport competition in this region," Mr. Eckes of Indoswiss said.
If only people would start flying again.

file: Bank Rules Are Eased By China.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's Finance Minister agreed today to allow some American and foreign banks to expand into some cities of China now closed to them and to accept deposits in Chinese currency.
American and other foreign banks have been pressing the Beijing Government to open more areas of the country to foreign financial service companies, which hope to play a lucrative role as a bridge between China's tremendous appetite for investment capital and the huge interest abroad in investing in the development boom here. 
Infrastructure investment in China alone between now and the end of the century is expected to top $500 billion.
Â 
Joint Effort Is Revived
Finance Minister Liu Zhongli's announcement of wider access in financial services came as part of a joint statement from himself and Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen, after a meeting of the two nations' Joint Economic Committee. 
The committee, founded in 1979, had been a forum in which China and the United States worked out economic problems, but it had not met since the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre. 
It was revived today by Mr. Bentsen and Mr. Liu.
They agreed to start meeting again annually and to establish sub-Cabinet groups that would deal with monetary and banking policy, exchange-rate reform and investment and economic cooperation.
Â 
Planning a Visit
Mr. Bentsen also announced that the chairman of the Federal Reserve, Alan Greenspan, planned to visit Beijing to consult with the Chinese authorities on monetary policy. 
The Securities and Exchange Commission, Mr. Bentsen also said, is discussing an agreement to help China establish and regulate "an effective securities market."
And, he said, the Treasury's Customs Service will provide China with assistance in monitoring trade.
All of this reflects the Clinton Administration's effort to step up engagement with China along a broad front. 
The idea is to give the Beijing authorities a greater incentive to meet American human rights demands that are the condition for renewing China's preferential trade benefits in June.
The most important initiative from the Chinese side was the Finance Minister's commitment to expand the range of opportunities in China for American banks and financial service companies, particularly the right of foreign banks to do business in local currency -- the renminbi.
American officials said that what this commitment meant was that some American and other foreign banks would be allowed to expand the number of cities in which they could open branches. 
Also, a few of them would be allowed for the first time to accept accounts in Chinese currency. 
This would also give foreign banks the opportunity to expand beyond the relatively limited area of financing trade, to providing small-business loans, mortgages, car loans and inventory loans -- all in local currency.
Most of the world's largest banks are doing business in China in a limited way now, including some of the largest financial institutions in Japan, Western Europe and the United States. 
Among the American banks are Citibank, Bank of America, Chemical and Chase Manhattan. 
Generally, these banks have representatives in Beijing and Shanghai or other cities in China to offer trade financing and other services. 
But they cannot accept deposits under existing regulations.
Like so many other Asian nations, China has been reluctant to open domestic banking markets to foreign financial institutions for fear of losing some control over the money supply. 
At a time when inflation in China is running at 20 percent annually and the Government is trying to better control credit, this is an important issue.
Chinese officials refrained, for now, from specifying which new cities will be open to foreign bank branches, or which foreign banks will be involved in the experiment with local currency deposits.
Secretary Bentsen said this experimental move was important, but he added that he had strongly urged his Chinese counterpart to liberalize the financial services market quickly to benefit "both China and the United States."
Before leaving Beijing for Shanghai, Mr. Bentsen summed up his talks with Chinese leaders by saying that "there has been progress but more remains to be done," if the Chinese hope to have their most-favored-nation trade benefits renewed in June.
While Mr. Bentsen expressed the Administration's satisfaction with Thursday's agreement allowing more inspections of Chinese prisons to insure that their factories are not producing goods for export to the United States, he stressed that this was only part of what President Clinton was demanding as a condition for renewing the trade benefits, which allow China to export its products to the United States at the lowest possible tariff rates.
An accounting of China's political prisoners and visits to them by the International Committee of the Red Cross were two other important American demands, which China is considering but has not yet met.
"I hope sufficient progress can be made so we can put this issue behind us and there will not be an annual review" of the most-favored issue any longer, Mr. Bentsen said.

file: Banned Movement_s Head Urges Talks With China.txt
text:
ï»¿
The leader of the fast-spreading spiritual movement banned this week by the Chinese Government asserted yesterday that his group had no political ambitions and called on the Government to engage in dialogue.
"I hope the Chinese Government will try to resolve the matter through dialogue rather than through violence," Li Hongzhi, leader of the newly outlawed Falun Gong movement, which claims to use exercises to harness cosmic forces, said in an interview yesterday in New York. 
"The people's hearts cannot be changed."
"I don't want to get involved in politics ever," said Mr. Li, who in 1992 developed a cosmic theory and a movement that says it now has more than 100 million members worldwide. 
Estimates of the number of followers in China range from two million given by the Government this week to tens of millions claimed by supporters, numbers that cannot be verified.
From his self-imposed exile in New York, Mr. Li is embroiled in one of China's sharpest social rifts in years, as the Government tries to stamp out a movement that has been wildly popular among many retirees, middle-age women and others, mainly in urban areas around the country.
The Government this week described Falun Gong as an illegal political and social force and Mr. Li as an "evil figure who, by deceiving, has been seriously disrupting social order."
Mr. Li, a youthful-looking 48, was dressed in a navy blue suit and spoke in mild terms, becoming most animated when countering Government contentions that he has lied about his past and his personal gains. 
He seemed to be anything but the plotting charlatan portrayed in official Chinese statements this week or even the charismatic leader of a new spiritual movement that has spread quickly in a few years, putting the most populous country on a near crisis footing.
Alarmed by the rapid spread of a movement outside the control of the Communist Party, China's leaders detained scores of Falun Gong leaders and mounted a campaign of invective against Mr. Li. Authorities dispersed resulting protests by tens of thousands of followers in at least 30 cities
"I really can't understand what the Chinese Government is doing," Mr. Li said yesterday. 
"I think the crackdown is going to do damage to the state, do damage to human rights and attract the attention of international public opinion."
"If a state cannot even tolerate a part of its cultural heritage like qigong, then what can it tolerate?" he asked, referring to traditional exercises thought to channel cosmic forces on which major elements of his own movement are based.
Falun Gong was developed by Mr. Li after decades of study under various masters, he said in a personal history that the Government disputes. 
It combines elements of qigong, Buddhism and Taoism. 
In Mr. Li's formulation, by performing certain physical exercises people can harness cosmic forces to improve their health and well-being.
The movement takes its name from the falun, the "law wheel" that is said to spin in the abdomen, drawing in good powers and expelling bad forces. 
Advanced students gain supernatural powers, his writings suggest.
Many followers in China simply say that they feel better after having practiced the exercises and that they also enjoy the morning group exercises as a hobby. 
It is unclear how many Chinese are fervent followers.
But the Communist Party is unwilling to tolerate any competing allegiance. 
Surprised and shocked in April when 10,000 Falun Gong adherents held an unauthorized demonstration outside the leadership compound in central Beijing, the authorities apparently began planning the crackdown for this week.
"If they want to outlaw the organization, then let them do it," Mr. Li said. 
"We don't have an organization."
Followers insist that volunteers carry out all activities, teaching neighbors and friends. 
Mr. Li professed yesterday to have no control over the activities of practioners, who carefully study his books and speeches for direction in their meditation and exercise regimens. 
Critics have likened the group to a cultish religion, an idea that followers vehemently dispute.
Mr. Li has communicated with a spreading worldwide network of followers through the Internet, where his latest thoughts are often posted at several sites.
Chinese authorities this week called Falun Gong "highly organized," with 39 teaching centers, more than 1,900 instruction stations and more than 28,000 designated exercise spots around the country. 
The authorities said Mr. Li had amassed large sums of money from sales of his books and his lectures, had bought cars and houses through relatives and had "hoodwinked" and "corroded the minds" of followers.
Mr. Li angrily denied the charges of personal gain as "sheer fabrications."
He also said the authorities had highlighted rare cases of followers who had committed murder or suicide without noting that those people were mentally ill.
"It is a proven fact that more than 100 million people have become healthier by practicing Falun Gong," Mr. Li said. 
"And many patients with cancer or other terminal diseases are still living because of this practice."
In the interview, Mr. Li was more muted than in his writings about supernatural powers like X-ray vision, an ability to fly and the radically lengthened lives that may be achieved through proper harnessing of cosmic forces.
Mr. Li said he felt that the reason for the persecution of Falun Gong was that so many people had become involved, including many Communist Party members, and that the growth had made officials nervous. 
Authorities have tried to distinguish publicly between the "ordinary" practice of qigong as a health-promoting exercise and the practice of Falun Gong.
In fact, most Chinese loosely believe in the supernatural forces evoked by various qigong sects. 
The Communist Party has worked unsuccessfully to stamp out such beliefs as superstition.
In detailing the case against Mr. Li this week, the Chinese authorities said records showed that he quietly visited Beijing on April 22, leaving for Hong Kong on April 24, the eve of the giant demonstration in Beijing by thousands of followers who were protesting harassment of the group and who called for the group's official approval.
In his interview, Mr. Li said he had visited Beijing then, but insisted the timing was coincidental. 
He said that he was on a layover en route to Australia by the cheapest flight, and that he did not meet with any followers and had not known of any demonstration plans.
Mr. Li, his wife and daughter have lived since last year in Queens, where they moved from China. 
They moved in part because he feared Government interference, he said, but more because his daughter wanted to attend an American high school.

file: Behind Japan_s Furor Over Tiny Isles, Gangland Fingerprints.txt
text:
ï»¿
As he relaxes in his office, smoke circling from an endless parade of cigarettes while he cheerfully explains that gangsters are sometimes very honorable people, Toyohisa Etoh seems an unlikely figure to have created an international mess.
Yet Mr. Etoh, a benign-looking man with graying temples and a scholarly look, has emerged as a key figure in Japanese foreign policy. 
He heads a mob-affiliated rightist organization that has built a lighthouse on a remote cluster of uninhabited islands, claiming them for Japan and thereby setting off a major dispute with China and Taiwan.
"I don't deny it when people call us yakuza," or gangsters, Mr. Etoh said firmly, "because if you're doing the right thing, that's what matters."
Doing the right thing, as Mr. Etoh sees it, means supporting Japan's claim to the islands, which in Japanese are called the Senkakus. 
The Japanese Government has been reluctant to act on its own, for fear of provoking China and Taiwan, and Mr. Etoh is bitterly contemptuous of Japanese Government officials.
"I despise the current members of Parliament and Government officials," Mr. Etoh said, waving his cigarette furiously through the air. 
"They're pigs!
Really pigs!
They have no patriotism whatsoever."
Japanese rightists have had a longtime interest in the Senkakus, a group of five islets and three barren rocks that lie between Taiwan and the Japanese island of Okinawa. 
Chinese nationalists are equally passionate about the islands, which they call the Diaoyus.
"It's very bad," fretted an official from one of the Governments involved, who insisted on not being identified. 
"I'm afraid this is getting out of control. 
But it's very hard to say to your citizens, 'No, you can't go to a territory that belongs to us.'
"
"Maybe America can send ships to the area and ask for all countries to be restrained," said the official, who called a reporter at home to make the suggestion. 
"Otherwise, I'm afraid this will get out of control."
One Hong Kong man drowned last month while trying to approach the islands, and Chinese nationalist groups have called on China and Taiwan to use military force to seize the islands from Japan. 
Tensions rose this week when some members of a protest group from Taiwan and Hong Kong managed to break through a cordon of 50 Japanese coast guard vessels and planted the Taiwanese and Chinese flags before withdrawing soon afterward.
Governments covet the islands for a reason deeper than nationalism: oil. 
The geology around the islands is said to be promising for petroleum.
Still, the Japanese Government last week put off indefinitely an application by Mr. Etoh's organization for the new lighthouse to be officially recognized on navigation charts. 
Mr. Etoh's organization, the Japan Youth Federation, has been involved in the islands since 1978, when it erected its first lighthouse there. 
It was a second lighthouse, erected in July of this year and repaired last month, that caused the present furor.
Over the years, Mr. Etoh says, he has spent more than $1 million to build the lighthouses and assert Japan's claim to the Senkakus, but he declines to say where the money comes from. 
The Japanese police say the federation has close ties to the yakuza, and Mr. Etoh acknowledges that the group's founder was a well-known mobster, Kusuo Kobayashi, who died six years ago.
The Chinese Government has condemned Japan for allowing Mr. Etoh to build the lighthouse, but the Japanese Government retorts that Japanese are allowed to travel anywhere in Japan -- including the Senkakus -- and that therefore there is nothing the Japanese Government can do.

file: BEIJING ARRESTS RIGHTS DEFENDER.txt
text:
ï»¿
Harry Wu, a Chinese-American human rights campaigner known for his daring and secretive travels through China to document prison labor abuses, was charged with espionage today.
Mr. Wu has been detained since June 19, when Chinese border authorities discovered his identity at a remote checkpoint in western China as he entered the country from Kazakhstan with an associate.
His arrest comes at a time of fraying relations between Washington and Beijing, and the start of legal action that could return Mr. Wu to a Chinese prison cell for the rest of his life is certain to bring an outcry from human rights groups and members of Congress.
Mr. Wu, 58, spent 19 years in Chinese labor camps, from 1960 to 1979. 
In a memoir published last year, he wrote that his secret forays "meant risking my own rearrest and reimprisonment," but he insisted on taking such risks to expose the abuses in the system under which he suffered.
One human rights advocate in Hong Kong today called the arrest an effective "declaration of war against the United States on the human rights issue."
"This move by Beijing calls for the most robust and sternest response from Washington," said Robin Munro, Hong Kong director of Human Rights Watch.
Though Mr. Wu has been a singular irritant to the Communist Party leadership, the timing of the arrest and the seriousness of the charge are likely to worsen the strains between Washington and Beijing. 
In addition to conflicts over human rights, trade issues and missile sales, tensions have been growing since President Clinton's decision in May to allow a private visit to the United States by the President of Taiwan, Lee Teng-hui.
In the current inflamed atmosphere, it may be politically impossible for Commerce Secretary Ronald H. Brown to lead a business delegation here this summer as planned, or for Hillary Rodham Clinton to address the United Nations International Women's Conference to be held in China in September. 
A spokesman for Mrs. Clinton said on Friday that she was considering accepting such an invitation.
Western officials and some Chinese said today that Mr. Wu's risky enterprise made his arrest somewhat predictable.
Chinese officials say that since 1991, Mr. Wu, in an effort to deceive them, has entered the country under the names Harry Wu and Peter H. Wu.
The official New China News Agency, in a dispatch from the central city of Wuhan, said Mr. Wu had been arrested "on charges of entering into China under false names, illegally obtaining China's state secrets and conducting criminal activities."
Mr. Wu, the press agency said, "slipped into China's areas and units closed to foreigners on several occasions, engaged in espionage and bought secret information and stole secret documents."
"He carried these secrets abroad," the dispatch said, "and provided them to foreign organizations and institutions."
Senior State Department officials say Mr. Wu has had only one American passport, as Peter H. Wu, the name under which he was naturalized as an American citizen in January 1992.
Mr. Wu has often testified at Congressional hearings on human rights abuses in China after collecting evidence by sneaking into labor camps and secretly filming what he has seen there. 
In 1991 he used a hidden camera to film a report for the CBS News program "60 Minutes."
Last year, in cooperation with the British Broadcasting Corporation, Mr. Wu tried to document on film that China was removing organs from executed prisoners for use in transplants to wealthy or powerful Chinese recipients.
While human rights experts say they believe that abuses in the organ donor system occur in China, the BBC discovered that Mr. Wu's videotape, ostensibly showing kidney transplant surgery, was actually a routine heart operation. 
A BBC investigation is under way.
It was not clear what legal representation Mr. Wu will be afforded to defend himself against the espionage charges. 
In Washington, Nicholas Burns, the State Department spokesman, said the United States had been informed that "we will be allowed access to Mr. Wu."
"We have decided to send our top consular official to Wuhan with the expectation that we may be able to see him on Monday," he said, adding, "We very much regret the detention of Mr. Wu and the accusations made against him."
Attempts by an American Embassy officer to reach Mr. Wu after his initial detention in Xinjiang Province failed, and led to recriminations between Washington and Beijing over whether China was adhering to consular agreements.
Chinese officials said that since Mr. Wu immigrated to the United States from the central city of Wuhan, his case had been turned over to the Wuhan Public Security Bureau, which carried out the arrest.
Mr. Wu and his wife, Ching Lee Wu, has been living in Milpitas, Calif., 40 miles south of San Francisco, where he is the director of the Laogai Research Foundation. 
Laogai is Chinese for China's "reform through labor" prison system, in which sentences of up to three years are handed down without trial, legal representation or appeal.
Born in Shanghai in 1937 as a wealthy banker's son and educated by the Jesuits of prewar Shanghai, Mr. Wu was of the class of Chinese that had risen from chaos to an almost European living standard. 
This way of life was shattered when the Communists won the Chinese civil war in 1949, and Mr. Wu's family suffered the indignities of the enforced social leveling.
By the time he reached the Beijing Geology Institute in the early 1950's, Mr. Wu was a stranger in the new culture of the Communist Party. 
The capitalist background of his family put him under constant suspicion and, in 1958, when he accepted Mao Zedong's invitiation to "let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend," his criticisms of the party, like those by thousands of other intellectuals, led to swift retribution.
He was judged guilty of being a counterrevolutionary rightist and put under the "supervision of the masses," a form of social persecution. 
For two years he was a virtual prisoner in his college and, the morning after his graduation, he was arrested and imprisoned. 
His stepmother, upon hearing of his arrest, committed suicide.
The next 19 years, including the tumultuous period of the Cultural Revolution, were spent in one "reform through labor" camp or another, unfolding for him the gulag that the Chinese Communists had built to capture millions of "bad elements," which included common criminals, former Nationalist opponents of the Communists and political dissidents of every stripe.
"Despair at life with no meaning after being dumped in China's human dustbin drove many inmates who should have been respected professionals to suicide," Mr. Wu later wrote. 
Human life, he said, had "no more importance than cigarette ash flicked in the wind."
After the death of Mao in 1976, it took three years for Mr. Wu's case to be reviewed so he could be released, and then he waited another five years for a passport to visit relatives in the United States. 
Once settled there, his fervor to document abuses in the Chinese penal system drew him back to China again and again.
"I felt urgently the responsibility not just to disclose but to publicize the truth about the Communist Party's mechanisms of control, whatever the risk to me, whatever the discomfort of telling my story," he said. 
"Each time I revisited my past, I hoped it would be the last time."

file: Beijing Buys a Stake in Hong Kong Phone Company.txt
text:
ï»¿
A company controlled by China's central Government has bought a minority stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications, the territory's dominant telephone company and a major subsidiary of Cable and Wireless of Britain.
The buyer, China Everbright Holdings Company Ltd., which is under the umbrella of China's State Council, the Government's highest administrative body, acquired 7.74 percent of Hong Kong Telecom for $8.6 billion (Hong Kong), or $1.11 billion (United States), from Citic Pacific, a publicly listed company that is also controlled, although far more loosely, by Beijing.
Some analysts here surmised that China was using the deal to gain access, and, down the road, possibly control, of one of the world's most sophisticated telecommunications companies. 
On July 1, China will resume sovereignty of Hong Kong after 156 years of British colonial rule.
"My view is they want to get into Hong Kong Tel and pick the bones of the knowledge base," said Robert Medd, an analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. 
"It's one of the most advanced telecommunications companies in the world."
Cable and Wireless controls 59 percent of Hong Kong Telecom. 
In trading this week on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, Honk Kong Telecom shares closed at $14.50 (Hong Kong), up nearly 10 percent from a week ago. 
The share price began rising Tuesday on rumors of a deal.
Already, China has moved, through various companies here, to acquire stakes or control of a range of British-owned companies, including two airlines and a local power company. 
Many analysts contend that China intends to exercise influence over a range of industries it considers "strategic," a term that seems to encompass airlines, power and telecommunications. 
Some analysts even believe that one of Hong Kong's banks, Hang Seng Bank, the leading consumer bank in the territory, is also being scrutinized by Beijing. 
Hang Seng is a subsidiary of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, which is owned by HSBC Holdings.
In a statement issued by the company here this afternoon, Brian Smith, the chairman of Hong Kong Telecom and Cable and Wireless Group, was quoted as saying: "We welcome the proposed investment by China Everbright Holdings in Hong Kong Telecom. 
This substantial investment of Chinese state capital demonstrates continued confidence in Hong Kong Telecom and Hong Kong through the 1997 transition and beyond."
Linus Cheung, the chief executive of Hong Kong Telecom, was quoted in Hong Kong papers this morning as saying that the company has maintained a close relationship with China's Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, China's regulatory agency for telecommunications.
Lloyd Fisher, the regional head of telecommunications research at BZW Asia Ltd., said that he did not know what the impact on Hong Kong Telecom would be. 
"It is basically a transfer of shares from one Chinese entity to another," he said. 
"If the company was a telecommunications firm from the mainland, that would make this transaction more significant."
But, he said, one of Everbright's publicly listed arms, China Everbright Technology, "has a stated interest in expanding into Hong Kong's telecommunications market."
From Citic's perspective, Mr. Medd said, the deal brought the company some badly needed cash. 
"Citic definitely needs to raise cash," he explained. 
"If they held onto shares of Hong Kong Tel it would be very difficult for them to do a deal. 
To do another deal they still have to go out and raise money. 
Basically from Citic's point of view it's a cash-raising exercise."
But as to the originator of the deal, Mr. Medd and others said they were uncertain. 
"I have no idea who instigated this," Mr. Medd said. 
"At that point you're starting to get into deep tea leaf reading."

file: Beijing Defends Arrest of a Top Dissident.txt
text:
ï»¿
In response to criticism from home and abroad, Chinese officials broke their silence today to defend their arrest this week of a prominent dissident who was trying to form an opposition political party.
"Xu Wenli is suspected of involvement in activities damaging to national security and has violated relevant criminal codes of the People's Republic of China," said a statement from the Foreign Ministry, which on Tuesday declined to comment on the arrest.
The sudden arrest on Monday night of Mr. Xu, as well as several other activists involved with him in trying to form the China Democratic Party, set off strong protests from human rights groups, other Chinese dissidents and Washington.
"We view his detention for peacefully exercising fundamental freedoms guaranteed by international human rights instruments as a serious step in the wrong direction," the State Department spokesman, James P. Rubin, said in Washington the day after the arrest.
American officials in Beijing urged the Government to release Mr. Xu and asked for clarification as to the exact nature of his crime.
China signed the International Covenant of Civil and Political Rights with great fanfare in October, and Mr. Xu's arrest is seen by human rights groups as a test of the nation's commitment to its tenets.
Dissidents in and out of China rose to Mr. Xu's defense, with more than a dozen activists around the country announcing that they would begin fasts in support of Mr. Xu and another leader of the China Democratic Party, Qin Yongmin, who was arrested in his home in Wuhan on Monday.
Almost 200 dissidents signed a letter to the Government protesting the detentions, said the Information Center for Human Rights and Democratic Movement in Hong Kong.
Three other Democratic Party organizers were also detained on Monday, although two of them were released early today.
But the two more prominent dissidents, Mr. Xu and Mr. Qin, are likely to face a longer haul since both have been charged with "criminal acts."
Mr. Xu's wife, He Xintong, said tonight that she had still not been informed of the specific charge against her husband, although she surmised from the aggressive behavior of the arresting officers that the sentence "could be long."
Mr. Qin's family was told that he was charged with "plotting to subvert the Government," a crime that for serious offenses commands sentences of three years to life.
In the Chinese criminal code, this charge comes under a grab-bag section called "threatening state security," which makes almost any political activity that questions or hampers the authority of the Communist Party illegal.
Mr. Xu's and Mr. Qin's trouble almost certainly stems from their efforts to gain recognition for the China Democratic Party, a loose network of pro-democracy activists in more than a dozen cities around China that was formed this year.
In the last six months they have become increasingly aggressive and defiant in their attempts to register the party with the Government, submitting repeated applications even after the local authorities had declared the concept of an opposition party illegal. 
They say the Chinese Constitution does not specifically forbid the formation of new political parties, although there have been none since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949.
In fact, the by-laws of the China Democratic Party are fairly tame, careful to acknowledge the central role of the Communist Party, but also supporting free speech and free elections for public officials.
"My husband thought the time was right to begin working to form a new party, since China recently signed the covenant on human rights," Ms. He said.
In September, a few Democratic Party members got some slightly encouraging signals from local governments, which initially accepted their applications to form a social organization to develop a party. 
But in recent weeks, as the organizers like Mr. Xu have become more insistent and defiant, harassment by the police has been increasing.
"All this past week we felt something was going to happen," Ms. He said. 
"It seemed that anyone who came to visit us was later detained for a while."

file: Beijing Delays Trial Of Man Who Urged Greater Democracy.txt
text:

Chinese officials have postponed the trial of a democracy advocate, which was scheduled to start this week, after the United States Embassy here urged them to drop or postpone the case.
Last week, Beijing courts said the trial of the advocate, Fang Jue, on charges of fraud and illegal business activities would begin on Tuesday.

file: Beijing Journal_A Dissident Finds the Political Prospects Bleak.txt
text:
ï»¿
Though the poplar trees are showing green along the capital's busy boulevards, for China's beleaguered democracy movement, there is no "Beijing spring."
Its leaders are either back in jail or under tight surveillance. 
It seems hardly possible that mass demonstrations for democracy like those in Tiananmen Square in 1976 and 1989 could recur.
"The craft of suppressing the people is more sophisticated than before," said Xu Liangying, the 74-year-old translator of Albert Einstein's works who -- along with six other scientists and intellectuals -- petitioned the Communist leadership last month to free the country's political prisoners and embrace political reform.
As a result, he was placed under house arrest during the visit of Secretary of State Warren Christopher, and his apartment is still being watched.
Neither President Jiang Zemin nor Qiao Shi, chairman of the National People's Congress and a young revolutionary comrade of Professor Xu's 45 years ago, has responded to the petition, except by clamping down even more harshly on dissent.
After the surveillance on his building slackened recently, Professor Xu agreed to an interview and greeted his visitors at the metal grate that serves as the outer door to his chilly seventh-floor apartment in the Academy of Sciences compound.
Inside, the walls are lined with well-stuffed book cabinets. 
An uncurtained window bathes a cluttered desk with afternoon sunlight. 
A single strand of wire arches across the glass as a shortwave radio antenna, to improve reception for Voice of America and British Broadcasting Corporation news.
Professor Xu studied physics and the history of science. 
He helped to translate Einstein, who glares down from a wall poster with a favorite Einstein aphorism: "Great spirits have always encountered violent opposition from mediocre minds."
His gray hair in flighty disarray, Professor Xu shuffled in slippered feet to fill teacups for his guests. 
He said he had joined the Communist underground as a youth in his native Zhejiang Province, before the civil war that brought Communist rule in 1949, and he remained a dedicated Marxist until 1974.
In 1957, he admitted, he only winced when Mao Zedong purged thousands of Communist Party members who had taken up his invitation to criticize the leadership.
"I thought some of the actions taken by the Communist Party were a little cruel, but I never felt the actions were a violation of human rights," he said.
Still, he voiced his disagreement with the purges. 
It cost him his post at the Institute of Philosophy and his Beijing residency permit and began 20 years of persecution. 
Toward the end, he realized that he had been carrying around the intellectual seeds of democratic thought all his life.
He recalled that in 1938, as he was going off to college, he had read Einstein's "Ideas and Opinions" and underlined this passage:
"May I begin with an article of faith?
It runs as follows: The state is made for man, not man for the state. 
I regard the chief duty of the state to protect the individual and give him the opportunity to develop into a creative personality."
But what is democracy for China?
Dissidents are likely to give different answers.
Some of the younger reformers -- even some of the older ones -- want to work within the Communist Party system. 
Professor Xu calls the most enthusiastic of these "boot lickers."
Middle-aged dissidents tend to be deeply influenced by their Maoist upbringing, and they articulate their democratic yearning for the government to empower and serve the proletarian masses. 
Professor Xu has concluded that they are at times misguided.
"The people who were brought up in the 1960's and 1970's did not know much about democracy," Professor Xu said, adding that the reason was they had no access to the literature of democracy from the West.
Many of China's democracy advocates, he said, "believe that if you are not satisfied with the Government, you ought to stand up and overthrow it."
After all, Mao taught them that power comes out of the barrel of a gun.
Professor Xu's close friend Fang Lizhi, who was China's most famous dissident until he was exiled in 1990, also disapproves of this view. 
Now a professor of astrophysics at the University of Arizona, Mr. Fang said by telephone: "Even many Chinese students here, they don't know democracy. 
They still use the concept of Mao, which is mass democracy: the majority can do anything it wants, and if there is a small number in opposition, the majority can ignore their existence. 
That is total dictatorship or proletarian democracy."
Professor Xu said he believes that the student leaders of the Tiananmen Square uprising of 1989 did not really understand democracy, "and so they ended up making chaos," though he does not blame them for the military crackdown that followed.
"In 1989, I said the number of intellectuals in China who really understand democracy does not exceed 100," Professor Xu said. 
"Today I am still saying the same words."
Now Professor Xu and his colleagues are searching for a non-threatening forum to keep the discussion of democracy alive. 
He plans to write a book about the history and theory of democracy.
His wife, the historian Wang Laili -- who also signed the petition -- will be the co-author.
"My wife and I are a life-and-death couple," Professor Xu said. 
"Both of us were underground revolutionaries."

text:
ï»¿
When she walks down a city street, Jin Xing effortlessly draws attention with her noble bearing and her elegant clothes. 
But there is something else about her, and many people seem to sense it.
Jin Xing is a transsexual.
At 32, Jin Xing (pronounced jin SHING) already has an impressive resume: a prize-winning dancer and choreographer, a former colonel in the army, founder of China's first independent dance troupe, owner of one of Beijing's hottest nightspots.
Yet it is Ms. Jin's leap across the gender barrier, from male to female, that fascinates many people here. 
Ms. Jin is the first transsexual in China to talk about it openly, and it is making her a celebrity.
"If people pay more attention to my dance because of who I am, that's fine," Ms. Jin said between sips of cappuccino at an outdoor cafe near her home. 
"If more people think about who they really are, because of me, that's fine too."
Ms. Jin evidently revels in the attention she is attracting, voraciously soaking up publicity in any form. 
In addition to a cascade of requests that she choreograph or direct stage performances, spurred by her fame as well as her talent, she is also accepting invitations to pose for magazines.
"I like being famous," she said.
A growing number of people are undergoing sex change operations in China, and several have thanked Ms. Jin for setting such a public example, saying it gave them the courage to proceed.
Although no precise statistics have been made public, sex change operations have become numerous enough that Beijing Medical University recently published guidelines for people requesting the surgery, including a five-year waiting period, extensive psychological counseling and a year of hormone treatment before the operation. 
One doctor at the university has performed 26 operations.
It may seem remarkable that a Government as conservative as China's allows sex change operations, though the medical authorities recently disclosed that the first one was performed, in secret, in 1983. 
No law ever expressly forbade or permitted such operations.
Yet what seems an even greater surprise is the ability of someone like Ms. Jin to operate freely in Chinese society, a distinct sign of how permissible unconventional styles of life are becoming here.
Not long ago, China's control-obsessed Government made sure that all non-approved ways of life were kept out of view, including homosexuality and even premarital sex.
But deep social change in recent years, forced by economic loosening, has meant that ordinary Chinese have gained more freedom over private life and that transsexuals and the more eccentric branches of youth culture like punk rockers can express themselves without fear.
"I don't feel any discrimination," Ms. Jin said. 
"Many people do not understand, but no one is saying, 'You can't do this.'
"
Chinese society is highly homogeneous, and individual expression is often snuffed out at an early age. 
At the same time, overcrowding and a lack of privacy also put a premium on discretion. 
As long as no one feels threatened, Ms. Jin's sex change is regarded with fascination but also with acquiescent respect.
As a man, Jin Xing emerged as China's top dancer in 1987, winning a national competition and then going to New York for four years of study. 
Living in the Chelsea section of Manhattan, he opened his eyes to American society, among other ways by spending a night in jail when a rival Chinese dancer falsely accused him of robbery to try to keep him out of a dance competition.
Real artistic distinction came in 1996, a year after Ms. Jin's sex change operation, when she established China's first independent dance troupe and began performing a set of startlingly original pieces that explored issues of love and identity, winning accolades as China's leading modern choreographer.
China's state-run media, reporting on her performances that year, also wrote about her sex change, a sign of official approval.
Like many transsexuals, Ms. Jin said she had known from childhood that she had a gender conflict. 
Living in New York and in Europe, where she spent three years, Ms. Jin became aware that a sex change was a realistic possibility.
"My whole being is female," she said. 
"I always knew I should be a girl."
Coming from a military family, Jin Xing joined a dance troupe run by the army at age 9 in the northeastern city of Shenyang. 
Dance instructors remember a willful child, fiercely determined and extraordinarily talented as a dancer. 
And crafty, too. 
One time the young dance student went on a hunger strike for a week when the army blocked a move to study with a more advanced dance troupe.
"They sent me in to talk to him, and I told him he was hurting his body by not eating," recalled Zhang Aijuan, a dance teacher at the military troupe. 
"He looked at me with a long face and whispered, 'I'm not stupid, I'm sneaking chocolate.'
"
The military superiors eventually relented and allowed the transfer.
Ms. Jin credits her success, in part, to the discipline learned in the army.
"The more you give, the more you get," she said. 
"Success takes three things: talent, hard work and opportunity. 
I am very lucky to have had all three."
She did not discuss her decision to become a woman with her parents until she was about to go ahead with the operation, performed in a Beijing hospital in 1995. 
She was most terrified about telling her father, a military intelligence officer and a professionally conservative man.
Yet he surprised her, congratulating her for being so brave. 
His help was needed to get the sex designated on Ms. Jin's national identity card switched from male to female, which she says has been the most difficult bureaucratic obstacle she has faced. 
She felt no need to change her name, which means "gold star" and unlike many names in China is not gender specific.
Ms. Jin said she had not undergone the psychological therapy now required of sex change patients in China, and had refused to take hormones for fear they would make her fat.
"I'm a dancer," she said. 
"My appearance is very important."
Ms. Jin, whose broad shoulders and strong hands hint at a masculine past, said she had become accustomed to standing out in a crowd. 
Most days, she wears a qipao, a long body-hugging gown.
"People look very carefully at me," she said. 
"I have it much harder than ordinary women. 
They can dress sloppily, but I have to be perfect every day. 
People are looking for my faults."
She also feels that she grew up in a discriminatory atmosphere as a member of an ethnic minority, since her parents are ethnic Koreans.
"Chinese people can be very racist," she said. 
"I felt a lot of discrimination as a child. 
My teachers were always telling me: 'Don't let anyone know you are Korean. 
You will never get into competition.'
"
Finding the right mate is never easy, Ms. Jin also said, pointing out that even the most open-minded Chinese men were often intimidated by a strong woman.
Although dance has been her life, Ms. Jin says she would like to become an actress and perhaps a talk-show host. 
She was recently cast as a Chinese dance instructor in a Hungarian-Chinese film, to be shot next year.
After she won an award from the Culture Ministry last year, a seal of official approval, many Government-backed organizations commissioned her to choreograph performances. 
She recently staged a performance of monks from Shaolin Monastery who practice martial arts and is currently working with a children's acrobatic troupe at the military academy where she herself studied.
"They didn't dare approach me until they knew that the Government approved," she said. 
"It has taken a lot of work, but I am finally getting there."

text:

Ever since Prime Minister Li Peng signed State Council Proclamation No. 129 last month banning the purchase or possession of satellite dishes by ordinary Chinese, millions of people on the broadcasting and receiving ends of the television business in Asia have been trying to determine whether Mr. Li will risk the draconian steps necessary to enforce the order.
So far, no police officers have been sent to start ripping dishes off rooftops, but the Government is talking tough. 
Many in Beijing feel the Politburo has invested too much of its prestige to back down.
"The large majority of Beijing dish owners will have to tear their dishes down," said Wei Dangjun, a spokesman for the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television, whose Minister, Ai Zhisheng, is known for his zeal in attacking the "spiritual pollution" infecting China from the West.
"Most owners have already broken rules by installing their dishes without application," Mr. Wei said in an interview. 
"Those that didn't listen to orders prohibiting installation," he said, "and then didn't listen to orders to disassemble, we will punish according to relevant laws."
The most compelling test of this latest crackdown is whether it is too late. 
The thought-control officials in China's old guard may find that the genie of the information explosion has been out of the bottle too long.
In the Fang Village neighborhood of south Beijing, even the apartment buildings that house retired officers of the dreaded public security bureau are wired up for satellite programming from the United States, Britain and Hong Kong.
Inestimable millions of Chinese have already been swept into the information era by foreign newspapers that have arrived with the flood of foreign business people and through television programs arriving via the "heavenly thread," which is the literal translation of "satellite antenna" into Mandarin Chinese.
While there are an estimated 500,000 satellite dishes in the country, because of cable hookups on apartment buildings the Government estimates that there are 15 million subscribers to multichannel systems that import English-language programs.
Â 
A Sense of Crackdown
The announcement of the ban coincided with a conference in early October on state security attended by Mr. Li and President Jiang Zemin. 
It concluded that "hostile forces outside our country have never stopped endangering the safety of our country" using "all means to infiltrate, split and damage us."
The ban also followed the decision of the International Olympic Committee to award the 2000 Games to Sydney, Australia, a crushing setback to the Chinese leadership.
The order banning satellite dishes contributed to a sense of crackdown in the capital this month. 
Two prominent journalists have been arrested: Xi Yang, a reporter for the large Hong Kong daily Ming Pao, and Gao Yu, a mainland reporter who was detained days before she was to leave for an academic year at Columbia University.
For several tense weeks, tens of thousands of Chinese who have bought the dishes from private and state-owned companies, including from the People's Liberation Army dish factory, have been hoping that this order will simply go the way of previous threats to enforce the ban.
The companies marketing the dishes have suddenly taken a low profile, though purchases are still possible, as one Beijing resident discovered last week.
"Hello, I would like to know if you still have any satellite television dishes available in your store?" the resident first asked in a telephone call.
"No, haven't you heard about the new regulations?" the clerk asked. 
"We're not allowed to sell them now."
The same day, the caller visited the department store and approached the salesman at what had been the satellite antenna service counter.
The man behind the counter seemed to be speaking on a different frequency. 
If the customer really wanted a dish, he said, it could be arranged for the equivalent of $650, including installation.
The fact that the Government is moving deliberately to enforce the ban reflects the struggle in the leadership between those who believe China should continue to open up to Western influences and those who believe China's economic boom can be sealed in a cocoon of Communist ideology.
Satellite dishes have become a way of life in China in the last two years. 
Even as the Clinton Administration complains that China is jamming Voice of America broadcasts, the same Chinese leaders appear helpless as millions of Chinese tune in to the Star TV network.
Star TV is the Hong Kong-based communications company that beams its five-channel menu -- including the BBC and CNN news, sports and MTV music videos -- into 4.8 million Chinese households.
In July Rupert Murdoch bought 63.6 percent of Star TV and has identified the mainland as his largest future market.
"Some leaders have installed satellite dishes with public funds," complained one Government worker who insisted on not being identified and who owns a $570 dish and receiver. 
"It's the authorities who have the power to do whatever they like. 
We are the victims."
As reported in People's Daily, the penalties for failing to take down the dishes will be anywhere from $900 to nearly $9,000. 
This does not include the cost of the dish, which would be confiscated.
At the ministry, Mr. Wei said he did not know when the decision would be made to start tearing hardware off rooftops.
"We await specific measures from above," he said.

text:
ï»¿
There was a time, nearly 50 years ago, when revolutionary fervor in China attracted left-leaning Americans, with its mantras of self-reliance and manual labor, and its promise of achieving a socialist dream.
Joan Hinton, for one, gave up a promising career as a nuclear physicist in 1948 to come and work on a farm, enduring severe hardship in the name of a political ideal. 
Most Chinese who labored beside her believed in the same dreams, although they abandoned them when other options -- fresh vegetables, telephones and television -- eventually came along.
Ms. Hinton, however, is still here, working at a dairy on the outskirts of Beijing. 
She toils on, a practicing believer in proletarian values, even though almost everything she has worked for in China has been washed away by an onslaught of change, much of it economic.
"I always say you need three things to survive in China," said Ms. Hinton, relaxing in jeans and army-issue green sneakers. 
"A sense of humor, a sense of history and a sense of struggle. 
If we didn't know how to struggle, we'd still be up in the trees."
Ms. Hinton is one of a handful of veteran leftists from the United States and Europe who remained in China through years of political turmoil, and are disillusioned by the transformation that has both brought the nation's economy to life and allowed an array of social ills to flourish.
Once oddities only because they stood out physically, these "foreign experts," as the Chinese Goverment still classifies them, even though some have become Chinese citizens, attract attention for the way they cling to political beliefs that most Chinese abandoned years ago.
Sidney Shapiro, 80, a lawyer from Brooklyn who came to China in 1947, and Ruth Weiss, 87, an Austrian who moved here in 1951, say they still believe that socialism will somehow prevail, even though, in China, it seems further out of reach each day.
Among the dozen or so long-staying "foreign experts," however, none are as hard-core in their devotion to Maoist ideals as Ms. Hinton, 74, and her husband, Sid Engst, 76. 
And yet their admiration for the militant leftism that erupted in the Cultural Revolution of the late 1960's and early 70's, and their disdain for the changes that followed, do not seem to have dampened their enthusiasm for living here.
With her husband, and with the three children who came along the way, Ms. Hinton lived in rural Shaanxi Province for 18 years -- first turning old scrap metal into cooking utensils, then raising cattle and then ducks -- before moving to the Beijing area, living on a commune and, after it was disbanded, settling in at the dairy. 
The grown children no longer live in China.
Ms. Hinton speaks nostalgically of "the 30 years" -- 1949 to 1979 -- a period that many Chinese see as essentially wrong-headed in its efforts to mold human nature to be something it is not.
"It was like that journalist who went to Russia and said 'I've seen the future and it works,' " said Ms. Hinton, referring to Lincoln Steffens's trip in the 1920's. 
"That's how I see the 30 years. 
It worked. 
There was very little stealing, there was great community spirit, there was a common goal. 
That's all been thrown away now, except for the memory."
Ms. Hinton, whose mother founded the Putney School in Vermont, began her professional career in the 1940's as a nuclear physicist at Los Alamos to help produce the first atomic bomb in 1945. 
She became disillusioned as the cold war began, and quit physics.
After coming to China in 1948 to join Mr. Engst in an area "liberated" by Communist soldiers, she was accused by McCarthy-era Americans of being a spy who spilled nuclear secrets to China.
Ms. Hinton giggles girlishly as she shows a visitor a laminated copy of a magazine article about her, "The Spy Who Got Away," with a drawing that depicts her as a Lauren Bacall look-alike in a trenchcoat, scribbling in a notebook as she observes a nuclear test in the desert.
"I never looked that good," said Ms. Hinton, her blond hair now silver. 
Nor, she said, did she ever use her physics expertise in China.
If they cling to political views that sound antiquated in today's China, Ms. Hinton and Mr. Engst are acute critics of problems in Chinese society.
"It's a mess," said Mr. Engst. "Nobody listens to the central government anymore. 
They keep putting out laws, and nobody listens. 
You can pass all the laws you want, it makes no difference."
Mr. Shapiro, a translator whose Brooklyn accent is still healthy after 49 years in China, similarly mourns the rise of crime and corruption, and the loss of the communal spirit he once knew in Beijing. 
Yet he blames something deeper than current policy.
"The great flaw of Chinese society has been recognized: It is not Socialism or Communism, but Confucianism," said Mr. Shapiro, who became a Chinese citizen in 1963. 
"That means blind worship of authority, which has been used very much to the advantage and to the disadvantage of the Communist Party over the years."
Ms. Weiss, a retired translator, seems perplexed by what she sees out her window at the Friendship Hotel, where she lives alone in an apartment cluttered with Chinese knickknacks.
"In the 1950's, there was a real feeling of cohesion among people," she said. 
"Now, everything you have to pay, no one takes responsibility for anything. 
For me, Mao Zedong was always a father figure. 
I thought he was really interested in the welfare of the people. 
Obviously, he wasn't."
Ms. Hinton, however, is still a believer in Mao.
"Mao started the Cultural Revolution to cure the disparity between the few and the many," said Ms. Hinton. "How could that be wrong?"
She dismisses the current view, that Mao's misguided policies led to the deaths of more than 30 million people in the famine of 1960-62, as revisionist history.
"We were in the countryside then, and there was malnutrition, not starvation," said Ms. Hinton. "Without socialism, we would have starved. 
We banded together, sharing grain coupons."
Mr. Engst chimed in: "The Cultural Revolution achieved a lot. 
It identified the main problem, which is the dark side of the party. 
It just didn't succeed in eradicating it."
The "dark side" of the party means those led by Deng Xiaoping, who championed the transformation of the last 17 years.
In fact, Mr. Engst had a condition for being interviewed: "You have to promise not to describe us as pro-Deng Xiaoping or pro-reform."

text:

"How much do you charge for delivery?" a customer asked, leaning on the handlebars of his bicycle in front of a truck- sized heap of cabbage on the side of the street in western Beijing.
"Charge for delivery?"
Wang Zhenping fired back in a mocking tone that turned a few heads in the Horse Tail Gully vegetable market. 
"Did you just crawl out of a cave or something?
It's free!"
The great cabbage migration has begun, and it's a buyer's market.
Mountains of Chinese cabbage -- 396 million pounds by the reckoning of the Beijing authorities -- began advancing on the capital this month, as one of old Beijing's agricultural rhythms persists against the onslaught of modern supermarkets and glitzy shopping centers that have sprouted here.
Rough-hewn peasants who have been sleeping with their crops for weeks in a 100-mile arc of farmland outside Beijing have converged for the annual ritual of selling what was once a survival crop for many Chinese.
They come in trucks, horse-drawn carts and pedal-powered three-wheelers, all straining under billowing loads of cabbage that within the space of a week fill acres of sidewalks and alleyway space.
Ten thousand city workers help the farmers with a fleet of 1,400 trucks, which haul cabbage to 500 city-run markets.
From these and from hundreds of freelance cabbage heaps, the hawking begins.
"People will always buy cabbage," Mr. Wang said. 
"That's the food you get through the winter on."
Lan Wei, a 26-year-old worker in a state factory who was out marketing the other day, said, "In the past, there used to be nothing else to eat."
Smiling, she repeated a ditty of the Communist era, "When you've got your winter cabbage, in your heart you feel secure."
Buying winter cabbage is no simple chore. 
Volume is the key, as is buying early to get the best price, as little as a penny per pound.
"It used to be that people would get in long lines and really stock up on the stuff -- 400 to 500 pounds," Ms. Lan said. 
It was stacked on balconies and in stairwells and hung outside windows as a strategic food reserve for every family.
By December it freezes and turns black from the coal soot that makes China's wintertime air famous for its density, but Beijingers just peel away the outside leaves and plop it in boiling water.
"You can fry it, you can make it into dumplings, you can put it into soup," said Wang Yanhong, a young woman who works for an American company in Beijing. 
She defended it against the disdain of today's youth in China.
"It's not that all young people don't like it," she said, "It's the same as any vegetable. 
If you eat it every day, you'll get sick of it."
Ms. Lan said that "in recent years, a lot of cabbage hasn't been sold."
The reason is that prosperity, greenhouse farming and year-round vegetable crops shipped from southern China have cut into the northern custom of stocking up on baicai, which in Chinese literally means "white vegetable."
(Chinese cabbage is not the soccer-ball-shaped stuff familiar in the West. 
The Chinese version is cylindrical, with broad white leaves that trend toward a green crown.)
But there seems to be a larger cultural shift afoot.
"Of course, young people don't like cabbage as much as the older generation does," said Hu Bei, 23, another shopper in western Beijing, "but it's also that lots of young people are too lazy to cook, especially the ones who are earning high salaries or working for foreign enterprises."
Many newly well-off Chinese simply identify the annual cabbage haul as a relic of past privation. 
And to the young, it seems downright unfashionable.
But if anything has spurred the sales of this year's crop of cabbage, it has been soaring urban inflation, which has pushed up vegetable prices 50 percent in the last year. 
Even households with new income are watching their food budgets.
"In the past few years people haven't bought so much cabbage," Ms. Hu said. 
"Now, though, they're worried about the prices going up on vegetables, so they're buying more."
It may seem hard to imagine that while millions of Chinese are getting rich, millions of other Chinese seem to be slavishly following the habits of an earlier era.
"The farther north you go, the more people rely on it," Ms. Lan said.
Back at the Horse Tail Gully market, Mr. Wang, his brother and sister-in-law, Gao Aijun, 27, had been selling for three straight days and it looked like it might take two more days to reduce their cabbage heap to the dregs.
"This year it's been a pretty good harvest," Ms. Gao said, "and we'll do a lot better this year than last," perhaps with a total profit of more than $1,200 on 55,000 pounds of cabbage.
That is, Mr. Wang added with a note of caution and a sideways glance up and down the street, "depending on whether any competition arrives."
In the cabbage business, a competing heap could come around the corner at any moment, he said.

China has turned down efforts by the Vatican to arrange a visit by Pope John Paul II to Hong Kong when he tours Asia later this year, dashing hopes among Catholics in China that ties between Rome and Beijing might improve.
A Roman Catholic bishop in Hong Kong who recently returned from the Vatican said today that China had decided against a visit by the Pope.
"The mainland says the Vatican has ties with Taiwan" and no ties with Beijing, Bishop Joseph Zen told Reuters. 
"Therefore, such a visit is not convenient."
Although the Vatican is eager to improve relations with Beijing eventually, the real obstacle seems not to be Taiwan so much as the wariness among Chinese leaders about the Pope's moral authority over 10 million Catholics in China.
Many of them worship in underground churches to evade the Communist Party's ban on recognizing the Pope as the Catholic Church's supreme earthly authority.
A possible visit by the Pope to Hong Kong was supported by some Catholic leaders in China, even those who swear allegiance to the party, in the hope that it would be a first step toward warmer ties between Rome and Beijing.
Yet Beijing's negative answer did not come as a real surprise.
The Vatican's Secretary of State, Angelo Cardinal Sodano, has said in the past that Rome will gladly move away from Taiwan if it can establish ties with Beijing.
China's Foreign Ministry issued a statement today containing its familiar criticism of the Vatican's ties with Taiwan, which Beijing has considered a renegade province since the Chinese civil war ended in 1949.
"Currently, the Vatican still maintains so-called diplomatic relations with Taiwan," the statement said. 
"Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China. 
The issues involving the Pope visiting Hong Kong are rather complicated. 
The Vatican is clear on this."
A Hong Kong newspaper reported today that Chinese officials had rebuffed inquiries from Rome made after the Pope expressed interest in visiting the territory, over which China resumed sovereignty in 1997. 
The newspaper, The South China Morning Post, ran an accompanying editorial saying the decision called into question the high degree of autonomy that Hong Kong had been promised.
Although Beijing's Foreign Ministry did not say so, the two matters excluded from Hong Kong's theoretical autonomy are foreign affairs and defense. 
Relations with the Pope, recognized as the head of state of the Vatican, clearly falls under China's jurisdiction over foreign affairs.
A visit by the Pope to Hong Kong would have been the first since Pope Paul VI visited in 1970. 
Hong Kong has about 370,000 practicing Catholics -- 250,000 ethnic Chinese and roughly 120,000 Filipinos, most of whom work as domestic helpers.
Mary Seung, a spokeswoman for the Catholic Diocese of Hong Kong said local Catholic leaders learned several weeks ago that the Pope would not be visiting.
"Officially we have not heard any explanation from Rome at all," Ms. Seung said.
As excited as Hong Kong Catholics would have been by a visit by the Pope, the larger issue that looms behind any such proposal is the question of a long-term rapprochement between Beijing and Rome, which have had not formal diplomatic ties since the Communist Party came to power in 1949.
A Catholic bishop in Shanghai said in an interview with an Italian magazine several months ago that the Vatican and China had held secret talks about improving relations but had yet to achieve any significant progress. 
The bishop, Jin Luxian, expressed a yearning for reconciliation.
"The Pope represents the supreme leader of all the world's Catholics, including those in China," Bishop Jin said at the time, adding that he dreamed of seeing a papal nuncio in Beijing.
China is officially atheist and bans Christian worship outside the "patriotic churches" set up under the control of the Communist Party, which is inherently suspicious of any organization it does not control. 
Many Chinese leaders are also wary of the role that the Catholic Church played in the downfall of Communist rule in Poland in 1989.
