file: CHINA AFTER DENG_ DIPLOMACY_U.S. AND CHINESE SEEN NEAR A DEAL ON HUMAN RIGHTS.txt
text:
ï»¿
After seven months of secret diplomacy, American and Chinese officials seem to be within striking distance of a breakthrough in their longstanding dispute over human rights. 
At issue is the fate of thousands of Chinese political and religious dissidents held in prisons, labor camps or just at home under heavy guard or surveillance.
Under the terms of a deal that Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright will seek to nudge toward agreement when she arrives in Beijing on Monday for her first official visit, China would agree to sign two important United Nations covenants on human rights, release a representative group of up to eight political prisoners and restart talks with the International Committee of the Red Cross aimed at establishing a program of prison visits to determine the status of the thousands of prisoners of conscience in China.
In return, China could expect to bring an end to the annual confrontation over its human rights record at the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva.
For President Clinton and President Jiang Zemin, this prospective breakthrough comes at a time of extraordinary opportunity and risk.
With the death last week of Deng Xiaoping, it accords the new generation of Chinese leaders an early chance to end the period of harsh repression that has followed the Tiananmen massacre of 1989.
[Ms. Albright arrived in Beijing on Monday, stepping off her plane only hours after the body of Mr. Deng arrived at the Babaoshan cemetery for cremation.]
To emerge from their long "defensive crouch," as a former American Ambassador, J. Stapleton Roy, once called it, China's new leaders would have to stand up to the hard-line forces in the Communist Party. 
Those forces see any act of political tolerance or human rights concessions to Washington as appeasing those who would like to topple Communist rule here.
It is anyone's guess as to whether the Chinese feel confident enough to go forward. 
But American officials point to two important factors.
First, the leading hard-liner, Prime Minister Li Peng, has predicted in internal leadership discussions that he can pull off an acceptable deal with the Americans that would help China's case before the Human Rights Commission in Geneva.
The commission meets from March 10 to April 18 this year and will again take up a resolution calling for an investigation into human rights conditions in China. 
Beijing has defeated the resolution each time, often by narrow margins.
Chinese officials say such an achievement by Mr. Li would boost his campaign to gain a prestigious party post and retain supervision of China's foreign affairs after he steps down as Prime Minister next year.
The second factor is that both Chinese and American officials have known since November that Wang Dan, a student leader of the 1989 Tiananmen democracy movement who was sentenced to 14 years in prison last fall, is willing to go into exile in exchange for his freedom.
Mr. Wang is one of the best known of the eight dissidents on the list presented in July by Anthony Lake, who was then Mr. Clinton's national security adviser, in talks with Communist Party leaders. 
Mr. Wang's release and arrival in the United States, which has already privately conveyed a willingness to provide him asylum, would be a dramatic 11th-hour concession by China.
Since November, China has released three other political prisoners on the list, apparently in response to the American requirements: Chen Ziming, sentenced as one of the "black hands" behind the 1989 demonstrations; a dissident from Inner Mongolia named Ulan Shovo, and Xi Yang, a journalist.
For Mr. Clinton, who took political risks in breaking the link between China's human rights performance and its trade status that was imposed by his predecessor, a demonstration of tangible gains would vindicate his policy of engagement.
But Mr. Clinton, whose Presidency now faces an extended investigation into Asian fund-raising efforts during his re-election campaign, will need concessions that are able to withstand Congressional scrutiny.
One difficult issue for Mr. Clinton is deciding how many prisoners among the eight cases raised would have to be released to declare progress. 
One is Wei Jingsheng, China's best-known dissident, who has served 17 years of a total of 29 years and for whom Mr. Clinton once showed great public concern.
With both China and the United States constrained by domestic political considerations, Ms. Albright appeared to be lowering expectations for her first meeting with Chinese leaders since she became Secretary of State. 
Her senior aides indicated that she was maneuvering to give the Chinese an opportunity to get through the period of Mr. Deng's funeral before the final hard bargaining on the Geneva resolution.
"The emphasis in China over the coming weeks and months is likely to be on continuity, on stabilityI within the leadership, on building consensus within the leadership," said a senior official who briefed reporters traveling with Ms. Albright. "In other words, nothing risky."
"Our expectations are not too high," he said, adding, "Based on the current situation, we expect to proceed with the resolution."
Last week, the State Department sent cablegrams to the 53 nations on the Human Rights Commission saying that without a breakthrough in the talks, Washington intended to go forward with plans to sponsor the resolution in Geneva calling China to account for human rights abuses.
But Administration officials have been careful to say the final decision to go forward will be made closer to the Geneva meeting. 
American officials also hope that the brinksmanship in the talks, or recriminations over failure, will not disrupt the visit of Vice President Al Gore to Asia in March, but Beijing has withheld final dates for his stay.
"While one can always hope for human rights progress, we shouldn't expect any dramatic movement forward in the next few days," the official traveling with Ms. Albright said. 
"We obviously would welcome a gesture now or at any point in next few months."
Mike Jendrzejczyk, the Washington director of Human Rights Watch, said: "Mrs. 
Albright is hoping that the Chinese will make significant enough concessions that the Administration could credibly back off on going forward in Geneva. 
For the Chinese, they want to avoid the kind of loss of face that would arise from another debate and from a vote in Geneva."
John T. Kamm, a former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong who regularly travels to Beijing on behalf of political prisoner cases, said that for the Chinese, "with the passing of Deng, a new beginning is possible."
"There is now a window of opportunity for China to demonstrate that it intends to live by international standards of human rights," he said. 
"If Jiang Zemin were to make this decision, it would demonstrate to the outside world and especially to Hong Kong that he is stepping in and being very decisive. 
But there is going to be considerable opposition in the party to doing this."
A crucial issue this year has been whether China would sign and then ratify the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and a similar document on economic, social and cultural rights. 
Together, they would obligate China not only to uphold freedom of speech, assembly and religious worship while also adhering to due process of law, but also to report on its human rights situation to the international community.
"We think signing the covenants would be an extremely important step forward for China," said a French diplomat here.
China has said only that it will sign the documents without committing itself to a specific date and has used that vague commitment to try to split the American and European alliance that has formed each year in Geneva. 
Last year China tried a similar tactic, but after "consideration," did not sign the covenants.
Similarly, while China has invited a senior Red Cross official to visit Beijing, it has refused to make a specific commitment to go ahead with the agency's prison visit program, which has been the subject of many fruitless negotiations.
"We look for progress on various issues," said the official with Ms. Albright. "We don't expect the visits themselves to be merely symbolic. 
We want them to provide evidence of an improvement in relations."
Stanley Roth, who is expected to become Ms. Albright's assistant secretary of state for Asian affairs, told an interviewer in Washington this weekend that "the relationship cannot be a one-way street."
"If there is no improvement in all the issues the United States cares about," Mr. Roth said, it will be "very hard to create support for a broad relationship."

file: CHINA AFTER DENG_ THE ECONOMY_Deng_s Legacy_ Finishing Long March to Capitalism.txt
text:
ï»¿
Deng Xiaoping, the architect of China's policy of economic openness, seemed to possess a magic touch with China's economy in its rocky transition from Communism to capitalism.
But Mr. Deng has left his successors facing even tougher challenges, ones that he may not have been brave enough to take on.
Jiang Zemin, Mr. Deng's designated successor, and his circle of colleagues and adversaries have far less political legitimacy and influence than Mr. Deng. That may be crucial in pushing ahead with the next era of restructuring -- tackling the cumbersome state-run sector and adopting unpopular but necessary economic policies, like raising taxes, hiking prices or allowing large-scale layoffs.
This leaves one pressing question: will Mr. Deng's death threaten to derail the pace of China's progress on economic restructuring?
Or is it possible his death might pave the way for even swifter change?
Today, business leaders in the United States expressed an almost stubborn optimism that China would remain on its current course of economic modernization. 
And markets around Asia seemed to take his death in stride, with stock indexes in Tokyo, Hong Kong, Taipei and Shenzhen edging higher.
Trading in the Hong Kong stock market opened smartly Thursday, as the Hang Seng Index jumped more than 200 points. 
The market finished the day up more than 300 points to close at 13,411.3, for a 2.3 percent gain. 
That would have been inconceivable a few years ago, when people were talking about a drop of 30 percent after Mr. Deng's death, and it is a sign that more and more people accept that a leadership transition has taken place.
Mr. Deng's death was not only anticipated, but Mr. Deng had already set in motion an economic revolution in China that stretched far beyond what any one man could control.
"It is still a market of taxicabs and chauffeur-driven vehicles," said John F. Smith Jr., chairman and chief executive of the General Motors Corporation, which has a sizable business in China. 
"The roads are currently missing, so that has to come first."
Mr. Deng's death does not change the fundamental strength of the economy, which grew nearly 10 percent last year. 
Savings rates are still high, labor remains cheap. 
China's public works and legal systems both remain weak but they are improving.
"Nobody in China has really lost from economic reform, and in the beginning that was very important," said Nicholas R. Lardy, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. 
"But somehow along the line, you've got to start making some tough choices."
Those tough choices loomed while Mr. Deng was still alive, and they remain China's greatest challenge for the future. 
And yet, Mr. Deng's presence was so pivotal to China's economic restructuring that his own gradualist approach suggests how difficult it must have been at times to bring China this far.
It will certainly be hard to match the magic of China's former patriarch. 
When Mr. Deng made what has become known as his imperial journey to the south in 1992, a time when economic restructuring was stalling, he was nominally just a retired old man.
But in fact, his trip paved the way for remarkable changes in national economic policy. 
A "socialist market economy was in favor;" central planning was out. 
And suddenly, a new economic vitality spread rapidly throughout the country.
Mr. Deng was a decisive leader, and when problems arose or critics swooped down on him, he forged ahead steadily and determinedly. 
That is exactly the opposite of the approach taken by Jiang Zemin, China's cautious Communist leader.
Mr. Deng had the influence to override conservatives who thought economic modernization should proceed much more slowly. 
China still has a clutch of elderly leaders, some of whom are ardent, revolutionary purists, and they may now press for a slower pace of economic restructuring. 
It is unlikely they will win, but there may at least be a tortuous, protracted battle that itself could delay economic change.
Finally, Mr. Deng had the political capital to make dramatic and painful changes in China. 
He did not always exercise it, but he did begin to allow companies to lay off workers and he gingerly began to accept the concept that companies could go bankrupt.
Still, in a sense, one of Mr. Deng's critical economic contributions survives him: economic restructuring is no longer an ideological question. 
It is more of a technical one.
When the Chinese leadership debates how to introduce capital markets or dissolve inefficiencies in the state sector, the debate is not over whether these steps are allowable. 
Instead, they are about the concrete process of how to go about orchestrating the change.
For example, how can welfare benefits be taken away from people?
How can workers be laid off, and how can new jobs be found for them, to keep them from protesting in the streets?
They are issues that are as much a headache for any capitalist leader.
In some ways, China's younger, more technocratic and worldly crop of leaders are better equipped than their elderly predecessors to handle the next stage of economic challenges. 
Mr. Jiang and Mr. Li probably understand the technical issues about the economy better than did Mr. Deng, and they are acutely aware that a vibrant, flourishing and progressing economy is the core of their legitimacy.
But they may not have a strong enough political will, the discipline or the mandate to carry out unpopular measures. 
Moreover, if the Chinese leadership is divided, neither Mr. Jiang nor Mr. Li may have the ability to break the impasse.
There are a cast of characters surrounding Mr. Jiang and Mr. Li in the collective leadership, and one or another of them may be potentially daring and shrewd enough to emerge as a kingmaker.
One leader who sometimes has demonstrated a flair for the bold is Zhu Rongji, a Deputy Prime Minister who is often considered China's new economic czar. 
He helped steer China's overheated economy to a soft landing in recent years, curbing inflation without choking growth.
Some even see him as China's Gorbachev, or a future emperor, though, those who do are mostly foreigners. 
Indeed, with Mr. Deng gone, some economists like Mr. Lardy say there may be possibilities for faster or more substantial progress to be made if well-informed, better-trained technocrats are allowed to proceed with restructuring.
China's economic successes have been phenomenal. 
But along with this wealth has come signs of the evils of 19th century industrial capitalism in the West. 
Fly-by-night companies in China often produce dangerous products, families send their children to sweatshops instead of schools, inequalities are expanding, and the get-rich-quick mentality creates its own excesses.
Mr. Deng was perhaps not courageous enough to confront the most troublesome remnant of Communism: the inefficient state sector and the circle of financial and systemic problems surrounding it.
"I think there were some things that it was harder to raise and debate openly while he was still alive," said Robert A. Knapp, president of the U.S.-China Business Council.
China's state sector used to be the core of its economy, but now it is draining the economy dry, Mr. Knapp added. 
Loans to inefficient state-owned enterprises have doubled as a percentage of gross national product, according to Mr. Lardy.
"When we look back in 5 to 10 years, I think his legacy will not look so strong," said Mr. Lardy. "Because it will be more readily apparent that part of the success of Deng's strategy has been one of deferring reform. 
So he has left it to the next generation of leaders to make some of the tough choices."

file: China Agrees to Resume Talks With U.S. on Human Rights.txt
text:
ï»¿
Claiming both diplomatic and commercial victories today, Commerce Secretary Ronald H. Brown said he had won a commitment from Chinese leaders to resume a high-level dialogue with the United States on human rights.
At the same time, Mr. Brown said that his trade mission to China had led to the signing of agreements totaling $4.9 billion with Chinese Government industries.
Mr. Brown, who is leading a delegation of 24 American executives on a six-day Chinese tour, said that if all the agreements reach the final contract stage, more than $2 billion of the total would go to American firms participating as equipment sellers or joint-venture partners.
Â 
A Modest Step
The resumption of the human rights dialogue, broken off last March after a stormy visit to Beijing by Secretary of State Warren M. Christopher, is regarded as a modest but important step by Western officials concerned about the deterioration of human rights conditions in China during the last three months.
Since Mr. Clinton announced May 26 that he would no longer link progress on human rights in China to the annual renewal of Beijing's trade privileges, Chinese security agencies have continued to clamp down on political dissidents and religious activists. 
Beijing has also broken off talks to open its prison system to visits by the International Committee of the Red Cross.
At a news conference this afternoon, Mr. Brown said the success of the delegation's visit "speaks volumes about the wisdom of the policies President Clinton has pursued" in dealings with China.
"There hasn't been a meeting in which we haven't raised human rights issues," Mr. Brown said. 
"But we haven't tried to bludgeon them about it."
Mr. Brown said the first positive indication that China was ready to resume a human rights dialogue came from Prime Minister Li Peng in a meeting Monday. 
Mr. Li said China was willing to have a dialogue on human rights, but only on an "equal footing" and with "mutual respect."
Mr. Brown said he raised the issue today in a meeting with President Jiang Zemin, and an aide in Mr. Jiang's office telephoned later to advise that China was ready to resume the dialogue with a meeting between China's Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, and Mr. Christopher in Washington in late September. 
At the same time, the State Department's top human rights official, John Shattuck, will meet with a senior Chinese Foreign Ministry official in New York.

file: China and Taiwan Agree to Keep Their Discussion Going.txt
text:
ï»¿
As a senior official from Taiwan ended a landmark visit here, China and Taiwan promised to continue talking but also reiterated their profoundly different visions about the island's political status.
The differences, extending even to what they ought to discuss, suggest that a solution to one of Asia's most dangerous rifts remains distant.
"Only when the Chinese mainland has achieved democracy can the two sides of the Taiwan Strait talk about reunification," said Koo Chen-fu, the 81-year-old tycoon representing Taiwan here. 
His statement followed an hour-and-a-half discussion with China's President and Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin.
This morning, after Mr. Koo had a blunt exchange of views with Deputy Prime Minister Qian Qichen, Mr. Koo complained that Beijing still failed to recognize "one simple fact, which is the existence of the Republic of China."
His use of that name reflects the decades-long rift. 
In 1949 the Republic of China, governed by the Nationalist Party, lost a civil war to the Communists, who then founded the People's Republic of China. 
The Nationalist Government fled to Taiwan, which Beijing has considered a renegade province ever since.
After the morning meeting a Chinese spokesman, Tang Shubei, said Taiwan must "look upon the mainland objectively and bravely face up to the international situation."
He added, "Don't be an ostrich."
Still, both sides seemed eager to put the best face on this visit and to keep the diplomatic wheels spinning. 
Even if they produce no breakthrough, continued talks are seen by both sides -- and by keenly interested bystanders like the United States -- as a way to head off a disastrous conflict that nobody wants.
China is anxious to negotiate Taiwan's return to the motherland. 
Taiwan has become a relatively prosperous democracy. 
More and more its people have an independent identity, and its Government vows that it will not even consider reuniting with the mainland until China, too, is transformed.
Mr. Koo, leader of Taiwan's semiofficial Straits Exchange Foundation, came to the mainland on Wednesday to meet with his counterpart, Wang Daohan, 84, the leader of China's Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Straits.
The two elder statesmen met in Singapore in 1993. 
But a second meeting scheduled in 1995 was canceled by China, which was angered by what it saw as moves by Taiwan toward independence. 
Relations reached a dangerous low in the next year as China shot missiles near Taiwan during the island's presidential election and the United States warned China to back off by sending two aircraft carriers near the area.
China has vowed to attack Taiwan if it declares independence and is pressing for political negotiations aimed at bringing the island under its wing. 
It has offered greater autonomy than that granted last year to Hong Kong -- if Taiwan will accept Chinese sovereignty. 
The offer includes the right to preserve its capitalist economy, hold elections and maintain its own army.
But Taiwan refuses to negotiate about its political status, insisting that China must acknowledge that Taiwan's Government is already sovereign in practice. 
Instead, Taiwan wants to talk about matters like fishing disputes and the treatment of cross-strait visitors and businesses.
During the current visit, the two sides pledged to continue the newly reopened dialogue, and Mr. Wang accepted an invitation to visit Taiwan at an undetermined future time.
Reflecting both sides' desire to keep up positive momentum, the question of future agendas was blurred: the Chinese said Taiwan had agreed to include political matters, while the Taiwan representatives said today that the practical issues they wished to discuss included, of course, a political element.
The meeting this morning between Mr. Koo and Mr. Qian included the most pointed and honest exchanges in a visit mostly filled with smiling toasts and visits to tourist sites.
In his meeting with President Jiang late this afternoon, which lasted half an hour longer than scheduled, Mr. Koo said in an interview, the divisive central question of Taiwan's political future was not directly discussed. 
He described the meeting as pleasant and friendly, and said the two had engaged in a general discussion about the meaning of democracy, with Mr. Jiang emphasizing that the mainland had its own needs and path.
A central goal of China, and of many of Taiwan's business leaders, is for Taiwan to lift its restrictions on direct travel, commerce and communications across the strait at a time when the island's investment and trade here are climbing. 
Mr. Koo said the restrictive policy represented Taiwan's effort "to strike a balance between security and commercial concerns."
"If we could get assurance that China will not use force against us, then we could talk about this," he said in the interview.
The Taiwan representatives, while expressing a desire for friendly dialogue, took several opportunities to publicize their positions.
When Mr. Wang, the Chinese official, agreed to make a return visit to Taiwan, the Taiwan delegation immediately suggested that he go in early December, so he could view at first hand the country's democratic legislative elections. 
The Chinese said that would be a bit too soon.
During the current visit, officials back in Taiwan complained that China was aggressively continuing its strategy of isolating Taiwan diplomatically, courting some of the 27 countries that still recognize Taiwan.
In this morning's meeting, Mr. Qian, the Chinese Deputy Prime Minister, said it was only a natural development that more countries would switch allegiance from Taiwan to the mainland, since that was the official United Nations position, according to Chinese media accounts.
The third-ranking member of the visiting delegation, Kang Ning-hsiang, has a well-known history as a democracy advocate on the island and is now associated with a pro-independence opposition party. 
The Taiwan officials asked if he could be one of the small group attending the Koo-Jiang meeting, but the Chinese refused. 
So this evening, when Mr. Koo gave a final news conference, Mr. Kang was also given a chance to speak, and he made his plea for democracy in China.
This morning, Mr. Koo surprised the Chinese by announcing that Taiwan was considering asking to join an American-led multinational program in North Korea that aims to forestall production of nuclear weapons ingredients by helping to provide other energy sources. 
China is generally annoyed by such efforts by Taiwan to gain international acceptance, but today it had no clear reaction.
Mr. Koo said he was encouraged by the visit. 
"We'll keep talking, and we'll find ways to narrow the differences," he said in the interview. 
"We do have the patience."
But diplomats here wonder and worry how patient China will be on reunification, which it calls its overriding foreign policy goal.

file: CHINA AND TAIWAN IN HIJACKING PACT.txt
text:
ï»¿
Officials from China and Taiwan signed an agreement today intended to end a recent string of hijackings from China. 
Diplomats on both sides described the accord as a breakthrough in the relationship between the two old rivals.
The agreement was welcomed because the hijackings had undermined Beijing's latest air safety drive and threatened its tourism industry. 
But more importantly, the accord represented a first step in cooperation between the two Governments, which have no formal diplomatic relations. 
Both describe themselves as the sole legitimate authority in all of China.
China, which considers Taiwan to be one of its provinces and has long threatened to reclaim it by force, appeared to make most of the major concessions. 
For the first time, China has agreed to recognize Taiwan's authority to decide which hijackers should be returned to China, and which are political refugees who may remain.
Under the accord, China also will recognize Taiwan's authority to patrol fishing in the Strait of Taiwan.
The pact sets up a framework for the return of hundreds of illegal Chinese workers being held in Taiwan.
In the statement signed today in Taipei, the two sides also committed themselves to "increasing communication" that will "eliminate misapprehensions, reduce differences and nurture trust."
China was apparently willing to compromise on the issue of returning air pirates in the hope of ending the hijackings, which kept reminding the world that some citizens found China so oppressive that they would do almost anything to get out.
Taiwan is holding all 16 Chinese citizens involved in the 12 hijackings since April 1993. 
All the hijacking suspects but one have been convicted of air piracy and sentenced to prison. 
The 16th is awaiting trial. 
Under the accord, it is not clear if Taiwan is willing to send any suspects back.
Most of the hijackers were seeking political asylum, apparently fearful that the recent talks would close their last escape route.
China had initially demanded that the hijackers be returned unconditionally for trial in China, where they would have faced the death penalty.
Officials on both sides hailed the agreement, which they described as the most important step toward closer ties between the two Governments since their first landmark meeting 16 months ago in Singapore.
"You can say there has been a major breakthrough," said Chiao Jen-ho, secretary general of Taiwan's semi-official Strait Exchange Foundation, which handles relations with Beijing in the absence of formal ties.
But Taiwanese officials were reported to have warned that the accord did not indicate that the two countries had moved closer to reunification. 
Taiwan has moved in the last few years to acknowledge the Communist Government's de facto authority over the mainland, increasing Beijing's fears that Taiwan would eventually seek recognition as an independent nation.
Mr. Chiao's counterpart, Tang Shubei, secretary general of China's Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Strait, was quoted in news reports as agreeing that the accord, reached Sunday in Taiwan after eight days of talks, was a breakthrough.
Mr. Tang was the highest-ranking official from the Chinese mainland to visit Taiwan since the Nationalists fled to the island in 1949 and banned official contact with Beijing. 
His association acts on behalf of China's Government on issues involving Taiwan.
While trade and tourism between the two countries have increased rapidly in recent years, diplomatic relations remained ice-bound until the Singapore meeting last year, which produced little beyond a schedule for further contacts. 
Relations deteriorated rapidly last March when 24 Taiwanese tourists were killed in an arson attack on a pleasure boat on Qiandao Lake in southern China.
The killings, and efforts to cover up their cause, set off a wave of anti-Chinese sentiment, with polls showing increasing support for Taiwan to declare itself independent.

file: China Announces Arrest of a Senior Aide.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese authorities announced today that a former senior national police official had been arrested in connection with the government's investigation of corruption and smuggling in Xiamen, a southern port city.
It was the highest-level arrest announced so far in a billion-dollar smuggling scandal surrounding the Yuanhua Corporation. 
Several trials of lower-level officials implicated in the scheme began earlier this week in five cities in Fujian province.
In the announcement today, Zhao Dengju, deputy head of the Supreme People's Procuratorate, the country's top antigraft body, told Chinese journalists at a news conference that Li Jizhou, a former vice minister of public security, had been arrested late last year for taking "huge bribes" in connection with the Yuanhua smuggling case.
He added that Mr. Li had also been charged with taking bribes in two other smuggling cases in Guangdong province, according to the state-run China Radio International.
Until a recent government crackdown on graft, vast smuggling rings in southern China -- generally working in collaboration with government officials -- made huge profits by illegally importing a wide range of goods, including fuel, cars, cigarettes and electronic equipment.
As part of the same crackdown, the former vice chairman of Parliament, Cheng Kejie, was executed today for taking $5 million in bribes and kickbacks. 
Mr. Cheng, who was sentenced in July, is the highest-ranking official executed for corruption since the Communists took power in 1949.
"There is no place for corrupt elements to hide in the Party," said a commentary in People's Daily, the main Communist Party newspaper.
Corruption is widespread at virtually all levels of government, a fact that has greatly tarnished the party's image. 
China's leaders and, according to opinion surveys, ordinary citizens both point to corruption as the country's greatest problem.
The central government began a major campaign late last year to clean up government, led by Prime Minister Zhu Rongji. 
Hundreds of investigators were dispatched to Xiamen to delve into the Yuanhua smuggling empire and collusion with dozens of local officials.
But critics have complained that the investigations tended to focus on low- and mid-level officials and that the government's enthusiasm for public arrests went cold when the trail led to senior officials.
For example, when it seemed like government investigators were poised to implicate the wife of Beijing's Communist Party chief, Jia Qinglin, a protege of President Jiang Zemin, in the Yuanhua case, a government press office took the offensive to clear the couple's names.
The exact extent of the crackdown is unclear, since most high-level investigations are kept under wraps. 
But over the past six months, the arrests have slowly moved up the chain of command and have become somewhat more public -- presumably in part to satisfy public demands for more action.
Indeed, though the arrest of Mr. Li took place late last year, Mr. Zhao announced it only today. 
The deputy procurator-general's relatively candid discussion of the Yuanhua case also marks a change from the general secrecy.
Mr. Zhao said that from January to August this year, the national prosecutor's office had investigated 4 officials at the rank of minister or provincial governor and 100 at the rank of head of a bureau.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: China Appears Ready for Trial Of a Leader of Outlawed Party.txt
text:
ï»¿
One leader of a suppressed new political party will be tried on Dec. 
17 on a charge of colluding with foreign enemies of China "to incite the subversion of state power," according to court documents given to his wife today.
The decision to try the leader, Wang Youcai, a founder of the China Democracy Party, with unusual speed suggests how serious the Communist authorities are in their campaign to destroy the fledgling party and silence dissidents who had begun to speak out over the last year.
The charges that Mr. Wang faces, in a trial that will almost certainly be secret and quick, could bring a sentence of five years or more. 
Mr. Wang, 32, has been imprisoned in his home city, Hangzhou in eastern China, for a month, but was formally arrested on Nov. 
30. On that day two prominent dissidents, both promoters of the new party, were detained.
One, Qin Yongmin, 45, of the central city of Wuhan, and the other, Xu Wenli, 55, of Beijing, are being held on suspicion of subversive activities. 
Detailed charges have not been filed.
Mr. Wang was a student leader in the pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in 1989. 
After the army crushed the movement Mr. Wang was arrested and served two years in prison.
Mr. Qin and Mr. Xu became known as democracy advocates in the late 1970's. 
Mr. Qin was imprisoned for eight years. 
In 1993 he was put in a labor camp for two years. 
Mr. Xu spent 12 years in prison.
Mr. Wang announced the formation of the Democracy Party when President Clinton visited in the spring. 
He and other dissidents hoped that China's new friendship with the United States and its decision to sign a global covenant on political and civil rights would give them room to promote political alternatives.
After Mr. Clinton returned home Mr. Wang was detained, warned and released, only to be re-arrested as authorities began what now appears to be a major crackdown on dissent. 
Today, Mr. Wang's wife, Hu Jiangxia, was handed the bill of prosecution, according to the Information Center of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in Hong Kong.
Mr. Wang is charged with helping draft a party manifesto that states, in part, "Only by establishing an opposition party can we be rid of this despotism."
That is cited as grounds for the subversion charge, the information center said.
In addition to detailing Mr. Wang's organizing activities, the prosecutors charge that he colluded with enemies of the state abroad, making his crime far more serious.
He used E-mail to send 18 copies of the party's founding documents abroad, met with a member of a subversive foreign organization and received money from foreign sources to buy a computer, the indictment reportedly says.

file: China Appears To Crack Down On CD Pirating.txt
text:
ï»¿
Off a meandering dirt road that cuts through soft hills laden with tropical foliage, a pair of young women tended to thousands of newly hatched ducklings in a rundown shack one recent afternoon, enveloped by a gentle chorus of chirping.
Behind this innocent-looking setting lay a workshop where copyright pirates hid a crude but lucrative operation that illegally copied millions of compact disks until an anonymous caller told the local authorities, who came and shut it down in February.
The duckling hatchery is still in business, but two compact disk production lines were confiscated and three men who ran them were taken into custody by officials who said later that they had rarely seen such a well-disguised operation.
The caller was given $36,000, an enormous sum in a rural area of southern China where duck tenders make $25 a month.
After years of dragging their feet, and ignoring demands from the United States and elsewhere, China's copyright police are finally pursuing and arresting pirates, even well-hidden ones. 
The authorities are also being creative, trying to pierce the shell of local secrecy by offering informants bricks of cash.
Since a concerted effort began in December here in Guangdong Province, the acknowledged center of copyright piracy in China, the authorities say they have arrested more than 100 offenders and shut down 28 underground factories, where each disk-making machine could copy 10,000 disks a day.
Dozens more factories are believed to exist, but many have suspended production, apparently in the hope that the current campaign will subside after a few months. 
After all, the history of Communist China is a catalogue of political campaigns, most of which last just a few months or a year before they are overtaken by new ones.
Fighting copyright piracy in China, one of the world's biggest violators of intellectual property rights, often looks like an unwinnable task. 
Yet industry experts say Beijing seems serious about the current crackdown, in part because it is beginning to recognize the dangers that piracy poses to China's own legitimate music and movie industries.
The stimulus for the current crackdown, officials here and in Beijing say, is a domestic crusade for "spiritual civilization" that President Jiang Zemin is trying to make his political signature as he consolidates his power as the successor of Deng Xiaoping, the political patriarch who died in February.
Mr. Jiang is expending a fair amount of political capital on the drive, because it has been opposed by many local officials, army officers and members of the secret police who have profited from the trade.
To overcome such opposition, which stymied previous attempts to enforce laws against piracy, Mr. Jiang is framing his campaign as one aimed at pornography, something China's leaders strongly object to. 
Even though dirty movies account for only about one-tenth of the pirated videos in China, the current crackdown is called "Sweep Away Pornography; Combat Illegal Copying."
While devised as a purely domestic campaign, Beijing is also using the crackdown to comply with parts of an agreement signed with the United States in February 1995. 
Current efforts are winning guarded approval from industry experts who monitor intellectual property abuses.
"Since December they've been doing really well," said Cheng Ching-ming, the representative in China of the International Federation of Phonographic Industries, a London-based organization representing more than 100 music companies. 
"The question is whether they will keep up the pressure, which they need to do for a few years to succeed."
In perhaps the strongest sign yet of greater confidence in Chinese enforcement, Warner Brothers recently signed an agreement with a Shenzhen-based company that was suspended in 1995 for copyright violations to start legally producing video compact disks of 100 movies owned by Warner.
Similarly, many other compact disk factories that pirated music in the past are now getting more legitimate music business than they can handle, a sign that the crackdown is having an effect, said William A. Brent, a consultant specializing in China's entertainment industry.
Until this year, the Guangdong authorities acknowledged the existence of only 19 compact disk factories in their province, because they only counted the legally registered outfits, many of which were investigated and found guilty of piracy.
With most legitimate factories behaving legally, local officials now admit that there are several dozen underground factories that were churning out large quantities of illegally copied disks until recently, and continuing on a smaller scale now.
"There's so much money to be made, people will continue to take risks," said Chen Jiakui, who heads Guangdong Province's office on copyright violations. 
"It's not something that can be stopped in a day, but we're making a difference."
United States trade officials say they deserve at least some credit for Beijing's new resolve. 
But the fact that the Chinese authorities began a serious crackdown only in recent months, after years of pressure from Washington, suggests that China's domestic politics are the greater influence.
The decision seems to have been made by Communist Party leaders at a Central Committee meeting last September. 
Even so, Mr. Chen said, the Guangdong authorities held meetings for three months before they announced a plan of action on Dec. 
11.
On that day, officials here publicized new efforts to ferret out underground pirates, who have begun to hide their compact disk copiers in increasingly obscure places. 
One method is to offer the $36,000 reward to any caller whose information leads to the closing of an illegal operation. 
"We recognize now that we can't find all these offenders without help from ordinary people," Mr. Chen said.
More than 20 of the 28 illegally operating factories that were shut down since last year, he said, were identified through information from anonymous callers.
Even so, Mr. Chen conceded that winning the fight against piracy would involve far more than arresting the factory managers, and that backers -- often Hong Kong and Taiwan businessmen involved in organized crime -- are harder to catch.
"If you put the workers in jail, that doesn't solve it," Mr. Chen said. 
"The real problem is the big bosses."
The nexus of organized crime, the Chinese secret police and movie piracy came to light in late 1995 in an incident involving the International Federation of Phonographic Industries.
Mr. Cheng, the group's representative, pushed the Guangdong authorities to prosecute a local company, which he had learned was run by a senior official in the Guangdong State Security Bureau and was copying a high volume of pornographic movies supplied by shady Hong Kong businessmen. 
In late 1995, secret police agents came to Mr. Cheng's office and demanded that he retract his allegations.
After Mr. Cheng persisted, the police agents jailed him for a week, saying he had "threatened China's security."
They never formally charged him, apparently a violation of China's legal procedures.

file: China Applauds as Its Officials Plunge Into Profit.txt
text:
ï»¿
Happily married, his career flourishing, a 31-year-old midlevel city official named Lu Zhoukui abruptly decided last August to xia hai, or plunge into the sea.
Mr. Lu was not feeling suicidal, and in fact it may have been the best decision he ever made. 
"Plunging into the sea" is the new slang in China for going into business, and it is becoming a nationwide craze.
Tens of millions of Government and Communist Party officials are plunging into the sea. 
Deng Xiaoping's youngest son has dived in, along with the children of most other top leaders, and the official newspapers are full of praise for the phenomenon.
"From top to bottom, the Government is encouraging us to do business," Mr. Lu said as he sat in the anteroom of his plush new office in this eastern Chinese city. 
"The only restriction is that the business must be legal."
Â 
Cash Over Politics
It says something about the giddiness of the economic and social revolution under way in China that the Communist Party is hailing its officials for abandoning their posts to the temptations of capitalism. 
More fundamentally, the rush to plunge into the sea reflects the growing sense among China's elite that power and comfort and prestige in the coming years will no longer derive from political position, but rather from hard cash.
One measure of the trend is that the number of registered companies in China soared 88 percent last year alone, rising to 486,000. 
The registered capital of private enterprises surged 79 percent in the year, to $3.9 billion.
Fragmentary statistics suggest that about one-third of China's 103 million Government employees have leaped into the sea, or at least waded in far enough to get a second, part-time job. 
Many more Chinese are expected to take the plunge, for the word is getting out that the sea is warm and inviting -- and that almost no one sinks.
Mr. Lu, for instance, started a company in August to engage in everything from running restaurants to placing Chinese laborers in foreign jobs. 
The company turned a profit of $219,000 in the four months it was operating last year, and this year Mr. Lu is expecting a profit of almost $1 million.
By comparison, his income at his old Government job was $46 a month.
Â 
Some Troubling Questions
Nevertheless, the trend toward leaping into the sea raises some troubling questions. 
Some people worry, for instance, that China is becoming a nation of money-grubbing materialists, in which intellectuals are obliged to sacrifice more important work just to keep up with the Wangs.
There was considerable disquiet when a Beijing newspaper reported that a Communist Party secretary at the Forestry University was selling meat pies on the side. 
It is not clear which of two items bothered readers more: that the man would stoop to be a vendor or that by doing so he tripled his income.
"I am totally appalled," a commentator wrote in The Guangming Daily News, a newspaper for intellectuals. 
"I'd like to read the professor's works rather than eat his meat pies."
A broader question is whether those leaping into the sea are unfairly taking advantage of their guanxi, or connections. 
Good guanxi are paramount in China, for they make the difference in getting bank loans, electricity, running water and tax waivers. 
Guanxi are often more important than rules.
Â 
How He Hired Russians
Mr. Lu, for instance, is about to open a restaurant with Russian waitresses. 
Many other bars and restaurants around China have lately been forbidden to hire Russians, partly because of concern that some engage in prostitution.
Perhaps Mr. Lu has obtained permission through luck, or through astute preparation. 
But it cannot hurt that he knows all the city officials, and that calligraphy given to him by the provincial governor is hanging in his office.
"Some of these people going into business worked for many years in Government offices, and they have lots of contacts," said Zhang Huafu, the Deputy Mayor of Yantai. 
"I can't deny the problem. 
But because of this problem, we shouldn't oppose the whole idea of people going into business."
The term "plunging into the sea" reflects the sense of daring and uncertainty that is associated with business in China. 
Much of that is dissipating, but one recurring problem is finding housing.
Â 
Having to Return Apartments
Government employees normally get low-cost apartments from the state, and unless they have good guanxi, they often have to return their apartments when they go into business. 
Private housing is difficult to obtain and extremely expensive.
Wang Quanjie, a 42-year-old engineer in Yantai, is now grappling with the housing question. 
Mr. Wang, who used to oversee leather factories for the city government, left his job in July with 10 colleagues to form a leather research institute.
Mr. Wang and his friends have done extremely well, winning consulting fees from factories and making back their starting capital of $17,000 five times over. 
Like most Chinese who plunge into the sea, they raised the money by dipping into savings and by borrowing from friends and relatives. 
Also like most, they are trying to use their guanxi with friendly officials to get large loans from Government-run banks.
The problem is that the Government gave them a one-year grace period to leave their housing. 
So the staff has to find new apartments this summer.
"That's a huge headache for all of us," Mr. Wang said. 
"I've got to figure out how to house all my staff."
Â 
Quitting Is Avoided
Partly to avoid losing their apartments, many Chinese leap into the sea without formally quitting their other jobs. 
They neglect their work, but keep the salaries and housing, knowing that it is very difficult to be dismissed.
A result is that while not enough officials have resigned to create staff shortages, many schools and offices have a very clear shortage of employees concentrating on their work.
Policemen moonlight as pimps. 
Factory workers wave rags on street corners as an offer to wash cars. 
University students sell photocopiers and X-ray machines on commission. 
Professors become corporate consultants, working with such enthusiasm that The Economic Daily complained recently about faculty members who rush out of class when their beepers go off.
As for Chinese journalists, a joke going around says there are now five kinds of reporters. 
The top tier is made up of those who run a business on the side, and they are followed by those who play the stock market.
The third kind sells advertisements as a sideline, winning a typical commission of 7 to 12 percent from their business departments. 
The fourth kind freelances for other publications.
"The bottom rank of journalists is the least respected," said a reporter for one of China's most distinguished newspapers. 
"They're the ones who actually do the work and write the front-page stories."
Â 
Traditionally Demeaned
Traditionally in China, Confucianism looked down on business people, and until recently officials and intellectuals disdained commerce as demeaning. 
Many Chinese also regarded business as risky, because of fears that private enterprises would be confiscated if hard-liners returned to power.
The term "plunging into the sea" apparently originated early in this century in Shanghai but then migrated to Taiwan, where it was a pejorative expression for young women working as prostitutes. 
The term returned to mainland China last year, and fell into common use only in the last six months.
But on the journey from Taiwan, the meaning of the phrase was twisted to reflect the broader concept of going into business in any way. 
Now it encompasses moonlighting professors as well as prostitutes.
Because of the traditionally negative associations of engaging in private business, in the early and mid-1980's a hugely disproportionate share of entrepreneurs in China were ex-convicts. 
They could not get any respectable job and so were forced into business.
Â 
Ex-Convicts Are Prosperous
A result is that perhaps in no other country are ex-convicts so prosperous. 
China often boasts about its low recidivism rates; one reason is that released prisoners -- mostly common criminals, but also some dissidents -- are part of an old-boy network that offers some of the most lucrative jobs in the country. 
For making useful business connections, Beijing No. 1 Prison is the Harvard Business School of China.
As time passes, fears of a major policy reversal by the hard-liners are diminishing, and so is the scorn for private business.
A well-known writer, Zhang Xianlang, has just started his own holding company, setting up a huge billboard as its first project. 
And China's most famous movie actress, Liu Xiaoqing, has started the Xiaoqing Industrial and Commercial Company, with interests varying from cosmetics to real estate.
Â 
Favorite Job Preference
A survey of young people found that their top job preference was to be an entrepreneur. 
National Government work ranked 8th out of 16 choices.
All this is very heartening to those who have plunged into the sea, like Wang Qian, who left her Government post last summer to join the private leather research institute in Yantai.
"A few years ago, it would have been tough for somebody in my present situation to find a boyfriend," said Ms. Wang, 24. 
"Then a woman in business could look for a boyfriend only among other traders."
"But now it's very different," Ms. Wang added, beaming. 
"People accept the fact that it's a market economy. 
Anybody will go out with you."

file: China Asks Auction Houses to Withdraw 4 Relics.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese government has thrown the art market in this capitalist outpost into an uproar by asking Sotheby's and Christie's to withdraw four relics -- which Beijing says were stolen 140 years ago -- at next week's auctions of Chinese antiquities here.
An official at the State Cultural Relics Bureau said that the objects, a vase and three sculptures, were taken from a Qing dynasty palace when it was ransacked by British and French troops. 
The official, Wang Limei, said that the bureau was asking Sotheby's and Christie's not to sell them in Hong Kong because "it is insulting and deeply painful to the Chinese people to have these things sold before their eyes."
Hong Kong, the former British colony that is home to some of the world's richest Chinese, has long been a fertile market for dealers in rare Chinese antiques. 
But Beijing has steadily tightened its grip on Hong Kong since it reverted to China in 1997. 
Now it is making its presence felt in the art market, declaring that the city should no longer be a clearinghouse for treasures stolen from imperial China.
Sotheby's and Christie's said on Saturday morning that they would proceed with the sale of the relics as planned. 
The Christie's auction is scheduled to begin Sunday in the ballroom of an upscale hotel here. 
Sotheby's will open bidding on its collection on Tuesday at an equally deluxe hotel nearby.
"It's full-speed ahead for us," said Carlton Rochell, the managing director of the China and Southeast Asia division at Sotheby's. 
"We're doing everything we can to satisfy their concerns about the objects in question."
Victoria Cheung, a spokeswoman for Christie's, said the sale of the items was "part of our routine calendar of auctions."
She declined to comment on Christie's negotiations with the Chinese government.
It is not clear that Beijing would have the authority to prevent Sotheby's and Christie's from holding the sales even if it tried. 
Hong Kong is a separate legal jursidiction from mainland China, and mainland laws that protect China's national treasures do not apply here.
Chinese government officials said they had not demanded that the relics be returned because, 140 years after the looting of the palace, it would be difficult to prove that they were taken from the country illegally.
In late March, United States Customs officials seized a 10th-century marble sculpture that was to have been auctioned at Christie's gallery in New York City. 
In that case the Chinese government said it had proof that the sculpture, a painted relief panel, had been stolen by raiders who had broken into the Five Dynasties tomb of Wang Chuzhi in Hebei Province in northeastern China.
Neither Sotheby's nor Christie's disputes that the four relics were taken from the old summer palace, known as Yuanmingyuan. 
Indeed, Christie's is promoting its auction as "The Imperial Sale: Yuanmingyuan," and the company's Web site promises that the sale will feature "some of the most sumptuous artworks made for the Manchu emperors of the 18th century."
Beijing objects to the sale of two bronze heads -- an ox and a monkey -- that were part of a set of 12 in a zodiac fountain in the palace garden. 
Christie's estimates the value of the ox head at $500,000 to $580,000. 
It did not value the monkey head or disclose the owners of either piece.
Sotheby's is auctioning a bronze tiger's head that it says was part of a water clock commissioned by the emperor and designed by a French astronomer for the grounds of the Old Summer Palace. 
The catalog does not estimate the value of the sculpture or disclose its owner.
The second of its disputed relics, a hexagonal vase, is featured on the cover of the catalog. 
Sotheby's speculates that the vase "may have been brought directly from the Old Summer Palace, Beijing, by Lord Loch of Drylaw, after it was burned down in 1860."
By playing up the Old Summer Palace, Sotheby's and Christie's have resurrected one of the most sensitive chapters in Chinese history. 
The palace, an 870-acre estate in Beijing, was sacked and burned by British and French troops during the second Opium War.
Though there are only a few ruins left, the Chinese government has kept the episode alive in history books and propaganda as an example of the country's humiliation at the hands of foreigners.
Mr. Rochell said he was mindful of the emotions stirred by artifacts from the Old Summer Palace. 
But he noted that the Sotheby's auctions here often result in relics' being transferred from Western owners to Chinese owners, whether from Hong Kong, Taiwan or even mainland China.
"I don't want to exaggerate this point," Mr. Rochell said. 
"But in a sense, these auctions have been repatriating a great deal of objects back to China."

file: China Bans One of Its Own Films_ Cannes Festival Gave It Top Prize.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a bleak omen for the Chinese cultural world, the Government has banned one of the nation's most acclaimed films after just a few showings.
The leaders had approved a censored version of "Farewell to My Concubine," a movie that follows the lives of two Peking Opera actors through five turbulent decades of recent Chinese history. 
But last week the authorities abruptly halted its release and distribution without offering an explanation.
The ban will not affect the movie's planned release in the United States in the fall. 
But it means that Chinese audiences will be unable to see the first Chinese film to win the top prize at the Cannes International Film Festival.
From the Politburo's point of view, the problem is that "Farewell to My Concubine" deals with homosexuality and depicts some of the turmoil in the Communist period.
Worst of all, a leading character commits suicide. 
That might be tolerable if the death occurred during the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976, when most of today's leaders were out of power. 
Instead, it takes place in 1977, when Deng Xiaoping and other Chinese leaders were already clawing their way back to the top.
Normally the Chinese authorities ban a film in obscurity and almost no one hears about it. 
But to their huge embarrassment, a quiet execution is impossible this time.
Â 
The Praise and Prizes
In May, "Farewell to My Concubine" was a co-winner of the Palme d'Or, the top prize at the Cannes International Film Festival. 
The other film was "The Piano," a romance set in New Zealand.
"Farewell to My Concubine" also received the International Critics' Prize for "its incisive analysis of the political and cultural history of China and for its brilliant combination of the spectacular and the intimate."
Critics have given the movie some excellent reviews. 
Vincent Canby described it in The New York Times as "a handsome, exotic, beautifully acted film, full of the kind of humanism that festival juries like to commend."
The ban is a retreat in what has overall been a process of cultural liberalization in China. 
Books, magazines, music and art have all been flourishing and mostly finding ways to evade the cultural commissars.
The Propaganda Department, which is adjusting to the times by changing the translation of its name to Information Department, is loosening controls over news organizations and is even allowing a wave of talk-radio programs. 
Satellite dishes and cable systems are sprouting around the country, allowing millions of citizens to watch Hong Kong and Taiwan films and serials.
Speaking of the ban, Chen Kaige, the director of the film, said today, "When this kind of thing happens in my country, I feel very hurt."
He said his intention in the film had not been to pass political judgment on the Government, and he noted that films like "The Godfather" and "Platoon" were not regarded as anti-American even though they depicted violence by organized crime and the trauma of the Vietnam War.
Officials from the Chinese Film Bureau and the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television declined to comment today. 
The Chinese distributor, the Beijing Film Studio, also refused to say anything. 
By some accounts, the Politburo itself screened the film and decided to ban it unless major changes were made.
"Farewell to My Concubine" opened in Shanghai on July 26, and two weeks' worth of tickets promptly sold out, reportedly setting a record in the city. 
The authorities have allowed the film to continue its run there for all the performances whose tickets have been sold, apparently for fear of angering audiences who had paid nearly $4, half a week's salary for a typical worker, for each ticket.
In Beijing, the Government allowed a premiere on Wednesday last week but no other showings. 
The film has not been allowed in any other cities.
The ban already is having a chilling effect on other productions. 
Mr. Chen, the director, said he had put aside plans to film "Life and Death in Shanghai."
The book, by Nien Cheng, describes the sufferings of one family during the Cultural Revolution.
Mr. Chen said that for now at least, he had also dropped the idea of making a movie of the early life of Jiang Qing, the actress who became Mao Zedong's wife. 
Both projects would be far more sensitive than "Farewell to My Concubine," which is not directly political.
Harvey and Bob Weinstein, the co-chairman of Miramax Films, which is to release "Farewell to My Concubine" in the United States, expressed outrage at the ban.
"We have been through this sad situation before and were hopeful that the blatant suppression of artistic freedom in China had changed since then," the Weinsteins said in a statement. 
"Obviously that is not the case."

file: China Buying U.S. Computers, Raising Arms Fears.txt
text:
ï»¿
Since President Clinton deregulated the export of computers in 1995, China has gone on a shopping spree, buying 46 American-made supercomputers and many more that are nearly as powerful, according to Government officials.
The newly acquired computers could be used by the Chinese to design more efficient or lighter nuclear warheads that could be put on missiles capable of reaching the United States, American intelligence officials and nuclear experts said.
Several officials said they have suspicions -- but no direct evidence -- that China is using the powerful computers for this purpose.
Clinton Administration officials who defend the 1995 policy said they believe that the civilian purchasers in China are making sure the equipment is not diverted to military uses.
Gary Samore, the senior director for nonproliferation and export control at the National Security Council, said, "We don't have any information that these computers are being used by the Chinese for military purposes, including nuclear weapons."
At the same time, Mr. Samore said, there were no formal military or intelligence investigations of that question. 
The Government's knowledge, he said, was drawn largely from the computer companies.
There are disagreements among American officials about the importance of the Chinese purchases of supercomputers. 
But Gary Milhollin, a nuclear expert in the private sector, said of the 46 supercomputers, "For the first time these give China access to a larger number of computers in this range, and that's a big jump for the Chinese."
The supercomputers sold to China would allow the country to significantly improve its nuclear weapons by processing huge amounts of data from very small underground nuclear weapons tests. 
The tests are currently banned by international treaty, but the high-performance computers would allow the Chinese to conduct weapons tests with explosions so small that they would be undetectable by outsiders, said American Government officials who requested anonymity.
Under the 1995 policy, most supercomputers sold for civilian purposes do not need to be licensed for export by the Federal Government. 
Exporters consequently cannot be required to track how they are used.
The disclosure earlier this year that American companies had sold supercomputers to two Russian nuclear installations prompted Congress to ask for an accounting of how many had been sold to other countries.
At the time, the Republican chairman and the ranking Democrat on the House National Security Committee asked the President to "refrain from further" deregulation of supercomputer exports and to reassess the national security risks of allowing exporters to decide whomay buy supercomputers.
"We think many of the supercomputers sold to China are being integrated into the military weapons development area in a way that is going to make their weapons more sophisticated and lethal, and this could jeopardize our own national security interests," said Senator Thad Cochran, Republican of Mississippi, chairman of a Senate subcommittee overseeing the issue.
Clinton Administration officials said today that they were satisfied with deregulation. 
They argued that it would be nearly impossible for the United States to effectively prevent the Chinese from obtaining the computers from other sources.
The Commerce Department has been investigating last year's sale by Silicon Graphics of a supercomputer that performs almost six billion operations per second, operating at 10 times the speed of the fastest personal computer, to a Chinese science academy. 
The company says the buyer is a benign civilian institution, but according to nuclear experts, the academy has other functions, including helping China develop long-range missiles. 
The Justice Department is also investigating another Silicon Graphics supercomputer sale in 1996, to a Russian research institute that also serves as a nuclear weapons laboratory, the officials also said.
"One reason I ran for President was to tailor export controls to the realities of a post-cold-war world," President Clinton wrote in a September 1993 letter to Edward McCracken, the chief executive officer of Silicon Graphics.
In his 1992 campaign, Mr. Clinton received important political support from executives of high-technology companies, including Mr. McCracken.
Shortly after the President's 1993 letter, the Administration took its first steps toward decontrol. 
In October 1995 President Clinton announced that he would relax export controls on all but the most powerful supercomputers to help American companies compete abroad, saying the system would "adjust to the global spread of technology while preserving our vital national security interests."
But by eliminating the need for licenses on most computer exports, the President shifted some national security responsibilities -- avoiding the misuse of sensitive technology -- from the Government to the computer industry.
The Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration, William A. Reinsch, said the department was investigating some cases of unlicensed export of supercomputers to China and Russia, which could uncover more information about how the computers are being used. 
But he insisted that the relaxation of controls was a realistic solution since rapid changes in the flexibility and availability of computer technology make it easy for purchasers to circumvent controls.
"Where do you draw the line to be absolutely certain that no one in China has a supercomputer?"
Mr. Reinsch asked. 
"The only way is to insist on validated licenses on all computers and then deny them."
Another obstacle was thrown up when diplomatic and intelligence officials, wanting to protect their sources, refused to allow the Commerce Department to publish a list of buyers suspected of nuclear activity, according to Mr. Reinsch. Then earlier this year, 16 months after the White House promised that the Commerce Department would keep manufacturers informed of nuclear proliferation risks, the department publicly disclosed one name of a suspected nuclear installation -- an Israeli university.
Mr. Reinsch says more names will be disclosed soon, a move industry officials say they favor.
Robert Rarog, a spokesman for Digital Equipment Corporation, which has sold supercomputers to China, said his company feels that the deregulation "basically works" but that "the Government has to step up to the plate" and disclose questionable buyers "to level the playing field for U.S. companies" who compete with foreign manufacturers that may be less diligent.
In early 1996, Government nuclear experts asked the Commerce Department to provide supercomputer manufacturers with a list of sensitive nuclear sites in Russia and China to prevent misuse of their technology, but the Administration turned down the request, according to Mr. Milhollin, the director of the Wisconsin Project on Nuclear Arms Control. 
A Department of Energy spokesman confirmed Mr. Milhollin's account.
In an interview, Mr. Milhollin compared the relaxation of export controls to the 1980's deregulation of the savings and loan industry.
"The decision to decontrol supercomputers, without adequate safeguards was the equivalent to the deregulation of the savings and loans -- the industry benefited but the public welfare and security was sacrificed, he said."
A Senate subcommittee headed by Mr. Cochran will hold a hearing on the deregulation issue on Wednesday.Â Â Â Â Â Â

Leaders of the official Protestant church defended China's policies on religious freedom this week, asserting that a record 15 million Chinese now worship in approved Protestant churches and that persecution of so-called underground Christians is rare.
At a news conference that appeared intended in part to contradict reports -- like one from the State Department this month -- that religious persecution in China is on the rise, the church leaders charged that meddling by hostile foreign evangelists has caused many of the reported conflicts between Christians and the police.
They also said the claim that tens of millions of Chinese attend illegal "house churches" is exaggerated.
"Some hostile forces overseas are still reluctant to see the Chinese Protestant church become independent," said the Rev. Cao Shengjie, deputy director of the China Christian Council, one of two government-affiliated organizations that run the nondenominational Protestant church. 
Foreign religious groups use secret donations "to attract Chinese into illegal activities," she said, and their secret missionaries seek to "undermine the stabilityI of the country and the running of the official church."
The news conference by four elderly church leaders on Thursday was tied to their celebration of the 50th anniversary of the Chinese Christian Three-Self Patriotic Movement, founded to direct Protestant affairs after the Communist victory in 1949.
At midcentury, building a new church dedicated to "self-government, self-support and self-propagation" was essential, the leaders said, because the Chinese people saw missionaries as agents of Western colonialism.
"The imperialist powers used Christianity to invade China," said Luo Guanzong, chairman of the Three-Self organization.

We've shown that Christians can love the country and actively participate in building a socialist society."
Although Christians were severely persecuted during Mao's Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976, over the last 20 years the government has allowed the gradual growth of official Protestant and Roman Catholic churches.
Within the legal constraints -- pastors, liturgy and church construction are subject to official controls, public proselytizing is forbidden and children may not be baptized, for example -- many followers say they enjoy genuine Christian worship. 
On Sundays, legal churches tend to be packed.
But groups that refuse to register with the authorities have come under increased pressure, with leaders sometimes fined, detained or sent to labor camps, giving rise to charges that human rights and freedom of worship are being violated.
According to the State Department's Sept. 
5 report on religious freedom, in 1999, "some unregistered religious groups were subjected to increased restrictions -- including, in some cases, intimidation, harassment, and detention," but the degree of repression varied by region.

Their leaders say they cannot pledge allegiance to the atheistic Communist Party, or accept restrictions on their work to spread the Gospel.
Evangelical Christians from Asia, Europe and the United States provide encouragement and funds for this "house church" movement, and in one recent case three Taiwan-born Americans on a brief mission were detained in central China and expelled.
"It's true that some groups have not registered due to theological difficulties," said Han Wenzao, chairman of the China Christian Council.

"This is unrealistic," said Mr. Han, who argues that Christians should be thankful for the growth of the official church and the fact that a church-run company can print large numbers of Bibles.
The Roman Catholic Church here is also split, with an official "patriotic" church that rejects the authority of the Vatican and a large, illegal church that is loyal to the pope.

text:
