In a major step toward greater cooperation by China in rebuking North Korea at the United Nations, the Security Council expressed its "serious concern" today about the intrusion of a North Korean submarine into South Korean territory last month.

file: China Keeps Up Criticism As U.S. Welcomes Dissident.txt
text:
ï»¿
While Harry Wu was being celebrated as a hero in the United States, Chinese authorities continued their campaign against him today, portraying him as a thief, a fraud and a womanizer who wanted revenge against his native land.
Beijing's decision to release Mr. Wu, the Chinese-American human rights advocate, is widely expected to ease tensions between China and the United States. 
But the old Communist-style denunciations of him today are a reminder of how far apart the two countries remain on human rights.
Undersecretary of State Peter Tarnoff flew from Shanghai to Beijing this evening, and is scheduled to meet with Deputy Foreign Minister Li Zhaoxing on Saturday and with Foreign Minister Qian Qichen on Sunday. 
Mr. Tarnoff may also meet one or more senior leaders, who often wait until the last minute before confirming appointments.
Whatever benefits these diplomatic meetings bring to bilateral relations, they are unlikely to break much ground on the seemingly intractable issue of human rights.
Chinese leaders apparently decided to expel Mr. Wu less as a human rights concession than as a gesture to improve cooperation with the United States on other matters.
Political prisoners in China have often been used as diplomatic bargaining chips. 
Chen Ziming, a leading dissident, was released last year just before President Clinton decided to remove China's human rights record as a condition for extending its most-favored-nation trade status.
But Mr. Chen was taken back into custody in June as relations with the United States deteriorated. 
In recent months, China has taken dozens of other dissidents into custody. 
Just last week it detained Ding Zilin, a university professor who has pressed the authorities for a full accounting of how many people were killed in the June 4, 1989, massacre near Tiananmen Square.
Today, the harsh invective and detailed accusations hurled publicly at Mr. Wu seemed intended to communicate within China that the authorities were as tough on him as they would be with anyone who directly challenged the leadership.
"A man who was morally corrupt and did many evil deeds," is how an article in today's People's Daily characterized Mr. Wu.
It said Mr. Wu's thievery began in 1959, when he was a student at Beijing Geological College, saying he had stolen money from a classmate and was punished with three years of "reform through labor."
The article went on to accuse him of stealing public property, faking documents to get radios and electric fans, and forging his superior's signature on travel expense forms. 
It also alleged that he later tried to seduce a student at a university where he taught.
The article drips with innuendo, describing him as "morally degenerate," and accusing him of a lack of patriotism.
"His heart was full of hatred," the article said. 
"He felt China owed him, and he wanted to settle an old score with China."
Political prisoners in China often face trumped up charges with only a vague basis in fact.
Mr. Wu has said he was first taken into custody in China's radical campaign against political "rightists" in 1957, and was sentenced to life imprisonment in April 1960.
By his own account, Mr. Wu spent 19 years in prisons and in forced labor on state farms, coal mines and chemical factories. 
He was freed only in 1979, after Deng Xiaoping came to power and pardoned some political prisoners.
It was those years of suffering, and the memory of fellow prisoners whom he watched die, that Mr. Wu has said made him determined to expose the abuses of China's vast penal system.
Mr. Wu was allowed to leave China in 1985 to go to the United States as a visiting scholar. 
He became an American citizen and in 1992 set up the Laogai Research Foundation, named laogai for "reform through labor," a reference to forced labor camps. 
He returned to China several times to obtain fresh information about the labor camps and prisons.
Communist Party authorities insist on repentance from prisoners, as a way of showing submission, and official accounts of Mr. Wu's case have gone out of their way to say Mr. Wu recognized his wrongdoing.
"After considering his admission of guilt, his signs of repentance and the fact that he had been used by others, the court gave Wu a lenient sentence," one agency report said.
Yet, after all his years of experience in Chinese prisons, Mr. Wu appears to be expert at expressing respect and submission while evading any actual admission of guilt for the most serious charges leveled against him, in this case spying and stealing state secrets.
A New China News Agency report said Mr. Wu had signed a confession in court. 
Yet the account says he conceded only that "his actions had damaged the interests of the Chinese Government and the Chinese people, and violated Chinese laws."

file: China Licenses Four Foreign Insurers.txt
text:

China granted licenses to four foreign insurance companies today on the eve of Prime Minister Zhu Rongji's departure for a 14-day visit to the United States and Canada. 
He hopes to win a deal in Washington for China's entry to the World Trade Organization, and insurance and other financial services are a sticking point in the protracted negotiations.
The licenses were issued to the Chubb Group and the John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Company, both of the United States. 
The other two were the Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada and Prudential P.L.C. of Britain, which is not related to the American company of the same name. 
They join nine other insurers doing business in China.
China requires all foreign life insurance companies to find Chinese partners before they can sell insurance here. 
Foreign companies are not allowed to hold a controlling stake and life insurance companies may sell only individual life insurance plans.

But industry executives say insurance regulators are prepared to open as many as 10 more cities for foreign insurers soon.

file: CHINA MAY ALLOW RED CROSS TO VISIT DISSIDENTS IN JAIL.txt
text:
ï»¿
Signaling what would be a major policy shift on human rights, China said today that it would give "positive consideration" to allowing the Red Cross to visit more than 3,000 political prisoners.
Speaking with United States journalists, Foreign Minister Qian Qichen also said China viewed a meeting next week between President Clinton and the Chinese Communist Party Secretary, Jiang Zemin, as not for "picture taking," but as a discussion of "a broader and longer-term perspective" on bilateral relations.
The talks are to be held in Seattle during a meeting of national leaders from both sides of the Pacific.
Â 
'Left Over From the Cold War'
Mr. Qian indicated that Mr. Jiang would take a hard line against Washington's policy of linking trade preferences to China's human-rights record, a policy that the United States has insisted on since the 1989 military crackdown at Tiananmen Square.
"China does not accept linking questions unrelated to trade," Mr. Qian said. 
"This method is a means left over from the cold-war era. 
It is a means to exert pressure, and therefore one cannot expect China to accept this."
Mr. Clinton said in May that "overall, significant progress" in improving China's human-rights record would be the main criterion for whether he renewed China's favorable trade status with the United States next June.
Â 
Skepticism From Christopher
Just three weeks ago, Secretary of State Warren Christopher said he did not think he could recommend renewal of China's trade privileges because of China's human-rights record.
But in answer to a question about the desire by rights groups to inspect prisons, Mr. Qian said, "I believe that if the Red Cross does put forward such a request for exchanges, we would give positive consideration to that request."
[State Department officials said in Washington that the apparent decision by China to allow the Red Cross access to prisoners would be an important factor in determining whether China's favored trade status would be extended.]
Western diplomats and human-rights workers, who have been urging China to take such a step for years, applauded the move. 
If carried out, it would reverse four decades of refusals to allow any outside humanitarian organization access to the tens of thousands of Chinese who have been imprisoned, tortured or persecuted for their political beliefs.
Coming as it did days before Mr. Qian and Mr. Jiang leave for the United States, the statement was clearly timed to defuse the contentious atmosphere over China's record on rights.
Even though Mr. Qian rejected a link between trade and human rights, the turnabout on access to prisoners is clearly part of China's strategy to improve relations.
Access to prisoners is an explicit condition of Mr. Clinton's executive order on China's future trade relations. 
The order says China must make progress within one year on "insuring humane treatment of prisoners, such as by allowing access to prisoners by international humanitarian and human rights organizations."
The Asian representative for the International Committee of the Red Cross, Christophe Swinarski, said in a telephone interview from Hong Kong that the Red Cross would take Mr. Qian's statement "very seriously."
He hinted that talks on prison access could begin this week when Mr. Swinarski passes through Beijing on his way to North Korea.
John T. Kamm, an American businessman who has carried on private humanitarian work in China for years, characterized Mr. Qian's statement as "a significant change in the opinion of the Chinese Government."
"To me, the immediate impact of this announcement," he said, "is that it delivers a message to every warden holding prisoners that they better clean up their act because there is a very good chance the Red Cross is coming."
Apropos the talks in Seattle, business leaders in the United States have urged the Clinton Administration and the Chinese leadership to repair their relationship, which has been dominated by Washington's reprisals and threats on trade since China's crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in 1989.

Welcomed in Washington
WASHINGTON, Nov. 
9 (Special to The New York Times) -- State Department officials said today that the apparent decision by Beijing to allow the Red Cross access to political prisoners would be an important factor in whether Secretary of State Christopher would recommend extending China's preferred trade status.

file: China Migrants_ Economic Engine, Social Burden.txt
text:
ï»¿
With his possessions bundled in plastic and hung from his shoulders, and his trousers rolled up to beat the heat, 30-year-old Ren Jun drifted into Beijing this month, part of a migrant tide of 50 million peasants that is threatening to swamp China's urban landscape.
To the Communist Party leadership, they are the engine of China, an inexhaustible supply of cheap labor, a floating population helping to build the country. 
They are one reason that 5,000 factories can be simultaneously under construction in China's coastal provinces.
But they also are becoming a huge and at times unstable and exploited force rampant on the fringes of China's overcrowded and polluted urban centers, where crime, corruption and unemployment threaten stabilityII.
The migrants are easy to spot. 
Most large cities along China's coast have a million or two living in shanty towns, dormitories or public spaces. 
At Beijing's main railway station, a thousand migrants an hour pass through the green metal gates. 
And vast numbers of laborers like Mr. Ren appear each morning here at an impromptu labor market, hoping local coal-mine supervisors will pick them to work.
Â 
'A Positive Development'
"So far, I think it has been quite a positive development," said Fan Gang, a leading economist at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. 
"It has helped to transfer wealth from rich to poor areas of the country."
Richard Baum, a political science professor at the University of California at Los Angeles, called the mobile population "a shock absorber" that can flow from one sector of the fast-changing economy to another "to cushion the transformation of the Chinese economy."
At the same time, today's migration could be the harbinger of an even greater one to come, Chinese and Western specialists say. 
With 130 million surplus workers in China's farm belt and a surge in population growth that will push that number to 200 million by 2000, China's migrants are an X factor in China's future.
"In five years, this could become a very big problem," Professor Fan said.
Â 
Estimate of 70 Million
In March, Agriculture Minister Liu Jiang estimated that 50 million peasants had left their farms in 1993 to seek employment in the cities, more than double the 24 million who set off for the cities in 1992.
Some estimates put the "floating population" at 70 million to 100 million, said Dorothy Solinger, a China scholar at the University of California at Irvine. 
She also argued that the migrant problem "may not be as bleak as it is made out to sound."
"First, they are not all going to the big cities," she said. 
Many migrants simply move off farms into township enterprises nearby, or even far away, but not necessarily to large cities.
Second, she argued, where migrants do cluster, crime is the largest potential worry, not political rebellion. 
She pointed out that the Mayor of Zhuhai, the special economic zone adjoining Macao, recently said 75 percent of the crime in his city could be attributed to migrants.
But much is simply unknown, she said. 
The growth of the migrant phenomenon came from nowhere in a country that enforced rigid residency rules just a decade ago, making it impossible for peasants or city dwellers to stray from their work units.
What seems undisputed is that Pearl River delta in Guangdong Province has the largest concentration of migrants, an estimated 10 million. 
At least 500,000 are child laborers, Chinese surveys have shown; many work in sweatshop conditions.
Â 
Dangers of a Downturn
In Jiangxi Province, the outflow of farmers leaped from 200,000 in 1991 to more than 3 million last year. 
Shanghai's 13 million residents are now supporting 2.5 million rural workers attracted from all over the Yangtze valley to construction work on the city's vast redevelopment.
As long as China's economic growth gallops along at more than 10 percent a year, this floating population is likely to remain relatively well employed, prosperous and stable. 
But an economic downturn or recession could easily leave the migrants stranded and aggrieved.
"This is the labor of an exploited class," said a longtime Western diplomat here. 
"There are no wage laws to protect them, and they can be fired on a whim."
Professor Baum added: "It is a double-edged sword to be sure. 
They may be an efficient buffer helping to transform the economy, but they are also a large pool of marginal people subject to the vagaries and insecurity of having no rice bowl they can count on. 
They are dying in grotesque industrial accidents, they are locked in the dormitories at night, and they create a pocket of potential human misery wherever they cluster."
Â 
Building Subways and Hotels
Farmers from Sichuan Province are building Beijing's new subway, just as peasants from Zhejiang Province are building new freeways, hotels, office buildings and ministries. 
Many leave their villages because $1.25 a day on a sweltering construction site is more than they can earn working the land.
Others are "environmental refugees" from northern and western China where the land has just given out from degraded soil, dried up water resources or the relentless advance of the Central Asian deserts.
Many go home with money in their pockets, but many also go home nurturing grievances.
On a recent afternoon, six unkempt men lying on bedrolls in Beijing's main railway station explained why they were returning to Jiangsu Province after less than a month at work here. 
Their spokesman was a 24-year-old farmer named Liu with a face lined by weather and worry.
"We just don't want to work here any more," he said. 
"We left our construction team yesterday without notifying the boss. 
It serves him right."
The construction boss had come to Mr. Liu's hometown and promised to pay the villagers $1.72 a day to lay bricks and pour concrete. 
He said he would also pay for their train tickets. 
But when they got to the site, near Beijing's international airport, the boss cut their wages to 57 cents a day and told them they would have to pay for their own train tickets.
Â 
The Uses of Money
Their tempers simmered for a month before they decided to head back to the farm, where their wives were looking after the rice crop.
Speaking in a tone that reflected their intimidation in the big city, Mr. Liu said: "We dare not walk in Beijing alone. 
We are new here. 
Some people might find faults with us, or fine us."
Remittances from peasants who do find work are dramatically redistributing the new wealth.
Professor Fan said that in one county in Sichuan Province, migrants remitted $138 million last year, more than the total economic output of the county, which was $115 million. 
A recent study of China's rural economy said migrant farmers from Anhui Province sent home $862 million, which exceeded the provincial government's annual revenue by $230 million.
What is most remarkable, however, is the sheer mass of migration.
During Lunar New Year celebrations, when all 1.2 billion Chinese are drawn home to their families, train stations became encampments for hundreds of thousands of travelers a day, Woodstock-sized crowds of peasants waiting for trains in dozens of rail hubs.
Â 
52 Trampled to Death
At the New Year in February, China's overburdened rail system pressed special freight trains into service, each one bulging with human cargo packed so tightly that some passengers became hysterical with claustrophobia. 
In one accident, 52 people were trampled to death when 10,000 migrants were herded onto a freight train in Hunan Province.
Mr. Ren arrived recently in Beijing hoping to land a job in the local coal mines. 
He made his way to the labor market, becoming one face in a sea of laborers for hire.
Alarmed at the rapid growth of Beijing, the municipal authorities have posted signs saying the market has been closed. 
This has not stopped the peasants from coming, nor has it stopped gangs of criminals from prowling the market, looking for women and children to abduct and sell into China's booming trade in prostitutes and wives for sale.
Â 
From One City to Next
Policemen on foot patrols often scatter the workers like so many chickens.
One laborer who kept well away from the police was Wang Xinmin, 24, who has migrated from one city to another since he left Henan Province at 17. 
Too much work on not enough land put him on the road, he said.
He has worked in the far south, at a garment factory in the special economic zone of Shenzhen, adjacent to Hong Kong, but it did not last.
"The local people there bullied us because we were from the countryside," he said. 
And the factory boss, who had promised high wages, delivered only half of that on payday.
"The working conditions were really unsafe and chaotic," he said, "and though we were supposed to work eight hours a day, actually we had to work much longer."
Having lost his most recent job, as a busboy, Mr. Wang said he would try for two more weeks to land another job in Beijing before heading home.
Â 
Farming 'Not Worth It'
Mr. Wang sat cross-legged under a pine tree near the labor market, and when he finished telling his story, he listened to one from Mr. Ren, who comes from a line of farmers in the hardscrabble hills of Hebei, 120 miles northwest of Beijing.
"People like me don't want to work on the land anymore," Mr. Ren said. 
"It's backbreaking work. 
I've tried it. 
The land is not fertile, and it is far from any water. 
It's just not worth it."
If he stayed home and worked the land, Mr. Ren said, he might earn $345 a year if rain were plentiful. 
But working in a Beijing coal mines, he might take home nearly $700.
In either case, it is not enough to get a wife these days. 
"I would like to have a wife," he said. 
"But the dowry demands of girls are very high," higher even than the wages of a migrant coal miner.

file: China Moves To Cut Power Of Microsoft.txt
text:
ï»¿
Janet Reno is not the only one worried about Bill Gates's software monopoly. 
China's leaders are, too.
They are concerned that the country is growing overly dependent on the Windows operating system, which controls computers running everything from banks to President Jiang Zemin's e-mail box. 
But the Chinese government, itself a master at monopoly, is taking its case against Microsoft not to the courtroom but to the marketplace, albeit with a bit of administrative fiat. 
It is backing the Linux operating system, which was created by a Finnish university student in 1991 and is distributed free to anyone.
"We don't want one company to monopolize the software market," said Chen Chong, a deputy minister of information industries who oversees the computer industry in China. 
With Linux, "we can control the security," he added, so "we can control our own destiny."
A growing number of Chinese have likened dependence on Microsoft to leaving the keys to the country's increasingly computerized economy in the hands of a potential enemy. 
Some warn that secret holes in Microsoft's computer code might allow the United States access to Chinese networks or even enable it, in time of war, to shut those networks down.
Such concerns were only heightened last year when a cryptographer for a Canadian software firm working in the United States said he had found a feature in Windows called an NSAKey -- as in National Security Agency, the United States government agency that gathers electronic signal intelligence worldwide. 
Though Microsoft said the key was innocuous and no support has been found for any sinister explanation, "no one can guarantee that Windows does not have back doors," said Liu Bo, a former Microsoft executive who is now chief executive of Red Flag, a government-backed company set up to create software based on Linux and to encourage a homegrown software industry.
In addition, various arms of the government have been warning of the security risk posed by the country's reliance on Microsoft. 
"Without information security, there is no national security in politics, economics and military affairs," declared an editorial in People's Liberation Army Daily earlier this year.
Microsoft calls such fears nonsense and says it continues to enjoy a strong working relationship with the government. 
"We have shared product information with them," said Michael Rawding, Microsoft's regional director in China, "and I believe that their comfort with our product information led them to allow the launch" of Windows 2000, Microsoft's new business-oriented operating system, in China last spring.
Unlike the Windows source code, which Microsoft keeps secret, the Linux code is open for all to see and is freely distributed with the stipulation that anybody can improve it as long as any modifications are shared with the rest of the world. 
The almost communistic "from each according to his ability, to each according to his need" approach appeals to China's Marxist leaders.
Despite the government's stand, no one is suggesting that Microsoft is finished in China. 
Though it will not provide specific sales figures, the company says its software sales in China surged 80 percent last year and continue to grow. 
But the government's move to diversify reflects a broader dissatisfaction with the company and its founder, Mr. Gates, who just a few years ago was hailed as a hero by China's young technology enthusiasts.
The turning point in Microsoft's image was the introduction of its Chinese-language Windows 95 operating system, which was programmed to display references to "Communist bandits" and to exhort users to "take back the mainland."
Beijing, infuriated to learn that Microsoft had used computer programmers in Taiwan to write the software, demanded that the company hire mainland programmers to fix it.
Chief among the company's critics is its former general manager for China, Juliet Wu, who has become a national celebrity with her withering, best-selling expose, "Up Against the Wind: Microsoft, I.B.M. and Me."
The picture she paints of Microsoft as an arrogant Goliath feeds into the irritation many Chinese computer users feel toward the company.
Ms. Wu and other critics say Microsoft's pricing -- a software program can cost as much as an average office worker's monthly salary -- forces users to buy pirated copies of the company's software. 
(The Business Software Alliance, a nonprofit trade group, estimates that as much as 95 percent of all software in China is pirated, though the industry hopes China's expected admission to the World Trade Organization will change that.)
Liu Dongli, an Internet entrepreneur in the southern province of Fujian, was so enraged by having to pay $241 for Windows 98 that he sued the company for unfair pricing. 
The suit was withdrawn when Mr. Liu realized that Microsoft charges no more for its products in China than it does elsewhere. 
"But that doesn't mean we lost the case," he fumed, vowing to bring suit again when he has more evidence. 
"Monopoly is not a good thing."
The news media, meanwhile, have criticized Microsoft for suing a company last year over the sale of pirated software. 
Microsoft, which was asking for $200,000 in damages, lost the case because the Chinese court ruled that it had sued the wrong company. 
The defeat only darkened Microsoft's ominous silhouette in the eyes of many Chinese.
"Microsoft is a bully," said Hua Yuqing, a young Internet entrepreneur, who complains that Microsoft's high prices and proprietary computer code squelch creativity. 
He is building a business creating software programs that run on Linux. 
"I don't want to feel that I'm subconsciously controlled," Mr. Hua said, referring to the dependence on Microsoft that comes with using its products.
Mr. Hua and a half-dozen computer programmers peck away at their keyboards here in a drab office empty except for computers, desks, chairs and a shelf stocked with bottles of orange soda and boxes of chocolate milk. 
He and his colleagues are using Linux to start a company that provides services to subscribers over the Internet -- in this case, the use of accounting software and sales-tracking software. 
The software stays on Mr. Hua's server computer, and customers rent it rather than buy their own.
Microsoft's public relations disaster has been a boon for Linux. 
So far, several companies -- including Red Flag, which is backed by President Jiang's son, Jiang Mianhang, and TurboLinux, based in San Francisco -- have introduced Chinese-language versions of the Linux operating system in China. 
Many other companies have started to provide software and services for China's Linux users.
The Chinese government tried for more than a decade to develop an operating system of its own, but was unable to keep up with the fast-changing industry. 
Linux gives the country the tools to build that system now -- and, in the Chinese view, the fact that the Linux code is not privately held assures that any security it wants to build into its computer systems will not have undetectable vulnerabilities.
But even Linux enthusiasts profess ambivalence about the government's interest. 
Linux developers in China say some overseas colleagues worry that China may not play by the rules for collaborating and sharing and may adapt Linux to create a proprietary system instead.
In any case, China represents a market potential of such size, and government influence over the market is still so strong, that Beijing's support can turn almost any product into an industry standard domestically. 
By the end of next year, the country may well be the third-largest PC market in the world, and software sales are expected to grow more than 30 percent a year for the foreseeable future.
As China's economy becomes increasingly integrated with that of the region and the world, much of Asia is likely to follow its lead.
Mr. Liu, the chief executive of Red Flag, says a third of the country's Internet servers -- the computers that power Web sites -- are already using Linux operating systems. 
He estimates that by the end of next year Linux will run half of all servers in China and as much as a third of the country's desktop computers.
Those estimates may be overblown; the technology research firm IDC Asia-Pacific says its data shows less than 3 percent of all servers shipped to China last year were loaded with Linux. 
But IDC expects the number to more than double this year, and Linux's real market share is most certainly higher because the operating system can be downloaded free from the Internet.
"Linux, without doubt, has gained some headway among software developers in China," Mr. Rawding said. 
"However, I have yet to see any mission-critical organization deploy Linux because the truth of the matter is that in businesses, you want the support and service to be available to you instantly when something does go wrong."
Nonetheless, Great Wall Computer, one of China's biggest PC makers, has already shipped 200,000 desktop computers loaded with the Linux operating system, which looks much like Windows though it cannot yet match all of Microsoft's features.
Ma Li, marketing chief at Great Wall, says his company shifted toward Linux at Beijing's urging. 
"As a leading enterprise," he said, "we should respond to the call of the government."

file: CHINA OPPOSES U.N. OVER NORTH KOREA.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a major blow to international efforts to force North Korea to give up its nuclear weapons program, China announced today that it opposed the imposition of any sanctions against North Korea.
Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, speaking at his annual news conference, said that his Government not only opposed sanctions but also was against bringing up the matter before the United Nations Security Council.
North Korea announced earlier this month that it was withdrawing from the treaty to halt the spread of nuclear weapons and would not allow international inspections of suspected nuclear weapons laboratories. 
The United States and other Western countries hope to pressure North Korea to reverse its position.
Because Beijing has a veto in the Security Council, today's announcement means that there is little chance of using the Security Council to coordinate an international response. 
And without China's cooperation, sanctions would have little meaning, as it is one of the few countries that still trades with North Korea.
"We support patient consultations to reach an appropriate solution," Mr. Qian declared. 
"If the matter goes before the Security Council, that will only complicate things."
Â 
Quiet Pressure From China?
China may be applying quiet pressure on North Korea to return to the nuclear pact and give up its nuclear aspirations, which have alarmed the entire region. 
But if there is no threat behind the pressure, it is unclear that China's pressure will be successful.
For several years, Beijing has apparently been urging North Korea not to develop nuclear weapons. 
However, Western experts believe that the hard-line Communist Government in North Korea has quietly continued its program and is near to building a nuclear bomb or may already have constructed one or more.
China is North Korea's most important friend left in the world, and even Beijing has been clearly annoyed by North Korea's actions lately. 
Mr. Qian did not endorse North Korea's position, and he reiterated China's view that nuclear weapons should not be introduced to the Korean Peninsula. 
China itself is a nuclear power.
Mr. Qian's opposition to international pressure on North Korea is almost certainly linked to China's discomfort with the idea that international bodies can tell sovereign nations what they can and cannot do. 
Western countries have frequently accused China of human rights violations, of making destabilizing arms sales, and of brutal repression in places like Tibet, and China's standard answer is that no nation has the right to interfere in another's internal affairs.
In his news conference, Mr. Qian also said that the time was not right for a meeting with the British Foreign Secretary, Douglas Hurd, about the dispute between China and Britain over Hong Kong, which is to revert to Chinese control in 1997. 
Mr. Qian disclosed that Mr. Hurd had suggested a meeting, but he added that "conditions are not ripe."
But Mr. Qian did not rule out negotiations at some point in the future, and he did not issue quite as fierce a denunciation of Great Britain as some other Chinese leaders have in recent days.

file: China Picks Local Banker After Portugal Cedes Macao.txt
text:
ï»¿
For 442 years, Portuguese officials have ruled this spit of land on the southeast coast of China. 
Today, Macao got its first Chinese leader. 
A committee appointed by Beijing chose a local banker, Edmund Ho, to administer the colony after it reverts to Chinese rule in December.
Mr. Ho's ascension had been widely anticipated here. 
He is the de facto leader of Macao's Chinese business community and has close, longstanding ties to the Chinese Government.
There was a palpable lack of suspense as the 199 committee members -- a lone Portuguese among them -- filed to the front of a wood-paneled auditorium and deposited their ballots in a box. 
After 30 minutes of counting, Mr. Ho was declared the winner with 82 percent of the vote.
The meticulously choreographed ceremony recalled one in Hong Kong more than two years ago in which a shipping magnate, Tung Chee-hwa, was selected as the chief executive of the former British colony.
But unlike Hong Kong, where demonstrators burned tires to protest Mr. Tung's selection, people here had few reservations. 
Most regard Mr. Ho, the 44-year-old scion of a prominent Chinese family and a longtime member of the legislature, as the obvious choice for chief executive.
"There were no real alternatives," said Ricardo Pinto, the editor of Ponto Final, a Portuguese-language newspaper here. 
"If you look around the local political scene, there is no one with the same stature."
Macao is in a deep recession, which has been aggravated by a violent gang war for control of its lucrative gambling trade. 
Many people here believe the departing Portuguese have given up trying to control the violence, and most are more relieved than alarmed about returning to China.
"I fully understand that the people of Macao are concerned about law and order," Mr. Ho said at a news conference after his selection. 
But he said it was too early to offer details on how he would tackle the problem.
Mr. Ho pledged to defend "one country, two systems" -- the arrangement under which Macao, like Hong Kong, is supposed to function as a semi-autonomous region in China with its own legal system.
"With the support of our motherland, the people of Macao shall enjoy a high degree of autonomy and become self-governing," said Mr. Ho, who switched seamlessly between Cantonese, Mandarin, and English.
Despite Mr. Ho's skills, people worry that Macao will be swamped by China. 
Its civil service is not as well developed as that of Hong Kong. 
Chinese officials have expressed anger at Macao's crime rate. 
And China has already sent troops to the colony, ignoring the objections of Portuguese officials, who said their agreement with China does not provide for a military garrison.
Gazing down from a dais during the ballot counting were two aging men who will arguably wield more power over Macao than Mr. Ho: Qian Qichen, the Deputy Prime Minister of China who is overseeing the handover, and Stanley Ho, a Hong Kong tycoon who owns the colony's nine casinos. 
(He is not related to the chief executive).
On the issue of troops, Edmund Ho served notice that he did not plan to provoke officials in Beijing.
"I believe the stationing of troops is in total accordance with the sovereignty of the Chinese Government," Mr. Ho said. 
"My position is in 100 percent agreement with the central Government."
Ng Kuok Cheong, one of Macao's few pro-democracy politicians, said Mr. Ho's response was typical of his outlook. 
Mr. Ng, who said he had lost two jobs because of his political views, predicted that under Mr. Ho, debate about China would be even more sharply curtailed than it is now.
Despite his allegiance to Beijing, Mr. Ho is also popular with the Portuguese, who regard him as tactful and reliable. 
Macao's Governor, Gen. Vasco Rocha Vieira, warmly welcomed his selection.
While Mr. Ho is respected, his father, Ho Yin, is venerated. 
The elder Mr. Ho, who died in 1983, dominated Macao society for decades, playing middleman between the Chinese and Portuguese. 
When anti-colonialist protests exploded during the Cultural Revolution in the 1960's, Mr. Ho calmed both sides.
"For a long time, Edmund has been living under the shadow and patronage of his father," said Fok Kai Cheong, a professor at the University of Macao. 
"It's time for him to prove himself."
Mr. Fok said it was in China's interest to insure that Mr. Ho succeeds. 
Macao's handover is the second act in what Chinese officials hope will be a three-act drama, culminating with the return of Taiwan. 
"This is considered another step in the ultimate reunification of China," he said.

text:

President Jiang Zemin today told a Congressional delegation led by the House majority leader that China "is going to make an effort" in coming months to meet President Clinton's concerns about the country's human rights record.

But the delegation took the Chinese President's positive tone as an encouraging sign.
Mr. Jiang's remarks to the majority leader, Richard A. Gephardt, and five other House members came at a crucial time, just before the release of a State Department human rights report that is critical of China and could affect its trade status as a most favored nation. 
His remarks also came in the middle of important talks with Washington on China's textile imports.
Â 
An Unusual Response
Although Mr. Jiang did not present any detailed course for improving China's human rights record, his remarks were significant in that Chinese officials almost never respond directly or positively to any admonition from foreigners about their human rights record. 
In public statements, Chinese officials uniformly reject American intercessions on human rights as interference in China's internal affairs.
In Washington, a State Department official said today that Mr. Jiang's comments, as reported by the delegation , were "very, very encouraging."
The official said that several recent developments suggested that China understood Western concern about its human rights practices. 
But he said the United States was looking for more evidence.
Â 
'Let's See What Happens'
"Today's meeting was quite positive and encouraging, but let's see what happens," the official said.
At a news conference, Mr. Gephardt praised the extensive diplomatic engagement that is under way with China and said he hoped that it would lead to a resolution of disputes.
"We are hoping for progress on human rights," Mr. Gephardt said. 
"To date there has not been sufficient progress, but we are not at the end of the process. 
We have another six months to go."
Â 
Chinese Seriousness Seen
After the news conference, Mr. Gephardt said the most positive aspect of his visit was that he felt for the first time that the Chinese leadership was "really serious" about resolving its most contentious issues with the United States, beginning with human rights.
"We have a number of important differences," Mr. Gephardt said, "but we are working hard to resolve those differences."
The delegation members, who said they were in Beijing at Mr. Clinton's request, also met with China's economic czar, Zhu Rongji.
The visit is part of the torrent of diplomatic contacts between Washington and Beijing aimed at averting a confrontation later in the year over China's poor human rights record.
China has until June to demonstrate "overall, significant progress" in human rights or Mr. Clinton has threatened to end China's most-favored nation access to the American market, which entitles Chinese companies to export their goods to the United States at very low tariffs.
Human rights abuses also played a major role in the rejection of China's bid to be the host of the Olympic Games in the year 2000, despite a vigorous campaign by Beijing.
In case the Chinese did not get the message from Mr. Gephardt, the White House is sending Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen here this week.
Â 
Bush on Private Visit
The sometimes blunt exchanges with Mr. Clinton's emissaries were overshadowed in the Chinese press by coverage of former President George Bush's private visit to Beijing.
"I think the U.S.-Chinese relationship is very, very important," Mr. Bush told the Chinese President. 
"It's very important to stay on track."
Officials at the United States Embassy said they were unaware of any coordination between Mr. Bush and the White House over his visit, though former Presidents as a matter of courtesy often carry messages and report on the results of their trips.
American officials said that before leaving the United States, Mr. Bush was briefed by the State Department and the staff of the National Security Council, but that he is carrying no official messages.
Mr. Bush also met with the Chinese Prime Minister, Li Peng, whom most American officials avoid because of his role in ordering the military crackdown that led to the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989.
Mr. Clinton issued his conditions for continued favored trade status in a May 1993 executive order, and Mr. Gephardt's visit to China is part of the "midterm" review of its progress on human rights.
In deciding whether to extend China's trade privileges, American officials said they would use criteria specified in Mr. Clinton's executive order. 
At a minimum, there must be greater freedom of emigration and less use of prison labor. 
In addition, the Administration will consider whether China has made progress on other human rights issues, including respect for the religious and cultural heritage of Tibet.
A member of Mr. Gephardt's delegation, Representative Norm Dicks, Democrat of Washington, and the American Ambassador, J. Stapleton Roy, both described Mr. Jiang's statement to the delegation.
Mr. Roy said the Chinese leader's remarks were consistent with other recent positive responses senior Chinese officials have been making to American officials regarding the human rights abuses that routinely occur at the hands of China's security services and the judicial and prison authorities.
Â 
Talks With Red Cross
Chinese officials also told the Congressional delegation today that China would begin detailed discussions this weekend with the International Committee of the Red Cross on a program that could allow the first Red Cross visits to Chinese political prisoners in the history of Communist rule.
Western diplomats here said the release this week of two Tibetan human rights campaigners was also an important development indicating that the Chinese leadership is taking some early steps on Tibet, where larger issues of autonomy and freedom of expression are proving very difficult to solve.
American officials saw the release as a good-will gesture coming before Secretary of State Warren Christopher meets with China's Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, in Paris on Jan. 
24 and 25, but some human rights groups cast it as a move timed to coincide with the State Department's annual human rights report. 
A draft of the report, which is to be released in the coming week, states that China has not made substantial progress on human rights.
The remarks also coincide with last-minute talks to prevent a trade war over a threat by Washington to cut Beijing's textile export quota by 25 to 35 percent. 
China has said it will strike back if the United States proceeds with the plan.
Besides Mr. Dicks, the House members accompanying Mr. Gephardt here are George Miller of California, Mike Synar of Oklahoma, Chet Edwards of Texas and Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, all Democrats.
Â 
'Mixed Message' Possible
Mr. Gephardt acknowledged that some members of Congress are opposed to canceling China's trade privileges at a time when American companies are seeking new markets in China's booming economy, and he said the Chinese leadership might be receiving a mixed message from Washington.
"Anyone who observes the United States for any period of time will always be able to get a mixed message," Mr. Gephardt said, but he added that "it would be a grave mistake for anyone to think" that China's trade privileges "could not be stopped."
The delegation also delivered a list of 19 political prisoners who are reported suffering from medical problems and asked that they be released on parole.

file: China Puts Director In Suspense Over a Film.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Jiang Wen's powerful wartime film, "Devils on the Doorstep," won the Grand Prize in Cannes in May -- second only to the festival's Palme d'Or -- the word was that he faced trouble with China's film censors.
Two months later, that seems an understatement. 
His film languishes unscreened, officially condemned for political reasons that seem drastically out of kilter with China's increasingly buoyant, sophisticated society.
He has also fought with his investors over their demands, on commercial grounds, to shorten the 2-hour, 40-minute movie.
And now Mr. Jiang, one of China's most acclaimed actors as well as a second-time director -- he starred in Zhang Yimou's classic "Red Sorghum" in 1987 and the recent hit television series "Beijingers in New York" -- sounds utterly despondent.
"It's all too much like a Hitchcock thriller," Mr. Jiang, 37, said in an interview. 
"There's terror all around me, but I can't see what's going on."
Strangely, Mr. Jiang said, he personally has never been officially notified of the long list of demands made by the notoriously conservative Film Bureau. 
The bureau vets all scripts of films made in China and then must approve the finished product for release, often nit-picking scripts and nixing topics that can be broached in newspapers, magazines and books.
Mr. Jiang said the film's producers, the Asia Union Film and Entertainment Company of Hong Kong and the China Film Co-production Company, a required government-run partner that ushers foreign companies through the bureaucratic maze, had been told not to show him the Film Bureau's document.
More ominous, Mr. Jiang and his friends have heard repeated rumors that the Film Bureau plans to bar him from making or acting in films for many years. 
He said he had tried to meet with the authorities to discuss the matter but had been repeatedly rebuffed.
An official of the bureau's film censorship committee, Zhou Jiandong, said today: "The film hasn't been banned. 
It just hasn't passed the inspection process."
"This film has lots of problems," Mr. Zhou said in a telephone interview. 
"It was shown at a film festival abroad without prior approval, which is a clear violation. 
This film is at odds with a number of regulations concerning film content and distribution."
Asked about the rumors that Mr. Jiang might be barred from making new films, the official would only say: "We're still dealing with the matter. 
I can't say how they will resolve these problems."
"Devils on the Doorstep," which features Mr. Jiang as an actor as well as director, tells the story of a wounded Japanese soldier held prisoner by Chinese villagers in the last winter of World War II, as the Japanese invasion is crumbling.
In a story replete with ironies and cultural misunderstandings, most of the villagers treat the man well for a time, before they decide to trade him back to the Japanese for grain.
The rapacious Japanese occupation of China is a deeply sensitive historical topic here, a source of persistent personal bitterness and of frosty exchanges between the Chinese and Japanese governments.
This has led to contradictory attacks on Mr. Jiang. Long before the film was completed, government censors, not known for their appreciation of irony, began demanding that he change the title, apparently worried that characterizing the Japanese as devils might cause a furor. 
His producers, too, urged him to find a new title, worried about alienating potential Japanese viewers as well as about Beijing's approval. 
But Mr. Jiang would not budge.
Virtually all of the points raised by the censors in their review of the finished movie, though, involve its failure to paint every character in politically correct colors.
Copies of the April 21 appraisal have been faxed around Beijing, and it has even appeared on the Internet. 
It reads almost like a parody of censorship from the heyday of Mao's Cultural Revolution in the 1960's.
"The Japanese military anthem is played many times throughout the film," the letter says. 
"This signifies the strength of the Japanese military and severely hurts the feelings of the Chinese people."
"The Chinese are called 'chink pigs' by the Japanese many times throughout the film," it says. 
"This severely damages the image of China."
More generally, this "Official Opinion From the Film Censorship Committee of the State Administration of Radio, Film and Television" complains that too many Chinese in the film behave in a friendly manner toward the Japanese, "creating the impression that Chinese civilians neither hated nor resisted the Japanese invaders."
Mr. Jiang is berated for changing previously approved scenes and for failing to make previously demanded changes.
"There is a shot of a naked female," the letter says. 
"In general the style of the film is too vulgar."
The film's producers are invited to resubmit the film after complying with a lengthy list of demands for cuts and changes, and so far the matter remains at an impasse. 
But given the sweeping condemnation, it is hard to see how Mr. Jiang could make the film acceptable even if he tried.
"I feel pulled in all directions, and my will has been completely exhausted," Mr. Jiang said today.
"I'm just a filmmaker," he said. 
"I wanted to show how people react under extreme danger, how Chinese and Japanese responded and how in the middle of a war, people can lose all humanity.
"I never expected it would become so tangled up and politicized."
Mr. Jiang's plight is hardly unique. 
Since the mid-1990's the Film Bureau has if anything tightened its grip on filmmaking, causing anguish and humiliating choices for many directors and sending some abroad, leaving others to stick with innocuous topics.
The bonds of convention, prudery and ideological correctness imposed on domestically made movies seem all the more outdated considering some of the Hollywood films that are approved for showing -- and which are clobbering domestic films at the box office.
Most of the up to 10 foreign films allowed in each year are the likes of "Gladiator" or "Titanic," adventures and romances. 
But one of this spring's biggest hits in China was "The General's Daughter," which features a woman's corpse, naked and spread-eagled on the grass, and references to kinky sex that would never be allowed in a Chinese film.
"It's all right to portray Americans as decadent," one movie fan here explained with a laugh.

file: China Raises Military Budget Despite Deficit.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government today announced a 15 percent increase in the military budget for this year, adding to a series of increases in military spending that is alarming neighboring countries.
Although China no longer faces a major threat on its borders, its military budget is almost double the figure for 1988. 
Other Asian countries fear that China is trying to intimidate its neighbors and resolve longstanding boundary disputes in its favor. 
More fundamentally, some diplomats suggest, China is trying to fill a vacuum in the Pacific after the collapse of the Soviet Union and the withdrawal of United States forces from the Philippines.
Chinese officials made no attempt today to justify the increase in military spending. 
But on Monday, Prime Minister Li Peng told the National People's Congress that China needed to turn the three-million-member army into "the best armed forces that China's conditions permit."
Without citing any threats, Mr. Li said the army must "constantly increase its combat effectiveness and defense capabilities under modern warfare."
The spending figures were included in a budget speech today by Finance Minister Liu Zhongli to the congress, a rubber-stamp parliament that is meeting in its annual session. 
Mr. Liu said the military budget was 42.5 billion yuan, or $7.4 billion. 
That compares with military budgets of 37 billion yuan last year and 21.5 billion yuan in 1988.
Military spending increased even though Mr. Liu released figures indicating that by Western accounting methods the budget deficit grew to $19.8 billion, or 27 percent of revenues last year. 
Other areas like education, culture and health care increased much less than military spending.
In fact, the publicly announced military budget includes just half of all military spending, experts say. 
It does not include money spent on acquiring new equipment, on weapons research or on relocating and supporting retired officers. 
Those amounts are disguised in other areas of the budget. 
In addition, the military has other substantial sources of income, including arms exports and the sales of the refrigerators, radios, clocks and other civilian items made by military-owned factories.
Even so, total military spending probably accounts just only a bit more than 3 percent of the gross national product, a smaller share than in many other countries. 
Other Asian countries are nervous largely because China has boundary disputes with at least seven neighbors and has lately been aggressive in pressing its claims.
Diplomats and other military experts say among the improved weapons that China is building or obtaining from Russia or other countries are fighter planes, surface-to-air missiles, destroyers, frigates, tanks and radar equipment. 
Chinese documents also say the country will acquire an aircraft carrier.
Distressed by suggestions abroad that China is becoming a threat, officials in Beijing have mounted a vigorous counteroffensive. 
"Recently, some people in Western countries have deliberately spread slanderous rumors that China is building up its national defense to a level 'seemingly beyond a capability for defense,' " the official New China News Agency complained a few weeks ago.
Mr. Li referred to such analyses in a meeting last month with former Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. and added, "All these fabricated rumors and absurd tales are totally ridiculous."
The New China News Agency asserted last week that critics of increased military spending here were "simply unhappy that there is no chaos in Asia, and they are trying to drive wedges among the Asian nations."
One Chinese official cited inflation as a factor in the rising military spending. 
But according to official statistics, retail prices rose less than 7 percent last year, and they have increased 32 percent since 1988, the same period in which the military budget has increased 98 percent.
Sympathetic diplomats, usually from countries that are not adjacent to China, also say it is natural for a country to increase its military spending as its overall economy grows.

file: China Reaffirms Drive to Overhaul Bloated State Industries.txt
text:
ï»¿
Senior Chinese officials today reaffirmed their determination to squeeze dead wood and red ink out of bloated state-owned enterprises, vowing to make nearly all of them competitive and profitable by the end of next year.
Reporting on his first year as Prime Minister, Zhu Rongji told the annual session of the National People's Congress that, despite the "grim environment at home and abroad," China would forge ahead with the overhaul of state industries as well as a streamlining of Government bureaucracy.
While his speech was mainly devoted to economic policy, Mr. Zhu implicitly acknowledged the social unrest that has flared as urban unemployment grows and farmers protest taxes and corruption.
In a statement that seemed to be aimed as much at local officials and the police as at potential protesters, Mr. Zhu said such conflicts should be resolved promptly, "eliminating them before they grow."
Mr. Zhu said the Government projected 7 percent economic growth in 1999, compared with an official figure of 7.8 percent for 1998, and would continue its effort to stimulate the economy -- which has been battered by the Asian financial crisis and a shrinkage of domestic demand -- by pumping large sums into capital investments.
But the determination to wring out state-owned enterprises was the clear theme of the day.
In a news conference after today's opening of the congress, the official in charge of revamping state industry sought to rebut the perception that economic reforms had stalled.
"We have continued to quicken the pace of state enterprise reform," said the official, Sheng Huaren, chairman of the State Economic and Trade Commission, noting progress in closing of excess textile mills and coal mines, and restructuring of the petroleum, petrochemical and metallurgical industries.
Mr. Sheng gave a surprisingly upbeat assessment of some of the challenges facing the Chinese economy.
Mr. Sheng said the Government aimed to stabilize 7,680 large and medium-size public companies, of which 2,300 are now losing money. 
The goal, he said, is to end the losses of one-third of those companies this year, and the losses of an additional one-third next year, leaving no more than 15 percent of the surviving companies in the red.
Last year, 48,000 company officials were demoted or fired for poor management, Mr. Sheng said, and under a system of inspection by outside auditors, more incompetent or corrupt managers will be removed.

file: CHINA REJECTS CALL FROM CHRISTOPHER FOR RIGHTS GAINS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese officials today flatly rejected Secretary of State Warren Christopher's demand that Beijing improve its human rights performance and warned that stripping China of its trade privileges would backfire.
In a day punctuated by harsh and often acrimonious exchanges, the Chinese also accused the United States of breaking Chinese law by meeting secretly with a leading dissident last month.
Mr. Christopher's first visit to China as Secretary of State, initially planned as the culmination of the Administration's six-month-long strategy of intensive high-level engagement with the Chinese, has instead reduced China's chances of winning renewal of trade privileges that expire in June.
Â 
Internal Affairs Cited
This took place against a backdrop of heightened American demands for steady and substantive progress on human rights, and in large part they clashed with China's traditional resistance against being told what to do about its internal affairs and with the authorities' desire to maintain strict control as democracy advocates begin to become more assertive.
Mr. Christopher told Foreign Minister Qian Qichen this morning that China's actions toward its citizens, including the recent detention of a number of prominent dissidents, "suggest that China attaches relatively little weight to core human rights issues," the State Department spokesman, Michael McCurry, told reporters.
If that is so, the Secretary added, it "certainly bodes ill" for the chances of renewing the most-favored-nation trade status that gives China lower tariffs than those accorded to most American trading partners.
Â 
A Rancorous Exchange
The exchange was so rancorous that as he said goodbye to Mr. Qian after four hours of meetings that extended through lunch, Mr. Christopher made no effort to hide his frustration, saying, "I wish the meeting had been as good as the lunch," Mr. McCurry reported.
In an afternoon meeting, Prime Minister Li Peng seemed to reverse China's earlier pledges this year to try to make progress on human rights.
"China will never accept the U.S. human rights concept," Mr. Li told Mr. Christopher, according to a Foreign Ministry spokesman, Wu Jianmin. 
"History has already proven that it is futile to apply pressure on China."
Mr. Christopher's aides have acknowledged that they are both shocked and bewildered by the Chinese decision to greet Mr. Christopher's arrival with a sweeping crackdown on dissidents instead of conciliatory gestures on human rights.
But at the same time, it was impossible to judge whether the sudden Chinese belligerency was a tactical rebuff to Mr. Christopher, who has been publicly scolding the Chinese for not making enough progress, or a tough, new overall attitude on human rights. 
Only a month ago, President Jiang Zemin told American Congressional leaders in very conciliatory tones that China would make an effort to respond to Mr. Clinton's demands.
In taking a tougher line than at any time since the Clinton Administration took office, the Chinese appear willing to gamble that Washington has too much to lose by revoking the trade privileges, a policy they see as driven by anti-China lawmakers in Congress. 
Both Mr. Qian and Mr. Li warned Mr. Christopher today that the United States would suffer more than China if its trade privileges were revoked.
Â 
Boast of Self-Sufficiency
China is nearly self-sufficient economically, Mr. Li boasted, adding that if the United States were to revoke its trade status, "it means the United States would lose its share of the big Chinese market."
He said Chinese imports were growing at a rate of 9 percent a year and would reach a trillion dollars by the turn of the century.
But Mr. Christopher, the highest Clinton Administration representative to visit China, told his hosts that reports in China that the United States had already decided to extend preferential trade privileges or would accept only modest improvements in human rights to extend them were "unambiguously wrong," Mr. McCurry quoted Mr. Christopher as saying.
In an extraordinary allegation that prompted a strong response from Mr. Christopher and his aides, the Chinese accused John Shattuck, the Assistant Secretary of State for Human Rights, of breaking Chinese law by meeting late last month with Wei Jingsheng, China's most prominent dissident, whom Mr. Wu described to reporters as "a criminal on parole."
The official New China News Agency quoted Mr. Qian as telling Mr. Christopher, "A top U.S. 
Government official came to prepare for Christopher's visit, and in disregard of Chinese laws, the official took actions interfering in China's internal affairs."
Â 
U.S. Refuses Diplomatic Limits
In reply, Mr. Christopher was quoted as saying the United States "cannot accept any limits on the ability of its diplomats to meet with foreign citizens."
Although Mr. Christopher chose not to speak publicly today about his first day of meetings, Winston Lord, the Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs, chastised his hosts. 
He told reporters that the Chinese assertion that the United States was poisoning the well in advance of Mr. Christopher's visit because of human rights was "really Alice in Wonderland," and "an extraordinary leap of chutzpah."
Mr. Lord, a former Ambassador to China, tried to put the best face on the trip, saying, "Let's hope the next couple of days are better."
But Mr. Christopher's aides conceded in private that any real progress would have to come after the meeting is over.
Â 
Two and a Half Months Left
The Chinese still have two and a half months before the Administration must decide whether they have made enough progress in improving their human rights record to warrant annual renewal of their preferential trade privileges. 
And despite Mr. Christopher's threats to revoke China's trade privileges, the United States has no intention of abandoning its strategy of high-level diplomatic engagement, Mr. Lord told reporters.
Still, there is deep concern on the American side that China may do too little too late in meeting the requirements of a 1993 executive order linking extension of the trade benefits to China's progress on releasing political prisoners, ceasing the jamming of international broadcasts, carrying out the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, protecting Tibet's cultural and religious heritage, permitting the right of emigration and opening Chinese prisons to international relief groups.
The executive order was the result of intensive consultations with Congress, which has pressed for deeper concessions from China on human rights.
In an unusual departure from Chinese hospitality and courtesy, Mr. Wu, the Foreign Ministry spokesman, acknowledged to reporters that the Chinese had suggested that Mr. Christopher postpone his trip because it coincided with the opening of the National People's Congress, but that when the Americans said they could not change their arrangements, "in the end we have accommodated the Secretary."

file: China Releases Dissident and Sends Him to U.S. for Treatment.txt
text:
ï»¿
A prominent leader of the Tiananmen Square democracy movement was released today and immediately sent to the United States to seek treatment for hepatitis and a heart ailment.
The dissident, Wang Juntao, was one of five political prisoners with serious medical problems who were the subject of a letter signed by a majority of United States Senators and sent to President Jiang Zemin in February.
[Mr. Wang arrived at Kennedy Airport in New York Saturday and was met by his wife, the Reuters news agency reported.]
The release of Mr. Wang, a 35-year-old physics graduate from Beijing University, may be the first step in a series of releases leading to the June 3 deadline President Clinton has set for China to improve its human rights record or face loss of its trade privileges for $30 billion in annual exports to the United States.
In Hong Kong, John Kamm, an American businessman and human rights advocate, said the release of Mr. Wang was welcome news, but cautioned that other seriously ill political prisoners remained in jail, in particular Mr. Wang's closest colleague, Chen Ziming, and Bao Tong, who was an aide to Zhao Ziyang when he served as Prime Minister.
By sending Mr. Wang out of the country for treatment, the leadership has rid itself of a major figure from the Tiananmen period as China approaches the fifth anniversary of the democracy movement. 
The authorities may also refuse to allow him to return home after treatment.
"It has all the earmarkings of an exile," Mr. Kamm said. 
"But the Chinese Government has not taken a position on whether it will readmit him."
Mr. Wang's mother, Ge Yumei, told the Reuters news agency that Mr. Wang had been taken to the airport, where he was allowed to see his family before he boarded a flight to the United States.
"I am very relieved that the Government has allowed him to be released on medical parole for treatment in the United States," she said.
A short statement in the official New China News Agency said Mr. Wang "has left for medical treatment abroad after the Chinese judicial authorities released him on bail according to law on account of the conditions of his illness."
Mr. Wang was arrested in 1989 and was in detention until he was tried and sentenced to 13 years in prison on Feb. 
12, 1991. 
He and Mr. Chen were co-directors of the Beijing Social and Economic Sciences Research Institute, whose newspaper, Economics Weekly, was a strong advocate for political reform and democracy before the 1989 crackdown.
The two dissidents spent many hours advising the student leaders at Tiananmen Square, and were regarded as voices of moderation during the long standoff leading to the declaration of martial law and the military crackdown on June 4, 1989.
Mr. Wang and Mr. Chen were accused of manipulating the Tiananmen protesters in an attempt to overthrow the Government, a charge they denied during their secret trials.
Mr. Wang's wife, Hou Xiaotian, has been in the United States campaigning for her husband's release while serving as a visiting scholar at Columbia University.
Â 
--------------------
U.S. Says More Is Needed
WASHINGTON, April 23 (Special to The New York Times) -- Clinton Administration officials said today that they welcomed the release of Wang Juntao but that more needed to be done for China to have its preferred trading status renewed.
"There are other cases very similar to Wang's, and we hope in the future to see other prisoners released in this way," said Michael McCurry, the State Department spokesman.
He also said the Administration "expects the Chinese Government to honor his right to return" to his homeland.

file: China Reportedly to Start Trial of Four Sect Leaders Tomorrow.txt
text:
ï»¿
China plans to put four leading members of the banned Falun Gong spiritual movement on trial on Sunday. 
The move is the most significant prosecution since the government outlawed the group five months ago, a rights group in Hong Kong said today.
Relatives of the four members were formally notified today of the trial and told that each defendant could have one relative present at the No. 1 Intermediate People's Court here, the Information Center of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China said. 
The background of the defendants -- Li Chang, Wang Zhiwen, Ji Liewu and Yao Jie -- underscores the reach of Falun Gong, the government's fear of the group and the difficulties in suppressing it. 
All four were Communist Party members with positions of some influence in government or business.
The news about the trial spread late today, and the court did not answer calls. 
The court is expected to sentence the four to 20 years or more in prison for "using an evil cult to undermine the implementation of laws" and other crimes, the Information Center said.
The trial may also spark renewed protests here by Falun Gong members. 
Members in the United States, who have previously helped mobilize followers in China by e-mail and other means, confirmed that a trial has been set for Sunday, citing family members of the accused.
Two times this month -- on Dec. 
4, when the trial was to have originally started, and again on Dec. 
18 -- followers gathered outside the courthouse in western Beijing, and the police arrested 20 of them, the Information Center said. 
Followers have embarrassed the government and the police by repeatedly staging peaceful acts of protest in defiance of the ban, on July 22, and a crackdown that has seen thousands detained and pressured to recant their beliefs.
Falun Gong advocates a mixture of traditional meditation exercises and ideas drawn from Buddhism, Taoism and the group's founder, Li Hongzhi, a former government grain clerk who lives in New York. 
Practice is said to promote health and morality and in the seven years since the group was founded it has attracted millions of followers here. 
Chinese leaders say the group had caused the deaths of more than 1,400 people by discouraging them from seeking conventional medical care. 
In outlawing the group, the government called Falun Gong a menace to public welfare and a threat to Communist rule.
The state-run media have accused one of the four defendants, Wang Zhiwen, an engineer for a materials company in the Railways Ministry, of having organized a protest on April 25 by 10,000 members at the Communist Party leaders' compound here.
Mr. Wang, 50, and the other three were arrested on July 20, two days before the ban. 
According to the information center, Mr. Li, 59, was a senior official in the computer bureau of the national police; Mr. Ji, 36, managed a subsidiary of a Chinese nonferrous-metals company in Hong Kong; and Mr. Yao, 40, headed the party committee of a large Beijing real-estate company.
All four have been charged with undermining laws. 
In addition, Mr. Wang, Mr. Li and Mr. Yao were accused of illegally gathering and disseminating state secrets. 
Mr. Yao and Mr. Ji were also accused of involvement in illegal business, the information center said.
The center said Mr. Wang, Mr. Li and Mr. Yao had already been tried behind closed doors on the state-secrets charges and that the trial on Sunday would focus on the other charges.

file: China Reports Trade Deficit Doubled in Only 2 Months.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's overheating economy suffered a new blow today with the release of official statistics showing that its trade deficit had doubled in just two months.
Soaring imports, driven by frenzied consumer and state spending, pushed the trade gap for the first six months to $3.54 billion, meaning it more than doubled in May and June, according to customs figures released by the Xinhua news agency. 
The deficit had reached $1.7 billion by the end of April.
China's imports surged to $40.69 billion in the first six months, up 23.4 percent from the comparable period in 1992. 
Exports grew a scant 4.4 percent, to $37.15 billion.
Â 
Â 
Economic About-Face
The growing deficit reflects a remarkable about-face for the Chinese economy after more than a decade of export-fueled growth and strict controls on imports and foreign exchange.

file: CHINA SAYS TAIWAN CANNOT CONTINUE DELAYING REUNION.txt
text:
