file: CHINA_ PROFIT _ OR PRINCIPLE__The Chinese Are Coming. Wait. They_re Already Here.txt
text:
ï»¿
Early in January a group of Hong Kong's wealthiest tycoons boarded an Air China flight to Beijing for three days of meetings to promote the territory's interests with some of China's most senior officials. 
The visit reached its climax in a meeting with Li Peng, China's Prime Minister, the man widely regarded as having ordered the 1989 massacre of protesters at Tiananmen Square.
The tycoons assembled in the Pavilion of the Purple Light, one of the ceremonial halls of the old imperial compound in the heart of Beijing. 
Bit by bit the flattery and obsequiousness seeped out.
One member of the delegation asked whether Li's feelings had been hurt by the relentless negative coverage he had received in Hong Kong's free press. 
Another suggested that China buy a television station in Hong Kong so that it could more easily propagandize the people there. 
And another raised eyebrows even among his sycophantic colleagues when he praised Li for his "extraordinary leadership" of China's Communist Party. 
Li himself was taken aback at this. 
"I'm not the leader," Li reminded him. 
"President Jiang Zemin is."
The Union Jack still has 16 or so months to fly on Hong Kong's flagpoles, but many members of the city's elite are hurrying to cozy up to their new colonial master. 
Yet Hong Kong doesn't have to travel to China for that. 
In some respects the master is already there. 
You can find him on the top three floors of the old Bank of China, where China's Communist cadres once hung streaming banners denouncing British colonialism and hailing the glories of Mao Zedong. 
David Tang remembers those days. 
"One of my early memories was how mysterious that building was," says the 41-year-old Tang. 
"And there was a distinct smell. 
There was a Communist smell about it."
Today, Tang wishes he could bottle that smell because, for him, it is the smell of China. 
Tang is selling China, or at least the romance of it, here at the China Club, where nearly 2,000 of Hong Kong's toniest have shelled out $19,500 in membership fees for the privilege of eating fairly ordinary Cantonese food in a Chinese memory palace.
Waiters pad about in black slippers on worn plank floors. 
Dark wood columns are sconced with faintly Art Deco lamps. 
Rotary telephones sit beside old stuffed-leather chairs draped with antimacassars. 
And paintings of Mao cover the walls. 
Mao orating to the masses. 
Mao cheek by jowl with Whitney Houston.
Many of those who live in Hong Kong now were once victims of Maoist persecutions, but Tang, the founding spirit and part owner of the club, doesn't worry about the paradoxes. 
"Mao is an intrinsic part of Chinese history," he says. 
"We are not condoning everything Mao has done. 
I think people ought to be a little more relaxed about these kinds of things."
The transfer of Hong Kong will soon become part of Chinese history, too, and relaxing about Mao, and about China, is the message of the day in some of its inner circles.
"The message of the China Club is to create a new Chinese superiority based on being Chinese, based on being privileged Chinese," says a prominent Hong Kong lawyer. 
"And who are the privileged Hong Kong Chinese?
Those with relations with privileged Chinese. 
This is the new comprador class. 
The China Club is the new symbol."

file: CHINA_ PULLING TOGETHER _ OR COMING APART__Class Climbing.txt
text:
ï»¿
Exploding economic growth is introducing new wealth and values in China and even eroding the bedrock of society, the family. 
Consider the Gao family of Nanjing, a city of 2.2 million residents about 200 miles from the mouth of the Yangtze River. 
The father, Gao Made, 76, is a professional painter, and the mother, Chen Ruqing, 70, is an art designer. 
As artists and intellectuals, they have benefited from the economic changes.
"After 1949, painting had to serve the people -- workers, farmers, soldiers," says Made, whose paintings of opera characters sell for as much as 6,000 yuan -- about $720. 
"During the Cultural Revolution, I was not allowed to paint. 
Now life is good. 
One can draw what one wants."
The couple's elder son, Gao Huan, 40, is also an amateur painter, but he has little time these days for artistic pursuits. 
One of a growing number of relatively wealthy entrepreneurs, he runs a factory that makes electronic components for the credit card industry and employs 20 workers. 
Weeknights and weekends are spent on his cellular telephone, paving the way for his next venture: a cement factory, which he hopes will thrive on a Yangtze River dam project.
Like an increasing number of urban Chinese, Huan is divorced, and he has remarried. 
He has a daughter from his previous marriage, Gao SinSin, 12, who lives with her maternal grandmother, and a second daughter, Gao Gage, 3, with his wife, Si Hui. 
(The one-child policy is relaxed in some cases, including divorce.) By law, Huan must pay child support. 
He initially gave SinSin half his earnings, which several years ago totaled 40 yuan a month. 
These days, he says, he gives her much more -- thousands of yuan at a time -- and hopes one day to send her to college.
It is a moral and constitutional obligation in China to support one's parents. 
Although a growing number of children have reneged on this contract, Huan has not: he shares his home with his parents as well as his wife and their daughter. 
His sister, Gao Qing, 46, lives nearby with her husband and 20-year-old son, a photography student. 
Although a heart ailment keeps her at home, she has achieved moderate success as a cartoonist for a children's magazine.
Inevitably, however, the new China is proving inhospitable for some. 
In 1992, Huan's younger brother, Gao Duo, 38, quit a longtime teaching job and, using money from his father, opened a restaurant in Nanjing. 
It quickly went bankrupt. 
He now works the late shift as a designer at a state-owned newspaper in Nanjing, a job gained through family connections. 
Though he earns a respectable salary -- about 1,000 yuan a month, or $120 -- Duo is burdened by a sense of failure. 
Divorced, he still lives with his former wife. 
Last year he tried suicide. 
His parents offer emotional support and he visits them every evening before work, but he has few friends. 
"Forging ahead now is difficult," he says.
Huan, meanwhile, is busy with his latest investment: a stud farm outside Nanjing, the first in the region. 
Though it has yet to turn a profit, it offers him a respite from his usual stress and provides a creative outlet.
"When I was young, I envied the democratic freedom of the West, their sexual liberty," Huan says. 
"Now I envy their horses."

file: China_s Arrest of Pennsylvania Librarian Alarms Scholars.txt
text:
ï»¿
The arrest here of a Pennsylvania-based Chinese researcher as he collected documents from the Maoist era has caused an uproar among Western scholars, who say it imperils academic research and exchanges with China.
Today, 101 China scholars, including many leading experts from American, Australian and British universities who favor broader ties with China, released a letter to President Jiang Zemin calling for the immediate release of the researcher, Yongyi Song.
The letter warns that Mr. Song's arrest -- on vague charges of providing confidential information to foreigners -- could undermine support for the academic exchanges that China has fostered over the last two decades as it sought to modernize and end its former isolation. 
Each year, thousands of Chinese students and professors study abroad while smaller numbers of Western experts visit China to study its history, politics and society.
"Continued prosecution of this case will make it impossible for foreign scholars or Chinese scholars associated with foreign universities to conduct research in open sources in China with the confidence that they will be safe from criminal prosecution," says the letter, which was faxed to the Chinese Embassy in Washington today.
One of the signers, Michel Oksenberg, a political scientist at Stanford University and a former White House adviser on China policy, said in an interview that by arresting an academic researcher who was apparently seeking materials already in the public domain, China may have violated basic principles on which scholarly exchanges are based.
"As a sponsor and adviser of students who wish to do research in China," Mr. Oksenberg said, "I have some responsibility to insure that their research will not place them, or those in China who assist them, at risk."
Mr. Song, 50, is a scholar and librarian at Dickinson College in Carlisle, Pa., and an authority on the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, when China was in turmoil and largely closed to outsiders. 
Mr. Song has written a book and numerous articles in Chinese, but is best known for his exhaustive bibliographic work on that chaotic decade.
Last summer -- as he often had before -- he visited China to collect materials from the period, such as newspapers of the radical young Red Guards, old books and mimeographed records that lurk in second-hand book stores, street markets and private collections.
Many Western and Chinese scholars, including Chinese graduate students at American universities, routinely engage in the same kind of historical treasure hunt here.
But on Aug. 
7, Mr. Song -- a Chinese who was on the verge of becoming an American citizen -- was detained by security forces in Beijing.
After months of interrogations, on Dec. 
24 he was charged with "the purchase and illegal provision of intelligence to foreigners."
The charge is less severe than that for divulging "state secrets," but depending on how the courts define the gravity of his offense, Mr. Song could receive anything from a light sentence to more than 10 years in prison. 
No trial date has been announced.
The Chinese authorities have not revealed which of his activities resulted in the arrest. 
Mr. Song's wife, Helen Yao, a jewelry designer who was detained along with her husband and held for over two months, said in a recent interview that when security officers asked him about particular government documents he had acquired, he argued that each had formerly been published.
Roderick MacFarquhar, a Harvard professor and author of a multi-volume history of the origins of the Cultural Revolution, said that the prosecution of Mr. Song would create two classes of China scholars abroad: "Westerners who can come and go with relative freedom, and current or former Chinese citizens who will have to tread very carefully for fear of being arrested or at least having their relatives harassed."
Perhaps most affected will be Chinese scholars who live and work in China, who fear that their already limited ability to pursue historical evidence may shrink even further. 
One historian in Beijing said that he and his colleagues also fear that collaborative research with foreigners may become more dangerous.
The international group of scholars, organized by David Strand, a historian of China at Dickinson, also sent a copy of today's letter to President Clinton and Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright in the hope that the administration will step up efforts on his behalf.
A spokesman for the American Embassy in Beijing said today that senior Embassy officials have "brought up the matter of Yongyi Song several times" with the Chinese government.
A subject of endless fascination for historians, the Cultural Revolution remains among China's most politically sensitive topics, and accounts published here are carefully censored in an effort to protect the legitimacy of the Communist Party.
Under Mao's banner of continuing revolution, millions of people were persecuted, imprisoned or killed, schooling came to a halt and the economy was nearly destroyed.
After Mao's death in 1976, his successors declared the Cultural Revolution to have been a disastrous mistake and said that Mao had erred under the baleful influence of a small group of leaders, including the "Gang of Four."
But Mao's achievements greatly outweighed his missteps, the official line declared, and his memory as the heroic father of the People's Republic has been carefully nurtured ever since.
Many key documents from the Cultural Revolution remain in closed archives, including Beijing directives that might implicate Mao or other leaders such as the late, revered Prime Minister Zhou Enlai in vicious purges or other misdeeds.
But during the early years of the Cultural Revolution in particular, fanatical young Maoists often published leaders' speeches and other documents. 
Such materials have been avidly collected by scholars and libraries, largely without trouble until now.
In recent weeks, as word spread about the criminal charges against Mr. Song, members of Congress and the State Department have expressed concern and China scholars have been up in arms.
"Because of its unpredictability and the absence of clearly stated rules," said Thomas P. Bernstein, an expert on Chinese politics at Columbia University, the case "is dangerous from the point of view of anyone doing research on contemporary China."
Mr. Strand, Mr. Song's colleague at Dickinson, said today, "This case strikes at every aspect of the work we do, both practical and ethical."
"Every day I think of Song in his jail cell," he said.

file: China_s Bid To Send Astronauts Into Space.txt
text:
ï»¿
China is closer to becoming only the third nation in history to launch humans into space, a feat that could come as early as next year, say international space experts.
After years of saying it would "one day" or "soon" put people into space, and initiating and postponing efforts to do so, the Chinese government has finally embarked on a serious program to make it happen, these experts believe.
"I think evidence of a manned space program in China is very real and that they are serious," said Charles Vick, a space issues expert with the Federation of American Scientists, a Washington policy group.
According to specialists following Chinese space developments, Chinese officials had hoped to put two astronauts into space by October to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the Communist takeover of China. 
But, they said, delays in developing a new rocket for lifting heavy payloads, and problems with other equipment, make such a crewed flight unlikely until at least next year.
Nonetheless, the first flight in the program, an unmanned test of the new rocket and spacecraft, could still come in October.
"Assuming there is no major failure during the first unmanned flight of the system, I would expect a Chinese manned flight a year to 15 months afterwards," said Phillip S. Clark, a British space consultant who closely follows the Chinese program. 
"Only the United States and Russia have the capability to send people into space and China seems ready to become only the third nation to join this exclusive club."
Lynn Cline, the official in charge of external affairs at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, said the space agency had no detailed knowledge of China's plans. 
"For many years, they have set as a goal building a manned spacecraft, and earlier said they wanted to make a manned flight this year," Ms. Cline said. 
However, she said, the agency has heard that this flight has been delayed for unknown reasons and that there will be an unmanned mission instead this year.
Renewed interest in human spaceflight by China flared last month when pictures said to show the Chinese spacecraft and rocket suddenly appeared on the Internet from an anonymous source. 
The pictures depict a spacecraft based on the Russian Soyuz design atop a large rocket with four booster motors attached to the sides.
Mr. Clark, in an article to appear next month in the British magazine Jane's Intelligence Review, describes the rocket as the Chang Zheng 2F, an upgraded version of one of China's largest satellite launchers, the Long March CZ-3E. 
The new version is capable of placing a 10 metric-ton payload into low Earth orbit, he said, while the Chinese manned spacecraft weighs about 8.4 metric tons.
The spacecraft itself resembles the Russian Soyuz, which is built in three sections -- a propulsion section, an orbital section and a return module -- but it is larger and carries two pairs of solar-power panels instead of one set as the Russian craft does, Mr. Clark said. 
The central orbital module, instead of being spheroidal like the Soyuz, is more cylindrical, he said. 
The Chinese version is designed to make docking with other craft and transferring crew members easy.
The detailed color photographs were supposedly taken by a construction worker at China's Jiuquan launching site near the Gobi desert. 
They show a completed rocket and spacecraft being rolled out of an assembly building to a gantry and firing pad.
The new building looks a lot like NASA's giant Vehicle Assembly Building at Cape Canaveral, Fla., where Apollo moon rockets, and now space shuttles, were put together for missions. 
The rocket is on a mechanical crawler with tank-like treads that slowly move it to a launching pad, just as American shuttles are transported. 
Previously, Chinese space rockets were assembled from components on the pad before launchings, not transported there ready to fly.
Initial discussion about the pictures focused on whether they were clever fakes. 
Some spacecraft experts questioned whether the pictures were of small-scale models or images put together with computer-aided drawing and photo manipulation software. 
After carefully examining details in the pictures and calculating the size and positions of elements in the images, most experts now believe they are authentic, for the most part.
"There's too much detail there to be faked," Mr. Vick said.
However, Mr. Clark and other experts said the image of the large assembly and integration building where the rockets are prepared may have been enhanced in some way. 
The pictures taken by the worker are supposed to be from a promotional brochure created for the construction company that put up the building, and that company may have been trying to emphasize its work in the images, Mr. Clark said.
Some experts also question the relatively close proximity of the assembly building to the launching pad, compared with the arrangement at Cape Canaveral, as evidence of possible photo manipulation. 
But Mr. Vick noted that the launching arrangement for the new European Ariane 5 rocket also has the service building and launching pad similarly close together.
China launched its first satellite in 1970 and has maintained an active space program that includes launching commercial satellites for clients in other countries.
Chinese officials began discussing sending humans into space in the late 1970's and reports of astronaut training began emerging in the 1980's. 
Talk of manned spaceflight then ended for several years, partly because of social upheaval in China, and revived in the early 1990's.
The push toward the current manned flight effort, dubbed Project 921, began in March 1995, when China made a deal with Russia to acquire space technology, including information on life-support systems, docking mechanisms for spacecraft and spacesuits. 
In October 1996, two Chinese astronauts and more than a dozen trainers and support workers arrived at the Russian cosmonaut training center outside Moscow and stayed for about a year, experts said. 
At about the same time, Beijing announced plans to fly a manned spacecraft for the nation's anniversary celebration, but has said little about the program since.
Officials and scientists questioned about the program in China give conflicting answers, with many declining to comment on possible dates for manned flights until the government announces them.
But one thing Chinese scientists and outside experts agree on is that most of the technology being developed is Chinese, even though some is an adaptation of Russian ideas and equipment.
Dr. Joan Johnson-Freese, an instructor at the Asia Pacific Center for Security Studies in Honolulu, and author of the book, "The Chinese Space Program: A Mystery Within a Maze" (Krieger Publishing, 1998), said the Chinese always have multiple agendas. 
China wants to prove that it is a technically sophisticated nation and a great power that does not need outside help, she said.
Recent investigations by Congress and the Pentagon that accuse China of stealing secrets and benefiting from American companies illegally transferring rocket and satellite information to China have embarrassed the Chinese and given them something to prove, she said.
"There is no economic payback for a manned space program," Dr. Johnson-Freese said. 
"The manned space club is very exclusive. 
It's all for the prestige."
China is willing to spend part of its limited funds to develop technology that is distinctly its own for sending humans into space, she said.
"This way, China can say: 'This is not U.S. technology. 
This is not Russian Technology. 
This is very much Chinese technology,' " she said. 
"It's saying, 'We don't need to steal your secrets and expertise -- we have our own.'
"

file: China_s Chief Tells Army To Give Up Its Commerce.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Jiang Zemin ordered China's military to relinquish its sprawling multibillion-dollar commercial empire, saying it is the only way to combat an epidemic of smuggling, which the army dominates, the state news media reported today.
Addressing an extraordinary meeting of top military commanders, Mr. Jiang called on the armed forces to regain their "purity" in order to regain public confidence and to safeguard the nation's long-term stabilityI.
Yet business -- and smuggling -- are so entrenched in the army that separating the military from its commerce could take years.
The announcement, broadcast nationally this evening on China Central Television, offered scant clues about whether Mr. Jiang has the political will or the support from military leaders to carry out such an ambitious undertaking.
Most remarkable, perhaps, was his indirect admission of the degree of lawlessness that exists in the army. 
Never before in 49 years of Communist Party rule has the military been so publicly questioned, suggesting that Mr. Jiang may be serious about deep-seated change.
"The army and armed police forces must earnestly carry out checks on all kinds of commercial companies set up by subsidiary units, and without exception from today must not engage in their operation," said Mr. Jiang, looking somber in a pea-green Mao suit at an anti-smuggling conference convened Monday and Tuesday in Beijing.
In the television broadcast, dozens of military leaders were shown earnestly taking notes. 
As chairman of the Communist Party's Central Military Commission, Mr. Jiang is China's Commander in Chief. 
Yet the army wields wide power, and it is unlikely that he would make such a bold pronouncement without the support of top generals.
All of the army's senior leaders attended the conference. 
Seated beside the President were Gen. Zhang Wannian and Gen. Chi Haotian, vice chairmen of the Central Military Commission. 
Four other generals, Fu Quanyou, Yu Yongbo, Wang Ke and Wang Ruilin, also appeared.
The vast array of businesses the army owns or partly controls ranges from commercial airlines to pharmaceutical companies and from vegetable growers to arms dealers.
Army-related businesses earn billions of dollars each year, though they are so numerous and disparate that virtually no one inside or out of China can accurately estimate their full scope.
Although China's military often appears a stern-faced monolith to outsiders, its money-making role is a hodgepodge of ventures, essentially built by military officers taking advantage of their authority in the political apparatus to build lucrative operations.
The army's role in smuggling appears to have grown in tandem with the nation's stunning economic growth over the last 20 years. 
Although the true volume of goods smuggled into China cannot be measured, officials conservatively estimate that it has reached tens of billions of dollars each year.
More than $10 billion a year in tax revenue is lost to smuggling, the New China News Agency reported. 
Chinese Customs, alternatively seen as corrupt and unable to stand up to military smugglers, confiscated just $330 million of smuggled goods in the first five months of this year.
The main contraband is not drugs or illegal arms, but rather high-end goods that face such onerous import duties that customers are willing to pay handsomely for an army transport that escapes scrutiny at a border.
Mr. Jiang, echoing comments he made last week at the opening of a broad anti-smuggling campaign, said that all party and Government offices and law enforcement agencies would also be required to cut ties with companies they own. 
That will be a gargantuan task.
When any national campaign begins, several political elements may be at work. 
Yet decison-making in China is so opaque that it is difficult to know if the driving force behind the anti-smuggling campaign is Mr. Jiang's desire to flex his muscles over the military, or to buttress his reputation as a corruption fighter.
There may also be financial concerns.
