The police were out in force in several Chinese cities this weekend, seeking to head off rumored plans for new demonstrations by a spiritual sect that staged a giant vigil in Beijing a week ago.
No incidents have been reported, and national leaders are pondering how to deal with the group, called Buddhist Law, which has gained millions of fervent followers. 
The Government normally maintains control over mass movements and religions and does not allow social groups to be directed from abroad, as this group is.
Though it is not political and insists that it is not a religion, Buddhist Law has pushed the edge of what is allowed. 
With last week's demonstration by 10,000 members seeking legal approval, the group also showed a remarkable ability to muster its believers.
The Communist rulers have tried to avoid provoking the organization, whose members are seen as decent citizens. 
But the leadership cannot be happy to see the emergence of a social wild card.
Buddhist Law, or Falun Gong, was first preached in 1992 by Li Hongzhi, who was already a master of the ancient art of qigong (pronounced che-goong) in which breathing and meditation are used to channel vital forces. 
Mr. Li, now 48, combined concepts from qigong, Buddhism and Taoism with his own mystical theories. 
Last year, saying he was under official pressure, Mr. Li moved to New York, but he remains the sect's absolute leader.
The word Falun means "law wheel," a high-energy rotating body said to be in a practitioner's abdomen that harnesses cosmic forces and expels bad elements. 
Followers are told to harness this power, rather than using medicines, to cure disease.
Traditional martial arts like qigong were suppressed here as superstition in the 1960's and 1970's, but in the more open climate that followed they have revived. 
Leaders of traditional groups here who blatantly cross over into fraud have been imprisoned.
Although it obviously has great popular appeal, particularly among retirees and middle-aged women, Mr. Li's new sect has had critics. 
More traditional qigong sects are mainly devoted to health and fitness. 
The Government's limited oversight is wielded through the martial arts department of the Sports Commission.
Last year, that department began evaluating qigong sects for legal approval. 
But a scholar who advised the department, Luo Shao, said that the evaluation methods were ill-defined and that many officials were followers of qigong, insuring a lack of critical oversight.
So far the agency has studied only 11 sects out of hundreds, not including Buddhist Law, and approved them all, said Mr. Luo, an expert on Buddhist history at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and a strong critic of the group.
New offshoots like this one, with charismatic leaders and broad-ranging mystical beliefs, have been attacked as heretical cults by some scholars here as well as by mainstream qigong groups and Buddhist leaders. 
Members resent the characterization.
Buddhist Law was accepted into the semi-official China Qigong Science Association in 1993, but expelled in 1996 for what were considered its extreme claims. 
In a letter sent to followers in December, Mr. Li said he had withdrawn because the purpose of "so-called fitness-maintenance qigong" is to "swindle money."Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: China_s Sniping Heeded By Some Taiwan Voters.txt
text:
ï»¿
With Taiwan's presidential election only 10 days away, China has uncorked its vitriol on the Democratic Progressive Party candidate, Chen Shui-bian, calling him a separatist and a silver-tongued liar. 
To hear Mr. Chen tell it, Beijing is doing him a favor.
"We have a precedent here," he said in an interview during a campaign swing that took him from Taipei to this southern port city. 
"The person China hates, Taiwan voters love."
When Beijing fired missiles into the ocean near Taiwan before the 1996 election, hoping to scare people away from President Lee Teng-hui, they responded by re-electing him in a landslide. 
Mr. Chen, who is viewed as less acceptable to Beijing than either of his two main rivals, said China's latest barrage of threats would play to his advantage as well by raising the hackles of voters.
But Chen Shui-bian is not Lee Teng-hui, and this is not 1996.
Interviews with party officials, political analysts and voters this week suggest that Mr. Chen's identification with the cause of Taiwanese independence could hurt him, particularly among the one-quarter of the electorate that is still undecided.
Mr. Chen is running neck-and-neck with Vice President Lien Chan and James Soong, an independent. 
Mr. Chen's campaign manager figures the election will hinge on 200,000 to 300,000 voters, who may not make up their minds until they step into the polling booth.
In the meantime, these people are being subjected to a daily drumbeat from Beijing. 
On Monday, the Chinese Army accused a "prominent figure" -- read Chen Shui-bian -- of pushing for independence and said it had put its troops on alert to crush such a move.
"Under no circumstances should we be fooled by his sweet talk," said the army's newspaper, Liberation Army Daily, in a front-page editorial. 
"One minute he is brazenly howling 'Long live Taiwan independence,' while the next he is using beautiful and pleasant words to lie that he wants 'good will, reconciliation, vigorous cooperation and everlasting peace' with the mainland."
Today in Beijing, President Jiang Zemin told a group of foreign journalists, "If you seek Taiwan independence, it will be a case of brother fighting brother."
One of those who is listening is Chen Yen-yang, 22, a political science student at National Taiwan University. 
Mr. Chen, who will cast his first vote in this election, said he always assumed he would support Chen Shui-bian. 
But he starts compulsory military service next year. 
That has changed his mind, and he now plans to vote for Vice President Lien of the governing Nationalist Party.
"Everybody around me, my family and friends, is talking about the possibility of war between Taiwan and China," Mr. Chen said. 
"I can't ignore that."
His classmate, Chen Yu-wen, said, "I think Chen Shui-bian underestimates China's willingness to take military action against Taiwan."
She said she planned to vote for Mr. Lien because the Nationalist Party "understands China."
"They know how to deal with them," she said.
Mr. Chen's rivals have seized the chance to portray him as a threat to peace. 
The Nationalists are running a newspaper advertisement that shows a man in army fatigues, his face hidden by a black gas mask, staring into a wall of flames. 
The figure represents Taiwan in the aftermath of a Chen victory.
Mr. Chen counters these charges by noting he is the only candidate with a son who would be drafted into the military if Taiwan were invaded by China. 
"As a father, I understand the fear of parents who don't want to put their children into danger," he said.
In his zeal to appear moderate, Mr. Chen rivals even the hypercautious Mr. Lien. If elected, he has pledged not to declare independence, not to hold a referendum on the issue, and not to put the phrase "special state-to-state" relations into Taiwan's Constitution. 
Those words, which President Lee uttered last July, infuriated China and set off a war of words across the Strait of Taiwan.
The problem for Mr. Chen is the platform of the Democratic Progressive Party, which calls for "the establishment of a sovereign and independent Republic of Taiwan."
Mr. Chen insisted today that such a move would come only after a plebiscite, the timing of which would be up to the people.
Some political analysts dismissed Mr. Chen's more conciliatory tone as a political ploy rather than a shift in his bedrock beliefs. 
And they said the fervor of 1996 -- in which Taiwanese people rose up to defend their first native-born president -- was missing from this election.
"People in this country are no longer fanatical," said Wang Jin-pyng, a Nationalist Party stalwart who is the president of Taiwan's legislature. 
"They believe that maintenance of stabilityI is the best policy. 
If the threats from China reduce Chen's support by 3 percent, he will lose the election."
Kaohsiung is one of Mr. Chen's strongholds, and tonight thousands of his supporters turned out here for an earsplitting, and defiant, rally.
Lee Chia-shin, 27, who has a mix of mainland Chinese and native Taiwanese roots, said she did not worry about China's hostility. 
"I think Chen Shui-bian will be flexible enough to deal with it," she said.
Cheng Wen-shiung, a 47-year-old tailor, also said the threats from China would not intimidate him.
"We Taiwanese have the courage to repel any invader," he said. 
But he added, "Of course, some people won't vote for Chen because of China."

file: China_s Top Justice Official Ousted, Some Say for Corruption.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's minister of justice was removed from office this week, officials acknowledged today, and according to some accounts he is under investigation for corruption.
As of tonight, the departure of the minister, Gao Changli, 63, had not been announced. 
But during the day, as rumors swirled in legal circles, Justice Ministry employees were told that Mr. Gao had quit because of poor health, a ministry worker said.
If his departure involves financial improprieties, Mr. Gao's case would be another blow for the Communist Party, which is reeling at the scope of corruption coming to light.
Adding to the party's concern is a legal battle brewing in Vancouver, Canada, over the fate of China's most wanted suspect, Lai Changxing. 
Chinese officials say he was the mastermind of a smuggling operation in the southern city of Xiamen that drew hundreds of high party, police and customs officials into crime.
Officials said Mr. Gao had been replaced by Zhang Fusen, deputy secretary of the Beijing Communist Party and a former deputy justice minister.
Over the last two days, a few newspapers in Hong Kong and the West have reported that sources in the ministry were saying that Mr. Gao had been detained for interrogation about economic misdeeds. 
While some legal officials also said today that he was under investigation, others said that they were unaware of it, and details could not be confirmed.
Mr. Gao rose to power in Shandong Province, then in 1993 became a senior member of the national Supreme People's Court before being appointed to the top justice post in 1998.
Though traditionally weak, the ministry oversees prisons and legal education and regulates the legal profession. 
While Mr. Gao had no direct power over prosecutors and courts, which are notoriously susceptible to political control and corruption, he had taken a leading role in promoting the rule of law, a professed goal of the top leaders as China opens to the global economy.
Mr. Lai, the detained businessman, began as a barely educated farmer in Fujian Province but by the 1990's was a corporate kingpin living in Hong Kong, with his Yuanhua Group a dominant corporate presence back in Xiamen, a port in Fujian. 
The authorities say that by spreading bribes widely, Mr. Lai, 42, imported more than $5 billion worth of cars, fuel and other goods without paying duties. 
By the time the case broke earlier this year, Mr. Lai had disappeared. 
Now, with the detention of him and his wife, Tsang Mingna, by Canadian immigration authorities last week, it is known that Mr. Lai, his wife and three teenage children fled to Vancouver in August 1999, using Hong Kong passports.
The couple's detention has put Canada in a delicate spot. 
In hearings this week, officials made it clear that they hope to deport them to China, stressing that Canada does not want to be seen as a refuge for criminals. 
But Canada does not have an extradition treaty with China or a death penalty and has often declined to extradite criminals to countries where they are likely to be executed.
Eleven others in the smuggling case have been sentenced to death, and Mr. Lai would be almost certain to receive the same punishment.
In a court statement this week, Mr. Lai denied the smuggling charges and gave sensational but unverified details of past ties to senior Hong Kong and Chinese officials as well as his work as a Chinese double-agent against Taiwan.
Mr. Lai said that he met three times in 1999 with Chinese prosecutors who wanted him to help frame the vice minister for public security, Li Jizhou, who had been a longtime friend. 
It was his refusal to cooperate in a political struggle, Mr. Lai said, that led prosecutors to go after him.
In contrast, accounts leaking from government sources say Mr. Lai kept a pleasure house in Xiamen where he set up Mr. Li and other officials with mistresses, ensuring cooperation in his scheme.

file: China_s Trade Status Remains _Open Question_ as Vote Nears.txt
text:
ï»¿
With animosity toward China growing on the right and left in Congress, President Clinton's national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, said yesterday that it remained "an open question" whether Congress would vote to revoke China's normal trading status.
Mr. Berger spoke as the Republican leadership in the House rescheduled this year's vote on the trading status for late June, a month earlier than expected, to assure a vote before the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule on July 1.
Mr. Berger said that even a close vote that preserved China's status could prove "corrosive," undercutting the Administration's efforts to deal with China's leaders on a variety of issues, from the environment to the spread of weapons.
"It is difficult for us to move this relationship to a new level where we have a greater chance of solving problems if we don't have a national consensus behind the policy," Mr. Berger said in an interview in his office at the White House.
The trade arrangement is called "most favored nation" status, although it is the normal trading arrangement accorded most countries by the United States. 
China's status is currently subject to yearly review, and advocates of renewal this year have been concerned that any problem in the handover of Hong Kong, especially televised protests that could provoke police reaction, could jeopardize passage.
One Republican aide said yesterday that the vote was being moved up to deny opponents the opportunity to rally support. 
That suggested confidence that the House will preserve the status but concern that opposition could be stronger than it has been in recent years.
In a speech delivered in New York at the Council on Foreign Relations, Mr. Berger said that the fight to revoke China's status was the "one development" that could undercut American policy toward China and "do grievous injury to the interests of the United States."
In his speech, Mr. Berger defended the Administration's policy, which seeks to engage China through trade and economic development, while making clear American objections to violations of human rights, among other things. 
He also said the United States would monitor how China takes control of Hong Kong to insure that its traditions and freedoms thrive, but that punishing China by revoking its trading status would only isolate Hong Kong.
"The goals of the opponents to normal trading relations with China are ones we share -- advocating human rights and religious freedom, promoting fair trade, strengthening regional and global security," he said in his speech. 
"But the method they have chosen -- destroying our economic relations with China -- is profoundly misguided."
In the interview, Mr. Berger said the Administration was articulating what he called a "clear and coherent" policy toward China as Congress moves toward what is expected to be a pitched fight.
The Administration hoped this year would bring calmer relations with China, culminating in a summit meeting between President Clinton and President Jiang Zemin in the fall. 
Last year's debate ended quickly, as members in the House voted solidly -- 286 to 141 -- to renew China's status.
But this year the debate has flared, driven by a lack of improvement in China's human rights record, the impending takeover of Hong Kong and the controversy over campaign finance.
Mr. Berger argued that critics of China had chosen the wrong way to register their outrage. 
He said that the United States had "an arsenal of tools" to punish China, including more targeted sanctions, like those imposed last month on two Chinese companies for helping Iran develop chemical weapons.
As for Hong Kong, he said the United States expected China to abide by the agreement reached with Britain in 1984 to maintain Hong Kong's freedoms under autonomy. 
The United States would gauge that, he said, by seeing whether elections for a new legislature take place soon, the civil service and judiciary continue to work unmolested, the economy remains open, and freedom of religion, speech and association is maintained.
"Living up to that pledge is as much in China's interest as it is in Hong Kong or in ours," he said in the speech.
"A smooth reversion will promote China's international prestige," he said. 
"Handled badly, the transition will tarnish China."
He did not, however, specify what steps the United States would take if China at some point in the future violated those standards.

file: China_s Transport Gridlock_ Cars vs. Mass Transit.txt
text:
ï»¿
Until recently, officials of this port city famous for its Tsing Tao beer and its German architecture boasted that they were investing heavily in basic infrastructure as part of their strategy to attract more foreign industries.
Last fall, Deputy Mayor Min Xiangchao could hardly contain his enthusiasm when he told an interviewer that "the pace of growth of Qingdao is difficult to hold back now" because the city had won approval from the central Government in Beijing to build a subway system, a cross-harbor tunnel connecting the city's industrial zone with its downtown area, which are on opposite sides of Jiaozhou Bay, and a 10-mile bridge to span the bay.
"These will be the engines of growth in later years," he predicted.
Today, however, these projects have been suspended for lack of financing.
What has happened here in the last 12 months is happening all over China: basic transportation projects, especially mass transportation, are being canceled or cut back dramatically for lack of capital and as Beijing's leaders debate the best way to move 1.3 billion Chinese from one place to another in the next century.
While money is a key issue, basic issues of transportation policy also remain unsettled.
Although most Chinese still walk, bicycle or ride a farm animal to get around, the migration by millions of people to urban centers is creating a transportation crisis.
Where there is public transport, bus and train fares stay frozen for years, part of the cradle-to-grave subsidy system under socialism that has undermined new investment. 
Meanwhile, in dozens of large cities, traffic gridlock is threatening the very growth that must occur to meet the transport needs of tens of millions of new job seekers arriving in the cities over the next five years.
In large part, the policy debate centers on whether scarce money should be directed more toward better roads for the swelling number of automobiles, or toward mass transit. 
Which way China goes will have enormous environmental consequences not only for urban residents here, already choking in smoggy air, but for the whole world -- a vast new fleet of cars in China would use up so many resources and add to the problem of planetary warming.
The debate over how to manage this crisis has pitted the powerful Ministry of Machine-Building Industry and its two million workers in dozens of automobile plants against China's scientific establishment and many municipal authorities, who see their streets descending into a choking paroxysm of traffic and pollution.
The ministry is busy implementing the "pillar industry" strategy formulated in 1994 by China's State Council under Prime Minister Li Peng. 
Its aim is to create a half-dozen giant Chinese automakers in partnership with General Motors, Volkswagen and other foreign companies to feed the growing demand by newly rich Chinese for cars.
The ministry wants China's central and local governments to divert more money into highway and road construction to support an automobile-based economy.
But China's scientific community, in a major report last summer, began a campaign to challenge this policy.
"It would be inappropriate for China to encourage the use of family cars on a large scale in the next few years because of the country's serious shortage of land, oil and other resources and its huge population," the scientists' report said. 
It recommended "a public transportation network that is convenient, complete and radiating in all directions."
As it is, China's relatively small road network is already under strain. 
For every one million Chinese, there are only 541 miles of roads, most of them unpaved and rutted. 
By comparison, there are 15,195 miles of paved road per one million Americans, 5,457 miles per one million Japanese and 1,070 miles per one million Indians.
One of China's leading physicists, Prof. He Zuoxiu, who worked on the country's first atomic bomb, has thrust himself into the transportation debate by trying to persuade the Communist Party leadership to get behind mass transit.
Ticking off the problems of China's future energy supplies, worsening pollution and the shortage of land, Professor He said in a recent interview in Beijing that "China just simply cannot sustain the development of a car economy."
Professor He said that he fears that Government policy is being driven by a desire to keep two million auto workers employed. 
In addition, many top officials in Prime Minister Li's Cabinet come from the auto industry. 
Even President Jiang Zemin got his start as a Soviet-trained electrical engineer.
"Right now, the Government still has no clear policy and so this issue is still very much under debate," Professor He said, even though "almost every scientist in China favors the development of mass transit systems."
As the debate rages, many experts say other factors are influencing China's choices, notably the country's inability to attract the kind of capital needed to construct a modern transport system.
Limits set by Chinese authorities on rates of return foreigners can earn on long-term investments in power plants and toll highways in China have engendered a wariness in world capital markets about making long-term commitments here.
Still, there is a sense of urgency.
China's infrastructure bill includes the Yangtze River's Three Gorges Dam, the largest hydro-electric project in the world, and dozens of major power plants that must be completed to meet electrical demand and stop the blackouts that idle many industries.
In addition, money must be found for an aquaduct system to save northern China from perpetual drought, for new rail networks to open China's internal markets, for oil refineries, an updated telecommunications system and dozens of new airports and shipping terminals.
The central Government's budget revenues, chronically weak, cannot hope to pay for such a prodigious agenda, estimated by the World Bank to cost $300 billion or more during the 1996-2000 period.
"China's needs today are enormous and immediate," concluded a recent study by Nicholas Bradbury of The Economist Intelligence Unit in Hong Kong. 
"Without dramatic improvements to its infrastructure, and foreign expertise to implement them, China's economic progress will stall."
In December, China's State Council, or cabinet, issued orders to shut down subway and light rail projects in Qingdao and three other major cities -- Nanjing, Shenyang and Tianjin. 
The order was not made public until late March.
"Funds needed for metro construction are beyond the means of the central and local government and operating expenses are too high," the semi-official China Daily newspaper quoted a Cabinet statement as saying.
The latest estimates show that the cost of subway construction have soared in the last decade and now range from $53 million to $91.5 million per kilometer.
"These programs are extremely capital intensive," said Robert S. O'Neil, president of De Leuw, Cather & Company, a Washington, D.C., subway design and consulting company now working on Shanghai's subway system. 
"They don't pay for themselves," he added.
Wang Yuexian, a senior transportation planner at the State Planning Commission in Beijing, said that under the cabinet edict, only subways planned for Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou would go forward, and even in these cities, schedules would be stretched out and work limited to a single line.
"A total of 17 cities have applied for subway financing," said Jiao Ying, a senior engineer at the Ministry of Railways, who has stayed behind in Qingdao to complete a test tunnel section should the project ever be revived. 
"But the Government only considers three or four of them important, and the rest will have to wait," he added.
In Beijing, a new eight-mile subway line that was to open in 1997 will now be delayed another 10 years. 
Shanghai will be allowed to complete a new 16-mile line and Guangzhou will complete an 11-mile line.
The central Government edict has done little to dampen enthusiasm in Qingdao.
Xue Liai, the vice director of the city's Major Projects Office, said in an interview that "we still hope we can build the subway because every citizen here wants it."
Construction crews had nearly completed the largest station on the first 10-mile segment of the Qingdao system when the order to stop work came in December. 
City officials quickly shifted their plans and persuaded the Miramar Hotel group from Hong Kong to convert the station into an underground shopping mall.
Now, where the trains should be running, there is an endless line of boutiques, and above ground on the streets -- gridlock.

file: China_s Troops Enter Macao And Are Cheered by Residents.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's troops streamed into this new Chinese territory today, in a joyful procession that revealed how deeply people here yearn for law and order after the gangsterism that stained the last years of Portuguese colonial rule.
At noon, 12 hours after the ceremony in which China gained sovereignty over Macao, a convoy of armored personnel carriers, buses and trucks rumbled across the border from Zhuhai, on the Chinese mainland. 
Less than an hour later, the 500 troops secured their objective: a makeshift barracks in a vacant apartment building in the center of Macao.
Tens of thousands of people lined the route, cheering and waving Chinese flags, in a largely unscripted expression of hospitality. 
It was a contrast to the handover of Hong Kong two years ago, when the arrival of the Chinese Army was met with a mixture of curiosity and dread.
"I am thrilled because the soldiers give me confidence," said Lau Kit Leng, 34, a homemaker. 
"Security has been such a big problem in Macao. 
The troops give me a reason to hope."
The Chinese Army seems destined to play a very different role in Macao than in Hong Kong. 
In well-policed Hong Kong, the troops have kept a very low profile. 
They arrived in predawn darkness on July 1, 1997, and headed to their barracks, where they have essentially remained.
In Macao, where the colonial administration could not stop a gang war for control of the territory's lucrative casinos, officials said the army would play a powerful symbolic role in restoring law and order. 
On the streets today, several people said that if the local police were not up to the job, they would be happy to see the army go after the gangsters.
Edmund Ho, the new chief executive of Macao, insisted that the troops would not be used for police work. 
But he said they would give people a sense of safety. 
And he added that having a garrison nearby would help him reform the Macao police force, which has been plagued by corruption.
The deployment of troops was a bone of contention between China and Portugal in an otherwise smooth handover. 
Portugal withdrew its soldiers shortly after its revolution in 1974, and Portuguese officials said the joint declaration governing the return of the colony did not provide for stationing troops there.
But early this year, China's deputy prime minister, Qian Qichen, said the government planned to send an advance guard to the colony even before the handover.
In March, President Jorge Sampaio of Portugal briefly threatened to boycott the handover ceremony if the Chinese did not explain why they were not abiding by the agreement.
In an interview here on Sunday, Mr. Sampaio seemed eager to wash his hands of the issue. 
"China is China," he said. 
"China has sovereign rights. 
Macao is going to be a special region of China."

file: Chinese Action On Copyrights.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's legislature approved prison terms and stiffer fines for copyright violators today, meeting a principal United States demand five days after Washington threatened trade sanctions.
The new rules were approved by the National People's Congress and take effect immediately. 
The rules for the first time include prison terms. 
Violators of copyright laws face up to seven years in jail, the state-run New China News Agency reported.
The United States said last Thursday that it would give China six months to curb what Washington said was widespread piracy of intellectual property, like computer software and movies.
If the United States remains unsatisfied, it could impose punitive tariffs on up to $800 million worth of Chinese goods -- the amount that Washington says American companies are losing each year from Chinese piracy.
The regulations approved today also require violators to compensate copyright owners for losses, according to the Chinese news agency. 
American companies had complained that violators previously had to pay only modest fines.

file: Chinese and Indian Leaders Vow to End Border Tension.txt
text:
ï»¿
Nearly 35 years after a border war that left China occupying a sprawling region of Himalayan uplands claimed by India, the two countries agreed in principle today on mutual troop withdrawals from disputed areas along their 2,500-mile frontier and pledged that "neither side shall use its military capability against the other."
The pact was a centerpiece of the visit to New Delhi by President Jiang Zemin of China, the first Chinese head of state to visit independent India. 
He arrived here on Thursday for a four-day stay that has been billed by both countries as a fresh opportunity to rebuild a relationship that has wavered between bitter and wary for three decades.
Apart from the pledge that they would not go to war, which has appeared in past agreements between the two countries, details were deferred for another round of negotiations, and no deadline was set for a final accord.

Sooner or later someone was going to discover a way to make money on the Chinese craze for America. 
Now it looks as if someone has -- perhaps at the expense of thousands of naive Chinese.
All across the country, from the ice-glazed terrain of Harbin in the north to this moneyed metropolis in the south, Chinese people are talking about the chance to buy a "piece of America."
"I want to be a landowner in America!" said Bi Fei, a young financier who carries a cellular telephone and dashes around from luxury hotel to fancy restaurant. 
"How many Chinese people can say that they own American land?"
Driven by a belief that possessing land in the United States gives the owner the right to inspect the property -- and therefore obtain that sorely wanted visa -- tens of thousands of Chinese are rushing to buy tiny bits of America.
Â 
A $1,700 Gimmick
In the United States, a "Deed of Land to the United States of America" is a deed to a square inch of terrain in each of the 50 states. 
It sells for $49.95 as a novelty gift, like a pet rock or canned air.
But in China, the deed represents a dream, and prices are going berserk. 
In Guangzhou, the price this month was $468, in Beijing $700. 
In Shanghai, the price once hit $1,700.
While the novelty was intended for sale primarily in the United States, 100,000 Chinese have purchased the deeds since they arrived on the market in China last November. 
That is twice as many as bought the deeds in the United States, where they have been available for more than a year.
The mania reflects the infatuation with most things American. 
But what really captures the Chinese imagination is the prospect that as American landowners, they will be allowed to visit their property. 
This is coupled with the fear that, as with real estate in China, there is not much around.
Â 
An Inch Here, an Inch There
In fact there is plenty, according to American Acres Inc., which sells the product in the United States. 
The company, which says it has purchased an acre in each of the states, divided its holdings into 6,272,640 shares, one for each square inch. 
Three of the properties are in Saint Lawrence County, N.Y.; Danbury, Conn., and Oldmans Township, N.J.
About 250,000 deeds have been sold around the world, with China by far the largest market.
In Guangzhou, where enough people have hidden bank accounts that they can begin to appreciate the concept of buying novelties, a few business executives are thinking about the deeds as a collector's item or a speculative stock.
But for many Chinese the land offers a remote possibility: the chance to clinch that visa to America. 
Unfortunately, the Chinese are mistaken.
United States Embassy and consular officials deny that a deed will help obtain a visa. 
The calls and the questions, however, are still coming in.
The fine print is in English, and many buyers ignore it.
In a dilapidated Guangzhou office, a middle-aged engineer tells how he was sadly disappointed when the United States Consulate told him his property would not win him a visa.
Â 
The Fine Print
"What we bought is not a piece of land at all," he complained. 
"What we have is just a piece of paper. 
We can't even resell the land on our own. 
The only thing we can resell are the pieces of paper."
The engineer said his company had purchased several hundred shares in the hope of reselling them at a profit. 
But after discovering that the deeds do not help to get a visa, the company decided to drop its plans and absorb the loss.
In fact, the deed states that owners shall not resell it as a security, but a secondary market has sprouted anyway in several cities.

Â 
The Real Estate 'Market'
"The sellers tell us to buy now, when the price of land in America is low, and then sell later, when the economy and the real estate market rises," said a Chinese reporter who covers business and the economy.

"We sell it at one price.

text:
ï»¿
EAST AND WEST
China, Power, and the Future of Asia.
By Christopher Patten.
Illustrated. 304 pp. 
New York:
Times Books/Random House. 
$25.
We now have the book that Rupert Murdoch refused to allow HarperCollins, owned by the news corporation he controls, to publish, presumably because he thought it would be offensive to the Chinese Communist authorities. 
That alone may persuade many people that Christopher Patten's "East and West" is important enough to buy -- even, perhaps, to read. 
If it does, Murdoch will have done us all an unintended service. 
This is a book we need to read, even though the tumult over its publication gave us little idea of what it is really about.
Those expecting sensational disclosures or gossip about scandalous personal behavior will be disappointed. 
Patten's book has none of that. 
Those expecting a defense of Patten's record as the last British Governor of Hong Kong and a critique of Chinese conduct during the negotiations over the handover of the city will find that, but it is only the start. 
The author's experience in Hong Kong makes up a relatively small, though critically important, part of the book.
Even its full title, "East and West: China, Power, and the Future of Asia," fails to do justice to its scope. 
It is, in fact, no less than the defense of a political and economic philosophy to guide public policy as we approach the next century. 
This description (which Patten does not use) may seem pretentious and, indeed, forbidding, so I should hasten to add that this volume is neither a dreary academic summary nor a tedious apologia by a politician who has just left office. 
It is, rather, a beguiling mixture of memoir and maxim, of well-chosen anecdote and pithy analysis, of experience and erudition. 
The result is that rarest of literary products: a book that is as delightful to read as it is enlightening to ponder.
When Christopher Patten was Governor of Hong Kong, his critics charged that his attempt to introduce elective democracy into the colony on the eve of its transfer to Chinese rule was misguided; it was, they said, too late in the day for reform to be carried out successfully and any attempt would only offend the leaders in Beijing, who would not only take out their resentment on Hong Kong when they had a chance but (infinitely more important in the eyes of many of the critics) deprive British businessmen of their fair share of trade and investment opportunities.
Patten's rejoinder is that, though British concern for democracy in Hong Kong may have been belated, it was nonetheless motivated by both principle and practicality. 
Hong Kong's civil society had matured to the point that it would not tolerate a secret deal struck behind its back. 
Furthermore, he argues that everything he did to make the legislative elections in Hong Kong as democratic as possible was consistent with what had been formally agreed to by the Governments of Britain and China before his arrival. 
It was not he, therefore, who was the problem, but rather the Chinese, who tried to undermine the clear purpose of that agreement. 
As for trade and investment, he doubts that political disputes ever had much effect on Chinese business decisions, despite occasional threats by officials in Beijing.
The record of negotiations, the pattern of trade and the course of events since July 1997, when Hong Kong became a province of China, strongly support Patten's view on all these questions. 
No fair-minded person who has bothered to read the Joint Declaration and looked at the facts can seriously charge that Patten violated the agreement in the arrangements for elections to Hong Kong's legislative assembly. 
The disputes with Beijing stemmed from a Chinese effort to subvert the clear meaning of agreements they had signed and thereby to avoid being confronted by too many awkward democratic institutions when Hong Kong came under Chinese rule. 
Despite occasional doubts stimulated by some "old China hands" and gullible businessmen, the British Government supported Patten most of the time, and there is no evidence that trade and investment have suffered.
While China dissolved Hong Kong's legislative assembly when it took over, it scheduled new elections for May of this year. 
Changes in the election rules handicapped the democratic parties, but they still won the largest single bloc of seats in an election with a record turnout of voters. 
So much for the argument that people in Hong Kong were interested only in making money, not in politics.
Who can doubt that, absent the precedent for limited representative democracy set by the citizens of Hong Kong during Patten's tenure as Governor, Chinese treatment of the erstwhile colony would have been harsher, and attempts to limit Hong Kong's autonomy more vigorous?
And who can doubt that, if China's Communist leaders had been encouraged to lay a heavier hand on Hong Kong's liberties, this would have weakened the city's economic performance and made it more difficult for China to resist the bout of Asian flu that spread through the region last fall?
Governments, preoccupied with staying in power, often fail to understand what is in their country's best interest.
The Chinese leaders, of course, understood that a prosperous Hong Kong would be useful to China. 
What they did not understand was the intimate connection between economic prosperity and a free society based on the rule of law. 
As Patten puts it, they had little comprehension "of the relationship between Hong Kong's hardware, a capitalist economy, and its software, a pluralist society."
If China is able to master the daunting problems now facing it (failing state industries, a vulnerable banking system, the social pressure of rising expectations, pell-mell urbanization), it will need more than Hong Kong's wealth; it will also need to heed Hong Kong's experience. 
Again, in Patten's words, "Hong Kong is at one and the same time China's window on the world, bridge to the world, shop front for the world and paradigm for the world of what China as a whole could become."
Following the spirited and persuasive defense of his record in Hong Kong, Patten turns to broader themes: what has brought about economic advance in Asia (and elsewhere)?
Is there a culturally determined "Asian" way that is either superior to the "Western" way or -- at least -- more suited to the Asian environment?
Are our civilizations doomed to clash?
Is democracy necessary for economic development?
What is the proper role of government, in the East, the West, or anywhere?
The claim that Asia's economic success resulted from specific Asian virtues has suffered a severe blow since the monetary and economic setbacks that became apparent last fall. 
Even so, the fallacy of this argument should have been obvious earlier. 
As Patten contends, what brought rapid economic development to the Asian "tigers" was the same thing that brought it to countries elsewhere: capitalism, hard work, frugality, limited government. 
There was no Asian miracle; if development was more rapid in some Asian countries than it had been in the West, that was because modern technology and communication have accelerated the process of change and because these countries were playing catch-up. 
It takes longer for a pioneer to clear the way than for late starters to follow a well-marked trail.
Patten heaps particular scorn on the thesis that authoritarian government fits the Asian character better than dem-
ocratic institutions. 
It is understandable that dictators, their sycophants and those who aspire to dictatorship would make the argument; it is harder to explain why intelligent scholars and businessmen should be taken in by it. 
After all, in country after country we have seen that as people become more affluent they demand a part in their own governance. 
If this is denied, governments eventually fall (witness South Korea and Indonesia) and sometimes the entire fabric of the state is left in tatters, as in most of the former Soviet Union.
While Patten is firm in his conviction that human rights are universal and that democratic countries should reflect that in their policies, he would not place human rights at the center of a foreign policy or attempt to promote them by ineffectual means. 
He praises the United States for supporting democracy in Hong Kong, but ridicules the annual farce in Washington when Congress debates extension of most-favored-nation trading status for China, to no useful effect whatever. 
He is uncomfortable with the choice to go with what he terms "Carter or Kissinger, with high-minded waffle or cynical common sense."
Such a choice does, indeed, create an awkward dilemma, but Patten's advice to treat China as we would any other country, while sound as a general principle, does little to resolve it. 
The fact is that the Chinese leaders will not respect the rights of their own people until they see that it is in their interest to do so. 
We have no means of forcing them to do what they should, and public lectures are more likely to engender acts of defiance than willing compliance.
Does this mean that the cause is hopeless?
Far from it: if in fact a civil society, the rule of law and democratic institutions are essential to a productive and stable polity, governments that block their introduction will only handicap their countries in today's and tomorrow's competitive world. 
This is something that some Communist officials have come to understand. 
Zhao Ziyang, the Chinese leader who was ousted in 1989 for opposing repression of the demonstrators in Tiananmen Square, seems to have understood; in a different country both Mikhail Gorbachev and Eduard Shevardnadze came to the same conclusion.
We should have no hesitation in explaining why respect for human rights is vital to every society and why it influences our attitude toward the countries we deal with. 
But in doing so, we must be careful not to leave the impression that treating one's own people properly is in some way a concession to us, or deserves a reward from us.
Eloquent, compact and far-reaching in its range, Christopher Patten's "East and West" is a must for anyone who wishes to understand the forces that will shape the world of the 21st century. 
We should thank Rupert Murdoch for calling it to our attention. 
The leaders of the democratic China of the future will doubtless remember his signal service to their cause.

A loose-knit group of veteran democracy advocates has started a campaign to promote independent labor unions among China's workers, who face vast layoffs as the Government strives to close money-losing enterprises.

In a letter sent this week to foreign news organizations, the campaigners say workers now have a clear right to set up new unions to fight for their interests in this period of drastic downsizing, mergers and sales of state-owned industries. 
Currently, unions not sponsored by the Communist Party are illegal, and the Government has given no sign that it will relent, United Nations covenant or not.
The proposals in the letter go to the heart of China's most explosive political challenge: how to cope with the legions of victims as it unleashes market forces to streamline the bloated, often bankrupt Communist economy.
In recent months, there have been numerous reports of small-scale worker protests around the country over such concerns as nonpayment of wages or pensions, fear of job losses after corporate takeovers, and conflicts over dismissals and severance pay.
The dislocation of millions of industrial workers is occurring even as the growing private and semiprivate sectors bring new prosperity to millions of other Chinese -- a visible gap that only adds to the tensions.
"Workers in state-owned enterprises, especially, should immediately form their own unions to monitor their leaders and prevent leaders from engaging in bribery or stealing public properties," said the letter, signed by four leaders of the 1979 "Democracy Wall" movement, each of whom has served time in prison. 
"Only by depending on ourselves can we fight those who punish workers arbitrarily or fire workers without reason."
In a telephone interview from Cambridge, Mass., Wang Xizhe, one of the signers, said: "China's workers don't understand that China has agreed to this international agreement. 
We're going to use every method we can to educate them about it."
Mr. Wang, 49, who spent 15 years in prison for earlier pro-democracy activities, fled China last year under threat of arrest after he signed a letter calling for impeachment of President Jiang Zemin.
The agreement in question is the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights of 1966, which China's United Nations representative, Qin Huasun, signed in New York on Oct. 
26, just before President Jiang visited the United States. 
The covenant is one of two that Washington had urged China to sign to improve its human rights record.
The covenant guarantees "the right of everyone to form trade unions and join the trade union of his choice."

China could easily cite these loopholes.
Because of tight Government control of the press, few people here may learn directly about the pro-union letter, which is dated Dec. 
20. But Mr. Wang said many people around China were spreading the message through the Internet and private channels. 
He said the group also hoped that foreign radio news broadcasters, who are widely listened to here, would take note.
Mr. Wang added that the signers were only trying to raise awareness, not organize unions, something he said workers must do themselves.
