file: CLINTON LAUNCHES EFFORT TO RENEW CHINA TRADE TIES.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Clinton began a campaign today to win Congressional renewal of normal trading status for China, in an annual exercise that threatens to be more contentious than ever this year.
In an announcement before a group of business executives, Mr. Clinton said that trade ties are "the best way to bring China into the family of nations and to secure our interests and our ideals."
Mr. Clinton is facing growing anti-China sentiment on both the right and the left in Congress, with an unlikely combination of opponents lining up against renewing China's trade privileges. 
The coalition ranges from labor, which is concerned about economics and human rights issues, to the Christian right, which is opposing China on human rights grounds as well.
Once Mr. Clinton formally sends his decision to grant China what is known as "most-favored-nation status," the House and Senate have 90 days in which they can try to overturn his recommendation.
Originally the White House had hoped that this year relations with China could be put on a firmer footing. 
Mr. Clinton is expected to hold a summit meeting with President Jiang Zemin of China later this year, and the Administration is negotiating with China over entry into the World Trade Organization.
Admitting that it would not have the votes, the White House quietly shelved any hope that it might be able to win permanent, instead of annual, approval of normal trade ties for China this year.
The only debate inside the Administration, officials said, was over how much the President should personally put himself on the line to support China in the face of the campaign finance controversy.
The President won an important ally of sorts today in Representative Newt Gingrich, the Speaker of the House. 
Although Mr. Gingrich assailed Mr. Clinton as being "virtually absent without leadership on issues of religious tolerance, human rights, and democratic freedoms," he said he would support normal trade relations with China.
Other irritants in this year's debate are China's transfer of missiles to Iran and its huge trade surplus with the United States. 
Congress is also swayed this year by increasing concerns over Hong Kong. 
The assumption in Washington is that the handover of the British colony to China will go smoothly. 
If it doesn't, as one senior Administration official conceded this afternoon, "this whole effort sinks in the Pacific."
The White House today sought to address concerns about Hong Kong's transition by noting that Hong Kong's governor, Chris Patton, and Hong Kong's most prominent advocates of democracy , like Martin Lee, the leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, support extension of China's trade status.
"Even those people in Hong Kong that have been most passionately identified with the cause of freedom and human rights and have been most in conflict with the Chinese have argued that we have to maintain an open trading relationship with them so we can continue to work with them," Mr. Clinton said.
Other Administration officials argued that Hong Kong is the gateway of trade between the United States and China and that to cut off China's trade status at this moment would deal a blow to Hong Kong precisely at this crucial moment of transition.
While last year's announcement about China's trade status was made in a major speech on Asia policy, this year the President made the announcement at the business leaders' event, which was held in the Old Executive Office Building.
Mr. Clinton said that stopping normal trade relations would "cut off our contact with the Chinese people and undermine our influence with the Chinese Government."
Mr. Clinton originally came into office accusing President Bush of "coddling dictators," but in the spring of 1994, under pressure from American business groups, Mr. Clinton backed down from his early attempt to link China's most-favored-nation status to significant progress in human rights. 
Since then Mr. Clinton has called for renewal of China's trade status annually.
Mr. Clinton has argued that economic engagement is the best way to get China to improve its treatment of dissidents. 
But his national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, had to concede at a White House briefing today that "we cannot say that human rights conditions in China are better today than they were a year ago."
But Mr. Berger argued that commercial cooperation and openness to the world would eventually change the Beijing Government's behavior.
Yet the Administration's admissions that little has changed in human rights encouraged those who argue that Mr. Clinton's attempt to use commerce in the service of human rights has failed.
"They have to change the subject from human rights because they have nothing to point to," said Gary L. Bauer, the president of the Family Research Council, which is pressing its traditional Republican allies to abandon the party's longstanding support for renewing China's ordinary trading rights.
"It's a corrosive debate," Mr. Berger said in an interview in his office this afternoon. 
"Everyone in Congress knows that cutting off trade relations is far too blunt an instrument. 
Instead of debating how to influence China, how to shape the direction, we wind up debating a piece of the relationship. 
It doesn't work."
Mr. Clinton said today that "the United States has a huge stake in the continued emergence of China in a way that is open economically and stable politically. 
Of course we hope that it will come to respect human rights more and the rule of law more."
But Human Rights Watch/Asia immediately issued a statement asking how the Administration planned to exert influence on China on human rights, noting that the Administration's efforts to condemn China's human-rights practices in Geneva last month had failed. 
"What other measures is the Administration willing to use?" asked Mike Jendrzejcyk, the group's Washington director. 
"Or has it abandoned human rights altogether?"
Despite the growing anti-China sentiment in Congress, Administration officials and opponents of most-favored-nation trade status say that Mr. Clinton would ultimately have the votes to prevail on the issue.
The United States has economic incentives to continue the trade relationship. 
United States officials say that 170,000 American jobs are dependent on exports to China and that ending normal trade status would cost consumers $600 million annually in higher prices on certain consumer goods.
In fact, at this point the United States and China are so economically intertwined that even many members of the growing anti-China lobby in Congress concede that denying trade privileges to China would be tantamount to breaking off political relations with the world's most populous nation.
As the debate plays out over the next months, the only question, officials say, is whether the President will be forced into a bruising veto fight to preserve most-favored-nation status. 
That would occur if the House and Senate pass a joint resolution turning down normal trade status. 
Both chambers would then have to muster two-thirds votes to override the President's veto.
The last time there was such a confrontation over China was in 1992, a Presidential camapign year, when Congress tried to stop most-favored nation status but failed to override Mr. Bush's veto.

file: CLINTON PLANNING DIPLOMATIC WHIRL ON NEW YORK TRIP.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Clinton's foreign policy aides say he plans a diplomatic whirlwind in New York over the next three days, including what one senior official called "the last real chance" to jump-start the failed talks between Israel and the Palestinians and what may be prove to be a tense session with China's president over Beijing's continued missile exports to Pakistan.
Those meetings are part of a jammed schedule for Mr. Clinton, who arrives in Manhattan today for one of his last opportunities for major foreign policy accomplishments in his second term. 
Tomorrow, he is to open a three-day series of speeches and discussions by more than 150 world leaders at the United Nations.
Clearly intent on not sitting on the sidelines while the presidential campaign speeds into its last two months, Mr. Clinton plans to announce American support for a plan to strengthen the United Nations peacekeeping department.
But Mr. Clinton also plans to use the United Nations meeting to insert himself in an array of simmering world conflicts -- from the Middle East to Cyprus to the Korean Peninsula.
Samuel R. Berger, Mr. Clinton's national security adviser, said in a lengthy interview over the weekend that much of Mr. Clinton's time will be spent on one last effort to reconstruct a deal between the Palestinian leader, Yasir Arafat, and Prime Minister Ehud Barak of Israel. 
Mr. Clinton is said to want that foreign policy achievement more than any other in his short time left in office, and he watched in frustration and anger as it slipped from his grasp at Camp David in the early morning hours of July 25.
He put most of the blame on Mr. Arafat, who was unwilling to sign on to any agreement that gave him only partial sovereignty over contested parts of Jerusalem. 
Mr. Arafat also was apparently unwilling to go along with Mr. Clinton's alternative proposal, to announce a settlement on all issues except Jerusalem. 
Mr. Clinton later likened the sessions to "going to the dentist without having your gums deadened."
In advance of this week's meetings, Mr. Clinton dispatched Dennis Ross, his special Middle East envoy, and George Tenet, the director of central intelligence, to try out new formulations. 
"There needs to be some flexibility that would indicate we have some chance of getting real momentum here," Mr. Berger said. 
"If we are not any further than we were in Camp David, it will be tough to get this done."
Both President Clinton and Mr. Berger have contended that Mr. Arafat's inflexibility was the chief obstacle to an agreement at Camp David. 
American officials have made it clear that little has changed since then.
Mr. Berger said that currently there are no plans for three-way meetings between Mr. Arafat, Mr. Barak and Mr. Clinton. Instead, the president will shuttle between the two at the Waldorf-Astoria, starting tomorrow afternoon.
No other meetings are formally scheduled, but Mr. Clinton's aides have already laid out a plan for at least two more days of talks.
Nonetheless, the atmosphere of the chaotic week at the United Nations may work against Mr. Clinton's hopes. 
In the seclusion of Camp David, the president could shut out distractions and some of the outside pressures bearing down on the leaders in the heat of their talks. 
News blackouts were easy to manage, because the press was kept miles away. 
Cell phones do not work at Camp David, leaving just a few land lines for each delegation.
New York will be the opposite: Mr. Arafat will be negotiating with other Arab leaders just blocks away, and Mr. Barak will be talking as he entertains American Jewish groups and others with a strong interest in how a deal is constructed.
Thousands of reporters will be milling about; the delegations will have every form of communication at their fingertips.
"It's not an ideal atmosphere," a former senior official who was deeply involved in past negotiations said recently. 
"I think the effort is to get enough progress to justify more meetings or maybe whisking them back to Camp David at the end of the week."
Mr. Berger said he believed that any thought of reconvening at Camp David was premature; nonetheless, Clinton's schedule for week's end has been left vague, save for a few New York appearances on behalf of his wife's candidacy for the New York Senate seat.
Mr. Clinton's meeting on Friday with President Jiang Zemin of China may be Mr. Clinton's last chance to show that he has made a lasting imprint on American relations with China. 
He has not seen Mr. Jiang in more than a year, and not since the two countries reached agreement over China's entry into the World Trade Organization. 
Although Mr. Clinton contended that the trade accord would yield broader diplomatic benefits, encouraging China to be more cooperative in dealing with hot spots around the globe, so far there has been little evidence of a change in China's attitude.
Mr. Jiang, under increasing political pressure at home because of the scope of China's market-opening concessions, is not likely to be in a mood to offer Mr. Clinton much. 
Moreover, while the House approved the W.T.O. accord in the spring by a surprisingly large margin, the Senate has yet to act. 
Passage there seems all but assured, but the Republican leadership has yet to schedule a vote, part of an elaborate maneuver for political advantage in the last days of the Congressional session.
Mr. Berger said that even as the administration works to secure Senate passage of the trade bill, "we will be pressing the Chinese on the question of implementation" of the W.T.O. accord. 
Those are code words for American concern that China will drag its feet on market openings and continue its efforts -- stepped up in recent months -- to control Internet content in China.
Mr. Clinton said earlier this year that such efforts were fruitless and that eventually, the openness spawned by increased commercial contacts would undermine the Communist Party's power. 
He is unlikely to repeat that prediction, which presumably angered China's leaders, to Mr. Jiang.
One focus of the Friday meeting will be to win Mr. Jiang's assurance that China's missile exports to Pakistan, its longtime ally against India, will cease. 
"We have to get this resolved and we are seeking further commitments on restraint," Mr. Berger said. 
But he quickly added that he did not expect an accord at this meeting. 
The two men are expected to see each other again after the presidential election, at a meeting of Asian leaders. 
But by then Mr. Clinton's powers will be all the more diminished in China's eyes.
Mr. Berger also said that the two men would discuss Taiwan at some length, for the first time since the island's longtime opposition won the presidential election. 
China made threatening indications to Taiwan before the election, in an effort to keep independence forces far from power, but has been far more moderate since the Nationalist Party lost. 
Still, there has been little communication between Beijing and the new government in Taipei.
"We have been urging flexibility, restraint and dialogue and we have had more success on one and two than three," he said.
Mr. Clinton's United Nations speech tomorrow will also endorse a report, issued by a special advisory group to Secretary General Kofi Annan, that the peacekeeping department be augmented by an interdepartmental panel that could do more continuous planning and make peacekeeping less of an ad hoc operation. 
"In principle we are supportive of what is in the report for a peacekeeping operation," Mr. Berger said. 
"It parallels what we have been recommending for several years."

file: Clinton Renews Trade Privileges For China Despite Rights Record.txt
text:
ï»¿

President Clinton today sent Congress his bill to usher China into the World Trade Organization. 
He then opened a new front in the debate on the subject in his own party, arguing that opening China's markets will undermine Communist Party control.
In a speech at the Johns Hopkins University's foreign affairs graduate school here, Mr. Clinton tried to float above the bitter economic debate in his party about the wisdom of the legislation, and he said little about Taiwan, whose tense relations with China have been worsening.
But he made an argument that opening up China's economy amounted to a poison pill for China's Communist leaders.
"In the new century, liberty will spread by cell phone and cable modem," Mr. Clinton told a crowd that included students, lobbyists and many cabinet members, who are now making daily calls to Congress about the issue.
When it joins the Geneva-based trade organization, the president said, China will be obliged to make "the tools of communication even cheaper, better and more widely available."
"We know how much the Internet has changed America, and we are already an open society," he said. 
"Imagine how much it could change China."
Excerpts, Page A10.
Mr. Clinton acknowledged that since the deal was signed four months ago, China's leaders have tried to control the kind of sites Chinese can reach via the Internet and to prevent foreign ownership of Internet-related companies. 
But to the Chinese leaders trying to control the Internet in a country as vast and hard to police as China, he said he had only two words: "Good luck!"
The long-delayed transmission of the bill to Congress -- it appeared timed to arrive after Vice President Gore had the Democratic presidential nomination firmly in grasp -- set off a battle within the Democratic Party that intertwines the politics of trade, the presidential election and Mr. Clinton's final effort to recast relations with Beijing.
The legislation's prospects are unclear. 
Only 50 to 60 Democratic members of the House appear ready to support the bill, which would grant permanent "normal" trade status to China. 
That is the one legal prerequisite that would let American companies benefit from market openings China promised in 13 years of negotiations that ended in November.
That means that Mr. Clinton is dependent on support from House and Senate Republicans to pass what may be the last major foreign policy legislation of his presidency. 
Senate passage is thought likely. 
But the vote in the House is expected to be very close. 
By most estimates, President Clinton would have to win over at least 20 more Democrats in the House to secure passage.
He is getting little help from Vice President Gore, who, to appease labor unions that vociferously oppose the deal, said three weeks ago that he would negotiate something better if elected to office. 
Mr. Gore later reiterated his support for the deal the administration struck, but his aides did not return calls on the subject today.
Ari Fleischer, a spokesman for the presumed Republican nominee, Gov. George W. Bush of Texas, said Mr. Bush remains a "vocal supporter" of China's entry into the trade organization, because "it is in our interest, and it is in the interest of the Chinese to grow an entrepreneurial middle class."

Mr. Clinton was introduced today by Paul Wolfowitz, dean of the Paul H. Nitze School of Advanced International Studies.

One senior administration official said this week that he feared that "China's own efforts could backfire on us big time."
But Mr. Clinton noted today that even if Congress votes against normal trade relations, China will still get into the world body.
A vote against the bill, Mr. Clinton said, "will cost America jobs as our competitors in Europe, Asia and elsewhere capture Chinese markets that we otherwise would have served."

file: Clinton Takes Political Risk in Talking to Chinese.txt
text:
ï»¿
In meeting China's President in Seattle on Friday, President Clinton is gambling that the strategy of tentatively embracing Beijing's leaders rather than castigating them will work better for him than it did for President George Bush.
The one-hour meeting, the highest-level contact since China suppressed pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in 1989, comes after a formal policy review in September that led to a decision to shift away from threats and finger-pointing and substitute what a top Administration specialist called "enhanced engagement."
Mr. Clinton was so determined to turn the deteriorating relationship around that in September he opened high-level exchanges with Beijing and sent President Jiang Zemin a letter announcing that the United States would help promote a "strong, stable and prosperous China."
It did not seem to matter that Mr. Jiang's most important title is General Secretary of the Communist Party, or that in last year's campaign Mr. Clinton had accused Mr. Bush of "coddling" China's leadership.
There are some differences in both the policy and the risks for the two Administrations. 
President Clinton started off in office as a far tougher critic of the Chinese and, unlike Mr. Bush, he is willing to link trade benefits to Beijing's human rights performance, at least in the abstract.
Because of Mr. Bush's close association to China, dating from the 1970's when he was the American envoy, he was excoriated in Congress and in the press for meeting with Prime Minister Li Peng at the United Nations in January 1992. 
By contrast, there has been virtually no criticism of Mr. Clinton's planned meeting with Mr. Jiang. Administration officials maintain that this is due to a tougher track record that they hope will now make the switch to a softer line more effective.
On the lofty political level, the American goal is to convince China that it is in its national interest to liberalize its political process. 
Mr. Clinton will tell his Chinese counterpart that if China wants to continue to export its goods to the United States under the same low tariffs enjoyed by most other nations, it must make broad changes in its human rights policies now, rather than wait until the benefits face renewal in June.
Â 
What China Must Do
The concern is that China may do too little too late in meeting the requirements of a May 1993 executive order linking extension of the trade benefits to China's progress on releasing of political prisoners, ceasing the jamming of international broadcasts, implementing the Universal Declaration on Human Rights, protecting Tibet's cultural and religious heritage and allowing visits by international humanitarian organizations.
On a more mundane level, the Administration's policy is driven by Mr. Clinton's determination that the United States get a larger chunk of the world's fastest-growing market. 
China's trade surplus with the United States could exceed that of Japan's by the end of the decade.
That means a renewal of China's trade benefits, because China has threatened to retaliate against American companies if the privileges are withdrawn. 
And all of the Administration's economic agencies have begun to weigh in heavily on China policy, arguing that the interests of commerce should prevail over other policy considerations.
Â 
Criticism From Christopher
Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who has not acted on Foreign Minister Qian Qichen's invitation to visit China, is the Administration's most vocal advocate of Beijing's need to do much more if it wants to keep its preferential trade status.
At a briefing Monday, Mr. Christopher characterized as helpful but inadequate such isolated gestures as China's announcement last week that it will give "positive consideration" to allowing the Red Cross to visit prisoners.
The latest indication of China's attitude toward human rights came on Monday, when two dissidents were apparently seized by police and disappeared after attending a meeting to promote nonviolent political reform.
In a speech to a business group in Hong Kong today, Mr. Bush could not resist criticizing his successor's attempts to impose democratic values abroad. 
Saying China's economic leap forward had made its society much freer than when he was the envoy, he warned that to revoke China's trading privileges would isolate China and narrow Washington's influence.
Â 
Questions of Missiles
But kind gestures and sweet talk in Washington do not necessarily produce results in Beijing, as evidenced by China's determination to sell ballistic missiles in violation of an international accord.
During a visit to Beijing in 1988, Secretary of State George P. Shultz was unable to dissuade the Chinese from going forward with contracts to sell such missiles; three years later, Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d ended talks in China under the erroneous impression that the Chinese would adhere to their pledges not to export missiles or technology that violated the accord.
The Clinton Administration is fighting the same battle and, thus far, the Chinese are winning.
The Administration imposed sanctions on an estimated $1 billion in high-technology trade with China last August, as required under United States law, after intelligence agencies reported that China had shipped technology and components for M-11 missiles to Pakistan.
China has refused to pledge adherence to the accord. 
In a meeting with senior State Department officials in Washington early this month, the Deputy Foreign Minister, Liu Huaqiu, said Beijing would be willing to open a formal dialogue with the United States only after Washington lifted the sanctions.
Â 
Gesture of Good Will
As a gesture of good will to the Chinese, Mr. Clinton's senior advisers are recommending that he accept a broad interpretation of the law requiring sanctions. 
That would enable him to announce to Mr. Jiang that he was allowing the export of two of the seven satellites affected by the sanctions.
Mr. Clinton's advisers are also urging that he approve the sale of a supercomputer for meteorological purposes that some nonproliferation experts in the Administration fear could be put to military uses.
The Clinton-Jiang meeting will certainly be Mr. Clinton's most important encounter during an economic summit meeting that will bring together leaders of the 15-member Asia-Pacific Economic Conference.
But a subdrama of another sort may also play out in Seattle: Mr. Christopher's search for a deputy after the forced resignation of Clifton R. Wharton Jr. last week.
Â 
Post Turned Down
Senior Administration officials said Mr. Christopher's first choice was Michael H. Armacost, who served as Ambassador to Japan and was the third-ranking official in Mr. Baker's State Department. 
But Mr. Armacost, now a visiting professor at the Asia-Pacific Research Center, turned it down.
While senior officials said Mr. Christopher may try to change Mr. Armacost's mind, he is also focusing on several other candidates, including two officials who will be demonstrating their diplomatic mettle in Seattle this week: J. Stapleton Roy, the Ambassador to China, and Winston Lord, the Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs.
The front-runner -- at least on the lists of some officials among State Department executives -- remains Thomas R. Pickering, the Ambassador to Russia; unlike Mr. Armacost, he is said to be very interested in serving as Mr. Christopher's No. 2.

text:

President Clinton arrived here today and prepared to repair the damage from what some of his aides call one of his biggest foreign policy mistakes this year: walking away from an agreement to get China into the World Trade Organization.
In preparation for a meeting scheduled for later today with President Jiang Zemin, Mr. Clinton's aides have been scrambling to make sure that China is still willing to make the broad market-opening concessions that it offered in April. 
At that time Mr. Clinton rejected the deal, after some top aides advised holding out for an even better deal.
Within days, the President decided that this was a mistake. 
Business executives flooded the White House with protests, complaining that he underestimated the extent of Chinese concessions.
But subsequent events -- from the accidental bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade to the accusations of Chinese nuclear spying -- led Beijing to suspend the talks, amid a vigorous debate in China over whether Prime Minister Zhu Rongji and Mr. Jiang were giving away too much.
That debate continues. 
But the mood in the Clinton Administration has changed, and Mr. Clinton is clearly primed to move a deal along -- even if one is not achievable at today's meeting.
"There is a sense that if we are going to get the relationship with China back on track, this is the only concrete step we can take," one of Mr. Clinton's top foreign policy advisers said.
The chief negotiator for the deal, Robert Cassidy, went to Beijing last weekend to lay the groundwork for today's meeting. 
Then his boss, Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, met her Chinese counterpart here and agreed that the two nations would work to get China into the World Trade Organization within three months. 
That would be before the world's top trade officials gather in Seattle in December to begin a new round of negotiations over agriculture.
Assuming a deal is struck, the big remaining obstacle is Congress. 
Any agreement with the United States would require that China be given permanent preferential trade status -- depriving Congress of its annual trade debate, which has become a venue for venting frustration with China's human rights record.
Another problem in Congress is whether Democrats can be convinced that the deal protects American workers. 
Labor unions vow to lobby against getting China into the trade organization.
One of the mysteries for the Administration is how badly Mr. Zhu, and perhaps Mr. Jiang, were hurt by Ms. Barshefsky's decision in April to publish a summary of China's trade concessions. 
That list helped build support for a deal among American business executives. 
But it outraged many powerful Chinese, who fear that the deal would remove protections against foreign competition.

file: Clinton Urged to Meet Top China Dissident.txt
text:

A group of 55 democracy advocates from around China called on President Clinton today to meet with a prominent Beijing dissident during his visit to China next week as a visible symbol of commitment to human rights.
In a letter to President Clinton faxed to foreign news agencies and to the American Embassy, the group said the planned official welcome for Mr. Clinton "on the bloody red carpet on Tiananmen Square," where the military crushed student-led demonstrations on June 4, 1989, was "a source of great grief."
After meeting President Jiang Zemin, the letter said, Mr. Clinton should meet with Xu Wenli, a veteran of democracy activities from the late 1970's who spent 12 years in prison. 
Mr. Xu has recently re-emerged as one of the most active dissidents in the country, making public demands that the Communist Government allow free labor unions, multiple political parties and an independent human rights monitor. 
In the last few months he has been briefly arrested several times and warned to curtail his activities.
"We hold that meeting with Mr. Xu Wenli, or at least strongly demanding to meet with Mr. Xu Wenli, is a way to indicate that you are genuinely concerned about the cause of democracy and human rights," the letter said. 
If Mr. Clinton does not make the effort, it said, "we will not be able to believe that your trip to Beijing will have any significance other than helping the Chinese Government to cast off the diplomatic shadows of June 4 in exchange for your own political interests."
In Washington, Stanley Roth, an Assistant Secretary of State, said. 
"At this point, I don't believe we're going to have dissidents on the schedule."
He said that a meeting might lead to penalties against dissidents, in which case "instead of advancing the cause of freedom and democracy and human rights, you'd end up worsening it."
Diplomats here said it was extremely unlikely that Mr. Clinton would want to provoke the outrage of the Chinese Government by seeking a meeting with an outspoken critic like Mr. Xu.
Mr. Clinton has said he will firmly press the cause of human rights during his visit, from June 25 to July 3. 
But overall, the trip has been carefully scripted to cast light on China's growing diversity and progress, in keeping with the desire of both Governments to cement smoother ties.
Since Mr. Jiang's state visit to the United States last year, China has sent from prison into exile its two most famous dissidents, Wei Jingsheng, a contemporary of Mr. Xu's, and Wang Dan, a student leader of 1989. 
But rights monitors abroad say that thousands of people remain in jail or labor camps for publicly advocating democratic change.
Today's letter was written by Wang Zechen, a lawyer in Liaoning province. 
Most of the remaining signers are, like him, little known but are part of a network of people who, in the face of steady police harassment, are communicating by E-mail and fax to call for major political change.
Earlier this year Mr. Xu, with the best known among the signers of the new letter, Qin Yongmin of Wuhan, started faxing out reports on arrests of dissidents and other rights developments. 
But the reports recently ceased after both men were detained overnight and their fax machines and computers were confiscated.
American officials are hoping that China will offer at least one nod to rights concerns during Mr. Clinton's visit, by announcing a firm date for signing the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.
When China said in March that it planned to sign the international convention, which calls for free speech and assembly, the American Government said that it would stop pursuing resolutions critical of China's human rights policies in an annual United Nations meeting.
China did not say when it would sign or how soon after signing that it might ratify the convention, nor did it say what reservations it might make that would exempt it from selected obligations.
When China does join the convention, American officials argue, it will be subject to inspections and probing reports, a useful way to nudge legal improvements here. 
But in the years before that occurs, both countries will avoid confrontations over rights in the United Nations forum.

Following are excerpts from an interview of President Clinton in the Oval Office by The New York Times:

Q. Looking back now, are you convinced that this approach that you developed of using this web of economic engagement . . . has actually worked, and that's proved your thesis that as you engage more economically, you actually do bring countries around to democracy -- this despite the Vietnam and Chinese examples?
Â 
A. Well, the short answer is, yes, I think it is -- I think it will work. 
But I think it's a question of whether you -- whether we're prepared to pay the price of time, and what the options are.
I don't think there's any way for us to bring openness and freedom to China or to Vietnam more quickly than the one we've adopted. 
I don't think that either country -- I don't think we have any levers of pressure, for example, that would bring change more quickly. 
And I think the downsides of adopting a different approach are greater than the upsides.
I think the -- first, let me back up and say my whole view of this period in which we're living is that the world is becoming exponentially more interdependent, and with all kinds of new opportunities and all kinds of new dangers -- that if you want to make the most of an interdependent world, you have to let people within your country have more freedom over the basic aspects of their lives. 
. . .
Â 
Q. What kind of time frames are we talking about for China and Vietnam, do you think?
Â 
A. I don't know. 
I think, if you look at Vietnam, it was really interesting to me when I was there to see the differences in the approaches taken sort of in gradations from the mayor of Ho Chi Minh City to the prime minister to the president to the general secretary of the party. 
And if you -- the way they -- even the way they talked was so much a function of their responsibilities and the extent to which they are dealing with the emerging world. 
I was actually, on balance, quite encouraged by what I saw there and where I think it's going.
In China, I think it's really just a matter of time. 
If you go to -- as I've said, you've got a lot of different things going on in China. 
It's a vast country. 
But if you go to Shanghai, or just go out in those villages -- like I went to a couple of those little villages, where they elected their mayors and all -- I think there's more and more personal freedom, freedom of movement, freedom of choice of career, freedom in educational choices, things that did not exist before.
And I think that eventually the country will become more open and free if we do the right things and they do the right things.
There is always the possibility you will have people get in office in either country that will make mistakes. 
But I think that the policy is right, and the direction is right.
Â 
Q. Coming back to Vietnam from a domestic side, were there ways in which you felt your going there and the trip had brought you full circle kind of culturally and politically?
. . .
Â 
A. Well, it was interesting. 
I had this encounter with the general secretary of the party, sitting there with Pete Peterson, who was a P.O.W. for six and a half years.

But -- and some of this has been reported, but basically, the general secretary was saying -- he was the most hard line of all the people I talked to -- and he said:
Well, we can talk all about the future here, but we've got to get the past straight. 
And we didn't invade your country, you invaded our country, and it was terrible. 
And I'm so glad that so many of the American people opposed it, I'm glad you opposed it, I'm glad the people were in the streets. 
But it happened, and we've got to somehow work this out.
And I looked at him, and I said, "If you want to talk about history, we can, but -- and it's true that we were deeply divided over the war."
I said, "Most of our division related to what the character of the conflict was, and what if any impact we could have on it."
But, I said, "Mr. 
Chairman, we were not France.

And I said, "I think it would be better if we had these discussions looking to the future."

text:

The Coca-Cola Company expanded its status as the world's leading producer of soft drinks this morning by signing an agreement in Beijing with the Chinese Government to build or upgrade 10 bottling plants in the interior of the country.
The deal will enable Coca-Cola to move well beyond the coastal regions of China, where it has had a relatively strong presence, and build what it hopes might eventually become one of its largest national markets.
Roberto C. Goizueta, Coca-Cola's chairman and chief executive, said yesterday that the company would invest $150 million in China over five years. 
He said the expansion would enable Coca-Cola to produce and sell significantly more than the 75 million cases of its drinks that it sold in China last year. 
That is roughly the same quantity sold in France.
But with China's population nearing 1.2 billion, as compared with 55 million in France, that meant that each Chinese, on average, drank only one and a half cans or bottles of Coke a year.
Mr. Goizueta said the company's goal was to increase Chinese consumption of Coca-Cola drinks to that in the United States, where on average, each person drinks nearly one can or bottle a day -- the highest in any of the 195 countries where Coca-Cola sells.
The beverage company currently operates 13 plants -- one each in Shanghai, Beijing and 11 other cities near the east coast. 
Of the 10 plants covered by the deal signed today, some are situations in which existing soft-drink plants operated by the Chinese will be upgraded to produce Coca-Cola products.
"This is a monumental step for the Chinese to have taken," Mr. Goizueta said in an interview. 
"We don't have exclusivity in China, but we do have the lion's share of the market and we need to increase the per-capita."
Pepsico, the world's second-leading producer of soft drinks, ranked second to Coca-Cola in China last year, selling 27.4 million cases from seven bottling plants.
Coca-Cola's agreement was the culmination of several years of negotiations with the Chinese Ministry of Light Industry and the expansion of Coca-Cola's presence in China, which began in 1981.
Â 
A Chinese Staff
The company intends to operate the new plants with Chinese managers, many of whom were educated in the United States, and with 5,000 local employees. 
They will produce not only Coca-Cola products but also a Chinese brand of cola known as Jinmeile.
Mr. Goizueta said the new plants would be operated as joint ventures, the way eight of the company's existing plants are run. 
The five others are state-owned.
Linda Peek, a Coca-Cola spokeswoman, said that the jobs in the new plants would about double the number of Chinese people working for the company and would increase its investment in China to about $250 million.
It would also maintain Coca-Cola as one of the largest American investors in China, particularly among consumer-products companies.
Richard Brecher, a director of the United States-China Business Council in Washington, said that most American companies operating in China were involved with industrial or technology products and that most were joint ventures, with the American investment ranging from $5 million to $10 million.
Â 
Money, and Lots of It
But that is changing. 
"In the last two years, we have seen a real explosion in China again," Mr. Brecher said. 
"Consumers suddenly have money and they are spending it on foreign products."
Referring to the size of Coca-Cola's investment, he said that five years ago "only a handful" of American companies were so involved in China.
"Now," he added, "we are seeing quite a few, and there are a lot more in the pipeline."
Mr. Goizueta said Coca-Cola's expansion reflected the company's confidence about the increased buying power in China and the people's growing interest in American products. 
Last year, Coke's sales there were the highest among the Asian countries in which the company's products are sold.
"Our plans for further investment in China are testimony to the very bright future of this country and its soft-drink industry," he said.

But he indicated that Israel expects to proceed with the promised sale of at least the first radar-equipped aircraft.
"We are aware of the sensitivity in the United States with regard to China," he said. 
Then he quickly added, "We are, of course, aware of our commitments in the contracts that we signed."
Mr. Jiang's arrival here on Thursday will be the first official visit to Israel by a Chinese leader, making this a singularly awkward week to renege on the deal. 
But American Congressional leaders have warned Israel that proceeding with the contract could jeopardize support for the huge $17 billion military aid package Israel is seeking in connection with an eventual peace treaty with Syria. 
Among the items Israel is requesting are American Boeing Awacs, considered far more sophisticated than the Israeli version.
According to Israeli military officials, Israel notified the United States four years ago of its intent to offer airborne radar surveillance systems for sale to China. 
Pentagon officials reviewing the proposed contract determined then that Israel would not be providing China with proprietary American military technology, the Israelis said.
But American objections to the sale are based not on narrow interpretations of agreements but on the broader principle that Israel as an ally should defer to Washington's strategic judgments in regions beyond the Middle East. 
The United States has not supplied arms to China since 1992.
Mr. Cohen voiced concerns privately before, but had never spoken out publicly here against the sale.
"We are aware of the need to be in close coordination and contact with the United States on every issue that might pose a risk to American interests," Mr. Barak said today.
Yet Mr. Barak has also placed great emphasis on the self-sufficiency of Israel's military industry, which Pentagon officials readily acknowledge can survive only through an aggressive sales program. 
Israeli Aircraft Industries is the country's largest export earner, selling weapons systems and refurbished fighter jets to dozens of countries, as well as civilian commuter aircraft.
Mr. Barak and his predecessors have also put great stock in a strengthened relationship with China, seen as both a critical market for Israel and a bulwark against diplomatic isolation.
Though Israel did not establish full diplomatic relations with China until 1997, it has provided arms to Beijing since the 1980's. 
Israel aided the development of China's F-10 fighter jet, which is expected to carry a version of Israel's Pitun missile. 
But the potentially billion-dollar order for four Awacs-type planes would, if realized, be its largest sale to China yet.
Chinese officials also clearly consider it important. 
Li Peng, the chairman of China's National People's Congress, and Che Ho Tien, China's defense minister, have personally inspected the converted Ilyushin surveillance planes on visits to Israel in the past six months.

file: Colonialism Ending in Asia As China Reclaims Macao.txt
text:
ï»¿
Five hundred years of European colonialism in Asia sputters to a close here this weekend on a desolate, rain-swept waterfront dredged out of Macao's once beguiling harbor. 
At the stroke of midnight on Sunday, China will reclaim this tiny enclave from Portugal, raising its red flag over another patch of Chinese soil and setting the stage for what it hopes will be eventual reunification with Taiwan.
Unlike Britain's handover of nearby Hong Kong two years ago, which was heralded by years of Chinese anticipation and British angst, this is not the reluctant surrender of a prized possession. 
Portugal tried to give back this enclave of 430,000 people once before, after the revolution that ended decades of dictatorship in Portugal in 1974, but China's leaders, fearful of losing a trading channel to the outside world, demurred.
Since then, the Portuguese administration has presided over Macao's steady deterioration into a disreputable, vaguely sinister gambling destination for weekend wagerers from Hong Kong. 
As feuds between rival Chinese gangs have terrorized the colony over the last few years, the economy has withered and Macao has become ever more hooked on the casinos, which generate more than half of its tax revenues.
"As a local, I'd have to say the Portuguese haven't done a good job," said Eric T. M. Yeung, a prominent Macao businessman who makes toys. 
"But in fairness, they had their own problems and couldn't pay attention to a little spot of land on the other side of the world."
A senior Chinese official in the future local government, who asked not to be identified to avoid offending the Portuguese, said: "Hong Kong is so successful that Hong Kong people always think they are superior to the Chinese. 
We are happy in Macao, but I don't think anyone is proud."
Portuguese officials are keenly aware of their checkered legacy. 
They were the first Europeans to colonize in Asia, driven by a lust for adventure and discovery, and a desire to spread the Christianity that had helped free Portugal of Moorish, Muslim rule. 
But for all the centuries they have lingered here, the Portuguese have left behind no lasting political culture.
In the last few weeks, they have worked diligently to promote the artifacts, old and new, of 442 years of colonial rule: meticulously restored buildings in Portuguese pastels, a state-of-the-art airport and gleaming causeways that connect Macao with its outer islands.
Portugal's president, Jorge Sampaio, said that in the last decade Macao had taken on many of the hallmarks of a liberal Western state, including the rule of law, freedom of religion and a free press. 
"Well, it could have been done 300 years ago," he said in an interview on the eve of the handover, "but that was not the habit of time."
For Sunday's ceremony, the departing colonial masters from a small nation on the other side of the world have produced the trappings of a momentous occasion. 
This week, workers frantically hammered the last planks on an $8 million pavilion where President Jiang Zemin of China will take control of the eight-square-mile territory from Mr. Sampaio. Officials say the translucent building is meant to resemble a Chinese lantern. 
In truth, it looks more like a giant, softly lighted bathtub.
The Portuguese have also sought to account for the dark side of their rule: a stunted political system, with few local Chinese trained to take over the government, shaky courts, a corrupt police force, and a democracy movement that can be summed up by the fact that it has exactly one elected legislator.
"We can build an airport in five years; we can build a bridge in two," said Jorge Alberto Rangel, the secretary for public administration, who is coordinating the handover ceremony. 
"But forming people takes time. 
We really did what we thought was best for Macao."
Mr. Rangel's sense of conflict is deeply felt. 
A native Macanese -- part Portuguese, part Chinese -- he comes from one of the colony's oldest families.
But he also served in the Portuguese Army as an infantry commander in Guinea-Bissau, in West Africa. 
There, Mr. Rangel witnessed Portugal's chaotic departure from its African colonies after the 1974 revolution. 
With no leadership and no capacity to govern themselves, formerly Portuguese Mozambique and Angola fell into bloody strife, and in Angola, it continues today.
"What happened in Africa was disaster," Mr. Rangel said. 
"We made no preparations, like we have here. 
I believe Macao deserved to have it done differently."
Portugal's sudden renunciation of empire was not just a tragedy in Africa. 
Its retreat from East Timor 25 years ago opened the door for Indonesia to invade and turn the colony into an unwilling province. 
Guerrilla rebels fought the Indonesian Army until this year, when Jakarta unexpectedly agreed to allow the East Timorese to decide their own future. 
The Indonesian Army left, but not before reducing much of the territory to cinders and attacking the Roman Catholic Church, whose strength in East Timor is arguably Portugal's most lasting legacy there.
Macao was spared such predations, mainly because China effectively gave Portugal squatter's rights after its seafarers landed here in 1557. 
Satisfied as long as the Portuguese paid tribute, the Chinese allowed them to build a bustling trading post in the 17th and 18th centuries. 
Along with the traders came the Jesuit priests, who used Macao as a base to launch missions into China. 
The richly detailed facade of Sao Paulo, the surviving fragment of a church that burned down in 1831, attests to the church's deep roots here.
"It's amazing that a European power could remain on Chinese soil for all this time," said Fok Kai Cheong, a professor of history at the University of Macao. 
"They survived every kind of Chinese government: dynastic, xenophobic, nationalistic, Communist."
But while Macao kept the peace with China, it could do little about the thrusting British colony 38 miles across the Pearl River delta. 
Hong Kong, which was ceded to Britain in 1842 after the Opium War, rapidly supplanted Macao as the preferred trading hub in the region. 
By the early 20th century, Macao was a backwater known mostly as a refuge for families fleeing from China's war with Japan.
Macao's next shock came in 1966, when Chinese laborers caught up in the fever of the Cultural Revolution rose up against the Portuguese. 
The unrest was quelled, but it shook Macao's administrators and soured Lisbon's appetite for its vestigial foothold in Asia. 
As the Portuguese retreated, local Chinese -- mostly bankers and traders -- emerged as the de facto powers in the colony.
Among those shadow leaders was Ho Yin, a banker who is revered by many here for mediating between the Chinese and the Portuguese. 
His son, Edmund Ho, was chosen to be the first postcolonial chief executive of Macao by a Beijing-appointed committee last May.
Like his counterpart in Hong Kong, Tung Chee-hwa, Mr. Ho is a conservative businessman who is not likely to ruffle the feathers of the Chinese leaders. 
He even looks a bit like Mr. Tung, with razor-cut hair that would pass muster in boot camp. 
But unlike the courtly Mr. Tung, he can be blunt.
In an interview here on the eve of taking control, Mr. Ho, 44, came across like a big-city mayor who wanted to let people know who was boss. 
His target was the Chinese gangs, or triads, which have waged an ugly war for control of Macao's casinos since the mid-1990's.
"My basic policy on the triads is that they have to learn how to behave," he said. 
"I don't think we'll have to go house to house, arresting people and putting them in concentration camps. 
But they must know how to behave. 
If you are in the underworld, learn to keep it under."
Mr. Ho also welcomed Beijing's decision to deploy army troops in Macao after the handover. 
Portugal had protested the move, noting that it had withdrawn its troops in 1974. 
Mr. Sampaio even briefly threatened to boycott the ceremony Sunday.
Although Mr. Ho said the troops would not be used for police work, he clearly relished having a garrison at hand.
"One major advantage is that I will have psychological support for making drastic changes in the police," he said. 
"Because if they say, 'We're not happy, we don't want reforms, we don't want to do our jobs,' I'll say, 'You can just step aside and I'll put in the soldiers.'
"
Remarks like that would cause a tempest in Hong Kong, where pro-democracy leaders are on the lookout for any authoritarian tendencies in the government. 
Among Macao's overwhelmingly Chinese population, however, they are seen as an overdue return to law and order.
"Most local people don't object to the Chinese Army coming to Macao," said Ng Kuok Cheong, the lone pro-democracy member in the territory's legislature. 
"They believe that mainland China can control crime, but that the Portuguese government can't."
China is happy that most Macanese see it that way. 
For Beijing, the ceremony Sunday is another step in its push to reunify all of China, including Taiwan, the seat of the Chinese Nationalist government whose 22 million people seem unlikely to accept any move that would place them under Communist rule.
Mr. Ng, a soft-spoken former loan officer at the Bank of China who lost his job because of his politics, said that democracy had little future in Macao. 
But he blames that less on China than on Portugal. 
"The British established a pro-Western capitalist elite in Hong Kong," Mr. Ng said. 
"The Portuguese never did that. 
Their primary concern was preserving Portuguese culture."
A magnificent salmon-pink edifice housing the public security department here attests both to that Portuguese concern and to the accompanying failure to curb the gang wars that have killed government officials, scared off tourists and brought gun battles and car bombings to otherwise tranquil streets.
Last month, Macao sentenced its most flamboyant triad leader, Wan Kuok-koi, to 15 years in prison. 
It was a victory for the authorities, who had seethed as Mr. Wan strutted around town with an aura of invincibility. 
Yet Mr. Wan, who goes by the nickname Broken Tooth, got in some telling last words. 
As he was being led away, he screamed at the police: "You're corrupt. 
You've taken dirty money."
Few people here believe the Mr. Wan's demise will end the mayhem. 
But they note approvingly that China has arrested hundreds of suspected triad members in neighboring Guangdong Province. 
Now, they say, the new government must figure out how to clean up Macao's casinos, which have contributed to the crime wave by allowing gangs to take control of V.I.P. rooms that cater to high rollers.
Cramped, dark and crawling with prostitutes, Macao's casinos are worlds away from the theme-park ambience of Las Vegas. 
The gambling industry is controlled by Stanley Ho, a Hong Kong billionaire who has held an exclusive government license since 1961. 
That license expires in 2001, and Edmund Ho, who is not related to Stanley, is not revealing whether it will be renewed.
In the meantime, Macao's next leader is busy building a government -- "from ground zero," he notes in a swipe at the decamping colonials. 
Mr. Ho is also putting out the word that Macao intends to remain a distinct enclave, with its own laws and customs. 
Even he acknowledges, however, that it will live mostly in memory -- Europe's last foothold in Asia, soon to be lost in the enormity of modern China.
"Everyone here would like the world to remember that there's a Macao somewhere in this region," Mr. Ho said a bit wistfully. 
"But we have to be realistic."

file: Commercial Property_Asian Investment Is on the Rise in Los Angeles.txt
text:
ï»¿
JAPANESE investment in the top hotels and office towers in Los Angeles soared during the 1980's and then crashed with the real estate market in the early 1990's. 
Now, Asian investment is once again increasing, mainly from Taiwan, Hong Kong and Indonesia, driven partly by bargain real estate prices here and political uncertainty at home.
In the last three years, Asian-based companies have bought at least 15 buildings in the Los Angeles area, each priced at more than $10 million, according to the Financial Capital Investment Company, which helps Asians buy American property. 
Analysts and Asian buyers say these transactions -- which the company says total nearly $450 million -- reflect Asia's growing prosperity and a belief that Southern California's struggling commercial property market has hit bottom.
For instance, a Hong Kong-based syndicate, B. W. Hotels, bought the luxury Regent Beverly Wilshire in February for a reported $100 million. 
The landmark 275-room, 12-story Beverly Hills hotel, featured in the film "Pretty Woman," is near the chic shopping street Rodeo Drive.
"We think Los Angeles has turned around in hospitality," said Ambrose Cheung, president of B. W. Hotels. 
"It is now on the upswing. 
We think the real estate situation is positive. 
It's about coming in at the right time."
For years, Taiwanese entrepreneurs have been major investors in small-scale projects like shopping centers, warehouses and apartment buildings in the Los Angeles area, and they typically have focused on those communities with a large Asian presence. 
But Randall J. Lee, an Asian economic consultant with Lilly Enterprises here, said the new wave of Asian investment was increasingly of a larger scale.
"We are going to continue to see the mom-and-pop guys buying the small shopping centers," Mr. Lee said. 
"But we are beginning to see the bigger players, their equivalent of Goldman Sachs."
In the Chinese style, many investors are low profile, which makes tracking sales difficult, said Richard Alter, managing director of Financial Investment Capital. 
He said investors typically formed a syndicate, paid in cash and focused on second-tier properties like midsize office towers and business-class hotels that do not draw as much attention or attract as much competitive bidding.
"We try to go after some properties that the big Wall Street firms would not go after," Mr. Alter said. 
"Size makes a difference. 
We go for commercially viable properties, but not the Statue of Liberty. 
We don't want to pay for the marquee value."
Real estate brokers and Asian investors here say the recent interest in Los Angeles real estate is partly a product of confidence in Southern California's improving economy and partly an example of bottom fishing. 
Investors are capitalizing on real estate values that are down nearly 50 percent from their peak in the late 1980's after years of recession coupled with cutbacks in the defense sector.
Despite the city's budding recovery, downtown is suffering from a glut of office space and hotel rooms. 
Office vacancy rates downtown have hovered near 20 percent for some time, according to the Los Angeles County Economic Development office, while the area's hotel occupancy is 59.9 percent for the year through June, according to PKF Consulting, a hotel industry advisory service.
ON the other hand, downtown is regarded as having a solid market base since there are only a few convention-sized hotels. 
And the city's center is being considered as a site for a new sports arena, which could help revitalize the area.
"Asian buyers are getting great bargains on all these properties and they sense that there is great economic potential here," said Jack Kyser, chief economist for the county's economic development office.
Those companies selling big properties bought during the boom years are generally losing millions of dollars in the process. 
In a few cases, the losers are Japanese companies, part of a multibillion-dollar divestment of their American assets.
For example, TAT Los Angeles Ltd., one such Japanese company, bought the ornate, 11-story, 683-room Biltmore Hotel and its adjoining 22-story office tower for a reported $219 million in 1989 and then sold it in June to Hong Kong-based Regal Hotels at a 70 percent loss. 
Many Japanese companies bought American property with borrowed money, and now their banks are demanding payment.
Peter Zen, a director of the Taiwan-based Forward Time Corporation, which paid nearly $50 million last year for Los Angeles' largest hotel, the 1,368-room, glass-faced Westin Bonaventure Hotel and Suites, said property in Los Angeles is relatively inexpensive compared with many Asian cities. 
He said land in Los Angeles could cost only $300 a square foot, versus $2,000 a square foot in Taipei.
Moreover, he said, many Asian investors regarded the United States as a safe haven for capital, especially in light of recent events in their home countries. 
For instance, Indonesian protesters clashed with the police in Jakarta in July. 
At the same time, Taiwan is frequently swept by fears of invasion from China and the British colony of Hong Kong is 10 months from reintegration with mainland China.
"The United States is a country where you don't have to worry about expropriation, or that the government is going to topple every day," Mr. Zen said.
But, he added, there is a trade-off to investing in Los Angeles versus Bangkok or Kuala Lumpur. 
Profits are generally lower in Los Angeles, and its land values are expected to increase much more slowly than in Asia's prospering cities.
"You can't compare Los Angeles to the Far East, where you have a lot of upside," Mr. Zen said. 
"Here, it's very stable. 
You turn out some earnings every year."
Asian companies often do not get involved with the demands of owning industrial space, and instead focus on office towers and hotels, which are considered to be easier to operate. 
Frequently, Asians hire an American company to manage the property.
Since profiting from significant short-term property appreciation in Los Angeles is unlikely, many Asian buyers say they have a longer-term commitment to their acquisitions, at least for the near future. 
As a result, many investors plan property improvements to attract business.
FOR example, the Biltmore Hotel, built in 1922, will get a $10 million to $20 million renovation. 
The Regent Beverly Wilshire will get 100 new suites on five vacant floors in roughly 18 months.
"Suites, bungalows and villas are in very high demand," Mr. Cheung said. 
"These are the rooms that can command a very high rate from the entertainment, performing arts, and fashion industries."
Asian real estate buyers generally cited an increasing familiarity with the United States, either through their own education here or that of their children, as a major investment factor. 
Asian companies are focusing most of their purchases on New York and North America's major Pacific cities, all of which are easily reached from Asia and have large Asian communities. 
Los Angeles County's Asian population in 1995 was estimated at 907,000 by the state Department of Finance.
"These investors go where there are more Asians and more infrastructure," Mr. Alter said. 
"That makes them more comfortable than in Salt Lake City or Cleveland."
Mr. Lee said investment in Los Angeles real estate should increase as wealth spreads to more Asian countries. 
In particular, he said companies from mainland China, some of which have already participated in a few medium-sized deals in Los Angeles, should be a growing source of capital.
"A lot of people don't realize that there is a lot of wealth being created in China," Mr. Lee said. 
"Before it was the government people, now it's the entrepreneurs."

file: COMMITTEE IS TOLD A DONOR RECEIVED FOREIGNERS_ CASH.txt
text:
ï»¿
Yah Lin Trie, a friend of President Clinton who is suspected of donating foreign money to the Democratic Party, received $1.4 million in wire transfers from abroad from 1994 through 1996, an agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation testified today in the Senate inquiry on campaign finance practices.
The agent, Jerome Campane, who has been working as a special investigator for the Senate committee, said $905,000 of the $1.4 million came from a single source, Ng Lap Seng, a business associate of Mr. Trie from Macao, a Portuguese territory on the coast of China near Hong Kong.
This money was used in part to cover the $220,000 that Mr. Trie and his wife gave to the Democratic National Committee, Mr. Campane (pronounced campaign) testified. 
It was also used, he said, to reimburse donations made by associates of Mr. Trie, who is a United States citizen, and Mr. Ng.
Donating foreign money to American political parties or disguising the source of contributions is against the law. 
Republicans hold that Mr. Trie is a prime exhibit of how fund-raising by President Clinton and the Democrats got out of hand in the last election.
The Democrats have returned all the money Mr. Trie and his wife donated, as well as an additional $425,000 that he raised from others for the party. 
Party officials did so, they have said, because they believed it was foreign money or because they were suspicious of the source of the money.
Among the money Mr. Trie received from overseas that did not come from Mr. Ng was $100,000 from Charoen Pokphand, a business conglomerate in Thailand.
The Washington representative of the conglomerate was Pauline Kanchanalak, another large Democratic contributor whose donations are being investigated.
Pressed by the senators, Mr. Campane said he could not determine whether any of the money wired to Mr. Trie had originated in China, whose possible effort to influence American elections through major, illegal campaign contributions is a prime target of the Senate investigation.
But he said Mr. Ng was wealthy in his own right and could easily have afforded the money he sent. 
And he indicated he thought the ultimate aim of Mr. Ng and Mr. Trie was to gain political influence for themselves, not someone else.
Mr. Campane also said he had found no evidence that Mr. Clinton, Vice President Al Gore or anyone at the Democratic National Committee knew Mr. Trie's money had come from overseas at the time it was donated.
Asked by Senator Bob Smith, Republican of New Hampshire, whether he thought Mr. Trie had laundered campaign contributions, Mr. Campane responded, "It's what we call in the business a slam dunk, Senator."
Mr. Trie, who is called Charlie, is said to be in China and is refusing to cooperate with investigators. 
In an interview last month with NBC-TV, he adamantly denied wrongdoing and said of the Senate investigators, "They'll never find me."
A native of Taiwan who is now an American citizen, Mr. Trie owned a Chinese restaurant in Little Rock, Ark., that was frequented by Mr. Clinton and other politicians when Mr. Clinton was Governor.
After Mr. Clinton was elected President, Mr. Trie sold his restaurant, moved to Washington, opened an office and tried to use his connection in business activities.
He was "always trying to find a deal and find the next deal," Mr. Campane testified. 
But the deals almost always fell through and none seemed to have made much money.
Many of Mr. Trie's activities have been covered in news reports over the last six months, including how he gave $640,000 to the trust fund collecting money for President Clinton's legal expenses, money that the trustees returned before its existence was publicly known.
But Mr. Campane's testimony today, especially the details of how much money was received from abroad, was more complete and authoritative than any of the news accounts.
The agent described how Mr. Trie had visited the Clinton White House at least 23 times and how he had arranged for Wang Jun, China's most important arms dealer, to attend a coffee with the President.
Asked why Mr. Trie had become involved in politics, Mr. Campane said that he seemed to enjoy hobnobbing with politicians and also hoped to use his political connections to make money.
"Trie understood and practiced an important lesson of Asian business culture: important political connections enhance one's reputation as a businessman," Mr. Campane said.
The same appeared to have been true of Mr. Ng, the businessman from Macao, whose name in Mandarin is Wu and who was referred to in today's hearing as "Mr. 
Wu."
After listening to the testimony, Senator Robert F. Bennett, a Republican from Utah, explained why he thought the businessman was willing to give Mr. Trie almost $1 million.
"I think Mr. Wu got what he paid for," Mr. Bennett said. 
"He was interested in establishing his own credentials or the credentials of his man in the United States, if Mr. Trie would be so characterized, as having very high-level contacts. 
And it's been my personal experience that this is very valuable, can open a lot of doors in a lot of places in ways that American business people simply do not understand, because we don't do business that way in the United States."
As was the case two weeks ago when the committee explored the activities of John Huang, another Chinese-American fund-raiser, the implication throughout today's hearing was that somehow Mr. Trie might have been a conduit of money from China.
At the outset of the hearings early this month, Senator Fred Thompson, the Tennessee Republican who is heading the investigation, spoke of a plot by the Chinese Government to funnel money into the American election campaigns last year.
So far, the Governmental Affairs Committee, headed by Mr. Thompson, has produced no public evidence to substantiate the plot.
On Monday night, several Senators on the committee received a classified briefing on the China question from Louis J. Freeh, Director of the F.B.I., and George J. Tenet, Director of Central Intelligence.
The Senators would not talk publicly about the substance of the meeting. 
But Democrats said they thought Mr. Thompson had overstated his case.
The Democratic view is that while the Chinese may have had some intention of trying to influence the election, there is no evidence that any money was actually put into the presidential race, and only scanty evidence that Congressional elections were involved.
After Mr. Campane left the witness table today, two Chinese immigrant homemakers testified to taking part in an elaborate three-cornered money transaction involving Mr. Trie. They gave $25,000 in their own names to the Democratic National Committee last year and were then reimbursed from a bank account held here in the name of Mr. Trie and Mr. Wu and supported by Mr. Wu.'s overseas resources.
The money was used to purchase a ticket to a Democratic fund raiser for the President's re-election at the Hay Adams Hotel here on Feb. 
19, 1996. 
After the campaign abuse scandal broke, the Democratic National Committee returned the money.
Given immunity from prosecution, the two women, Yue F. Chu and Xiping Wang, testified in Chinese, their words translated by a State Department translator.
They said they did not understand the transaction or its connection to American politics. 
But Ms. Chu, whose husband is an employee of Mr. Wu, repeatedly explained the situation this way:
"Mr. Wu was my husband's boss, and he wanted to buy a ticket to pass the gate. 
The boss wanted to go to the White House."

file: COMPANY NEWS_A.T.& T. Signs Pact In China.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a deal that could be worth billions of dollars over the next several years, China agreed yesterday to discuss buying a wide range of equipment from A.T.& T., including switching and transmission systems, cellular telephones, and business phones and computer networks.
Formally, the agreement signed by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company yesterday with the State Planning Commission of China is merely a memorandum of understanding to study possible investments.
But Randall L. Tobias, vice chairman of A.T.& T., said a major project would be announced "within a matter of months because we're moving at warp speed."
Â 
Equipment Sales Limited
The cold war, however, still looms over the deal. 
Cocom, the 17-nation Western trade organization that polices high-technology exports, limits the kind of telecommunications equipment that China can buy.
When A.T.& T. gets down to negotiating a specific deal on fiber-optic transmission lines, for example, it may find that it can supply only a line that carries 1,900 simultaneous conversations, a 10-year-old technology that A.T.& T. is about to phase out of production. 
Export to China of the more modern cable, for 8,000 conversations, is illegal.
Still, the agreement yesterday represents a significant advance for A.T.& T., which despite its $64 billion in revenue last year, has relatively little foreign sales except from its NCR computer subsidiary.
The world's most populous country would be the largest potential market for any company, but especially so for A.T.& T. The company's largest overseas market for phone equipment has been in Spain, one of the tiniest European markets for such sales.
For China, the agreement promises a major technological jump-start to an already fast-growing economy. 
A.T.& T. has also agreed to make computer-switching equipment and integrated circuits in China, combine corporate telephone systems and computer networks, and provide services like voice mail and toll-free "800" numbers.

file: COMPANY NEWS_AST to Build PC Factory Near Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
AST Research Inc., the fourth-largest American personal computer maker, today announced a joint venture with China to build a $16 million computer factory near Beijing that would make 100,000 PC's a year.
The deal, which will include efforts to develop China's nascent market for computers in schools and homes, could help AST solidify its position as China's best-selling computer maker. 
AST is so popular in China, where its PC's have been sold since 1985, that rivals promote their machines as "AST compatible" and clone makers turn out counterfeits of AST products.
"Establishing a leadership position in an early stage market has proved very key here," said Richard Zwetchkenbaum, a computer analyst for the International Data Corporation. 
"If they can do well in that country, they can do well in other countries in the region."
In addition, he said China's low labor costs could help AST remain competitive in the PC business. 
"This has implications for AST as a worldwide vendor."
Part of AST's strategy in Asia will be to capitalize on a recently acquired technology that permits data to be entered by pen on a screen. 
The Tandy Corporation's pen-based Grid system was part of a $160 million acquisition made by AST in July.
Currently, up to four keystrokes are needed to create a single Chinese character on AST machines.
"Clearly, Chinese can write far faster than they can use a keyboard," said Howard Elias, AST's marketing vice president. 
"We will be taking advantage of that technology."
AST stock rose 37.5 cents today, closing at $15.50 in Nasdaq trading.
AST, which was founded by three Asian immigrants, had 25 percent of China's $440 million market in 1992.
This year, International Data forecasts that 250,000 PC's will be bought in China, compared with 13.5 million in the United States, where growth is below 12 percent a year. 
China, the world's fastest-growing economy, will be snapping up PC's at a 22 percent annual rate through 2000.
"China represents the world's most promising market for PC's and other high-technology products," Safi U. Qureshey, AST's president, said in a statement.
AST declined to specify China's contribution to the venture.
