SWORDFISH FRIED IN SAGE OLIVE OIL
Adapted from "New Food Fast" by Donna Hay
Time: 10 minutes
Â 
3 tablespoons fruity extra virgin olive oil
8 large fresh sage leaves
2 teaspoons grated lemon zest
1/2 teaspoon cracked black pepper
4 thin ( 3/4-inch) swordfish steaks.
1. Heat olive oil in a large saute pan over medium-high heat. 
Add the sage leaves, lemon zest and cracked black pepper. 
Saute until sage is crisp, about 2 minutes.
2. Add swordfish, and saute about 1 minute on each side, or until just cooked through; be careful not to overcook. 
Quickly transfer to serving plates, and drizzle with the oil and sage from the pan. 
Serve immediately.
Yield: 4 servings.
Â 
ORANGE, DATE AND CARDAMOM TART
Adapted from "Spice" by Christine Manfield
Time: 2 hours, plus overnight refrigeration and 3 hours' cooling
Â 
1/2 cup confectioners' sugar
3/4 cup flour
5 1/2 tablespoons chilled unsalted butter, cut into cubes
2 large egg yolks
1/2 vanilla bean, split
4 large eggs
3/4 cup plus 2 tablespoons extra-fine
granulated sugar
Zest of two oranges
1/4 cup fresh orange juice
Seeds from 4 green cardamom pods, ground
1/3 cup heavy cream
18 fresh dates, halved lengthwise.
1. Sift together powdered sugar and flour, and place in food processor. 
Add butter, and pulse until mixture resembles fine bread crumbs. 
Add egg yolks, and scrape in pulp from vanilla bean. 
Blend until dough just comes together in a soft ball. 
Wrap in plastic film, and refrigerate overnight.
2. In a medium bowl combine eggs and sugar, and whisk until pale and creamy. 
Add orange zest, juice, cardamom and cream. 
Mix well, and refrigerate overnight.
3. Lightly dust a work surface with flour, and roll dough into 10-inch circle. 
Fold into quarters to transfer to a 9 1/2-inch nonstick tart pan. 
Unfold and fit snugly into pan, trimming and patching as necessary. 
Refrigerate 30 minutes.
4. Preheat oven to 325 degrees. 
Prick tart shell all over with a fork, and bake just until dry and golden, about 15 minutes.
5. Strain egg mixture through a fine sieve. 
Place tart shell on baking sheet, and arrange dates inside. 
Gently pour in egg mixture.
6. If edges of the tart shell are already browned, cover with strips of foil to prevent burning. 
Bake until custard is lightly browned and set, about 30 minutes. 
Allow to cool at least 3 hours before removing from pan.
Yield: One 9 1/2-inch tart (8 servings).
Â 
WARM SALAD OF BARBECUED LAMB
Adapted from "Australian Food"
Time: 1 hour and 15 minutes
Â 
2 tablespoons Asian plum sauce
2 tablespoons light soy sauce
1 tablespoon mirin (sweetened rice wine) or sherry
3 tablespoons light vegetable oil
1 teaspoon sesame oil
1 tablespoon rice vinegar
Chili oil, optional
4 cups mixed baby spinach, arugula and tatsoi
18 green beans, trimmed
4 lamb loin chops, boned and trimmed of fat
1/4 cup char sui sauce or Asian plum sauce
1/4 cup Sichuan peppercorns, finely crushed with a rolling pin
3 tablespoons vegetable oil
12 oyster mushrooms
15 snow peas, ends trimmed, each cut diagonally into two
3 tablespoons bean sprouts
6 fresh water chestnuts, peeled and sliced, or 1/3 cup canned whole water chestnuts, thinly sliced.
1. In a small bowl, combine 2 tablespoons plum sauce, soy sauce, mirin, light vegetable oil, sesame oil and vinegar. 
Mix well, and add chili oil to taste. 
Set aside.
2. Prepare a grill, or lightly oil a heavy ridged or flat skillet. 
Place spinach mixture in a bowl, and set aside. 
Bring a pot of lightly salted water to a boil, and blanch green beans until just tender. 
Rinse under cold water, drain and set aside.
3. Coat lamb chops with char sui sauce, and roll very lightly in peppercorns. 
Allow meat to rest 30 minutes. 
Grill or sear over high heat until charred but pink in the center, about 2 1/2 minutes on the first side, and 1 1/2 minutes on the second. 
Transfer to a plate, cover with a bowl and let rest for 2 to 3 minutes.
4. Heat vegetable oil in a separate skillet, and fry mushrooms until crisp. 
Add to spinach mixture. 
Add snow peas and green beans to skillet, and saute for 30 seconds. 
Add bean sprouts and water chestnuts, and toss just until heated. 
Add to spinach mixture.
5. To serve, whisk dressing until blended, and add to spinach mixture. 
Toss gently, and place an equal portion in the center of each of four serving plates. 
Slice the lamb thinly on the diagonal, and arrange over greens. 
Serve immediately.

"I told him about some of my experiences in dealing with the Chinese Communists," Mr. Wei told reporters at a briefing later, "and I expressed the hope that in dealing with the Chinese Communists, the United States would not be deceived.

text:

Wei Jingsheng, China's most prominent democracy advocate, said in an interview in New York yesterday that he would tell President Clinton that only continued pressure from the West could help free more Chinese political prisoners. 
He said he intended to use his time in exile to act as a campaigner for human rights.
"This will be the very first issue that we discuss," said Mr. Wei, who is expected to meet Mr. Clinton later this month or early in December. 
"If you want to have a dialogue with a Communist Government, you have to use pressure, otherwise they will never talk with you."
Excerpts, page A5.
Still weakened by his 16 years of imprisonment, Mr. Wei nonetheless appeared to be in fairly good health. 
Reports that he was suffering from life-threatening illnesses appear now to have been part of a strategy by family members and rights groups to press Beijing's Government to release him on medical parole, as it did last weekend.
Mr. Wei's assertions that he intends to become a strong public advocate for improvements in China's human rights situation could complicate relations between Washington and Beijing.
Mr. Wei's message may prove controversial to the Clinton Administration, which won praise yesterday from rights organizations for pressing Mr. Wei's case in private meetings with Chinese leaders in the last three years. 
Mr. Clinton has stepped back from the campaign of trade pressure on China that he advocated at the outset of his Administration, arguing that "engagement," not confrontation, was more likely to produce improved rights conditions in China.
Speaking at a news conference in New York and in an interview afterward, Mr. Wei said he saw himself becoming an evangelist for greater freedom and democratic reform in China using the Voice of America, Radio Free Asia and other news media that would enable him to build an audience among the Chinese.
Many people in China do not recognize his name because it is banned from being mentioned by state-run news outlets and because he has been imprisoned almost continuously since March 1979.
"Most of the Chinese people would very much like to hear other voices," he said. 
"Otherwise they would not know that they have choices. 
That is why this is very important."
He quarreled good-naturedly in the interview at being labeled a dissident. 
"Most of the Chinese people all want democracy," he asserted. 
"And the people who are different are just this little group of ruling elites of the Chinese Communist Party, so they are really the dissidents."
In the news conference, he exhorted China's democracy forces, saying, "You should not pay attention to the immediate low tide, because after a low tide there is always a high tide that follows."
The State Department earlier this year reported that political dissent in China had effectively been completely stifled through a campaign of repressive measures including jailings and forced exiles.
Mr. Wei's entrance this morning into a large hall at the New York Public Library packed by waiting reporters and well-wishers was greeted by applause and cheers. 
The 47-year-old activist wore a brown corduroy jacket and a red plaid shirt, his uneven prison crew cut looking in need of a trim.
In an opening statement, Mr. Wei thanked the "people and governments around the world that have made enormous efforts to press the Chinese Government for the release of political prisoners" and admonished those who already live in freedom in the world not to become complacent about those who do not.
"Democracy and freedom are among the loftiest ideals of humanity, and they are the most sacred rights of mankind," he said. 
"Those who already enjoy democracy, liberty and human rights, in particular, should not allow their own personal happiness to numb them into forgetting the many others who are still struggling against tyranny, slavery and poverty, and all of those who are suffering from unimaginable forms of oppression, exploitation and massacres."
Though he evaded questions during the news conference about what message he would deliver to Mr. Clinton, during the interview afterward, Mr. Wei was emphatic that he would seek continued pressure from Washington and other Western capitals for improvement of rights conditions in China and the release of prisoners.
The only reason Chinese leaders have ever engaged in dialogue over the country's internal human rights conditions has been pressure from the United States and other countries whose markets have become important export destinations for Chinese goods and a source of technology for China's modernization.
Mr. Wei said he would like to visit all parts of the United States in the coming months. 
While in New York, he has been assigned a New York police detective as a bodyguard. 
Columbia University and the University of California at Berkeley have offered him office space and living quarters to pursue academic studies and pro-democracy work.
His immediate plans are to write a book about the beatings, abuse and psychological pressure that the Chinese prison authorities used to try to break him and, ultimately, to force him into exile by refusing him further medical treatment in prison.
Among the techniques were shutting off heat in his cell, using other inmates to torment or beat him and housing him in a cell where lights were left on 24 hours a day as a way of denying him sleep.
Mr. Wei was released from Jidong Prison, about 150 miles southeast of Beijing. 
"When I was a prisoner there in 1989, they used to brag that they were the largest salt factory in Asia, exporting to Japan and many other countries. 
But when I returned in 1993, I asked them if they were still exporting salt to other countries, and they denied it."
Mr. Wei indicated that international criticism of China's use of prison labor for exported products had caused the prison authorities to change their story.
He said that if he becomes active as an opposition figure in the United States, he is concerned that the Communist authorities might retaliate against members of his family left behind in China.
"I am concerned about their security," he said at the news conference. 
"They have suffered a lot. 
But there are hundreds of millions of Chinese who have been oppressed, and I am concerned about them equally."
Beijing's leaders are apparently calculating that with Mr. Wei out of the country, his threat to rekindle a democracy movement has been neutralized and his effectiveness as a political troublemaker will be minimized by his distance from China.
But rights groups based in the United States, with Mr. Wei's cooperation, already appear to be developing a strategy to give him a new voice in China, something he has scarcely had since 1978-79, when he pasted his pro-democracy essays on a stretch of wall in central Beijing that became known as the Democracy Wall.
Among Mr. Wei's first interviews yesterday were with correspondents for the Chinese-language service of the Voice of America, Radio Free Asia and a major Chinese daily newspaper in Hong Kong. 
He was also interviewed by The New York Times.
For a man who has spent long years in solitary confinement and watched as more than a dozen teeth dropped out from years of malnutrition because of a poor prison diet, Mr. Wei seemed to enjoy parrying the questions of a New York news conference.
Asked about his views on Taiwan and Tibet, where there are strong independence movements with support in the United States, Mr. Wei was careful not to challenge China's claims of sovereignty over both territories.
"On Tibet," he said, "this is a rather complex question. 
I don't agree with the Government's policy of oppressing and killing Tibetans and carrying out the destruction of Tibetan culture, but as to how to resolve this issue, I think that calm Chinese and Tibetans should sit down and figure out a good solution."
Asked to tell the greatest lesson he learned from his 16 years of imprisonment for the views he expressed during the Democracy Wall period, Mr. Wei said: "I have learned many things in prison, but the most important thing is that for a human being, there is no difficulty that cannot be overcome. 
You just have to rely on yourself and you can get through anything."
The man most responsible for Mr. Wei's jailing was Deng Xiaoping, the Chinese leader who emerged in the years after the death of Mao in 1976 and opened an era of economic reform that is turning the nation of 1.2 billion into an Asian powerhouse.
Mr. Wei's trenchant essays on Democracy Wall pointedly criticized Deng for failing to carry through with his promises of democracy as part of the program for China's modernization. 
When Mr. Wei called Deng a dictator in early 1979, he was arrested and Democracy Wall was torn down.
Mr. Wei said he sent a letter of condolence to Deng's family when the 92-year-old leader died in February.
"If he could have expanded reform to the political arena," Mr. Wei said, "then -- even if he had abused me even worse than he has -- I still would not hate him."
Mr. Wei took questions for a little more than 40 minutes at the library hall and then asked politely that he be excused because he was feeling tired and dizzy.

file: Dole Wavers On Extending Trade Rights For China.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the first indication that Washington's dealing with China could become a major campaign-year argument in Congress, Senator Bob Dole appeared to back away today from years of support for extending broad trade privileges to Beijing, saying he had not decided whether to oppose the Clinton Administration's efforts to renew those trade rights this spring.
Mr. Dole has been under sharp pressure from the right wing of his party to abandon the traditional Republican position that the best way to influence China's behavior is to engage it economically. 
But as recently as a few days ago, when he canceled a major speech on his policy toward China, his advisers insisted that he was still firmly in favor of "most-favored nation" status for China, on which billions of dollars of trade with American companies -- and perhaps the economic futures of Hong Kong and Taiwan -- depend.
Today, however, Mr. Dole wavered. 
Emerging from a meeting with former President George Bush, who has just completed a trip to China, Mr. Dole said, "We'll be developing our position on it very soon."
For Mr. Dole, as for Mr. Clinton, China's trade status poses some agonizing problems. 
His home state of Kansas is the site of a major Boeing plant, where one in seven jets goes to China. 
Agricultural companies, among his biggest supporters, have warned that ending China's trading preferences would be a disaster for them.
And Mr. Dole has a long record of statements in support of trade concessions that sound much like Mr. Clinton's arguments.
"I strongly support most-favored nation status for China," he said on "Larry King Live" on March 23, 1994. 
"I think we make a mistake when we tie it to human rights."
Cancellation, he said, would "cost us a couple of hundred thousand American jobs."
In 1992 and 1993, when Mr. Clinton was wavering on the issue, Mr. Dole was urging him to "move ahead on most-favored nation status for China where, again, Republicans would support the President if he'll come out and do that."
Some Republicans have urged Mr. Dole to turn the extension of trade privileges into a referendum on Mr. Clinton's dealings with China, with an eye toward putting Mr. Clinton in the embarrassing position of vetoing a Congressional resolution to end China's trading rights here.
"It would be a very tough veto in an election year," one of Mr. Clinton's top aides said recently, worrying that the President could appear to be defending China's leadership.
American business has strongly urged the extension of China's trading rights, and successfully pressed Mr. Clinton two years ago to reverse himself and "delink" favorable trade status from China's human rights performance. 
Until today, Mr. Dole -- whose Kansas constituencies include major exporters to China -- seemed firmly in the Clinton camp.
Like Mr. Dole, the Administration is also concerned that its policies not cost America lucrative contracts. 
Just today the Export-Import Bank of the United States approved a $160 million loan guarantee for a Chinese airline to buy three Boeing jets. 
In February, Secretary of State Warren Christopher had asked the bank to suspend consideration of loans for all projects in China for 30 days until he decided whether and how to sanction China for selling $70,000 of ring magnets to Pakistan. 
But Mr. Christopher is still weighing his decision, both because of legal complexities and because the Administration is still trying to hone in on a sanction that would show American toughness but not prompt retaliation.
No decision is expected until he meets Foreign Minister Qian Qichen of China on Friday, American officials said. 
Mr. Christopher is to break off from President Clinton's trip to Russia to meet Mr. Qian in The Hague. 
Officials at the Ex-Im Bank, an independent agency, said they had to move ahead because China was already giving more aircraft contracts to Europe.
The sanction Mr. Christopher has in mind would prevent the Ex-Im Bank from aiding a Chinese company that was linked to the ring magnet sales. 
But it would also hurt two major American companies, Westinghouse and Bechtel.
The Administration had hoped that its threats of sanctions against China would defuse the calls for the repeal of favorable trade status, which permits the Chinese to get the benefits that America extends to its other major trading partners -- including low tariffs for its goods. 
But liberals outraged by the human rights record of China and conservatives outraged by its threats against Taiwan are aligning in the House of Representatives to vote against the trading rights after Mr. Clinton formally notifies Congress of his intentions. 
He must do so by June 3.
"We're going to lose the House on this," a top Administration official said recently. 
"The issue is the Senate, and specifically Bob Dole."Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: Don_t Joke About This Stock Market.txt
text:
ï»¿
In his private trading room at a local securities firm, Millions Yang peers intently at a parade of price charts flowing across a computer screen. 
Mr. Yang, a rotund former Red Guard who earned his nickname the easy way, by making millions in the stock market, breaks into a smile.
"Today I made 100,000 yuan," almost $20,000, he says, laughing. 
"Not bad for a day."
Outside Mr. Yang's office during one recent lunch break, several hundred small investors line up, eager to place orders when trading resumes two hours later. 
Millions Yang goes to the door and they ask him for advice.
"Millions Yang!" call dozens of voices. 
"Millions Yang, what should I buy?" one man shouts. 
"Give me some tips," yells another. 
Millions Yang -- which translates to Yang Baiwan in Chinese -- chats with those in front of the line. 
Heads crane as those in back try to overhear.
"I'm trapped in a loss," one woman tells him despairingly. 
"What should I do?"
"You must be willing to take a loss," he answers, and people nod, taking mental notes. 
"If it's going down, sell it and accept the loss. 
Otherwise you'll be stuck with a bigger loss."
That's the way it is at the Chinese stock market these days. 
The market used to be just a curiosity, a sort of masquerade in which Communists cross-dressed as capitalists and waved share certificates in place of little red books. 
American financiers and journalists dropped by the stock exchanges to chat patronizingly with the traders: "So, Mr. Yang, how much money did you make today?
A dollar!
That's wonderful -- you're going to be a rich man."
Â 
2 Million Shareholders
No one is patronizing these days. 
Now China has two million shareholders, with the number growing by about 50,000 a week. 
The market index in Shanghai soared 167 percent last year, and these days even the small American investor can buy into the Chinese market, although some experts suggest it might be just as prudent to visit Las Vegas.
On a good day, the two-year-old Chinese market trades $350 million worth of shares, more than Hong Kong in a slow session. 
And it is growing at a prodigious rate: in the first quarter of 1993, the Shanghai Stock Exchange enjoyed a trading volume 2.2 times that of all of 1992. 
With the number of listings expected almost to double this year, some experts think that in a year or two the Shanghai market will regularly enjoy the highest volume in Asia outside Japan.
In short, the Chinese stock market is transforming itself from a curiosity to a major force. 
The metamorphosis is quite a spectacle. 
Thousands of Chinese companies yearn to go public, at home or on foreign exchanges. 
Hundreds of foreign accountants and lawyers are struggling to make sense of nonsensical Chinese balance sheets. 
Western investment banks are opening offices in China and paying huge sums for anyone who knows how to say "P/E ratio" in Chinese. 
Above all, tens of millions of ordinary Chinese are desperate to become shareholders. 
Last August, a million Chinese lined up for days under a fierce sun to buy stock -- more precisely, to pay several weeks' salary for an application form that would give them a 10 percent chance of being allowed to buy new shares. 
When the forms ran out, the would-be investors rioted. 
Securities executives in the West could be pardoned for feeling a bit envious.
The growth of the stock market is having an important effect on China as a whole. 
First, state-owned companies, perennially inefficient, begin to care about profitability. 
"You can see that when the companies issue stocks, they have to have a board of directors, they have to be audited, and they pay a lot more attention to efficiency," said Pan Muping, the Shanghai representative of Crosby Securities, a Hong Kong-based brokerage that was one of the first to be bullish on China.
More broadly, the rise of the market legitimizes the kind of quasi-capitalism that has been around for a dozen years but is steadily becoming less quasi and more capitalism.
Also, it helps create the kind of urban middle class that is the foundation for a modern civil society. 
In the past, the Communist Party was the sole source of power and prestige. 
While the party remains awesomely powerful, it is no longer the only show in town. 
Business interests are becoming an alternative power base, an alternative source of values, a rival source of prestige.
Â 
A Westerner Impressed
The changes impress William A. Schreyer, chairman of Merrill Lynch & Company, who was in China last month to open the firm's new office here in Shanghai. 
"The modernization of China's economy, I think, is one of the most exciting endeavors in this century," he said, "and we want to be there and be part of it."
Mr. Schreyer said he was impressed from the moment he took the road from the Beijing airport and saw what seemed a continuous construction zone. 
He grew more enthusiastic when Prime Minister Li Peng and Communist Party General Secretary Jiang Zemin both received him and expressed interest in improving corporate accounting standards.
"If I were 25 years younger," the 65-year-old Mr. Schreyer said, "I'd study Chinese and ask Merrill Lynch to post me there."
He added that Merrill Lynch is positioning itself in China in the hope of growing with the local market just as it did in Japan 32 years ago.
What?
Mention the Japanese and Chinese stock markets in the same breath?
A couple of years ago that would have been regarded as foolish. 
Now it's regarded as visionary.
"China is the world's fastest-growing economy," said Duncan P. F. Mount, managing director of CEF Investment Management Ltd. in Hong Kong. 
"There are about 300,000 incorporated companies, of which about 70 are listed. 
In time, it's obviously going to be Asia's biggest stock market, probably bigger than Japan. 
The question is how long it's going to take, not is it going to happen."
Â 
Some Caveats
To be sure, the same could have been said back in 1914, when Shanghai first opened a securities exchange. 
Fund managers and brokers who promoted Shanghai back then may eventually be proven to be visionaries, but from beneath their gravestones their clients will be unimpressed.
Even now, the Chinese market faces enormous challenges that Westerners do not always appreciate. 
Like the rest of the economy, the stock system is laced with corruption that alienates many ordinary citizens. 
Most of the trading is a speculative froth that bears little relationship to fundamentals, and some of the excitement seems to be of the flavor-of-the-month variety. 
At various times, other emerging markets -- South Korea, Indonesia, Taiwan, Mexico, etc. 
-- have been the toast of international investors, but often the small investor showed up as the party ended, just in time to pay the bill.
What is more, most of the Chinese companies that list stocks are from the state-owned sector, which is the weakest part of the economy. 
The companies that are behind the Chinese boom are the small township factories and private enterprises that operate on a small scale, bribe local officials, dodge taxes and keep miserable accounts. 
It is virtually impossible for foreigners to buy shares in them.
This may well be the make-or-break year for the Chinese stock market, which is still formally dubbed an experiment. 
If all goes smoothly, China's leaders are expected to decide next year that the experiment is over, and that they can implement the shareholding system on a far wider scale.
The stock market in its current form began in December 1990 with the formal opening of the Shanghai Securities Exchange. 
About the same time, the southern city of Shenzhen, next to Hong Kong, was also allowed to open an exchange.
These days the Shanghai exchange trades in 62 stocks, with several more to be listed over the next month. 
The exchange now has 600 seats; in June that will rise to 2,500. 
The Government has agreed in principle that 50 or 60 more companies from all over the country can list this year, issuing shares with a par value of $1 billion.
"Late this year or early next year, we'll regularly have higher trading volumes than Hong Kong," said Wei Wenyuan, the executive director of the Shanghai exchange. 
"Then it'll keep going up from there."
The Shanghai exchange has gradually left the Shenzhen exchange behind and become the premier market in the country. 
A half-dozen other cities are desperately trying to start their own stock exchanges, but the Government has refused to allow them to do so.
Many Chinese buy stocks with the giddy excitement they might show in entering a casino. 
Investors have heard about a few people who committed suicide after losing their money, but mostly they hear stories about folks like Millions Yang. 
The losers keep quiet. 
So the emphasis is on speculative in-and-out trading. 
Chinese speak of "chao gu," or stir-frying stocks, meaning to turn them over quickly.
Chinese do not telephone their brokers; instead they swarm into the brokerages. 
Each of the dozens of brokerages in Shanghai has a huge trading room in which individual investors stand shoulder to shoulder, watching a huge screen with share prices. 
To trade, they fill out a form and stand in a long line, sometimes for hours, to give it to a broker.
In Shanghai alone, more than 100,000 people have become professional investors. 
Some have quit their jobs; others -- in what local people say with a wink is a demonstration of the superiority of socialism -- simply don't show up at work while still being paid. 
They spend every day in the trading rooms of a brokerage.
The "da hu" -- big rollers, those with more than $90,000 in their accounts -- get favored treatment. 
At Shenyin Securities, for example, a da hu is allowed to pay $40 a month and get a pass to enter a basement room with sofas and computer monitors. 
A purchase order can be handed to a broker without waiting in line.
"A year ago we had 15 da hu here," said Zhu Weidong, a 22-year-old broker who looks after them. 
"Now we have 60."
Mr. Zhu said the richest of them once had the equivalent of almost $2 million in his account.
The securities boom has created a shortage of employees in the field. 
Companies lure brokers by paying $200 a month, several times the prevailing wage, and offering bonuses.
For now, of course, the stock markets are essentially local ones in just two of China's innumerable cities. 
But this year they are supposed to go national. 
The Shenzhen exchange just listed a company from Hainan Province, and one or two major companies from each of China's 30 provinces are supposed to go public in Shanghai or Shenzhen in the coming months.
At the same time, the Shanghai exchange is eagerly targeting investors in other cities. 
Fifty cities, in every province but Tibet, are now hooked up to the Shanghai stock computer system. 
On April 26, the exchange began to broadcast share information by satellite to a network of receiving stations all over the country, and two-way trading by satellite is scheduled to begin in November.
The transformation of the Shanghai market into a national one would be hugely important. 
It would multiply the pool of potential investors by a hundred, and allow more long-term investors to join the speculators.
Â 
Little Regulation
Still, the market faces a host of problems. 
One of the most important is that there is little regulatory control. 
A new Securities Regulatory Commission has been established, but nobody seems inclined to pay it much heed.
"The foundation for China's stock market is seriously inadequate, creating equally serious problems," a confidential Government report declared recently. 
The 18-page report, classified secret, strongly supported the continued development of the market but warned of far-reaching corruption, inter-ministry rivalries and other problems. 
In particular, the report warned against "power shares" -- gifts of stock to Government figures to win favors.
"We're approached by companies every day, banging on our door and saying that they want to go public," said Gao Xiqing, an American-trained lawyer who is chief counsel to the Securities Regulatory Commission. 
"It's remarkable how the whole country is so gung ho."
Perhaps too gung ho. 
Because the Government is restricting the numbers that can go public, there is a natural temptation to offer bribes.
"Some people come in and offer us X number of shares in their company," said Mr. Gao, who is in charge of public offerings. 
"They don't have the concept of a conflict of interest. 
I say I can't take it, and they think I don't have the money. 
So they say it's free. 
And then when they understand that I just can't accept it, they say it doesn't have to be in my name."
Millions Yang acknowledges that there are problems in the stock market, but he thinks they will be easily overcome. 
Shanghai, he says, will eventually become the financial capital of the Far East.
Asked whether hard-liners might close the stock market after Deng Xiaoping dies, Mr. Yang paused for only a second. 
"I don't worry," he said, then offered a novel interpretation of Marxism: "The goal of the revolution was to make people rich, and now they're rich. 
The Government won't allow folks to become poor again."
Â 
VARIOUS WAYS TO GET IN ON THE CHINA PLAY
ASIDE from rushing to Shanghai and "stir-frying" shares alongside Millions Yang, foreigners can participate in the Chinese stock market in several ways.
One of the simplest is to buy into one of the 30-odd China funds, with $1.3 billion in assets, offered by international securities firms. 
Some of these funds are traded, like shares, on the New York Stock Exchange and other exchanges, or are available directly through brokers.
The problem with that is that some of the funds are not what their names might imply. 
Some hold mostly cash rather than China stocks, or their "China holdings" may be almost entirely companies in Hong Kong that do business in China. 
The recent fascination with "China concept" stocks has led many Hong Kong companies to put China in their names so that they can enjoy the premium afforded to China plays.
Another possibility is to invest in Chinese companies listed abroad. 
One such company, Brilliance China Automotive Holdings, was listed on the New York Stock Exchange last year, and others hope to follow. 
In addition, nine Chinese companies are expected to list on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange later this year. 
The best known is Qingdao Brewery, which makes Tsingtao Beer.
The final possibility is to invest directly in Chinese shares. 
While foreigners are not allowed to buy ordinary shares in Chinese companies, 10 companies in Shanghai and 9 in Shenzhen have listed a special kind of foreign currency-denominated stock -- called B-shares -- that only foreigners may purchase. 
Some large brokerages can arrange a purchase of the B-shares.
However, transaction costs in B-shares are relatively high, trading volume is low and the B-shares change hands at less than half the price of the A-shares held by Chinese investors.
One reason in the past for the limited demand was that the clearing system in Shanghai did not meet standards of the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, effectively keeping out many American investors. 
But the Shanghai exchange has started a new settlement system, and last month the S.E.C. agreed to allow China funds to buy B-shares.
Buying by American fund managers may give the B-shares a boost, but they would get an even bigger boost if Chinese nationals were allowed to use their United States dollars to buy them. 
China's central bank and foreign exchange agency have so far blocked proposals to allow Chinese to buy B-shares.
Â 
Â 
Â 
RED GUARDS TO HOT PROFITS
BEFORE Millions Yang became an investment legend, he was active as a Red Guard during the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976. 
Those were chaotic years in Shanghai. 
Vehicles were instructed to go forward at a red light and stop at a green light -- the Red Guards reasoning that red, as the revolutionary color, should not be associated with coming to a halt. 
Not all drivers got the message, however, and accidents were common. 
Finally traffic lights were given special dispensation to pursue their bourgeois ways. 
A red light again meant to stop.
After the Cultural Revolution, Mr. Yang, whose real name is Yang Huaiding, found that making money was more fun than making revolution. 
He entered the securities business in 1988, buying Government bonds in rural areas and selling them in Shanghai. 
This was a lucrative business, and partly as a result it was suspect. 
While there was no clear law against it, the authorities periodically denounced such arbitrage with the ugliest of words in the official vocabulary: speculation.
When the stock market opened, Mr. Yang began reading about equities, quickly developed a knack for trading and became the nation's most famous investor. 
In China, he says, it is still pretty easy to make a quick profit. 
"In New York, the market is more mature so it's harder to get a profit," he said. 
"Here everything is still being developed, so it's a lot easier."
