The London stock market led a widespread upward surge on European stock prices yesterday, rising to its highest close since April 15.
In China, meanwhile, profit taking took some of the shine off a spectacular rebound on its stock markets.
The strength of the European markets surprised many traders. 
In London, the Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading shares soared 60.1 points, or 1.94 percent, in a jump unmatched since June, to close at 3,157.5.
In Frankfurt, the DAX 30-share index advanced by 1.5 percent, led by a strong chemicals sector, while in Paris, the CAC 40-share index ended 47 points, or 2.3 percent, ahead on lively overseas interest and strong futures.
British shares were helped by a report from the Bank of England saying that it expected underlying inflation to peak just above 3 percent in the first quarter of 1996, then fall back. 
It also said disinflationary pressures generated by the slack in the economy had been greater than anticipated.
The Bank of England's forecast was based on the assumption that the current 5.25 percent prime lending rate would not change.
Elsewhere, China's two stock exchanges gave back part of their gains from a spectacular rally on Monday that sent prices surging more than 30 percent.
Shanghai's A-share index dove 3.19 percent to 433.42 points as buying stalled just below the 500-point mark. 
The Shenzhen A index shed 1.75 percent to 125.80 points.
Brokers said Beijing's pledge to freeze all new issues and listings this year, which sent Shanghai's market rocketing by 36.14 percent and Shenzhen's up by 33.96 percent Monday, was still buoying sentiment.
Small investors and institutions alike placed great trust in Beijing's resolve to rescue the market, brokers said.
"The new measures are different from former steps taken by Beijing because they are concrete and resolute," said Yan Yulong, a broker with Guo Tai Securities.
Past attempts by China's top securities regulator, Liu Hongru, to talk up the market served only to further frustrate investors and sparked new rounds of selling.

file: Ex-General, Member of Banned Sect, Confesses _Mistakes,_ China Says.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese authorities disclosed today that a retired army general, the highest-ranking leader in Beijing of the spiritual movement that was banned last week, has confessed his "mistakes" and renounced his allegiance to the organization.
The admission by the general, Li Qihua, is a milestone in China's crackdown on the movement, Falun Gong, and a sign that despite widespread resistance by members, the authorities appear to be succeeding in dismantling the group's core.
Mr. Li, 81, who carried the rank of lieutenant general in the People's Liberation Army, was head of the 301 Hospital in Beijing, an extremely sensitive post because the enormous military-run hospital is where China's top leaders are treated.
He retired 15 years ago after a lifetime in the Communist cause that he said began at age 10. 
His seniority, impeccable credentials and continued access to the highest circles in China made him strategically important to Falun Gong, and equally threatening to the country's leaders.
Today, the military newspaper, Liberation Army Daily, printed a question-and-answer interview with Mr. Li in which he offered a classic Communist Party-style confession as he endorsed the party's crackdown, the nation's most sweeping political campaign in a decade,
"I felt I was cheated," Mr. Li said, according to the account. 
"The party's decision is very wise, very correct and very prompt."
In the secretive and shadow-prone way of Chinese politics, however, Mr. Li's former position and rank were not described in the article, which simply referred to him as an old cadre who had "wrongly written an article propagating Falun Gong."
To the casual reader, Mr. Li's long admission might look like just another item in the anti-Falun Gong propaganda that has swamped China's official media over the last week.
But as Chinese insiders know, Mr. Li has been identified by Chinese authorities as Falun Gong's top officer in Beijing, and the article he wrote was a critical item in the Government's decision to mount such a wide-reaching political campaign against the movement. 
Falun Gong advocates an amalgam of traditional qigong breathing exercises and meditation, with elements of Buddhism and Taoism, to enhance spiritual and physical well-being. 
The Communist Party has mobilized its vast apparatus to demand that government offices and work places all over the nation purge Falun Gong members and swear allegiance to the party's Marxist ideology.
Mr. Li's article was brought to the attention of President Jiang Zemin on May 5, 10 days after a huge demonstration by Falun Gong supporters outside China's leadership compound in central Beijing, said a Chinese political analyst with access to internal documents.
In his article, which was circulated among senior military officers, Mr. Li wrote that China's leaders should look kindly on the spiritual movement. 
What is more, Mr. Li urged leaders to study Falun Gong personally to improve their own physical and mental health.
Gen. Zhang Wannian, China's top military officer and vice chairman of the Central Military Commission under Mr. Jiang, sent a copy of the article to the President recommending that action be taken against Mr. Li.
Mr. Jiang, who was deeply alarmed by the boldness of the challenge to his authority implicit in the April 25 demonstration, wrote a sharply worded memorandum to fellow Politburo members identifying Falun Gong as a serious threat to the Communist Party's existence.
The memo was dated May 8, the day after NATO bombed the Chinese Embassy in Yugoslavia, which caused such outrage here that most Chinese saw it as an affront to their national dignity. 
The authorities permitted students to hold anti-American demonstrations, which included throwing rocks at the United States Embassy in Beijing.
If Falun Gong masters can foresee everything, Mr. Jiang wrote, how could they not predict the bombing of our embassy?
At the same time, Mr. Jiang instructed Gen. Wang Ke, the director of the People's Liberation Army's General Logistics Department, to visit Mr. Li to help him see the party's position more clearly.
Mr. Li apparently buckled right away. 
Yet his confession was only made public today.
In the confession, Mr. Li made it clear that he will now oppose the teachings of Li Hongzhi, who founded Falun Gong in 1992 and now lives in New York City. 
The two Li's are not related.
"When Li Hongzhi says that Falun Gong can cure all disease, that is a ridiculous position and must be a way to trick people," Mr. Li was quoted as saying. 
"Seeking medical treatment when you are sick is common sense. 
If Falun Gong is really so powerful, why do we need doctors, why do we need hospitals?"
Mr. Li, a veteran of the Communist military forces' Long March in the mid-1930's, the defining political event of the party's founding generation of leaders, has apparently been permitted to stay at home, while many other Falun Gong leaders have been taken into custody.
Although the organization of Falun Gong has remained mysterious, staffed by adherents who have gone to extreme lengths to protect what they believe is a sacred mission to propagate the teachings of Li Hongzhi, the crackdown is gradually disclosing clues about its structure.
The official media have reported that under the central leadership of the Falun Dafa Research Society, there were 39 provincial-level "general guidance stations" and 1,900 lower-level "guidance stations" spread all over China. 
For ordinary practitioners, the authorities said, there were more than 28,000 practice sites, mostly in urban parks and public places.
In recent days, the authorities have started producing confessions from the heads and deputy heads of "general guidance stations" in Jilin Province and Shandong Province.
In a nationwide political campaign, Communist Party leaders in each province are expected to produce the confession of the chief local culprit, in this case Falun Gong leaders, so the number who are actually brought forward may provide the best indication of how well Beijing's campaign is going.
One difficulty that Chinese leaders face is Falun Gong's amorphous nature, which makes it difficult to control. 
Another difficulty is the group's home-grown nature, which makes it hard to cast as a foreign plot, a favorite tactic in identifying a political enemy and one that was used against the democracy movement of 1989 at Tiananmen Square.
Yet Chinese officials have pointed to a foreign role in Falun Gong anyway, apparently because Li Hongzhi is based in the United States and because much of the Internet communication among the group's leaders has come from outside China.
"Hostile Western forces are using 'Westernization' and 'separatist' strategies to constantly carry out ideological and cultural infiltration," the New China News Agency reported this week.
A Hong Kong newspaper, Ming Pao, also reported that Mr. Jiang's memo specifically pointed to "behind-the-scenes involvement of foreign forces" in Falun Gong.

Citing environmental concerns, the Export-Import Bank refused today to help finance a huge dam in China that is intended to be the largest hydroelectric project in history.
The agency's board voted unanimously not to issue letters of interest -- a preliminary step in subsidizing loans for foreign countries to buy American goods and services -- to Caterpillar Inc. and other equipment makers that have sought to take part in the project.
The Clinton Administration had recommended against Ex-Im financing for the Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River, in Hubei province of central China. 
The dam, which is expected to cost more than $25 billion to build, is to be about a mile and a half wide and 600 feet high, flooding farmland and towns and creating a 400-mile-long reservoir.
The bank said it would reconsider if China provided extensive new information about how it would protect water quality and preserve endangered species, and meet other concerns about the project. 
But the decision not to proceed with applications for loan subsidies from American companies could be a substantial roadblock to these companies ambitions, though it is not likely to affect progress on the dam itself.
The bank's president and chairman, Martin A. Kamarck, noted that companies were free to participate without its support, and that several American companies had already sold $60 million to $100 million of equipment and services for the project. 
To date, he said, Canada was the only other nation whose export-credit agency had offered financing.
Among the American companies that are interested in the project are Caterpillar, which makes earth-moving equipment; Rotec Industries of Elmhurst, Ill., which makes concrete-handling equipment, and Voight Hydro of York, Pa., which makes turbines.
The three companies had been seeking initial approval to apply for financing of equipment sales worth an estimated $500 million, with the potential for greater sales in the future.
The bank's environmental requirements were established by Congress in 1992 in response to complaints by environmental advocacy groups that the bank was supporting destructive projects.
Mr. Kamarck said that to qualify for loans, the Chinese would have to provide plans for waste-water treatment plants upstream of the dam to reduce the pollution discharged into the reservoir. 
They would also have to supply plans for cleaning up toxic waste sites that would be flooded and for dredging contaminated sediments.
Beyond that, the bank wants a better plan for protecting endangered species, more information about how to minimize destruction downstream in the river's other lakes and estuaries, and explanations of how resettlement would be controlled to protect forests and other natural resources.
He said the bank had found no financial or technical weaknesses in the dam project, other than the environmental concerns.
Last year, President Clinton's National Security Council, citing environmental and human rights concerns, recommended against providing Ex-Im Bank financing for the project. 
Its recommendation followed a study by several Government agencies.
While the Ex-Im Bank, as an independent Government agency whose board is appointed by the President, can disregard such a recommendation, it was widely considered unlikely to do so.
Marsha Hausser, a spokeswoman for Caterpillar, criticized the decision but said that the company would continue to try to persuade the Chinese authorities to purchase American products for the project. 
Previously, company officials had described the bank's role as crucial in allowing Caterpillar to sell equipment.
"America's export competitiveness has suffered as a result of today's decision," Ms. Hausser argued.
The bank recently resumed consideration of several requests for financing of Chinese projects after delaying decisions since February because of a dispute between the United States and China over the Chinese sale of nuclear technology to Pakistan.
The Ex-Im Bank helps encourage the sale of American goods and services around the world by guaranteeing and otherwise subsidizing commercial loans, which makes American companies more able to compete with foreign concerns.
China says the benefits of the dam include protecting millions of people from seasonal flooding and producing more than one-tenth of the current annual energy output. 
China is highly dependent on coal for generating electricity, which emits extensive pollution.
United States environmental groups strongly oppose the project, and welcomed its rejection today.
So did human rights groups, who have objected to both the forcible resettlement of the local population near the dam and the repression of dissidents in China who oppose the project.

text:

Two months before the 10th anniversary of the crackdown on student protesters in Tiananmen Square, a former top Chinese official has sent an impassioned letter to China's leaders urging them to end a decade-long "cover-up" and to renounce the order that sent soldiers to disperse the demonstrators, killing hundreds.
"I have only one thing to say and that is to urge you to reverse the assessment of the 1989 student demonstrations without delay," wrote Bao Tong, a former leading Central Committee member jailed from 1989 to 1996 for sympathizing with the protesters. 
"The events of June 4, 1989, are shameful to humanity."
China's leaders have repeatedly defended their decision to forcefully move out the protesters, who they said were involved in a "counterrevolutionary rebellion."
Mr. Bao's letter, dated today, is an opening public salvo in what is likely to be a tense prelude to the anniversary. 
Despite constant surveillance and warnings not to speak out, Mr. Bao has remained the most prominent Chinese critic of the Government's actions in 1989, expressing the misgivings that many citizens feel but dare not utter. 
The Tiananmen crackdown remains the most forbidden topic in China.
Ever the politician, he argues in the letter that the decision to fire on students must be re-evaluated because it was morally wrong and because it undercuts public support for China's ruling Communist Party.
"Letting the wrongful assessment of the events to remain without reversal means the continuation of severe pain for the Chinese people," Mr. Bao wrote.
Chinese leaders have taken pains to insure that June 4 will pass uneventfully, hoping to focus attention instead on the country's lavish 50th anniversary celebration, planned for Oct. 
1.
Authorities have recently become more aggressive in closing down political discussion groups and publications that were tolerated just a year ago. 
And several former student protesters say they have been visited by local public security officers and warned "not to make trouble."
But perhaps the biggest deterrent is that Tiananmen Square -- the only open space in this packed city of 14 million -- is currently boarded up with high walls, closed for renovation in preparation for the Oct. 
1 celebrations. 
The project was originally scheduled for completion this spring but local officials recently announced that the reopening had been postponed until July.
Most ordinary Chinese still regard June 4 as far "too sensitive" to discuss in public. 
But privately, many remain deeply chagrined about the decision to use force.
"Millions of people in Beijing and hundreds of thousands of bystanders from other parts of the country watched the events unfold," Mr. Bao wrote, adding: "The history of bloodshed remains in people's hearts; they will not forget."
In a telephone interview, Mr. Bao said he wrote the letter out of the conviction that "when each of us begin to speak out and make our own views known, it will become increasingly necessary for the leaders to reconsider the decision."
Although Mr. Bao has been warned about his "unapproved" contact with foreign reporters and the police screen visitors to his home, he is cryptically optimistic about his current situation: "My life seems free, it should be free and I hope it stays free," he said.
The letter is addressed to President Jiang Zemin, Prime Minister Zhu Rongji and the members of the Politburo Standing Committee. 
In the late 1980's, Mr. Bao was chief of staff for Zhao Ziyang, then the Communist Party chief.
But in May 1989, both Mr. Zhao and Mr. Bao opposed the used of force to disperse the demonstrators. 
Both lost their jobs in the days before the June 4th crackdown.
Mr. Zhao has been under house arrest ever since. 
On May 28, 1989, a Government driver picked Mr. Bao up at his home in Beijing for a supposed meeting -- and drove him to prison. 
He spent the next seven years in solitary confinement, followed by a year of house arrest.
He was freed just before President Clinton's visit last summer and immediately started speaking out on issues like free speech and the rule of law. 
Expressing a common view on the streets in Beijing, Mr. Bao says the student leaders were naive and certainly "made mistakes," but adds that their protests were "orderly" and nonviolent. 
"Whatever they did or said should be dealt with according to democratic principles and the law," he said.
Mr. Bao, a political insider in the spring of 1989, places responsibility for the crackdown on Deng Xiaoping, China's former leader, who died in 1997. 
He takes issue with the conventional wisdom that China's current leadership could never criticize the crackdown because many were already in power at that time.
"When the tragedy happened most of you were not in the highest level decision-making positions in handling the event (except for one who bore a lesser responsibility) and had no involvement in the case," he wrote. 
"It is unnecessary for you to bear such a burden now."
The "one who bore a lesser responsibility" is a reference to Li Peng, the current head of the National People's Congress, who was China's Prime Minister in 1989.
Mr. Bao's letter also contains a Cassandra-like warning: That if the Party does not reverse the verdict, 1.2 billion Chinese will rise up and do it themselves.
"If you were to initiate the reversal of the judgment of the 1989 students demonstrations, the benefits to China would be great and the cost would be minimal," he wrote. 
"Such a course of action would be beneficial to the people and to all of you, and especially in strengthening the reputation of the Party. 
Therefore, I believe it best for me to urge you, rather than others, to take such action."

file: Ex-Prisoner of China Seeks Insights at Old Gulag Site.txt
text:
ï»¿
On the outskirts of town, a former Stalinist prison stands behind a row of concrete slabs. 
Undaunted by warnings from local residents who wish to remember Stalin's horrors but are acutely aware that this is still state property, the Chinese-American guest scrambled up the wall.
The guest, Harry Wu, a former Chinese dissident, spent 19 years in Maoist prisons that were modeled on the Soviet gulag system and set up with the help of Russians. 
Now that he was visiting the Russian city that was once the center of a sprawling archipelago of sub-Arctic prison camps, he wanted a better look.
"You can't go in there," cried Miron Etlis, a former prisoner who was guiding Mr. Wu on a trip to a nearby monument to Stalin's victims. 
"That's military property."
Mr. Wu, 61, jumped off the wall into the yard.
Mr. Wu is a research fellow at the Hoover Institute at Stanford University and is active on behalf of Chinese political prisoners. 
He visited Magadan, a city of 134,000, as it was commemorating the 60th anniversary of its incorporation at the height of Stalin's purges and seven years after the Kolyma labor camps opened here.
The anniversary came complete with oompah bands in the square and cheerful drunks lurching down Lenin Prospekt in the midnight sun, apparently heedless of the tens of thousands of former prisoners buried in the tundra around here -- some of the two million or so who mined gold, silver, tin and uranium in the Magadan and nearby Chukotka regions from 1932 to 1957.
Mr. Hu flew in at his own expense to speak to a crowd of just 15 at a historical conference held as part of the 60th anniversary events. 
He has repeatedly returned to China to document prison labor and the harvesting of organs from executed inmates, and said he wanted to urge Russians both to treasure their nascent democracy and the memory of Soviet repression. 
"You have to remove all the Lenin and Stalin statues and put up gulag monuments," Mr. Wu said at one point, jabbing his finger at his hosts. 
"That's the only way to keep it from coming back."
Magadan residents, like Russians in general, are ambivalent about how best to commemorate the legacy of state terror. 
On a hill outside town, a monument to gulag victims looms like a giant head from Easter Island.
Yet a street and a school are named for Eduard Berzin, the director of Dalstroi, the state company that built the camps and ran the mining enterprises, and his muscular bust stands on a pedestal in front of city hall. 
Because he was purged in 1937, officials have recast him as a gulag victim.
Lyudmila Vronchina, a city librarian who helps former inmates garner the documents necessary to apply for federal aid for ex-prisoners, said the Berzin monument "sends chills down my spine."
"He is a murderer," she said.
Aleksandr Biryukov, a Magadan lawyer whose father was a camp prisoner, has compiled a list of every one of the 11,000 people documented to have been shot in Kolyma camps by the state security organ, the N.K.V.D. 
Tens of thousands of others died from disease, cold and overwork. 
Mr. Biryukov has also begun researching the location of graves and said some bodies are still partly preserved in the permafrost.
Mr. Wu had another idea: using the old prison as a gulag museum. 
The property is currently owned by the Russian military but partly occupied by a scrap metal dealership.
After jumping from the wall, Mr. Wu charged into the old prison, yanking open doors and testing locks, trying to calculate how many prisoners occupied each cell.
The cells, whose walls have been knocked down, measured about 10 feet by 11 feet and were unlighted and unheated. 
Prisoners sometimes froze to death overnight. 
Surviving prisoners would stack the dead in the corner and eat their bread rations until the guards noticed.
"So each cell was designed for 20 people," said Mr. Wu, pacing about. 
Mr. Etlis, 71, who had found his way in through a gate, arrived to hear this. 
"Ha!
I was in a cell like this in Kazakhstan and there were 50 people," he said. 
Mr. Wu eventually concluded that up to 3,500 prisoners had been crammed into the building.
After Mr. Wu had filmed every corner, the group filed out. 
But he hung back, apparently pondering the prison's history, then beckoned to a reporter and pointed out a 1930's-era padlock bolted to a jail door.
"Get it off," Mr. Wu said. 
"I want it."
After efforts to pick it with a pen failed, he said: "Just break it. 
Break it with your hands."
The lock held. 
Disappointed, Mr. Wu walked out. 
Just such a lock had hung on his own Chinese prison door. 
"This," he said, "was the lock produced by Lenin."

After heavy lobbying by the computer industry and the Clinton Administration, the Senate today rejected a proposal to tighten control of the sale of American supercomputers to China and Russia and instead voted for further study of the issue.
The question of whether to tighten supercomputer export controls will now be resolved in a conference with the House of Representatives, which last month overwhelmingly passed a measure requiring a license for sales of some computers to countries such as China and Russia. 
The different Senate and House measures are attached to the Defense Authorization Act.
In 1995, the Clinton Administration greatly relaxed export controls for supercomputers, transferring to the companies the responsibility for screening buyers to insure that they were not diverting technology to military uses.
The normally arcane subject of export controls became a lively debate earlier this year when it was disclosed that Chinese and Russian nuclear weapon facilities had acquired American supercomputers without Federal licenses.
This led to criminal investigations, diplomatic protests, legislative action and industry reaction. 
I.B.M., for example, mobilized a lobbying effort that ranged from low-level employees around the country to its chairman and chief executive officer, Louis V. Gerstner Jr., who called Senators such as Republican leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, according to a company spokesman.
The Senate originally considered an amendment similar to the one that passed the House, shifting responsibility back to the Federal Government by requiring licenses for sales of certain computers to dozens of countries, including Russia and China.
But in a vote of 72 to 17 today, opponents backed a substitute amendment that retains the current system but calls for a study of the national security implications of the issue by the General Accounting Office, an arm of Congress.
Senator Rod Grams, Republican of Minnesota, argued "it is not possible to effectively control" exports of mid-level computers and doing so would be "handing the mid-level computer business to Japan and other allies."
Secretary of Defense William S. Cohen wrote a letter supporting the Grams proposal. 
And Administration officials in Madrid for the NATO summit meeting kept tabs this week on the debate, making phone calls to Congress, officials said.
But Clinton Administration arguments also helped buttress the position of those Senators who wanted to reinstitute tighter controls.
For example, one backer of tighter controls, Senator Richard J. Durbin, Democrat of Illinois, said the possibility of lost business was overstated, since the Pentagon and the Department of Commerce had told the Senators that "the only country likely to step in was Japan" if licensing requirements were reimposed and "they have more restrictive controls than the United States."

text:

The White House tried last month to obtain sensitive counterintelligence information from the Federal Bureau of Investigation about Beijing's plans to influence American politics, but Director Louis J. Freeh of the F.B.I. rebuffed the inquiry, Administration officials said today.
The F.B.I. material was sought by Charles F. C. Ruff, the new White House counsel, for a briefing of Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright. In a Feb. 
18 letter to Jamie S. Gorelick, the Deputy Attorney General, people who have seen the letter said, Mr. Ruff posed a series of questions about what Federal investigators knew or suspected about the involvement of Chinese officials and citizens in a purported plan to make illegal contributions to American political campaigns.
Mr. Ruff said he was seeking the information on behalf of the National Security Council. 
At the time, Ms. Albright was preparing for a trip to China, scheduled for late February.
Mr. Ruff, who said today that there was nothing improper about his request, stressed in the letter that the White House wanted "information only concerning the activities of officials and nationals of the People's Republic of China" and not American citizens.
A reply was prepared, with the approval of top Justice Department officials, but Mr. Freeh, who was traveling in the Middle East at the time, intervened and ordered the document withheld, Federal law enforcement officials said.
The officials said Mr. Freeh had decided to stick to his earlier decision that no information relating to possible influence buying by China would be provided to anyone in Congress or the executive branch. 
Mr. Freeh, officials said, was worried that whatever information was passed on would leak and that the F.B.I. would be criticized for sharing information with the President's aides, officials said.
The F.B.I. director's refusal of the White House's request was a vivid example of the tensions among the White House, the Justice Department and the F.B.I. that have escalated in the unfolding investigation of the financing of the 1996 Presidential campaign.
The dispute over Mr. Ruff's request may also help explain why Mr. Freeh has seemed so personally at odds with the White House, to the point where the F.B.I. argued publicly with the President this month over accounts of briefings that the F.B.I. had provided to the National Security Council at the start of the China investigation.
In addition, the exchange showed the extent to which the investigation has tied the relationships among Federal agencies in knots. 
Indeed, some Government lawyers suggested today that it was Mr. Freeh who had erred by withholding the information from the White House and thus leaving the Secretary of State without critical information at a time when she was embarking on a diplomatic mission to Beijing.
These officials said Mr. Freeh, who had been accused in Congress of maintaining a cozy relationship with the White House, had simply decided not to risk further criticism.
In the summer of 1993, Presidential aides were embarrassed when they summoned the F.B.I. to investigate the White House travel office. 
Weeks later, there was more trouble when some investigators said they were blocked by White House officials during their inquiry into the death of Vincent W. Foster Jr., the former deputy White House counsel who had committed suicide that year. 
Last year, Republicans in Congress blasted the White House for obtaining F.B.I. background files on hundreds of Presidential aides.
In his letter, Mr. Ruff said, "We seek information only concerning the activities of officials and nationals of the People's Republic of China and wish only to obtain sufficient information to enable the National Security Council to formulate an appropriate policy with respect to allegations regarding those activities."
Mr. Ruff's letter said that he did not want information that might interfere with any criminal investigation and that any information he obtained should also be turned over to the House and Senate intelligence committees.
Even so, some senior F.B.I. officials were surprised by the request, which was marked "top secret," particularly because Mr. Freeh had earlier decided not to share investigative material with the White House or Congress.
Moreover, Mr. Ruff, who is Mr. Clinton's fifth counsel, has a reputation in legal circles as a tough litigator. 
In his current post, Mr. Ruff is responsible for supervising the defense of the President in the inquiries into campaign fund-raising and some F.B.I. officials feared his request could be interpreted as an attempt to learn how much information the the F.B.I. had collected.
But Mr. Ruff and Justice Department officials called the request a legally and ethically appropriate effort by the White House, acting on behalf of the National Security Council, to obtain information that could be helpful in Ms. Albright's meetings with Chinese representatives.
Moreover, Mr. Ruff said in an interview today, under interagency rules, requests for F.B.I. information that could interfere with a criminal investigation must be made by the counsel's office.
"This was a matter being dealt with by the National Security Council in its capacity as adviser to the President," he said.
Law-enforcement officials said that Mr. Ruff's letter arrived when Mr. Freeh had left Washington on a trip to the Middle East. 
In his absence, Attorney General Janet Reno and her deputy, Ms. Gorelick asked the Justice Department's criminal division and Mr. Freeh's top deputies to decide whether any information could be turned over to the White House.
The Justice officials, along with top officials at the F.B.I. like Robert Bryant, then head of the F.B.I. national security division, and William J. Esposito, the newly appointed F.B.I. 
Deputy Director, agreed that Mr. Ruff's narrowly phrased questions could be answered without jeopardizing the investigation.
After preparing several versions of a response, several officials described the result as a "plain vanilla" report that contained little information beyond accounts already described in news articles on the suspected influence scheme by the Chinese. 
The broad outlines of the effort had been gleaned from conversations intercepted by the National Security Agency, the secretive Federal intelligence unit that eavesdrops on global communications.
But before the Justice Department turned the report over to the White House, Mr. Bryant telephoned Mr. Freeh, who objected to releasing any information. 
The reply was held until Mr. Freeh discussed the matter with Ms. Reno. They agreed to send the White House copies of documents like the briefing materials that the F.B.I. had given to two national security council aides in June 1996 when the issue first arose at the White House.

file: FABLED ROAD TO THE FAR EAST.txt
text:
ï»¿
FOR SOME 1,500 YEARS, UNTIL ITS decline in the 15th century, the ancient trade route known as the Silk Road was a principal artery for goods and ideas passing from China to Europe. 
Finery, spices and porcelain were exchanged for such Western delicacies as walnuts and figs and, more importantly, gold.
Last year, my wife, Shareen, and I were privileged pilgrims on this route, following the presumed path of Marco Polo. 
Our journey only became possible after the Karakoram Highway was opened to tourism in 1986. 
Built jointly by China and Pakistan over two decades, this spectacular paved road winds from near Islamabad, the Pakistani capital, to Kashgar, an oasis city in Chinese Central Asia. 
We traveled by minivan for the first third of our trip; then, in China, we switched to bus, train and plane, passing from snow peaks to deserts on an itinerary that ended in Xian, once the caravan terminus of the Silk Road.
Although the rewards of the journey were generous, so were the discomforts. 
Lasting some three weeks and covering more than 2,500 miles, it is a trip more safely managed by a group. 
Shareen and I therefore chose to sign up on a Silk Road tour organized by the British Museum.
We joined the tour in London in late August. 
At an orientation lecture by our scholarly guide, Dr. Wang Tao, of London University's School of Oriental and African Studies, we studied our fellow travelers with guarded curiosity, having already improved the odds for congeniality by persuading three American friends to join the group of 20. 
Only after landing in Islamabad, however, were we able to take full measure of the rest of our troupe: an adventurous Tuscan matron, two Argentine women and Britons of varying vintage but with a common stiff-upper-lip demeanor. 
We guessed, during a first day spent visiting museums and mosques, that our companions had that essential steadying quality the English call bottom, and so it proved. 
We also guessed, accurately, that our tour manager, Lucy Turner, a young and energetic Briton, would be equal to the unavoidable screw-ups on a perhaps too ambitious itinerary.
On the fine clear morning of Aug. 
28, we clambered into two Toyota deluxe vans, each seating 14 passengers, along with our gear: everything from field glasses and canteens to an exotic miscellany of just-in-case pills. 
We left Islamabad for the Grand Trunk Road, begun centuries ago by a Mogul emperor, which once extended from Peshawar to Calcutta. 
Memorably described in the pages of Kipling, it churns today with an even thicker tide of humanity. 
We threaded among teetering polychrome trucks and three-wheeled pickups, the local buses, passengers protruding from their gaping rear doors. 
We slowed intermittently for herds of cattle and sheep, ambling with seasoned nonchalance.
Those of us in the lead van were accompanied by the first of a half-dozen locally assigned guides. 
He was a Pakistani of polyglot skills, who, like his successors in China, stuck mostly to a standard script, dealt vaguely with awkward questions and imparted a strong whiff of the currently correct political views.
Our first stop, an hour or so from Islamabad, was at the ruins of Taxila, in remote times a notable caravansary and monastic center. 
Its history provided a preview of multicultural themes that became familiar in the days ahead. 
Alexander the Great stayed here, so did the peace-loving and law-giving Buddhist emperor Asoka. 
Greeks settled here and so did Kushans, Scythians and Parthians. 
This cultural mix over the centuries yielded up fine Gandharan sculptures, combining Hellenic and Indian styles. 
Taxila was a civilized and civilizing crossroads in Central Asia for more than a thousand years, but it perished in flames and carnage, sacked by the horse-borne White Huns in the sixth century A.D. or thereabouts.
From 1912 to 1934, British archeologists exhumed the sprawling site, uncovering the stone and brick foundations of the Greek-built lower city of Sirkap. 
Nearby, they bared Buddhist temples, stupas and monastic cells, and later restored the most interesting. 
A rich selection of Gandharan Buddhas, with their Westernized features, and troves of coins, rings and bejeweled necklaces were also unearthed; these are well displayed in an on-site museum, complete with a guard who exacted a tip for showing us mildly erotic figures in an enclosed alcove.
In the lower city, we gathered for an introductory lecture by Dr. Wang Tao, soon to be called Tao by all of us. 
Chinese-born, soft-spoken and in his 30's, Tao interpreted Buddhist iconography and described the antique human handiworks that we would find scattered at intervals all along our route: huge rocks coated with pictographs and ancient scripts, giant statues of Buddha in improbable and inaccessible perches, caves with fading murals, old crumbling forts and roadside tombs.
WE THEN BEGAN a four-day journey along the Karakoram Highway that would take us about 600 miles through Pakistan and across the Khunjerab Pass into China. 
Engineers cut few tunnels for the mostly two-lane road, which hugs the mountainsides, challenging drivers with sudden pitches, axle-deep streams, hairpin turns and rockslides. 
More unnerving is the absence of shoulders as the road drops steeply into valleys with churning rivers. 
I confess to fixedly studying distant glaciers, the crystal skies, or the corduroy texture of slopes covered in evergreens, especially when we passed trucks or buses that had careened off the highway -- three during the trip. 
(I should add that our own drivers were exemplary and, with a single exception in China, invincibly good-natured as they kept to a tight schedule.)
Though we traveled each day from 6 to 10 hours, boredom was minimal, dispelled by a succession of natural and human spectacles.
Our first overnight stop was a riverside village called Besham, where we stayed in a simple, clean, dimly lighted motel. 
At the front desk, I happened to pick up a flier for visitors that explained why women were invisible in the valley. 
Devout Muslims in this region believe a woman should be seen outside her home only on her marriage, or in the event of hospitalization during childbirth, and in death. 
Every adult we saw that day, from shepherd to shopkeeper, was indeed male.
As our route ran parallel to the Indus River, we were becoming acclimated to the otherworldly landscape. 
After a few hours' drive, a roadside sign announced, "YOU ARE IN A UNIQUE PLACE IN THE WORLD."
Here three immense mountain chains visibly collided, leaning tilted sheets of shale drunkenly against each other. 
Ahead, in the east, lay the Karakoram Mountains, mostly velvety black, with K2 just beyond our vision. 
In the west loomed the Hindu Kush, brownish and severe. 
Southward were the bare and tawny Himalayas, crowned by the jagged whiteness of Nanga Parbat, among the 10 highest peaks in the world, and said to be still growing.
More than 150 miles from Islamabad and halfway to Gilgit, we became seasoned watchers of the dark and foaming Indus, and of the ingenious footbridges, cable cars and rope walkways that crossed it. 
At dusk, we arrived for a two-night stay at the Serena Lodge in Gilgit town, the administrative center of the region now known as the Northern Areas. 
Wedged between the frontiers of India, China and Afghanistan, this sliver of Pakistan was once, in the words of the British historian John Keay, "the hub, the crow's nest, the fulcrum of Asia."
Here, in the 1870's, the British established the Gilgit Agency, chiefly to keep an eye on ever-advancing czarist Russia, with the aid of such local warrior peoples as the Dards. 
After India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, Gilgit's Muslims rebelled against rule by Hindus, and Pakistan seized control of the Gilgit Valley. 
So sensitive is its location, so prevalent is smuggling, that the area surrounding Gilgit town remains restricted, dotted by military checkpoints.
Still a frontier trading and listening post, Gilgit town has many dust-colored brick buildings that enclose a thriving street bazaar and scattered remnants of the British raj (a cantonment, the agent's bungalow and a graveyard). 
The Serena Lodge was as good as its name. 
Its rooms were pleasant, and there was an excellent buffet and a spacious lobby, in khaki colors, adorned by polo gear (the game is still played by rough local rules on nearby grounds). 
These amenities were enhanced by well-kept gardens set against the white-capped mountains.
We kept a laptop diary and that night Shareen wrote: "Regretfully left the lodge after a delicious breakfast of yogurt and apricot compote. 
We followed the Gilgit River into the Hunza Valley: a striking assemblage of young jagged mountains with sometimes sinister overhangs. 
Our first stop was a cemetery memorializing the workmen killed in building the highway (one for each of 1,500 kilometers, according to our Pakistani guide). 
Their epitaphs were written in English, Urdu and Arabic, with a quote from the Koran and Rupert Brooke: 'There shall be in that rich earth a richer dust concealed.'
"
The last leg to the Chinese frontier took us through the Hunza Valley, said to be the charmed fictional locale of Shangri-La. 
Presiding over riverside villages and terraced orchards was Rakaposhi, with its mantle of glaciers, the most dramatic of the Karakoram peaks. 
In a garden cafe set amid blooming cosmos, whose menu promised tea "served with sympathy," we were overtaken by a kind of infectious giddiness. 
At a photo stop, we scooped garnets from a roadside cut; later we stopped for lunch at Karimabad, seat of successive Mirs of Hunza, and took a bone-crunching Jeep ride to several Tibetan-style forts.
We spent the night at Gulmit, a town near the Chinese frontier, and, in the morning, of what stretched into a long day, we drove from a Pakistani security outpost through the Khunjerab Pass, a broad plateau fringed by waterfalls, glaciers and meadows. 
Midway, multilingual tablets and heroic statuary marked the precise frontier and recorded the pass's opening to all traffic in 1982. 
After a box lunch, we switched from twin vans to a special shuttle bus, passing three Chinese checkpoints, the only notable episode being the general mystification when a People's Liberation Army private clambered aboard and shouted what sounded like "Cohens."
Shareen guessed correctly that he wanted nothing more sinister than coins.
At the checkpoint at Sust, we encountered the Chinese bureaucracy in its immemorial obduracy. 
Our papers, it appeared, were not entirely in order; we just might be delayed for hours. 
But a glowering official finally struck upon the perfect remedy: a special $60 group fine.
At Sust, we met our local Chinese guide, a young woman in her 20's, who disarmingly apologized for the delays as we boarded a brand-new red-and-green Toyota bus big enough for the entire group. 
All this was a foretaste of the frustrations and rewards in China, where personal goodwill compensated for official inflexibility.
We were now high in the Pamirs, cruising at a crisp 16,000 feet among rounded mountains tinted in orange and yellow-brown, reminiscent of the landscapes of the mystic Russian artist Nicholas Roerich. 
Tashkurghan, a grim frontier fortress town since imperial times, was less than welcoming. 
We stayed overnight at the Pamir Hotel, built in 1965 and the one truly unspeakable accommodation on the tour. 
Even the most stoic of our British companions blanched at the odious slop served at dinner, the cold and dark rooms (each with a foot-deep puddle in the bathroom) and a staff that was surly or invisible. 
Next door was a mysterious hot spot, the Princess Fort Kala OK Club (presumably meaning karaoke club).
A long day's drive took us through the Subash plateau, at more than 12,000 feet one of the highest in the Pamirs. 
Morale improved as we encountered one diversion after another: whistling ginger-colored marmots, munching herds of camels, solemn yaks and surreal dzus (half yak, half cow, with feather-duster tails) tended by Kirghiz herdsmen. 
The Kirghiz, a Turkic-speaking nomadic people, still greet foreigners with friendly curiosity, and, at two stops, we were courteously permitted to enter their richly carpeted, tentlike yurts. 
Lunch was at a cafe on Kara-Kul Lake, as cerulean as the sky.
Because all China is in the same time zone as Beijing, it was bright as noon when we arrived in Kashgar at 6:30 P.M. Auspiciously, our bus was greeted at the hotel by a troupe of whirling dancers, teenage boys and girls in flowing day-glo costumes performing a folkloric repertory with more zest than precision. 
This was our introduction to the Uighurs, an Islamic people who form the majority among Kashgar's 200,000 inhabitants and in the Xinjiang-Uighur Autonomous Region, an area roughly as big as Alaska, with a population of 15 million.
Once a Buddhist kingdom and flourishing Silk Road entrepot, Kashgar was the springboard of militant Islam, conquered but not really subdued by China in the 18th century. 
It was thereafter a contested cockpit in the Great Game, the clandestine duel between Russia and Britain for mastery of Central Asia. 
Appropriately, our hotel, the Chini Bagh, took its name from the former British Consulate, the decaying Victorian-Gothic building set just behind it. 
Here, before and after the Bolshevik Revolution, British operatives fenced with their counterparts at the nearby Russian Consulate, now the Seman Hotel. 
More colorful if less modern than the Chini Bagh, the Seman adjoins a compound that once sheltered White Russian emigres and still encloses a handsome garden lined with poplars.
In Kashgar's main square, a huge statue of Chairman Mao sits incongruously among open-air pool tables and medieval houses, not far from the Aidkah Mosque. 
Dating to 1442 and still the largest in China, the mosque is more imposing than handsome, a magnet for thousands of believers who flock to Friday services. 
On Sunday, there is a rival magnet: the fabled market, sprawling over more than a square mile and offering everything from spices and dowry chests to livestock and marvelous varieties of headgear. 
Between shouts of "Passu!
Passu!"
(Get out of the way!) and a cacophony of moos, baas, whinnies and the chirps of caged birds, one is irresistibly drawn into a labyrinth redolent of freshly baked cakes, saffron and dung.
If our two days in vibrant Kashgar were a high point, the next two in Khotan were a low. 
It took a 10-hour drive past irrigation canals lined with graceful poplars, willows and purple tamarisk to reach this city on the Silk Road's southern branch. 
Surrounded by the Taklamakan Desert (meaning, roughly, if you go in, you won't come out), Khotan has an imposing Buddhist legacy, evidenced by the vast ruined city of Yotkan, just six miles to the west, believed to have been an imperial capital, now a gloomy assembly of brick stumps and wind-carved dunes. 
But modern Khotan is undistinguished -- a center for cultivating silkworms and producing jade knickknacks -- and our hotel harbored spiders whose bites seemed to have doubled the size of one of our number's left leg. 
Even the normally chipper Tao gave his daily lecture a downbeat title: "Why the hell are we in Khotan?"
Morale soared as we were bused to the airport to fly north across the Tarim Basin to the industrial city of Urumqi. 
Here, in the middle of nowhere and seemingly overnight, an industrial metropolis with a million-plus population has sprung up, its growth fertilized by state and foreign investment in nearby oil and mineral riches. 
To us, as we headed downtown, it seemed as if a large slab of Chicago had somehow floated to Central Asia and planted itself near the Tien Shan or Celestial Mountains. 
We were to spend two nights in Urumqi's most modern hotel, a Holiday Inn.
Not a sneer was visible as our group savored the hotel's antiseptic joys. 
We responded warmly to the city's lively restaurants, department stores and a better-than-expected antiquities museum. 
Though Urumqi has gotten a bad press from many travelers, perhaps the right way to go to the city is by way of Khotan.
After a day, we traveled on a good highway, to Turfan, a major oasis city flanked by the Flaming Mountains on the Silk Road's northern route. 
Famous for its grapes and the longevity of its people, Turfan was once a flourishing cultural and political center. 
Ruins of local rulers are strewn in caves and tombs in the desert. 
Ten miles west of Turfan is Yarkhoto, the ruins of a fortress dating to the first century A.D.; it was captured by successive warrior peoples and then abandoned in the 14th century. 
Extensively excavated and restored (with help from Unesco), the site has a melancholy eloquence. 
So also does Gaochang, another long-forsaken desert metropolis; the ancient tombs of Astana, and the Thousand-Buddha Caves at Bezeklik, a limestone warren above the roaring waters of the Murtuk River Gorge. 
Yet I confess that I was more fascinated by the elaborate system of irrigation that still brings mountain waters to the Turfan oasis by means of pipes whose depth and complexity imply millions of hours of forced labor.
Turfan was a prelude to our encounter with the great Mogao Caves at Dunhuang (meaning Blazing Beacon), an oasis town of 14,000, some 250 miles from Turfan. 
Getting there involved a new experience: going to the Turfan train depot with boxed meals, waiting in the "soft" lounge reserved for privileged passengers, being saluted like royalty as we boarded an overnight sleeper and gazing through train windows at the endless undulating ribbon that was the Gobi Desert. 
But there was a hitch: no bus was at hand on our arrival in Dunhuang. 
Two days later, we were bumped from our flight to Xian because only 15 seats were available.
There was compensation. 
Our tour leader, Lucy, negotiated a third day in Dunhuang with special benefits. 
Benefit One was a meal at the Manhattan Cafe, which we had spotted by chance from a bus window. 
Recently opened by two New Yorkers, Beth Schifter and her husband, Tom Lee, it offers omelets, French fries and lamb burgers, as well as excellent coffee.
Benefit Two was a second visit to the Mogao Caves, which are on the cliff face of the Mingsha Hills, just outside Dunhuang. 
These man-made galleries, created from the 4th to the 14th centuries, contain the world's richest trove of Buddhist wall paintings, sculptures and manuscripts. 
In the 492 grottoes are 45,000 murals, 2,000 pigmented stucco figures and, carved within one cave, a giant Buddha, 113 feet high, with toenails as big as snow shovels. 
Initially, we were pointedly taken to the cave that once held 50,000 Buddhist manuscripts, some of the best of which were taken to the British Museum, in disputed circumstances, by the scholar-explorer Sir Aurel Stein, nearly a century ago.
We then discovered that many of the best Mogao caves were either closed or required a hefty additional admission charge. 
Nor did our local official guide inform us of a superb museum adjoining the site, jointly built by the Chinese and Japanese and opened in 1995, containing admirable replicas of the major caves and a fine collection of Tibetan bronze bells and sculptures. 
The extra day enabled us to see the museum, the bronzes and a dozen special caves, gratis.
That evening, we returned to Dunhuang Airport for our flight some 800 miles eastward. 
Xian, China's former imperial capital, was the starting point of the great Silk Road caravans, and its medieval walls and streets somehow escaped destruction during two wars with Japan and three revolutions: Nationalist, Communist and Cultural. 
The city's pagoda-shaped Great Mosque, nesting in a maze of tiny shops, was damaged by the Red Guards, but its elegant pavilions and gardens were restored in 1987.
Fortunately, the real riches of Xian were mostly underground and therefore safe from political turbulence. 
In 1974, a peasant digging a well a few miles from Xian unearthed the first life-size figure in a terra-cotta army that has now grown to 6,000 strong. 
The figures, each different, were meant to protect China's first emperor and founder of the Qin (pronounced Chin, whence China) dynasty, after his death in 210 B.C. So vast and various is this army that two huge structures, big as airplane hangars, have been built to permit visitors to look down from ramps to see the ghostly soldiers on the soil from which they emerged.
One could not help but be awed by Xian, as indeed Marco Polo was in his putative 13th-century journey to China. 
I say putative because in one of his talks, Dr. Wang Tao offhandedly remarked that, of course, Marco Polo's narrative was probably fiction and, in any case, the Venetian was probably not the real author. 
Fiction?
Pressed to amplify after an audible gasp, Tao recounted current scholarly research holding that a consortium of ghostwriters assembled long-familiar Silk Road tales and affixed Polo's name to enhance authenticity. 
A learned Briton in our group added that Marco Polo somehow never mentions the Great Wall of China or the widespread custom of drinking tea.
For myself, I prefer to believe that Marco Polo did, as tradition holds, dictate his memoirs while a prisoner in Genoa, and that he had so much to recount that he simply forgot about tea and the Wall. 
I find this plausible, for I am all too aware of what I have left out of my account. 
For example, there is . . . but I digress.
Â 
THREE FOR THE ROAD
British Museum, 46 Bloomsbury Street, London WC1 3QQ (telephone: 171-323-8895 or 171-323-1234; fax: 171-580-8677), will offer its "Taxila to Turfan" tour again in August 1997. 
The price is expected to be about $4,500 a person, including air fare from London. 
Dr. Wang Tao is scheduled to lecture.
Smithsonian Associates, 1100 Jefferson Drive SW, Room 3045, Washington, D.C. 
20560 (202-357-4700), is offering a Silk Road tour, from Sept. 
7 to 30, that includes stops in Urumqi, Kashgar, Xian, Dunhuang and Lanzhou. 
The $7,290 price includes air fare from San Francisco.
American Museum of Natural History, Central Park West at 79th Street, New York, N.Y. 
10024 (800-462-8687 or 212-769-5700), is planning a tour of the Silk Road by private train in April 1997. 
Stops include Beijing, Xian, Lanzhou, Dunhuang, Turfan, Samarkand, Bukhara and Tashkent.
