file: FALLOUT IN ARMS RESEARCH_ A special report._Amid Race Profiling Claims, Asian-Americans Avoid Labs.txt
text:
ï»¿
Asian and Asian-American scientists are staying away from jobs at national weapons laboratories, particularly Los Alamos, saying that researchers of Asian descent are systematically harassed and denied advancement because of their race.
The issue has long simmered at the laboratories, but it came to a boil last year with the arrest of Dr. Wen Ho Lee, who is accused of mishandling nuclear secrets at Los Alamos. 
Though officials vehemently deny it, many Asian-Americans said Dr. Lee, a naturalized citizen born in Taiwan, was singled out because of his ethnicity.
In any event, Asians and Asian-Americans said, security procedures implemented after Dr. Lee's arrest fall hardest on them. 
Since the arrest, some scholarly groups have even called for a boycott of the laboratories, urging Asian and Asian-American scientists not to apply for jobs with them.
Whether because of the calls for a boycott, the underlying claims of discrimination, or both, all three national weapons laboratories -- Los Alamos, Lawrence Livermore and Sandia -- have seen declines in Asian and Asian-American applicants for postdoctoral positions, according to their own statistics. 
Other Asian and Asian-American scientists have left voluntarily.
Los Alamos, for example, has seen the number of Asian applicants (those granted formal reviews by committees) dwindle to 3 in the first half of 2000 from an average of 28 in 1998 and 1999. 
The number accepting jobs at Los Alamos fell from 18 in 1998 to 9 in 1999 to 3 in the first half of 2000.
The combined acceptances of Asians and Asian-Americans at Sandia and Livermore, which compile statistics by fiscal years ending in late September, are similar to Los Alamos, falling to 3 so far in 2000 from 21 in 1998. 
At Los Alamos, the number of Asians applying for jobs declined in percentage as well, to 4 percent of total applications from 12 percent in 1998. 
Over all, postdoctoral appointments of Asian and Asian-American fell to 7 percent from 14 percent when the three laboratories, with their slightly different record keeping, are combined.
"To me, this is an indicator that some of the best have decided either not to apply, or even when they do apply, not to come when they're offered a position," said Dr. John C. Browne, director of Los Alamos.
The decline is troubling for two reasons. 
First, Asians and Asian-Americans represent a huge pool of talent -- more than a quarter of all Ph.D.'s awarded in science and technology at American universities each year. 
Second, postdoctoral appointments, which are generally filled by researchers who have recently earned Ph.D.'s, are an essential source of candidates for permanent positions. 
The appointments constitute "the primary means of recruiting future scientists and engineers for Los Alamos," said Jim Danneskiold, a spokesman for the laboratory.
In May, the National Science Foundation, a major source of research money, reported that "heightened security concerns" at the laboratories were hindering efforts to recruit and retain Asian and Asian-American scientists.
And last week, speaking before a panel of the House Armed Services Committee on reorganizing the Energy Department, Representative Ellen O. Tauscher, Democrat of California, referred to suspicions of racial profiling at Livermore and Sandia.
Mrs. Tauscher said there was "the sense that Asian-Americans are targeted or scapegoated as potentially coming to work at the labs because they can spy," adding that the problem "has a deleterious effect on our ability to recruit and retain."
Observers say they are not surprised by the comments.
"There's no question in my mind that the Asian-Americans are conscientiously avoiding working in Los Alamos and the other labs like the plague," said Prof. L. Ling-chi Wang, chairman of the department of ethnic studies and director of the Asian American studies program at the University of California at Berkeley.
Two organizations, the Asian Pacific Americans in Higher Education and the Association for Asian American Studies, have called for a boycott, urging Asian-Americans not to work at the laboratories.
Professor Wang, who helped organize the boycott calls, is not alone in thinking that they have contributed to the flight from the laboratories.
Dr. Browne said that an "overall black cloud" caused by the boycott was driving Asian and Asian-American scientists away, but said that he did not believe racial profiling had occurred at Los Alamos.
Still, it is difficult to say whether anger over security measures is the sole reason for the sharp drop in Asian and Asian-American applicants, particularly with laboratory budget cuts and a booming economy creating lucrative jobs in private industry. 
But the impact is apparent.
"The labs are falling apart," said Dr. Jonathan Medalia, a specialist in national defense at the Congressional Research Service and the author of a study on the laboratories, which he presented at a conference but has not yet delivered to Congress.
The loss of talent is most severe in computer science, Dr. Medalia said, and if it continues, could threaten the nation's ability to ensure the safety and reliability of its nuclear weapons.
He said that tightened security measures increased the losses among all ethnic groups, but that the economy and other effects contributed.
Accusations of racism have also led to formal complaints.
In December, nine Asian-American scientists and engineers at Livermore filed a discrimination complaint with the State of California that the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing is investigating.
The federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has also begun an investigation, said officials at the laboratory and a lawyer for the scientists.
Secretary of Energy Bill Richardson, whose agency oversees the laboratories, conceded that political pressures from Congress had created "an atmosphere of fear" among foreign-born scientists.
A year ago, Mr. Richardson named a committee to investigate complaints of racial profiling, and he appointed Dr. Jeremy Wu, a former official in the Agriculture Department's office of civil rights, as the department's ombudsman to review diversity issues and hear employee complaints. 
But the problems are so ingrained, scientists said, that those measures are not enough.
"For years, a lot of these things have festered, and it was typical of the Asian way to say nothing," said Kalina Wong, an American-born scientist of Chinese and Hawaiian descent who tracks inventories of nuclear materials at Livermore, and one of the employees who filed the complaint. 
Now, Ms. Wong said, "Pandora's Box is open."
Laboratory officials deny any systematic discrimination. 
If anything, they said, administrators are eager to promote members of ethnic groups.
Â 
The Complaints
A History Of Discrimination
The new security directives do not explicitly mention Asian-Americans or any other group; moreover, Mr. Richardson accompanied the directives with a warning that they should not be seen as an excuse to question the "loyalty and patriotism" of Asian-Americans as a group.
But the directives required scientists to report "close and continuing contact" with nationals of sensitive countries -- a designation that covers Russia and most countries in Asia, but few countries in Europe.
"If you have relatives in sensitive countries, you are under the microscope," said Dr. Aaron Lai, a climate researcher at Los Alamos and a naturalized citizen born in Taiwan. 
"Before the Wen Ho Lee case, the chance of getting promoted was very low," Dr. Lai said. 
But with the new rules, he said, "it's getting worse."
Joel Wong, an engineer at Livermore, who is from Hong Kong and is now an American citizen, said, "They associate foreign-born with being a threat."
The 19-member committee appointed by Mr. Richardson, issued a report earlier this year, based on interviews with workers. 
Its recommendations included appointing an ombudsman, as Mr. Richardson has done, and compiling data on minority groups across the department. 
Existing data are sketchy at best. 
The report also described pervasive feelings of unease and fear.
In October, the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus heard from several scientists who said Asian-Americans faced discrimination at the laboratories.
Ms. Wong, the Livermore scientist, told the group of a lagging salary, racially insensitive comments from officials, her removal from sensitive projects and an unexplained erosion of authority.
"The whole Chinese spy allegation has set us back further," said Ms. Wong, whose family has been in the United States for five generations and who has worked at Livermore for more than two decades. 
"It seems now that there is license to do as was done to me because we Asians are potential spies."
Livermore officials said racial bias has not played a role in the treatment of scientists, either before or after the Lee case.
"There is no underlying discrimination," a Livermore spokeswoman, Susan Houghton, said. 
"If anything, it's the opposite. 
It is still very much a goal to increase minority representation in management."
In an interview, Ms. Houghton and Tommy Smith, a mechanical engineer who is the laboratory's director of affirmative action and diversity, said Livermore had established goals for increasing the numbers of Asians and other minorities in management and held a one-day workshop for employees in April. 
"Obviously, we can always do a better job," Ms. Houghton said.
She also noted that the investigations into discrimination claims were not proof of wrongdoing.
Los Alamos has about 7,000 employees, including 3,500 scientists, said Mr. Danneskiold, the laboratory spokesman.
Over all, Asians or Pacific Islanders make up 2.4 percent of the staff and about 4 percent of the scientists, he said.
But of 99 senior managers, only 1 is of Asian descent, Mr. Danneskiold said. 
And of 322 leaders of technical groups, a lower rung in management, only 3 are Asian-American.
Similar if somewhat less pronounced disparities exist at Livermore; at Sandia, the proportion of Asians in management and the laboratory are nearly the same.
Michael Trujillo, the equal employment opportunity officer at Los Alamos, also rejected the idea that Asian-Americans' relatively low representation in management was a result of bias. 
But Mr. Trujillo said he could not offer an explanation. 
"I don't think that there's an easy answer on that," he said.
Â 
The Rules
Response That Some Called Racial Profiling
The Energy Department ombudsman, Dr. Wu, said in an interview that he believed new security rules had infringed on "individual rights and scientific freedom" and added that he hoped he could improve the situation.
He has been on the job since January, but he began visiting the laboratories last year and has already investigated several bias complaints. 
In two cases, involving the loss of a security clearance and the termination of a grant, rulings against Asian and Asian-American scientists have been overturned, he said.
Edward J. Curran, who directs the Energy Department's counterintelligence office, said a review almost two years ago led to increased reporting requirements for many employees and to polygraph testing of some scientists. 
He said the rules were intended to make intelligence officials aware of any unusual inquiries from foreign nationals and to help catch any American scientists who were spying, whatever their ethnicity.
Among the directives are two that Mr. Richardson issued last July in which scientists are required to report certain "close and continuing contact" during unclassified visits with people from countries deemed sensitive.
Dr. Al West, a security director at Sandia, said that at least one Asian-American scientist, whose fiancee was from Hong Kong, left for a longstanding job offer in private industry "because they got tired of dealing with all the inquiries into their personal affairs" as a result of the new rule.
And Dr. Shao-Ping Chen, a physicist at Los Alamos, criticized a requirement to list all contacts and relationships with people in sensitive countries.
"Where it should stop is not easy to tell," said Dr. Chen, originally from Taiwan but now an American citizen. 
"If you have a big family, those people are large numbers."
Henry Tang, chairman of the Committee of 100, a group of Chinese-Americans engaged in public policy issues, said that in enforcing the new rules, security officials "are no different than a highway patrolman suspecting someone merely by virtue of their physical characteristics."
Dr. Paul D. Moore, who was the F.B.I.'s chief of Chinese counterintelligence analysis for more than 20 years and is now at the Center for Counterintelligence and Security Studies, a nongovernmental training center in Alexandria, Va., said that belief was mistaken. 
But Dr. Moore said that it had ultimately taken root because, in his view, the Chinese government specifically courts ethnic Chinese in the United States when looking for potential spies. 
As a result, he said, counterintelligence agents focus on Chinese-Americans. 
"It's unfair," he said, "but what are you going to do?"
Â 
The Boycott
A Mixed Reaction Among Scientists
As racism accusations simmer, the moves that have sparked the most discussion -- and dissension -- are the calls for a boycott.
Dr. Shujia Zhou, who left Los Alamos last year, said, "The Asian people feel hit hard."
Dr. Zhou published research in journals like Science and Physical Review Letters but said he left the laboratory because officials made continuing his work difficult, revoking his computer access, for example, and because the atmosphere had soured for Asians.
He easily found another job. 
Dr. Browne, the Los Alamos director, said that revoking computer privileges for some Asian scientists was an "unfortunate" overreaction and that fairer procedures had been put in place.
The calls for a boycott have generated mixed reactions at the laboratories. 
Dr. Manvendra K. Dubey, a Los Alamos scientist and chairman of its Asian-American Working Group, said he opposed a boycott "because if we disappear from within, we will have no voice."
Some say the heightened sensitivity to race may eventually help the laboratories.
But for now, the security concerns about Asian countries, the lack of data on where and how Asian-American scientists work, and the near-absence of Asians in upper ranks are hindering progress at the laboratories, many Asian-American scientists say.
Perhaps more pernicious, they add, is the idea, prevalent among some Americans of European descent, that rational scientists must be immune to ordinary racial bias. 
That visceral difference in viewpoint may pose the most elusive but enduring barrier to improvements, some Asian scientists say.
"I think it's hard for a white person to appreciate the bias," said Dr. Huan Lee, a Chinese-American scientist at Los Alamos.

file: Familiarity Breeds Affection for Asian Vegetables.txt
text:
ï»¿
FOR thousands of years, Asians have treasured the delicate sweetness of pea shoots, the gentle bite of Chinese broccoli, the zest of Chinese chives.
What is common knowledge for them is now becoming more familiar to Americans, as a greater selection of Asian vegetables moves onto market shelves, next to culinary staples like shiitake mushrooms and fresh ginger that were considered exotic here just a few years ago.
Crisp bunches of bok choy, their stems an unblemished white, their leaves dark green, can usually be found in D'Agostino markets, and tender stalks of Chinese broccoli show up at Balducci's in Greenwich Village. 
Purple-veined amaranth lurks at the Union Square Greenmarket.
"Ten years ago it was ginger, then it was dried mushrooms, dried lily buds, and now it's the cabbage family" of Asian vegetables that is endearing itself to the American palate, said Bruce Cost, author of "Bruce Cost's Asian Ingredients: Buying and Cooking the Staple Foods of China, Japan and Southeast Asia" (William Morrow, 1988). 
"The explosion has been in the last five years."
American cooks are learning that these foods are not only tasty and versatile, but also healthy. 
Many Chinese, for example, are lactose-intolerant. 
What have they eaten to get calcium?
"Cabbages and broccoli," Mr. Cost said, adding that these vegetables also provide vitamins A and C.
Chefs of many cuisines are adding Asian greens to their shopping lists. 
Gray Kunz, the executive chef at Lespinasse in the St. Regis hotel in Manhattan, finds bok choy, Thai basil and lemon grass at the Union Square Greenmarket, to his delight. 
"You can integrate them into everyday cooking," Mr. Kunz said.
Most of the vegetables taste best when cooked simply, Mr. Cost said.
Pea shoots stay tender and sweet when sauteed for a scant 10 seconds and can be a delicious substitute for sauteed spinach or watercress. 
Chinese chives can take the place of scallions when scrambled eggs are in order.
Mr. Cost, who is also a chef and a partner in Big Bowl Restaurants in Chicago, went shopping recently at the Hong Kong Supermarket, 37-11 Main Street in Flushing, Queens, where he chose a basketful of Asian vegetables.
Here is a look at some whose flavors and textures could be instantly alluring to the Western palate.
AMARANTH -- Imagine a plant whose taste resembles the tastes of chard and kale, with a hint of sorrel. 
That is the flavor of the beautiful, red-veined amaranth, whose leaves and, at most, an inch of stem are edible. 
(The rest of the stem is hopelessly tough.) Cook quickly in a bit of oil, like pea shoots. 
Varieties of the plant are found throughout the world, and the Chinese have cooked the leaves for centuries.
CHINESE BROCCOLI -- Chinese broccoli is more refined than its Western brethren, although the flavor is similar. 
Every inch of it is delectable, from the smooth, slender stalks to the silky leaves. 
Slice the stems on the diagonal, in sections an inch and a half long and a quarter of an inch thick, with the leaves left whole.
The traditional Chinese preparation is to drop the broccoli in boiling water and blanch it for 3 to 5 minutes, until the stalks are tender. 
While the broccoli is cooking, heat equal parts of vegetable oil and oyster sauce in a skillet, add a dash of sugar and mix until the sauce is blended, about 10 seconds. 
When the broccoli is ready, drain it, turn it onto a plate and drizzle the sauce over it. 
The slight bitterness of the broccoli is offset by the sweetness of the oyster sauce.
DAIKON -- This lovely, crisp, juicy radish has a subtle bite. 
Unlike most root vegetables, it has a light, refreshing, thirst-quenching taste.
Koreans, Japanese and Chinese simmer it in broth until it is translucent and so tender that it can be broken into bite-size pieces by chopsticks. 
It is also pickled, or eaten raw -- shredded into fine white strands and served as an edible garnish. 
Mr. Cost cooks it in a long-simmered oxtail stew seasoned with soy sauce, sugar, star anise, ginger and garlic. 
Before it is used, it must be peeled.
GREEN CHIVES -- These chives are longer, and stronger in flavor (onion comes to mind), than Western chives, and have the ability to scent the entire interior of a refrigerator unless completely wrapped. 
They are cooked and stuffed into translucent dumplings, cooked with noodles and Chinese roast pork, and scrambled with eggs. 
The potent scent fades with cooking.
PEA SHOOT -- This appealingly fragile and tender vegetable tastes as it looks. 
It has a sweet-pea flavor and an evanescent crunch. 
Trim and discard the stems, where the leaves stop, and saute in oil for 10 seconds at most, with a dash of salt, sugar and rice wine or sherry.
SHANGHAI BOK CHOY -- Where the more familiar bok choy has green leaves and white stems, Shanghai bok choy is monochromatically green, and when cooked turns a brilliant shade of emerald. 
Although it can grow to a foot in height, it is often available as baby bok choy, with five plants to a bunch.
To savor this vegetable, strip away the outer leaves (and save them for sauteeing, or to toss into a soup), and use just the hearts, whole or cut in half lengthwise. 
Saute them in oil for two minutes, add chicken broth, and after a minute or two, when the broth is very hot, add a dash of cornstarch mixed with an equal amount of water so that the sauce thickens slightly into a glaze.
A silky Chinese dish places braised shiitake mushrooms atop the tender green hearts. 
This vegetable is a clean-tasting foil to rich or spicy dishes.

file: FILM_A Chinese Actress Blossoms on the Screen.txt
text:
ï»¿
In Chinese, Hua Ping, actually a flower vase, is a pejorative term for a beautiful but empty actress. 
Some Chinese-speaking moviegoers reportedly applied the words to Gong Li after her debut in Zhang Yimou's 1988 film "Red Sorghum."
But the criticism abated after Mr. Zhang's next two films -- "Ju Dou" in 1990 and "Raise the Red Lantern" in 1991 -- in which Gong Li played the leads.
Last year's "Story of Qiu Ju," with Gong Li in the title role, may have silenced the skeptics forever. 
The film, which opens on Friday at the Lincoln Plaza in Manhattan, won the top prize at the Venice Film Festival, and Gong Li took the award for best actress. 
When "The Story of Qiu Ju," also directed by Mr. Zhang, played last fall at the New York Film Festival, Janet Maslin of The Times praised the actress for emerging once again "as a figure of astonishing fortitude."
The film, a jab at the pervasive bureaucracy that cripples China, is a comedy about how society bruises one of its members -- literally. 
The 27-year-old Gong Li portrays the pregnant wife of a chili farmer, Quinglai, who has been kicked in the groin by the village chief for commenting that the chief fathers only "hens."
Qiu Ju trudges frustratingly through rural and urban courts just to get an official explanation for this offense. 
When she enters a life-threatening labor, the chief helps to save both mother and newborn. 
The child being a son, all forget the now-repaired damage to Quinglai's masculinity. 
Only then do the police arrive, with less than impeccable timing, to arrest the chief.
In drawing the character of Qiu Ju, Mr. Zhang recalled the gestures and speech patterns of expectant women in his birthplace, Shanxi, the city in northern China near the village where the film was shot.
"When they get pregnant, they walk slowly, and they're short of breath," he explained. 
"So when I drew this character, I made her short of energy. 
I told Gong Li, 'Slow -- psychologically and physically.'
Qiu Ju represents the perseverance of Chinese women, which contrasts with her slowness."
In preparing for her roles, Gong Li typically reads a script, then lays it aside until just before each take. 
Her performances are instinctive, she says, and her abilities as a mimic enable her to adopt regional accents quickly and convincingly.
"An actor should not memorize every line but should allow new things to happen," she said. 
"I need a collaboration with the director and other actors, something at the location that allows something else to emerge."
For two months before the filming of "The Story of Qiu Ju," Gong Li lived in a small farming community, committing herself so strongly to the role of a pregnant peasant that she wore only the heavy pads and oversized flannel jackets that enhance the frumpiness of the character.
Like Qiu Ju, she is persistent. 
Says Chen Kaige, who directed her in the recent Hong Kong-Chinese co-production "Farewell to My Concubine": "She would say, 'I don't think this dialogue is going to work. 
Think about it. 
You're the artist and decision maker.'
"
Her attitude toward her craft is workmanlike. 
"I like my job very much," says Gong Li, the daughter of a university professor and an archivist from Shantung province, in northeastern China. 
"I don't think of myself as a star. 
An actress is nothing remarkable."
Nevertheless, she notes a difference between her approach and that of more commercially minded actors in Taiwan and Hong Kong (despite her own occasional forays into the less arty fare that is characteristic of assembly-line film making in Hong Kong): "Those actresses don't have time to experience the lives of their characters, but I'm willing to take the hardships."
The 43-year-old Mr. Zhang and Gong Li are personal as well as professional partners. 
The film maker, who was married at the time, discovered the actress while casting "Red Sorghum," when she was a sophomore at the Central Academy of Drama in Beijing, and their relationship began soon after. 
In "Red Sorghum," Gong Li played a purchased bride, a role that displayed her physical beauty more than her dramatic talent, prompting some critics to brand her a hua ping.
In "Farewell to My Concubine," which will compete next month at the Cannes International Film Festival, the actress is a former prostitute named Juxian, who is married to one of two homosexual lovers from the Beijing Opera. 
As the character ages 40 years, Gong Li exhibits a new range of talents. 
"She comes completely alive at the moment when the camera starts rolling," says Mr. Chen. "She becomes a very different person."
Juxian and Qiu Ju extend a trajectory of portrayals by Gong Li that have become increasingly more complex. 
In "Red Sorghum," she ultimately instigates a village revolt against the occupying Japanese. 
Her young wives in "Ju Dou" and "Raise the Red Lantern" also rebel, gradually evolving into vengeful adultress and madwoman, respectively. 
In "The Story of Qiu Ju," she is quietly outspoken and independent: she fights what should be her husband's battle. 
At film's end, the camera frozen on her unadorned face, she seems to be preparing for yet another round of attacks on an elephantine system. 
While celebrating the strength of Chinese women, this final close-up also signals a victory for Gong Li over the stigma of hua ping.

text:

COULD it be that one of today's most important film artists -- the critic J. Hoberman calls him "the world's greatest active narrative filmmaker" -- is a Taiwanese director virtually unknown here?
American audiences, accustomed to gauging a movie's importance by its advertising budget and buzz, may understandably scoff at such a claim. 
Regardless, the director in question, Hou Hsiao-hsien, is a star of the international circuit. 
Six of his last seven pictures have been shown at this year's New York Film Festival, which ends today, yet none were released in the United States theatrically. 
His movies are considered "difficult" -- and they are, compared with the latest action picture. 
Yet it says something about how incurious American audiences have become that they must be "protected" from great, demanding cinema from abroad. 
The fault is not entirely ours: Mr. Hou's producers have sometimes made unrealistic demands for foreign sales.
Now Wendy Lidell, vice president of WinStar Cinema, is taking the chance. 
She has put together a package of seven Hou Hsiao-hsien films to tour nationally, beginning at Lincoln Center's Walter Reade Theater, on Wednesday through Oct. 
27; eventually the films will be issued on video and DVD. 
(The Walter Reade series will be fleshed out with three other Hou titles and will include a weeklong run of Mr. Hou's magnificent "Flowers of Shanghai.")
Mr. Hou's significance is that he is both a great humanist storyteller and a great formalist. 
Imagine a cross between the character-rich, domestically observant cinema of Satyajit Ray or Vittorio de Sica and the rigorously framed, meditative aura of Yasujiro Ozu and Robert Bresson, with gritty urban echoes of Martin Scorsese thrown in. 
His films constitute a running commentary on Taiwanese identity, while drawing deeply on classical Chinese art. 
If Mr. Hou's style bridges the old traditions and the jagged, modernist edges of rootless global culture, it is partly because he himself embodies those contradictions.
This maker of contemplative masterworks is, at 52, youthful-looking, roguish and a hard-drinking karaoke habitue, as we see in "'H.H.H.: Portrait of Hou Hsiao-hsien," an intriguing documentary by Olivier Assayas that is included in the Walter Reade series. 
We learn that Mr. Hou had a wild youth; many of his gang cohorts met violent ends. 
After military service, which settled him down, he was unsure whether to aim for pop singing, acting or filmmaking. 
He joined a movement of cinematic progressives (including Edward Yang, in whose "Taipei Story" Mr. Hou played the lead). 
The New Taiwanese Cinema identified with the French New Wave, rebelling against the previous Taiwanese studio comedies and melodramas and favoring real locations and socially conscious material. 
Their first effort was an omnibus film, "The Sandwich Man" (1983); Mr. Hou directed the title section, and already one can see his patient observation of ordinary people caught in a trap. 
Other early Hou films, "The Boys From Fengkuei" and "A Summer at Grandpa's," displayed a fresh, open storytelling approach that captured the irregular rhythms of growing up. 
But it was not until the more autobiographical "A Time to Live and a Time to Die" (1985) that Mr. Hou made his first genuine masterpiece.
He chose the story of a schoolteacher, much like his father, who transplanted his family from mainland China to Taiwan in 1948 for work reasons, then was unable to go back after the Revolution. 
The first generation's tragedy was that they died in Taiwan deluding themselves that they would one day return.
THEIR children, Mr. Hou's generation, accepted that they belonged in Taiwan, though that meant subscribing to an uneasy, fractured identity, buffeted politically between the Nationalists and the Chinese Communists. 
These larger tensions are reflected in the story of an exiled family, much like Mr. Hou's, in which the death of both parents led to the adolescent children's delinquency.
Praising the movie's "attractive plainness," Janet Maslin wrote in The New York Times: "Much of the film is about suffering and loss, detailing the painful circumstances in which family members, one by one, grow ill and die. 
It has been photographed, most effectively, with a streamlined ordinariness that amounts to a kind of eloquence."
Mr. Hou's camera records, with anthropological interest, life's task-laden dailiness, which continues through dramatic disruptions. 
The mournfully consoling noises and rituals of everyday go on in the surround (you can't even say "background," because the key dramatic action is not always in the foreground).
The performances also mimic a nonprofessional style, which makes you forget you're even watching acting, so absorbed is the camera with real-time behavior. 
For instance, there's a stunning, throwaway moment when the mother, who has throat cancer, is being clumsily strapped into a rickshaw by its driver, to be taken back to the hospital. 
You watch the rain falling, the driver buckling the straps around the mother, her own stolid, indrawn expression, her grown children more or less assisting. 
The scene's restraint lets you feel, and swallow, the full effect of severe illness.
Without overgeneralizing, perhaps one might speak in broader terms of a Taiwanese cultural sensibility, which is melancholy and fragilely quotidian, reflecting the apprehensive circumstances of this island's modern history (occupied for 50 years by the Japanese, then placed under martial law for 40 years by the emigre Nationalists). 
Hong Kong films tend toward the brashly kinetic; Chinese mainland films, toward the panoramically epic; Taiwanese films, toward the quietly moody. 
Mr. Hou's trademark poignant stoicism, humor-flecked, has been aided immeasurably by his two wonderful screenwriters: the novelists Chu T'ien-wen and Wu Nien-chen.
Mr. Hou's next work, "Dust in the Wind," based on Mr. Wu's autobiographical script, focused on the problems of country youth moving to the big city and getting lost in the shuffle. 
A small, wrenching film, it features some astonishingly beautiful long shots, which, like Chinese landscape painting, assign us humanity's place in a larger picture.
From this point on, Mr. Hou steadily perfected his technique, moving from that "attractive plainness" to a level of refinement justifying Peter Sellars's assessment that he was "one of the last great craftsmen in cinema."
Visual elegance permeated his subsequent film, the haunting "Daughter of the Nile," which portrayed disaffected Taipei teen-agers trapped in the aqua fluorescent glare of Burger Kings, and, even more, his ambitious, three-hour "City of Sadness," which won the grand prize at Venice in 1990.
"City of Sadness" was a breakthrough for Mr. Hou in many respects: by telling the taboo story about the "February 28 incident," a massacre of thousands of native Taiwanese in 1947 by the Nationalist Chinese, he struck a national chord (the film set box-office records in Taiwan). 
By layering so many characters and themes with a minimum of orientation, he created a new kind of epic, both richly textured and austere. 
The film traces the fortunes of a family, led by Older Brother, a brusque, gravel-voiced, irrepressibly endearing gangster, who tries to honor the codes of family, clan and professional confederates, while keeping wife and mistress happy. 
Meanwhile, we learn a lot about the Japanese occupation, competition from Shanghai gangsters, leftwing political movements.
The film's narrative reach, violence and fatalistic undertone owes something to that other gangster epic, "The Godfather," which Mr. Hou says inspired him. 
In "City of Sadness," violence often erupts from seeming tranquillity and then spends itself, the site returning to calm. 
A man is slowly walking up a mountain road; a rickshaw appears in the middle distance; the man turns and strolls toward the rickshaw occupants, then pulls a samurai sword and starts thwacking at them. 
This spasmodic aggression gets swallowed by the mountainous landscape.
(There is also a hint of Godard -- another influence of Mr. Hou's -- and his droll shootouts between gangsters in long-distance.) "I always tell my cameraman, 'Pull back!
More detached!'
" says Mr. Hou. By striving for a detached, objective point of view, without leading us ideologically by the elbow, he compels a more active spectatorship. 
It must be admited, though, that "A City of Sadness" is not easy to grasp in one viewing.
Mr. Hou's reputed difficulty for American audiences is only partly because he dwells so specifically on Taiwanese matters. 
Those particularities can be overlooked; more crucial is a willingness to surrender to a different pace and vision. 
American scriptwriters are taught to make one point per scene and move on. 
With Mr. Hou, you feel your way into a scene, sorting as you go the characters' relationships and objectives. 
As Kent Jones, co-curator of the Lincoln Center series, has written: "There is truly nothing but in medias res in Hou."
After a while you abandon your quest for the "key action" and surrender to the perplexing, multifarious life unfolding before you.
In a sense, Mr. Hou's work is not difficult at all: you need only slow down your metabolism and submit to the pace, the images, the information on screen.
What he offers, finally, is a plenitude of life as it accumulates in the moment; the screen fills with being like water in a fish tank. 
Mr. Hou forces you to attend to the unfolding present -- a quality he shares with other "ontological" filmmakers like Andrei Tarkovsky, John Cassavetes, Jean-Luc Godard, Andy Warhol and Frederick Wiseman, all of whom allow the moment to flower, rather than coercing it into plot functions.
"He probably understands framing better than any director in the world," observed Richard Pena, the New York Film Festival's director. 
He often subdivides the frame, with lattice or door frames, letting several actions go on at once. 
Increasingly, each scene is presented as a self-controlled whole, without interior cutting, which places more pressure on camera movement and choreographed action within the shot. 
Yet if you're not always sure why you're watching what you are, given his abjuring of transition shots, a second viewing of any Hou film reveals that it has been very tightly constructed, with no narrative flab.
"City of Sadness" was the first in a historical trilogy, which also included "The Puppetmaster" and "Good Men, Good Women."
Both paid their respects to the resilient optimism and sacrifices of an older generation, as a way of trying to understand Taiwanese history and to contrast it with the malaise and pessimism of young Taiwanese today. 
Having performed this filial duty, Mr. Hou next made "Goodbye, South, Goodbye," in which he brilliantly cut loose. 
Here he gives us Taiwanese punks talking on cell phones, riding motorcycles through the mountains (a joyously lyrical scene), hanging out after botched suicide attempts and trying to pull off harebrained cons. 
We also see how dominant the cultures of America and Japan are on the young Taiwanese. 
Mr. Hou paints Taiwan as a society so corrupt and lawless -- "pure" capitalism -- that only a frayed system of familial and clan loyalties is left to adjudicate disputes. 
There is an amazing nightclub scene that begins with an elderly man crooning a karaoke song about women and betrayal; then the camera moves to a row of banquet tables, where a senator and a policeman on the take discuss with a gangster how best to mediate a kidnapping. 
Around them sit various friends and retainers of both sides, eating with decorous politeness as the bribes are worked out.
In his most recent film, "Flowers of Shanghai," Mr. Hou abandoned Taiwan for the first time and focused on a period drama set in various brothels in turn-of-the-century Shanghai. 
This gorgeous, remorselessly controlled film is shot entirely in interiors: a succession of dimly gaslit parlors where background colors are muted -- plums and golds that open to reveal the players half-concealed in the shadows -- and where no one is ever left alone for long, though their inner isolation remains untouched. 
Elaborate rituals of opium pipes, feasts and gambling underpin the carnal intimacies and duplicities.
Mr. Hou takes the conventions of geisha melodrama -- the cruelty of sexual commerce, the women's debts, the madam's bossiness, the self-protective, two-faced nature of a courtesan's attachments -- and strips down the genre to its essence, by way of formal blackouts, frontal compositions, and gyroscopically rigorous camera movements, which capture each scene in a single setup. 
At the film's emotional center is a handsome, unhappy patron, Master Wang, played by Tony Leung, who is addicted to the pleasure quarters, not so much for reasons of sexual titillation as for the loneliness, lostness and languor obtainable there. 
We are left to witness the enormous gulf between male and female, as Wang gazes at his sometime-mistress Crimson, wondering what is going on inside her, while she prepares his pipe.
"Flowers of Shanghai" is one of the cinematic highpoints of the 90's, a tribute from one fin-de-siecle to another, by a master who keeps growing.

SAMUEL L. JACKSON WAS PACING backstage on the set, waiting for his cue. 
Decked out in a checked suit as a world-renowned violin expert, he was working on an attitude of weary sophistication. 
Although the film was being shot in English, he was practicing his French.
"Ca va?"
Mr. Jackson asked a production assistant. 
"That's cool, man. 
C'est bon."
It was the fourth day of shooting for the Canadian segment of "The Red Violin," which represents the first big international co-production of New Line Cinema. 
(Fine Line Features, a division of New Line, released "Shine," the hit film biography of the pianist David Helfgott.) Equally significant, "The Red Violin," which stars Greta Scacchi in addition to Mr. Jackson and features original soundtrack music by John Corigliano, is the second collaboration between Francois Girard and Don McKellar, who wrote the acclaimed 1994 movie "Thirty-Two Short Films About Glenn Gould."
"The Red Violin," which traces the imaginary history of a 1681 Italian instrument over three centuries, is as sweeping and ambitious in scope as "Thirty-Two Short Films" was intimate and insular. 
Though technically a Canadian film, with a modest $10 million budget, it is an international effort, co-produced by companies in Canada, the United States, England and Italy. 
It is being filmed in five countries: Canada, England, Italy, Austria and China. 
Each episode represents a different era, and the casts and languages change accordingly.
The tale puts forward a fictional Italian master, a maker of string instruments who paints the violin of the title with a varnish made from the blood of his beloved dead wife, in an attempt to keep her spirit alive. 
By 1792, the instrument has wended its way to the Austrian Alps, where a young prodigy determines to play it at the court in Vienna. 
From there, it is taken up by Gypsies, acquired by a Dionysian composer in England and, in 1966, sent on a boat to China, where it is hidden during the Cultural Revolution. 
Finally, in the present day, it lands at an auction house in Montreal, where the violin expert played by Mr. Jackson becomes obsessed with it.
As might be expected, there is already excitement about "The Red Violin" in musical circles. 
The soundtrack, to be produced by Sony Classical, is being created by Mr. Corigliano, whose work includes the opera "The Ghosts of Versailles" and the scores for the movies "Altered States" and "Revolution."
The American violinist Joshua Bell will play concerts on the East and West Coasts in the fall featuring a rhapsody written by Mr. Corigliano inspired by the film.
"Most music films are basically sports films with a music scenario," Mr. Corigliano said. 
"They have a competition and a superstar who is out to beat everybody else, like running the four-minute mile. 
Although there are virtuosi in it, 'The Red Violin' is a completely different look at music. 
It's more the idea of how music has gone through the ages, and the passion that people feel for it going through time."
Channel 4 in England, which has produced movies like "Four Weddings and a Funeral," is a backer of this film. 
"What first interested me in 'The Red Violin' was the script," said the channel's director, David Aukin. 
"I've never come across a story quite like this, and I was intrigued to see what someone of Francois's sensibility and talent would bring to it. 
It struck me as entirely unusual and idiosyncratic."
For the Canadian team at the heart of "The Red Violin" -- Mr. Girard, Mr. McKellar and Niv Fichman, the producer -- this is a far more ambitious project than "Thirty-Two Short Films," which was shot for less than $2 million. 
That movie, which looked at the artistic genius and personal eccentricity of the great Canadian pianist Glenn Gould from a variety of angles, was an unexpected critical hit when it opened in the United States. 
It "brilliantly breaks with tradition and gives us a movie that actually inspires us to think about what it was like to be this man," wrote Roger Ebert in The Chicago Sun-Times.
As a result, Mr. Girard received a number of proposals for films about musical figures. 
"I thought I wouldn't want to do another film about music," he said in French-accented English. 
"But then this idea came to me, of a violin traveling through time. 
It's not five stories; it's one story in five steps. 
And the auction is where the different stories finally meet."
Here, now, was the ornate auction room, which had been created in a former municipal swimming pool on Amherst Street. 
It was a grand space, ringed by a gallery and filled with gilt chairs. 
Extras wearing Gucci pumps and pearl necklaces stepped gingerly over wires. 
At one end, standing at a podium, was Colm Feore, the Canadian actor who portrayed Gould in "Thirty-Two Short Films," now playing the auctioneer.
Behind him stood a lone violin on a pedestal, an actual Stradivarius, which the cellist Yo-Yo Ma had helped the producers procure. 
In the script, it was being auctioned just before the red violin. 
The crew was proud to have the Stradivarius, valued at $1.8 million, on the set. 
"It could be the world's most expensive prop," said Mr. Fichman.
Mr. Jackson appeared at the back door of the auction room. 
"My character here is someone who looks at an instrument and knows its value, knows how music is created," he said later.
Playing the part of a violin connoisseur is a departure for Mr. Jackson, who has appeared in "Pulp Fiction" and "A Time to Kill."
Mr. Fichman said that he and his partners did not want to make a film that was completely "white and Eurocentric," hence the casting of a black actor for the part.
It didn't hurt, of course, that Mr. Jackson was a big star. 
He, for his part, was interested in making another low-budget film.
"The crafts services' food is not as good," he said. 
"But the passion that's surrounding me here is totally different from the energy that goes into a studio production."
For months, Mr. Girard and his team have been embroiled in lengthy talks with the Chinese Government, negotiating a deal to allow them to film in Shanghai. 
Resistance arose among officials, because the segment was to be set during the Cultural Revolution, a period the Government would rather not dwell on. 
But the latest news is positive: Mr. Fichman, who went to China in March with Mr. McKellar, has received word that the project has now met with a positive response from the Chinese Government. 
Although the film awaits one last stamp of approval, the crew is preparing to shoot in Shanghai in late June.
"We've come up with a script that is agreed upon by both sides," Mr. Fichman said. 
"We understand what their concerns are. 
We're not setting out in any way to denounce Chinese culture."
After filming in Montreal, the production traveled to Vienna, and to Cremona, Italy, and will shoot in England in late May. 
Since each segment is being shot in the language of its country, most of the film will be subtitled.
"It was very important to me that the film be shot in the different languages," said Mr. Aukin, of Channel 4. 
"To me, that was the whole point of the movie, that music is a universal language that goes beyond other languages and unites people. 
Everyone can understand the violin when it's played."
Mr. Girard finds deep significance in the immortality of the red violin. 
"I don't think we're making a movie just about music," he said. 
"If you ask me what this film is about, I would say it's actually about love and mortality. 
It's about surviving mortality through art, beauty and craft.
"I think that's what all artists are doing," he added after a pause. 
"This is the afterlife that art can give us."

text:

WHAT makes the subject of Tibet such a tricky one for filmmakers is that the moral lines of right and wrong in the China-Tibet confrontation have become so tightly drawn in the popular imagination that there is little room left for ambiguity or subtlety.
This is not to say that China's savage treatment of Tibet has left great ambiguity, but simply that such a good-guys-versus-bad-guys relationship makes it hard for anyone to break free from the powerful field of presumptive gravity that surrounds the subject. 
No matter how authentic the sets and costumes or how "big" the director or stars, films about Tibet find themselves inescapably bounded by a determinism that grows out of what we Westerners unconsciously think about when we imagine Tibet.
We tend to see Tibet through one of the most powerful utopian mythologies of this century -- of a fabled, Shangri-La-like refuge from the outside world. 
When the Chinese People's Liberation Army marched into Tibet's capital, Lhasa, in the 1950's, it occupied not only a geographic place but this beloved Western fantasy as well. 
It violated not only Tibet but our yearning to believe that there was still a place on this shrinking planet where spiritual purity, physical isolation and natural beauty endured and where legions of Buddhist monks spent their lives meditating rather than making Buicks.
Then suddenly the specter of China, land of revolutionary violence, godless (and Buddhaless) Communism and crypto-colonial occupation, intruded on Tibet and our Western reverie. 
Where we saw a benign spiritualism, they saw an oppressive feudal theocracy and a backward serf class in desperate need of Communist "liberation."
So deeply rooted in the Western psyche is our version of Tibet that it has become virtually part of our mental DNA. 
One way or another every article, book or film on Tibet must contend with the political and cultural determinism of this myth. 
But, alas, when a film's conclusion is more or less foregone, it loses the kind of literary tension and mystery that gets us involved. 
Of course, we may feel outraged, an understandable feeling when contemplating Tibet's sad modern history. 
But outrage is rarely enough to hold our attention.
Because conclusions are incipiently imbedded in the very subject matter, Tibet presents a difficult artistic challenge for filmmakers, a headwind against which the spate of recent Tibet films -- Martin Scorsese's "Kundun," Jean-Jacques Annaud's "Seven Years in Tibet" and numerous documentaries -- have had to sail. 
And the fact that Mr. Scorsese and Mr. Annaud could not go to Tibet to shoot only made their efforts more detached from the real place and more dependent on the "imagined Tibet."
Now comes "Windhorse," a low-budget feature film (it cost a mere $300,000, while "Kundun" cost $30 million and "Seven Years in Tibet" $65 million), written, directed and produced by the documentarian Paul Wagner, who won Academy and Emmy Awards for his 1985 film "The Stone Carvers," a portrait of the Italian-American craftsmen who work on the Washington Cathedral. 
With "Windhorse," which opened April 30, Mr. Wagner wanted to pick up where these other films left off.
"No one had covered what had happened since then," he writes of the 1950's in his production notes. 
"To date, over a million Tibetans have been killed by the Chinese. 
There is no freedom of speech and no free press in Tibet, and I've heard of teen-agers being tortured with cattle prods just for wanting to practice their religion. 
That's the situation as it is, not 40 years ago."
Mr. Wagner was determined to shoot at least some of "Windhorse" in Tibet itself. 
But realizing that the Chinese would never grant him permission, he set off in the grand tradition of other Western interlopers who have stolen into Lhasa. 
Posing as a tourist, he and a crew of nonprofessionals managed to film covertly with a Sony mini-DV (digital video) Handycam. 
He says he wanted "to push the envelope in terms of the authorities," to get a sense of what it was like to live and work under China's domination.
Recognizing that certain production values would be lost by using a guerrilla mode of feature filmmaking, Mr. Wagner tried to turn this liability into an asset. 
Indeed, being forced to operate in the same politically supercharged and fearful atmosphere that permeates Tibetan life under occupation does give "Windhorse" an edgy cinema verite authenticity missing in the other, bigger-budget Tibet films. 
And the fact that actors speak Tibetan and Chinese gives the film a further feel of verisimilitude.
THE story centers on a Tibetan family that becomes ensnared in the struggle for freedom from China after a cousin, Pema, who is a Buddhist nun, is arrested and tortured to death. 
The sister, Dolkar, leaves her Chinese boyfriend and quits singing syrupy propaganda songs about "the motherland" in a Lhasa disco, while her ne'er-do-well brother gives up his dissolute life to join the resistance and help smuggle a tape of Pema's story out of Tibet.
Mr. Wagner got interested in Tibet after his own niece, Julia Elliott, who had been living in Katmandu, Nepal, was detained, stripped of her film and camera, interrogated and forced to sign a confession by Chinese police officers while on a trip to Lhasa. 
As Mr. Wagner learned more about Tibet's plight, he became increasingly incensed.
"Tibet has a kind of urgency about it," he told me. 
"It's classic David and Goliath stuff. 
And in my professional work, I love to deal with underdogs."
With Ms. Elliott as his co-writer, Mr. Wagner set off in 1996 on an exploratory trip to Lhasa and quickly fell under the sway of Tibet's unique allure. 
"It is easy to become enamored of the incredible costumes, the intensity of religious faith, the elaborate culture and above all the mountains," he told me as he was editing his film. 
"Tibet has been a temptingly unreachable place. 
For us, it is wanting what we can't have."
Mr. Wagner has captured an elusive piece of this intriguing place's history. 
Yet, as in other Tibet films, we know before we begin that Tibetans will be abused by Chinese subjugators and that there will be no cathartic moment for the victims. 
In this sense, Tibet films are something like Greek tragedies, except it is not a tragic flaw in an individual that brings about inevitable downfall, but the hopeless situation in which Tibetans find themselves.
Although old Tibet has all but vanished and Lhasa is turning into a charmless Chinese city, we Westerners still love to retreat into virtual versions reconstructed on film sets. 
As one of the characters in Frank Capra's 1937 film version of James Hilton's novel "Lost Horizon" presciently says when asked by a colleague if he believes that Shangri-La actually does exist, "I believe it because I want to believe it."
But films like "Windhorse" present such a somber vision of Tibet that it is ever more difficult to conjure up our old fantasies of this fabled land. 
China's reckless occupation has turned this dream, and Tibet's reality, into something of a nightmare. 
That nightmare binds every Tibet film into a strange, subliminal confinement, which makes it not only harder to believe in Shangri-La but also harder to make a film that surprises us with its originality.

The Moroccans who were working on "Kundun," Martin Scorsese's movie about the Dalai Lama's boyhood, seemed unimpressed by the transformation of their hometown into the capital of Tibet, complete with Buddhas painted on the hillsides and golden rooftops topping houses in the casbah below. 
Then again, Jerusalem was just down the road, where Turner Network Television had recently shot "David," its latest work in the "Bible" series. 
Perhaps the locals are just inured to strange sights.
Into this town, where tempests are usually strictly of a meteorological variety, came the news that the Chinese Government had denounced "Kundun."
The Chinese have been anything but blase about the goings-on in this town, a gateway to the Sahara nestled in the foothills of the snowcapped Atlas Mountains.
On Nov. 
22, the news broke that the Chinese Government was complaining about the Walt Disney Company's involvement in producing "Kundun."
The movie chronicles the life of the Dalai Lama, who has called for Tibetan independence from China.
"We are resolutely opposed to the making of this movie," a Chinese official said last month. 
"It is intended to glorify the Dalai Lama, so it is an interference in China's internal affairs."
Those on the set when China's denunciation of "Kundun" broke preferred not to discuss their reactions, though the movie's screenwriter, Melissa Mathison, said: "I'm glad it's all out in the open. 
I'm sort of surprised at the dimensions, but I'm not surprised the Chinese would try to stop the movie."
The story has raged on in newspapers around the world, with Disney saying that it will go ahead with the domestic distribution of "Kundun" next year. 
For those involved in the project, which will finish shooting by the end of the month, this is yet another chapter in what has been the long, incident-filled story of the movie's development.
That story begins with the Dalai Lama. 
In 1937, a 2-year-old boy was identified as the 14th reincarnation of the Dalai Lama, the spiritual and political leader of Tibet. 
The boy, Tenzin Gyatso, and his family were taken to Lhasa, the country's capital, where he grew up in the Potala Palace. 
He spent his childhood in study, cared for by other lamas and abbots from the country's greatest Buddhist monasteries.
In 1950, China, led by Mao Zedong, invaded Tibet, its neighbor and former trading partner. 
In response, the Dalai Lama was officially enthroned, at the age of 15. 
At first, the Tibetans thought the Chinese would be supportive, but in 1954, when the Dalai Lama made an official visit to Beijing, it was clear that this was not the case.
"Religion is poison," said Chairman Mao, making his intentions clear.
Despite Chinese occupation, the Dalai Lama and his Tibetan Government refused to make concessions. 
When he turned to the West for help, it did not come. 
When the Dalai Lama's summer residence was shelled, the cabinet decided that he had to leave the country.
In 1959, he crossed into Dharmsala, India, where he still lives, heading a Government in exile.
Ms. Mathison, a screenwriter best known for "E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial," first heard of the Dalai Lama when she was a student at the University of California at Berkeley. 
"Even before I wrote 'E.T.'
I had thought that this would be a great movie," she said.
"I am sort of famous for little-boy stories, and this was a fantastic little-boy story, a story of destiny and nurturing and tragedy, the idea of finding a 2-year-old child and then investing in him everything that is good about human beings, your people and about your beliefs, and then asking that he try to save your country."
In 1990, she wrote a proposal and asked the actor Richard Gere, a well-known supporter of the Tibetan cause, for help in getting it to the Dalai Lama. 
The Dalai Lama himself wrote back to say he would be interested in discussing the project. 
A meeting was set up for April 1990, when he was to be in California to receive an award.
Ms. Mathison recalled that she and her husband, Harrison Ford, went to meet the Dalai Lama at the Red Lion Inn in Santa Barbara. 
"I did a pitch, basically," she said. 
"He said: 'Yes, you may do the movie. 
I'm going to Santa Cruz to rest for two days. 
Why don't you come up and we'll talk?'
"
They accepted that invitation, as well as the next one: to come to India.
A year after first meeting the Dalai Lama, with a draft of a screenplay completed, Ms. Mathison and Mr. Ford went to Dharmsala. 
For six days they talked, and Mr. Ford read the script aloud to him.
"His Holiness would make corrections, or his memory would be jogged and he'd say, 'This reminds me of something' and tell us a story," Ms. Mathison said. 
"And when Harrison got to the end of the script, his Holiness said: 'Good. 
Very good. 
Very strong. 
Very beautiful.'
"
Back home, she began the process of trying to interest a director in the project. 
The one she wanted was Mr. Scorsese, largely because she thought the issues would appeal to him.
"First of all," she said, "it's the story of the male society. 
Secondly, the story of a loyalty to an idea and this man who had the strength, with all of the universe working against him, to stand up to that idea. 
The religious overtones I knew would appeal to Marty. 
I saw it as a story of a kind of wise guy, and I knew he would get what it was about."
She was right.
"There was no doubt," said Mr. Scorsese. "Whether I like it or not, a lot of my movies have religious elements or themes. 
But the key for me in this story is the concept of how you live a life of compassion. 
And I think that goes all the way back to the first lines of 'Mean Streets': 'You don't make up for your sins in a church. 
You do it in the streets. 
You do it at home.'
"These are things that have always fascinated me. 
I've always been torn between what is preached in church and what is acted upon, how people really live. 
And how does one answer such incredible violence and upheaval with nonviolence?
Why is the man who is nonviolent actually stronger?"
After he agreed to take on the project, Mr. Scorsese worked with Ms. Mathison on the script, which he describes as a "story about a little boy who loses a lot in life and gains in other ways."
In March, Mr. Scorsese, Ms. Mathison and others went to India to begin preparation for the film they assumed would be shot there. 
The complex task of casting fell to Ellen Lewis, who has cast all of Mr. Scorsese's movies since "New York Stories," in 1989.
"To do it with people from Tibet is the only way you can do this kind of film," Mr. Scorsese said. 
"You go right back to the lesson of De Sica and Rossellini at the end of World War II. 
You just do it with the people in the street."
He added: "I've worked with a great many nonactors in the past 25 years, although I've never worked with nonactors from a different culture. 
Almost half the speaking cast in 'Casino' was nonactors. 
Many of the people in 'Goodfellas' were nonactors, including my mother."
MS. LEWIS EMBARKED on an elaborate tour of rural India -- "video camera in hand, cows mooing in the background," she said -- to gather people to play the 34 speaking parts, including four to play the Dalai Lama at various ages. 
From New Delhi, she went on to Dharmsala, where the largest population of exiled Tibetans now live.
She was accompanied by Namlha Taklha, the movie's chief technical adviser, who is the widow of Lobsang Samden Taklha, the Dalai Lama's brother. 
They traveled through India, visiting Tibetan enclaves. 
Since they needed Tibetans who spoke English, Ms. Lewis also visited a variety of American and Canadian cities. 
In the end, she cast 15 people from India and the rest from North America.
Although she found the Tibetans receptive to working on "Kundun," which in Tibetan means "the presence of a great incarnation," many were eliminated from consideration because they could not speak English. 
She also found casting difficult because "Tibetans are not an emotive society, they don't show emotion, and that doesn't work for acting."
Some of the cast were chosen solely on the basis of videotape auditions. 
Others had ties to the Dalai Lama's family. 
Mrs. Taklha's nephew, for example, plays the Dalai Lama as an adult. 
The Dalai Lama's niece plays his mother.
Ms. Mathison had already begun trying to get permission to shoot the film in India. 
"I did my stint in the ministers' office, sitting for hours, drinking cups of tea, hoping to talk to somebody," she recalled. 
When Mr. Scorsese became involved, he also tried. 
"We spent a year meeting with the Indian Government to try to get permits to shoot there," Mr. Scorsese said. 
"We met with practically everyone and tried everything. 
But when I went back this past April, we became aware that it was difficult for the Indian Government to give us permission for political reasons. 
China is on their border. 
Ultimately we were told that they 'could not make a decision at this time.'
"
Morocco was suggested as an alternative, partly because its high desert and mountains are extraordinarily similar to those of Tibet, and it is here that many members of the production staff have been working since May.
The production designer Dante Ferretti's journey, like Ms. Lewis's, began in India, where he met four times with the Dalai Lama, who made drawings of the layout of the interior of the Potala, which is controlled by the Chinese.
Mr. Ferretti also met with Mrs. Taklha, and benefited from her finds, including a tiny booklet about the enthronement and snapshots of the actual event. 
Fabrics for the sets and costumes were bought in India.
"I was overwhelmed to see the Tibetan civilization that no longer exists be re-created in Morocco," Ms. Mathison said.
Many of the Tibetans in the cast had seen Tibet only in photographs. 
Ms. Mathison said one young woman had said, on seeing the costumes, "Was Tibet as rich as this?"
Then she hid herself in a corner and wept for what was lost.
Mr. Scorsese witnessed similar displays of emotion. 
"The first day, when many of them had just arrived, I showed them the set of the Potala. 
A number of them prayed, and a few of them were crying."
About a 15-minute drive on the route to Marrakesh from Ouarzazate's hotel zone, the parking lot outside L'Hotel Oscar is filled with beat-up movie trailers. 
The hotel was built for a James Bond film and later appeared on an Egyptian street in "The Jewel of the Nile."
Lhasa rooftops have been affixed to existing structures. 
A sound stage has been built here, as has a replica of the facade of the Dalai Lama's summer palace in Norbulingka, near Lhasa.
Several tents are set up to house 1,600 costumes, including monks' robes and Chinese military uniforms, as well as elaborate Tibetan and Chinese headdresses, all made by hand. 
The budget for the film is $30 million.
On this brilliantly sunny November day, 550 extras were roaming around before the filming of the enthronement scene began on the sound stage. 
Draped in maroon robes, the 129 real Tibetan monks, some from the Dalai Lama's own monastery, were impossible to distinguish from 73 other Tibetans and about 350 Moroccans, who, with their shaved heads, had achieved a similar look.
Inside, the Palace's throne room was thick with the smoke of hundreds of yak butter candles (actually, honey-colored wax), which glinted off the ornate gilt Buddhas.
As the monks took their places, Mr. Scorsese headed for the set from his rickety trailer nearby. 
Despite his surgical mask and a hat to keep out dust from a sandstorm, he looked dapper. 
Tossing a maroon scarf around his neck, he announced wryly, "We love these windstorms."
Because of the intensity of the Chinese reaction to the project, a few of those connected with the film worry that there will be repercussions for some of the Tibetans involved. 
There has already been some discussion of altering their names in the credits, to conceal their participation. 
Even more troubling for the film makers is the fact that the parents of the man playing a main character still live in China.
Asked if there is a possibility that China would ban future Harrison Ford movies because she wrote the script for "Kundun," Ms. Mathison said she was not at all concerned, and pointed out that they had not banned any movies starring Mr. Gere, perhaps the most vociferous advocate of the Tibetan cause in Hollywood.
"It's a wonderful movie, and it's going to be released no matter who releases it," she said in her apartment on Central Park West in Manhattan the day the story about China's reaction to the project was emerging in The New York Times. 
"Disney has said they're very high on it."
Another movie being filmed in Argentina, "Seven Years in Tibet," has apparently escaped censure by the Chinese. 
Based on a book by the mountain climber Heinrich Harrer, "Seven Years in Tibet" is being directed by Jean-Jacques Annaud for Columbia Tri-Star and stars Brad Pitt as Mr. Harrer.
"It's interesting that suddenly, in 1996, a number of these movies are being made," Mr. Scorsese said. 
"It's very good for the cause of Tibet. 
And hopefully, one doesn't take away from the other."
Â 
North Africa's Tinseltown
THE MOROCCAN TOWN of Ouarzazate, 125 miles southeast of Marrakesh, bears a name that in Berber means "city of silence."
But this outpost, which was developed by the French as a garrison in 1928, is now anything but. 
First the tourists came, and then the movies. 
Ouarzazate (pronounced WAR-za-zat) has gone Hollywood.
dd French, Arabic and Berber are native tongues, and many film crews speak Italian or English. 
When Martin Scorsese scouted the location 10 years ago for "The Last Temptation of Christ," Ouarzazate had two streets and no electricity. 
There were no cars. 
Today, many still live without electricity or plumbing.
The only movie theater in town, population 20,000, closed six months ago, so it is doubtful whether "Kundun" will be seen here until it is released on video. 
But it has already become a custom to declare an official holiday here when TNT's Biblical productions are shown via satellite, since televisions are plentiful. 
The local residents, many of whom work as extras, are eager to see themselves and their hometown on the screen.
Since 1951, more than 50 movies have been made here. 
The draw is a ready-made Biblical setting that looks more than 2,000 years old and cheap labor. 
A scene from Bernardo Bertolucci's "Sheltering Sky" was shot here, as were Elaine May's "Ishtar," Franco Zefferelli's "Jesus of Nazareth" and David Lean's "Lawrence of Arabia," as well as "The Jewel of the Nile."
An airplane from that film still sits in back of the soundstage where part of "Kundun" is being shot.
Over the past four years, TNT has made six films here; the fifth, "Samson and Delilah," was shown this month. 
And filming for the network's "David," with Jonathan Pryce and Leonard Nimoy, has just been completed.
While on location, actors and crew can stay at the 225-room Berbere Palace hotel, built in 1991.

text:
ï»¿
THERE IS A SAYING IN CHINA: When two people talk, they tell the truth; when three people talk, it becomes a joke; when more than three people talk, it is all lies. 
Tian Zhuangzhuang, the Chinese director whose "Blue Kite" will open on Friday in New York, quoted this saying at dinner recently. 
In attendance were his translator; Lu Liping, the star of the movie and one of China's most popular actresses, and Peng Xia Lin, a director friend of Mr. Tian's. "Of course, this meeting is the exception," Mr. Tian said, laughing.
The 42-year-old director, who lives in Beijing, was in New York for a brief visit on behalf of his film, whose themes are truth and deception, face and mask, censorship and ritual -- in other words, how the domestic and the political intertwine.
"The Blue Kite," which opened last year's Cannes International Film Festival and, at the Tokyo International Film Festival, won awards for best film and best actress, is about a Beijing family from 1953 to the late 60's. 
Less obviously political than Chen Kaige's "Farewell My Concubine," which covers much the same period, Mr. Tian's film steers a course through domestic life. 
Aunts and uncles sit around tables; youngsters play on red-tiled roofs; mothers have hopes and fears for their children; the winter silence in the courtyard is broken only by a cat's meow.
The narrator is a boy named Tietou, whose childhood overlaps the Cultural Revolution. 
The kite in the title is made by Tietou's father just before he is sent away to a labor camp. 
Tietou's mother (Ms. Lu) is married and widowed two more times; other family members marry, fall ill, recover or die. 
Some are imprisoned; some are ardent Maoists; some dream of the Great Society; others merely survive. 
The child grows into a willful youngster and, by the film's end, a rebellious adolescent.
Richard Pena, the director of the New York Film Festival, which showed the film last fall, said of "The Blue Kite": "It's not about action, it's about atmosphere. 
It's the first film to really address how political and personal oppression just became a day-to-day affair. 
How you'd get up every morning and you'd live with it every day, and it affected who you married, who you made love to, where you got a job. 
Everything.
"As good as he's been in the past," Mr. Pena said of Mr. Tian, "with this new film he's reached a new level."
Martin Scorsese, who met Mr. Tian in Tokyo some years ago, was equally enthusiastic in his praise. 
"It's a film of deceptive simplicity that manages to convey the entire history of late 20th-century China," he said of "The Blue Kite."
(Mr. Tian, for his part, is an equally ardent fan of Mr. Scorsese's: on this, his first trip to New York, he had already had lunch with the director; he had seen Mr. Scorsese's "Taxi Driver" 11 times on videotape.)
While the film is not autobiographical, Mr. Tian's family, like most in China, experienced severe hardship and sorrow in the 1960's and 70's. 
His father, Tian Fang, was once head of the Beijing Film Studio, which is now an official Chinese film production unit. 
His mother, Yu Lan, a famous actress in China, is the director of the Children's Studio, which makes movies with and for children. 
Like tens of thousands of Chinese intellectuals, his parents were "re-educated" during the Cultural Revolution. 
"At that time, it was just the way it was," Mr. Tian said.
He remembers setting out one morning to say goodbye to his father. 
"He had been sentenced to hard labor, so I had to get there by 8 A.M., because that's when work began. 
I was 16, and the day before someone had introduced me to my first girlfriend. 
So the ride on my bicycle was quite pleasant. 
I knocked on the iron gates and told the guard I had come to say goodbye to my father."
He remembers hearing the sound of his father's soft cloth shoes approaching, and recalls that his father was carrying a spade. 
"It was his eyes I remember most," he said. 
"I felt like he wanted to say something, but he saw the way I looked, and he said nothing."
His father returned home after the Cultural Revolution but died a few years later. 
Mr. Tian, married and divorced, is the father of an 8-year-old son, Tian Zi, with whom he lives in Beijing.
Tian Zhuangzhuang is part of China's so-called Fifth Generation, a term used to describe the 100-plus students who were the first class to enter the Beijing Film Academy when it reopened after the Cultural Revolution and who graduated around 1980. 
The class included Chen Kaige and Zhang Yimou, whose "Raise the Red Lantern" was considered a breakthrough film for the new Chinese cinema. 
Indeed, some critics now compare China's Fifth Generation film makers with the French New Wave of the 1950's.
Yet it remains difficult for these film makers to get a movie made in China. 
Financing is scarce and dealing with the Central Film Bureau, a part of the Ministry of Broadcasting that functions as a gatekeeper for film making, can be bizarre. 
Mr. Tian learned this when making his second film, "The Horse Thief," an atmospheric work about tribal rights and Buddhist practices shot in Tibet. 
(His first project, "On the Hunting Ground," was an ethnographic movie made in Mongolia in 1985.)
The Central Film Bureau dragged out the process of approving "The Horse Thief" for eight months. 
"While I waited," said Mr. Tian, "my enthusiasm for film making almost went to nil."
He finally made a deal with the agency: He would cut whatever they asked him to cut. 
"I sat with two censors in a room," he said, "and they told me: 'You have to cut here. 
You have to cut there.'
I felt it was an insult. 
So I didn't want to make films anymore."
The film, shot in 1986, was subsequently shown at film festivals and at the Film Forum in New York in 1988.
Frustrated with working with the censors, Mr. Tian turned to making commercial movies and the usual dissipations -- drink, women, gambling. 
"I have traveled a very long and crooked road," he said. 
"But when I turned 40, I felt that if I didn't return to making the kind of films I wanted to make I would become more and more decadent."
Since Mr. Tian was on staff as a director of the Beijing Film Studio, he made "The Blue Kite" there, with money from Hong Kong. 
But when he finished shooting the film, the Beijing studio refused to submit footage to the Central Film Bureau for approval for post-production work. 
(Because China does not have first-class film editing facilities, almost all post-production work is done elsewhere, usually Japan.) Several sources said that his friends smuggled raw footage of the film to Japan and edited it there according to his written instructions.
"In China," he said, "the best way to deal with things is to wait patiently. 
And work hard. 
That's how you prevail."
Any Chinese film must also pass through the Central Film Bureau to be allowed out of the country for film festivals. 
Therefore, when "The Blue Kite" was shown at the Tokyo film festival, without official clearance, the Chinese delegation walked out in protest.
Mr. Tian says he is not interested in making films solely about history. 
"What I'm interested in," he explained, "is people in relation to the environment they are in, that has, of course, a historical setting. 
Movies should be made without aim," much less a narrow political one.
The Government, nonetheless, will not allow the film to be shown in China. 
And since no one in China can go on record as having seen "The Blue Kite," no one there can speak specifically about the film's merits. 
Instead, movie makers who still work in China talk in general about the film's director.
"Tian Zhuangzhuang is my classmate and friend," said Mr. Zhang, who directed "Raise the Red Lantern.""He's one of China's best film makers, and I'm very proud of his achievement."
Mr. Chen believes that Mr. Tian will one day be considered among the most important directors in modern China. 
"I not only admire his works but also admire him as a human being, as a film maker," he said. 
"He tries to find ways to express his feelings about almost everything -- life, the world and himself."
Mr. Tian, who returned to China last month, has resigned from the Beijing Film Studio, which makes his future as a film maker in China all that much more difficult. 
"I am interested in portraying people and their emotions," he said. 
"I like my country. 
I like my people. 
This belief is the education my parents gave me. 
I imagine my journey will be difficult."

A fire killed 79 people in a department store in the northeastern city of Tangshan on Sunday, the official New China News Agency reported today. 
A city fire department official in Tangshan, 100 miles east of Beijing, said 51 people had been injured.
The fire ripped through the three-story Linxi department store during peak shopping hours Sunday afternoon, transforming the store into an inferno, the report said.
"Inside, the three-story building was completely gutted," the news agency said. 
"Outside, walls were blackened by smoke and most windows broken."
The report attributed the fire to workers who neglected safety precautions while welding in the department store.

Concern Over Safety
Safety standards have become the object of increasing concern as China embarks on a nationwide construction boom, fueled by the country's rapid economic growth. 
New buildings and factories are being built quickly, while existing stores and restaurants are being remodeled to serve the emerging consumer society.
Official news reports have said accidents on building sites are on the rise, and safety precautions are said to be often ignored in the race to get things built in short order.
Department stores are seen as particularly dangerous since they are often packed with shoppers, crowded with new sales counters and flammable items, and frequently lack sufficient access to exits.
Â 
Delay in Reporting
Sunday's fire was not reported in tonight's main evening television news because China's official news organizations customarily delay reports about domestic disasters.
In 1991, China reported one of its worst factory fires when a blaze struck a rainwear factory in the southern province of Guangdong, killing at least 66 workers who were sleeping in dormitories attached to the factory building.
In 1976, Tangshan was struck by a major earthquake, measuring 7.8 on the Richter scale, that killed an estimated 250,000 people and destroyed huge sections of the city.
