file: Global Economy Slowly Cuts Use of Fuels Rich in Carbon.txt
text:
ï»¿
Even as the world's expanding population and economy increase atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide that scientists say are warming the earth, the global energy system is moving steadily away from the carbon-rich fuels whose combustion produces the gas.
Experts say atmospheric levels of carbon dioxide may be double that of the pre-industrial era by the end of the next century. 
But they also say the levels would be much higher except for a trend toward lower-carbon fuels that has been going on for more than 100 years, but has been largely unnoticed except by a small band of energy specialists.
The question now, they say, is whether the trend can be accelerated enough to stave off or lessen what many scientists believe is a potentially disruptive global warming.
For nearly a century and a half, fuels with high amounts of carbon have progressively been replaced by those containing less. 
First wood, which is high in carbon, was eclipsed in the late 19th century by coal, which contains less. 
Then oil, with a lower carbon content still, dethroned King Coal in the 1960's.
Now analysts say that natural gas, lighter still in carbon, may be entering its heyday, and that the day of hydrogen -- providing a fuel with no carbon at all, by definition -- may at last be about to dawn.
As a result, the experts estimate, the world's economy today burns less than two-thirds as much carbon per unit of energy produced as it did in 1860. 
In the United States, they estimate, the trend toward lower-carbon fuels combined with greater energy efficiency has, since 1950, reduced by about half the amount of carbon spewed out for each unit of economic production.
But because economic growth and population growth have been so rapid over the decades, overall atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide have steadily risen, to the point that the concentrations may well have doubled by the year 2100.
Mainstream scientists say that this much carbon dioxide could warm the earth, on average, by 3 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit. 
By comparison, that is about half as much as it has warmed since the depths of the last ice age 18,000 to 20,000 years ago.
A change of this magnitude would likely have widespread consequences for the world's climate, weather and human life.
Now, as representatives of 150 governments meet in Bonn in the latest round of global talks on measures to further reduce carbon-dioxide emissions, analysts both in and out of industry say that the next quarter-century is shaping up as a period of technological and economic ferment offering a chance to accelerate the trend toward a low-carbon economy and, eventually, a no-carbon one.
In Bonn, the delegates are trying to work out the details of an agreement forged two years ago in Kyoto, Japan, that could speed up the trend. 
Their work is not expected to be finished for at least a year, and the Kyoto agreement still must be ratified by a sufficient number of countries after that.
However that may turn out, "the decarbonization of the energy system is the single most important fact to emerge from the last 20 years of analysis" of the system, said Dr. Jesse H. Ausubel, an expert on energy and climate at Rockefeller University in New York City. 
Dr. Ausubel predicts that this evolution will produce a carbon-free energy system by the end of the 21st century.
Among some recent signs of the trend are these:
*The Federal Energy Information Administration reported last week that emissions of carbon dioxide by the United States had increased by an average of 1.37 percent a year in the 1990's -- only about half the 2.6-percent rate of growth in economic production. 
Analysts say the discrepancy is evidence that the economy is being decoupled from carbon.
*The agency reported this month that the same is generally true in China, the biggest consumer and producer of coal in the world, where coal production has been reported to be dropping lately. 
"China has dispelled a commonly held notion that economic growth and energy consumption are necessarily coupled," the report said.
*In December, Honda will introduce in the United States a high-efficiency, low-emissions automobile powered partly by gasoline and partly by self-generated electricity. 
It is said to run at 60 miles per gallon of gasoline in town, and 71 on the highway, and to travel 600 to 700 miles on a tank of gas.
Toyota has introduced a similar "hybrid" automobile in Japan, and these cars are "literally kick-the-tires examples of the decarbonized economy," said Hal Harvey, president of the Energy Foundation, a partnership of foundations that promotes energy efficiency and renewable energy.
Other auto makers are also planning hybrids, which are being viewed as a transition, ultimately, to vehicles powered by hydrogen fuel cells that emit no carbon. 
In its planning, the General Motors Corporation has "embraced fuel cells as the technology of choice," but with hybrids coming first, said John Williams, the leader of the company's internal team on global climate issues.
And while auto companies are looking down that track, some of the world's biggest energy companies are looking to provide the appropriate fuels. 
Hydrogen, in particular, has attracted fresh interest.
Until recently, "the hydrogen option was seen as rather distant," said Ged R. Davis, an executive of Shell International in London who analyzes such questions for Royal Dutch/Shell, one of the world's largest energy companies. 
"Now it is looking closer, perhaps over the next decade or two," Mr. Davis added. 
"Most of the energy and car companies are looking at this rather seriously."
Shell itself has established a hydrogen subsidiary.
In the nearer term, hydrogen would be used in fuel cells for cars, trucks and industrial plants, just as it already provides power for orbiting spacecraft. 
But ultimately, hydrogen could also provide a general carbon-free fuel.
The world energy system will not change overnight, of course, if it changes at all. 
And new products must ultimately stand the test of the marketplace. 
But some analysts say that the next two decades or so will be a time of unusual pressure for change, both for environmental and economic reasons, in which companies will be driven to compete for survival and dominance in some sort of emerging new energy system.
Whether companies are seriously pursuing new options or merely preserving them for the future, experts say there seems little doubt that the long-term trend toward decarbonization is real, and that it will most likely continue even in the absence of any shift to hydrogen or renewable energy sources like wind and solar power.
"The future decarbonization rate is likely to be at least as high as the historical one" of about three-tenths of a percent a year, said Dr. Nebojsa Nakicenovic, an expert on energy and the environment with the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis, a research group in Laxenburg, Austria. 
The institute was one of the first groups to study the question.
Oil accounts for the biggest share of global energy consumption today, followed by coal and, closely, by natural gas. 
In most of the world except the United States and China, said Dr. Ausubel of Rockefeller University, coal is either defunct or on the way out, and natural gas will increasingly displace it.
According to several recent analyses, Dr. Nakicenovic said, recoverable natural gas now appears far more abundant than had been previously thought. 
The burning of gas produces, on average, only about a third of the carbon dioxide per unit of energy of coal, and about two-thirds that of oil.
Gas not only can fuel fixed facilities like industrial plants and furnaces, it can also be processed to produce hydrogen for use in carbon-free fuel cells to power automobiles and generate electricity. 
In those cells, there is no combustion; instead, hydrogen reacts chemically with oxygen to produce electricity. 
But when hydrogen is extracted from gas, the residual carbon must somehow be disposed of, possibly by pumping it back into depleted oil and gas wells.
Dr. Ausubel predicts that natural gas will become the dominant fuel of the next 40 to 50 years. 
If so, that alone would be enough to continue the long-term decarbonization trend.
China, which some experts think will emerge as the biggest carbon-dioxide emitter of the 21st century, has greatly reduced its energy consumption per unit of economic output, has closed several coal mines, is seeking to modernize industrial and power plants and is moving toward natural gas, many analysts say.
Not least, they say, the Chinese are worried about the health effects of coal's air pollution. 
Nevertheless, the Energy Information Administration reported last week, China's coal demand is expected to double by 2020.
So while the trend toward a carbon-free economy may continue, Dr. Ausubel says, it might not move rapidly enough to assuage the fears of those who are most concerned about global warming. 
He says that if the trend continues to evolve more or less naturally, with business as usual, it will take another century or so to decarbonize the energy system fully.
By then, he predicts, atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide will be around 500 parts per million, nearly double what they were before the industrial revolution. 
Mainstream scientists say that would be enough to change the earth's climate substantially, make droughts, heat waves and floods worse and raise the sea level to heights that would threaten many low-lying coastal areas and islands. 
Some analysts say that 500 parts per million is a best-case estimate, and that business-as-usual could cause a tripling of pre-industrial carbon-dioxide levels.
Other experts think that concentrations could be held substantially below 500 parts per million if the trend toward decarbonization were to accelerate. 
Mr. Harvey of the Energy Foundation says "prospects are excellent" for an acceleration.
And Mr. Davis, the Shell executive, says his company's analyses suggest that if the proper incentives were in place, new energy technologies could be adopted broadly enough to bring about a peak in oil use and carbon-dioxide emissions by about 2020. 
After that, there would be a decline.
One sort of incentive might lie in the Kyoto agreement, which calls for a group of 39 industrialized countries to reduce their carbon dioxide emissions by an average of 5 percent below 1990 levels over the period 2008 to 2012. 
One mechanism for doing this is a system whereby a country that exceeds its reductions target can earn money by selling that extra reduction to another country that is having trouble meeting its target. 
A similar system, involving company-to-company trading, has been proposed for the United States.
While negotiators struggle over the terms of such arrangements and politicians wrangle over putting the Kyoto accord into effect, many energy analysts seem to agree on one thing: The ultimate goal ought to be a carbon-free economy based largely on hydrogen. 
Dr. Ausubel, for one, predicts that such an economy will materialize.
Many would agree with Mr. Williams of General Motors: "I think I'm on pretty solid ground in saying the long-term vision is hydrogen. 
But there's a lot of work between here and there."

file: Global Women_s Forum Fights China_s Barriers.txt
text:
ï»¿
Organizers of an international forum on women that was expected to draw more than 40,000 people to Beijing this summer are balking at a Chinese demand to move their conference 32 miles away from the Chinese capital and will ask Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali's help.
The meeting, called the NGO Forum on Women, a nongovernmental organization, is scheduled to be held almost simultaneously with the official United Nations-sponsored Fourth World Conference on Women, also in Beijing. 
All large United Nations conferences now have parallel sessions for nongovernmental organizations, and no host government has tried to control them like this, organizers said today.
Diplomats and United Nations officials say that Beijing appears to be wary of demonstrations by nongovernmental groups on political or human rights issues. 
In addition to trying to isolate the nongovernmental forum by relocating it to Huairou, a tourist area near the Great Wall, China is blocking delegations of Tibetan women, women from Taiwan and lesbian groups and is expected to deny visas to others.
"We have set a deadline of May 24 to resolve this," Irene M. Santiago, executive director of the forum, said in an interview today.
Ms. Santiago has just returned from four days in Beijing, where she and Khunying Supatra Masdit, a Thai politician who will preside over the nongovernmental forum, were invited by the Chinese to look at alternative sites after they protested the move to Huairou.
When the General Assembly decided in 1990 to give the conference to China, it was stated explicity in the agreement that nongovernmental groups play an important part in the deliberations by offering expertise and lobbying on various issues.
Two years ago, a site closer to the United Nations conference, the Workers' Sports Service Center, was selected. 
But in March, the Chinese informed the forum organizers that there were structural defects in a gymnasium at the sports center and that the forum would have to be relocated.
"We went to Beijing because we had been given two alternative sites along with Huairou," Ms. Santiago said today. 
"We visited the two sites, but then were told that they were not in fact available. 
Huairou was our only option."
She described Huairou as a scenic town that "doesn't have any of the facilities we need to have a successful forum."
She said that meeting rooms and accommodations were scattered all over the town, which took them 50 minutes to reach in a car with a police escort. 
Although they protested that they would be out of reach of official delegations and journalists covering the conference, they were told the site was better because they would have more space and more meeting rooms in Huairou.
Forum organizers listed several other possible sites, including an Olympic center, the Beijing Sports University and the original site minus the faulty gymnasium.

file: Go East, Young Man.txt
text:
ï»¿
MARCO POLO AND
THE DISCOVERY
OF THE WORLD
By John Larner.
Illustrated. 250 pp. 
New Haven:
Yale University Press. 
$29.95.
In 1392, John Larner tells us in this erudite and highly personal book, a Florentine patrician on winter duty as mayor in an isolated Italian village decided to transcribe the whole of Marco Polo's travels, "to pass the time and to keep melancholy away."
At the conclusion of the exercise, the patrician expressed his own views on Polo's manuscript: "What he says seems to me not so much lies as more than miracles. 
And yet what he speaks of could be true, but I don't believe it -- though in the world one finds very different things from one country to another. 
But these, it seems to me -- though I've enjoyed copying them -- are things not to be believed nor to give faith to, so it seems to me."
This sense of befuddlement mixed with awe is still true for readers of Marco Polo. 
Despite the opacities and repetitions of Marco's lengthy manuscript, the fact that almost nothing is known about him as a person and the knowledge that chances of finding any new information are slim indeed, Marco Polo resolutely refuses to go away. 
All we can be fairly sure of is that a Venetian merchant called Marco Polo, born around 1254, traveled to China by the overland route between 1271 and 1274, in the company of his uncle and his father. 
The three returned safely in 1295, bringing back with them some objects acquired in the Far East. 
A few years later, while under some kind of house arrest in Genoa, Marco Polo dictated a version of his adventures to a professional writer called Rustichello. 
Though the original manuscript is lost, various copies -- some distributed by Marco himself after his release -- began to circulate around 1307. 
He married in the period between his return to Venice and his stay in Genoa, and had three daughters. 
He died in 1324.
Virtually everything else has to be deduced, either contextually from what we know of the trade patterns and social customs of the medieval European world and the Mongols who ruled China at the time or from the raw contents of the different manuscripts -- which vary enormously. 
The result is a paradise for imaginative scholars, who are free to apply virtually any hypothesis to the sparse facts and ample wordage in front of them. 
A steadfast few further confuse the issue by denying that Marco Polo was ever anywhere near China. 
The harsh fact is that one cannot prove that he was in China; there are no Chinese or Mongol documents to substantiate his claim, no missionary letters giving even a glancing reference to him, no Arab travelers who ran into him. 
All one can do is take his manuscript at face value, and challenge the opposition to prove that he was not there.
Larner, a historian at Glasgow University, has a special expertise in the field of medieval and Renaissance geography, and "Marco Polo and the Discovery of the World" is an eloquent attempt to prove that Marco Polo's main importance was to the discipline of geography. 
This focus leads Larner to much creative rethinking of things that have puzzled many readers. 
For example, the attempt to recreate the exact route Marco took to China, as it is described in his manuscript, has absorbed scores of scholars, and countless maps have sought to record some version of "The Voyages of the Polos."
But as Larner ingeniously argues, what Polo seems to be presenting as the route he traveled is not in fact a route that he himself traveled at such and such a time. 
"It is an organizing device, the route along which Marco and Rustichello lead their readers from west to east and then back from east to west, the route through the book."
The book itself "is not a story of adventure and it is not a description of travels."
Nor is it any kind of merchant handbook in the sense of giving an accurate depiction of the trade flows of a precise area Polo visited at a specific time. 
It lists rare goods of many kinds and the huge volume of trade in various cities of China as a way of awakening a "sense of wonder" in Marco's readers for the extraordinary reach of the world that he now knew existed, and wanted to share. 
"The cumulative effect of these, for us, tedious repetitions, would have been to give the medieval reader an extraordinary vision of a whole hitherto unknown world of cities engaged in trade and commerce set within the East."
Marco Polo was thus, in a sense, a missionary of geographical knowledge.
In Larner's analysis, Polo was a man with an unusual, indeed unique, vision, who knew that he had an astounding geographical story to tell but no skill at how to tell it. 
Larner intuits that Marco had sheaves of notes, mementos of his journeyings in the East, but they were jumbled and disorganized, and he had no idea how to bring order to them. 
He also concludes that Marco had only a peripheral interest in his own personal experiences. 
Rustichello, on the other hand, a man moderately well known in the later 13th century as a storyteller and writer of courtly romances, saw the narrative possibilities of Marco's material, but had a different set of priorities. 
Their fortuitous meeting in Genoa led to a hybrid manuscript that is what has come down to us. 
In Larner's words, "What the modern reader is not looking for, but what he gets, is a work of geography which Rustichello has tried very hard to place within the transitions, formulas, dialogue and general rhetorical traditions of chivalric literature."
Larner adduces a grand range of sources to elaborate on this theme, and to trace the exact periods -- and even the precise atlases and globes -- in which we can find later Renaissance geographers seeing the value of Marco's work concealed within the Rustichello carapace. 
Much of this is fine scholarship, artfully argued. 
But Marco does have a way of running away with those who study him, leading them helter-skelter down the leafy avenues of inference.
This is especially true when scholars try to define his character and inner nature. 
Larner finds in one group of manuscripts -- a 1470 version known only in an 18th-century copy, and a version by the Venetian humanist Ramusio published in 1559 -- what he believes to be "a more personal authorial statement" by Marco, which included Marco's views on such dangerous topics as religious tolerance. 
He also tells us these manuscripts are "unquestionably authentic" -- though it appears to me they have much material that could easily have been inserted long after Marco's death. 
Marco's curious manuscript becomes "a mediation to the West of such Chinese geographical culture as has been absorbed by its Mongol rulers."
Marco himself is given an identity, as "a minor Mongolian civil servant," a student of topography and human geography, customs and folklore and Mongol authority structures. 
"Then, having taken early retirement, he has sought an audience for his memories."
The tone of Marco's book becomes for Larner that of a man whose "home was China," which explains why his book conveys no sense of "culture shock."
Marco's return to Venice was thus not a homecoming so much as a "virtually enforced exile from Mongolian China."
Marco -- and this is high romanticism on Larner's part -- brought back with him to Europe not simply the treasured objects later inventoried in his will "but the whole of the East where he had spent most of his life and which he would now attempt to recreate in words."
Marco was justified, Larner feels, in these grand hopes. 
His book turned out to give the European world "an unparalleled opening of horizons" and was a "triumph" for both him and Rustichello. 
Larner himself in conclusion reiterates his conviction that Marco's enigmatic book has "its own curious poetry, and the flavor of the author's own enigmatic personality."
To those less convinced, Larner is generous. 
For me, one of the grace notes in his study was the wondrous parody of Marco Polo found tucked in Boccaccio's "Decameron," quoted here: "So away I went, and after setting out from Venison, I visited the Greek Calends, then rode at a brisk pace through the Kingdom of Algebra and through Bordello, eventually reaching Bedlam."
It is only the most gracious authors who can thus tease their subjects, their readers and themselves.

file: GOODWILL GAMES_Wilkinson Leading the U.S. Toward a Diving Comeback.txt
text:
ï»¿
Until the 1980's, the world's best divers usually came from the United States and its college and club systems. 
Then the Chinese discovered and developed the sport, the Russians made a resurgence, the great American champion Greg Louganis retired and American diving struggled.
Now the Americans seem to be making a small comeback, although when the Goodwill Games diving competition ended tonight, China and Russia had won the most medals. 
After 9 of the 10 events, China had 12 medals (4 gold), Russia 7 (4 gold), the United States 3 (1 gold) and the rest of the world 5. 
The best diver here was Dmitri Sautin, a Russian who won the men's 3-meter springboard on Sunday and the 10-meter platform tonight.
But the Americans made a strong impression Sunday night when 20-year-old Laura Wilkinson, a University of Texas junior from Houston, won the women's platform title. 
Wilkinson had won seven United States championships, but never a big international competition. 
And this one was big. 
The field included the world champion (Olena Zhupina of Ukraine) and runner-up (Cai Yuyan of China).
Here, every contender except Wilkinson made at least one major error -- an overrotation here, an underrotation there, a failure to keep the knees straight or the legs together. 
Wilkinson made no big mistakes. 
And when she needed a solid last dive to overtake Cai, she made it, a back 1 1/2 somersault with 2 1/2 twists, that drew scores of 8.0 from all seven judges.
Starting the ninth and last round, Wilkinson trailed Cai. 
Then Cai, only 16 but more experienced than Wilkinson, barely finished a 3 1/2 somersault pike. 
The door was open for Wilkinson, who dived next. 
She said her nervousness disappeared, and she nailed her dive. 
But she said that for her and for the American team, this was only one competition.
"I need to keep working on everything," she said. 
"And since the other teams are so good, we've had to work twice as hard to be able to compete with them. 
I think we're making progress. 
I don't know if it was U.S. diving slipping so much as the Chinese and Russians getting better."
Li Hongping of Mission Viejo, Calif., a former Chinese champion and one of the three coaches of this American team, was cheered by Wilkinson's victory.
"It's very significant," he said, "because it shows our divers are as competent as anyone else. 
This builds confidence in her and in the whole diving program in the U.S.
"It's very difficult to compete with someone who is training more, like the Chinese and the Russians. 
We have to be mentally tougher than anyone and have a more positive attitude. 
I'm seeing that. 
It happened with Laura and that's why she won a gold medal, so this is a very good step."

text:
ï»¿
Despite a warning from the National Security Council that a fund-raising luncheon at a Buddhist temple should be approached with "great, great caution," Vice President Al Gore made the appearance anyway after his own national security adviser raised no objections to the trip, Mr. Gore's spokeswoman said today.
The issue arose today after documents released by the White House showed that in an E-mail exchange of messages between John J. Norris, a member of Mr. Gore's national security staff, and Robert L. Suettinger, one of the National Security Council's Asia affairs specialists, Mr. Suettinger raised concerns about how the 1996 event would be perceived by China. 
He also suggested that the donors might have a "hidden agenda."
The computer messages are also the latest document to make clear that members of the Vice President's staff were aware beforehand that the luncheon at the temple was intended to raise campaign money, despite Mr. Gore's initial assertion in the face of news reports last fall that he had thought it a "community event" and not a fund-raiser.
"Hsing Yun would host a fund-raising lunch for about 150 people in the V.P.'s honor," Mr. Norris said in a message to Mr. Suettinger on April 15, referring to Venerable Master Hsing Yun, a Taiwanese Buddhist leader. 
"Any problems with the V.P. participating in this event from the perspective of U.S.-China relations?"
On April 19, Mr. Suettinger replied: "This is terra incognita to me. 
Certainly from the perspective of Taiwan/China balancing, this would be clearly a Taiwan event, and would be seen as such. 
I guess my reaction would be one of great, great caution. 
They may have a hidden agenda."
Mr. Norris's E-mail message said the fund-raising event would be held at the end of June. 
In fact, it was held 10 days after Mr. Suettinger issued his words of caution. 
Mr. Gore appeared on April 29, as the main speaker at the Hsi Lai Temple, which is in the Los Angeles suburb of Hacienda Heights and is described by its founders as the Western Hemisphere's largest Buddhist monastery.
Lorraine Voles, the Vice President's spokeswoman, said today thathis office had taken the words of caution from the National Security Council "very seriously."
But, she said, Mr. Gore nonetheless went ahead with the event because his own national security adviser, Leon S. Fuerth, after consultation with the council and a separate inquiry to the State Department, "posed no objection to the event from a foreign policy standpoint."
Mr. Gore's appearance came at a tense time between the United States and China, just a month after the Administration had sent United States warships near Taiwan in response to Chinese military exercises that were timed to Taiwan's first direct presidential election.
Mr. Gore's stop at the temple has been a continuing source of controversy, because $140,000 in campaign money was raised in a religious institution and also because of questions about the true source of some of the money.
In addition, Mr. Gore has amended his account of what he knew about the event.
The Democratic National Committee has said that in hindsight, it considers the raising of donations in a religious institution, which has tax-exempt status, to have been a mistake. 
The Democrats reimbursed the temple for the $15,000 it spent on food and other expenses for the event, and later returned some of the campaign money.
The documents released today show that Mr. Gore's foreign policy staff was concerned enough about his appearance to inquire about its propriety. 
Ms. Voles said that on the advice of the State Department, Mr. Gore's staff had worked with the organizers of the event "to minimize any risk of negative reaction from the Chinese Government" by making sure that the luncheon was not identified as a Taiwan event, that there was no display of Taiwanese flags or political symbols and that no politicians from Taiwan "were allowed to exploit the event."
Ms. Voles also said Mr. Norris's description of the luncheon as a fund-raising event was not inconsistent with Mr. Gore's own remarks. 
"Some members of our staff may have known the event was a fund raiser, but he did not," she said. 
"The briefing paper provided for him did not say it was a fund raiser."
She added: "I'm not saying there wasn't a disconnect here. 
The senior political staff traveling with the Vice President also did not know it was a fund raiser."
Last autumn Mr. Gore initially said he had believed that he was attending a "community event" for Asian supporters of the Democrats. 
Then, in December, the White House released thousands of pages of documents that included one on the luncheon that had been sent to the Vice President's office by the Democratic National Committee's fund-raising division. 
Mr. Gore then acknowledged that he had known that the Asian Pacific Leadership Council, which he addressed, required membership payments to the Democratic Party. 
But he said he had not known that the luncheon itself was intended to raise money.

file: GRADING THE SECRETARY_ A special report._Albright, a Bold Voice Abroad, Finds Her Role Limited at Ho.txt
text:
ï»¿
With her bold public stands undermined by irresolution in the White House and her experience rendered less relevant by new economic crises, Madeleine K. Albright has had a tough 20 months as Secretary of State.
Ms. Albright remains the Clinton Administration's principal foreign-policy voice and the liaison with a recalcitrant Republican Congress, and is greeted like a celebrity very popular in the country beyond Washington. 
But a President averse to military risk, preoccupied by the fallout from his relationship with an intern and unwilling to offend core Democratic constituencies has not supported her on key issues like the Middle East and Kosovo.
Her assiduous courtship of Congress was instrumental in winning Senate ratification of NATO expansion and the Chemical Weapons Convention from a Congress verging on isolationism. 
But Ms. Albright has had little to do with the few other Clinton successes of the second term: a settlement in Northern Ireland and a reinvigoration of relations with China.
And now, as Russia melts, tainting one of the relationships of which Mr. Clinton has been proudest, this is a particularly vulnerable period for the Administration's foreign policy. 
Russia was part of widening international crisis that has now hit Wall Street, threatening the booming economy that has kept his popularity afloat.
But Ms. Albright and the State Department have not been crucial players, White House officials say. 
With Mr. Clinton so distracted, it is not immediately clear who is in charge.
The evidence appears to favor the national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, and the Treasury Secretary, Robert E. Rubin, though, instead of Ms. Albright.
In a recent interview, Ms. Albright bristled at specific criticism, but says it is only natural that the economic experts take the lead on their issues.
"For me, what's important is what people think in years hence," Ms. Albright said. 
"Whether I used this four-year period in a way that ultimately accomplished what I want: to create the underpinnings for the American role in the next century, while taking care of what needs to be done to problem-solve."
Ms. Albright attended only one recent meeting of the National Economic Council, the functional equivalent of the National Security Council, and that was on Japan.
She and her officials did regularly urge a broader view of American interests in Asia than simply the financial, including security and the stabilization of democratizing Asian allies, and coordinated interagency aid packages for Thailand and Indonesia.
But her call for President Suharto of Indonesia to step down occurred only hours before he did so anyway, and in general, Ms. Albright and her department have let Treasury run the show.
Was this an opportunity missed, or simply, as Ms. Albright and her aides contend, the most efficient and collegial way to coordinate a post-Soviet world with new, nontraditional challenges?
In the Middle East, on the other hand, Ms. Albright has been central, trying to coax and cajole Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel into a compromise that would refresh a deterioriating peace and help restore American credibility in the Arab world. 
But her intensive efforts have not yet produced the clear personal triumph that zero-sum Washington seems to require.
In May, she gambled that public pressure and an ultimatum would move Mr. Netanyahu, but the White House failed to support her in the face of a lobbying firestorm stoked by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
She kept the Administration engaged in Bosnia, where it could not reasonably retreat.
Here in Sarajevo on Sunday and again today, Ms. Albright spoke passionately and effectively about the effort required to make a multinational, democratic Bosnia come to pass, and she was eager to make it vividly clear that American aid would only come to those who worked to carry out the Dayton accords.
But her advocacy of an aggressive approach -- including a credible threat of air strikes -- toward the Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic, over his crackdown on ethnic Albanian separatists in Kosovo Province did not find wide support within NATO and was rejected by Mr. Clinton in the spring.
Her vow in March that "we are not going to stand by and watch the Serbian authorities do in Kosovo what they can no longer get away with doing in Bosnia" has proven hollow.
Other American threats have seemed equally empty -- against Iraq to defend United Nations weapons inspections, for example.
That has called into question the American commitment to a sustained war on terrorism, a commitment Ms. Albright and others pledged would begin with the missile strikes against Afghanistan and Sudan.
Â 
Some Early Victories For a New Secretary
Ms. Albright's accession as Secretary of State, becoming the highest-ranking woman in American history, prompted enormous popular and media interest. 
She attracted attention for her newly discovered Jewish background as well as for successful efforts to expand NATO and to her push to articulate a more forceful American position than her dry, quiet predecessor, Warren M. Christopher.
She quickly earned respect from her French, Russian, Chinese and Arab colleagues. 
Early victories in Congress were hailed, and she has won important policy shifts on Iran and Cuba, while helping to prevent a trade war with Europe over sanctions.
But with domestic problems undercutting Mr. Clinton's international credibility, the Administration foreign policy seems ever more reactive. 
And with the bombing of American Embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, followed by missile strikes in Afghanistan and the Sudan, with civil war in Kosovo, nuclear tests by India and Pakistan, the Russian economic and political problems and the unresolved crisis in Iraq flaring again, the world seems a more dangerous and unstable place than when Ms. Albright came to office.
Ms. Albright's greatest virtues -- clarity and an intelligent, forceful voice connecting with the public and Congress -- have not diminished, said a senior White House official who admires her. 
But as the Administration faces diverse and less manageable problems, many due to the economic problems that began in Asia, "her virtues seem less impressive or timely," the official said, "because neither economics nor strategy are her strengths, and her depth lies in European issues, not Asian ones."
Even Ms. Albright's hard work with Congress -- in particular with Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina -- has not yet produced a deal to repay Washington's debt to the United Nations or funds to replenish the International Monetary Fund reserves, both described as high priorities by her aides. 
Compromises have been stymied by a fight with House Republicans over abortion policy.
"My predecessors had a different world to deal with in which the parameters were fairly set," Ms. Albright said. 
"They had the possibility of focusing all their attention on one or two issues."
By contrast, she said, she is trying to "put into play a lot of issues that I see as challenges we're facing," like nuclear nonproliferation, economics and the effective use of sanctions, issues that were at the center of a January review of priorities.
Â 
The Land Mines And the War Crimes
Ms. Albright has failed to achieve some of the human-rights goals she described as among the most important to her. 
She was an early champion of a ban on land mines. 
Last year, however, in Ottawa, the United States was nearly alone in opposing a treaty.
As a Central European whose family fled first the Nazis and then the Communists, she has been especially concerned about crimes against humanity. 
She created an Ambassador for War Crimes and lobbied for a permanent international tribunal to prosecute them.
But at a Rome conference to accomplish that goal, the United States was part of a small minority refusing to sign a treaty to create a permanent tribunal. 
In both cases, the Pentagon and Congress successfully argued that the only superpower required special exceptions.
Ms. Albright said she continues to champion her principles, but she cannot forget America's responsibilities. 
"I have to balance enunciating the principles and leading the way with the pragmatism of getting things done and the power of the United States," she said.
But there is now a new expression in diplomatic circles -- "to pull an Ottawa" -- which means to promote a new initiative and then abandon it at the end.
Ms. Albright's fierce rhetorical battles with the Iraqis at the United Nations helped catapult her into the Secretary's elegant office on the seventh floor. 
And in a corridor leading off from it, she keeps a comic shrine, a collection of cartoons, newspaper cuttings and other mementos of her tussles with Iraq.
But the Iraq problem persists. 
The latest crisis is an outgrowth of the inconclusive standoff last March, which did little for the reputation of Mr. Clinton's foreign-policy team.
Iraq continues to serve as a reminder of the limits of American power, of the post-Soviet difficulties in orchestrating allies and of the continuing reluctance of Mr. Clinton to use force in risky circumstances.
Â 
The Big Fiasco In Columbus
But the televised town hall meeting in Columbus, Ohio, in February, was the most visible fiasco. 
Ms. Albright and Mr. Berger, the security adviser, and Defense Secretary William S. Cohen were unable to silence hecklers or to sound convincing about why a nearly isolated United States might need to bomb Iraq.
The Ohio meeting -- organized by the White House to use Ms. Albright's skills and popularity -- began the erosion of her reputation among the foreign-policy elite of which she has been a member for so long.
"If you look around the world for the big challenges now, where's the Secretary of State?" asked Robert B. Zoellick, former Under Secretary of State for James A. Baker 3d, who enjoyed a level of access to his President, George Bush, and influence over him that seems denied to Ms. Albright. "To an outsider, she's M.I.A. 
People run issues case by case, but there's a sense the show is being managed by Berger."
The Administration manages crises but has no clear strategic framework, Mr. Zoellick said. 
"How do different problems relate to one another?
It starts with the President, but it's not her forte or Berger's. 
If you don't have a sense of where you want to take the country, you won't get there."
Michael Mandelbaum, of Johns Hopkins University, who criticized first-term foreign policy as "social work," thinks the current team is doing decently at managing the smaller crises of the post-cold-war era, which have less to do with national security and diplomacy.
"Certainly in this second presidential term, by far the most important figures in foreign policy" are Treasury Secretary Rubin and his deputy, Lawrence H. Summers, Mr. Mandelbaum said. 
"For that we should be grateful. 
A world with a financial crisis is far safer than a world with a military crisis, and they've been doing pretty well. 
But Albright doesn't seem to be a player in all this."
Â 
Success With China: Who Gets Credit?
Richard N. Haass of the Brookings Institution, who was on the National Security Council staff under President Bush, said "the one significant accomplishment in the second term" has been to renew relations with China. 
"There you can see a policy initiative and presidential investment," he said. 
"One senses that the engine for that has been the President and the National Security Council."
In the interview, Ms. Albright defended her involvement and that of her strong team in the full range of foreign policy, from Asia and China to Iran and Cuba. 
On financial matters, she said, she has been working to insure that the diplomatic, human and security aspects are fully grasped.
As a former academic, she has been happy to reach down to the regional assistant secretaries and to urge them "to think outside the box," wanting career officers to compete for ideas with outsiders. 
She has encouraged Under Secretaries Thomas R. Pickering and Stuart E. Eizenstat, and Deputy Secretary Strobe Talbott, "to drive policy and make things happen," an official said.
"Economic issues we have brought right into the department," Ms. Albright said, "and we have an Under Secretary who's strong -- Stu Eizenstat -- really working on sanctions issues and on trying to meld the financial with the assistance part of the Asian financial crisis."
She has pushed hard, as she promised him she would, Mr. Eizenstat said, to make State a serious player again on economic issues. 
Treasury gets the headlines over Asia, he said, "but we and she have been intimately involved with the humanitarian and political dimensions."
She is confident about her managing role as Secretary of State, as the prime foreign-policy spokesman for the Administration and as a formulator of key policy. 
And she rejects the notion that Mr. Clinton's choice of Richard C. Holbrooke to be chief American delegate to the United Nations -- someone who was said to have been a candidate for Secretary of State before Ms. Albright was chosen -- is a sign that her own star is waning or wanting.
"Washington is what it is," she said, shrugging. 
"People think you're terrific, and then they think you're too terrific, so then they let you know that you're not. 
You can't be in a position of being the visible voice for the United States and not be out there to be praised and criticized."
Ms. Albright and Mr. Berger have a friendship dating back to the presidential campaign of Michael S. Dukakis of Massachusetts, when Ms. Albright was the chief foreign-policy adviser to a candidate who took almost unremitting heat for not having a strong foreign-policy view. 
Despite moments of annoyance -- usually over personnel -- presidential briefings or second-guessing about the results of specific diplomatic missions, Ms. Albright and Mr. Berger are each other's closest advisers. 
They hash out policy in advance and speak many times a day -- a sharp contrast to the tension between Mr. Christopher and Anthony Lake, or the raging warfare under Jimmy Carter -- the last Democratic President -- between Cyrus R. Vance and Zbigniew Brzezinski.
Â 
Albright and Berger Are Both Pragmatists
"This is not the foreign-policy President who wakes up thinking what notes he can pen to his foreign colleagues," a senior Administration official said, a reference, apparently, to Mr. Bush, who was famous for his hand-written correspondence to world leaders. 
"So Berger becomes the guy who doesn't make foreign policy so much as broker it."
In meetings, another senior White House official said, "she is pragmatic and a consensus builder, like Berger, despite her reputation outside as an uncompromising, six-gun shooting moralist."
She arrives well-briefed and armed with a collective department view, in contrast to Mr. Cohen, whose well-armed Pentagon often gets its way regardless. 
She is "articulate on issues she knows well, and tends to put aside the talking points and draw from her own experience, and she's best when she does that."
Ms. Albright dealt movingly with the emotional and security crisis surrounding the bombing of the American Embassies in Kenya and Tanzania and the deaths of many of her employees, and she has handled Mr. Clinton's personal troubles with dignity.
But her finest policy moment lately has been a shift in the treatment of Iran after the election of the moderate Mohammad Khatami as President. 
While maintaining demands for a halt to terrorism and Iran's nuclear, chemical and missile programs, she pushed Mr. Clinton to a more receptive Iran policy.
"It was hard and had internal criticism, but she got it done with Sandy and the President," avoiding an interagency battle, an official said.
After her recent speech laying out the new policy -- to which Iran has not yet responded -- the President took her aside to congratulate her, she said, "for threading the needle."
Similarly, she used contacts with Pope John Paul II, the Congress and Cuban exiles in Miami to allow direct relief flights from the United States to Cuba to resume and to let relatives send money.
Ms. Albright is also praised for her work with the Russian Foreign Minister, Yevgeny M. Primakov, which helped forge a new relationship between NATO and Russia.
At one point, aides remember, as Mr. Primakov argued for secondary military status for new NATO members, Ms. Albright said: "Neither the President nor I will negotiate over the heads of the peoples of Central Europe. 
That happened once before and it's not going to happen again."
Mr. Primakov was silent, then diverted the conversation, and never pressed the issue so hard again, the aides say.
But Russian policy is generally run by Mr. Talbott and is dominated by the economic and political crisis, making Mr. Primakov -- and Ms. Albright -- less important.
Ms. Albright also pushed the Pentagon to act more decisively in support of political goals in Bosnia and to keep troops there without a deadline.
Her conversations with the Bosnian Serb President, Biljana Plavsic, were crucial in encouraging her to challenge Radovan Karadzic.
On Kosovo, she argues that -- unlike in Bosnia -- Washington and NATO were involved early and got Europe to act. 
A resolution is not yet clear, she says, but the ground is prepared.
Ms. Albright is also proud of using her unprecedented telephone relationship with the Chinese Foreign Minister to organize the Security Council's five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain -- to condemn nuclear tests by India and Pakistan.
At their June meeting in Geneva, she told the others that they are "always talking about a multipolar and not a unipolar world."
This was their chance to prove it, she said, "so one country doesn't take a principled stand and the others sign up the contracts."
Â 
She Will Await History's Judgment
With all the "profound ideological confusion" facing a post-cold-war Secretary of State, said Moises Naim, editor of Foreign Policy, this is not a period for "grand strategy."
Ms. Albright's role, he said, is inevitably one of a goalkeeper.
But Secretaries of State are often defined by challenges. 
Mr. Baker, for instance, had a great crisis thrust upon him, the Persian Gulf war, and a great opportunity, the collapse of Communism.
So far, Ms. Albright has not had such a test or made such an opportunity of the growing world economic problems.
"I can't operate on the basis of instant gratification on any part of my daily work," she said.
"The policies that are being put into place are longer term. 
It may be the next Secretary of State will reap the rewards of what I've done. 
Sitting in this chair you get the sense that you are a part of history."
She noted her recent induction into the national Women's Hall of Fame. 
"When they say I'm the highest-ranking woman in the history of the United States, that's pretty amazing. 
I don't mind occasionally having someone criticize me."
Judith Kipper of the Council on Foreign Relations, while a fierce critic of United States Middle East policy, praises Ms. Albright for showing the way.
"She can be soft with her children, motherly and nice, and go shopping and be all the things a decent person can be," Ms. Kipper said.
"But when it comes to the work, she's tough and serious. 
There's no gender in the work."

text:
ï»¿
Police raids in New York and Hong Kong over the weekend took aim at a Chinese gang that has become New York City's most powerful Asian crime organization, gaining wealth and influence through the smuggling of Chinese immigrants, investigators say.
The gang, known as the Fuk Ching, has been operating in New York for several years, but came under increased police scrutiny recently because of its role in helping to organize the ill-fated voyage of a tramp steamer that ran aground off Queens in June with nearly 300 Chinese men and women aboard.
The leader of the gang, Guo Liang Chi, 27, a convicted extortionist who is widely known as Ah Kay, was among 14 members or associates of the gang taken into custody. 
Mr. Guo was arrested in Hong Kong.
Mr. Guo, who first entered the United States as an illegal immigrant at the age of 15, had left New York early this year as warfare broke out in the ranks of the Fuk Ching (pronounced fook-ching) over control of the profits from the smuggling of immigrants.
Federal investigators and New York Police detectives say the extent of Mr. Guo's influence over the gang after he went abroad is unclear. 
But they believe he remained an important figure in the financing and coordination of shipments of illegal immigrants, both by sea and air. 
The gang itself may have become somewhat fragmented, the authorities say, but its estimated 25 to 30 members and dozens of associates remain deeply involved in human smuggling and other crimes.
The gang takes its name from Fujian Province in southern China, a coastal area that has been the source of most of the illegal Chinese immigrants landing in the United States in recent years. 
The name, Fuk Ching, translates as Young People of Fujian.
Like other Asian gangs, the Fuk Ching are extremely secretive and operate in small groups or cells, the police say. 
Perhaps their greatest asset is their language, a dialect that is colorful and complex, unintelligible to most other Chinese and, of course, to the police.
No one knows how many Chinese immigrants the Fuk Ching has helped spirit into this country, but the police say the numbers run into the thousands, with each immigrant paying $25,000 to $30,000 for passage. 
Initially, the Fuk Ching, like some of the half dozen or so other Asian gangs in New York, worked as contractors for the businessmen in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan who ran the human smuggling operations, the authorities say. 
Now, they say, it takes shares in the profitable syndicates that put the smuggling ventures together.
The main role of the gangs, the authorities say, remains the same. 
They take charge of the immigrants on arrival and hold them in bare apartments, basements and warehouses until friends or relatives pay the smuggling fees. 
But as financiers of the smuggling operations, their cut is bigger.
Â 
Mistreatment of Immigrants
Many immigrants have been beaten and threatened with death when the money for their trips has been slow in coming, the police say. 
Others have been roughed up for no apparent reason.
In June, the police found eight Chinese immigrants being held in a house in Sheepshead Bay after a 21-year-old Chinese woman escaped by climbing out a window as her captors slept. 
Several men, she said, had forced her into a car shortly after her arrival without documents at Kennedy International Airport, taken her to the house in Sheepshead Bay and raped her repeatedly. 
Two men in the group said they were beaten every day.
Like other Asian gangs in New York, the police say, the Fuk Ching also make money by shaking down businesses in Chinatown for protection money, providing guards for illegal gambling houses and brothels and by serving as couriers and bodyguards for drug dealers.
"But they prefer smuggling people," said one Federal investigator who spoke on condition of anonymity, "because it's very lucrative and the risk is much lower. 
The worst they can get for an immigration violation is five years in jail. 
If they get caught with a package of heroin, it's much worse. 
They could go away for 20 years."
Â 
Pressure From the President
Until the tramp steamer, the Golden Venture, ran aground off Queens and 10 people died, the chances of a smuggler getting caught or even receiving a five-year sentence were slim because investigators focused on crimes that carried bigger penalties. 
But President Clinton has now ordered the Justice Department to apply racketeering statutes, which provide for stiffer penalties, to human cargo smugglers.
Law-enforcement officials said the Fuk Ching leader, Mr. Guo, would be charged with ordering the murders of two subordinates, gunned down while they were getting telephone beepers in an electronics shop on Allen Street in Chinatown in early January, in the start of the battle for control of the human cargo business.
In April, two of Mr. Guo's allies were wounded by gunmen as they sat in a parked van on a darkened street in Bridgeport, Conn. 
A little more than a month later, one of the men wounded in Bridgeport and two of Mr. Guo's brothers were shot to death in what the police described as a gang "safe house" in Teaneck, N.J. 
Another of Mr. Guo's supporters died in the Teaneck shooting and one other was wounded.

file: Growing Pains for a Doll Maker_A Model Case of Risks and Rewards in Small Business.txt
text:
ï»¿
It isn't all crinoline dresses and cute blinky blue eyes in the doll business.
Last Christmas, Georgetown Collection Inc., a hot maker of collectible porcelain dolls, bet the survival of its business on play dolls for girls aged 6 to 11. 
It called the line the Magic Attic Club, 80 percent of which would have to be sold during the holidays.
Then the newest shipment of dolls from the company's factory in China arrived. 
And suddenly, six weeks before Christmas Day, the company's 100 employees found themselves scrambling to correct a disastrous and unforeseen product flaw: the dolls' arms were falling off.
For thousands of parents and little girls who had sent in their orders, Christmas morning was in jeopardy. 
But Georgetown faced nothing less than its demise. 
And so, secretaries, accountants, managers and the company's president toiled long into the night for weeks to reassemble 40,000 dolls and fix 80,000 little arms.
That effort saved the company and gave Magic Attic such a smashing season that it is now poised for success. 
Takeover offers and deals from feature-film producers, television syndicators and CD-ROM entrepreneurs are pouring in.
But there is no happy ending just yet. 
The privately held Georgetown is still struggling. 
Rich with ideas, expertise and enterprise, but capital poor, it is trying to keep up with skyrocketing demand while eyeing its potential competitors warily.
In many ways, Georgetown can be seen as a paradigm for thousands of small American companies that are trying to exploit their specialized knowledge, pulling themselves up by their own entrepreneurial bootstraps.
Initial success inevitably leads to the more daunting problems of rapid expansion: staffing, warehousing, distribution demands and foreign sourcing crises, as well as a host of unforeseen competitive forces beyond their control.
"This is the point where companies grow or fail," acknowledged Gretchen Springer, Georgetown's 37-year-old vice president for marketing, a former new-product manager at Johnson & Johnson. 
"We're at that point -- in response to demand -- where the company now has to manage its success and make the transition to the theoretical opportunity."
In a matter of months last year, Georgetown had to expand drastically the capacity of its telephone order center and the software that served it and enlarge its inventory and order-fulfillment systems.
But even then, Georgetown found itself in a Yuletide competition for part-time phone-order-takers with the Maine mega-cataloguer L. L. Bean, which is only 15 minutes away.
Rapidly expanding entrepreneurial companies like Magic Attic "need capital and resources to take their business to a higher plane, yet it's hard to maintain consistency and credibility with their banks without a long track record," said Jill S. Krutick, an analyst with Smith Barney. 
"Managing the cost side of the business is crucial, because inevitably they will be tested on their pricing by new competitors."
Like many young businesses, Magic Attic Club is a refinement of an existing product. 
The market for high-priced vinyl dolls was created by the Pleasant Company of Middleton, Wis., 10 years ago with its then history-themed American Girls collection. 
Using glossy catalogues and books to fire older girls' imaginations, Pleasant established a growing new market niche as the age of girls who play with Mattel Inc.'s Barbie became younger, analysts say. 
Although giant toy companies have generally ignored older girls, small companies like Magic Attic and Pleasant Company are offering dolls that sell for $40 to $130 and more.
A former teacher and textbook writer and publisher, Pleasant T. Rowland, the Pleasant Company's founder and president, termed Magic Attic "the most extensive effort at imitation" among her competitors -- "a shameless rip-off."
Jeffrey H. McKinnon, the 44-year-old president of Georgetown, credits Pleasant with "pioneering a unique new marketing approach to bringing a new type of play experience to older girls."
But he added, "We felt there was room in the market for another entrant," specifically one that offered finely detailed dolls for $59 instead of Pleasant's $82 and that focused on contemporary dolls.
While retailers are even now busily preparing for the Christmas toy season, the key to Magic Attic's business plan is direct response: only 5 percent of its 18-inch dolls are sold in retail stores, mostly collectors' specialty doll stores. 
Demand for Magic Attic dolls is driven not only by the colorful world of its catalogue but also by 17 books from the Magic Attic Press. 
The company has shipped 1.5 million $5.95 books to date and also profits from orders for accessories ranging from nightgowns to bedroom sets.
The dolls in the Magic Attic Club -- Alison, Megan, Heather and Keisha -- are four best friends who discover a trunk full of costumes in the attic of a neighbor's house. 
In the books, which bear more than a passing similarity to C. S. Lewis's "The Chronicles of Narnia," the dolls are transported by a magic mirror on adventures through time and space.
The explosive growth of the high-end doll-and-book category "is one of the biggest changes in the toy business in years," said Maurene Souza, an independent toy-industry consultant in Greenville, R.I., who for 20 years headed up girls' toy lines at big companies like Hasbro and Tyco. 
"This doll category is very hot."
Sean P. McGowan, an analyst with Gerard Klauer Mattison & Company, estimates the potential market at about $500 million in retail dollars, exclusive of books. 
Mr. McKinnon thinks it could be $600 million.
Analysts see the smaller, less expensive Barbie as a factor in the creation of this new market for girls. 
"Barbie used to go to age 8 or 9, but it has become a very young product," Mr. McGowan said. 
"Mattel calls it KGOY -- Kids Getting Older Younger."
But Mattel contends that girls up to age 12 still buy Barbie.
Mr. McKinnon, Harvard '74, and Ms. Springer, Dartmouth '80, have mapped out a business plan that is the antithesis of the large toy companies' drive for instant success and quick shelf turnover. 
"We don't want boom and bust, and we don't want fad," Ms. Springer said.
In 1994 Georgetown distributed 100,000 Magic Attic catalogues and sold more than 2,000 dolls, a giddy success for an untested, expensive product. 
Last year Georgetown got a $5 million working-capital investment from State Street Bank and Trust in Boston and Key Bank of Maine in Portland. 
"If Magic Attic had failed miserably, we'd have bankrupted the business," Mr. McKinnon said of his higher-priced collectible doll business, "and 1995 was our make-or-break year."
To be sure, the arm disaster nearly put Georgetown over the edge. 
"We discovered that out of a desire to make the doll's arms more pose-able our manufacturer in China changed the way the arm was attached to the body," Mr. McKinnon said. 
"We stopped shipping -- but we couldn't stop the demand."
"In 24 hours we figured out how to fix 80,000 arms on 40,000 dolls," he said. 
It was a complex assembly-line process, requiring 20 minutes per doll, that involved opening the package, undressing the doll, fixing the arms, then redressing and repacking the dolls. 
In the process, all the profits for Magic Attic evaporated for the year.
But on the bright side, Georgetown had $3 million in sales in 1995, and the company hopes to double that in 1996, largely in the coming holiday season.
These sales are minuscule in comparison with the $187 million in 1995 for the Pleasant Company, the Coca-Cola of upscale play-doll purveyors. 
Pleasant has sold more than three million of its 18-inch dolls since their debut in 1986.
After working in the industry, Mr. McKinnon started his collectible-doll business, Georgetown, in 1987. 
His expertise in working with Chinese factories for a direct-mail supplier enabled him to manufacture lifelike sculptured porcelain faces and eyes that were superior in quality yet cheaper than many other collectible dolls, which are sold to a passionate group of adult collectors for as much as $10,000.
From a zero presence in 1987, Mr. McKinnon quickly won 19 percent of the market, which he continues to hold. 
The problem was that the total audience for porcelain dolls in the United States is limited, estimated as five million avid collectors.
So Mr. McKinnon found a factory near Shenzhen, China, that specialized in high-quality vinyl molds, then brought his doll-making expertise to the production of toys for little girls.
The success of Pleasant Company and the challenge of Magic Attic have not gone unnoticed in the commercial dollocracy. 
"It's been a real awakening for the toy industry," Ms. Souza said.
Right now, Mattel "has no plans to enter the category," Lisa McKendall, a spokeswoman, said. 
Mattel's 11.5-inch Barbie has been selling for 37 years and has the largest sales for any toy ever: $1.4 billion.
But there are a number of other competitors in the expensive play-doll category. 
My Twinn of Littleton, Colo., sells $160 dolls.
And the Ertl Company, the nation's eighth-largest toy maker, will roll out its Girlhood Journey line of dolls for between $40 and $50 in retail stores this Christmas.
This new doll category is welcomed by some parents. 
"I think it's great that my daughter is playing with these dolls so creatively," said Cindy Rosenfeld of Woodbury, L.I. 
"There isn't that much in the toy stores for girls, and we have buckets of Barbies that are never played with. 
Now suddenly the girls are into dressing up dolls, and it's so wonderfully old fashioned."
"We play school with them, plan trips for them, set up tents and pretend we go camping with them," said 8-year-old Allison; she and her sister Amy, 6, have four Magic Attic dolls.
Other parents are stunned by doll-price escalation. 
Carol S. Jimenez of Long Beach, Calif., refused to buy an American Girls doll for her daughter Emily because "I think it's outrageous to spend $82 on a toy for an 8-year-old," she said.
So Emily used her own money to buy Felicity, one of the Pleasant Company's American Girls.
"I'm now saving up to buy Heather," a $59 Magic Attic doll, she said.

file: Hard Choice for White House On Hillary Clinton and China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Of all the powerful people in the White House, there is probably no one -- not even the President -- to whom aides less like to say no. 
So Hillary Rodham Clinton's strong wish to lead the American delegation to the United Nations Conference on Women in Beijing next month has prompted much hand-wringing among senior diplomatic officials who are not sure she should go.
The geopolitics are plain enough: should the most prominent woman in the United States lend her presence to a conference on women's rights that happens to be held in a country with an abysmal record on human rights -- especially when China is holding the American human rights advocate Harry Wu on espionage charges and Chinese-American relations are rubbed raw.
The domestic politics are clear, too: Congressional Republicans are chomping to seize the issue as an example of the mishandling of foreign policy by Mr. Clinton, and to accuse him of coddling dictators as he once accused George Bush of being too soft on China. 
House and Senate leaders have called for an American boycott of the conference.
The office politics are murkier: knowing Mrs. Clinton's desire to lead the charge on an issue that has long concerned her, Administration officials, including the President in his news conference last week, have studiously avoided saying no, and some are ambivalent about the risks and benefits involved.
For her part, Mrs. Clinton argues -- as she did in a speech to a women's group in Denver last month that her aides took pains to fax to a reporter today -- that the conference is "an important opportunity to focus attention on women."
She said that the American delegation should "play a very big leadership role in shaping the agenda" and that "the United States should do all that it can to make sure that barriers to women's participation are broken down, and that training and credit and political involvement and health care and education are available to all women."
As the Clintons began the first full day of a 17-day vacation in the Grand Tetons this morning, the official word from the White House was that there was no official word. 
Unofficially, senior Administration aides in Washington gave slightly conflicting status reports.
Some in the West Wing and the State Department said the current plan was to wait a few more days to see if Mr. Wu might be released, before making a decision by next Monday, which they described as the last realistic point at which the logistical arrangements for such a trip could be made.
Aides to the First Lady insisted there was no "drop dead date," but they acknowledged pressure to make a decision soon, since Mrs. Clinton would leave for Beijing from V-J Day commemorations in Hawaii over the Labor Day weekend, and perhaps visit Mongolia, Cambodia and Thailand as well.
On Monday, Secretary of State Warren M. Christopher and the deputy national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, met separately with Mrs. Clinton to go over the pros and cons. 
Aides to both the First Lady and the President said today that Mrs. Clinton would rely on their judgment in making her decision.
Moreover, at least some officials outside the First Lady's staff have argued that Mrs. Clinton's visit could be good for Chinese-American relations in the long run. 
Winston Lord, the Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs and former Ambassador to Beijing, switched his vacation plans to be available to escort her.
The matter remains complicated, balancing the enormous attention Mrs. Clinton would win among the 50,000 delegates and reporters at the conference with practicalities as particular as the fate of one man.
Over the weekend, Mr. Wu's wife, Ching Lee, wrote to the First Lady, imploring her not to go. 
Mrs. Clinton has not yet replied, but officials said there was general agreement that it would be extremely problematic for Mrs. Clinton to attend if Mr. Wu remained in custody.
At the same time, these aides said the Administration was determined not to link Mrs. Clinton's decision too closely to Mr. Wu's fate, or to the status of Chinese-American relations in general, but to the mission of the conference.
Washington will be well represented at the once-a-decade conference in any event. 
The chief United States delegate to the United Nations, Madeleine K. Albright, is the official head of the American delegation, which includes the Secretary of Health and Human Services, Donna E. Shalala, and former Gov. Thomas Kean of New Jersey. 
Mrs. Clinton would be the honorary chairwoman.
Officials said today that if she went, Mrs. Clinton would most likely stay in Beijing one day, address the conference, spend the night and then move on, holding no meetings with Chinese Government officials or dissidents to emphasize that she was attending an international conference, not honoring the Chinese.
But among the Administration's concerns is that however brief her stay, Mrs. Clinton could easily become embroiled in disputes or demonstrations by the various delegations at the conference, and that her visit would almost certainly be interpreted by the Chinese as a sign of American nonchalance about its human rights record.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: Hillary Clinton in Beijing as Women_s Conference Opens.txt
text:
ï»¿
Hillary Rodham Clinton arrived early today to a Chinese capital under tight security for the Fourth World Conference on Women, the largest ever gathering of its kind.
During a stopover in Guam, she expressed hope that her participation would focus world attention on improving the condition of women, children and families.
"I have very high hopes that this will not be just a lot of talk, but will enable us to learn from one another," she said at a reception.
The conference opened here on Monday with a ceremony at the Great Hall of the People, featuring speeches, entertainment and the pomp that characterized the Chinese imperial court of old. 
The 10-day meeting of more than 4,000 government delegates will seek to produce a "platform for action" to influence the policies of world governments on women's rights in health, education, business and politics.
President Jiang Zemin and the Communist Party leadership welcomed the official delegations from 185 countries at the Great Hall of the People, where dancers in gilded costumes entertained an audience of 10,000 and where the secretary general of the conference, Gertrude Mongella of Tanzania, said: "A revolution has begun. 
There is no going back. 
There is no going back."
Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto of Pakistan cut to the core of the issues when she addressed the opening session of the conference on Monday, raising her voice against violence directed at women.
Wearing a white veil as she spoke, she condemned the cultural traditions of Asian nations, including China, that have led to the deaths of millions of baby girls.
"How tragic it is that the pre-Islamic practice of female infanticide still haunts a world we regard as modern and civilized," she said. 
"Girl children are often abandoned or aborted. 
Statistics show that men now increasingly outnumber women in more than 15 Asian nations."
Ms. Bhutto said the preference for boys among Asian men had created pressure to abort "innocent, perfectly formed" baby girls.
"As we gather here today, the cries of the girl child reach out to us," she said. 
"This conference needs to chart a course that can create a climate where the girl child is as welcome and valued as the boy child."
Her remarks demonstrated that the most forceful call for action that may emerge from here in 10 days' time is a demand for international protection for women from violence, whether it is the rape and terror of "ethnic cleansing" and armed conflict or domestic battering.
Absent from Monday's opening ceremony because of illness was United Nations Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose address was delivered by Ismat Kittani, the Under Secretary General.
With Beijing under a virtual state of martial law for several weeks, one of the victims of the pervasive security on Monday was Winnie Mandela, the estranged wife of the South African President, Nelson Mandela, and about 20 other South African delegates. 
Arriving late in Chinese-provided buses, they were barred at the door to the hall, and when they began chanting, "Let us in, let us in," they were surrounded by Chinese police officers.
After a vigorous shoving match that lasted several minutes, Mrs. Mandela and the group were forced to retreat..
Inside the Great Hall, the Chinese President, who made no reference to the many complaints about the intrusions of Chinese security forces at a related meeting of 30,000 women outside Beijing, said, "Such a propitious assembly of outstanding women has added luster to the city that radiates with the colors of the golden autumn."
"Women hold up half of the sky in human society," Mr. Jiang said, using a Chinese metaphor. 
But "over a long period of time," prejudice against women "like an invisible chain, fettered the hearts and mind of millions."
This conference, the first of its kind since the end of the cold war, will bring up uncomfortable issues arising from the collapse of Communist governments and the upsurge of ethnic conflicts that have brought enormous suffering to women and broadened their impoverishment in the third world.
In the eyes of millions of women, the "victory" of market-oriented democracies has remained indifferent to their transitional problems in the old Communist nations, especially where women are heads of households and care for children.
The underlying theme of the conference is the effort to get more women trained and ready for the political process in their countries and win for them the economic and educational rights that will raise them from their disproportionate poverty.
Of 1.3 billion people living in absolute poverty in the world, 70 percent are women. 
For many of them, the importance of this conference, the most ambitious of its kind since the first such meeting dedicated to women was held in Mexico City in 1975, is that it will again take up the issue that has sundered the national politics of many nations of the world: the reproductive rights of women and the issue of abortion. 
The forum met last in Nairobi in 1985.
In part, this meeting appears doomed to debate again policy statements and recommendations that were reached last year at the United Nations conference on population in Cairo, which formed what at the time seemed a strong international consensus that the most effective strategy for limiting population was providing women better access to education and reproductive health care, including contraception and safe abortion.
Thus armed, or empowered, many women chose to plan smaller families to balance the number of children against family resources, the conference found.
"For those of us in this field," said Dr. Fred Sai of Ghana, the president of the International Planned Parenthood Association, "we have learned the importance of teaching the balance of human numbers with human resources and human aspirations."
The debate will again pit the delegations of many national governments against the Vatican and an assortment of Islamic and conservative governments.
In the platform for action, much of the language on "reproductive rights" has been placed in brackets, indicating that one or more governments have registered an objection.
The platform carries no force of law, but women's advocates in many nations can invoke its influence in making arguments to legislatures to enact laws protecting women's rights.
A coalition of women's groups is circulating a petition calling on the United Nations to remove the Vatican's special status as the only religious organization with permanent observer rights in the body.
But the Vatican and other anti-abortion forces are expected to make a strong showing here.
In a letter to Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky, a former Congresswoman and deputy chairwoman of the 45-member United States delegation, the president of the American Life League, Judie Brown, said, "On behalf of the 300,000 families supporting the work of the American Life League, I want to express my outrage at the insidious, deceptive manner in which the U.S. delegation" to the conference "continues to promote abortion, contraception and population control, all under the guise of human rights."
Mrs. Margolies-Mezvinsky was equally adamant. 
"The majority of nations have made it perfectly clear that they are not going to backslide and lose ground from Cairo," she said.
