file: Honda, Beating Out G.M., Plans to Build Cars in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Beating out a competing bid by the General Motors Corporation, the Honda Motor Company announced today that it had won the right to manufacture passenger cars at a plant in southern China.
Honda executives said the venture, their first auto assembly operation in China's perplexing car market, would involve a $200 million investment with two local partners to produce a model resembling the Honda Accord. 
Honda will take a 50 percent stake.
Yet Honda is essentially betting it can succeed where the French auto maker PSA Peugeot Citroen failed. 
Honda plans to use the same plant in Guangzhou that Peugeot vacated early this year, frustrated by low output, rising debt and squabbles with its local partner.
Honda executives, like their counterparts at other auto makers, expressed faith that the long-term potential in China's passenger car market was worth the considerable near-term difficulties, like bureaucratic interference, inadequate sourcing and an insular distribution network.
"We believe the Chinese market has the potential for further expansion in the future," Yoshihide Munekuni, Honda's chairman, told a news conference in Tokyo. 
"We will study the possibility of exports from the Chinese plant in the future."
General Motors expressed disappointment, but said it would not affect a larger commitment to G.M.'s $1.5 billion plant now under construction in Shanghai, where it plans to produce Buicks in 18 months.
"We regret that it was not possible for Opel/G.M. to reach agreement with the authorities in Guangzhou," G.M. said. 
"We believe our proposal, which provided a substantial investment in Guangzhou, would have been a viable business opportunity for all parties concerned."
Honda's local partners are the Guangzhou Auto Group Corporation, which Peugeot executives blamed for making their venture more trouble than it was worth, and the Dongfeng Motor Corporation, already a partner with Honda at a plant that produces engine and suspension components for export to other Honda plants in Asia.
The new Honda venture plans to start modestly, calling for just 30,000 vehicles a year. 
The first cars will be assembled in late 1999, Honda said.
The new venture will also give Honda its first automobile sales channel in the Chinese market, Mr. Munekuni said in Tokyo, where the No. 3 Japanese auto maker's plans were announced together with an upbeat earnings report timed to coincide with a visit to Japan by China's Prime Minister, Li Peng. 
Honda said earnings rose 33 percent in the six months ended Sept. 
30, powered by strong exports to the United States and Europe.
Mr. Munekuni promised that the new venture would not assume Guangzhou Auto's existing debt, though its size was not disclosed.
"Debts of Guangzhou Peugeot Automobile will be settled by the Guangzhou government," he said.
The first step in a long series of approvals that Honda must win, the Honda chairman added, is to apply to the central Government for permission to start a feasibility study on the venture. 
Formal approval of the venture will follow at a later date, barring insurmountable obstacles.
Guangzhou Auto hopes to become one of a handful of auto-making conglomerates that emerge in China in the coming decade. 
Officials in Beijing have said they hope to consolidate the nation's 123 auto assembly plants into a dozen companies as part of an overall plan to make the nation's cumbersome state-run industry more efficient.
Though its potential is tantalizingly large, China's auto market is still relatively small. 
Passenger cars account for only about a quarter of the 1.5 million vehicles assembled here, which are mostly trucks and vans.
One perennially touchy issue in China's car manufacturing is the amount of local content in autos made by international car makers. 
Honda said 40 percent of the China-made Accords would be made with local components in the first year, though that number is expected to rise in subsequent years.
Required to work with a local partner, international auto makers have rarely been able to profit in China. 
The outlook for car makers has grown hazier in recent months, as car sales have dropped, and the recent economic downturn in Southeast Asia is not expected to help.
By contrast, Honda's most lucrative markets are in the West, which was reflected in the six-month earnings report the company released today. 
Helped by the diminished value of the yen, Honda's exports almost doubled to meet strong demand in Europe and the United States. 
Honda vehicle sales rose 16 percent in the United States, to about half a million. 
A popular seller was the CR-V sport utility vehicle, which Honda began selling in the United States in February. 
European buyers snapped up CR-V's and Civics.
The export markets compensated for weak sales in Japan.

"Because there has been such great concern in the community, we have decided to seek clarification."
Late last month, the Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal ruled that children born on the mainland who have at least one parent living in Hong Kong have the right to residency here.

Mr. Lam said the government was not acting on orders from Beijing, though he acknowledged it had taken China's objections into account. 
He also said Hong Kong was not trying to overturn the ruling.
"This is a very special case," Mr. Lam said.

Hong Kong's new government, which took office with the former British colony's handover to China a week ago, moved today to establish a new electoral system that is likely to reduce the number of pro-democracy members in future legislatures while insuring dominance of pro-business and pro-Beijing lawmakers.

file: Hong Kong Court Upholds China_s Rule.txt
text:
ï»¿
A constitutional challenge to China's rule in Hong Kong was rebuffed today when a three-judge panel ruled unanimously that the territory was powerless to question Beijing's decisions, particularly the scuttling of Hong Kong's elected legislature and its replacement by a handpicked assembly.
The challenge, which grew out of a criminal case involving the theft of a Rolex watch at a ferry terminal, claimed that the existence of Beijing's legislature violated the Basic Law, the mini-constitution that Beijing drafted for Hong Kong before China took over here from Britain. 
The Basic Law provides for a legislature that is in part elected, but it does not provide for an appointed assembly.
In the narrow sense, the case revolved merely around the survival of a criminal indictment through the transition from British to Chinese sovereignty, but more broadly, the ruling by the Court of Appeal, the second-highest court in Hong Kong, found that China has the power to impose its will on Hong Kong.
The case itself marked a significant moment in the era of Communist rule in China. 
For the first time in the history of the People's Republic of China, judges deliberated on constitutional matters affecting Beijing's governance.
Indeed, remarkably, only one of the three judges was Chinese, making this the first time that judges of foreign nationality have deliberated on Chinese laws; all Hong Kong's judges retained their appointments after China resumed sovereignty over Hong Kong on July 1.
It was not immediately clear what the complete implications of today's decisions are for Hong Kong's autonomy, or whether the jurisdiction of Hong Kong's courts has been circumscribed. 
The Government insisted afterward that the rule of law and the integrity of the courts had been maintained. 
But lawyers who brought the case, and other critics, warned of the consequences of the ruling and hinted at an appeal.
At stake was the fate not only of Beijing's appointed legislature, known as the Provisional Legislative Council, but also of the laws it has passed, including an omnibus law to insure the continuation of common law in Hong Kong as well as the appointment of the appeals court judges themselves.
In reading his opinion today, Chief Justice Patrick Chan said, "I am inclined to hold that the Provisional Legislative Council has been validly established under Chinese law and was ratified by the National People's Congress," China's rubber-stamp Parliament.
Addressing a courtroom packed with observers lining the walls and spilling out the double wooden doors, Mr. Chan said of the appointed legislature: "Its formation is an interim measure out of necessity."
He said, "It was not done as an intentional breach of the Basic Law. 
It is, strictly speaking, not a Legislative Council under Article 60 of the Basic Law," the provision that requires a partially elected legislature.
In a precisely reasoned ruling, Justice Chan took pains to support his ruling on principles of common law and under Chinese laws passed by China's parliament, as well as the decisions of various Chinese-appointed bodies and the text of the Basic Law itself. 
At no point did anyone, including harsh critics of the decision, suggest that Mr. Chan and his colleagues were pressured by Beijing to rule a certain way.
Ever since China declared it would abolish Hong Kong's elected legislature, because the elections in 1995 were held without its approval, there has been a debate here, especially among legal experts, over whether an appointed assembly would satisfy the constitution.
Both the Bar Council, which represents barristers, the lawyers who appear in court, and the Law Society, representing solicitors, lawyers who deal with clients, have maintained that the Provisional Legislature is not in accord with the Basic Law.
That argument was powerfully presented in this case last week by Gladys Li, a former chairman of the Bar Council and one of the most respected barristers in Hong Kong.
Opposite her was the Government's chief legal officer, the Solicitor General, Daniel Fung, who insisted that China had the authority to erect the governmental structure it deemed appropriate for Hong Kong and that in any event, the courts had no power to rule on those decisions.
Clearly relieved at the court's posture, Mr. Fung said afterward, "We welcome the Court of Appeal's decision, which was unanimous that the Provisional Legislative Council is a valid, competent body established by the National People's Congress."
"This has settled a constitutional controversy and we welcome the clearing of the air," said Mr. Fung, who, like the other barristers and judges, appeared in court in elaborate regalia of robes, starched collars and horsehair wigs.
Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping magnate appointed by Beijing to administer Hong Kong, also praised the ruling. 
"The rule of law is one of the important factors contributing to Hong Kong's success," said a statement issued by Mr. Tung's office. 
"The litigation demonstrates the respect the society have towards the rule of law."
Across Hong Kong, however, many pro-democracy activists, including lawmakers who had been dismissed from the legislature by China, were critical of the court's ruling and suggested that the issue would be raised again in Hong Kong's highest court, the Court of Final Appeal.
Martin Lee, the leader of Hong Kong's largest political party, the Democratic Party, which lost all 19 of its legislative seats, was equally critical. 
"This case raises very serious implications for the future of Hong Kong's rule of law and autonomy," said Mr. Lee.
"There must be something seriously wrong if the Chinese central Government can introduce an appointed body, ignore the Basic Law at will, and Hong Kong courts cannot do anything about it," he said.
Nihal Jayawickrama, a professor of law at Hong Kong University, called the implications of the ruling "quite serious."
He explained, "What they are saying is that the National People's Congress is supreme and whatever it does, the court will apply. 
That's not what the Basic Law says. 
The National People's Congress has no relevance in Hong Kong. 
If they can do this, where does the Basic Law stand?"
While it was unclear tonight whether there would be an appeal to the territory's highest court, Mr. Fung expressed confidence that today's ruling would be upheld. 
"There is no question the common law is part of the law of Hong Kong," said an ebullient Mr. Fung after the ruling. 
"We all accept the difference in nature and development between the Hong Kong system and the Chinese system. 
But we have to respect the basic law and the structure under which we were created."

file: Hong Kong Faces Loss Of Luster to Mainland.txt
text:
ï»¿
For a city that has prospered as an intermediary between the Chinese economy and the outside world, Hong Kong has lobbied hard to help China win full membership in the world's club of trading nations.
Now that the United States House of Representatives has voted to give China permanent normal trade status -- bringing normalized trade relations closer and easing China's accession to the World Trade Organization -- Hong Kong has to begin facing the consequences of its successful campaign.
A China more open to commerce with the outside world, many experts say, will jeopardize Hong Kong's historic role as a trading post.
"There's no question that companies are going to do business directly with China," said Robert C. Broadfoot, the managing director of the Political and Economic Risk Consultancy here. 
"It's not a question of if, but when, you're going to have shocks to Hong Kong's role."
Mr. Broadfoot contends that in the long run Hong Kong will benefit from China's integration into the global economy as the overall volume of China-related trade grows.
But in the short term, China's march into the World Trade Organization will pose a thorny challenge. 
As a former British colony and now a semiautonomous region of China, Hong Kong is a separate trading entity that already has its own membership in the W.T.O.
Hong Kong's stock market reflected this ambivalence, falling slightly today while shares in the mainland Chinese cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen roared ahead.
In 1998, more than $52 billion worth of goods passed through Hong Kong's port bound for mainland destinations. 
Mr. Broadfoot estimates that a third of that traffic will disappear after the United States and other countries start shipping directly to mainland ports.
Likewise in air travel, Hong Kong could lose its role as a gateway to China. 
As part of the W.T.O. negotiations last year between the United States and China, Beijing agreed to increase the frequency of commercial flights, which would enable more American cities to have more direct flights to mainland Chinese cities.
That could hurt Dragonair, a Hong Kong carrier that serves many mainland cities. 
It stands to lose Western passengers who fly to Hong Kong and transfer to planes to popular Chinese destinations like Xian or Guilin.
Hong Kong's position is further threatened by Taiwan, whose new President, Chen Shui-bian, has signaled that he is open to negotiating direct trade links with China. 
In 1998, Hong Kong's container port handled nearly $10 billion worth of Taiwanese exports bound for China. 
If Taiwan and China were to break down these barriers, some of that trade would also bypass Hong Kong.
"Once China gets into the W.T.O., Taiwan would presumably get into the W.T.O. soon as well," said Eden Woon, director of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce. 
"That means that Taiwan would have to deal more directly with China."
With all the troubling implications, why did Mr. Woon and other Hong Kong officials push so energetically for the House to pass the bill?
Part of the reason is political. 
Beijing has made entry into the trade organization the centerpiece of its economic agenda. 
In Hong Kong, where politicians and business leaders try to outdo each other to be seen as loyal to the motherland, supporting the trade campaign was a natural.
Even Martin Lee, Hong Kong's most prominent pro-democracy leader, traveled to Washington to lobby for the bill. 
Mr. Lee, a longtime critic of Beijing, said his motives were political rather than economic.
"I went to support the 1.2 billion people of China, not the Chinese government," Mr. Lee said. 
"I see in this bill a reasonable possibility that China will change its culture toward observing the rule of law."
Other supporters argue that Hong Kong can retain its middleman role -- with a few tweaks -- as a provider of services to the next generation of foreign companies that try to get into China. 
Hong Kong, with its legions of lawyers, accountants and consultants, is quite likely to remain a valuable guide for those companies.
"In order to handle all this trade, China will have to have a very well-developed service sector," said Victor K. Fung, the chairman of the Hong Kong Trade Development Council and the owner of a trading firm. 
"In the short run, it will be very difficult for China to ramp up those services."
But some more old-line Hong Kong industries will have to redefine themselves. 
With the United States set to lift import quotas on Chinese textiles and textile products by 2005, Mr. Woon predicted that many Hong Kong clothing makers would move their factories to the mainland to take advantage of lower production costs. 
Hong Kong, he suggested, could recast itself as a center for Asian fashion design, rather than a manufacturing center.
China's entry into the trade organization is also quite likely to deprive Hong Kong of its thriving gray market in goods like oil, cigarettes and agricultural products. 
Those are smuggled from mainland China by the truckload and exported from Hong Kong so that they will be subject to lower tariffs.
Despite its expected negative effects on some Hong Kong industries, China's trade campaign has made people here recognize that their economic fortunes are inextricably tied to the mainland. 
It seemed no coincidence that last week Hong Kong announced a $12 billion expansion of its rail system, including a direct link between central Hong Kong and Shenzhen.
Hong Kong's government estimates that China's joining the W.T.O. would add more than 5 percent to the territory's gross domestic product over the next decade. 
It also predicts that investment by Hong Kong companies in China will explode. 
Local companies have already poured in a cumulative $156 billion.
Because Hong Kong and China would retain separate memberships in the World Trade Organization, officials said Hong Kong would not necessarily gain access to Chinese markets earlier than other countries. 
But business people here are lobbying for special treatment. 
Even without it, officials say, Hong Kong will flourish.
"We do not mind if multinational companies go directly to China," the government's chief spokesman, Stephen Lam, said. 
"As long as the pie gets bigger, even if we get a smaller piece, it will still be more than enough for us."

file: Hong Kong Is Warned By Beijing On Press.txt
text:

Long accustomed to their boisterous, muckraking press, Hong Kong's journalists and news organizations are reeling from a series of body punches delivered by a senior Beijing official over the future of press freedom here.
Lu Ping, the Chinese official charged with setting up Hong Kong's new government after China retakes the territory from Britain on July 1, 1997, has issued a procession of comments starkly warning the crown colony's press that there will be limits on what can be published here under Chinese rule.
"It's all right if reporters objectively report," said Mr. Lu, while on a visit to Japan this month in his role as director of China's Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office. 
"But if they advocate, it is an act. 
It has nothing to do with freedom of the press."
Mr. Lu's reference to "an act" appeared to invoke Article 23 of the Basic Law, which China has pledged to respect and is often described as Hong Kong's future constitution. 
Article 23 allows the banning of any "act" deemed treasonous, subversive or secessionist. 
Mr. Lu went on to specify that advocacy of Taiwan's independence could be prosecuted under Article 23.
Hong Kong's 59 newspapers and 675 periodicals are filled with columns of advocacy, blistering articles of opinion and untempered appeals for community and political activism. 
With China's reassertion of suzerainty now in sight, anxieties among Hong Kong's journalists are mounting.
"The message is pretty clear," said Ivan Tong, president of the Hong Kong Journalists Association. 
"On the one hand he is talking about Hong Kong people retaining the same degree of press freedom after 1997. 
On the other hand he's talking about a bottom line, a limit on press freedom. 
It's not press freedom at all."
In addition to Hong Kong's huge Chinese-language press, there are many international news magazines published in Hong Kong, including The Asian Wall Street Journal, Time and Newsweek's Asian editions, the Far Eastern Economic Review and Asia Week. 
And while all insist publicly that they intend to remain here under Chinese sovereignty, many publications are quietly looking at alternatives to Hong Kong.
"Our plan is to remain in Hong Kong," Donald M. Morrison, the editor of Time's Asian edition, said. 
"Not only are we staying in Hong Kong, we are expanding."
But he also cautioned, "As for 1997, obviously we will wait and see what the climate is in terms of freedom of information."
Now in its 50th year, the Far Eastern Economic Review, widely regarded as the region's preeminent weekly and now owned by Dow Jones, also insists that it intends to remain in Hong Kong after 1997, and seems more optimistic about the future climate for journalism here.
"We have every intention of remaining in Hong Kong," said L. Gordon Crovitz, the magazine's editor and publisher. 
"It's important to us that we always be able to report fairly and accurately and we have every expectation that we will be able to do that from our base in Hong Kong."
Urban C. Lehner, the editor of another Dow Jones publication, The Asian Wall Street Journal, said that the paper would also continue to be based in Hong Kong after 1997. 
"We're staying," he said. 
"We're committed to being in Hong Kong. 
We think Hong Kong is the place to be. 
It's the central spot in Asia. 
It's the heart of covering the best story in Asia, which is China."
But a senior Journal executive acknowledged that the company had already scouted alternative locations to Hong Kong. 
"Losing Hong Kong is one fifth of our readers," he said. 
"Advertisers want those readers. 
Not delivering a morning paper to those readers would be the biggest loss. 
But basically, we could move in a minute."
For most of Hong Kong's printed press, however, the option of moving after 1997 does not exist, and editors here are taking a grim view of Mr. Lu's recent statements.
"His comments brought out the anxieties journalists have had for a long time," said Daisy Yet Wah Li, a senior editor at Ming Pao, one of the territory's most serious newspapers. 
"Is merely reporting on Tibetan independence or Taiwan independence advocacy?
What about commentary?
What about a survey that Hong Kong people want independence and we put it on the front page?
We always thought that this would be a problem."
John Schidlovsky, director of the Freedom Forum Asian Center, an independent research center on press issues and a training center for journalists here, said Mr. Lu's comments reflected an unfamiliarity with the role a free press plays in a free society.
"Advocacy is part of free speech and should be allowed," said Mr. Schidlovsky. "If he rules that out, then that's suppression of free speech."Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: Hong Kong Journal_Any Omens_ Colony_s Soothsayers Won_t Say.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the shadow of an old Buddhist temple, a curving alleyway known as Soothsayer's Arcade is full of tiny stalls where fortunetellers routinely predict the future and, for a few dollars extra, unlock some of life's deepest mysteries.
Yet even here, in icon-laden booths that reek of incense and the mystical power of Chinese fortunetelling, no one seems willing to venture a prediction about what will happen in Hong Kong after July 1, when China takes over from Britain.
"How can you know?" asked Leung Tin-che, a 50-year-old fortune-teller whose inviting smile turned to a puzzled frown when he was asked about Hong Kong's future. 
"None of my customers ask about that anyway. 
They want to know about their career, or love."
As Hong Kong nears its fateful date, people all over the world are wondering what will happen in a political situation that history has no script for. 
In Hong Kong itself, however, many people seem to accept that their future remains firmly in the realm of the unknowable.
But in a telling indication of the way things are going, in Soothsayer's Arcade and in so much of Hong Kong, new customers now come mostly from mainland China.
Fortunetellers say that many of the mainland visitors are actually mid-level Communist Party officials, who ignore the Party's rejection of superstitious practices when they come for a session.
"It makes sense if you think about it," said Chung Tak-ching, another fortuneteller. 
"If you're from the Communist Party, and no one believes in Communism anymore, wouldn't you have questions about your future?"
Probably no place is as obsessed with lucky numbers and talismans and fortunetelling as Hong Kong, perhaps because its very existence -- as a precarious dot on the long coast of China -- seems to have tempted fate over the years. 
Bankers and lawyers regularly consult fortunetellers, as do housewives and delivery boys, and the 200 fortunetellers in Soothsayer's Arcade may be the largest such grouping in the world.
A decade ago, despite China's promises to leave Hong Kong untouched, many people here feared that 1997 would mean the closing of places like fortunetelling stalls and nightclubs and race tracks, long banned in China as remnants of a misguided, and capitalist, past.
But few fear such a crackdown now, since change in recent years has brought capitalist pastimes like stock markets and nightlife to the mainland. 
Even if Chinese control does mean a loss of civil liberties, several fortunetellers said they found it hard to imagine their trade being affected.
"They come here as customers themselves, so why would they want to shut us down?" asked Priscilla Lam, a matronly fortuneteller who has brushed up on her Mandarin to accommodate mainland clients. 
"Maybe they'll figure out a way to make money off us."
In a simple example, Ms. Lam seemed to put her finger on some critical forces verging on Hong Kong's future: China's enthusiasm for capitalism, the eagerness of Chinese officials to enjoy the forbidden fruit within, as well as these officials' tendency to try to make money off anyone who is making money.
Yet all the reasons why China should leave Hong Kong alone may have to be balanced against Beijing's deepest concern: to control anything it perceives as a threat.
"We are not a danger to anyone," Ms. Lam said firmly. 
"No one here would ever make a prediction that is politically sensitive."
Described on her business card as a "physignomist," Ms. Lam prefers to divine an individual's future by examining palms and nose and eye shape, and by crossing her findings against one of many ancient charts listing personality characteristics based on year, date and hour of birth.
One customer, Evelyn Lau, a 24-year-old bank clerk wearing purple lipstick, came to ask about her prospects with a man she recently met. 
She demurred when asked what her palm-reading disclosed.
"I want to know about big issues that will affect me for my whole life," she said, trying to surpress a nervous giggle. 
Egged on by a friend, she admitted, "I really like this guy."
Mr. Leung said that, although most of his prognostications also deal with romantic concerns, there was a surge in the fortunetelling business about five years ago when many Hong Kong people were trying to decide whether to emigrate and to where.
"Everyone was afraid of the future back then," he said. 
"But everything depends on what happens in China, and China is changing fast."
Despite his own reluctance to predict Hong Kong's future, Mr. Leung said he had noticed a few things about people who do make predictions.
Hong Kong's most vocally optimistic people, he observed, are wealthy businessmen and women who, although they have the most to lose, also have the easiest ways out. 
Most of them arranged foreign passports or other escape routes years ago.
In contrast, he said, many working-class people are pessimistic about the future, though they have little to lose but their freedom.
"They're the ones with nowhere to go," he said. 
"Like me."
Ms. Lam has also advised many customers on choices about emigration, but she said it was always a question about where, not if.
"Everyone with enough money emigrates," she said simply.
With the fortunetelling business slow, Mr. Leung allowed that he makes his real money as a master of feng shui, the ancient art of geomancy, advising a tenant or home-owner on the proper placement and design of an office or dwelling. 
Even though the practice was banned in the mainland long ago, Mr. Leung thinks it inconceivable that Chinese officials would try to restrict it here.
Ms. Lam also complained that since much of her business now comes from mainland visitors, business has been slow this month, because Chinese authorities feared an onslaught of mainland visitors in the weeks just before and after the handover and put restrictions on how many could come.
"We'll have to wait until late July 1 before things pick up again," she said.

text:

It began with a dare.
"Two years ago I was doing this live radio talk show, and I was saying I had great confidence in the future of Hong Kong," David Chu said. 
"Then one listener called in and started giving me hell, saying, 'You have a U.S. passport, you're safe.'
He challenged me to give up my U.S. passport. 
I accepted that challenge. 
And for me, that was the turning point."
With less than two years to go before Britain returns this territory to China, the pursuit of a foreign passport has been elevated to a fine art by those here who fear for their future under Beijing's rule. 
Giving up foreign citizenship just isn't done.
Yet for David Chu, former banker and current real estate mogul, the future is not to be feared but welcomed. 
Not only has he ripped up his passport, Mr. Chu has also eagerly, and very publicly, been pounding the drum for Beijing.
Under American law he may obtain a new passport merely by applying for one. 
Still, as a reward for his demonstration of allegiance, he was one of 35 Hong Kongers chosen by Beijing to sit on the body that advises China what to do about Hong Kong.
"Some Chinese go overseas and become very Westernized, but some Chinese go overseas and discover their Chinese identity," Mr. Chu said. 
"I belong to the latter category."
His empathy for China's approach to Hong Kong -- an approach that is generally dismissive of British concerns while forcefully asserting Beijing's right to determine the territory's future -- mirrors that of many in the colony's business elite. 
While most Hong Kongers, according to opinion polls, still do not want to return to Chinese sovereignty, most Hong Kong business leaders, many of whom play a role in Hong Kong's current governance, have accommodated themselves to China's desires.
"I freely admit I'm pro-China," Mr. Chu said. 
"It's no different than Americans who feel pride about being American and are willing to go to war for their country."
So, in a way, Mr. Chu went to war for China. 
Three years ago, when Hong Kong's Governor, Christopher Patten, enraged China by pushing through a series of changes intended to expand democracy, Mr. Chu took up the cudgels for Beijing.
"That's when Britain and China started fighting," Mr. Chu said.
"We, the pro-China camp, had to do something," he said. 
"I think it is wrong to destroy what we have had with a headlong rush toward democracy. 
What has made Hong Kong very successful is a dictatorial or colonial government that is responsive to public opinion.
"Some people say, let's fight with China, let's be more free. 
I don't think that's a very responsible attitude. 
There is a price to pay for that."
Mr. Chu fled Shanghai with his parents in 1954, when he was 14, landing in Boston, where his father found work as an accountant.

text:

On clear days at this time of the year, Barrie Cook used to take out-of-town visitors to the top of Victoria Peak, where they could see the gleaming skyscrapers of Macao, a Portuguese colony 38 miles away. 
Now, he said, "you can barely see to the bottom of the hill."
For much of this winter, Hong Kong has been shrouded in a yellowish haze that has blotted out its legendary vistas. 
This is not brooding, rainy mist of the sort that supplies atmosphere in James Clavell novels. 
It is a dry, gritty smog that catches in the throat and gives the city an odd sepia-tinted glow.
As the haze has become an every-other-day phenomenon in this city of 6.7 million, it is setting off alarm bells in some unlikely quarters.
"If this is allowed to deteriorate further, it's going to be a major problem for the economy," said Mr. Cook, who runs a cement and concrete company for Hong Kong's most famous tycoon, Li Ka-shing. 
"Companies are very concerned about employees working in a deteriorating environment. 
They won't want to invest here. 
They won't want to put people or facilities here."
In Hong Kong, tackling pollution raises ticklish political issues. 
Much of the smog is generated across the border in mainland China, where a forest of smoke-belching factories has risen in Guangdong Province over the last two decades. 
In the winter, northerly winds blow the fumes into Hong Kong, where they mix with exhaust from buses and taxis to create what Kim Salkeld, the government's spokesman on the environment, calls a "horrendous cocktail."
Mr. Salkeld said the percentage of days when pollution reduced visibility to less than five miles doubled from 1991 to 1997, to more than 8 percent. 
Hong Kong hit a new low on Jan. 
19, when a particularly murky brew cut visibility to less than 3,000 feet, despite sunny skies. 
Ships in the harbor were forced to sound their foghorns as they crept forward in the midday gloom.
Hong Kong is still less polluted than Beijing or Shanghai -- not to mention famously blighted Asian cities like Bangkok and Manila. 
But experts here worry that Hong Kong could soon slip into their ranks.
With China's economy still humming, more factories are likely to spring up in Guangdong.
And Hong Kong, which is clawing its way out of an economic quagmire, may be reluctant to turn away industrial development, even if it degrades the environment and alienates foreign businesses.
"It really depends on what we're willing to put up with," said William Barron, a professor at the Center for Urban Planning and Environmental Management at the University of Hong Kong. 
"What we see in a place like Bangkok is how bad things can get, but the government still doesn't address the problem."
Mr. Barron said that while the Hong Kong government regards pollution as a major threat, it has been loath to confront China about its role in fouling its newest possession. 
"They don't even want to talk about the pollution coming across the border," he said. 
"It is way too sensitive."
Partly this is because of Hong Kong's general reluctance to ruffle the feathers of its new sovereign, whether it be over issues of judicial independence or environmental policy. 
But partly it is because the government knows that many of the factories in Guangdong are owned by Hong Kong companies.
Hong Kong also has no shortage of home-grown pollution. 
The number of cars, taxis and buses has soared in recent years as more people have moved into the New Territories, a once-bucolic hinterland that separates Kowloon from the mainland.
In Hong Kong's popular shopping district, Causeway Bay, the pollution readings are often so high that the government urges people with respiratory conditions to stay indoors. 
On a recent afternoon there, the fumes from taxis and double-decker buses all but choked two women who were standing on the sidewalk, handing out invitations to join a health club.
"In 15 years, Hong Kong will not be livable," Cindy Ho said as she packed her things and headed for a restaurant. 
"Everybody will be dead."
Mr. Salkeld said the government was determined to clear the air by banning leaded gasoline, converting taxis from diesel to liquefied petroleum gas, and expanding the rail system by 40 percent. 
But Hong Kong's close ties to southern China are not helping. 
Many trucks burn low-grade diesel fuel that is smuggled into Hong Kong from the mainland. 
The police recently uncovered an illegal pipeline that carried the cheap and far more polluting fuel across the border.
Politicians here said the government could no longer afford to tiptoe around China. 
Hong Kong's chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, declared in a speech last month that the environment would be "at the forefront of our agenda next year, year after next, and every year thereafter."
But Mr. Tung, a shipping magnate appointed by Beijing, has said little about cross-border pollution.
"What I don't want to see is the government saying, 'Just because the problem is from over there, we can't do anything about it,' " said Christine Loh, a pro-democracy leader who is active in environmental issues.
As a practical matter, it is not clear that Hong Kong can do much to influence Beijing's environmental policies. 
Mr. Salkeld said the two governments were cooperating to harmonize fuel standards. 
And they pledged $3 million each to install a pollution-monitoring system in Guangdong. 
But Mr. Salkeld noted that China's population and economic demands were so vast that they could make any environmental initiative seem hopelessly inadequate.
And anyway, he added, the seasonal wind currents work against China, too. 
"During the summer," he said, "when Hong Kong's air quality is pretty good, the wind is blowing our pollution into the mainland."

text:

Tendrils of steam plumed from the teapot's spout as Yip Wai-man splashed the parchment-thin ceramic thimbles with boiling water. 
Then, in a liquid ballet, he filled a tiny red clay pot with water, spilled tea into a blue and white china jug and carefully poured a mouthful of pale amber liquid into each thimble.
"This is Iron Buddha tea," Mr. Yip said, balancing the translucent china thimble in his fingertips. 
"Smell the bouquet and then sip it carefully."
In the frenzy of Hong Kong's day, executives in crisp suits scurrying into glass towers, the 24-hour roar of construction equipment, the buzz of business over hurried lunches, Mr. Yip preaches the need for tranquillity and harmony -- elements of the traditional Chinese tea ceremony. 
It is a ritual, he insists, that has been all but lost here.
"Basically everything of tradition in China was destroyed with the fall of the Qing dynasty," Mr. Yip said, referring to the collapse of China's last dynasty in 1911. 
"When I went to China, I was devastated to find there was no one to teach me about tea.
"Frankly speaking, China is not so useful; they've lost everything related to the tea culture. 
Nobody talks about the Chinese tea ceremony, only the Japanese ceremony. 
Of course, its origin was in China."
With nervousness growing as Hong Kong braces for the takeover by mainland China on July 1, 1997, Mr. Yip, cherubic in a Beatle-ish mop and white cotton Chinese jacket, extols the virtues of "cha dao," or "the way of tea," as a political healer and social pacifier.
In a city with some of the busiest McDonald's anywhere, where Coke and cognac consumption spirals upward and where tea is more an afterthought than passion, Mr. Yip's obsession nears the quixotic. 
But he is undeterred.
"I used to drink Coke," said Mr. Yip, 37, a former social worker. 
"I was like the Hong Kong masses. 
I was totally not into tea. 
I didn't even think it tasted good. 
Then I became interested in China's history and culture. 
It arose from my concerns about 1997, to dig into my past, my thoughts about being Chinese."
Being Chinese is apparently not at the forefront of many Hong Kongers' sensibility. 
A recent poll by the Chinese University of Hong Kong found that only 36 percent of Hong Kong's people see themselves as Chinese, while 49 percent identify themselves as "Hongkongese."
Mr. Yip said that escaping history was not so easy. 
"I realized that because of jitters over '97 and my sense of the growing distance between people here in Hong Kong, I want to use tea to spread harmony," he said. 
"What I want is a new Hong Kong tea culture, a product of the combination of the old and new China, of north and south and the ingestion of Western influences."
Already he has staked out land in the New Territories, Hong Kong's bit of the mainland, for a tea farm and the site of his members-only International China Tea Club.
Intended as a refuge from the frazzled existence of urban Hong Kong, the Tea Club, to open in September, will be a traditional two-story Chinese teahouse where the elaborate ritual of tea drinking can take place in leisure and relative solitude, a privilege that will cost the equivalent of about $6,500 a year.
"The idea is to relax, drink tea and make teapots if you wish," he said.
To be sure, Hong Kong is not lacking in tea. 
There is not a restaurant here where tea is not a staple. 
But hunched behind his desk in his tea shop on Argyle Street in Kowloon, Mr. Yip disdains the plebeian practice of sloshing plain green tea into mug-like teacups.
In his Jabbok Tea Shop, the paraphernalia of the tea ritual -- what he insisted are the essentials of the tea experience -- sit carefully on well-lighted shelves and in glass cases. 
On three glass shelves, 15 palm-sized red clay teapots are arrayed under spotlights.
"These are very special," Mr. Yip said, adding that they cost about $8,800 each.
Along the wall, fat canisters of tea displayed the profusion of regional vintages, from Pu-er to Long-jing, from Mu-dan to Iron Buddha, teas in a rainbow of colors, smells and tastes, with prices from $5 to well over $1,000 for a bit more than a pound of tea leaves.
"Tea," Mr. Yip declared, "is like French wine. 
It matters where the leaves are grown, on a hill or a valley, and when they are harvested, in the spring or autumn."
Mr. Yip spreads his devotion to tea, to the esoterica of ritual and his faith in the tea ceremony's palliative properties, in courses he teaches -- more than 8,000 students over the last decade, he said. 
But a few other tea masters in Hong Kong, less fervent perhaps, have brought the ferocity of competition to the genteel world of tea sipping.
Vesper Cha, the proprietor of the Best Tea House, a small chain of tea shops in Hong Kong, sells a wide range of ordinary and rare teas, teapots and the assorted utensils used in a traditional ceremony. 
But Mr. Cha, a former dealer in industrial lubricants, saw the lack of high-quality teas in Hong Kong as a marketing challenge.
"All over Hong Kong, I could not find one high-quality tea," he said. 
"So this was a big chance for me to open a shop with high-quality tea. 
My first shop was only 400 square feet."
Today, he has shops in Hong Kong and Canada.
Still, the infatuation of Hong Kong's young people for Coca-Cola and beer remains a hurdle.
"If your only customers are old people, you're doomed," he said with a laugh. 
"When people are too young, they don't know how to appreciate a cup of good tea. 
They have too much energy. 
But hopefully when they get to be 30, they learn to enjoy real tea."
Mr. Yip, who admitted that he is not immune to market pressures, insisted that his more refined approach to the tea business, and to tea culture, would endure.
"Tea has always been closely related to Chinese life for the last 3,000 years," he said. 
"It brings out the concept of harmony, which is a central theme of Chinese civilization. 
Tea is a real instrument of furthering harmony. 
It is a real linkage in relationships."

text:

In this status-obsessed city, where Rolls-Royces and Rolexes seem to outnumber Toyotas and Timexes, the most prized of all possessions these days is a 75-cent plastic beagle.
Every day since Sept. 
11, McDonald's has sold a new Snoopy figure, dressed in different national costume, as part of a monthlong marketing campaign. 
And with each day, the stampede to buy these toys has gathered force -- turning a fad into a phenomenon and, ultimately, into a public safety hazard.
On Tuesday, the Hong Kong police had to break up scuffles among tens of thousands of people who lined up -- many of them overnight -- in front of the city's 147 McDonald's restaurants to buy the "Hong Kong" Snoopy, a sturdy little fisherman clad in a yellow rain slicker and holding his daily catch.
"People have just gone crazy," a well-dressed woman said as she waited restlessly outside a McDonald's, alongside stockbrokers, department-store clerks, household servants, college students and even some children.
So pervasive is beagle-mania here that it has managed to trivialize even the most solemn of civic rituals. 
When Hong Kong celebrated China's National Day last week, there was more talk about the Golden Arches, where crowds flocked to buy the "China" Snoopy, than about the Gate of Heavenly Peace, where Mao proclaimed the founding of the People's Republic on Oct. 
1, 1949.
Fads are nothing new in Hong Kong, where the crowded living conditions and a gregarious population make it a hothouse for all sorts of trends. 
But the scale and nature of this fad has caught social observers by surprise. 
For one thing, people here normally pitch their consumer obsessions a bit higher.
Last spring, for example, Hong Kong people lined up by the thousands to buy shares in "red chips," mainland Chinese-owned companies listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. 
And in the fall, they besieged a fancy cake shop, after rumors circulated that it was about to close. 
Never, though, have so many upscale consumers turned cartwheels over something so resolutely mass market.
"Frankly, I'm baffled," said Michael Bond, a professor of psychology at Chinese University in Hong Kong. 
"The texture of these Snoopy toys isn't particularly appealing, the shape isn't particularly appealing. 
I guess nobody ever went broke underestimating the taste of the public."
Others say the Snoopy craze is merely the latest sign of Asia's economic distress. 
At a time when the recession has hammered Hong Kong's stock market, property market and even its race track, these brightly colored, three-inch beagles have become a low-cost outlet for people's consumer appetites.
"The Snoopy costs very little, but it represents something -- a status symbol," said Peter Tsoi, a local psychiatrist.
But economic misery alone does not explain it. 
Mcdonald's has run the same campaign in Thailand, Taiwan and Singapore, where it was popular but scarcely a sensation. 
The company said it would start the campaign in Japan soon and was considering whether to bring it to the United States.
Demand here is so intense that it has spawned a lively black market. 
Dealers loitered outside a McDonald's in central Hong Kong on a recent morning, haggling over particularly coveted Snoopys, like the ones representing China, Britain and the United States. 
The most sought-after Snoopy -- a sombrero-wearing Mexican -- commands nearly $40 at markets in the teeming neighborhood of Mongkok.
"Whenever people can smell a black market, they will come out in droves," said Thomas Wong, a 36-year-old employee at a finance company, who stood in line with his wife. 
"That is especially true during a recession."
Despite his financial bent, Mr. Wong insisted he was collecting the Snoopy toys purely for pleasure.
Still, the growing black market has exposed McDonald's to criticism. 
The company has declined to say how many Snoopys it has sold or how many it has in stock, which has further inflated their perceived value. 
Members of Hong Kong's legislature demanded that the restaurant chain halt the promotion because it was provoking unruly scenes outside the restaurants. 
It ended today.
McDonald's has tried to defuse the criticism by allowing customers to order an unlimited number of Snoopy toys through the mail. 
Until last week, they could only buy a single toy by lining up to purchase a burger, french fries and a soft drink. 
But because they could also buy up to five meals at a time, many were emerging from McDonald's laden down with plastic bags.
"We don't want long lines," said Mayee Tang, a spokeswoman for McDonald's. 
"People are lining up overnight. 
We're very concerned about safety in our restaurants. 
People are also really aggressive."
Among those lining up on a recent morning, however, the mood was more sheepish than surly. 
A well-dressed young man reading The Asian Wall Street Journal waved away a reporter without lifting his eyes from the paper. 
Several people argued that Snoopy offered valuable lessons about other cultures. 
And still others insisted they were only buying them for their children.
"This doesn't reflect the craziness of Chinese people, but the desire of parents to satisfy their kids," said a woman who identified herself only as Mrs. Tam, and was on her 10th consecutive day of lining up to buy a beagle.

text:

Two things changed Jimmy Lai's life forever: half a chocolate bar that he ate in 1957 and the massacre at Tiananmen Square in Beijing 32 years later.
"When I was 9, I was in Canton, just selling things on the street, stealing things," he said, recalling the young Lai Chi Ying.
"I tried to help this guy -- he had two big bags," he said. 
"A packet of something fell out of his pocket, and he broke it in half and said to eat it. 
I tasted this and said, 'What is that?'
He said, 'Chocolate, chocolate from Hong Kong.'
From that day, I said I wanted to go to Hong Kong."
Three years later, curled up in the bottom of a smelly, wave-tossed teacup of a boat, he was smuggled to Hong Kong.
The former street urchin came to run one of Asia's biggest chains of clothing stores, Giordano's, and to publish Hong Kong's largest circulation weekly magazine, which is as fat as a telephone book for a mid-sized town. 
The journal of politics, crime, fashion and life styles has managed with its exposes of corruption to enrage China and to provoke Hong Kong's triads, its violent criminal gangs.
In the last few months, firebombs have been thrown at Mr. Lai's home and paint at his clothing stores, and the police believe the gangs are responsible. 
Then in early July, China sued his magazine for libel.
"I don't care," said Mr. Lai, who is quick to smile, fond of talk and keeps his watch 30 minutes fast. 
"If we don't do it, someone else will."
When he arrived in Hong Kong, he left behind a China in the throes of Mao's Great Leap Forward industrialization program, which led to famines in which millions of Chinese starved to death. 
Like many of his fellow refugees, he brought with him little education or skills, but a ferocious determination to succeed. 
He went to work stitching gloves in a factory.
"I started studying English when I was 13," he said. 
"Whenever people shouted at me, were swearing at me, they shouted in English -- even the Chinese. 
I said I had to learn that damn language."
Seven years later, he had become the manager of a large textile factory. 
"From there I worked until I started my own factory," he said. 
"I found I could not take orders from other people."
His lack of education gave him an "inferiority complex," he said.
"So I studied and studied and studied," he said. 
"Even today, I will wake up at night and read."
In 1975, Mr. Lai opened his garment factory. 
"I sold to retailers like the Limited and the Gap," he said. 
"But I wanted to sell my clothes myself."
He picked the name Giordano's from an Italian resaurant in New York to camouflage the Hong Kong brand. 
The company took off after 1986, when he hired professional managers, he said, and now has 300 stores throughout Asia and $350 million in annual sales.
"But I was bored by retail," he said.
Then, on June 4, 1989, Chinese troops and tanks roared through the streets of Beijing, killing hundreds of people demanding democracy and protesting corruption. 
Mr. Lai watched on television, never moving from the images on his screen.
"There was no way back," he said. 
"I realized those guys had been closed from the world for 40 years. 
They had no information. 
And I realized information is the biggest business. 
So for me, to be in the media business became the greatest challenge."
Describing his publication, Next Magazine, he said, "I am, in effect, selling freedom."
Despite his wealth and the easier life he could have, he has kept the habit of hard work, focusing his energy on his new enterprise.
Since Next Magazine's inception three years ago, its circulation has soared to 180,000, the highest in Hong Kong. 
By paying high salaries, Mr. Lai has lured the colony's most aggressive reporters and its best writers. 
And while there are pages and pages of fashion, news of movie stars and social notes, the magazine's ground-breaking exposes have etched it clearly on the scene.
Mr. Lai's reporters have documented the way in which the Hong Kong gangs have insinuated themselves into the colony's life, controlling minibus concessions, extortion rackets and call girl rings. 
"They threw a Molotov in my house a couple of weeks ago," he said, laughing. 
"It exploded in the yard. 
They came in and destroyed my office, so now we have this security here. 
They destroyed my computers. 
They attacked my stores.
"I think they're very powerful -- no doubt. 
But if they threaten me, they won't kill me. 
If they want to kill me, they won't threaten me."
Then he took on the Chinese Government, reporting how about $9 million collected here in Hong Kong for poor children in China was misappropriated by local Chinese officials. 
"The kids never received any money, so we wrote about it," he said.
With China scheduled to take over the Government of Hong Kong from Britain in 1997, successful business people here are more inclined to curry its favor. 
But Mr. Lai believes that there is little point in capitulating to efforts at intimidation.
"The next three years will be very exciting, exciting in a positive sense and exciting in a frightening sense," he said. 
"In China, there is no trust left. 
That is the greatest disaster Communism has left behind in Chinese culture. 
There's no shame there. 
There's no sense of what is right, only of what is do-able. 
There has been a total corruption of the moral code."
Mr. Lai, who said he plans to stay after China takes over, heaved his work-shirt-clad shoulders. 
"Those Commies are fading very fast," he said. 
"They belong to the past. 
I think we are the future."

text:

After a year of economic despair, relentless criticism and growing doubts about his leadership, Hong Kong's chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, finally got a break last week.
Prime Minister Tony Blair of Britain, making his first visit here since this former British colony reverted to China, praised Mr. Tung for how steadily he was leading Hong Kong through the Asian financial crisis.
That the chief executive's most prominent defender these days is the former colonial ruler of this territory must be cold comfort to Mr. Tung, 61, a former shipping tycoon who took over Hong Kong when it was the pulsing heart of the Asian economy and has watched as it has gone into cardiac arrest.
"Am I frustrated?" asked Mr. Tung in a rare interview on Friday. 
"At times, I would say. 
But the important thing is to zero in on the things you can do and also zero in on the long-term perspective, because the turmoil will be over."
As if to underscore his point, Mr. Tung showed off a scroll that China's President, Jiang Zemin, painted and gave to Hong Kong as a gift during the handover. 
"Hong Kong will be better tomorrow," it says in Chinese calligraphy.
But to many people here, the economic crisis has settled into a debilitating illness, with little hope of a cure. 
Hong Kong's stock market has fallen by roughly half since its peak in August 1997, property prices have plummeted by as much as 60 percent and unemployment is soaring.
"People respect Tung as a sincere, elderly person," said Joseph Cheng, a professor of political science at the City University of Hong Kong. 
"His heart is in the right place, but people are looking for results."
As the man China chose to run Hong Kong, Mr. Tung faces a quandary unique among Asian leaders. 
He does not have a popular mandate, yet he must serve two very different constituencies: the 6.6 million people of Hong Kong and the Communist bosses in Beijing. 
Unless he comes to grips with the economic crisis, his critics say, Mr. Tung risks losing the faith of both groups.
With its economy in a free fall, some observers said they also feared that Hong Kong was turning away from the global market. 
In August the government intervened in the stock market to foil overseas hedge funds, which it accused of manipulating Hong Kong's markets.
In defending the intervention, senior officials played heavily on fears of unnamed "foreign traders," while a prominent member of the legislature referred to foreigners by a derogatory Cantonese word.
Mr. Tung said such remarks reflected public frustration with the hedge funds, which he said had destabilized Hong Kong's economy. 
But as someone who lived in Boston and New York for nine years and watches the football games of his favorite team, the San Francisco 49ers, on videocassette, Mr. Tung seemed disturbed by suggestions that Hong Kong had become xenophobic.
"The whole of Hong Kong overwhelmingly understands that Hong Kong is an international city, and the future of Hong Kong, the success of Hong Kong, is closely tied to being an international city," he said.
When it comes to domestic issues, critics said Mr. Tung seemed to miss the forest for the trees. 
In his annual policy address last week, he proposed to turn Hong Kong into a center for Chinese medicine, but he offered no major remedies for restoring the property market. 
During a radio call-in show with Mr. Tung after the 135-minute speech, one caller bluntly told him to resign.
"Obviously, you can understand it when the public is unhappy," Mr. Tung said. 
But he added, "Hong Kong is a very free-market economy, and what the government can do is really not a lot."
Some politicians here say Mr. Tung may be miscast in his role. 
Before the transfer to China, when Hong Kong was booming, a conservative businessman might have seemed an obvious choice to keep the cash registers ringing. 
Now, with the economy in a shambles and Hong Kong's confidence shaken, people here are yearning for more than Mr. Tung's gray-flannel style.
"He would make an excellent chief executive in Singapore, where the people are Chinese but are more old-fashioned," said Martin Lee, Hong Kong's most prominent pro-democracy politician.
Unlike his British predecessor, Christopher Patten, who was a Tory party leader before coming to Hong Kong, Mr. Tung does not relish kissing babies, glad-handing on the street or racing to accident scenes.
"This is one area in which I really have to learn a whole lot more -- transforming myself from a businessman," Mr. Tung said. 
"Could I communicate better?
Yes, I can and I will communicate better."
But while Mr. Tung wants to hone his political skills, he is not about to embrace the rough-and-tumble of democracy. 
Hong Kong held direct elections for one-third of the seats in its legislature in May, and pro-democracy candidates, who did well, are pressing for a speedier transition to full democracy.
Mr. Tung said the economic crisis made him more determined to stick to the timetable, which would not put his job or the full legislature up for election until after 2007.
"Right now we just have too many things going on," he said. 
"If you look at the changes that are around us, we need a stable environment."
In the final analysis, Mr. Tung's future depends on his relationship with the leaders in Beijing. 
And despite Hong Kong's travails, there is no evidence that he has lost their faith. 
Likewise, Mr. Tung's support among Hong Kong's powerful property tycoons remains generally solid.
Mr. Tung has worked hard to establish his credentials as the leader of a Chinese city. 
In his speech last week, he said Hong Kong people should be inspired by their brethren in China, who built earthen walls to hold back the waters during the recent floods on the Yangtze River.
But critics say the flood would not have been so calamitous if China had protected its environment. 
Hong Kong, they say, needs policies that avoid disaster, rather than appeals to heroism after disaster has struck.

text:
ï»¿
Over the last two centuries or so, Britain has ruled great chunks of the globe -- an empire, it was said, on which the sun never set.
Now, in a matter of hours, this easternmost shard of that empire will be relinquished, returned to China after 156 years of colonial suzerainty, leaving Britain with little more than a handful of islands, mostly in the Caribbean. 
Yet, the Hong Kong that returns to China is in many ways recognizable less as a place Chinese than a place indelibly touched by the ways of the West.
There are, to be sure, the obvious remainders of colonial rule -- coins with Queen Elizabeth's portrait still jingling in pockets, motorists hewing to the left side of the road, the local yacht club clinging stubbornly to its appellation "Royal," the tea and scones served on fine china at the Mandarin Hotel, and above all the use of English.
Yet, Britain has bequeathed Hong Kong more than visible trinkets of its reign.
Derek Davies, for decades the helmsman of Asia's pre-eminent news magazine, the Far Eastern Economic Review, assayed colonialism's central accomplishment in a speech he delivered not long ago titled, "Two Cheers for Colonialism."
"The British," he asserted, "were the Romans, the builders and administrators, no intellectual nonsense, although certainly they thought they were bringing civilization -- industry, modernity, the Christian religion."
"Harbors, roads, railways and imperial cities," were built, he continued, "in addition to less palpable but more important benefits such as the rule of law, the legal system, parliamentary democracy and a free press."
There are some here who are unimpressed by this heritage, preferring instead to see Hong Kong's entire colonial experience as an affront to Chinese history and civilization. 
Propounding this view most forcefully in the last year has been Zhou Nan, the senior Chinese official here, who invariably describes the return to Chinese sovereignty as the moment "when the yoke of colonialism" is shrugged off.
Indeed, Britain's resort to war from 1839 to 1842 to force the Chinese to buy opium from the firm of Jardine, Matheson and its wresting of the island of Hong Kong as booty from Beijing hardly presaged much in the way of morality or benevolence.
Official Chinese lamentations over British perfidy neatly overlook the venality and collaboration of a huge measure of Qing dynasty officialdom with the opium trade. 
Yet the fact remains that force of arms won Hong Kong for the British empire and cemented it, in 1898, with a 99-year lease on adjoining mainland territory.
In many ways, however, Hong Kong was different from other British colonial possessions, whether in the New World, Africa or the Indian subcontinent, virtually all of which are now long independent.
"I think Hong Kong is not a typical colonial situation," said Charles Aylmer, head of the University Library's Chinese Department at Pembroke College, Cambridge. 
"Rather paradoxically, I think the reason Hong Kong outlasted all the other colonies is because of the really strange situation with the lease."
"It is because everyone knew it was coming to an end that it lasted as long as it has," he said. 
"If it had been a simple occupied territory, there is no reason it would not have ended in 1949," the year Mao Zedong established the People's Republic of China.
The crude barbarity with which Hong Kong passed into British control was quickly supplanted by the rudiments of an administrative and legal system modeled on Britain's own. 
Democracy was not in the cards, though, for more than a century.
Still, Britain's last Governor, Christopher Patten, has been buoyantly defending the record of British stewardship. 
In his final appearance before Hong Kong's legislature, a fully elected body that China will dismiss on Tuesday, Mr. Patten summarized what he believes to be British colonialism's bequest to its last Asian territory.
"I think that Hong Kong is an astonishing Chinese success story," he told the 60-member legislature. 
"But I think it's a success story with British characteristics. 
I think that what Britain has helped provide as a result of the accidents of history is a framework within which people, particularly in the last 50 difficult years in this region, a framework within which Chinese men and women -- ordinary Chinese men and women -- have been able to do extraordinary things. 
I don't think any fair-minded observer would deny any role for British administrators or the rule of law in what has happened. 
But equally, any British observer, any of my predecessors as Governor, like this Governor, would stand back in awe at what Chinese men and women have managed to do here in Hong Kong given the chance, given the chance to be free in an economic and political sense."
More than any of his 27 predecessors, Mr. Patten in his five-year tenure moved Hong Kong toward a genuine measure of democratic governance and accountability. 
In 1995, for the first time, Hong Kong's Legislative Council was fully elected, directly and indirectly. 
Other local councils are all filled by elected members. 
It is one British legacy that will be nullified.
China will dismantle those institutions of governance on Tuesday. 
Indeed, the senior member of the new government's incoming Cabinet, Sir Sze-Yuen Chung, said this week that assemblies with appointed members marked "a step forward for democracy."
When the royal yacht Britannia, bearing Prince Charles and Mr. Patten, slips its mooring here on Tuesday, the Chinese flag will already be flying above them. 
But not all those who came here in the service of colonialism will follow.
Among those bits of empire that will remain are the likes of the stout and ruddy-faded Police Superintendent, Stephen Grinley Evans, who oversees a police team that watches the border for illegal immigrants passing into Hong Kong from China.
"I'm not ashamed to say I'm a bloody dinosaur," he said, laughing. 
"I came here from Scotland and I've been here since 1977. 
As long as they'll pay me, I'll stay."
And there is David T. Browning, a senior civil servant in the Customs and Excise Department who has seen the Union Jack lowered twice before on bits of empire.
"I joined the colonial service, partly for adventure and partly because I didn't really fancy staying in England," he said, hoisting a silver tankard of ale to his lips.
"I stayed on in Zambia after independence," he continued. 
"But I left the New Hebrides after it went independent."
The New Hebrides are now Vanuatu. 
"A friend in London said 'Why don't you go to Hong Kong?'
" he said. 
"Of course, I had in the back of my mind the impermanence of colonial regimes."
Now the last remaining British civil servant of 5,000 in his department, Mr. Browning said that Chinese rule would mean a rapid winnowing of the slightly more than 1,000 British citizens working in the Hong Kong Government.
"There are enough well-qualified, diligent, intelligent people here," Mr. Browning said. 
"The main thing is they have to maintain stabilityI under the S.A.R."
-- the Special Administrative Region, as Hong Kong will be known under Chinese rule. 
"I don't think it will be very many years before the expats leave," he continued. 
"Nobody's indispensable."
But for Governor Patten, his major regret, he insists, is not the disappearance of British civil servants -- for the civil service remains -- but the scuttling of democratic governance.
"I think there is a sadness," Mr. Patten said, "that this is the first time in recorded history that decolonization is followed by less democratization, not more."

Britain and China announced today that they would resume talks next week on Hong Kong's future, a decision that suggests a long and bitter impasse may have finally been broken.
The prospect of Beijing and London talking to each other instead of yelling at each other reflects the desire in each capital to defuse the uncertainty over Hong Kong's future. 
The talks mean that it again seems possible for Hong Kong to have a moderately smooth transition to Chinese rule in 1997.

'A Victory for Common Sense'
"I think that this is a victory for common sense," Mr. Patten told reporters in London.

text:

There are more sharks on the land in this want-to-get-rich town, Gordon Y. S. Wu likes to say, than in Victoria Harbor, the less than fragrant waters of Hong Kong's busy port where the 58-year-old engineer-developer will fearlessly take a plunge.
Nominally, Mr. Wu has lost a public bet that he could finish his Hong Kong-to-Guangzhou highway, the first superhighway into China, by September. 
Then he bet on Dec. 
31. He just keeps losing the bet, so jumping into the harbor is his self-imposed penalty.
But in the grander scheme of Mr. Wu's ambition, he seems to be winning. 
He wants to pave southern China with a modern and profitable toll-highway system while simultaneously building a dozen or more huge electric-power plants under license to the Beijing Government.
Â 
A Region to Contend With
Symbolically, the completion by early- to mid-1994 of the first six-lane, 76-mile superhighway will be a major event in burnishing the image of the Pearl River Delta as an integrated manufacturing corridor.
Though it will take years to repair the giant red scar that southern China's landscape now bears from the army of bulldozers rearranging its topography, Mr. Wu's transportation bridge will add to the economic nimbus that continues to billow in the region.
The $13-a-vehicle toll road will merge Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou into a single sprawling metropolis that the three cities will become after 1997 when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese control from its status now as a British Crown Colony. 
The area is already something of an urban megalopolis.
Â 
Respected for His Success
Though he is a number of months behind schedule in the mammoth highway construction project that has taken more than four years and, by the time it is finished, as much as $1.4 billion to build, Mr. Wu has developed an impressive record for overall performance in laying the foundations critical to sustaining southern China's economic boom. 
His longtime Hong Kong property-development firm, Hopewell Holdings Ltd., is listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.
By next year Mr. Wu's company, with two coal-fired power plants operating in Guangdong province, will be providing 35 percent of the south China province's electrical needs.
With the opening of the first leg of the highway project for the 30,000 vehicles a day crossing the frontier between Hong Kong and China, Mr. Wu will have established himself as a prototype developer, using foreign capital and management know-how to attack the bottlenecks in China's transportation and energy industries.
"There is no way China can get the money themselves to do the job," he said in an interview. 
"If I start working on nothing else but power generation until the day I die, I still can't fulfill 10 percent of what they want."
Largely because he has defined a market in a development area critical to China's leaders, Mr. Wu, as much as any Hong Kong businessman, has the confidence of top Beijing officials.
"China never wanted to open up this sector, and I was the first one to crack it in 1984," he said, recalling that his final negotiations were with Li Peng, an electrical engineer by training who is now Prime Minister. 
"I would say he reluctantly agreed at that time," Mr. Wu said.
As a result, these days the contracts just keep coming. 
And thanks to Beijing's enthusiasm and the China fever that is rolling through capital markets in the West, he has all the financial backing he can handle.
Mr. Wu started an eight-city American fund-raising tour in San Francisco last month to sell $374 million worth of stock to partially finance the power plants.
"By the time I hit Denver," he said, "the stock was all sold, so I suggested we forget about the Eastern cities because I had work to do, but the underwriters insisted that we go through the motions."
One key to Mr. Wu's China strategy is to make sure that his joint-venture partners in China, usually units of province governments, are making as much money or more than he is. 
Another is to remove himself from the distribution of electric power. 
His plants will sell wholesale to China's distribution network, which will add its own distribution charge.
"They are making more than we are," he said of the Chinese "We get a minimum of 15 percent.

In fact, the incentive clauses and special features of the contracts allow higher returns, analysts say.
Mr. Wu's friends say he has labored mightily on the highway project to overcome snags to land acquisition in China, where any of a hundred local village chiefs in the path of the highway could hold him up -- and did.
The six-lane road will rid the region of the grueling two-day, bumper-to-bumper round-trip from Hong Kong's port to Guangzhou's factories. 
Once the highway is open, it will be possible to make the round-trip in a morning's drive.

Some Negative Aspects
In an analysis of the roadway's progress, S. G. Warburg Securities said in a report issued in the fall that delays and cost overruns could conceivably push the opening of its final segments to the end of 1994, even into early 1995.

"Frequent press comments by Hopewell in respect of early completion and early revenue collection have not materialized," the report said, adding, "The risks that the company has exposed itself to by the apparent lack of programming and detailed budgeting are significant and it is this combination of unrealistic statements" and "the large sums of equity involved which give rise to concern."

Some eyebrows have been raised among Hong Kong stock analysts, who say that Mr. Wu's introduction of a new power subsidiary represents a prospective price-earnings ratio of about 40 times the unit's forecasted 1994 earnings of $27 million.

Vision to Last a Lifetime
A Princeton University-educated civil engineer, Mr. Wu is known for thinking big, and at times he dwells on the notion that he can now conceptualize projects that will take the rest of his working life.

"I am 58," he said. 
"I would really like to build that highway."
