It was class time at Beijing University, but at 10 this morning seven guys in shorts and T-shirts crowded around a color TV in dorm room 511, a spare cement cubicle decorated with three metal bunkbeds and yesterday's laundry. 
Nine student "shareholders" had bought the TV last month in anticipation of just such an occasion, and now hoots and jeers filled the air.
"Aya, that Malone he plays dirty."
"Nice ball. 
Go Rodman!"
"They're losing with three minutes to go. 
I can't stand it. 
Hit me with a hammer!"
Minutes later, half a world away, the Chicago Bulls clinched their sixth National Basketball Association championship with a final basket with only five seconds to play. 
The students jumped to their feet and began a refrain: "Qiao Dan, Qiao Dan, Qiao Dan."
Qiao Dan, of course, is Michael Jordan. 
Sure, Bill Clinton, President of the world's most powerful nation, is about to visit China. 
But to the Chinese, Michael Jordan remains America's king.
Mr. Clinton's state visit this month has brought out citizens' interest in all things American, from books to clothes to movie stars. 
But these all seem like passing fancies compared to the intense passion that Chinese, especially young Chinese, have developed for Michael Jordan and American basketball.
"Michael Jordan is much more famous than Clinton here," said Cheng Qian, 20, a Bulls fan and shareholder in the TV set who is a management major at Beijing University.
The Chinese have named him kongzhong feiren -- "space flier."
In the last week, businessmen, retired teachers, students and government officials have all paused to watch him, live on state-run television, as he led the Chicago Bulls to their 4-2 series victory over the Utah Jazz.
When Beijing Meilande Information Company recently asked 1,000 Chinese to name the best-known Americans ever, Michael Jordan came in second, trailing Thomas Edison by just a few percentage points. 
Behind him were Albert Einstein, Mark Twain and Bill Gates.
On the sidewalks of Jianguomenwai Avenue, vendors sell Michael Jordan posters. 
In department stores, Michael Jordan books and calendars sit beside those featuring Hong Kong movie stars and the late Chairman Mao.
"Of all American things, basketball is the most popular," said Li Fa, a junior, who could not join the crowd in 511 because he is a Jazz fan. 
"Everyone knows Michael Jordan."
State television began broadcasting prerecorded N.B.A. games in the early 1990's, and recently switched to live broadcasts. 
Today, Chinese viewers had three opportunities to see the final playoff game, which the Bulls won 87-86. 
The first was live at 7:30 A.M., then a taped game at 9 A.M. for late risers, and a replay at 9 P.M.
Chinese are hard pressed to say why they so adore the Bulls and Michael Jordan, who scored 45 points in the final game and was named Most Valuable Player.
"I don't know -- because of his skill, and because he alone carries half of the Chicago team," said Li Qixing, 20, another of the TV's shareholders.
American basketball is certainly more colorful than the home-grown variant, where the People's Liberation Army's August 1 team (named for the day the Army was founded) is the reigning champion. 
In skill and in entertainment value, Chinese players are no match for the likes of Dennis Rodman, who played the game with much of his hair dyed green.
Said Han Bai, a junior, sitting on his bunk bed in jeans and a T-shirt, "I couldn't accept this from a Chinese player, but he's an American so we expect it."
And American sportscasts have other attactions.
The students who gathered in 511 on this steamy morning, ooohed when they saw Leonardo DiCaprio, star of "Titanic," sitting at courtside. 
And, in a room full of male college juniors, the Jazz's cheerleaders, dancing in black leotards, got the thumbs up as well. 
Heads nodded in approval as Cheng Qian opined, "In this way, the Jazz are better than the Bulls."

file: In China, Incomes Are Low but Everything Is Cheap.txt
text:
ï»¿
One of the puzzles for many visitors to China is how to reconcile the apparent wealth around them with China's official per capita income of just $370 a year.
Part of the explanation is that interpreting China's economic statistics can be a nightmare. 
Prices, for instance, are so low that income statistics are misleading.
Take Zhu Huiyuan, a 46-year-old security officer at a company in the central Chinese city of Bengbu. 
His salary is only $25 a month, a fairly typical urban wage.
But Mr. Zhu also gets a half-dozen supplements -- for haircuts, for buying newspapers, for seniority and so on -- that add up to $14 more. 
His wife, a cook, earns a total of $30 a month in salary and supplements.
While their combined monthly income of $69 a month sounds meager, they pay no income or sales taxes, and expenses are minimal. 
Apartment rents in China average about $2.50 a month including utilities, bus fare is a penny, spinach costs 6 cents a pound, a winter down jacket is $22, and an evening newspaper costs 2.5 cents. 
Even a luxury like dog meat is only $1 a pound.
One way to come up with a more realistic value for China's gross national product is to adjust it by valuing production at international prices. 
This approach, called the purchasing power parity technique, yields a much higher value for the gross national product of China as well as for those of other developing countries.
A potential flaw in this method is that China's products are often of lower quality than Western commodities, so price comparisons sometimes overvalue the Chinese goods. 
Consider Chinese plates: they look terrific but are often contaminated with lead. 
Pricing them at the level of American plates would exaggerate their value.
Because of these kinds of ambiguities, different studies relying on this technique have come up with widely varying estimates of the size of China's economy, from about $650 per person to about $4,000 per person. 
One gauge is that China's figures for life expectancy and average calories consumed are close to those of countries with a gross national product of about $2,000 per capita.
At the highest estimates, China's G.N.P. is substantially bigger than Japan's. 
At the more reasonable level of $2,000 per capita, China's G.N.P. is about $2.3 trillion, behind the official G.N.P. figures for the United States and Japan but larger than Germany's.
When Japan's income is also adjusted for purchasing power, it drops significantly because of high prices in Japan. 
A World Bank analysis using United Nations data, for instance, suggests that in terms of purchasing power China's per capita income in 1990 may have been about $1,950, while in Japan it was $16,950 -- compared with the official Japanese per capita income in that year of $25,430.

file: In China_s Outlands, Poorest Grow Poorer.txt
text:
ï»¿
Life is unimaginably hard in the burnt umber hills of this part of northwestern China. 
In four of the last five years there has been no harvest and millions of poor farmers are living in a state of hunger, poor health and illiteracy that in some areas approaches the deprivation levels of China's great famine in the late 1950's.
Muslim villagers here in southern Ningxia, known as the Hui Autonomous Region, say that no official from the Xiji County government, 20 miles away, has ever hiked into this desperately poor hamlet to offer assistance to the peasants, most of whom cannot afford to send their children to school and for whom medical care is nonexistent.
To add to their misery this fall, a plague of rats has come down from the mountains to feed on the pitifully small potato crop that sprouted after the blessing of a late summer rain and is all that will keep hunger at bay this winter. 
This year, a farmer named He Delin put it ruefully, "Our life is potatoes."
Although China has made prodigious efforts under Communist rule to eradicate poverty, lifting tens if not hundreds of millions to a higher standard of living through the economic reforms led by the paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, since 1978, from 60 million to 100 million Chinese still live on the edge of starvation and despair.
And according to new World Bank estimates, more than one-quarter of all Chinese -- about 350 million -- are in substantial deprivation, subsisting on less than $1 a day. 
In addition, for the first time a significant number of urban dwellers -- perhaps 15 million or more -- are falling below the poverty line as moribund state factories jettison workers in cities with no social security or welfare nets to catch them.
The significance of the new estimates is that they show a larger part of China's population being left behind than previously thought, even as the overall economy continues to register impressive growth. 
Although an average Chinese is better off today than at any time in the last 150 years, a huge part of the population -- more than the population of the United States -- remains on the bottom rung of the economic ladder.
The new World Bank estimates, based on improved data from the Chinese, also show that the big reduction in poverty in the first 10 years of economic overhaul begun by Mr. Deng has slowed substantially, while disparities in income between the rich coastal regions and poor inland regions have only intensified.
Altogether, these new estimates suggest that China will not be the economic colossus in the next century that many experts have predicted. 
Some now believe that the weight of China's poor, added to the weight of its debt-ridden state industries and the degradation of its environment, will limit the pace of development and may well prevent China's emergence as a dominating power.
And the grievances of millions of peasants and workers slipping closer to the edge can only be a source of threat and volcanic instability for the Communist Party leadership, whose legitimacy now derives solely from its ability to deliver prosperity, not ideology, to the masses.
Here in the village of Niujuan, which means Cow Pen, the weight of poverty can be seen in the faces that reflect the grinding fatigue of malnutrition and the corrosion of untreated disease.
"Last year was the worst," said a farmer, Su Dikua, speaking by the light of the kerosene lamp in his one-room mud house, which is a step up from the cave where Mr. Su had lived for most of his 59 years. 
His wife has a "skin disease" acquired during those years in the cave. 
It is possible that it is leprosy, but she has never seen a doctor about it.
Last year, Mr. Su said, they had almost nothing to eat. 
"Those who had the energy, traveled to the city to beg," he said. 
Among those who fled because of the hardship was his eldest son, Su Sanwa, 22, and "we haven't had any letters from him since."
It now appears that the Communist Party leadership has little hope of reaching its goal of lifting this huge population out of its misery by the end of the century.
Although Beijing still spends about $1 billion a year to alleviate poverty, with additional help from the World Bank and the United Nations, "no one believes that the goal is achievable," said one antipoverty expert in a major Western aid institution.
Even senior Chinese officials are beginning to hedge.
Liu Junwen, a senior staff member of the "leading group" on poverty reduction under Prime Minister Li Peng, acknowledged in September that to reach the goal, "that means that we must lift 13 million people out of poverty annually, almost three times the figure we have managed to reach in the past few years."
Speaking to reporters after a poverty conference, he added, "the poverty in which these 65 million people are living constitutes the hardest nut to crack due to the various deep-rooted geographical and socioeconomic adversities."
In other words, the first easy step in poverty reduction is over.
The spurt of prosperity that came in the 1980's from breaking up Mao's communes and freeing 900 million peasants to sell their own produce has proved difficult to match in the 1990's. 
The early gains in living standards were made among the Chinese living in lowland areas with access to roads, markets and ports.
The hardest work lies ahead for hundreds of millions of Chinese who live in mountainous, desert and arid plateau regions where arable land and rainfall are rare. 
And many of the hard-core poor are from China's minority populations, who were flushed into the highlands centuries ago by conquering armies of the Han Chinese.
"You hike into these villages and people are putting dirt in backpacks to haul up onto these rocky slopes to try to get something to grow," said Alan Piazza, a leading specialist on poverty in China for the World Bank. 
"When I bring agriculturists to these areas, they look at the landscape and say, 'Declare this a national park and get everyone out.'
It's ridiculous; there is just no land."
He was referring to the eerily beautiful karst landscapes of southwestern China, where topsoil is scarce among the humpback limestone formations.
Mr. Piazza is the bank's most outspoken advocate for more focused, small-scale programs to put money into the hands of farmers, while also rebuilding rural education and health care so that families might have a chance to break the generational cycle of poverty.
"Most Americans could not begin to comprehend what 65 million Chinese have to endure and what that level of deprivation is all about," he said in a recent interview in Beijing.
"What you find in these villages is that one in 10 children dies in the first year of life," he said; "in some places it's one in five. 
Respiratory infections pick them off at incredibly high rates."
He added, "In poverty areas, the remnant of the health system that once was no longer exists."
As for education, he said: "In the Southwest, only one child in 10 gets through the sixth grade. 
There is no way you will eliminate poverty if you don't educate children through the sixth grade."
China's leaders may have begun to realize that their approach to poverty reduction has been flawed. 
A recent Government survey reported that about $800 million of the $1 billion allocated annually was being spent on subsidies to county governments in poverty areas. 
Other poverty experts say that money has been squandered by local officials who never travel to the countryside, and that other money has been diverted to rural industries that are favored by local party bosses.
"We have heard about poverty alleviation programs," said He Demin, a 43-year-old farmer with eight children who lives down the gully from the Su family and who sold off farm animals last year so the family could eat through the winter. 
"But it never arrives here."
He added, "The central authorities have a good heart, but their programs are not implemented by the officials below."
A neighbor, Yuan Wenqi, added: "It seems that the county government gets some money, and the township enterprises get some money, but not us."
The greatest failure in poverty reduction is in education and health, many experts say.
China has emphasized raising agricultural productivity on the assumption that rising farm incomes will allow peasants to buy the education and health services they need.
But because of the harsh terrain in China's upland areas, increasing agricultural production "is a pipe dream," Mr. Piazza said. 
The best solution, he said, is to educate children so they can find jobs in rural townships and small cities and leave the barren mountains behind.
"We are all illiterate here and so we don't know what is happening," said Mr. Yuan, as he offered boiled potatoes to a visitor. 
"If something is harmful, we don't know it. 
If something is good, we don't know it."
Ma Xinggui, a neighbor down the road, put it a different way as he paused from digging potatoes with his wife: "Because I have never been to school, I am like a blind person, even though I have eyes."

file: In Drive on Dissidents, China Gives 4th Severe Sentence in Week.txt
text:
ï»¿
Dealing out the fourth lengthy prison term to political dissenters in a week, China today convicted a man for "providing intelligence to hostile foreign organizations" because he gave an interview about farmer protests to the United States-financed Radio Free Asia, a human rights group said.
After an unusual Sunday trial in the southern province of Hunan that lasted less than three hours, the defendant, Zhang Shanguang, 42, was sentenced to 10 years in prison, according to the group Human Rights in China, based in New York.
Mr. Zhang previously spent seven years in prison for organizing an independent labor union in 1989. 
This year, before his detention in July, he had formed a group to protect laid-off workers and tried to register it with local officials.
Chinese authorities, fearing social unrest at a time of rising unemployment, appear to be especially fearful of any labor organizations outside Communist Party control, and of any efforts to link up disaffected workers with democracy campaigners.
Earlier this week, as part of the most severe crackdown on dissidents here in two years, three long-time activists who promoted a new China Democracy Party, Xu Wenli, Qin Yongmin and Wang Youcai, were convicted on subversion charges and given sentences of 11 to 13 years.
At his brief trial today in Huaihua City, Hunan, Mr. Zhang was charged with "illegally providing intelligence to hostile foreign organizations and persons," according to his lawyer and relatives.
The indictment specifically cited a telephone interview Mr. Zhang gave last March to Radio Free Asia in which he discussed a protest against high taxes by 70 to 80 farmers in one Hunan county, and another incident in which a farmer who refused to pay a tax was killed.
Numerous such farmer protests have been reported around the country in recent years and top national leaders have spoken out against high, unfair burdens put on peasants by local and county governments.
Radio Free Asia, which was set up in 1996 and receives all of its funds from Congress, broadcasts news and other programs into China from transmitters in Central Asia and the Pacific. 
The Chinese Government sees the network as hostile and tries, with some success, to jam the broadcasts, which often emphasize democracy-related subjects that are banned in the national media.
"We deeply regret this action," said Daniel Southerland, executive editor of Radio Free Asia, speaking by telephone from Washington today.
In the March interview, Mr. Southerland said, journalists called Mr. Zhang to verify reports of the farmer protests and "he didn't say anything that wasn't widely known -- certainly it wasn't national security information."
Radio Free Asia, which broadcasts in native languages to eight countries where news is censored, frequently quotes Chinese residents on its programs, though does not use names when it appears the speaker would be endangered.
Reeling from the recent trials, China's remaining dissidents are now waiting to see if the Government will stop with the jailing of a few leaders or continue on with more arrests.
In general, only those who have been actively involved in organizing the new political party or independent worker groups have been imprisoned for any length of time.
In contrast to earlier decades, Chinese people today are fairly free to voice dissenting opinions in private -- so long as they do not act on them.

file: IN ECLIPSE -- A special report._Empty Isles Are Signs Japan_s Sun Might Dim.txt
text:
ï»¿
After a dazzling century in which Japan emerged on the globe first as a feared military power and then as a formidable economic one, its influence may be on the wane.
The real problem is not the economic crisis that dominates the headlines, but a pair of intertwined long-run concerns: the work force is shrinking fast, and Japan undermines its economy's productivity by squandering money on life support for moribund industries and backward regions.
In the next few decades, unless Japan somehow manages to arrest current trends, it may find that its share of global economic output has shrunk considerably.
Japan's working-age population peaked in 1995 and is falling quickly. 
The overall Japanese population will still rise a tiny bit until 2007, because of the long life expectancy of today's retirees. 
But after that, the Japanese Government's official projections show the country's population tumbling rapidly, from 126 million today to 100 million in 2050 and 67 million in 2100.
"If influence is measured by G.D.P., then Japan's influence will decline," said Chikashi Moriguchi, a prominent Japanese economist who has studied the aging of Japan.
While other industrialized countries also face low fertility rates and aging societies, Japan is in a particular bind because for cultural and sentimental reasons, it cannot easily avail itself of the two obvious solutions: easier immigration to shore up the population and ruthless restructuring to bolster productivity.
Japan has some tremendous underlying economic strengths, ranging from well-trained and committed workers to huge private savings. 
Companies like Sony and Toyota may continue to expand and become even more titanic global businesses while their home market becomes relatively smaller.
Of course, the link between population size and global economic influence is far from absolute, as India demonstrates at one extreme and Hong Kong at the other. 
Even if Japan's share of the world's economy continues to decline, ordinary Japanese may live more enjoyable lives in a less crowded country.
"Japan will be more of a middling power, less important than it is now in the scheme of things, and it may be more comfortable with that," said Hugh T. Patrick, director of the center on Japanese Economy and Business at Columbia University.
But Japan's shrinking population, many economists argue, makes it difficult to see how Japan can continue to play the role of Asia's leading power. 
Historically, the world has usually adjusted more easily to the ripples from a declining power like Japan than to those of a rising power like China, but the economic and political ramifications will still be far-reaching.
Â 
The Safety Net
Picking Losers On a Huge Scale
What will Japan look like in a few decades?
No one knows, of course, but the late-night horror television scenario might be something based on life today in the little island of Akashima, in the Goto chain in southern Japan.
Yoshie Kokou, a friendly 70-year-old fisherman, stood on a bluff on Akashima the other day, smiling shyly and speaking lovingly of the many friends and family members who surrounded him. 
The only catch is that Mr. Kokou was standing in the cemetery. 
Akashima's hospital, school, stores and most of its homes are abandoned, and aside from Mr. Kokou only four people still live on the 128-acre island.
Akashima, its seaside cliffs jutting out of a blue-black ocean that is hospitable mostly to the passing whales, has lost people (it had 300 inhabitants at its peak a few decades ago) not so much because women had fewer babies as because people moved to the cities. 
But Akashima offers a glimpse of Japan's difficulties in generating the kind of boom in productivity that might help make up for a shrinking work force.
From the 1950's through the 1980's, productivity grew much more quickly in Japan than in the West. 
But Japan's Total Factor Productivity, the broadest measure, is now growing by only about half of 1 percent per year, much less than half the level of the United States.
Fundamentally, the reason is that Japan steadily lost its capacity for what the economist Joseph Schumpeter called "creative destruction."
Japan never built up a huge public welfare system, but it has instituted safety nets and subsidies to create a welfare state for companies and towns and declining industries.
The result is welfare dependency among inefficient corporations and moribund economic sectors and fading islands and villages. 
Instead of "picking winners," Japan is now picking losers and subsidizing them on a huge scale.
Even tiny Akashima, a minnow in the Sea of Japan, is taking up a whale's share of the national resources. 
Just the other day, several barges chugged into Akashima's port to begin a $2.5 million project to expand it and build a new pier.
It may seem odd to be spending so much money on a project that serves only five full-time residents, but that is only the beginning. 
The Government also provides a $490,000 annual subsidy to the twice-daily ferry to Akashima and a neighboring island, Oshima, which has 70 residents.
At a huge cost, the Government has also laid down under-sea cables to Akashima to carry electricity to the five residents. 
Indeed, to demonstrate its absolute disregard for expense and efficiency, the Government has laid down not just one cable but two.
"That is to insure a stable supply of electricity," said Choji Tanikawa, an official in the regional offices on the main island of Fukue.
Then there are the other subsidies: the underwater telephone cable, the postal delivery, the weekly clinic by a public doctor. 
The island of Oshima next door has what must be one of the best student-teacher ratios in the world: there are three students and nine teachers.
Â 
The Population
Low Birth Rates And Smaller Output
All the subsidies help reproduce mainland life even on the remotest islands.
"There's nobody left here, but I like it," said Tama Shiowaki, a 74-year-old woman who was bustling down the path on Akashima. 
"Feel this fresh air!
I get up at 5 A.M. to feed my chickens and ducks, and I'm so healthy here."
"I just hope young people come back," she continued. 
"When I was a kid, there was a store over there," she said, pointing to a collapsed building peeking from the thick brush. 
"And over there. 
And there. 
And down by the cemetery as well. 
And now they're all gone."
In another world, the bustle of downtown Tokyo, Kaoru Yosano is Minister of International Trade and Industry and is thus charged with maintaining Japan's future international competitiveness. 
Sitting at a conference table in his vast office, the size of a typical Japanese apartment for a family of five, Mr. Yosano sips his tea and admits that he is struggling for solutions to the population problem -- in vain.
"There is no easy answer," Mr. Yosano said bleakly. 
"My mother was one of 8 children. 
My father was one of 11. 
My wife and I were each one of 5 children, and we ourselves have 2 children. 
When we look further ahead at the next generation, well, I don't hear much from my sons about having babies."
(Mr. Yosano's two sons, both married, one with one child and the other without any, both declined to be interviewed.)
"Former Primer Minister Takeshita once told me that in the year 2500, Japan's population will be down to one person," Mr. Yosano said with a glum smile. 
"When that happens, I suppose Japan's global influence inevitably will have declined."
Japan is not, of course, the only country facing low birth rates. 
Japanese women give birth to an average of 1.4 children, while World Bank figures show Spain, Bulgaria and Latvia tied for the lowest "total fertility rate" in the world, at 1.1. 
Even the United States will grow primarily because of immigration, because its total fertility rate, of 2.0, is slightly below the level needed for a self-sustaining population (which is 2.1, to account for such factors as babies who die before adulthood).
So what sets Japan apart is not so much that its women are having fewer babies, but rather the combination it represents: the world's second-largest economy is now one of the world's least fertile and fastest-aging societies. 
Latvia's fertility crisis will affect Lithuania; Japan's will shape the global economy.
The essence of the challenge is a shrinking work force. 
The Government predicts that the working-age population of Japan will drop by about 650,000 a year over the next 50 years.
If those projections hold up, then even assuming that more women and old people hold jobs and that productivity continues to grow steadily at the same rate as in the 1990's, then Japan's gross national product in 2050 will be 5 percent smaller than it is today. 
Assuming that the rest of the world continues to grow economically at about the same pace as it has in recent decades, that will leave Japan with less than one-third the share of global output that it now enjoys.
Moreover, each Japanese worker will have to support more nonworkers, as the aged rise from one-sixth of the population now to one-third by the middle of the next century. 
This means that simply for Japan to retain its present per capita income, each worker will have to increase output to make up for the growing numbers who are idle.
"I don't think Japanese living standards are going to improve," said Robert Alan Feldman, chief economist at Morgan Stanley in Tokyo and one of the first Japan specialists to focus on demographic constraints. 
"Japan's G.N.P. is going to shrink, and on a per capita level it may also be a little bit lower."
Â 
The Puzzle
A Future Hampered By Past's Subsidies
None of this is fixed, of course. 
If Japan could shore up productivity dramatically, then fewer workers could still produce as much as today's work force or even more.
But the pattern of subsidies to Akashima -- repeated in small islands and hamlets around Japan -- helps explain why Japanese taxes and utility charges are so high, and why Japan has steadily seen its productivity growth slow down. 
Because it lays down undersea cables for people like Mrs. Shiowaki, NTT charges unified telephone rates across the country that are so high that they have stifled growth of the Internet in Japan.
The country has some dazzling technologies, and these could perhaps be the basis for increasing productivity and allowing Japan to hold its own economically for a time. 
But its strongest sectors, like technology, are hobbled by regulation and by the burden of having to support the weakest industries.
High per-minute phone connection charges mean that most Japanese do not spend much time surfing the World Wide Web, for instance. 
National law forbids discounting books, to protect small shops and consumers in remote areas, so there is no incentive to buy books on the Internet. 
The upshot is that Mrs. Shiowaki has her subsidized telephone, and Japan has no Amazon.com.
Likewise, high electrical charges, postal rates and taxes have made it increasingly difficult even for efficient Japanese businesses to compete internationally. 
It is, for example, more expensive to mail a letter within Tokyo than to mail it from America to Tokyo. 
Japanese companies began to do their mass mailings from America, to save on postage, so the Japanese Government banned the mailing of domestic advertising from abroad.
Why does Japan so obstinately subsidize its past at the expense of its future?
One reason is a political system in which small towns and rural areas wield disproportionate influence, such that an upper house member of Parliament from rural Tottori prefecture has only one-fifth as many constituents as a member from Tokyo. 
The economist Mancur Olson, in examining why great economies lose their dynamism, emphasized the rise of special interests that win protections and clog up the gears of a market economy; although he was writing primarily about the experience of the West, the same analysis applies to Japan.
Yet what is just as important as special-interest politics is a profound Japanese commitment to equality across the country, and a revulsion for "jaku niku, kyo shoku" society -- one where the strong eat the weak. 
Most Japanese accept that businesses may be predatory abroad, but there is some yearning for them to be vegetarians at home. 
There is a genuine and broad-ranging sympathy for the weakest elements of the economy, and there are virtually no calls for cutting off the spigots of cash for rural areas or declining industries.
In effect, Japan has fostered a gentle, merciful brand of capitalism, one that keeps dying businesses on artificial life support. 
The effort to run a country as if it were a Disney movie strikes Americans as deeply admirable and hopelessly naive, and Japan has indeed found it increasingly difficult to nurture an economy drawn entirely in cheerful pastels.
In a system too squeamish to let industries or islands die, taxes increasingly go to rescue the feeblest competitors, those that in a more ruthless system would have gone the way of blacksmiths and buggy-whip factories. 
Take Japan's ubiquitous sento, or public baths, for although they are a tiny industry they are symptomatic of Japan's difficulties letting go of its past.
These sento are glorious nooks of steam and history, privately owned, where people can go and scrub and then relax together in an oversize, overheated tub. 
After adjusting to the sensation of being boiled alive, it is difficult to think of anything more pleasant than a Japanese bath, or anything less essential.
In the old days, of course, the sento were necessary institutions, because many families had no bath or shower at home. 
Now nearly all homes have baths, and young people almost never use the sento, but Japan cannot muster the courage to let them go bankrupt. 
So, even though their time is past and they have no hope of competing in the marketplace, many sento are kept alive with Government loans and subsidies that each year total almost $100 million.
The result is not only higher taxes but capital and labor that, in the public bath industry, are at Indonesian levels of productivity and dropping. 
Everybody knows one way to raise productivity here -- let the sento go bankrupt -- but Japan is not prepared to pay that price.
The same kinds of sentimental subsidies keep islands like Akashima alive. 
There has not even been any discussion of cutting back the ferry service to once daily, and islanders seem stunned when they are asked whether the Government should continue to provide expensive services to a tiny, aging population.
"They've never talked about cutting off services," said Mankichi Kokou, 73, an Akashima resident. 
"Even if this becomes a ghost town, the services will continue. 
They have to."
There is a good deal of talk about how Japan may be beginning a "third revolution" of social and economic transformation as great as the late-19th-century Meiji period and the post-World War II era. 
Increasing mergers and the breakdown of the lifetime employment system give some evidence of this, and officials are talking a good game.
"It is essential that we radically transform this nation's system and character in order to promote further prosperity," Prime Minister Keizo Obuchi said earlier this month.
Nonetheless, as Mr. Obuchi suggested, the key changes are yet to come. 
Japan's steps have been tentative, and South Korea has more obviously embraced markets in just the last 18 months than Japan has in the last decade.
Â 
The Bottleneck
A Resistance To Immigration
Another way that Japan could stave off the demographic projections is by encouraging large-scale immigration.
The United States, in particular, has shown that a country need not worry too much about low birth rates so long as immigrants fill the ranks of workers. 
And America has brought in not only low-wage laborers, working as nannies or farm workers, but also computer technicians and software engineers who have contributed enormously to the dynamism of Silicon Valley.
"The great strength of America is that it draws in continually the best of everywhere," said Jagdish Bhagwati, a Columbia University professor of international economics who is from India. 
"Japan cannot really match that openness."
"Japan has the bottleneck," he said, "of not being really open to foreign cultures."
It has been 145 years since Japan abandoned its "sakoku" policy, which meant barring almost all foreigners. 
Yet even now Japan is more hostile to immigration than any other industrialized country. 
It is, for example, exceptionally difficult for a foreigner to acquire Japanese nationality without marrying a Japanese.
Tens of thousands of Chinese are sneaking into Japan to take dirty or dangerous jobs, and they are beginning to leave an imprint on the country. 
But because some of the Chinese immigrants are violent gangsters, many Japanese are more frightened than ever of large-scale immigration.
"I think the Government would try to find any other means of solving the labor shortage rather than mass immigration," said Charles Horioka, an American economist at Osaka University. 
"Japan is so concerned about maintaining cultural and racial homogeneity."
If Tokyo made an all-out effort, it could recruit many of the best young scholars and engineers from India, Taiwan, Vietnam and China to study and work in Japan. 
That could revitalize the economy and create a boom of entrepreneurship, but few in Japan seem enthusiastic about that idea, and many seem fatalistic about the waves of Asian migration that bypass Japan and continue on to the United States. 
"English has become a common language, so it's natural for the best and brightest to go to America to study," said Mr. Yosano, the trade official. 
"If they come to Japan, then they face the language barrier.
"I envy America for attracting them, but that's just the way it is."
Another alternative is for Japan to try to increase its own fertility rates, by persuading women like Miki Fujii to have babies. 
Mrs. Fujii, 32, has a good office job in Tokyo and the last thing she wants is a child.
"It's really a matter of whether having a child is worth all the stress and pressure," Mrs. Fujii said. 
"Besides, I'd get no help from my husband. 
He has this traditional idea that women should raise children and that they enjoy it."
"I've heard men say they're staying at work late because going home early means having to take care of children, and they'd rather work than do that," Mrs. Fujii continued. 
"I totally understand that. 
I think it's quite natural to feel that way. 
I know I would feel that way."
Â 
The Work Force
Making Babies, Keeping the Elderly
Japan is a difficult place for a woman to raise a child, partly because in practice this is a nation of single mothers. 
Husbands stagger home late from the office or a bar, and a Government poll found that fathers spend an average of just six minutes a day looking after their children.
Profound social changes -- like the emergence of husbands who changed diapers -- might help fertility rates. 
But the Japanese Government's bleak population projections already assume some recovery in fertility. 
If the total fertility rate stays where it is, then the population will plummet even faster: to 92 million in 2050 and 50 million in 2100.
Some Scandinavian countries have raised fertility a bit by offering improved child care and various other incentives, and some Japanese localities are even offering cash rewards for extra children. 
Still, in countries like Sweden that have tried this approach, the cost has been considerable and the long-term increase in fertility very slight.
Moreover, an increase in birth rates would take a long time to work through the system, for nearly all of Japan's labor force in the year 2025 has already been born.
"We cannot evade the phenomenal change in population structure and phenomenal change in population size," said Makoto Atoh, one of Japan's leading demographers. 
"It's an inevitability derived from the current level of fertility and longevity."
Dr. Atoh said that Japan could partly compensate for the decline in the labor force by having the elderly hold their jobs longer and by encouraging more women to work. 
Fewer women hold jobs in Japan than in most Western countries, so there may be room to expand the rate, he noted, but he said that Japan's population will shrink so quickly that adjusting to it will be very difficult.
Another problem of the aging of Japan's population will be how to pay for it. 
The social security system is underfinanced by a huge sum about equivalent to Japan's annual gross domestic product, and corporate pension funds are underfinanced by hundreds of billions of dollars, leaving them with a burden equivalent in scale to the banking crisis that has dogged Japan's economy for the last half-dozen years.
As for Akashima Island, it remains a gorgeous but depressing reminder of what can happen to a place when its population ages. 
Most of the people remaining on Akashima say they believe that there will still be at least one person living there for the next decade, but there is the sobering example of another nearby island, Himejima, which has been entirely abandoned.
"When I think of my young days, I remember how my friend lived over there, and another friend's house was over there," said Yoshie Kokou, the fisherman, pointing sadly at clumps of bushes. 
"And I long for the past."
"I hear young people aren't having kids now," he said. 
"I guess it's just the changing times."

text:
ï»¿
THERE may be prettier cities in Japan than Nagasaki, but there is none where beauty and tragedy are so intertwined, where a walk through the streets makes one alternately smile at the colorful carp in the canals and gasp at a plaque recording the city's wrenching past, where the hot springs in the surrounding hills -- the delight of countless tourists -- are also filled with memories of torture and death.
Largely obliterated by the atomic bombing of Aug. 
9, 1945, three days after the destruction of Hiroshima, Nagasaki has been rebuilt on the rubble and ashes of the old city. 
Set against a hillside overlooking a great natural harbor, Nagasaki is now a sprawling city of 440,000 on the southern island of Kyushu. 
Temples and mansions set among gardens on the hill preside over the bustle of office buildings and noodle shops on the winding streets below. 
Most of Nagasaki's historical sites and monuments are within walking distance of the center of the city, while a couple of miles away on the other side of town is a cluster of sights related to the bombing, including the new Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum, which gives powerful testimony to one of the pivotal events of the 20th century.
So Nagasaki is Asia's answer to Dresden, a city of light whose name is also almost synonymous with pain. 
Like Dresden, Nagasaki is thought of today mostly in connection with its wartime destruction, but Nagasaki resonated with tragedy even before 11:02 A.M. on Aug. 
9, 1945, when an atomic bomb exploded over the northern part of the city, missing its military target by a few miles and vaporizing a slum containing the largest Christian community in Japan.
As the most cosmopolitan city in Japan from the 16th through the 19th centuries, Nagasaki was a center for Christian missionaries -- and, accordingly, the center of religious persecution. 
This month marks the 400th anniversary of the first group of executions, when 26 Christians were crucified on a hill in Nagasaki. 
The city is marking the anniversary with special Catholic masses and with a new Japanese-language opera, based on the story of the executions, to have its premiere in November. 
During my latest visit, in October, I couldn't help contemplating those crucifixions as I visited the museums and memorials that recall Nagasaki's proud and tragic past.
I began near Dejima, an artificial island built in 1634 to house European traders in the city. 
Because of landfills, Dejima is no longer an island, and it is hard to tell where it starts and ends, but there are still some signs of its past. 
A stone sundial bears the initials of its Dutch owner of two centuries ago, and a few European cannons can be seen, while reproductions show what Dejima looked like in the old days: an island protruding into the great harbor that for centuries was the center for Japanese trade. 
These days the port is a minor one, but it is still filled with ships and gives Nagasaki a focal point -- as well as great views, since the city rises steeply into the hills from the bay. 
Sometimes called the "San Francisco of Japan" because of its hills, Nagasaki has the same salty charm as Hong Kong and the same historic links with Western traders.
Portuguese traders arrived in Nagasaki in 1571, and the authorities built Dejima to isolate them from Japanese society. 
The 130-acre island was big enough to accommodate not only the Portuguese but also their homes and warehouses and fields where their oxen and sheep could graze. 
After 1639, when the shogun ordered the Portuguese to leave Japan, Dutch traders were allowed to stay, but on condition that they move to Dejima. 
For more than two centuries after that, Japan tried to seal itself off from the outside world. 
Nagasaki was the only exception, and a tiny one: a few Chinese were allowed in a settlement in one part of the city, and a few Dutch were allowed to carry on their trade from Dejima.
The main Dejima Museum is closed indefinitely for renovation, but a nearby museum in Jurokuban-Kan, a mansion built in 1860 to house American consular staff, contains artifacts from the Dutch and Portuguese who lived on Dejima. 
The museum has no English labels on its exhibits, but it is chockablock with old European telescopes, clocks, guns and other antiques.
One of the main imports arranged by the Europeans was Christianity, and it is said that Hideyoshi, the great unifier and ruler of Japan, toyed with the idea of converting until he realized that he would be allowed only one wife. 
But the shoguns grew alarmed at how rapidly missionaries had converted some 300,000 Japanese, particularly around Nagasaki, and in 1597 the Government crucified six European missionaries and 20 of their Japanese followers; the youngest was Luis Ibaraki, a 12-year-old Japanese boy. 
All 26 were declared saints by the Catholic Church, and a small chapel and monument, built in 1962, mark the spot in the center of the city. 
After the crucifixions, the authorities seized those whom they suspected of being a Christian, branding them with hot irons, dunking them in boiling hot springs, burning them alive or suspending them upside down to die slowly in pits filled with filth and vermin.
The Government introduced all kinds of campaigns to stamp out Christianity, and it is said that Okunchi, an annual Shinto festival in Nagasaki, was founded for that purpose. 
Okunchi, which takes place every year from Oct. 
7 to 9, is one of the most famous festivals in Japan, with its 200-year-old floats and its dragon dances supplied by the Chinese. 
One of the aims, however, was to search for those who did not attend and therefore might be secret Christians.
An exhibit with floats from Okunchi and videos of past festivals is the centerpiece of the Nagasaki Museum of Traditional Performing Arts, one of many buildings in Glover Garden, a settlement containing the homes of the European traders who returned to Nagasaki after American gunboats opened up Japan in 1853. 
The centerpiece of this large outdoor complex is the home of Thomas Glover, a British merchant who came to Japan in 1859 at the age of 21, married a geisha and conspired with local lords to overthrow the shogun.
The home, built in 1863, is large and pleasant but would be unremarkable if it were not the oldest Western-style building in Japan. 
It is fun, though, to meander through the gardens and other Western homes, which are redolent of history. 
In Glover Garden these Western traders played on Japan's first tennis court, laid down Japan's first paved road and planned production of the beer now known as Kirin. 
Glover himself founded the Kirin brewing company, whose name apparently came from a couple of statues depicting him as a mustachioed kirin, a mythical Asian animal.
Chinese traders also left a mark on Nagasaki, apparent in the temples scattered on the hillside above Dejima. 
The oldest temple is Kofuku-ji, built in 1620, which presides sternly over the city below. 
Its peaked roofs and scattered halls surround a series of pleasant lawns and gardens, while forests begin just behind the temple. 
Most of Nagasaki is full of tourists, mostly Japanese schoolchildren, but Kofuku-ji was deserted when I wandered through its gardens and the cemetery behind it.
A more modern Chinese icon in Nagasaki is the Confucius Shrine, built at the end of the last century, but because there are few Chinese living in Nagasaki now, it has none of the authentic flavor of a Chinese temple, and the only people lighting incense and praying are giggly Japanese schoolgirls hoping to get into a good university. 
I am also suspicious of the temple's efficacy, for when I paid 100 yen (less than a dollar) for my fortune, the machine spat out a red slip of paper that advised me: "You will enjoy easy childbirth and bear a son."
Not likely.
A short walk away is a more familiar structure with a small steeple. 
In 1865 the Europeans who had settled in Nagasaki built the whitewashed concrete Oura Catholic Church on a hillside facing the spot where the Christians had been crucified in the 16th century. 
A few months after the church opened, its French priest was startled to get a visit from three Japanese, who, reassured by the statue of the Virgin Mary at the entrance, confided that their families -- and countless others -- had secretly been practicing Christianity for more than 250 years, long after everyone thought the faith had been wiped out in Japan. 
Word spread of this discovery, and the Government began cracking down on the Christians, exiling them to remote areas.
A museum attached to the Oura Church has displays, with explanations only in Japanese, about the religious repression, including the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637, in which some 37,000 people, many of them Christians, were slaughtered. 
They show religious documents, tiny crucifixes and religious sculptures, some disguised as Buddhist emblems, that were passed down from generation to generation.
But the most haunting part of any visit to Nagasaki, particularly for an American, is the other end of town. 
As it happened, the atomic bomb was dropped on those who had already suffered the most, for the Urakami neighborhood that was hit worst was a slum inhabited by Christians and by social outcasts known as burakumin, often described as the "untouchables" of Japan.
About 75,000 people died in the blast, and several memorials record the bomb's power. 
A pillar marks the epicenter of the explosion, and remains of the Urakami church are scattered around it on the ground, especially sculptures of saints, looking reproachfully at us. 
The area is now a pair of parks, bordered by a canal, and the peacefulness and prettiness are in a strange way disturbing.
The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum opened nearby last year. 
The exhibits are stark: a dimly lighted room with twisted debris and wrenching large-screen videos taken at the time of charred corpses and whitened skulls. 
Extensive displays show what Nagasaki looked like before the bombing and explain how the bomb worked, as well as offering hideous photos of victims and pictures of human shadows on rock and wood -- the only thing remaining when those near the epicenter were vaporized.
The problem with the museum is that it has almost no context: the atomic bombing is presented like a typhoon that suddenly swept in from the ocean for no reason. 
The subtext is not anti-American; it is anti-historical. 
To be sure, there is in one tiny nook a time line that mentions in a cursory way Japan's wartime activities. 
But this provoked a furor in Japan because of its reference to the Nanjing massacre, the incident in which the Japanese killed tens of thousands of Chinese civilians in 1937. 
Some Japanese deny that the massacre took place, and the photo that had illustrated it has been replaced by a blurred and rather meaningless picture of a crowd.
To leave Nagasaki on a more hopeful note, it is worth visiting the nearby home of Dr. Takeshi Nagai, a doctor and theologian who was a bit like a Japanese version of Dr. Albert Schweitzer. 
Dr. Nagai's wife was killed in the blast, and he lived with his two small children in a tiny hut, the size of an American closet, where he wrote powerful books exploring the meaning of what had happened. 
The most famous of these, "The Bells of Nagasaki," was once widely available in English but is now hard to find.
Dr. Nagai died in 1951, at the age of 43, and a little museum in his honor stands by the wooden shack where he lived and worked, a reminder that Nagasaki witnessed some of the best of humanity as well as some of the worst.
Â 
A port of many cultures, much history
Â 
Planning a Trip
About 10 flights a day on several airlines link Nagasaki with Tokyo, less than two hours away. 
There is a tourist information booth in the airport's arrivals area; information in English can also be obtained by calling 23-3631 locally. 
(The country code is 81, the city code 0958; drop the zero when dialing from abroad.)
The best hotel in Nagasaki is the Nagasaki Prince, 2-26 Takara Machi, telephone 21-1111, fax 23-4309, where a double room including tax and service costs $215. 
(Prices calculated at 116 yen to the United States dollar.) There are also some fine traditional Japanese inns in the area; the tourist office can help with bookings.
Â 
Local Fare
The most famous Nagasaki dish is kasutera cake, based on a Dutch version of a pound cake. 
It can be eaten in coffee shops all over town, but the most famous bakery is Fukusaya, 3-1 Funadaikku Machi, 21-2938. 
You cannot eat at Fukusaya, but you can buy a kasutera for $6 and up.
Another famous Nagasaki dish is shippoku, a multicourse meal that borrows from Europe and China. 
It can be eaten at such restaurants as Kagetsu, 2-1 Maruyama Machi, 22-0191 (reservations required), with its lovely garden; the price starts at $112 a person with tax and service.
Finally, Nagasaki is noted for Chinese dishes such as champon noodles. 
A meal of noodles, with shrimp, vegetables and broth, costs less than $10 a person at a restaurant such as Shikairo, 4-5 Matsugaecho, 22-1296.
Â 
Places to See
Jurokuban-Kan, 4-15 Minamiyamate Machi, 27-6111, is open 8:30 A.M. to 5 P.M.; admission $3.50.
Glover Garden, 8-1 Minamiyamate Machi, 22-8223, is open 8:30 A.M. to 5:30 P.M. in winter; admission $5.20. 
The Okunchi festival is Oct. 
7 to 9 every year.
Oura Catholic Church, 5-3 Minimiyamate Machi, 23-2628, is open 8:30 A.M. to 5 P.M. in winter; admission $2.15. 
The museum is to the right of the nave.
The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum, 7-8 Hirano Machi, 44-1231, is open 8:30 A.M. to 5:30 P.M., admission $1.70. 
The nearby Dr. Nagai Museum, 22-6 Ueno Machi, 44-3496, is open 8:30 A.M. to 5 P.M., admission free.
Kofuku-Ji, 64 Tera Machi, 22-1076, is open 8 A.M. to 5 P.M. and costs $1.70. 
The Confucius Shrine, and an attached museum of Chinese history, is open 8:30 A.M. to 5 P.M.; admission $4.50.Â Â Â N.D.K.

In 1992, the last time Bill Clinton talked economics at the University of Pennsylvania, he was a governor, times were tough, and his campaign manager kept saying, "It's the economy, stupid."
President Clinton returned to the same campus today, with just 11 months to go in his second term, to gloat a bit about his economic stewardship and suggest, without naming names, that Gov. George W. Bush's approach to economics might not be any more successful than that of his father.
Mr. Clinton's 1992 economics speech laid out his strategy of emphasizing education, investment tax credits and an overhaul of the nation's infrastructure. 
At the time, he was down in the polls, his throat was raspy and he pulled no punches in condemning his opponent, President George Bush.
When he talked of the state of the economy, Mr. Clinton derisively labeled it the "Bush recession."
Today, Mr. Clinton took no similar shots at the younger Mr. Bush, who is engaged in a fierce battle for the Republican presidential nomination. 
But Mr. Clinton suggested that Vice President Al Gore best understood how to keep the current prosperity going and he made clear his preference for paying down the debt rather than making large cuts in taxes.
"We have to maintain our fiscal discipline," Mr. Clinton said. 
Back in his campaign speech, which presidential aides distributed to reporters today, Mr. Clinton spoke of a battle to stay competitive in a world where Japan and Germany were "beating our brains in" with smarter investment and growth decisions.
Today, however, Mr. Clinton ignored those nations and focused on the need to admit China into the World Trade Organization. 
Addressing critics, he said differences between the United States and China should not prevent a deal.
"If we do this, 20 years from now we'll look back and wonder why we ever even debated it," he said. 
"And if we don't, 20 years from now we'll still be kicking ourselves in the seat of the pants."
Earlier in the day, Mr. Clinton made a vigorous pitch to the Business Council, a coalition of corporations that is pushing for congressional passage of China's admission to the World Trade Organization. 
Vowing "a full-court press from our administration," the president again took on the detractors.
"Most members of Congress don't question the economic benefits," he said. 
"Critics are more likely to say things like this: China is a growing threat to Taiwan and other neighbors. 
We shouldn't strengthen it. 
China is a drag on labor and environmental market rights and, if you put them in the W.T.O., they will block further progress on those issues. 
Or, China is an offender of human rights and we shouldn't reward it. 
Or China is a dangerous proliferator. 
We shouldn't empower it."
Mr. Clinton called the concerns legitimate but said "the problems will be worse if we do not bring China into the W.T.O."
Mr. Clinton's powers of prediction in his 1992 speech proved a mixed bag. 
He said, for instance, that bullet trains would be shuttling 500,000 passengers a day at speeds of up to 300 miles an hour. 
That did not happen.
But Mr. Clinton pointed out today that he had emphasized back in 1992, when the Web was in its infancy, the importance of a national informational network. 
"Just as the interstate highway system in the 1950's spurred two decades of economic growth," Governor Clinton had said, "we need a door-to-door fiber optics system by the year 2015 to link every home, every lab, every classroom and every business in America."

file: In Rich Hong Kong, Cages as Homes for the Poor.txt
text:
ï»¿
A rusty, sour odor skewered the gloom that enveloped ranks of steel cages jammed into a third-floor chamber of a decaying tenement. 
Dimly, the silhouettes of men appeared, one by one uncoiling from the stack of cages like cicadas casting off their shells. 
Ma Kwai-han, a feather of a man clad in a skimpy white undershirt and baggy gray pants, padded into a dim circle of light.
"I've lived here 36 years," he said quietly, his hand resting on the chain link cage he calls home. 
"I have no family and can't afford to stay anywhere else."
Here, in one of the world's richest cities -- last week Forbes magazine declared that 2 of the 10 richest men in the world live here -- the growth and persistence of poverty is hidden away, tucked into mildewed tenements and under highway overpasses. 
But the poorest of the poor live in Hong Kong's cage homes -- steel mesh boxes barely large enough for a mattress and a recumbent occupant, stacked in twos and threes -- in the heart of the other Hong Kong.
"These are among the poorest in Hong Kong," said Chong Chan-yau, the director of fund-raising for Oxfam, a private organization that assists poor populations, particularly in the third world. 
"There is undeniable poverty among the poorest section of our community. 
The poorest tenth of the population is getting a smaller and smaller share of the pie. 
The gap between the richest and the poorest is getting wider and wider."
By the time China resumes sovereignty of Hong Kong on July 1, 1997, said Mr. Chong, who said he relied on Government data, there will be 180,000 families on public assistance, in a society in which the dole is viewed with shame.
"That will be about 10 percent of Hong Kong's households," said Mr. Chong. "And there is this surviving Chinese attitude that 'I don't want to be dependent on the Government. 
I feel ashamed of my children not supporting me.'
"
It is not clear how many people live in cages here. 
The Government puts the number at 2,800, while Kalina Tsang, a social worker for a private agency that works in the poor communities and with cage dwellers, says that the number actually approaches 10,000.
"About 70 percent are elderly, single people with no families," Ms. Tsang said. 
"These are the people whose voices are not heard."
On Nam Cheong Street in Kowloon, on the edge of what used to be waterfront, before vast landfill projects moved the street well inland from Hong Kong harbor's fetid waters, sagging six-story buildings huddle together. 
A jumble of simple restaurants, machine shops and electrical supply stores line the narrow streets, and the clatter of jackhammers from never-ending public works echoes off building walls.
Mr. Ma has lived here since 1960, climbing the narrow concrete stairwell to the third-floor room filled with cages. 
His is No. 18.
"I came to Hong Kong in 1955," he explained, shifting from one foot to another as he spoke. 
"There was no food in China, so I came here. 
But life is difficult in Hong Kong. 
From my point of view, there's not much difference between Hong Kong and China."
Every day at 4:15 A.M., Mr. Ma rolls from his cage, hurriedly washes in the one cramped bathroom that serves the 25 people who live in the cages stacked in the room. 
Then he walks a few blocks to the restaurant where he works selling dim sum, a job that pays him about $273 each month.
"I used to work in a garment factory," he explained. 
"I worked there for 18 years, but they moved to China so I had no job. 
I'm illiterate, so that makes it difficult to get a job. 
Anyway, the only thing for me to do is to work hard every day so I can live. 
I don't really think my life will change after 1997, after China takes over."
For his cage, Mr. Ma, 58, pays $41 a month. 
"I'd like to move to a better place," he said, "but I don't see how."
Nearby, sitting on the edge of a floor-level cage, Zhu Qishui sucked on a cigarette. 
"This is O.K., not so bad," he said, glancing at the racks of cages. 
"I just came from China, from Jiangxi. 
Actually it's better back home, but this is not so bad."
Every day, 150 mainland Chinese are allowed to immigrate into Hong Kong, and countless others come on visitors' visas, which many of them overstay. 
Mr. Zhu, who came on a visitor's visa hoping to find some kind of work, has been here for three months. 
"I heard about Hong Kong from friends," he said. 
"They said it was easy to make a lot of money. 
But I still have no work, so I'll have to go home."
Ms. Tsang insisted that the persistence of cage homes in Hong Kong was intolerable. 
"This is one of the richest cities," she said. 
"We want the Government to resettle these people in affordable decent housing. 
But even if the Government resettles these people, new people will come in."
Already, slightly more than half of Hong Kong's population lives in subsidized Government housing, but the waiting time for an apartment now is nine years.
Still, Mr. Chong of Oxfam believes that Hong Kong's Government, with reserves of $57 billion, could do more for its growing poor population.
"The Government does have the resources to lessen the plight of those who are in poverty," he said.
On Nam Cheong Street, though, Mr. Ma does not believe his life will change any time soon. 
He nodded at the small shrine of Guangong, a figure of a robed Chinese god, the symbol of justice. 
A small pile of oranges was placed before the figure, illuminated by faint red bulbs. 
"Nothing can be improved here," he said, sighing. 
"This is our life."

text:
ï»¿
BLACK HANDS OF BEIJING
Lives of Defiance in China's Democracy Movement.
By George Black and Robin Munro.
Illustrated. 390 pp. 
New York:
A Robert L. Bernstein Book/John Wiley & Sons. 
$24.95.
AFTER street protests in 1976 against the hard-line Gang of Four, the Chinese Government denounced a young man -- a "crewcut shorty," it called him -- who had been photographed making speeches to the crowds. 
But the crewcut shorty vanished and the police never found him.
The crewcut shorty, whose name is Chen Ziming, was then a convicted "counterrevolutionary" on a weekend furlough from prison. 
By the time the Government denounced him, he was back behind bars -- the one place the police never thought to check.
The authorities finally caught up with him after he was released and played a major behind-the-scenes role in the 1989 Tiananmen democracy movement. 
Following the massacre of protesters, Mr. Chen tried to escape from the country. 
But he was betrayed by one of his associates and is now serving a 13-year prison sentence -- with no prospect of weekend furloughs.
Mr. Chen suffers from a malady that is universal among Chinese political prisoners: anonymity. 
There is no Chinese equivalent of an Andrei Sakharov, and one of the greatest challenges Chinese dissidents face in winning sympathy abroad is that few Westerners can even pronounce their names. 
Consequently, as Deng Xiaoping, China's de facto emperor, has boasted, the Government can lock protesters up without the West paying much attention.
"Black Hands in Beijing" is an attempt to address this problem by focusing on the lives of Mr. Chen and a couple of other important dissidents: Wang Juntao, an ebullient 34-year-old colleague of Mr. Chen's who is now also serving a 13-year prison sentence, and Han Dongfang, a 30-year-old railway worker whom the authorities released from prison because they thought he was dying from the tuberculosis with which they had infected him.
The Government dubbed these three people -- along with a few others -- the "black hands," and claimed they were responsible for the Tiananmen democracy movement. 
Yet as this book records, Mr. Chen and Mr. Wang in fact were relative moderates, who tried to persuade the student protesters not to force a dangerous confrontation with the leadership.
The authors know their stuff. 
Robin Munro is a Hong Kong-based researcher for the organization Asia Watch and one of the world's leading specialists on human rights conditions in China. 
George Black writes a column on foreign affairs for The Los Angeles Times.
"Black Hands of Beijing" is sensible, interesting and insightful, but it is not riveting. 
Part of the problem is that this is about the 30th book on the Tiananmen protests to have come out since 1989. 
Another part is those Chinese names again: non-Chinese speakers may have difficulty keeping track of all the characters who scoot in and out of the narrative.
The larger challenge is that Mr. Chen and Mr. Wang remain behind bars and impossible to interview. 
Thus the descriptions of them inevitably seem a bit austere and shallow, shorn of some of the passion and anguish of the times. 
For a richer account of their personal feelings and internal conflicts, we will have to wait until the "crewcut shorty" is released or gets another furlough and can again emerge into the daylight.

file: In Two Looks at Tibet, No Sign of Shangri-La.txt
text:
ï»¿
FROM THE TIME Ronald Colman stumbled into Shangri-La in the 1937 movie "Lost Horizon," Tibet in its various Hollywood manifestations has come to represent a kind of ultimate otherness, a golden-hued sanctuary teeming with a quiescent people too simple, too trusting, too good for this world.
For Mr. Colman's character, a disillusioned British gentleman yearning to escape a noisy and conflicted world, Shangri-La was a haven of peace, contemplation and unlimited reading time.
More recently, in "The Golden Child" (1986), Eddie Murphy rescued a Dalai Lama-like child monk from a band of demon kidnappers in a Tibet portrayed as a snowy, somewhat comical place full of chanting and special effects. 
In "Little Buddha" (1993), Bernardo Bertolucci told the improbable story of a young American couple who willingly surrender their child to monks who tell them that he is the latest manifestation of a Buddhist holy man.
Now, however, with two major films about to be released about Tibet and its exiled leader, the 62-year-old Dalai Lama, Hollywood seems to be trying to clear away some of that golden fog. 
Both "Seven Years in Tibet," directed by Jean-Jacques Annaud, and "Kundun," directed by Martin Scorsese, aim to present an exotic but more realistic version of Tibet's tragic recent history. 
The first film is opening on Oct. 
8; the second, on Christmas Day.
Both directors say they had no particular political motive in mind, but the release of these films is likely to focus popular attention on Tibet, coming at a time of growing international tension over China's behavior toward a land it has controlled since 1949. 
(The Dalai Lama, in India, said he did not want to discuss the films until he had seen them.)
Because of the political situation in Tibet, neither film could be filmed there. 
Mr. Scorsese's Tibet is actually the ragged peaks and arid plains of south-central Morocco; Mr. Annaud's is the sharp valleys and icy peaks of the Argentine Andes and the Canadian Rockies. 
Both filmmakers employed numerous Tibetan religious and political leaders to insure historical accuracy and realism. 
And both said their goal in such attention to detail was not the thrill of the exotic but the deeper feelings stirred by a sense of real life.
One afternoon last month, Mr. Scorsese peered between his outstretched hands as if they were an imaginary movie screen hanging in the air. 
"The idea," he said, "is to make the story as human and as emotional as possible, right?
So I thought the way to do that was to do it, as much as possible, through the eyes of the little boy. 
Very subjective."
Mr. Scorsese was describing the opening sequence of his straightforward, dreamlike evocation of the life of the Dalai Lama. 
The scene, which had just played on the screen in Mr. Scorsese's New York projection room, was replaying itself in his head as he spoke. 
He rattled off the sequence of shots, his small hands slashing through the air.
"We see what the boy sees: two parents talking," he said. 
"The boy turns and teases his brother. 
A door opens. 
We see someone's feet coming into the room, but it's sideways on the screen because the boy is lying in bed. 
A smiling face. 
We move across the room and the next thing you know----" Smack!
He clapped his hands. 
"Bright white light!
We're out in the courtyard in the sunshine."
Mr. Scorsese, 55, laughed nervously, occasionally plucking at his bushy eyebrows. 
"I wanted this to be a very human story," he said, "About real, recognizable people who just happen to live in Tibet."
Mr. Annaud, too, said he felt a very clear obligation to cut through some of the earlier Hollywood images of Tibet.
"YOU KNOW, I THINK for many people, Tibet is really a kind of fantasyland," said Mr. Annaud, 54, speaking from London, where he was putting together the final sound mix for his $65 million film. 
"What we really tried to do was to recreate Tibet, to bring it to life and to make it real."
Becky Johnston, who wrote the script for Mr. Annaud's film, said her chief desire was to bring the country to life for a Western audience "and for it not to be a glossy, laminated version of Tibet."
Melissa Mathison, who wrote the script for Mr. Scorsese's film, agreed. 
"I think part of the tragedy of Tibet is that it's been Shangri-La," she said. 
"Nobody believed it existed in the first place, so its destruction was the destruction of a fantasy."
In "Seven Years in Tibet," Brad Pitt portrays an Austrian mountain climber who escapes from a British prisoner-of-war camp in India during World War II and makes his tortuous way over the mountains into Tibet, where he eventually befriends the young Dalai Lama. 
Based on a memoir by Heinrich Harrer, who became famous in the 30's as a member of the first team to conquer the north face of the Eiger, this film chronicles the real-life redemption of the arrogant mountain climber through his relationship with the young spiritual leader.
The film drew unwanted publicity earlier this year when it was revealed that Mr. Harrer had been not only a member of the Nazi Party when he went on his Tibetan expedition but a member of Hitler's SS, a fact that he had never revealed. 
Nevertheless, Mr. Annaud decided that his film did not need to be updated.
"It was not what our movie was about," Mr. Annaud said. 
"I had always suspected that -- how shall I say -- that Harrer had a sympathy or a connection with the Nazi movement."
In the early scenes in "Seven Years in Tibet," Mr. Harrer is portrayed as a selfish, obnoxious character who is only gradually humanized by his encounters with the Dalai Lama. 
"Our film is about guilt and redemption, so this latest issue does not really affect it," Mr. Annaud said.
"Kundun," Mr. Scorsese's $28 million movie, is less an adventure film than a contemplation of nonviolence through the life of the Dalai Lama. 
The director said he had been attracted to making a movie about the Tibetan leader because he wanted to explore the implications of the philosophy. 
"I felt I knew what a violent life was all about, after growing up in lower Manhattan," he said. 
"I wanted to explore the other side."
The film follows Tenzin Gyatso from 1937, when he was discovered by Buddhist monks at the age of 2 and "revealed" to be the 14th incarnation of the Dalai Lama, the earthly manifestation of the Buddha of Compassion, to his final escape from Tibet in 1959 in the face of a Chinese invasion. 
(The word "Kundun" is an affectionate, reverent form of address used by those close to the Dalai Lama.) There are no Hollywood stars; everyone in the movie is either Tibetan or Chinese, all of them amateurs except for the Chinese actors who play Mao Zedong and one of his generals.
Tenzin Tethong, who works with Survivals International, a human-rights group in San Francisco that helps victims of torture and political abuse, is directly connected with both films. 
A former personal representative of the Dalai Lama in New York, Mr. Tethong acted as an on-set consultant during the filming of "Seven Years in Tibet," and his son, Guyrme, now 11, plays the Dalai Lama as a young teen-ager in Mr. Scorsese's film.
"There is a considerable amount of sympathy for Tibet," Mr. Tethong said, "but it is limited to people who are well informed, well intentioned or have some special connection to that part of the world. 
These two movies are obviously going to bring the stories directly to the ordinary person. 
I think the impact will be considerable."
Mr. Tethong is concerned, however, that the films still may not be realistic enough to dispel the well-entrenched Western image of Tibet as an otherworldly place.
"I think it is still perhaps going to keep fueling this fantasy image of Tibet," he said. 
"When you see the movies, you will see Tibet in its very exotic colors, in a golden glow. 
Sometimes, that seems to help because it draws attention. 
But other times, it doesn't help, because it makes everything look like it's not in this real world, it's something in the imagination."
Robert Thurman, a professor of Indo-Tibetan studies at Columbia University and a founder of Tibet House in New York, thinks that Tibetans like Mr. Tethong "want to be thought of as real people who are suffering atrocities and genocide."
"They make much of the fact that Tibet becomes a Western fantasyland," he said, "which excuses Western people from taking action to stop the suffering."
But Mr. Thurman believes that the inevitable benefit of having two such high-profile films about Tibet released around the same time should outweigh any concerns about perpetuating Western fantasies.
In the real world, Tibet's recent history has been anything but golden. 
Citing a 200-year-old document that they said proved Tibet was a part of China, Communist Chinese forces pushed into the once-secluded nation in 1949, first promising to respect Tibet's religious traditions but soon closing monasteries, sending monks to re-education camps, killing some, torturing others and resettling tens of thousands of Chinese farmers in the country, a process that continues today. 
When Chinese forces put down a Tibetan insurrection in 1959, the Dalai Lama and many of his followers felt they had no choice but to flee to India, keep their religious traditions alive and argue their case to the outside world.
IN 1991, THE DALAI LAMA WAS awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. 
The cause of the Tibetans has been adopted by many figures in the entertainment industry, including Richard Gere and Harrison Ford, Ms. Mathison's husband. 
But Western nations have been reluctant to embrace the Tibetan cause, in part because of concerns about alienating the Chinese leaders.
In November, while filming was still under way in Morocco on "Kundun," Chinese officials complained about the film to the Walt Disney Company, which was to release it under a subsidiary, calling it an intrusion into China's internal affairs. 
But Disney officials said they intended to go ahead with the movie.
Mr. Scorsese said last month that he had heard nothing directly from either the Chinese Government or Disney about whether China continued to object to his film, though he had heard "indirectly" that Beijing was still very much concerned.
The Chinese may be right to be concerned. 
Mr. Thurman believes that these two films, coming out at around the same time, will succeed in raising the level of understanding of Tibet's recent tragic history.
"I think these films will be inspiring people, and they come at a very desperate time for Tibet," he said. 
"For the world to get a look at this, the reality of the Tibetan story, and for them to have a sympathetic perspective on Tibet from two sources, kindles a spark of hope in the Tibetan community."
Ms. Mathison said she spent about two years researching the Dalai Lama's life, meeting with him and others and roughing out a first draft of the script. 
She and Mr. Ford then flew to India and Mr. Ford read the script to the Dalai Lama while Ms. Mathison sat, quietly watching.
"The Dalai Lama was very astute," she said. 
"It's really very difficult to talk about him without sounding like a Moonie. 
With the script, his concerns were often technical. 
How could I move from this room to that room?
Things like that. 
He was also very concerned about the way some Tibetan characters and ceremonies might be presented, such as the Dalai Lama's court oracle. 
He knows how that might appear to Western audiences."
Mr. Scorsese also met with the Dalai Lama several times and particularly remembers one meeting at Mr. Ford's ranch in Wyoming. 
"The Dalai Lama came in," Mr. Scorsese said, "and the first thing he said was, 'Does that bird have enough water?'
He also thought the dog wanted to go outside. 
He was more concerned about the animals than anything else."
It was a rough shoot, Mr. Scorsese said, made none easier by the unskilled cast. 
"I'd come out of my trailer in the morning," he recalled, "and there would be the assistant director with that day's problems. 
This person is sick. 
That thing is broken. 
The sandstorm is due to hit in an hour. 
And over at the side there would be these Tibetan monks bowing to me. 
It's far from downtown Manhattan, you know what I'm saying?"
