text:
ï»¿
Hong Kong's Governor, Christopher Patten, has been called a colorful assortment of names by Chinese officials in recent months, including "prostitute," "serpent" and -- his own favorite -- "tango dancer."
So it was unusual for Mr. Patten, during a visit to Washington and New York last week, to find himself squarely on China's side of a debate over its trade status in the United States. 
A man China regards as its enemy came to argue China's case to President Clinton, Congress and whoever else would listen.
"It's very agreeable to find myself in such good company," Mr. Patten said with a smile, referring to his fresh alliance with Beijing. 
"I admit that I'm not quite used to this."
No, he said, he had not exactly come to do China's bidding. 
But yes, he allowed, his case for renewing China's "most favored nation" trade status is virtually identical with Beijing's.
Hong Kong could lose more than $20 billion of trade that now passes through the colony on its way between China and the United States if China's trade status were revoked and tariffs increased, Mr. Patten estimated. 
More trade, not less, he argued, is the best way to promote China's evolution into a modern nation.
But politics is a different story. 
Since last fall, when he proposed expanding the right to vote for a legislature in 1995 -- the last election before Hong Kong is returned to Chinese rule in 1997 -- Mr. Patten has been tagged with a stream of invective from Beijing.
"A cunning political trickster" and "colonial oppressor" are among the names he was recently called in public by Chinese officials, who oppose broadening the base of voters. 
They argue that in the past Britain has never shown much interest in more democracy for Hong Kong and that there is no reason for it to do so now.
Mr. Patten, 48, who left his post as chairman of the Conservative Party in Britain to become Governor of Hong Kong in July, has refused to alter his plan for the election, which would to the voting age to 18 from 21 and would allow more people to vote for legislators selected by industry.
Mr. Patten's tough stance against Beijing has earned him credibility with those in Washington who most oppose his views on trade, and who favor linking China's trade status with progress in human rights and other issues.
"He is a person who has taken risks, who is courageous," said Representative Nancy Pelosi, Democrat of California. 
"You listen more carefully to someone like that."
Ms. Pelosi introduced legislation in the House last month to revoke China's most-favored-nation status in 1994 if measurable progress is not made in human rights and other issues. 
She said that although Mr. Patten did not change her mind, he had persuaded her to adjust her proposal by eliminating its references to Hong Kong.

file: INSIDE ART.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese Treasures
Chinese art has attracted a flurry of attention recently. 
Over the last two years the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, have given it considerable time and space. 
Now the National Gallery of Art in Washington is weighing in.
It announced this week that together with the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City, Mo., and the State Administration of Cultural Heritage and Art Exhibitions in China, it has put together "The Golden Age of Archeology: Celebrated Discoveries from the People's Republic of China."
The show, to be on view in Washington from Sept. 
19 through Jan. 
2, will travel to the Museum of Fine Arts in Houston and the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco.
The National Gallery is calling the show "the greatest survey of Chinese art and archeology ever lent by the People's Republic of China."
The show commemorates the 50th anniversary of the People's Republic. 
It will have about 200 examples of recent archeological discoveries, objects dating from 6000 B.C. to A.D. 960, as well as sculpture, ritual implements, musical instruments, paintings and calligraphy, plus decorative objects made of jade, stone, wood, bamboo, gold and bronze.
"It's very different from other Chinese shows in the U.S. because it focuses on archeological finds of the last 20 years," said Earl A. Powell 3d, director of the National Gallery. 
"It's a fascinating and beautiful show that tracks the evolution of Chinese art."
In 1974 the National Gallery presented a similar exhibition, "Archeological Finds of the People's Republic of China."
The forthcoming show is expected to present new perspectives on early Chinese civilization and art, documenting the most recent excavations and theories while showing the various ancient cultures that flourished simultaneously throughout China.
Mr. Powell said the show would demonstrate that Chinese civilization sprung not only from the valley of the Yellow River, as previously thought, but from the interaction and achievements of various cultures throughout the country.
Â 
Raising the Flag
Since he painted his first flag in 1954, Jasper Johns has created nearly 100 versions of what is now his most famous image. 
He has drawn flags, painted flags, produced flags in watercolor and as prints and created lead and bronze-relief sculptures of them. 
With so many examples of Mr. Johns's flags in such a variety of guises, why do auction houses consider it a coup when a Johns flag painting comes on the market?
"It's an icon of American art," said Franck Giraud, who heads Christie's 19th- and 20th-century art departments worldwide. 
"Flags just don't come on the market that often."
In November, at Sotheby's in New York, a small 1959 "Flag" drawing that was estimated to bring $500,000 to $700,000 sold for nearly $1 million. 
In February 1998 Christie's in New York sold a collage of a "White Flag" from 1960 for $1.2 million, twice its $600,000 high estimate.
On May 13 Christie's in New York will auction a "Flags" painting from 1973. 
It is made of two sets of three canvas panels, and depicts two vertical flags in red, white and blue. 
The work is estimated to sell for $7 million to $10 million. 
Some art experts suggest that the price may be high; they recall that in November Sotheby's unsuccessfully pushed its luck by offering "White Numbers" (1958), an important Johns encaustic-on-linen painting of numerals in a progression from 0 to 9, with a $7 million to $9 million estimate. 
No one was willing to pay more than $6 million.
Mr. Giraud said the estimate for "Flags" was justified because of "the tremendous popularity of the three Johns's we sold from the Ganz collection last year, each for way above their estimates, and for the rarity of the object."
The painting has been for sale before. 
In 1989, at the height of the auction market, Sotheby's in New York sold it for $11 million to Bo Alveryd, a dealer who purchased the painting on behalf of Renault, the French car manufacturer. 
While officials at Chrisite's will not identify the current seller, art world experts who know the painting say it is being sold by Renault.
"The flag is Johns's most desirable image," Mr. Giraud said. 
In October the Metropolitan Museum acquired a "White Flag" from 1955 directly from the artist. 
It has become one of the jewels in the museum's 20th-century collection.
Â 
American in Paris
The sale of the super-contemporary $41 million Frank Gehry building that had housed the American Center in Paris from 1994 to 1996 has been completed. 
The French Ministry of Culture bought the building for about $21 million and plans to turn it into a film center, with three screening rooms, a film library and spaces devoted to a museum, educational activities and a film and video research center. 
A lack of money forced the American Center to put its large building, in eastern Paris, up for sale in 1996.
"The American Center has continued out of a small office in Paris and now it will have an endowment," said Frederick B. Henry, the center's chairman. 
"We will be a grant-making foundation, which will support a variety of artistic endeavors."
Mr. Henry said that the exact focus of the grants has not been determined, but that the center was committed to "innovative philanthropy."
He added that the institution may join with two or three other arts organizations or foundations to develop special projects.
Â 
A New Venture
Alexander Apsis, a 25-year veteran of Sotheby's, who for the last five years has headed its department of Impressionist and modern art in New York, has resigned. 
He is to become a partner of C&M Arts, the Manhattan gallery on East 78th Street that was founded seven years ago by Robert Mnuchin, a retired investment banker.
"I've spent my whole working life at Sotheby's, and I wanted a new challenge," Mr. Apsis said. 
When he starts his job in May, Mr. Apsis will concentrate on Impressionist and classic 20th-century art.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS -- Global Tug, National Tether_As Companies Look Overseas, Governments Hold t.txt
text:
ï»¿
For nearly three years, Caterpillar Inc. has been banging its head against the Clinton Administration door, trying to get Government-sponsored loans for the sale of its big earthmovers to China. 
Beijing is buying them by the dozens to build the giant Three Gorges Dam, which the Administration considers damaging to the environment.
So the Chinese have turned to suppliers in Japan and Europe, where governments are less concerned about the environment and more forthcoming with credit. 
"We've only managed to sell the Chinese a few off-highway trucks," a Caterpillar official said.
That is hardly the description of a giant multinational ranging unfettered across the world. 
For all the talk of economic globalization, the process is still in an early stage.
A few multinationals, such as I.B.M., Royal Dutch/Shell or Imperial Chemical Industries, are ahead of the pack in spreading their revenues, research, financing, stockholders and management over many countries. 
But the majority are more like Caterpillar in America, the Mitsubishi Corporation in Japan or Volkswagen in Germany. 
For all their involvement in overseas sales and investment, nationality still binds them to home.
"What we have is United States, European and Japanese corporations trying to dress in global clothing," said William W. Keller, executive director of the Center for International Studies at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. 
"But if you conceive of globalization as being the rootlessness of corporations, that is a paradox. 
You don't have corporations without states attached to them. 
When they need help, you find out who they really belong to."
Many corporations have invoked the competitive pressures of an increasingly borderless global economy as the reason for moving operations and jobs abroad and to press for other concessions.
But a proliferation of treaty negotiations in recent months, aimed at setting rules for the global economy -- most of them favorable so far to business -- has raised a fresh question: just how untethered are these companies and who, therefore, should have a voice in the rule-making?
"We have to keep separate that the mobility of corporations has increased from the notion that we are living in a completely seamless integrated world market that gives national government no bargaining power to set standards," said Dani Rodrik, an economist at Harvard. 
"The latter has not happened."
Some want to stop the process of globalization. 
But others, including a re-energized American labor movement, are more interested in setting international rules of the road. 
Indeed, 12 different rule-making negotiations are currently under way.
Most are inspired by the North American Free Trade Agreement and the treaty that set up the World Trade Organization, in which the United States and 116 other nations agreed essentially to recognize W.T.O. rulings as having the power of national law. 
Several of the agreements now being discussed would require Senate ratification and would be similarly binding. 
That would push the setting of global rules beyond the voluntary guidelines that have characterized most such agreements since World War II.
"Thus far, the corporations, more than any other group, are shaping the new global regulations," said Raymond Vernon, an economist at Harvard's Kennedy School of Government. 
"It is not that they are abandoning their countries for a global identity. 
They are simply pushing abroad and arguing that if the obstacles are cleared away, they will produce enough for everyone and raise all boats."
The recent surge in rule-making brings out strange bedfellows. 
Corporate America and the A.F.L.-C.I.O. find themselves on one side, favoring an international stage, while the most visible advocates of those who want the rules made in America include Patrick J. Buchanan, the conservative commentator and politician, and Ralph Nader, the liberal consumer advocate.
"Rather than international negotiations, the rules should be written through Congress, where you can have discussion and debate," Mr. Nader said. 
As an example, he argued, Congress can no longer effectively ban imports of products made with child labor. 
Because the W.T.O. does not specifically prohibit such trade, such a law could be challenged before the organization, which could then fine the United States.
American corporate executives see in the new wave of rule-making not only the elimination of remaining trade barriers but also the removal of restrictions on investment abroad and greater freedom to purchase foreign companies. 
For Mr. Nader and Mr. Buchanan, however, these are hidden tools to make the shifting of jobs abroad that much easier. 
Mr. Buchanan advocates protective tariffs to keep companies at home, while Mr. Nader would discourage job-shifting by canceling tax breaks, imposing a "social tariff" and prohibiting Export-Import Bank loans for exports that contain too many foreign parts.
The bank once financed only those exports manufactured entirely in the United States. 
But it has relaxed that rule in recent years and now, for example, provides credits to customers of the Boeing Company to purchase aircraft that have as much as 15 percent "foreign content," and sometimes more.
Bucking such trends is futile, says John J. Sweeney, president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. 
He calls the Nader-Buchanan approach simplistic. 
"It is a very good feeling to tell the workers we are going to bring all the jobs back," he said, "but it is not realistic."
With that in mind, the American labor movement has joined corporate America in embracing global rule-making. 
Instead of waging a losing battle to keep jobs at home, the A.F.L.-C.I.O. is demanding a seat at the rule-making table, with only limited success so far. 
The intention is to preserve labor standards at home by raising them abroad.
That would be done by writing into every agreement a ban against child and prison labor, as well as guarantees that foreign workers can assemble freely and engage in collective bargaining. 
"If you can get rid of repression, workers can negotiate their own conditions," Mr. Sweeney said. 
The Administration included the A.F.L.-C.I.O. prescription in a bill now before Congress asking for $18 billion in new American financing for the International Monetary Fund. 
The language has survived so far in the House and Senate.
The treaty talks draw little public attention. 
They range from negotiations to eliminate tariffs on products such as cellular phones and computers to high-level talks between European and American business executives to develop common product standards that would then be incorporated into binding treaties.
The World Trade Organization, born in the tariff-cutting Uruguay Round agreement, plays a big role in this process, setting new standards, reducing more tariffs and eliminating other barriers to trade and investment.
"This is about international commerce," said Diane Sullivan, director of international trade at the National Association of Manufacturers. 
"Labor and the environment are not excluded, but they are not at the center of the W.T.O's concerns."
These outsiders are clamoring to make their views known in the negotiations for a treaty that is to be called the Multilateral Agreement on Investment.
The agreement is being negotiated under the umbrella of the 29-nation Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. 
Government negotiators, most representing major industrial powers, have met periodically at the organization's headquarters in Paris. 
The last session took place in mid-April. 
The group's main goal is to produce a binding treaty that would give foreign corporations a legal status equal to that of domestic companies, establish rules for prompt and sufficient payment in cases of expropriation and give foreign companies equal bidding rights in privatizations of state enterprises.
The United States already has a number of similar, bilateral agreements, but this would be the first multilateral treaty. 
And it is drawing fire from Mr. Nader and others, including labor, which is pressing for a greater say in the talks. 
As a result, the early May target date for completing an agreement has been postponed at least six months to allow for "consultation and assessment," the organization said this week.
Acknowledging the pressure, Alan Larson, Assistant Secretary of State for Economic and Business Affairs, who represents the United States in the negotiations, said: "There is strong support for measures in the treaty that would advance this country's environmental goals and our agenda on international labor standards. 
This treaty will not interfere with the ability of the United States to regulate in a normal and nondiscriminatory fashion to protect the environment or worker safety or health."
Faced with such regulation, Mr. Rodrik of Harvard argues, corporations will not decamp. 
"We exaggerate how effectively corporations can evade national rules," he said.
Indeed, many top executives of United States multinationals see their companies as essentially American in identity. 
That was evident in interviews with a half-dozen of them, and in the replies of others to a letter from Mr. Nader, who has been campaigning for companies to recite the Pledge of Allegiance, in the company's name, at each annual meeting of shareholders. 
The pledge would be a gesture of corporate loyalty to the United States in return for the tax breaks and other advantages that companies receive.
None of the 45 corporations that replied to Mr. Nader have agreed to such a proposal. 
Many argue that it would interfere with efforts to be good corporate citizens elsewhere in the world. 
Yet most spoke of their companies as essentially American in their management, headquarters, ownership and workers.
"It would be difficult to disassociate ourselves from America, even if we wanted to do so," Steve Burrow, president of the Anheuser-Busch Companies' international operation, said in an interview. 
"Our packaging is even red, white and blue, and the American eagle is part of our image. 
But our obligation is to our shareholders, and our international operation is an important part of increasing share value."
All these themes run through Caterpillar's effort to get low-interest credit. 
The company has moved about 25 percent of its production abroad; the rest is concentrated in the Midwest, where management and research are also centered. 
But overseas sales are rising rapidly, and the corporate goal is to have 75 percent of sales from abroad by 2010, up from 50 percent today.
The Export-Import Bank plays a significant role in this strategy, already providing low-interest credits for $300 million of Caterpillar's $19 billion in annual revenue. 
If sales for the Three Gorges project on the Yangtze River in China were to be similarly financed, the total would be $350 million or more.
Capital, of course, now flows relatively easily around the world, making loans available practically everywhere. 
But when Caterpillar is competing to sell diesel engines to Zambia, gold mining equipment to Russia and earthmovers to China, the global lenders are not so quick to offer low-interest loans.
So Caterpillar and other multinationals continue to turn to their home governments. 
"In really tough, high-risk, high-opportunity markets, a government will always have greater leverage for repayment than a bank," said William C. Lane, a Caterpillar executive in Washington. 
"You really have to have someone in your corner."

text:
ï»¿
At the Sidaokou wholesale market they have been snapped up, these strange golden orbs bedecked with American flag stickers and the name Ocean Spray.
Some people have driven two hours to purchase them. 
But most just regard these fruits with curiosity -- are they oversized oranges?
-- and read the poster that explains: "Grapefruits from Florida . . . Famous Brand Name . . . Healthy and Tasty . . . Good for Your Blood and for Beauty."
"It's my first imported product, and sales are very very good," said Rong Zhifang, a saleswoman, hovering behind her cartons.
When China joins the World Trade Organization, probably later this year, it will be forced to allow a huge range of foreign goods greater access to its vast markets. 
But a few American agricultural items -- including citrus fruit and pork -- have already attained sharply improved entry in the last few months, under a recent United States-China agricultural agreement.
And, in Beijing, the fate of the invading oranges and grapefruits is seen as a glimpse of China's future, presaging the sudden new opportunities and problems that free trade will bring.
"The arrival of American agricultural products is just a start," said The Beijing Morning News, in one of many articles that have appeared recently about the American fruit. 
"Once China joins the W.T.O., the story about the boy crying wolf will soon become a reality."
Indeed, Western companies are drooling at the prospect of China's potentially huge market, aggressively promoting their products.
At the annual Food China 2000 Exhibition last week in Beijing, American producers of chicken, ice cream and fruit juice -- to name a few -- turned out in stands decorated with red, white and blue bunting to give buyers from Chinese restaurants, supermarkets and hotels a taste of the future. 
There was even a booth promoting American pork, to a country where a surplus of pigs has driven pork prices to near record lows this year.
But it was the citrus booth -- with its free fruit slices and drinks -- that commanded the longest lines. 
"This will certainly open up new business opportunities for me," said Ding Yong, a food distributor for cafeterias. 
"The juices are great."
Price, of course, is something of an issue. 
Imported oranges are about three times the price of Chinese products. 
Grapefruits here cost about $1.50 each, compared with about 10 cents for somewhat similar Chinese fruits, called youzi (pronounced yo-zuh) and huyou (pronounced hoo-yo).
These price differentials will narrow somewhat when China enters the W.T.O., since the fruits now carry an average import tariff of 40 percent. 
But even as tariffs are cut, imported fruit is likely to remain quite a bit more expensive.
And other hurdles are likely to remain for a long time, as China's slow-moving bureaucracy adjusts to the realities of more imports. 
The Florida grapefruits that arrived in China on April 20, for example, were stuck in quarantine for the next four weeks, their release blocked by a series of logistical problems.
First, the inspection documents provided by the Florida producers were considered invalid by Chinese customs authorities. 
Then the quarantine inspectors sealed the warehouse after noticing that some cases contained dead insects. 
The inspectors ultimately cleared the fruits, but not before Chinese distributors had paid them thousands of dollars in storage fees.
"I have met with so many troubles from these fruits, and I still have many grapefruits in the ports waiting to be inspected," said Zhang Zhimin, the sales manager for the China Cereal Import and Export Company, which is handling the citrus imports. 
"Although sales are good now and I am quite optimistic, there are still many problems."
The citrus fruits are coming in under the United States-China Agricultural Cooperation Agreement signed late last year. 
Under the accord, China said it would drop barriers that had previously prevented the import of some American agricultural products.
China agreed to recognize the American pork inspection system, for example, which it had called inadequate. 
It also dropped what had previously been a near-blanket ban on citrus imports, put in place to protect against infestation by the Mediterranean fruit fly, or medfly.
Under the new agreement, the United States promised not to send fruit to China from counties experiencing medfly infestations.
Since April 20, more than six huge shipments of fruit have arrived here, including 16 tons of Sunkist oranges in the northeastern part of Dalian and 60 tons of grapefruit in the coastal city of Tianjin. 
By the end of May, they could be found in upscale markets in Beijing, where the press has provided detailed analyses of their flavor, appearance, breeding and value.
In Shanghai, the 1,800 cartons of oranges that arrived on May 11 sold out within two hours. 
In Dalian, they lasted just three days. 
Tens of thousands of grapefruits have sold in Beijing since they arrived on May 20.
"Will the high prices affect sales in China?" asked The Beijing Morning News. 
"It seems not. 
The Chinese people have showed unexpected enthusiasm for these fine-quality oranges."
Chinese experts urged their compatriots to carefully observe the invasion and learn from American farmers.
Of course, the initial burst of enthusiasm for the fruit may not be surprising in a country where consumers worship all things American. 
American fruit growers and distributors are determined to maintain the momentum.
Calling grapefruit the "No. 
1 Fruit in the U.S.," material from the Beijing Shiyi Futai Trade Company says its grapefruits help "protect your heart, blood vessels and kidneys."
The fruit "has the natural anticancer element of folic acid, and natural fruit colloid, which can lower cholesterol."
A series of flashy television ads, featuring a popular music TV host named Ke Lan, is planned to promote American oranges.
There is still much work to be done. 
At the China Food 2000 Exhibition, Sunny Chen, an executive chef from a hotel in Xian, declared that consumers there were "not ready" for the flavor of grapefruit, as he threw a rind into the trash can -- even though he personally liked the fruit and predicted success with the more worldly palates of Beijing.
But at the huge Xidan Market in the capital, six flag-festooned grapefruits sat forlornly on the shelves one recent day, more museum pieces than comestibles.
"Look!
Fruit from America," said Gui Shufeng, a retiree who was strolling in the market with his wife.
"I like them -- a little tart and a little sweet," said Mr. Gui, who had tasted grapefruit while visiting his daughter in New York. 
"But I'm not sure if Chinese will buy them. 
They're expensive."

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_ Fraying the Trade Ties_Politics in Taiwan Are Straining Business Links With.txt
text:
ï»¿
Ask Stan Shih about personal computers, the Internet or his native Taiwan, and he holds forth enthusiastically. 
Not for nothing is Mr. Shih, the voluble founder of the computer maker Acer, regarded as the head cheerleader and unofficial spokesman for corporate Taiwan.
But ask Mr. Shih whether he favors an independent Taiwan, and he turns monosyllabic. 
"No," he says, as his Cheshire-cat smile tightens.
Mr. Shih, 56, has good reason to be wary. 
As the chairman of one of Taiwan's biggest multinational corporations, he has major investments in mainland China. 
Since Taiwan elected Chen Shui-bian, a onetime supporter of independence, as president in March, being identified as a person who favors independence -- or who even seems to -- has become a sure way to derail one's prospects in China.
"I am always neutral in election campaigns," Mr. Shih said. 
"The fact is, President Chen appointed me as one of his advisers. 
I couldn't say no."
Mr. Shih says he did not even vote this year. 
Yet his advisory role looked awfully close to a vote of confidence. 
And worse, he appeared to be endorsing a man whose party espouses independence for Taiwan, which Beijing considers an inseparable part of Chinese territory.
The reaction of the Chinese government was swift and angry: it put out the word that Taiwan businessmen with ties to the new president or who favored independence for Taiwan were putting their China operations at risk. 
The statement was widely interpreted as a warning to Acer and Mr. Shih.
Stan Shih is one of several captains of industry here who have been caught in the treacherous political waters between Taipei and Beijing. 
Some, like the plastics tycoon Hsu Wen-lung, have been frank advocates of independence. 
Others, like Chang Yung-fa, a shipping magnate, are longtime supporters of Mr. Chen. Still others, like Mr. Shih, simply like to oblige future leaders.
For the first time, Beijing is scrutinizing the political beliefs of Taiwan's business leaders and warning those who stray from the official line that there is only one China. 
Political analysts say the crackdown could undermine the historic role of commerce as a bridge between Taiwan and China, binding the countries closer even when they diverge politically.
"In the last election, China came to realize that businessmen can play a very strong role in Taiwanese politics," Tien Hung-mao, Taiwan's foreign minister, said in an interview last month. 
"So China has begun politicizing the economic relationship between the two countries."
Mr. Tien worries that Taiwan business executives may be forced to take a loyalty oath to protect their investments in China. 
Those who refuse may become the targets of tax audits, surprise inspections and other forms of harassment by the Chinese government. 
In the worst case, some companies may be forced to leave China and take their capital and skills with them.
Since China opened its doors to Taiwan two decades ago, trade between the two has proved to be remarkably resistant to politics. 
In the first quarter of this year, while Beijing was threatening military action if Taiwan elected Mr. Chen, Taiwan exported $6.2 billion of goods to China, a 16 percent increase over 1999. 
It imported $1.3 billion, a 33 percent jump.
But Taiwan's investment in China is showing signs of weakness. 
While the amount of investment contracts rose 46 percent the first quarter, the actual volume of Taiwan money flowing into China declined 9.5 percent, to $420 million, according to China's Foreign Trade Ministry.
Experts say that could be an early barometer of trouble. 
Even investors like Mr. Shih, who were once wooed by Beijing to build factories with promises of tax breaks and reduced import duties, acknowledge they can no longer plow money into China without thinking twice.
"I have to be concerned," Mr. Shih said. 
"But I cannot control their opinion. 
If they welcome me, I will contribute to their country. 
If they don't welcome me, I have so many other things to do."
Mr. Shih is not as passive as he sounds. 
He traveled to a technology conference in Beijing in April, enduring a snub when high-level officials did not meet with him. 
And he plans to return in August to promote a new Web site, which features a series of lectures by him. 
By sharing his insights on entrepreneurialism with mainland students, Mr. Shih clearly hopes to mend fences.
Acer has a lot riding on Mr. Shih's charm offensive. 
Earlier this year, the company opened a $50 million factory in the province of Guangdong to make personal computers. 
Five more plants are on the drawing board. 
The company is also testing an Internet service in Shanghai. 
It hopes to roll out the service commercially, which would make it a pioneer in China's interactive communications business.
For Acer, China is the linchpin in its plans to become a global leader in the technology industry. 
Mr. Shih said that Taiwan, with 23 million people, was simply too small to supply it with enough workers or customers to compete with giant overseas rivals like Dell or I.B.M.
Acer is also struggling in the fiercely competitive American PC market. 
The company is counting on rapid growth in China to offset its tribulations in the United States. 
Mr. Shih believes that despite the political uncertainty, companies in Taiwan are still the best positioned to dominate the mainland market. 
Someday, he predicted, Taiwan and China will be parts of the same greater China.
"I don't know how long it will take," he said, "but sooner or later, after China becomes more competitive and self-confident, we will treat China as our home market."
Not everybody shares Mr. Shih's optimism. 
Dennis Chao, managing director of a Taiwan sportswear manufacturer, opened a plant in the southern city of Guangzhou in 1987. 
He said he was drawn by the Chinese government's promise of favorable treatment for Taiwan companies.
Seven years ago, however, Beijing stopped treating investors from Taiwan differently from other foreign investors. 
Mr. Chao, 48, said that losing breaks on import duties on machinery and raw materials has made it uneconomical for him to install new equipment or otherwise expand his factory, which employs 1,200 people.
Then, in the last month, the Chinese government warned Taiwan investors in the provinces of Guangdong and Fujian that they would be subject to unspecified sanctions if they advocated independence for Taiwan. 
Mr. Chao says he has studiously steered clear of politics. 
But he said such threats only added to China's reputation as an impossible place to do business.
"We're not enemies; we're all Chinese," Mr. Chao said. 
"It's enough to drive you crazy."
Some analysts said China's crackdown had been fueled by its irritation with a few high-profile personalities in Taiwan rather than any overall objection to where most business leaders stand on the issue. 
In particular, Beijing is angry with Hsu Wen-lung, the chairman of Chi Mei Industry, a petrochemical giant.
Mr. Hsu, whose company has six plants in China, staunchly supports Mr. Chen and has proclaimed his desire for an independent Taiwan. 
The Chinese government has subjected Chi Mei to numerous inspections and ordered state companies not to do business with it. 
It is the only known case of retaliation so far.
Experts said Beijing could play hardball with Mr. Hsu because it had a large and competitive domestic petrochemical industry.
"This is a policy of selective sanctions," said Andrew Yang, secretary general of the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies, a research organization. 
"It is not a unified policy toward Taiwan companies."
For example, Mr. Yang said China would be unlikely to take Draconian steps against Acer, which, as a high-technology company, provides expertise and thousands of skilled jobs. 
Despite the contretemps with its founder, Acer has not lost its license to test Internet services in Shanghai.
Moreover, Mr. Shih is going out of his way to protest his political innocence. 
He says he hopes for the eventual reunification of Taiwan and China. 
In case there is any misunderstanding, he adds, "I also agree with the Chinese government's position that businessmen shouldn't support independence."
Analysts here say that Mr. Shih, who learned business by helping his mother sell duck eggs and stationery, was probably turned into more of a symbol than he ever wished during the election campaign.
"Stan Shih has been very conservative his whole life," said Antonio Chiang, the editor of The Taipei Times, an English-language newspaper that supports Mr. Chen. "But he is sympathetic to the cause of reform. 
Chen Shui-bian is the only one who can reform Taiwanese politics."
Other experts say Beijing does not pay attention to such subtleties. 
They believe the Chinese government is using commercial ties as a lever to subdue Taiwan. 
Beijing pursued a similar campaign with Hong Kong investors before the British colony reverted to Chinese rule in 1997.
In Hong Kong, even tycoons who had been knighted by Queen Elizabeth swore fealty to Beijing. 
Some experts say the mainland market's lure is so strong it will get similar allegiance from Taiwan's tycoons.
"In the early days, China relied heavily on Taiwanese investment, but now foreign investors from many countries are in China," said Liang Su-Yung, head of the Strait Peaceful Reunification Association, a pro-China lobbying group. 
"Taiwanese companies need China more than it needs them."

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_ Soar Like a Falcon . . ._. . . Sink Like an Overextended Investment Bank.txt
text:
ï»¿
With the collapse of Peregrine Investments Holdings today, Asia's biggest underwriter of stocks has disappeared off the map of Asian investment banking just one decade after it was created by a swashbuckling former British racing driver and his Hong Kong partner.
The factors behind Peregrine's downfall were many and complex, and had much to do with its brash -- some would say insolent -- culture. 
Yet some executives at Peregrine, as well as financiers familiar with its final days, said its demise became inevitable only after First National Bank of Chicago, a unit of First Chicago NBD, its lead banker and an investor in the firm's putative restructuring, pulled out of a proposed rescue effort and canceled financing for Peregrine at the last moment.
The flame-out of Peregrine, the largest investment bank in Asia outside of Japan, spread panic through the Hong Kong stock market and raised further questions about the depth and duration of the economic crisis that is ravaging the fruits of more than a decade of explosive regional growth.
Yet, in many ways, Peregrine's downfall was emblematic of the fault lines in the foundations of Asia's once-vaunted economic miracle. 
Its headlong rush to do deals, its reliance on connections in high places and its willingness to skim the edges of legality and propriety mirrored the region's reckless economic growth and its tolerance of widespread corruption and cronyism.
But even in a part of the world where risk-taking had become the key to economic success, Peregrine stood out. 
It largely pioneered the market for junk bonds in Asia. 
After cozying up to the Chinese authorities in Beijing, it became the powerhouse behind virtually every initial listing by Chinese companies on Hong Kong's stock exchange. 
And it foraged markets -- North Korea, Vietnam and Myanmar -- that few others would go near because of their horrendous human-rights records.
Today, as Peregrine filed for liquidation, Hong Kong's stock market plummeted 8.6 percent, continuing a meltdown that has stripped it of more than one-quarter of its value so far this year. 
Even so, Hong Kong monetary authorities played down the threat the bank's collapse posed to the financial system. 
Donald Tsang, Hong Kong's financial secretary, turned down Peregrine's request for assistance over the weekend after a rescue package with a Swiss financial group fell apart. 
Mr. Tsang said a bailout would not be "in the public interest."
The market rebounded Tuesday, with the main index rising about 5 percent in midmorning trading.
In the end, analysts here and elsewhere said, it was arrogance that did Peregrine in -- an arrogance emanating from the personality of its founder, Philip Tose of Britain, and his Hong Kong partner, Francis Pak To Leung, and that pervaded the bank's culture. 
That arrogance, they said, led the company to lend too much money for questionable projects and to exercise too little supervision over managers, and especially over Andre Lee, who ran its highly profitable and nearly autonomous bond department.
As a result, when Asia's financial crisis broke last summer, Peregrine was ill equipped to cope with the fallout. 
Indeed, it was the failure of an Indonesian taxi-cab company that fatally undermined Hong Kong's premier investment bank.
Sometime last summer, when bullishness was still the sentiment of the day, Peregrine made a bridge loan of $260 million to Steady Safe, run by one of Indonesia's flashiest wheeler dealers, Jopie Widjaya. 
Mr. Widjaya's dream was to move from his profitable but humdrum Jakarta taxi business, with its fleet of 4,000 cabs, to rail projects, ferries and toll roads. 
Mr. Widjaya had the right connections; he had even bought a stake in a toll road owned by Siti Hardiyanti Rukmana, the eldest daughter of President Suharto.
Steady Safe had all the elements of a Peregrine-style deal: access to the corridors of power, seemingly assured earnings and sweeping opportunity. 
The problem was that Peregrine lent the $260 million in American dollars -- fully one-third of Peregrine's capital -- against Steady Safe's revenues in Indonesian rupiah. 
At the time, Peregrine seemed convinced that the rupiah was sound and that it could soon resell the bonds backing the loan. 
Moreover, the fixed-income team that cut the deal had earned 38 percent of Peregrine's profits the previous year; this was just one more deal.
Analysts say such confidence was misplaced. 
Any lender entrusting the equivalent of one-third of its capital to any borrower, much less a little-known company in a country notorious for corruption, shows poor financial judgment, they say.
But far from having second thoughts after the financial turmoil that shook Thailand last July spread throughout Asia, Peregrine remained upbeat. 
In late October, even though the rupiah had by then lost 30 percent of its value, Peregrine's own weekly analytical reports, boldly titled Greed and Fear, argued that the rupiah's collapse "certainly looks overdone and suggests a countertrend rally may be overdue."
It was not to be.
That same month, rumors began percolating in Hong Kong that Peregrine had taken $1 billion in trading losses, rumors denied by Mr. Tose. But even as he insisted on the bank's solidity, the rupiah was slipping and Peregrine's chairman was looking for an investor to replenish the company's capital.
In November, Mr. Tose, 51, announced that he had struck a deal with Zurich Center Investments Ltd., part of Zurich Group, a Swiss financial-services company, to buy a 24.1 percent stake in Peregrine for $200 million.
But the deal never went through.
According to Zurich Group, the two companies planned to set up an Asian investment fund, called the Peregrine Direct Investment fund, with a commitment of $50 million from each partner and an expected infusion of $350 million to $500 million from institutional investors.
But the continuing financial tumult in Asia apparently made Zurich nervous. 
A spokeswoman declined to go into details about the group's decision to back away, saying only it was the "end result of the negotiations to rework the conditions" of Zurich's participation.
Meanwhile, events in Indonesia tumbled out of control, and its currency collapsed. 
Steady Safe, with its earnings in rupiah, could no longer meet payments on its dollar loans, particularly the huge loan from Peregrine. 
The taxi company's stock sank to a sliver over one penny and, last week, it locked its doors.
As Peregrine's stock continued to slide, trading in the bank's stock was suspended. 
As Zurich Group was preparing one final offer to Peregrine, there seemed little hope of a deal. 
"When Zurich came back last week," said a senior Peregrine official who only agreed to speak anonymously, "they were going to buy our bond portfolio for 16 cents on the dollar. 
The bond portfolio was $600 million plus; there's a lot of good paper in that portfolio. 
But when you have a situation where they say you have $260 million, $270 million worth of bad paper, they say, 'What else have you done?'
It just snowballed."
At the table with Zurich was First Chicago, one of Peregrine's principal creditors. 
At about one o'clock in the morning on Friday, First Chicago left the negotiations. 
"Zurich walked away six hours later," said the Peregrine official. 
"It just unraveled from there."
A spokesman for First Chicago declined to comment. 
But executives at both Peregrine and Zurich said today that First Chicago had initially pledged $25 million for a small stake in Peregrine, then had a change of heart. 
First Chicago's departure from the negotiations Friday morning prompted Zurich's decision to throw in the towel, they said, in part because it did not wish to raise its stake in the company significantly beyond 24 percent.
"They did not want to go up to 35 percent and make a general offer," as required by Hong Kong law whenever a buyer's stake exceeds 30 percent, a Peregrine executive said.
Meanwhile, Peregrine executives desperately tried to salvage something from the fiasco, maintaining that the firm's brokerage and corporate-finance businesses would make good acquisitions for the right buyer. 
"We still have a first-class franchise and it would be highly regrettable if that was not kept intact," said Timothy Voake, chief executive officer of Peregrine Brokerage Inc., which has headquarters in New York.
After the collapse of negotiations in Hong Kong, a news conference announcing a deal was abandoned. 
Swiftly, the Securities and Futures Commission ordered Peregrine to stop all trading activities. 
Peregrine's seat on the stock exchange was also suspended.
Peregrine was bust. 
Scarcely six months ago, Peregrine was the enfant terrible of Asian banking, a champion of "buccaneering" as Mr. Tose put it.
"One of Peregrine's great advantages in its heyday was to commit its own capital rapidly to transactions, with bridge loans, for example," said Richard Margolis of Merrill Lynch (Asia Pacific) Ltd. 
"It could take decisions quickly."
Peregrine was created in 1988 on $38 million raised by Messrs. Tose and Leung -- both refugees from Citibank's foundering investment banking venture -- from some of Hong Kong's tycoons, including Li Ka-shing, a leading property and infrastructure developer; Gordon Wu, an Asian infrastructure developer, and Larry Yung, China's principal investment banker here. 
Peregrine grew exponentially, with Mr. Tose and Mr. Leung capitalizing on personal contacts cultivated over the previous decade. 
Both men enjoyed lavish life styles.
Connections, combined with speedy decision-making and a penchant for risk, catapulted the bank forward. 
And it rushed in where others hesitated to tread. 
Typical was Peregrine's response to China's massacre of civilians in Tiananmen Square in June 1989. 
"These events were just a hiccup," Mr. Leung said in an interview two years ago. 
"We decided we wanted to take advantage of depressed market conditions at the time."
Quickly, Peregrine emerged as one of the largest underwriters in Hong Kong. 
And while China and Hong Kong remained the core of the bank's business, it spread its wings and splashed offices across 14 countries.
Even Asia's widespread culture of corruption did not seem to trouble Mr. Tose. After all, he said in an interview with The South China Morning Post last year, it is "quite an open form of corruption."
"It is not stalling advances in Asia," he added, "but is an accepted way of life in many ways."
Unfortunately for Peregrine, though, it often ruffled the feathers of local authorities. 
In Vietnam, it formed Peregrine Capital Vietnam with a fast-talking nightclub owner and car dealer named Nguyen Trung Truc, for example. 
Shortly afterward, Mr. Truc's other businesses were raided by tax authorities, and he wound up spending most of the year in jail for tax evasion. 
Peregrine itself was fined for operating a business without proper licenses.
Last June, although storm clouds were rapidly gathering on Asia's economic horizons, Peregrine was buoyant. 
It reported hefty profits for the first six months of $82.5 million (United States) on revenues of $19.6 billion.
When the end came this weekend, however, many people were asking why Peregrine's vaunted connections with some of Hong Kong's wealthiest and most powerful people did not result in the firm's rescue.
As the day wore on today, hundreds of customers shuttled in and out of Peregrine's brokerage operations to close their accounts.
"I was very surprised," said K. Chan, a 60-year-old retiree. 
"I've been with Peregrine for six or seven years. 
I'm going to transfer my stocks to another company."
But, Mr. Chan continued, Hong Kong was not to blame. 
"What happened to Peregrine was caused by external forces, the Southeast Asian currencies," he said. 
"It's not because of Hong Kong itself."

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_A Bug Turns Up in U.S.-China Trade Relations.txt
text:
ï»¿
To halt the invasion of a devastating insect pest, the United States said today that it would ban the import of all Chinese goods shipped in raw wood packing material, a move that is likely to strain China's economy -- as well as United States-China relations.
Officials said wooden crates and pallets used to ship Chinese goods to North America sometimes harbor the comely but voracious Asian long-horned beetle, which has emerged from the packing material after it arrived in warehouses to kill trees in five locations around New York and Chicago in the last two years.
The ban is likely to result in delays or higher costs for a third to half of China's $62 billion in exports to the United States -- at a time when China has already seen its export growth slowed by weak economies in other Asian countries.
United States officials acknowledged during a news conference conducted by video hookup in Beijing that the restrictions, scheduled to take effect in 90 days, would cause pain for Chinese business -- and for American importers as well. 
But they said that when Agriculture Department inspectors found the beetles boring through maple trees in suburban Chicago neighborhoods this summer, they felt compelled to act.
"We are very concerned," Dr. Isi A. Siddiqui, Deputy Assistant Agriculture Secretary, said during the news conference. 
"These new regulations are based on sound science and a real threat to U.S. environmental resources."
Government studies estimated $138 billion of damage to the United States economy if the beetles, which have no natural enemies in the United States and cannot be eradicated with pesticides, move to United States forests.
Dan Glickman, the Agriculture Secretary, said the action should not be seen as a trade sanction, adding that trade between the United States and China had grown to $80 billion this year from $5 billion 15 years ago.
"Our intention here is not to disrupt trade, but to lock out an unwanted guest that poses a serious economic and environmental threat," Mr. Glickman told an audience in Chicago.
The new regulations require that goods from China be packed in non-wood packing material or wood that has been treated with heat or fumigation to kill the insects. 
It was not clear whether Chinese exporters would be able to adopt new practices in the next 90 days or how much their costs would rise.
Although the Chinese Government had no official comment on the ban, Chinese officials have been aware of the looming possibility for weeks and were hoping to avert it.
"If the ban is imposed, China's exports will suffer, because a considerable amount of our export trade is packed in raw wood," one Agriculture Ministry official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity.
The Chinese Government has recently issued billions of dollars in Treasury bonds in an effort to stimulate the economy and insulate it against a slowdown caused by economic crises elsewhere in Asia or the summer's devastating floods in China. 
Although China's exports are still growing, the rate of growth has slowed this year, and a reduction of its thriving export sales to the United States would be hard to bear.
Dr. Siddiqui said the United States Government had been discussing the problem with China's quarantine agency for many months, ever since the beetles were discovered in warehouses. 
He stressed that the United States hoped to cooperate with the Chinese to minimize disruption to trade.
"Look, this is not an action we wanted to take, but this bug is eating trees in people's back yards and their front yards," said one United States official in Beijing. 
"Inspectors from the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service are knocking on doors and saying, 'We have to cut down all the trees around your home.'
"
In the United States, the beetles have so far been detected in wood packing from China in warehouses in 14 states. 
They have been found free in the environment in and around Chicago as well as in Brooklyn and Amityville, N.Y.
The beetle was identified as the Asian long-horned beetle by a Cornell University entomologist, Richard Hoebeke, after Brooklyn residents noticed mysterious half-inch holes in their trees. 
The beetle's larvae drill through trees' bark into the wood, where they undergo metamorphosis into large black beetles with bright white spots and long elegant antennas.
In Brooklyn, as in three subsequent infestations, inspectors had to order the destruction of all affected trees, since there is currently no other way to control the pests.
United States officials disagreed somewhat over just how much of China's exports were packed in untreated wood, with estimates ranging from 25 percent to more than 90 percent, and on how difficult it would be for Chinese to adjust to the new requirements.
Ma Zhongmei, an official at the export department of the North China Air Transportation Company in Beijing, said about one-third of her company's customers packed goods in raw wood. 
She added that this sort of packing was most commonly used for high-value items, like large machines and factory equipment.
"These customers could have used plywood, but they chose raw wood to reduce cost," she said.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_A New Horizon for China in Trade.txt
text:
ï»¿
Liang Bingjun, chatting on his mobile telephone, is one reason the West ought to be excited about China joining the World Trade Organization next year.
A quarter of every dollar spent on the phone by Mr. Liang and other mobile phone owners in China could belong to a foreign company as soon as China joins the W.T.O. 
That's not small change. 
With more than 65 million cell phone users, China is already the world's second-largest wireless market and is expected to surpass even the United States by the end of next year.
Telecommunications is just one way in which China's trade organization membership will make an immediate splash. 
While reams of questions remain about what will happen after the world's most populous country joins the global trading club, there are some reasonable certainties about instant changes that will alter the global market forever. 
Others will happen gradually over five years.
China's W.T.O. membership will not change everything: the country will continue to protect many of its sectors from foreign competition. 
But joining the organization will force open the nation's economy more in the first five years than during the previous 20 years of reforms. 
Some of the biggest changes will come on the first day.
Tariffs are set to fall on a wide range of products. 
On the first day of China's W.T.O. membership, for example, the import duty on some automobiles will drop to 63.5 percent from 80 percent now, the first step in a five-year decline that will bring all car duties down to 25 percent.
Finance companies like GMAC, meanwhile, will be allowed to offer car loans, putting millions of Chinese consumers within sudden reach of buying an imported car.
And China has promised to scrap the murky, politicized process by which it decides what companies have access to its market.
Insurers, for example, will no longer wait years to hear if they are among the anointed ones. 
The day after China joins the W.T.O., the country's insurance regulator is supposed to have applications on hand for qualified companies that want to sell insurance in the country. 
And, under W.T.O. rules, the regulator will have to act on the applications within a set period of time, giving a written explanation to companies whose applications are turned down. 
That will be a relief to insurers that have spent millions of dollars waiting for word from the regulators with no information at all.
Insurers are eager to start: China's entire insurance market is still smaller than Taiwan's, but the government expects it to expand at a double-digit rate for at least the next decade.
"With incomes rising, there's little doubt the market will grow quickly," said Patrick Cranley, the Cigna Corporation's representative in Shanghai and the chairman of the American Chamber of Commerce here.
As a W.T.O. member, China won't be able to arbitrarily limit the number of foreign insurance companies operating here.
Other foreign services will become immediately legal. 
Foreign law firms, which have operated in a gray area for years, will at last be allowed to counsel clients on Chinese laws and rules related to commercial transactions, though they will not yet be allowed to argue cases before Chinese courts.
In some cases, China is already amending those laws and regulations to comply with W.T.O. standards. 
The country's legislature has drafted amendments that will lift burdens from foreign investors setting up factories in China. 
Those amendments will take effect when they are approved by the full legislature, a largely rubber stamp body, at its next session early next year.
Among other changes, foreign companies will no longer be required to use a certain amount of local materials or components in the products they make in China. 
And factories that are 100 percent foreign-owned will no longer be required to export at least half their China-made goods. 
Nor will licenses for wholly foreign-owned manufacturers be granted based on the level of technology they bring to China.
"That should make it easier for foreign companies to invest," said Patrick Norton, a Shanghai-based lawyer with the American law firm O'Melveny & Myers.
Few of the immediate changes will be as momentous as the opening of China's telecommunications industry, though, which itself is on the verge of explosive growth. 
Upon China's joining the W.T.O., foreign companies will be allowed to buy up to 25 percent of Chinese mobile telephone networks, and up to 49 percent within three years.
Foreign telecommunication giants are already jostling for position: Britain's Vodafone Group paid $2.5 billion for a 2 percent stake in China's biggest mobile telephone company, China Mobile Communications, earlier this year and has said it is ready to buy more. 
Hong Kong's Hutchison Whampoa holds a 2 percent stake in China Unicom, China's second mobile telephone operator, which is shopping for a still larger strategic investor. 
And there may also be more mobile telephone licenses issued in China after the country joins the W.T.O.
Mr. Liang, 25, who keeps his cell phone glued to his ear at a coffee shop on Shanghai's bustling Nanjing Road, said he was happy about the changes W.T.O. entry will bring. 
"If there are foreign companies in the market, there will be more competition and prices will come down," he said.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Asia Guide Calls Local Partners Key to Success.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Jim Rohwer was writing about Asia from the genteel surroundings of the London offices of The Economist, he was convinced he knew what he was doing. 
It turned out, he confesses now, that he did not.
"I realized within three or four months of arriving in Asia that I understood nothing about it at all," he said recently. 
"The same is generally true about Western business people who haven't set foot here."
After four years in Asia, three for The Economist, the weekly news magazine owned by Economist Newspaper Ltd., and the last as the chief economist for the CS First Boston Corporation, Mr. Rohwer now seeks to share his epiphany with Western readers. 
(Asians already pretty much know what he has discovered.) In short, he wants to explain why Asia has become, in his words, "the miracle" of late-20th-century free markets and economic development.
In a new book, "Asia Rising: Why America Will Prosper as Asia's Economies Boom" (Simon & Schuster), Mr. Rohwer explores the fundamental causes of Asia's prodigious growth and suggests how America's economy, and companies, can benefit from the jarring transformation of the global economy.
His analysis and suggestions might trouble Westerners, but that discomfort is essential, he said, if they are to grapple with Asia's complexities.
Indeed, the successful companies here, the ones that are defining how business is done and how economies are shaped, are not the multinationals of the United States and Europe, but the great conglomerates of Asia, like the Charoen Pokphand Group of Bangkok, Thailand, which have been built mostly by a vast diaspora of Chinese-born business families. 
Moreover, his analysis largely diminishes Japan's role in Asia, a view that runs counter to most judgments about growth in the region.
Mr. Rohwer is emphatic that his work is not a prescription for American companies, but he does believe there is one fundamental tenet that emerges from his book. 
"The biggest single thing for companies to do is to figure out how they can plug themselves into local conditions," he said. 
"Mostly that means finding the right partner, someone to guide you through that maze in Asia."
Yet, he cautioned, "this is very much a book of strategy more than a book on how to do it."
In an interview, Mr. Rohwer called Asia's success dependent on "being open, especially in terms of trade, investment and technology transfer. 
Second, it's linked to not providing protection -- social protection, protection from competition, protection from change. 
And third, it is having a very small role for government. 
The family is central and not government institutions in absorbing the shock of change."
Across Asia, government spending accounts for a very small share of gross domestic product, usually less than 20 percent, Mr. Rohwer said, compared with Western economies in which it ranges from 30 percent to 50 percent.
"How did this develop?
These countries were under threats to their survival," he said. 
"Their backs were to the wall and they had choices of fighting or collapsing. 
Secondly, America's role in the cold war of defending them gave them a stable structure. 
There also was a tremendous amount of American generosity. 
But far more important was the willingness to protect these countries and absorb their exports. 
And this was grounded in very strong family-based societies, where learning and hard work were highly valued.
"And last -- and this is the thing Americans have the hardest time understanding -- most places are run by highly authoritarian governments that unlike authoritarians in Africa or the Middle East were actually committed to the national interest."
Economies that have thrived under the apparently paradoxical combination of political and social authoritarianism and market freedoms are apparent: Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore, Malaysia and China. 
In Mr. Rohwer's view, the countries destined to follow these examples are Indonesia, which is well on the road to sustained economic growth, and Vietnam.
The great Asian failure, Mr. Rohwer argues, is India, which has too long practiced oppressive planning and a cloistered approach to economic development. 
As a result, he said, India has been left behind.
Driving the growth, Mr. Rohwer said, have been the multitude of Chinese families that turned small businesses into vibrant conglomerates across Asia. 
Together, the World Bank estimates that this "greater China" had a gross domestic product of $2.5 trillion in 1990, nearly half that of the G.D.P. of the United States in 1990.
"It's one of the most interesting business phenomena in the world," he said. 
"Scattered across Southeast Asia are 50 to 60 million Chinese. 
They have as a group created one of the most successful business empires in the world. 
It's the business equivalent of a neural network and the Chinese have come to dominate business, finance and commerce throughout Asia, outside Japan, even though they are a minority."
For American companies, Mr. Rohwer contends, Asia is the future. 
But protectionist impulses in the United States could damage the possibilities for American companies. 
Indeed, he said, the emergence of a huge Asian middle class augurs both great opportunity for American business -- and great competition.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Asian Markets Ending 1999 On Steep Internet Ascent.txt
text:
ï»¿
Stock markets across Asia are riding out the millennium on a cloud of euphoria generated by -- what else?
-- the Internet.
Shares in Tokyo, Seoul, Hong Kong and Kuala Lumpur rose again today, providing fresh evidence, if any were needed, that the information revolution has replaced the Asian economic crisis as the preoccupation of investors in this part of the world.
"Asia has lagged the West in information technology," said Dong Tao, a regional economist with Credit Suisse First Boston in Hong Kong. 
"But with Asia recovering from the crisis, companies are now willing to invest in this area. 
People see the possibility of a real breakthrough."
In South Korea, the market rose 2.2 percent to a five-year high, while stocks in Taiwan were up four-tenths of 1 percent, in the last trading sessions of 1999 for those markets. 
The gains capped a rally that began early in the year, as fears about Asian finances receded. 
After a setback during the summer, the rally reignited in October as companies began pursuing a flurry of Internet-related ventures in the region.
This jolt of excitement helped the benchmark South Korean index gain 82.78 percent for the year -- and more yet in dollar terms, 92.58 percent -- the best performance of any Asian market outside Japan. 
Taiwan's exchange, despite the devastating earthquake there in September, rose 31.63 percent from its final trading session of 1998.
Nowhere has the giddiness over technology been more pronounced than in Hong Kong. 
The benchmark Hang Seng index has moved from strength to strength over the last week, up more than half a percent today, to 16,928.29. 
It has risen 68 percent so far this year, and is higher now than it was at the peak of the territory's real estate boom in the mid-90's.
Analysts said today's gain was led by a company that did not exist a year ago: Pacific Century Cyberworks, which invests in Internet start-ups and is creating its own satellite-delivered Internet service. 
Its shares jumped 22 percent today, after soaring 44 percent last Thursday and Friday. 
The surge began in the United States last Wednesday, when the company's shares doubled in over-the-counter trading.
Pacific Century Cyberworks -- which was founded by Richard Li, the son of the Hong Kong tycoon Li Ka-shing -- loses money and will for several more years. 
Still, the company is being hailed as the vehicle that could turn Hong Kong into a technology mecca. 
And the younger Mr. Li spent last week denying rumors that he was about to swap shares with Microsoft or seek a listing on the Nasdaq market.
"Pacific Century does not even have a core business yet," Mr. Tao of Credit Suisse First Boston said. 
"But it has demonstrated its ability to raise funds, and that's what's important in this business."
With a market capitalization exceeding $30 billion, Pacific Century is worth almost as much as the elder Mr. Li's flagship company, Cheung Kong Holdings. 
Mr. Tao suggested that Richard Li had created as much wealth, on paper, in five months as his father did in 50 years.
Hong Kong's Internet bubble has expanded to encompass Internet-related companies like Cable and Wireless HKT, Hong Kong's local phone provider, and China Telecom (Hong Kong), the publicly listed arm of the entrenched mainland Chinese phone company.
China Telecom, which owns the gateways that Chinese use to gain access to the World Wide Web, is regarded by investors as a way to capitalize on the rapid growth of the Internet there. 
Cable and Wireless HKT recently signed a deal with Star TV, an Asian satellite television company controlled by the News Corporation, to provide high-speed Internet access and television programs throughout the region.
Despite the resurgence of Asian stocks, many analysts do not think that Hong Kong and other Asian markets are as steeply priced as those in the United States. 
Brokerage firms here predict that the Hang Seng index will finish next year significantly above its current levels, even with 1999's ascent.
"The Hong Kong market could easily pull back a bit from here," acknowledged Richard Margolis, a regional strategist at Merrill Lynch here. 
"But it's not as heavily underpinned as the U.S. markets by companies whose only valuation is a multiple of their losses."
One reason for the optimism is that Asia's underlying economies have recovered faster than almost anyone predicted. 
Mr. Tao, for example, recently increased his forecast for Hong Kong's economic growth in 2000 to 5.1 percent, from 3.2 percent. 
He says the territory is enjoying a sharp, "V-shaped" rebound.
With exports from South Korea booming and foreign investors pouring money into stocks there, the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade estimated that the country's gross domestic product will increase this year at an outsized rate of 9.5 percent, and a very respectable 6.5 percent in 2000.
Still, analysts are wary of projecting a future of unbroken gains. 
The enthusiasm for Internet shares is an export of the United States, and it has made Asian markets more dependent than ever on stock performance in New York, especially on the Nasdaq in recent months. 
If either the Nasdaq or the Dow Jones industrial average were to fall significantly from their current levels, analysts said it could halt the rebound in the region.
Simon L. Ogus, former head of Asian economics at Warburg Dillon Read, said: "There has always been a lot of correlation between the U.S. and Asian markets, because many of them are small, trading economies. 
But there is more correlation than ever now. 
We've got one huge correlative bet going on here."

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Behind Sumitomo Scandal, a Drive to Be the Copper King.txt
text:
ï»¿
When a typical Japanese trading company gets an order for copper in Bangkok, Thailand, it might take two months to move the metal from the mines in Africa to the docks in Bangkok.
But the Sumitomo Corporation can do it in 10 days.
"Their response to customers is incredibly quick for any brand, any amount and any time," said a rival copper trader.
Sumitomo's disclosure that the company's star copper trader lost $1.8 billion in futures has led traders and investigators to suspect foul play. 
But what the scandal obscures is Sumitomo's efforts in recent years to become a leading world player in copper itself, from mines to phone lines, not just in copper futures and options and other fancy trading instruments.
The copper wire that carries telephone conversations, the copper coils in compact disk players and the copper in car radiators may all have been supplied in some earlier shape by Sumitomo. 
Already, some analysts say, Sumitomo controls from 5 to 20 percent of the world market.
That could mean, as some traders say, that the company's copper trading influenced prices and supplies in ways that likely benefited Sumitomo's business in mining and smelting, as well as in the physical copper business. 
Thus, when commodities trading led to higher prices, that may have helped Sumitomo and other copper-related companies in the Sumitomo group at every step of the way -- from extracting the copper to smelting and refining it and finally to shipping and delivering loads of the metal around the world.
Copper has always been special to Sumitomo, partly because copper is the business that gave birth to this conglomerate three centuries ago. 
And more than other trading companies, Sumitomo has been rapidly expanding its copper business lately, stockpiling and blanketing copper buyers with an assertive sales strategy.
With a surging appetite for copper in Southeast Asia and China, Sumitomo and its affiliated companies have stepped up investments in the more profitable areas of copper mines and smelters around the world, as well as in the trading of the flat metal itself.
At the center of this boom was Yasuo Hamanaka, the Sumitomo copper trader accused of hiding losses of $1.8 billion over 10 years. 
Coincidentally, it was just a decade ago that Sumitomo began its resurgence into copper mines and smelters, and Mr. Hamanaka seemed to soak in business. 
Foreign partners came with new venture proposals, seeking to work with Sumitomo's copper king, and Mr. Hamanaka visited copper mines around the world.
Mr. Hamanaka won awards from Sumitomo's president and helped resurrect the copper business within the company. 
And with his complex trading strategies dovetailing with Sumitomo's growing copper empire, Sumitomo executives may have been less eager to investigate deeply into his activities, much less halt them.
"I find it very difficult to believe that a guy could run up a loss for 10 years," said Paula J. Sugawara, an analyst covering trading companies at Lehman Brothers Japan Inc. 
"It makes me wonder whether the company was turning a blind eye because he was making profits."
Sumitomo has rejected any suggestion that its top executives were involved in the scandal and says it is conducting its own investigation.
Other copper companies affiliated with Sumitomo would also have received a boost, of course, but no evidence has emerged that Sumitomo was deliberately trying to push up prices to bolster profitability in its other copper operations. 
Indeed, some analysts say that is implausible, partly because companies in the Sumitomo Group are decentralized and the traders at Sumitomo would not be inclined to take risks to help distant cousins in the group.
Still, the trading scandal and the motivations behind it are murky, and some traders say that Sumitomo's diverse copper holdings may have played some role. 
In addition, it is clear that Sumitomo stood to gain from higher copper prices in ways that other trading companies did not.
"As a total copper business, compared to trading groups like Mitsubishi or Mitsui, Sumitomo gained greater benefits because its operation is larger," Hiroaki Kawabe, a metals analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute, said about the effect of higher copper prices on Sumitomo.
Earlier this year, Sumitomo and the Sumitomo Metal Mining Company, one of Japan's largest copper mining and smelting companies, held an opening ceremony in Copiapo, Chile, for a $600 million copper mine. 
Sumitomo companies, which took a 20 percent stake, developed the mine with the Phelps Dodge Mining Company, and it has been operating since September 1994 with the capacity to produce 400,000 tons of copper concentrate each year.
Also earlier this year, Sumitomo announced a minority stake in a new $1.5 billion copper and gold mining venture in Indonesia with an American company, the Newmont Gold Company, and P. T. Pukuafu Indah of Indonesia. 
The operation, in which Sumitomo is investing $100 million and financing up to $800 million more, is expected to produce 245,000 tons of refined copper, beginning in 1999.
Next year, a $185 million joint venture among China and other investors, including Sumitomo and Sumitomo Metal, will begin a smelting operation with a capacity of 100,000 tons of copper in Anhui Province. 
In addition to this smelter, Sumitomo also has a technical cooperative arrangement with a Chinese partner in Jiangxi Province.
And two years ago, copper production began at a $200 million mining project in New South Wales, Australia, a venture among Sumitomo, Sumitomo Metal and an Australian company, North Broken Hill Peco Ltd.
Sumitomo also has a 10 percent stake in a $37 million mining venture in Mexico. 
It has interests in a highly successful mining operation with Phelps Dodge in Arizona, as well as another venture in the development stage in British Columbia, Canada.
"They are trying to integrate their business and they are targeting upstream, natural mining in particular," said Kenichiro Yoshida, a senior analyst at Nikko Research Center. 
"Trading and distribution margins are quite thin, but mining companies' profits are very high."
Other Japanese trading companies were also expanding, but Sumitomo was more aggressive, perhaps because it could take comfort in its large, captive clients. 
Sumitomo Electric Industries, for instance, is Japan's largest maker of electric wires and cables, and a member of the Sumitomo Group.
When asked if Sumitomo as a whole profited from Mr. Hamanaka's trading activities, Yoshinao Nemoto, a Sumitomo spokesman, said: "It may have produced profits. 
We cannot say if it increased because of Hamanaka. 
It may have, but we cannot tell you."
Instead, Mr. Nemoto provided a copy of a 1995 report by Brains, an industry newsletter, saying that Sumitomo was by far the most competitive Japanese company in the copper business, and was expanding aggressively. 
The report added that the overall "rise in copper prices had contributed greatly to an increase in sales in its network of copper businesses."
Revenues on Sumitomo's copper business were $11 million in the fiscal year ending in March, slightly less than for the corresponding period last year, and copper trading volume this year was $8.8 billion, also a small dip from last year.
Though this may suggest a less than distinguished performance for an influential trader like Mr. Hamanaka, trading volume surged 23 percent in the year ending March 1994 from the previous period, and was a significant 5 percent of the trading company's overall business, analysts said.
Copper traders and analysts said that Sumitomo had amassed large holdings of the physical copper -- it may have had as much as one million tons at one point, according to one Japanese rival trader.
Sumitomo stores vast quantities of copper in both its own and other warehouses in Singapore, California, Europe, India, Japan and elsewhere. 
With more warehouses spread around the world than other trading companies, Sumitomo can fill orders quickly, particularly with rapidly expanding demand for copper in Southeast Asia and China.
Japanese traders, however, said that Sumitomo might have initially achieved this stature at a price. 
It seemed to gain market share, they said, by shaving commissions and offering price quotations below the market level.
"They must have made a loss on the physical business to gain a big share," said another Japanese copper trader. 
He added about Mr. Hamanaka: "But the big share means he has big power in the market."
