text:
ï»¿
The first of China's leading Internet companies is set to go public in the United States later this week -- sort of.
The initial public offering of the company, Sina.com, will be the first of what are expected to be many new Nasdaq listings of China-based Internet content providers. 
But investors who buy the stock will not actually own a stake in China's most popular Internet portal. 
Instead, they will own a piece of the company's marginal Hong Kong, Taiwan and North American portals -- a fraction of its core business.
Sina.com, incorporated in the Cayman Islands, holds various licensing agreements with a Chinese company that owns the Chinese portal.
People in China's Internet industry are closely watching the offering, somewhat aghast that American investors may be willing to buy into a company gutted of content. 
Still, Sina.com's stock offering will determine whether other Chinese Internet companies take the plunge now or choose to wait until China's ever-shifting regulations change.
"I can't believe it will fly," a Chinese Internet entrepreneur said today at an industry party in Beijing.
Sina.com, founded by a 32-year-old Beijing University graduate, became the hottest Web site in China last year after it posted reports of the NATO bombing of China's Belgrade embassy within minutes of the official news media.
And Sina provided more information on the bombing than any other mainland source, relying heavily on foreign reports.
The company's main Chinese portal is linked to nine different "channels," Chinese-language Web sites that offer everything from news to online shopping for cellular phones, flowers, even food. 
The company's free and fast e-mail accounts and timely news updates have made it the most popular portal in China for nearly a year.
Investors in the initial public offering, however, will own none of that, because of regulations intended to allow Chinese Internet companies to raise capital on overseas stock markets while adhering to China's longstanding ban on foreign investment in the telecommunications and media industries. 
Those rules are supposed to change when China joins the World Trade Organization.
While the country has welcomed private foreign investment in the Internet, it remains fearful of allowing ownership of its new e-businesses slip overseas.
Earlier this year, Beijing-based AsiaInfo listed its shares on the Nasdaq, but that company provides technical services and software products, not Internet content.
Sina's staff quickly grew from a handful of people to more than 500 today in Zhongguancun, a section of Beijing akin to Silicon Valley. 
Investment bankers were soon offering the company bundles of cash, and it subsequently raised nearly $100 million.
The company's boldness won it fans, but not among China's conservative officials, who made it clear that Sina.com would not be given approval to list abroad unless the company toed Beijing's line.
To win regulators' favor, people familiar with the company say, Sina dropped news from all sources other than the state-run press and removed links to foreign media sites.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Catbird Seaton Great European Phone Deal Is in Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
As Mannesmann of Germany and the British company Vodafone Airtouch roll out the heavy artillery for their bitter takeover battle, there is already one undisputed victor: a Hong Kong tycoon who is watching Europe's great corporate war from the penthouse of a skyscraper half a world away.
He is Li Ka-shing, the billionaire developer and chairman of the Hong Kong conglomerate Hutchison Whampoa. 
With its deal to sell its British mobile-phone operation, Orange P.L.C., to Mannesmann, Mr. Li's company has become the largest single shareholder in the German company.
Mr. Li has already made an enormous profit because of the Orange-Mannesmann deal and could make more if Vodafone buys Mannesmann.
That would be the latest of many shrewd moves for Mr. Li, 71, who has amassed a $12 billion fortune since he came to this former British colony in the 1940's as a penniless refugee from mainland China.
As Vodafone seeks to entice Mannesmann's shareholders with its $127.7 billion hostile bid, analysts said the British company would have to win over Hutchison, which in addition to its 10.1 percent stake has a seat on Mannesmann's supervisory board. 
That will not be easy, since Mr. Li said on Tuesday that he would back Mannesmann's chief executive, Klaus Esser, in rebuffing Vodafone's advances.
Analysts and bankers noted, however, that Hutchison's loyalty stemmed at least partly from a legal obligation to hold its shares in Mannesmann for 18 months after the mobile-phone deal. 
Should Vodafone further sweeten its offer, Mannesmann would probably feel obliged to let Hutchison sell its shares.
"They've been incredibly lucky," said Peter Milliken, an analyst at DBS Securities here. 
"But Li Ka-shing isn't just a lucky guy. 
Some of it is foresight."
Mannesmann paid $14 billion in cash and stock to buy Hutchison's controlling stake in Orange -- a sky-high price that analysts said was driven by Mannesmann's urge to protect itself from a predatory Vodafone.
When Vodafone started its hostile bid for Mannesmann, the value of Hutchison's shares soared 25 percent. 
If Mannesmann accepted the current bid, Mr. Li would make more than a 40 percent return in barely a month.
Moreover, Vodafone has indicated that if it won control of Mannesmann, it would spin off Orange to the German company's existing shareholders. 
Although that move would be aimed at mollifying British regulators, it would also leave Hutchison with a stake in the same company it just sold.
"First they sold Orange at a huge premium," said an executive close to Hutchison who spoke on condition of anonymity. 
"Now they're getting a double-dip with the Vodafone bid for Mannesmann. 
If Vodafone were to spin off Orange, it would be a triple-dip."
Neither Mr. Li nor his lieutenants would comment beyond a statement on Tuesday in which Hutchison said it viewed its stake in Mannesmann as a long-term strategic investment. 
"Jointly with Orange, Mannesmann will be an outstanding company and better positioned than Vodafone for the future opportunities in the telecom sector," said Canning Fok, the managing director of Hutchison.
Analysts said that reaction was not surprising. 
If Vodafone took over Mannesmann, Hutchison's stake in the new company would be diluted to 4.5 percent. 
Though that might be enough to secure a board seat, Mr. Li would clearly not enjoy as much influence.
Hutchison cannot stand in the way of a takeover. 
Under Mannesmann's bylaws, no single shareholder exercises more than 5 percent of the vote. 
Mannesmann's fate will be determined more by Vodafone's next move -- it has declared it will not raise its bid -- than by the wishes of an Asian tycoon.
The beauty of Mr. Li's position, according to analysts, is that regardless of the outcome, Hutchison will be a player in the global mobile-phone business. 
In addition to its interest in Mannesmann, Hutchison controls cellular companies in Australia, India and Israel. 
The company is also active in wireless in the United States, through an investment in the VoiceStream Wireless Corporation.
In Hong Kong, a city where nobody leaves home without a cellular phone, Hutchison is the leading service provider, with 1.6 million subscribers. 
The company also competes with the dominant local phone company, Cable and Wireless HKT, in fixed-line telephone service.
Last week, Hutchison announced a $1.2 billion joint venture with Global Crossing Ltd., the operator of a worldwide fiber optic network, that will further expand its presence in its home market. 
The new venture, to be called Hutchison Global Crossing, will build a high-speed fiber optic voice and data network. 
Global Crossing will contribute $400 million in stock and $50 million in cash.
"It's really a classic Hutchison deal," said Tim Dattels, the head of investment banking in Asia for Goldman, Sachs & Company, which advised the company. 
"They've chosen their partners well."
Mr. Li took over Hutchison Whampoa in 1981, becoming the first Chinese businessman to control a traditionally British trading company in Hong Kong. 
The company's roots are in ports, and it now runs container ports in Hong Kong, mainland China, Indonesia, Britain and the Panama Canal. 
That last franchise recently landed Hutchison in a tempest in Washington. 
The Senate majority leader, Trent Lott, said the canal would fall under Chinese influence after the United States departs in December because Mr. Li had links to the Chinese Army.
United States officials have dismissed Senator Lott's claims, though nobody denies that Mr. Li has cultivated close ties to China's leaders. 
That could come in handy in the aftermath of a landmark trade deal between the United States and China. 
As part of the agreement, Beijing has pledged to open its telecommunications market to foreign companies. 
Few are better positioned than Hutchison Whampoa.
"That's the reason Global Crossing was willing to pay so much," Mr. Milliken said. 
"They were paying for Li's connections -- and not just telephone connections."

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_China Airlines Tries to Fix Its Reputation on Safety.txt
text:
ï»¿
For China Airlines, the 1990's were a recurring nightmare: three fiery crashes in six years that resulted in nearly 500 deaths. 
The only cold comfort for Taiwan's flagship carrier is that travelers seem to have developed shorter memories.
When a China Airlines' Airbus crashed near Taipei's airport in February 1998, killing 202 people, it scared away passengers for months and contributed to the airline's first net loss in 12 years. 
But when a China Airlines MD-11 flipped over and burned after landing during a typhoon in Hong Kong last August, killing three people, it depressed the airline's bookings for just two weeks.
"The total casualty rate was lower," said Sandy K. Y. Liu, the president of China Airlines, in an interview this week. 
"And the incident occurred during severe weather conditions. 
So, except for in Taiwan, a lot of people assumed that the weather caused the accident."
In the airline's home country, Mr. Liu acknowledged, many people immediately assumed that the pilots were to blame. 
That skepticism sums up the enormity of the task facing Mr. Liu, a 30-year veteran of China Airlines who is laboring to mend its reputation. 
While Taiwan travelers continue to fly China Airlines, they do so out of necessity and convenience -- not a sense of trust.
"I don't blame people for jumping to the conclusion that it must be China Airlines' fault," Mr. Liu, 51, said. 
"Our responsibility is to bring passengers from A to B and land there safely. 
We did not do that in Hong Kong."
China Airlines is not the only Asian carrier with a poor safety record. 
Korean Air and Garuda Indonesia both rank near the top of the list of major carriers involved in fatal crashes. 
But China Airlines has some unenviable distinctions: it is the only airline to have crashed two Airbus A300-600's, and it is the only carrier to have crashed twice in Hong Kong. 
In 1993, a China Airlines 747 overshot the runway at the old Kai Tak airport and landed in Victoria Harbor.
In some ways, the problems that plague China Airlines are typical of Asian companies generally. 
Founded by retired Taiwan air force officers in 1959, the airline is controlled by the China Aviation Development Foundation, a quasi-government organization. 
Analysts say those ties bind China Airlines, by preventing Mr. Liu from carrying out a much-needed top-to-bottom reorganization.
"The people who control those shares have connections to the pilots, so to some extent, the pilots dictate things at the airline," said Jim Eckes, a consultant at Indoswiss Aviation in Hong Kong. 
"As long as the management can't crack the pilot culture, they can't solve the bigger problems."
After the Taipei crash, the government ordered the aviation foundation to privatize the airline by selling its 71 percent stake. 
China Airlines seemed close to that goal early last year when it entered negotiations to sell an equity stake to Singapore Airlines. 
But the talks foundered after the two carriers could not agree on the size of the stake or on management control.
Last June, China Airlines made another push for the private sector. 
It hired Salomon Smith Barney to find a buyer for half the foundation's stake, or roughly 35 percent of the shares. 
But a self-imposed Dec. 
22 deadline passed without a deal. 
Mr. Liu declined to comment on the status of the search, except to say that the foundation was still determined to sell its holdings.
Analysts say the latest problem is that the airline's shares are trading well below the foundation's asking price. 
Mr. Liu noted that one of the foundation's missions was to "generate a lot of money" from the privatization, which it plans to use to nurture the aviation industry in Taiwan.
Some analysts contend that China Airlines will benefit from the delay. 
In addition to forgetful customers, the waning of the Asian economic crisis has revived traffic. 
"The longer the delay, the better it is, because their position can only improve," said Barry Grindrod, the publisher of Orient Aviation, a trade publication in Hong Kong. 
"Their financial projections are getting stronger."
But that assumes China Airlines will not relive the disasters of the last decade. 
Mr. Eckes and other experts said the airline was still overly reliant on former air force pilots, whose imperious style is poorly suited to the more collegial environment of a commercial airplane cockpit.
The Taipei accident, as well as a crash in Nagoya, Japan, in 1994 which killed 264 people, were both attributed to pilot error. 
China Airlines denies its pilots erred in the last Hong Kong crash, although the Hong Kong Civil Aviation Department said in a report in November that the wind speeds were above the recommended limits when the captain, who was Italian, decided to land.
Mr. Liu said China Airlines had instituted a rigorous retraining and recertification program. 
And he said the airline was recruiting expatriate pilots, as well as new college graduates, to complement its air force pilots.

Talks between South Korea and China on a project to develop passenger jets collapsed today.
An official at the South Korean Trade Ministry said the negotiations in Beijing, which opened on Monday, had broken down over differences on where to base final production.

text:
ï»¿
China Everbright Group, one of the nation's largest financial conglomerates, announced today that its chairman had resigned and been replaced by a deputy governor of the People's Bank of China.
The move, officially described as a normal transfer, appeared instead to be one of several personnel moves related to the shifting fortunes of Prime Minister Zhu Rongji, whose reform program has been under attack from conservative rivals in Beijing.
The departing chairman of China Everbright, Zhu Xiaohua, was one of China's most prominent executives, a relatively aggressive and ambitious financial operative in an environment that favors political caution and bureaucratic timidity.
Mr. Zhu, China Everbright's chairman since 1996, was widely reported to enjoy a close relationship with Prime Minister Zhu, who is no relation. 
The Prime Minister has been trying to spearhead sharp reform in China's lumbering financial sector, where state-run companies are plagued by mismanagement and bureaucratic politics.
Although China Everbright is considered one of the brighter stars in the collection of Hong Kong-based, China-owned financial companies, it is widely regarded as lacking the efficiency and flexibility of private competitors in Hong Kong.
China Everbright runs a wide range of businesses that extend from securities trading to banking to toll collection. 
It reports directly to China's State Council, or cabinet. 
It has three subsidiaries that are publicly listed in Hong Kong: China Everbright, China Everbright Technology and China Everbright International.
Like other state-run companies, China Everbright does not publicly report revenue or profit, and much of its other financial data are not disclosed.
China Everbright's commercial banking arm, Everbright Bank of China, had more than $10 billion in assets at the end of 1998.
Hong Kong newspapers reported rumors that Zhu Xiaohua was under investigation for his role in bad deals that had lost more than $200 million.
But in a field of state-owned financial companies where enormous losses are routinely written off, other, still unclear factors may also have been at play.
An investment banker at another Chinese company said Mr. Zhu's removal had more to do with Beijing politics than with China Everbright's balance sheet. 
A related move, the banker said, is the expected removal of Wang Qishan, deputy governor of Guangdong Province, who was sent by Prime Minister Zhu to sort out the financial mess left there by state-run companies, namely the Guangdong International Trust and Investment Corporation.
"We can't see what the whole picture is," the banker said. 
"But these moves are all related."
Prime Minister Zhu's aggressive reform program is said to have been sharply criticized by fellow Politburo members in Beijing, where the political atmosphere has become unusually tense and volatile. 
Leaders are currently confronted with crises over Taiwan, the spiritual movement Falun Gong, and strained United States-China relations, on top of a vulnerable economy and rising unemployment.
China Everbright's new chairman, Liu Mingkang, served for 11 years as a deputy governor of China's central bank.
Yet his background is as much in politics as finance. 
Before joining the People's Bank, Mr. Liu was a vice governor of Fujian province. 
He has an M.B.A. from London's City University.
At a news conference in Hong Kong, where Everbright is based, Mr. Liu said he would not change his predecessor's strategy of focusing on financial services businesses.
"The financial industry is our core business," Mr. Liu said. 
"That means commercial banking, including personal banking, institutional banking, corporate banking, and I am very happy to see that our commercial banking is getting stronger and stronger."
He denied that Mr. Zhu's removal was unusual in any way.
"As far as I'm concerned, this is part of normal operations, nothing more, nothing less," Mr. Liu said.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_China Grows Impatient With Its Ailing Banks.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government shutdown of a prominent state-run investment company, the Guangdong International Trust and Investment Corporation, shows that China may finally be getting tough with insolvent financial institutions.
Although debt problems plagued Guangdong International, the nation's second-largest trust and investment company behind the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, what surprised economists and bankers is that the Government decided to take decisive action against such a well-known institution.
China's official media reported that the central bank revoked the operating license of Guangdong International, also known as Gitic, on Tuesday because it could not repay its debts. 
The Bank of China, one of China's four policy-making banks, was ordered to take charge of repaying those liabilities.
The size of the debt was not made public. 
Like many Chinese companies, Guangdong International operated such a web of subsidiaries and shell companies that it is difficult for outsiders to calculate the true size of either its debts or assets.
In financial terms, the collapse was seen as relatively insignificant. 
Salomon Smith Barney analysts in Hong Kong estimated Guangdong International had assets of just $2.8 billion at the end of 1997, with nearly $1 billion in foreign debt. 
Domestic debt may have been far larger.
What is significant is that until now, it had been virtually inconceivable for Beijing to close a prestigious investment company like Guangdong International. 
In the past, state-run companies with good connections to the central Government have generally been able to rely on bailouts, often based on endless debt restructuring.
But Beijing's leaders have been alarmed at the crisis facing several Asian neighbors, which have been swamped by the same kind of financial overexposure that plagues many Chinese financial institutions.
Although China has so far been spared the worst of Asia's crisis, officials in Beijing have said they intend to make China's notoriously debt-ridden banks and investment companies more accountable. 
Economists estimate that Chinese banks have more than $200 billion in outstanding debt to failing state industries that are unlikely ever to repay it.
Yet without shareholder or market pressure to have a full accounting, many of China's banks indefinitely postpone any genuine inventory of their creditworthiness. 
That sort of endless rolling over of debt may now finally be changing.
A critical but partly hidden factor in the fate of Guangdong International has been a political revamping in Guangdong Province, beginning early this year. 
After enjoying breakneck development with skimpy regulation in the 1980's and early 1990's, Guangdong has recently come under greater scrutiny from the Prime Minister, Zhu Rongji.
Mr. Zhu traveled to Guangdong repeatedly this year to confront local officials about financial irregularities and helped Wang Qishan, a rising star in Beijing who headed the China Construction Bank, become deputy governor in charge of financial restructuring.
Guangdong International was set up in 1980 to manage investments on behalf of Guangdong Province, the fast-developing region that borders Hong Kong. 
Its investments included the Guangzhou-Shantou railway, power plants in Dongguan and the Shenzhen Science and Technology Park. 
It sold more than $400 million of international bonds.
In recent years, its heavy exposure to real estate in southern China went sour. 
Like other state-run investment and trust companies, it often relied less on creative or strategic planning than on local connections.
Now, Guangdong International's debt repayment has been suspended until January 1999 as Bank of China officials determine how to establish priorities for the debts.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_China Stews_A U.S. Trade Deal Falters.txt
text:
ï»¿
While China officially remains committed to joining the World Trade Organization, Chinese economists say that apparent divisions in the nation's leadership are likely to further stiffen Beijing's negotiating position and make agreement difficult to achieve in coming months.
With China experiencing a wave of nationalist politics after the NATO bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade on May 7, orthodox politicians, skeptical about the benefits of forcing open Chinese markets, as membership in the global trade group would require, seem to be gaining influence.
Prime Minister Zhu Rongji is widely considered China's strongest proponent of entry into the trade group, which sets the rules of global commerce. 
But Mr. Zhu has become vulnerable to accusations that he was giving too much away in the broad concessions he offered to American negotiators during his visit to the United States last month.
Foreign Trade Minister Shi Guangsheng said today that China had not changed its basic negotiating position. 
But he also re-emphasized that Beijing would join the trade organization on its own terms. 
"China will never enter the W.T.O. at the expense of its own basic interests," Mr. Shi said at a meeting with visiting Australian officials in Beijing.
An assistant United States trade representative, Robert Cassidy, had been scheduled to return to Beijing this week to resume talks, but his visit has been indefinitely delayed.
A Beijing economist with ties to the Government said the mood surrounding the trade talks had darkened and many economic changes were likely to be delayed while the leadership was preoccupied with a campaign to promote nationalism. 
"No one dares do or say anything until they see a direction from the center," the economist said. 
"It limits everyone's ability to work."
After President Clinton turned down a deal on Chinese membership in the trade group during Mr. Zhu's visit, Chinese and American negotiators looked to early June as a deadline to reach an agreement, when China's most-favored-nation trading status expires.
Reaching a deal by then would enable the Clinton Administration to advocate a single vote in Congress to give China permanent favorable trading status, as required under trade organization rules.
Without a deal, Congress would have to vote once to renew Beijing's most-favored-nation status, and then vote again on giving China that status permanently. 
With so many anti-China voices in Congress, made louder by recent accusations of nuclear spying, the Administration wants to avoid giving Congress two chances to oppose an agreement.
Yet reaching a deal before June now looks increasingly unlikely. 
Former Prime Minister Li Peng, now the chairman of the Chinese legislature, has been leading the ranks of old-line leaders in attacking the United States for aggression in Yugoslavia, charges that have no direct connection to the trade talks but that inevitably affect the flexibility of Chinese negotiators.
Over the weekend, Mr. Li argued that the bombing had enabled the Chinese people to see "the hypocrisy of the democracy and human rights advocated by the United States."
He denounced the Western view that student demonstrations in Beijing and other cities had been orchestrated by the leadership to gain better leverage in the trade negotiations.
United States officials have said that the final areas of disagreement with Beijing are over financial services. 
The Americans have sought full rights for foreign banks operating in China to do business in local and foreign currencies and to serve both Chinese and foreign customers.
Too many operating restrictions on American banks, insurers and other financial companies are discouraging them from doing business in China, American negotiators have said. 
In response, Chinese officials maintain that changing the rules to make them even for Chinese and foreign banks could be disastrous for China.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_China to Overhaul a Heavily Indebted State Company.txt
text:
ï»¿
Softening its tone toward foreign lenders, China announced a plan today to overhaul a debt-ridden state company, with the banks and the Government sharing the losses.
The company, Guangdong Enterprises, is staggering under $5.6 billion in debt and other liabilities. 
It stopped making loan payments in January, after its owner, Guangdong province's government, announced that it would overhaul operations with the help of Goldman, Sachs.
China's handling of Guangdong Enterprises is in stark contrast to its treatment of another troubled state company, Guangdong International Trust and Investment, known as Gitic. 
When Gitic capsized under $4.3 billion in debt last October, Beijing forced it into bankruptcy and told banks that they would lose most of their loans.
As the next-most-prominent corporate casualty, Guangdong Enterprises has been scrutinized by foreign banks as a test of how unforgiving the Government will be in cleaning up troubled state businesses.
"If this one went badly, it would have spelled trouble for creditors generally in China," said Gordon G. Chang, a bankruptcy lawyer in the Beijing office of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison.
Today, officials of Goldman, Sachs and of Guangdong outlined a plan for Guangdong Enterprises. 
It would recapitalize the company's main Hong Kong subsidiary by selling the subsidiary a profitable water business. 
The plan would also swap equity for a portion of the parent company's debt and would carve out $238 million of bad loans and place them in an asset management company.
In what amounts to a grand exercise in financial triage, the Chinese Government would revive the healthiest parts of Guangdong Enterprises while asking the banks to accept losses on the hopelessly sick parts.
"There should be a mutual sharing of loss," said Wang Qishan, the executive vice governor of Guangdong province, at a news conference after he presented the plan to several hundred creditors in Hong Kong.
While Guangdong Enterprises' creditors said in a statement that the plan was "not satisfactory on initial inspection," their relief seemed palpable. 
"It's definitely an O.K. place to start negotiating," said Ted Osborn, a partner at PricewaterhouseCoopers, which is advising the creditors. 
"The Guangdong government didn't have to give anything; these companies are bankrupt."
Mr. Osborn said the creditors would certainly negotiate on the finer points of the proposal, such as how to value the debt-for-equity swaps and the water plant that the Guangdong government would contribute to Guangdong Enterprises' publicly listed Hong Kong flagship, Guangdong Investments Ltd. 
But he added: "The Guangdong government has put down its marker. 
Now at least the banks know where they stand."
Goldman, Sachs, which has labored since January to make sense of Guangdong Enterprises' tangled finances, said that if the new stock issued to the creditors performed well, some of them could wind up with no losses over the long term.
"There is no forced loss for any of the creditors -- none," said Steven M. Shafran, a Goldman managing director in Hong Kong.
Mr. Shafran was particularly enthusiastic about China's contribution of the Dongshen Water Supply Company, which supplies 75 percent of Hong Kong's water and which he said was worth more than $2 billion.
Still, creditors are skeptical about Guangdong Enterprises, given that many of its assets are in sad shape and some former executives are suspected of corruption. 
One executive who advises the creditors estimated that the plan would result in 20 percent to 40 percent losses to the banks on their loans.
In the case of Gitic, the banks are likely to recover less than 20 percent of their loans. 
Mr. Wang said that if the Government had chosen to liquidate Guangdong Enterprises, its banks would have received a similarly paltry return.
As with Gitic, Guangdong Enterprises' creditors are a who's who of global institutions, including Sumitomo Bank, Citigroup and Deutsche Bank. 
Chinese, Japanese and French banks have greater exposure than American banks.
Although Gitic and Guangdong Enterprises bear similarities, there are crucial differences. 
Gitic is an investment trust company, while Guangdong Enterprises is a state-owned enterprise whose main subsidiary is a "red chip" company listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. 
The Chinese Prime Minister, Zhu Rongji, has expressed his distaste for investment trusts, which he contends are outmoded vehicles to raise capital.
Red chips, on the other hand, remain China's most dependable way to tap global capital markets. 
Mr. Wang said he took special care with Guangdong Enterprises because he did not want to throw Hong Kong's red-chip market into turmoil. 
Shares in Hong Kong eased today, as investors waited for the Guangdong Enterprises proposal to be announced, after having risen Monday as initial details of the plan leaked out.
"Regardless of the province," Mr. Wang said, "we feel we should make a contribution to the stabilityI of Hong Kong."
Mr. Wang, who was appointed last year by Prime Minister Zhu to rein in the freewheeling financial practices in Guangdong province, gave a freewheeling performance of his own today. 
By turns playful and scolding, he reiterated Mr. Zhu's campaign to reform China's economy and banks.
And he switched seamlessly between free-market evangelist and dutiful party functionary.
Asked whether China would suffer more corporate failures, Mr. Wang said, "The fundamental principle of a market economy is that the winners win and the losers lose."

text:

China appears to have toughened its stance in talks aimed at gaining entry to the World Trade Organization, making United States negotiators pay for President Clinton's decision earlier this month to delay a final deal.
In the latest turn in China's long and complex path toward membership in the group that makes the rules for global commerce, Chinese negotiators have accused American officials of making excessive demands.
"Some negotiators are reaching out for a yard after taking in an inch," Wu Yi, a State Councillor and senior trade official, said in Beijing. 
"They are demanding too high conditions that are impractical and unacceptable for China."
China also seems to be trying to use international leverage with European trade officials to put pressure on the United States to agree to a World Trade Organization deal more quickly.
Today, Chinese negotiators met for a third consecutive day in Beijing with negotiators from the European Union, in preparation for a visit by Sir Leon Brittan, the European trade commissioner, who is scheduled to arrive in Beijing on May 5 and is expected to announce an agreement that China should finally be allowed into the world trade body.
Two separate groups of negotiators met about tariffs and on trading services, the New China News Agency reported.
Long Yongtu, China's chief negotiator, was quoted by the agency as saying that China was prepared to make extensive efforts to push forward the negotiations, apparently appealing for international support to counter American demands in its trade talks with China.
Just before Prime Minister Zhu Rongji's trip to the United States early this month, China made a broad array of concessions aimed at overcoming United States opposition for Chinese entry to the trade body, which China has sought for 13 years.
China agreed to import more American beef, citrus products and wheat, and to allow more openness in the telecommunications, financial services and entertainment fields. 
President Clinton rejected a proposed agreement, though, apparently judging the anti-China mood in Washington to be too strong to accept an accord.
After vigorous protests from United States business leaders that a good deal had been within reach, the Clinton Administration authorized a fresh round of negotiations aimed at preserving the momentum that had been achieved.
With the Americans on the defensive for what is widely seen to have been a lost opportunity during Mr. Zhu's visit, Chinese negotiators seem to want to take advantage of a suddenly strengthened negotiating position.
American officials now say that their latest round of talks with China, held last weekend, focused on financial services, an area where they say the most obstacles remain. 
They have demanded full rights for foreign banks operating in China to conduct business in local and foreign currencies and to serve both local and foreign customers.
The American negotiators say that China is insisting on too many restrictions on United States banks, insurers and other financial companies that want to enter the country. 
In response, Chinese officials argue that equalizing market access for Chinese and foreign banks could be disastrous for domestic banks.
"Excessive growth of nonbank financial institutions could lead to a financial crisis," The China Economic Times reported, quoting a position paper from the State Development and Planning Commission. 
"Foreign-invested firms, supported by their banks, could easily take over sectors of the market and monopolize industries."Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_China Turns Blind Eye to Pirated Disks.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the downtown area of almost every major Chinese city, the signs are now prominently displayed on store windows: open advertisements for pirated video compact disks of Hollywood movies that sell for less than $2 each.
In recent months, even new releases have become available all over China, as copyright pirates distribute their wares unchecked. 
"Titanic," as popular here as everywhere else, has been sold in Shanghai since late November, a month before its theatrical release in the United States.
After three years of cat-and-mouse enforcement of anti-piracy regulations, Chinese authorities have essentially given up efforts to prevent the sale of illegally copied videodisks, a new technology that has swept this country with remarkable speed.
The open sale of pirated movies signals a failure of the intellectual property rights agreement that China reached with the United States in 1995, pledging vigorous enforcement. 
Yet American officials, apparently slow to pick up on the change, have let the protection of intellectual property drift off their list of priorities as they prepare for President Clinton's visit to China in June.
Chinese authorities concede that enforcement has fallen off, but say there is little they can do about it, and American officials, when asked, acknowledge that they did not even know the problem had become so serious. 
The United States-China agreement remains in force on paper, though the effectiveness of other joint pacts could suffer if this one remains so badly neglected.
Paradoxically, industry executives say that the principal cause of the current boom in video compact disks stems from China's success in cracking down on copyright piracy a year ago, chasing pirates into Macau, the tiny Portuguese colony near Hong Kong. 
There is no copyright law in Macao, where it is easy to mass-produce movies, some copied from master tapes and others simply videotaped with a hand-held recorder in a screening room.
Roughly 500,000 pirated disks are now smuggled into China from Macao each day, estimates Cheng Ching-ming, who monitors piracy in China for the International Federation of Phonographic Industries, an organization representing the world's major music companies.
"The situation is out of control," Mr. Cheng said. 
"For movies, there has been a complete breakdown in enforcement. 
The authorities seem to have lost all interest in trying to prevent sales."
Mr. Cheng said China's customs officials pose little threat to copyright pirates, who easily bribed or sneaked past them. 
In Macao, where piracy is believed to be controlled by organized crime, no effort is being made to quell the booming industry.
Although industry executives estimate that American businesses lose more than $2 billion a year to piracy in China, it is impossible to accurately estimate how many Chinese customers would actually purchase nonpirated movies or music at a higher, legal price.
Yet the fast growth of pirated movies on such a vast scale is a reminder of the risks and unpredictable nature of business operations in China, where law enforcement remains highly political and combating wrongdoing requires both diplomatic pressure and creative solutions.
Piracy of musical compact disks is now not as rampant as that of movies, for instance, in part because Mr. Cheng's organization aggressively pursues violators in Chinese courts and in private negotiations, while the international film industry has been relatively passive.
Chinese authorities, while still officially committed to protecting copyrights, seem resigned to accepting piracy as a fact of life. 
Arguing that it makes little sense to go after retailers when producers of pirated movies are the real culprits, officials say there is now little they can do.
"We used to be able to locate the production, but now we can't," said Shen Wenping, a senior official at Shanghai's Industrial and Commercial Administration, responsible for anti-piracy efforts here. 
"It's very hard to control."
Joe Papovich, assistant United States trade representative in Washington, said he was unaware of the wide availability of pirated movies in China, but insisted that fighting piracy in China remained a long-term goal. 
He added that he knew that the center of production had moved to Macao and, to a lesser extent, to Hong Kong.
"We're trying to make contact with someone in Macao about this," Mr. Papovich said. 
"We're banging hard on Hong Kong."
The United States trade representative office, he said, depends on industry sources for information, and the Motion Picture Association, which is supposed to track movie piracy on behalf of Hollywood's major studios, has not made any complaints about it.
Michael Connors, the Motion Picture Association's chief representative in Asia, said he had not complained because he was unaware that the availability of pirated films had become so open. 
The Motion Picture Association, Mr. Connors said, has recently focused its efforts on helping Chinese customs officials detect smugglers, even though recent seizures of millions of disks represent a small fraction of what is smuggled into China each month.
"We don't have any complaints," said Mr. Connors, who is based in Singapore but spoke from Beijing, which he visits regularly. 
The Motion Picture Association says that pirated movies are a problem throughout the world and it recently set up a team of investigators in New York City to crack down on the problem there.
The boom in video compact disks, or VCD's, has transformed China's electronics industry with remarkable speed, shifting to embrace a technology that remains largely unknown to consumers in the United States. 
While VCD's were introduced at trade shows several years ago, they have not caught on, and appear likely to be bypassed by another format, digital videodisks, known as DVD's.
Video compact disks, the same size as music compact disks, typically contain up to 70 minutes of a movie on each disk, using two disks for a Hollywood feature. 
DVD's can capture far more information, covering more than one entire film per disk. 
In China, video cassettes are rapidly being replaced in the typical urban home by a video compact disk player, even faster than CD players replaced cassettes in the United States, both because it is a superior technology and because pirated movies are widely available at such a low price.
The boom in pirated movies also supports a home-grown industry of video compact disk makers, already so popular that domestic producers are expected to manufacture 50 million VCD players this year, up from about 30 million in 1997.
Although legitimate VCD's are sold in Chinese department stores for $5 to 10 each, smaller stores openly sell pirated movies for $2 or less in almost every Chinese city outside Beijing, Mr. Cheng said. 
His view is borne out by random visits to cities in northern and southern China.
On Nanchang Road in downtown Shanghai, a store called the Music Box has a sign on its window advertising VCD's for under $2, a price that store retailers readily acknowledge can only mean they were copied illegally.
"Of course they're pirated," said a middle-aged proprietor behind the counter at the Music Box, "Otherwise how could we sell them so cheap?"
The proprietor, who declined to give her name, said she used to keep pirated VCD's under the counter, taking them out only when a customer asked. 
But since last autumn, she said, Shanghai's copyright police had stopped coming around to check, so she has felt no fear.
"There's nothing wrong with selling pirated VCD's," she said. 
"My son loves watching them."
"Titanic" has been one of the best- selling VCD's at the Music Box, long before it is available for home viewing in the United States, and it is anyone's guess if "Titanic" will remain as popular after it appears in movie theaters in China on April 1.
When the United States trade representative, Charlene Barshefsky, signed a landmark intellectual property rights agreement with China in 1995, both sides promised to enforce anti-piracy provisions strictly with regular progress reports.
Yet trade talks between the United States and China have inevitably been an extension of diplomatic politics. 
When United States-China relations were strained in 1996, the Clinton Administration wanted to appear tough on China, and copyright piracy was an obvious lever to pull.
This year, as President Clinton prepares to come to China for a summit meeting in June, pressuring China on trade disputes has receded as a political priority, as has enforcing the intellectual property rights agreement. 
Mr. Papovich, the assistant trade representative, maintains that long after President Clinton departs, anti-piracy efforts will continue.
Yet without constant pressure, lawyers and industry executives agree, Chinese authorities are unlikely to exert much effort.
Only under the threat of billions of dollars of trade sanctions did Chinese officials begin to take the protection of intellectual property rights seriously, even though Chinese producers suffer from widespread piracy as much as Americans do.
Last year, local authorities in Guangdong, the southern province that had become a center of illegal copying, finally got tough on copyright pirates, closing down dozens of underground producers, as well as legal producers who were pirating movies and music during off hours.
Ever resourceful, pirates simply moved their operations across the border to Macao and Hong Kong.
Xu Guoji, a senior official in Shanghai's Industrial and Commercial Administration, said that Chinese authorities had been overwhelmed by the pirates' relentless efforts to take advantage of China's enormous market.
"The profits are so great, they will take any risk," Mr. Xu said. 
"They're like drug dealers. 
It is very difficult to arrange a crackdown. 
You have to coordinate all these different departments, the copyright publication department, the police, the Industrial and Commercial Administration.
"We take copyright violations very seriously," he went on. 
"But when it comes to copying a disk, most Chinese people don't see what's wrong."

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_China Unicom Shares Jump Nearly 9_.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a sign that China is again drawing the ardor of foreign investors, shares in the country's second-largest telephone company soared nearly 9 percent on the first day of trading here, even as the rest of the Hong Kong market slumped.
Shares of China Unicom Ltd. rose 8.9 percent, to 16.80 Hong Kong dollars, or $2.16. 
That followed a 12 percent jump on Wednesday in the company's first day of trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most heavily traded stock.
China Unicom's performance did not surprise analysts, who had forecast a sparkling debut since the company expanded the size of its offering to nearly $5 billion last week. 
Indeed, executives close to China Unicom seemed mildly disappointed that the first-day gain here did not match that in New York.
Given the dowdy reputation that China Unicom once had, however, the company has made a remarkable transformation. 
Its stock offering was the largest ever in Asia, outside Japan, eclipsing the 1997 offering of China Telecom.
Part of the success reflects persistent marketing by Unicom's executives and investment bankers. 
Even more goes to China's improved image since it signed deals with the United States and Europe to enter the World Trade Organization, and won a crucial trade vote in the United States House of Representatives.
"People who follow this company know it from the bottom up," said Duncan Clark, a partner in BDA China Ltd., a consulting firm in Beijing. 
"But investors view it from the top down. 
They think, 'Gee, another cellular operator in the world's largest market, which is about to enter the W.T.O.'
"
China Unicom's success augurs well for other Chinese state-owned companies, which hope to enter the stock market later this year. 
The nation's second-largest oil company, the China Petrochemical Corporation, plans to sell up to $5 billion in shares. 
Its prospects have been brightened by a 40 percent rise in the shares of its rival, Petrochina Ltd., which went public in April.
The improved prospects extend to smaller companies. 
Two Internet start-ups, Netease and Sohu.com, are planning initial public offerings later this year, after delays in the face of a hostile market and skepticism about Chinese ventures.
Still, as in previous periods of euphoria over China stocks, some analysts are urging caution. 
Investors bought into the first wave of Chinese companies, known as red chips, in the mid-1990's, only to find out that many were poorly managed and cobbled together with shoddy assets.
Unlike the red chips, China Unicom is in a single line of business, with cellular and paging franchises that have a measurable value. 
The company also has indisputable growth prospects. 
China's cellular market has more than tripled since 1997, to 43.2 million subscribers. 
With only 4.2 million customers -- and franchises that cover 578 million people -- Unicom's horizon is virtually limitless.
For all that, the company's future hinges on its treatment by the Chinese government. 
Beijing granted Unicom several assets -- including the nation's largest paging company -- to dress it up for the stock offering. 
But it must still compete against China Mobile, which was spun off from the state telephone monopoly. 
China Mobile is much larger and has stronger political connections.
"Right now, people are buying Unicom because it is in favor with the government," said Douglas Hansen-Luke, the chief executive of Asia Strategic, a research firm here. 
"But that could change. 
It's a very dangerous reason to buy equities."
In the short term, analysts said investors would probably profit by owning one of only two major Chinese phone companies. 
Mr. Clark said that having taken the first steps toward a more competitive phone market in 1999, the Chinese government was unlikely to shake things up further this year.
But he said that Beijing would probably issue the next generation of mobile-phone licenses in 2001. 
There are several companies lining up. 
One is China Netcom, a carrier owned by several state ministries and backed by a son of China's president, Jiang Zemin. 
Another is China Telecom, the former parent of China Mobile, which owns the nation's dominant fixed-line network.
Under the terms of its agreement to enter the W.T.O., China will also allow foreigners to own 49 percent of telecommunications companies within four years. 
That opens the door to well-financed competitors like AT&T, the NTT Corporation of Japan and Deutsche Telekom.
Mr. Hansen-Luke said investors in China Unicom could reap a windfall if foreign companies chose to acquire stakes in domestic Chinese operators rather than build their own networks. 
But Unicom's track record in alliances is dismal: it spent several years and $1.6 billion unraveling a series of partnerships with foreign companies that the Chinese government declared illegal.
The more basic question is whether China Unicom -- with untested management, uncertain ties in Beijing and an underdog position -- can compete in China's rapidly changing market. 
"Even an idiot can make money in a managed duopoly," Mr. Clark said. 
"But duopolies don't leave you in much of a position to compete when the market opens."

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Chinese Raise Interest Rates on Dollar Deposits.txt
text:
ï»¿
China raised interest rates today on United States dollar deposits in an effort to stem a flow of hard currency out of the country that has come as international banks cut credit lines to Chinese borrowers.
The Bank of China, acting on orders of the central bank, raised the rate on one-year dollar deposits in Beijing to 4.66 percent from 3.75 percent. 
It also increased one-year rates for deposits denominated in the Hong Kong dollar -- which is linked to the American currency -- to 5.25 percent from 5 percent.
The rate increases "will encourage repatriation of hard-currency earnings by Chinese exporters," said Fred Hu, executive director of Asian Economic Research at Goldman, Sachs in Hong Kong. 
He called the increase a "correction" that brought Chinese bank rates more in line with international rates.
Other Chinese banks typically follow the lead of the Bank of China, a large commercial bank here. 
The new rates will vary among Chinese cities and banks.
Despite the higher rates paid on deposits of dollars, local currency rates "still have room to go lower," Mr. Hu said.
Seeking to rekindle economic growth, and to lower the interest payments that state-owned companies must make, China has cut interest rates paid on deposits of the local currency, the yuan, five times since November 1996. 
The economy is projected to grow 7 percent this year; although that is much faster than the growth expected in other Asian countries, it would be the slowest expansion in China since 1990.
Chinese banks currently pay 3.78 percent on one-year yuan deposits.
In 1997, China's foreign-exchange reserves rose by an average of $3 billion a month. 
But last year, despite increases in the trade surplus and in foreign investment, exchange reserves rose about $400 million a month.
The concern over currency reserves comes as foreign banks have instituted a near-freeze on new loans to Chinese companies. 
The foreign banks curtailed lending after the collapse in October of the nation's second-biggest trust company. 
Many of them are also demanding early repayment of loans to minimize further losses if more Chinese companies fail, bankers say.
Still, the $5 billion gain in reserves last year brought China's total to $144.96 billion at the end of 1998, second only to Japan's.
Today's interest-rate increase will narrow the gap between Chinese and foreign rates. 
The Bank of China's rate of 4.66 percent for one-year dollar deposits in Beijing is below the average of 5.23 percent offered by banks in the United States. 
The 5.25 percent rate offered for Hong Kong dollars is still below the 7 percent that Hong Kong banks are paying in Hong Kong.
Still, the increases may prove to be an incentive for Chinese exporters to repatriate some of their foreign funds. 
Exporters are permitted to retain 15 percent of their foreign-currency earnings, much of which is believed to remain outside China.

Hundreds of thousands of Chinese, many with little or no experience trading stocks, have recently rushed to buy shares, hoping to cash in as prices reached dizzying heights.

"The present overheated state of China's share markets makes us think of the stock crash in America in 1929," the statement said. 
"Chinese shareholders should draw lessons from stock crashes that have happened repeatedly worldwide."
The announcement reflected official concern about the markets as a potential source of popular unrest. 
Set up in the early 1990's to draw funds into ailing state enterprises, the markets are looked at suspiciously by Communist Party hard-liners.
The number of stock investors has more than doubled this year, to more than 21 million, with 8 million new trading accounts opened in the last few months, and one major Chinese stock index has more than tripled.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Christmas Trimmings Brighten a New Market.txt
text:
ï»¿
Zhang Guoyang is packing up his six-foot Santa Claus samples today, but come March he'll be taking orders again for plastic reindeer, flocked Christmas trees and Styrofoam snowmen.
Sales of Mr. Zhang's Christmas kitsch are growing by about 50 percent a year, and the volume he ships is growing even faster because prices are falling. 
About half of his products go to the United States, but his fastest-expanding market is right here at home, where hotels, restaurants and shops bought nearly $50 million worth of Christmas decorations this year. 
That's a lot of tinsel.
Christmas has been co-opted by the Communists as good for stimulating business and is already a bigger deal than New Year's Eve in China's cities. 
Thousands of vaguely Asiatic Santa statues stand guard across China in November through December. 
And millions of paper Santa-head cutouts adorn shop windows, his face beet red, in China's traditional celebratory color.
That, despite the fact that few Chinese have any idea who the "old foreigner" is, or what Christmas is all about.
"It's the foreigners' New Year," Jiang Hui, a 20-year-old waitress at a small Shanghai restaurant festooned with Christmas decorations, said a few days ago. 
She compared it with the Chinese lunar New Year celebration that, for now, still eclipses Christmas as China's most important holiday.
Eyeing the red-cloaked effigy standing on the sidewalk outside the restaurant, she put her hands together in a gesture of prayer and suggested uncertainly that Santa Claus "makes wishes come true."
Even Mr. Zhang, a Santa expert to the Chinese who visit his crammed showroom, laughed nervously when asked who the rotund bearded mannequins represent. 
"He's a character in the story about Jesus, that's all I know," he replied.
The spread of Christmas in China has less to do with the growth of Christianity in this officially atheist country than it does with the growth of foreign joint-venture hotels. 
When foreign hotels began opening here 20 years ago, their annual Christmas decorations were hugely popular among locals.
Soon, Chinese hotels were putting up decorations of their own to pull in business, and before long restaurants were offering Christmas Eve banquets to state-owned companies. 
They readily subscribed, using the events as novel year-end perks for their employees.
Mr. Zhang was working for a trading company at the time, importing Christmas decorations from America and selling them to hotels. 
Most of the decorations were made in China, so bringing them back added an expensive round trip to their cost.
He quit the trading company eight years ago and started his own business to make and sell Christmas decorations in China. 
Today, his company is one of the top three domestic Christmas trimming suppliers in the country, having sold more than $1 million worth of synthetic trees, tinsel and other Yuletide items this year.
Like the other domestic suppliers, he copies American designs or has factories fashion items based on his specifications -- often to strange effect. 
The country is populated at this time of year with his and other vendors' fiberglass interpretations of Santa, some with odd pear-shaped bodies or maniacal eyes that look plain freakish to Westerners.
The decorations often overlap with more traditional Chinese ornamentation. 
At the restaurant where Ms. Jiang works, a plastic, tinseled Christmas tree stands beside a gaudy, red-lit shrine to the Chinese God of Fortune. 
The Saint Nick standing outside looks like Ronald McDonald in a Santa suit.
Year by year the Santas and associated paraphernalia make their way to increasingly remote places. 
Mr. Zhang has shipped his oversized Santas to every Chinese province except Tibet and Qinghai. 
Even the Muslims of far western Xinjiang province now have dozens of Chinese Santa Clauses in their midst.
He still exports decorations to the United States, but he said the future is here in China. 
Competition from other low-cost manufacturing countries like Pakistan and the Philippines has cut the profit margin on exports to less than what he makes selling decorations at home.
For the next month, Mr. Zhang will be busy shipping beanie-topped fiberglass boys and golden Styrofoam coins and fish for the Chinese New Year at the end of January. 
Then he'll turn his attention to designing next year's Christmas novelties and wait for the Noel orders to start rolling in.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Hong Kong Bounces Back, But Faces New Challenges.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a report that made the Asian crisis seem like a distant memory, Hong Kong said today that its economy grew 4.5 percent in the third quarter of this year. 
The government also upgraded its forecast of growth for the full year to 1.8 percent from 0.5 percent.
The numbers, which were well above estimates, attest to Hong Kong's remarkable recovery from its worst recession since World War II. 
Like other Asian economies, Hong Kong has shrugged off the calamitous events of two years ago and is regaining its strength far faster than analysts had predicted.
"Hong Kong is poised for a dramatic rebound," said Victor Fung, the chairman of the Hong Kong Trade Development Council. 
"The conditions were there, but we needed a strong confirmation and a boost to confidence. 
We've now had a whole series of such events."
In addition to the new data, Hong Kong has been buoyed in recent weeks by the Walt Disney Company's announcement that it would build a theme park here, by the successful debut of a government-linked investment fund, and by the landmark trade deal between the United States and China.
That last milestone, however, could prove to be a distinctly mixed blessing. 
As China opens up its economy in an effort to enter the World Trade Organization, analysts said, this former British colony could lose its prized role as the middleman between China and the outside world.
Nor is that the only cloud looming over Hong Kong. 
Today's numbers also show that the territory is caught in a deflationary spiral unique among the recovering economies of Asia. 
The consumer price index declined 3.9 percent in the first 10 months of 1999, and the government increased its projection of the full-year decline in the index to 4 percent from an earlier forecast of 3.5 percent.
Prices of everything from office space and imported wine to designer clothes and cars are plunging here. 
Although people are spending more in stores -- retail sales rose 2 percent in the third quarter -- they are lured by deep discounts. 
The number of tourists visiting Hong Kong is up 11 percent so far this year, but they are spending much less per person, economists said.
Much of this deflation is viewed as necessary. 
Hong Kong's prices were among the highest in the world, and made the territory a forbidding place to do business. 
But the falling prices are cutting profits at local companies, a trend that discourages them from resuming investment. 
"This is what I call a profitless recovery," said Dong Tao, an economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in Hong Kong.
Mr. Tao said the recovery would remain tenuous as long as companies did not have the confidence to take out fresh loans and begin spending. 
Also, even though commercial rents have fallen by more than 40 percent, Hong Kong is still more expensive than New York or London, he said.
Ian K. Perkin, the chief economist of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce, said the government had masked the effect of weak corporate investment by starting several costly projects, including the $3.6 billion Disneyland, which will be built largely with public money.
"We have to persuade domestic companies to begin investing again -- and real investments, not just the stock market," Mr. Perkin said. 
"I don't know how we do that."
The new trade agreement between the United States and China is a more long-term challenge for Hong Kong. 
The government's economist, K. Y. Tang, said that it was premature to estimate what impact the deal would have on economic output. 
"In general terms, I agree with those who say that it must be a very positive development for both the mainland and Hong Kong," he said.
Mr. Fung, of the Hong Kong Trade Development Council, and others contend that Hong Kong will benefit from the agreement because it will generate vast new trading opportunities for China. 
As the world's largest container port and the main clearinghouse for Chinese exports, Hong Kong will get a share of that increased traffic.
But a growing number of experts are questioning whether Hong Kong will miss out on most of the new wealth. 
As China opens its markets to foreign companies and products, American and other foreign companies could start dealing directly with the mainland Chinese.
"Hong Kong has been very successful in exploiting the gray areas of doing business in China," said Jason Felton, the chairman of the American Chamber of Commerce here. 
"But the W.T.O. is going to force the Chinese to be more transparent. 
Hong Kong companies will lose that niche, and they are clearly worried about it."
Mr. Fung said the trade agreement would encourage hundreds of small and midsize American companies to try to crack the China market. 
Lacking the resources or connections of major corporations, these companies would need the advice of people in Hong Kong, he said.
"If you're talking about the Fortune 100, it's probably true that these companies will put increased emphasis on dealing directly with China," he said. 
"What I think we'll get is a rush of medium-size multinationals, who have heretofore not dealt with China."
Mr. Fung acknowledged that Hong Kong would be forced to change. 
But he predicted that the territory would remake itself -- much as it did in 1979, when Deng Xiaoping opened the Chinese economy. 
At that time, Hong Kong was a center for low-cost manufacturing. 
But companies here recognized that China would usurp that role, so they moved their factories to neighboring Guangdong Province.
Now, Mr. Fung said, Hong Kong needs to retool its economy to provide information-age services to the growing Chinese market. 
The territory has become a hothouse for Internet companies that are focusing on the mainland. 
On Thursday, in an effort to create a Nasdaq exchange for Asia, the Hong Kong Stock Exchange opened a second board for technology-related stocks.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Hong Kong Is Debating Its Land Policy, a Vestige of Colonial Rule.txt
text:
ï»¿
With a solemn raising of the Chinese flag and the dulcet tones of Hong Kong schoolchildren singing the Chinese national anthem, this former British colony observed the third anniversary of its reversion to Chinese sovereignty this morning.
Hong Kong may seem more like China with each passing year, but it is still wrestling with the legacy of 156 years of colonial rule. 
Last week, this prosperous city was treated to the spectacle of 2,000 well-dressed homeowners taking to the streets to protest a plunge in property prices.
Brandishing signs with such unproletarian messages as "Negative Equity Is Eroding Our Society," the crowd demanded that the government prop up the real estate market. 
Some may have poked fun, but the rally has started a genuine debate about one of Hong Kong's most durable colonial-era practices.
Property prices here are effectively set by the government through a system of land auctions that dates from the time when the British Crown owned all the land in Hong Kong and parceled it out through 99-year leases. 
That arrangement worked nicely as long as asset values in Asia rose year after year.
In recent years, though, residential property prices have dropped 50 percent -- a lingering effect of the Asian financial crisis. 
Unlike other parts of Asia, in Hong Kong the real estate market shows little sign of recovery. 
And the government, as the regulator of prices, is being blamed.
"There are a lot of middle-class people who are under financial strain, and they're angry," said David Dodwell, the author of a book, "The Hong Kong Advantage," about the local economy. 
"A lot of them paid very high prices for apartments because they assumed the price would continue to go up."
One of those people is Thomas Lo, the sales director of a health care company here. 
Mr. Lo bought his two-bedroom apartment in April 1997, near the peak of the market, for $610,000. 
Two months later, on the eve of Hong Kong's handover to China, a real estate agent offered him $650,000. 
Mr. Lo decided to hold on to it. 
Today, he thinks the apartment is worth no more than $320,000.
"With my kind of income, I should be able to live a comfortable, relaxed life," Mr. Lo said. 
"But now I'm looking at buying a used car. 
Before, I would always buy the latest model of a car."
Mr. Lo, 38, said he did not feel sorry for himself. 
He can still afford to make his mortgage payments. 
But he said he could not imagine selling the apartment at a big loss. 
So, rather than trading up to a bigger place in a few years, he fears he will be stuck in this one until retirement.
Peter Churchouse, a property analyst at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, estimates that 20 percent of Hong Kong residents are in Mr. Lo's situation -- that is, the current market value of their apartments is less than the amount they still owe on their mortgages.
But far more people have suffered significant losses of wealth, which has led to bitterness toward Hong Kong's postcolonial government. 
The organizers of the homeowners' rally, the pro-government Liberal Party, were nonplused when demonstrators shouted "Down with Tung," a reference to the city's chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, who was appointed by Beijing.
The collapse in property prices is also rippling through the economy in the form of weak consumer spending. 
Although Hong Kong is enjoying a robust economic recovery, it is driven largely by exports. 
A decline in export markets, particularly the United States, could derail the recovery.
"There is a cliff here," said Nicholas Brooke, chairman of Brooke International, a real estate agency. 
"There is the potential to fall off that cliff, either by inactivity or intervention."
Hong Kong's land policy has also widened the gap between rich and poor. 
Because the government doles out undeveloped land sparingly, it commands high premiums. 
Private developers recoup their huge investments by charging astronomical rents. 
More than 70 percent of residents cannot afford to own homes.
About half of Hong Kong's seven million people live in public housing. 
Twenty-five percent buy private housing subsidized by the government. 
With salaries frozen in the wake of the Asian crisis, these middle-income people have little hope of moving up to better apartments.
"As Hong Kong becomes gradually more democratic, the divisions between the rich and poor are no longer tenable," Mr. Dodwell said.
He and other experts say Hong Kong needs to overhaul its land policy. 
During the Asian crisis, the government suspended land sales to stabilize prices. 
In mid-June, under pressure from property tycoons, it took a more modest step -- pulling off the market 16,000 subsidized apartments it had planned to sell.
A few commentators have called on Hong Kong to get out of the property business. 
They say that as long as the government controls the land, the territory will be doomed to cycles of boom and bust. 
But even these advocates concede that it would be extraordinarily difficult to unravel a system so deeply rooted in Hong Kong's colonial past.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_In Rebound From Weak Year, Chinese Stocks Are Surging.txt
text:
ï»¿
Shares in Chinese companies have been surging on world markets since the year began, a marked contrast to their weakness in 1995. 
While analysts and fund managers say that some of the stocks are likely to maintain their gains, they warn that other issues have been merely pulled up in the excitement and could fall sharply if corporate earnings weaken.
Lifted by an improving Chinese economy, an appetite among American investors and strength among Asian stocks over all, Chinese share prices rose sharply this week on the New York Stock Exchange, in Hong Kong and on China's two stock exchanges. 
Because the shares fell sharply last year, investors are buying them at bargain prices.
"China has engineered a very good economic landing, and conditions will improve this year," said Ean Wah Chin, a Singapore-based managing director at Morgan Stanley Group Inc., which manages $4 billion in Asian equities outside of Japan. 
Fund managers in the United States, flush with cash from investors betting that American stocks may run out of steam, are looking for inexpensive stocks in Asia, she said.
But Simon Lee, manager of the $8.8 million China Fund at Sun Hung Kai Fund Management, was cautious. 
"The consolidation should happen any time now," he said. 
"Share prices have been going up 50 percent and 60 percent and no one can explain it."
Mr. Lee said that low trading volumes in some of the stocks suggested that investors with large holdings were trying to manipulate prices to feed the frenzy.
Chinese stocks have drawn attention in the United States this week. 
On Thursday, for example, five of the eight leading percentage gainers on the New York Stock Exchange were Chinese companies. 
The issues ended the week with strong gains. 
Among them, Brilliance China Automotive Holding closed today at $7.25, up 87 percent from its closing price at the end of 1995, and China Tire Holding closed at $8, up 47 percent.
Overseas, the index of stocks in Chinese state-owned companies that trade in Hong Kong rose 2 percent, bringing its gain for the week to nearly 19 percent. 
Last year, the index fell 29 percent, in contrast to a gain of 23 percent in the Hang Seng Index, which tracks the stocks of major Hong Kong companies.
In trading in China today, B shares, which are shares in Chinese companies that foreigners can buy, rose 1.8 percent on Shenzhen's stock exchange but fell nine-tenths of 1 percent on Shanghai's exchange. 
So far this year, B shares are up 7 percent in Shanghai and 1.2 percent in Shenzhen.
Through the close of Hong Kong trading today, the CLSA China World Index, which tracks leading Chinese companies listed on world exchanges, was up 13 percent for the week. 
It had fallen 11 percent during the last two months of 1995.
One reason for the strength in share prices is the improving state of the Chinese economy. 
The Government announced in Beijing today that economic growth slowed slightly last year but still remained above the official target. 
The Government has been trying to hold down growth to restrain inflation, which did show a sharp slowdown last year.
Another factor aiding stocks is an absence of changes in Chinese taxes that would hurt corporate earnings. 
There had been speculation that such changes were near, but the Beijing Government, which usually announces any tax changes on Jan. 
1, did not disclose any revisions as the year began.
"If there were any more tax reforms, they would have come out by now," said Sonja Jong, assistant director at Mees Pierson Capital Management, which has $1 billion invested in Asian equities. 
"People think it's safe to get in, especially at these low levels."
The improvements in China's economy have come at a cost, however. 
As part of its efforts to fight inflation, the Government restrained credit last year, making it difficult for companies to finance operations and expansions.
As a result, analysts expect some companies to report 1995 earnings that were weaker than had been expected. 
The analysts said they did not expect earnings to improve until this year's second half. 
Corporate reports for 1995 are due in April.
"Some of the buying was indiscriminate," Graham Muirhead, director of HSBC Asset Management, said about this week's activity. 
"There is an improved economic environment, but slower economic growth means severe problems for companies."
HSBC oversees $200 million in specialized China investment funds.
The earnings reports may not tell the whole story. 
Many state-run enterprises are poorly managed and are routinely late in informing investors of negative news. 
Even well-managed companies can have clients that refuse to pay their bills.
