file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_New Economic Chief Sees Slow March to Open China Markets.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's newly elevated economic chief, Zhu Rongji, said today that he planned to move cautiously in opening the nation's markets and exposing its sclerotic state-owned enterprises to foreign competition.
But Mr. Zhu, in his first public comments since becoming one of the country's three top leaders last week, also declared that it was "unreasonable to exclude China from the W.T.O.," a reference to the continued insistence by the United States that China agree to a rigorous timetable for liberalizing its economy before it can join the World Trade Organization.
The Clinton Administration, officials in Washington say, is under growing pressure to relax some of those requirements before President Jiang Zemin makes a state visit to Washington late next month. 
Later this week, Secretary of the Treasury Robert E. Rubin will spend two days in Beijing to set the stage for that meeting.
While Mr. Zhu doled out morsels to a hungry audience of bankers and investors here today -- about new tax policies, protecting China's currency and finding work for millions of laborers whose jobs are threatened by privatization plans -- what he said was nearly overshadowed by how he said it. 
He joked easily, answered questions right from the floor, and made no effort to minimize the problems of China's deeply troubled banking system.
"It wasn't exactly Oprah," a senior American official said afterward, "but it wasn't the China we are used to seeing."
On a key question many in the audience wanted answered -- how, exactly, China plans to transfer ownership of industries from the Government to some form of shareholding without casting millions of workers into the streets -- Mr. Zhu bobbed and weaved. 
But that was expected, mainly because he is considered the likely successor to Prime Minister Li Peng next spring. 
He has nothing to gain by further angering local officials who already view him as the architect of the downsizing process sweeping through China's resolutely noncorporate factories.
For the Clinton Administration, perhaps the stickiest issue Mr. Zhu raised today was Chinese membership in the trade organization, a group of nearly 130 nations pledged to lower tariffs on imported goods and a regimen of steady economic liberalization. 
Two years ago, the Administration sent China a road map of changes it would have to make before it qualified, including a rapid end to subsidies of state enterprises. 
While some progress has been made in negotiations, officials fear there has not been enough for Mr. Clinton to declare at the talks next month that China is well on its way to membership.
"This problem will be solved eventually," Mr. Zhu said with a broad smile today. 
"It is unreasonable to make such demands on China, which is still a developing economy."
There are some hints that the United States may soon back away from its hard-line stance, showing flexibility over the amount of time China will be allowed before it must comply with the rules. 
Japan has said it is ready to let China into the organization, which also acts as a court of world trading rules. 
Mr. Rubin is expected to talk about the issue when he meets Mr. Zhu and President Jiang at the end of the week.
There were also hints today that China has been alarmed by the speed with which its Southeast Asian nations fell into a contagious currency crisis in recent weeks. 
Mr. Zhu said he had been advised to take his time before allowing investors to freely move capital of all kinds across Chinese borders.
The Government-controlled China Daily said today that Liu Jibin, vice minister of finance, was backing away from any quick move to make the Chinese currency fully convertible into dollars, and vice versa. 
Mr. Liu was quoted as saying that the Southeast Asia crisis had sent "a warning signal" to other developing nations about the dangers of surrendering control of the currency to speculators and investors.
Unlike the smaller Southeast Asians, though, China is coming to the markets well armed. 
Mr. Zhu disclosed today that foreign exchange reserves now stand at $131.6 billion, one of the highest levels in the world. 
They are so high, in fact, that officials traveling with Mr. Rubin say they believe the decision to keep that war chest securely in the bank may be unwise when the money could go toward buying power plants and other equipment that could help modernize industries that have changed little since Mao Zedong's death in the mid-70's.
But over the long haul, Mr. Zhu declared today, Washington will get what it seeks: a far more transparent financial system.
"To step up the reform of the financial system," he said, "China will strengthen the currency-regulation function of the central bank and the financial supervisory systems, and promote the commercialization of state-owned banks."
It is unclear, however, how he will dispose of huge loans that the banks made for political reasons rather than on the basis of credit-worthiness to failing state industries.
"China will also improve the capital structure and quality of the commercial banks," he concluded, "vigorously but steadily develop and regulate the financial market, improve and enact financial laws and regulations, and learn modern financial-management expertise."
Already, Chinese leaders have found something in common with President Clinton that they can talk about next month: They have all been surprised that revenue has flowed into Government coffers faster than anyone expected.
As a result, Mr. Zhu said, China would restore a series of tax exemptions for foreign technology and other goods that was revoked last year.

text:

Five years after announcing that it would pull out of China because of what it called pervasive human rights violations, Levi Strauss & Company said today that it would expand its manufacturing in the country and start selling its clothing there.
"It's clear to us that the environment is getting better there," said Peter A. Jacobi, the president and chief operating officer of Levi Strauss, which makes its trademark denim pants and shirts in 12 Asian countries. 
"We basically felt that we should untie our hands."
Mr. Jacobi, who disclosed the decision in an interview here, said the company's action was less a judgment of China's overall human rights record and more a belief that its local contractors would adhere to the company's guidelines for labor conditions.
"Levi Strauss is not in the human rights business," he said. 
"But to the degree that human rights affects our business, we care about it."
The action by Levi Strauss, a privately held company based in San Francisco, comes at a time of easier political and commercial relations between the United States and China. 
Several American companies, including Eastman Kodak and Coca-Cola, have announced major new investments in the mainland in recent weeks. 
With President Clinton scheduled to visit Beijing in June, business people here expect a flurry of new ventures.
But the decision may exacerbate concerns about the harsh conditions in Asian factories that churn out goods for American companies. 
Nike Inc. was criticized last fall when an audit found unsafe working conditions at a plant that produced Nike athletic shoes in Vietnam. 
A new report by the National Labor Committee, an advocacy group in Washington, says that factories in China routinely work their employees 60 to 70 hours a week.
When Levi Strauss announced its intention to withdraw in 1993, it was a lone holdout in corporate America's stampede into China. 
Indeed, it never fully withdrew, and no other American company followed suit -- a situation that human rights advocates said demonstrated the difficulty of using corporations to push for social reform.
"Levi's decision to go back into China should not be taken as evidence that the labor situation in China has improved," said Robin Munro, director of the Hong Kong office of Human Rights Watch Asia. 
"It has not."
And while Levi Strauss reduced its production, it still makes 800,000 units of clothing a year in the country, compared with three million units a year before 1993.
When the company decided to stop making jeans in China, it also decided not to sell them there. 
At the time, it was motivated by more than concern for human rights. 
Thousands of counterfeit jeans were being produced with the Levis label. 
Now, Mr. Jacobi said he believed the Chinese Government would play an aggressive role in helping the company track down and root out manufacturers of counterfeit products. 
And since Levi Strauss initially said it would leave China, competitors from around the world, including Lee Apparel, part of the VF Corporation, and Esprit, have established a strong position in the growing Chinese market.
Mr. Jacobi said Levi Strauss decided to withdraw after it found evidence of child labor, forced labor and a military presence at factories that produced Levi Strauss clothing.
The company does not actually own any factories on the mainland, but uses Chinese subcontractors in manufacturing. 
Its guidelines prohibit it from using producers that permit child labor, forced labor or excessive work hours.
"We were concerned that our association with these kinds of things would put our reputation at risk," Mr. Jacobi said.
But he said Levi Strauss temporarily halted its "phased withdrawal" from China two years ago amid signs that labor conditions were improving.
Its current decision to increase production and resume sales came after intense lobbying from its Asian division and after consulting other multinational companies active in the country.
The company now even plans to start a direct-marketing operation on the mainland. 
It already has such an operation in Hong Kong. 
Jim Fraser, the president of Levi Strauss Asia Pacific, said China could become the key manufacturing nation for the company's Japanese and South Korean markets, which generate two-thirds of its $468 million in Asian revenue.
The United States' current relationship with China -- in which disagreements are often muted in public and argued in private -- did not play a part in the company's decision, Mr. Jacobi said. 
But he acknowledged that it was easier to make such a move in this climate. 
In 1993, Levi Strauss's decision to leave put an uncomfortable spotlight on the company when no other company followed suit.
In choosing to expand its China presence, Mr. Jacobi acknowledged that Levi Strauss was balancing its carefully honed reputation for corporate idealism with a bottom-line business calculation about the value of the Chinese market.
"You're nowhere in Asia without being in China," he said.
Mr. Jacobi said Levi Strauss would vigilantly monitor its new Chinese factories to make sure that they complied with the guidelines. 
But some labor advocates said that even well-intended companies found it difficult to police every factory -- in part because the main contractors often dole out such assignments as sewing buttons or stitching trousers to other, smaller factories.
"We can't imagine how you could effectively manage these codes of conduct," said Jennifer Porges, a spokeswoman for the Asia Monitor Resource Center, a human rights group that focuses on labor issues.
A prominent Chinese labor activist, however, gave Levi Strauss the benefit of the doubt. 
Han Dongfang, who formed China's first independent labor union during the Tiananmen Square uprising, said he believed that the company could do more good by providing jobs in China, rather than by shunning the country. 
Mr. Han added that he hoped Levi Strauss would be open to allowing rights groups to monitor factories used by the company.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Stakes in China Suddenly Seem Less Appealing.txt
text:

Wall Street's top-drawer investment firms are falling all over each other to take China's state-owned companies public. 
After the furor unleashed by the latest deal, they may wonder whether it is worth the grief.
Goldman, Sachs & Company set the price today for its initial public offering of the PetroChina Company, China's dominant oil and gas producer. 
At 1.28 Hong Kong dollars a share, or about 16 cents, it is at the low end of the company's predicted range. 
That will hardly soothe the architects of the deal, who spent months putting it together, only to see it ripped apart by critics ranging from Republican lawmakers to Tibetan monks.
"The PetroChina offering has been a very complex and grueling process," said Paul Shapira, a managing director at Goldman, at a news conference here last Sunday.
When PetroChina's bosses traveled to the United States on March 20 to sell the offering, they were hit with charges of human-rights and labor abuses. 
Critics said the listing would lead to a million layoffs at PetroChina's parent, China National Petroleum. 
They also said the company was damaging the environment in Tibet and abetting an outlaw regime in Sudan through a joint venture there.
Not content just to criticize, the A.F.L.-C.I.O. organized a shadow road show in New York and other cities to persuade investors to steer clear of PetroChina. 
Fund managers in Hong Kong said today that the campaign had an impact -- scaring off some American funds.
"The political concerns have been a major overhang," said a fund manager, who, like most people interviewed for this article, spoke on condition of anonymity. 
"Not that many Asia-Pacific funds invest in oil and gas companies, so you need demand in the United States."
PetroChina's bumpy ride has far-reaching implications for China's campaign to overhaul its sclerotic corporate sector. 
As part of that effort, Beijing hopes to sell shares in dozens of huge state-owned companies, including Sinopec, the second-largest oil company; China National Overseas Oil, the No. 1 offshore oil company; and China Unicom, the No. 2 telecommunications company.
With PetroChina limping into the market, however, the prospects for these other deals are now cloudier. 
The A.F.L.-C.I.O., emboldened by its success, said it planned to protest future Chinese stock offerings that it feels are bad investments or represent companies that violate human rights and labor practices.
"Our understanding is that there is going to be 120 of these I.P.O.'s coming out of China," said Richard Trumka, the secretary general of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. 
"On ethical issues and shareholder governance issues, most of these are going to be just as bad as PetroChina."
In the face of such criticism, PetroChina may feel vindicated that it was still able to raise about $3 billion from the offering, which values the company at roughly $30 billion. 
China National Petroleum will retain a 90 percent stake and will appoint the entire board, including the two independent directors.
Shares of PetroChina begin trading next Thursday in New York and next Friday in Hong Kong. 
In New York, they will trade as American depository receipts that represent 100 Hong Kong shares, or $16.44 at the price set here today.
China National Petroleum had initially hoped to raise $5 billion or even $7 billion. 
To meet even the more modest goal, Goldman was forced to round up strategic investors to soak up the shares. 
BP Amoco agreed to buy 20 percent of the offering, or as much as $1 billion, while three politically friendly property developers in Hong Kong agreed to chip in another $350 million.
Goldman's performance was also tainted by an unauthorized e-mail message that four of the firm's sales representatives sent to 83 clients. 
Because the note contained claims that the firm feared may have violated securities laws, Goldman tried hard to recall it. 
Later, on the advice of lawyers, it took the extraordinary step of reprinting the e-mail message -- and correcting portions of it -- in the prospectus.
"It clearly was a mistake," Mr. Shapira said tersely at the news conference.
The disputes surrounding PetroChina obscure the fact that it is, in many respects, a trail-blazing company for China. 
It has instituted an incentive plan for its top 300 managers, tying as much as 75 percent of their compensation to profit targets. 
That is unheard-of among state-owned companies in China, which only recently began paying attention to profits, let alone the role of managers in producing them.
"We are a world-scale oil and gas company, and the flagship of China's reform," said Ma Fucai, the chairman of PetroChina, in the news conference in Hong Kong.
Because China National Petroleum is a classic state-owned enterprise -- with a vast network of hospitals and schools in addition to oil and gas operations -- the company decided to carve out its most valuable assets and place them in a separate venture, PetroChina.
By doing that, the company also removed the burden of its bloated payroll from PetroChina. 
The new public company will retain 480,000 employees, while the remaining one million workers will stay at China National Petroleum, where most are likely to be laid off.
These layoffs were a main reason that the A.F.L.-C.I.O. decided to oppose the deal. 
But the labor federation also warned that the proceeds from the stock offering could be siphoned off by the parent, where they could contribute indirectly to its activities in Tibet or Sudan.
"The fire wall they created between PetroChina and C.N.P.C. is illusory at best," Mr. Trumka said, "so money will find its way back into the parent company."
According to the company's prospectus, 90 percent of the proceeds will be used by PetroChina to pay off debt and finance capital expenditures. 
The remaining 10 percent will go to China National Petroleum to reduce debt and pay for employee severance and retraining. 
Mr. Ma said the company had hired outside auditors to guarantee that the money would not be used for other purposes.
Mr. Ma also tried to distance PetroChina from its parent's activities in Sudan. 
China National Petroleum is an investor, along with Malaysian and Canadian companies, in a pipeline there. 
"PetroChina does not have any overseas assets and operations," he said. 
"We do not have any plans to expand overseas."
Even aside from questions about Sudan, PetroChina has been hurt because it is indisputably an old-fashioned company. 
At a time when investors are bewitched by technology stocks, PetroChina's discussion of benchmark crude prices does not send hearts fluttering -- even though the company has proven oil reserves of 10.3 billion barrels, making it the world's fourth-largest publicly listed oil company.
Given the low price of its shares, analysts said PetroChina might prove a shrewd investment. 
For its labors, Goldman, Sachs also gets a high fee. 
The firm can expect to split a payment of 3 percent to 4 percent of the offering, or about $90 million, with the other underwriters.

text:

A surge of imports driven by the continued strength of the American economy pushed the United States trade deficit to another record in May, more than $21 billion, fueled both by rising oil prices and growing evidence that China is using exports to support its lagging economy.
The China deficit comes at a politically inopportune time for the Clinton Administration: Next week, the House of Representatives is expected to vote on a one-year renewal of China's preferential trade status. 
While the House is expected to approve the measure, the rising deficit with China -- it totaled more than $23 billion in the first five months of 1999 -- further complicates a relationship already deeply strained by the accidental bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade and China's renewed threats to use force if necessary to keep Taiwan from declaring itself an independent state.
The trade deficit is also one of the few economic indicators that Republican Presidential candidates can seize on to argue that not all is well with the American economy. 
But it is, in fact, a byproduct of American economic health; with unemployment at record lows, low-cost imports have helped keep inflation near zero.
"The May trade figures reflect the continuing large gap between the strong growth in the United States and weaker conditions in many foreign countries," Commerce Secretary William M. Daley said today. 
He estimated that the deficit was running at an annual rate of $224.8 billion, which would be nearly 37 percent higher than last year's record, $164.3 billion. 
China is not the only cause. 
The trade deficit with Japan remains large, though it dropped slightly in May, and there is a rising deficit with Canada and Mexico, the two other members of the North American Free Trade Agreement.
The size of the May deficit surprised many economists and led a few today to lower their predictions for American economic growth in the second quarter a bit. 
But perhaps more important, it was a strong indication that the American consumer spending binge is moving ahead unabated, which is bound to worry the Federal Reserve.
"Five years ago if we had seen numbers like this, what you would have heard on Capitol Hill was politicians blaming the Japanese and the Chinese," said Richard Medley, who heads Medley Global Advisors, an international investment firm in New York. 
"Now what you hear more often is that this proves we are spending too much and saving too little."
In fact, a number of economists and American officials are increasingly concerned that the accumulating current account deficit could ultimately hurt the value of the dollar -- and that, in turn, could set off an international exodus from the stock market.
The Japanese, meanwhile, are clearly worried about the effects of a weakening dollar -- not on the United States but on their own hobbled economy. 
They intervened Monday night to weaken the yen and prop up the dollar, in hopes of making their own exports cheaper on world markets. 
While the purchase was carried out through the New York Federal Reserve, acting as Japan's agent, there are increasing signs that the United States and Japan are at odds on exchange rate policy. 
A stronger dollar would further hurt declining American exports.
Today's report suggested that the decline is modest, but is made worse by the growing demand for foreign-made cars, crude oil and medium-technology electronics. 
Oil prices increased in May to an average of $14.54 a barrel, the Commerce Department said, from $12.71 a barrel in April.
Exports decreased to $77.6 billion from $78.2 billion in April, but they were up fractionally from May 1998. 
Imports increased to $98.9 billion from $96.8 billion in April and $92 billion in May 1998.
The latest figures suggest that some of the areas that the Clinton Administration concentrated the hardest on bolstering during Mr. Clinton's first term in office -- autos, auto parts and machinery -- are the exports now in greatest decline. 
They are also the products that are being imported in increasing numbers. 
Administration officials who once boasted of the auto and auto parts agreement they reached with Japan in 1995, after a trade dispute that nearly resulted in an embargo on Japanese luxury cars, now rarely discuss the subject.
Nor is there much discussion from the White House about how to deal with the complex trade problems with China. 
Over all, Chinese exports to the world are in decline. 
But their continued rise here suggests that the United States, now more than ever, has become the market of last resort for the Chinese.
The politics of the trade deficit with China are messy. 
Opponents of President Clinton's China policy -- on both the left and the right -- say the trade figures show that the President's decision to delink human rights and the annual renewal of China's trade status has helped neither dissidents nor American companies. 
Arrests by Chinese authorities continue -- there was a major crackdown today -- and exports to China are clearly not increasing.
Yet there has been little real resistance to the renewal of what was once called "most favored nation" trade status, and which has been delicately renamed "normal trade relations."
American companies have argued annually on Capitol Hill that unless China has the benefit of low tariffs on their imports here, the Chinese market will gradually be shut down for them.
If China and the United States reach an agreement this year on Beijing's entry to the World Trade Organization, the terms of its move to join the group should, in theory at least, open more markets to American goods. 
But opponents on Capitol Hill, both those on the left who are concerned with China's human rights record and those on the right who see China as a growing threat, view its admission as a favor to the Chinese, and not one that will necessarily benefit American workers.

The figures were released today just as China and the United States entered a critical phase in negotiations over China's push to enter the World Trade Organization, which sets the rules for international trade. 
China wants the international prestige that comes from joining the trade organization and would also get a measure of protection against trade barriers to its exports.
Intense talks are under way in Geneva over the terms of China's entry in hopes of reaching an agreement before the Prime Minister of China, Zhu Rongji, visits Washington in early April. 
The deadline has breathed life into talks that have sputtered for a decade.
One American negotiator said this week that "we've made more progress with the Chinese in the last three weeks than in the last three years," and this morning President Clinton's top economic advisers met at the White House to assess China's intentions.

The United States, however, ran a $6.4 billion surplus in services, from consulting to insurance.

The sharp increase occurred even though there was no rise in the value of imported gasoline and other petroleum products, now selling at prices lower than at any point in the last quarter-century.

Most of Hutchison's profit, however, came from a special one-time gain after the sale of its European mobile phone operations. 
And the company's encore, an ambitious plan to offer next-generation cellular services throughout Europe, is in doubt. 
Last week, Hutchison unexpectedly gave up a coveted license to offer advanced mobile services in Germany, saying it was too costly.
Today, even as Mr. Li and his lieutenants basked in the glow of rich earnings, they had to explain why the German setback had not scrambled their plans.
"We don't for a moment concede that we will be out of Germany," Canning Fok, the group managing director of Hutchison, said in an interview. 
"But we have to be more creative about getting into that market. 
To throw money around is not the way to do it."
In the great race to carve up Europe's electromagnetic spectrum, Hutchison Whampoa has emerged as an unpredictable outlier. 
Aggressive in bidding for a British license, abrupt in backing out of Germany, Hutchinson Whampoa, a conglomerate that can trace its roots to Hong Kong's early colonial days, has left many telecommunications experts scratching their heads.
Mr. Fok insists that there is no mystery. 
The company could someday buy back its share of the German license from its partners, Royal KPN of the Netherlands and NTT DoCoMo of Japan. 
Even if it never breaks into Germany, he said, Hutchison will create a valuable cellular franchise in Britain, where it recently won a license, and in other countries like Italy, where it is still in the running.
"Each asset is valuable as long as you get it at the right price," Mr. Fok declared. 
"We haven't lost anything from Germany. 
I won't say we've gained, but we haven't lost."
Despite their qualms, most analysts are willing to give Mr. Li the benefit of the doubt. 
Hutchison has become one of the most highly valued companies in Hong Kong on the strength of its chairman's ability to sniff out good deals and steer clear of bad ones. 
At a price for the three partners of more than $7 billion, Hutchison considered the German mobile license extremely expensive.
"Hutchison is a company where pragmatism is very much the watchword," said John Tysoe, a telecommunications analyst at the investment firm WestLB Panmure in London. 
"They avoid the mistake that other telecom operators make, which is to fall in love with their businesses."
By ceding Germany, however, other analysts say that Hutchison has effectively abandoned its dream of building a pan-European cellular network. 
Had the company been able to assemble such a network, it would have been an enormously valuable franchise -- perhaps even more valuable than Orange, the British mobile network that Hutchison sold last year to Mannesmann of Germany for $14 billion.
"The reason everybody owns Hutchison's stock is because they expect Li Ka-shing to pull off another massive deal," said Anil Daswani, a Salomon Smith Barney analyst. 
"We were all expecting them to build a European network, and then sell it off or spin off part of it."
Hutchison's recent attack of caution has deflated its shareholders. 
The company's stock has declined 6.4 percent since Aug. 
18, when it gave up the German license. 
The shares fell 1.8 percent today, to 110.5 Hong Kong dollars, or $14.17, though the earnings were released after the market closed. 
Hutchison stock traded lower early Friday as Hong Kong share prices declined.
The first-half earnings show a generally healthy company, even subtracting the one-time gain of $3.2 billion. 
Operating earnings rose 32 percent, to $1.3 billion. 
Hutchison's container ports, telecommunications and energy divisions turned in particularly strong performances, while the results of its property group remained lackluster.
The company would have reported even greater profit if it had not taken a $3.8 billion provision against fluctuations in the value of its 3 percent stake in Vodafone AirTouch, the British cellular giant. 
Hutchison picked up the stake when Vodafone acquired Mannesmann earlier this year.
Some experts say that Mr. Li's phenomenal record as a deal maker has placed unreasonable expectations on the company. 
Last year, after a previous round of blockbuster asset sales, Hutchison reported a profit of $14.25 billion. 
On that basis, it made the company, whose annual sales were around $7 billion, the most profitable in the world, ahead of General Electric.
"Our shareholders have gotten accustomed to big numbers," Mr. Fok said. 
"We've done it for two years now. 
But I won't guarantee it for every year."Hutchison's investors, he went on, recognize that no company can produce an endless stream of $14 billion transactions. 
The trouble is, they may have become spoiled: Mr. Li has pulled off more lucrative deals since the sale of Orange.
Hutchison's earnings do not include the roughly $9 billion profit it reaped last month when Deutsche Telekom agreed to acquire VoiceStream Wireless, a United States cellular company, for $53 billion. 
Hutchison began investing in VoiceStream late in 1997. 
It paid a total of $1.2 billion for a 23 percent stake, which is now worth about $12 billion.
If Hutchison's shareholders seem hungry for deals, it is because they have been trained by Mr. Li. Since he took over the company in 1981, he has treated it more as a collection of assets than an industrial empire. 
This reflects Mr. Li's background -- he came to Hong Kong from mainland China in the 1940's and traded his way up from selling plastic flowers to building skyscrapers.
But it also reflects Hutchison's roots in the mutable world of Hong Kong. 
Founded in the 1860's as the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, it built dry docks and ship-repair yards on the South China seacoast when Hong Kong was a young British colony. 
Over the years, it cobbled together a disparate array of assets, ranging from drugstores and supermarkets to container ports.
By 1980, Hutchison was losing money and was ripe for the picking by Mr. Li, the most aggressive of a new generation of Chinese entrepreneurs eager to supplant the British. 
Under Mr. Li, Hutchison's reach expanded beyond Hong Kong and into new industries like telecommunications. 
But its trading mentality never changed.
"There was never a strategy to dominate the world," said Simon Murray, a British investor who was managing director of the company in the 1980's and still sits on the board. 
"Hutchison always moved forward on an add-on basis, accumulating assets, building on the bricks we had."
Although the company's telecommunications holdings have accounted for its multibillion-dollar asset sales, they contribute only 6 percent of the operating profits. 
Indeed, Hutchison has made much more money selling telephone networks than running them.
Despite its retreat in Germany, Mr. Fok said Hutchison was ready to "go for it" in bidding for a third-generation license in Italy. 
He said the company would also consider investing in such networks in the United States, when Washington begins auctioning the airwaves.
Further down the line is China, which is still building its first generation of mobile phone networks. 
Hutchison has a $400 million stake in China Unicom, the second-largest telephone operator nationwide. 
Mr. Fok said, however, that Hutchison would not expand its presence there until the rules on foreign investment in the telecommunications industry became clearer.
For all his prudence, Mr. Fok seems exuberant when discussing the prospects for third-generation mobile service. 
With its emphasis on data transmission, Mr. Fok says this technology has more in common with the Internet than with traditional cellular service. 
And the German pullback notwithstanding, he says the scramble for licenses in Europe is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to seize a dominant position in a new industry in a single year.
"It's like there is a piece of triple-A land available for development in every major city in the world at the same time," Mr. Fok said. 
"When do you see that?
You don't."

text:
ï»¿
President Clinton promised today to wage an all-out campaign to get Congress to back a landmark trade deal with China, and administration officials have enlisted numerous corporate chief executives for what they describe as the most aggressive pro-trade lobbying effort since the United States opened its borders to free trade with Canada and Mexico seven years ago.
The campaign will pit the administration and its business allies against a network of labor, environmental and consumer groups, which oppose the new trade agreement with China and are eager to test their strength after successfully mobilizing street demonstrations that helped to scuttle world trade talks in Seattle late last year.
The vote concerns the November agreement between the United States and China that paves the way for China to enter the World Trade Organization. 
American companies will not benefit from the deal, which sharply cuts tariffs and clears barriers to freer trade in agriculture and services, unless Congress grants China the same access to the United States market that most other major trading partners have, forgoing an annual review of that country's trade status.
Clinton administration officials say they are guardedly optimistic that Congress will approve the terms of the deal. 
But having been stung by surprise defeats on previous trade accords and by the collapse of trade negotiations in Seattle, they are promising a steady stream of pro-trade events, speeches by Mr. Clinton and high-level administration attention until Congress votes on the issue in the spring or summer.
"I will be working hard over the coming weeks and coming months to make sure we don't let this opportunity slip away," Mr. Clinton said at a news conference to announce the members of an administration team appointed to oversee the campaign. 
"This is something that is in the national interest."
Mr. Clinton named William M. Daley, the commerce secretary, to lead the effort, a signal to many in the business community that the China trade deal has a higher political priority than some other recent votes on trade. 
Mr. Daley led the successful effort to win backing for the North American Free Trade Agreement in 1993 and 1994, and is now seen as one of the few members of the administration who can orchestrate a successful political campaign.
Mr. Daley will be working on the issue with Steve Ricchetti, Mr. Clinton's deputy chief of staff, and they have already begun lining up some top corporate leaders, including the chiefs at Boeing, America Online and Intel, to become directly involved in selling the benefits of the trade accord to Congress and the public. 
The hope is that the lobbying campaign will have a high-technology edge, with popular companies that are pillars of the new economy supplementing stalwart trade supporters like Boeing and General Electric.
Technology companies and farmers have much to gain from the trade deal, which will, at least on paper, pry open parts of the Chinese economy that Beijing has tended to shelter from foreign competition. 
These include telecommunications, the Internet, and grain and meat products, all which are particular areas of American strength.
But the vote is nonetheless seen as a close contest. 
Trade divides Democrats like few political issues, pitting core labor and environmental supporters against business support. 
The administration fears that the Republicans, who control Congress, will seek to delay the vote until the fall, when the election season is at its peak, to make the vote as politically costly as possible for their opponents.
In part for that reason, Mr. Clinton vowed today to put pressure on Congress to bring the China trade accord to a vote before the summer.
Labor groups, meanwhile, have vowed to see the China trade deal defeated, with many expressing optimism that the momentum generated in Seattle will propel opposition to the China accord. 
Unions say that Congress cannot treat China like any other big trading partner because it treats its workers badly and regularly violates trade agreements.
"We will flood every Congressional office with phone calls, letters and visits," James P. Hoffa, president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, said. 
"We will do whatever it takes. 
And with the momentum from Seattle, we will win."

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Will Hong Kong Pay if China Joins Trade Bloc_.txt
text:
ï»¿
For China, which has spent years trying to claw its way into the world's club of trading nations, the benefits of such an expanded reach and strong connections are clear.
But for Hong Kong, which has thrived as a middleman between China's closed markets and the outside world, the possibility of a more open China raises hard questions about the future of this trading post.
At first blush, China's success in moving closer to joining the World Trading Organization has buoyed local investors, on the theory that Chinese membership would be a good thing for Hong Kong. 
Stocks rose to their highest level in 12 months today, capping a week of powerful gains, in part because investors liked the progress they had seen in negotiations between the Chinese and American Governments.
"There are lots of people who think if China wins, Hong Kong wins," said Marc Faber, the managing director of Marc Faber Ltd., an investment firm here. 
"But I'm not sure. 
I think, on balance, the entry of China into the World Trade Organization is a negative for Hong Kong."
Although a deal would greatly expand business with China, Mr. Faber said it could also threaten Hong Kong's role as the broker for much of the wheeling and dealing that surrounds the China trade. 
With so many more ways into China, foreign companies may be ready to cut their own deals.
"This is further marginalizing Hong Kong," he said.
As a former British colony and now a semiautonomous region of China, Hong Kong is a separate trading entity with its own membership in the W.T.O. 
But its economic fortunes are so intertwined with China that people here have followed Beijing's campaign as if it were their own.
"The W.T.O. issue has helped sentiment in the market," said Miron Mushkat, global head of economics and strategy at Indocam Asset Management. 
"But it doesn't take much for sentiment to turn around."
Indeed, investors might have second thoughts if they scrutinized the implications of China's admission to the organization that sets the rules of global commerce and arbitrates disputes.
Already, some of the concessions Beijing has made in trade negotiations pose a threat to companies here. 
On Wednesday, just before Prime Minister Zhu Rongji flew to Washington, Chinese and American officials agreed to double the frequency of commercial flights between their countries and to increase the number of Chinese cities that United States air carriers can serve with direct connections.
That could deprive Hong Kong of its role as a gateway to China. 
Dragonair, the regional airline that serves many mainland cities, could lose Western passengers who fly to Hong Kong and switch carriers for the short hop to popular Chinese destinations like Xian and Guilin.
As China opens other industries, like telecommunications, financial services, and accounting, some analysts said foreign companies would rely less on Hong Kong as an interlocutor. 
That shift is already occurring in shipping, where Hong Kong's role as a gateway is still most pronounced.
In 1997, half of all Chinese exports passed through Hong Kong's container port on their way out of the country. 
But as China has opened more ports on the mainland, Hong Kong's share of exports declined, from 60 percent in 1992. 
Last year, container traffic rose less than 1 percent in Hong Kong, while Shenzhen, a large city nearby in Guangdong Province, reported a 70 percent increase.
"Clearly, more and more trade is carried out between China and other countries directly, rather than through Hong Kong," Mr. Faber said.
Yet for every downbeat consequence of freer trade with China, there is an offsetting positive one. 
Even if China opens its markets and adheres to global trade rules, analysts say it will still be a bewildering place to do business. 
The only difference is that more foreign companies will be taking the plunge.
"If you have a proliferation of people outside who are dealing with China, you need someone to act as a go-between," Mr. Mushkat said. 
"It doesn't necessarily mean pushing cargo through Hong Kong. 
But it may mean more skill-intensive activities, like lawyers or bankers."
Other experts said Hong Kong could assume a new role as an anchor of stabilityI in a commercially freer China. 
Once China gains entry into the W.T.O., analysts said it would be likely to make its currency, the yuan, fully convertible. 
The Hong Kong dollar, with an exchange rate linked to the United States dollar, could offset fluctuations in the value of the Chinese yuan.
Hong Kong's local companies would also benefit from having greater access to Chinese markets. 
Although Hong Kong is the largest source of direct foreign investment in China -- a cumulative $99.3 billion through 1996 -- its companies are still classified as foreign entities. 
Like American companies, they are barred from ownership in many Chinese industries.
Once those restrictions were lifted, Hong Kong companies could have an edge over others. 
For example, the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, a unit of HSBC Holdings, has decades of experience in China and would be well placed if foreign banks were allowed into Chinese consumer banking. 
Shares of HSBC helped propel the stock market rally here in recent days.
"Hong Kong should have demanded that its companies be classified as Chinese when it was negotiating the handover," said Robert C. Broadfoot, managing director of the Political and Economic Risk Consultancy in Hong Kong. 
"Now, it has a second chance to invest in China."
Regardless of the links between Hong Kong and China, some economists said it would be several years before the impact of a Chinese membership in the World Trade Organization made itself felt here.
"There's no doubt the business community would regard this as a positive," said Ian K. Perkin, chief economist of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce. 
"Just how positive is impossible to tell without knowing the details."

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORTS_ A CHANGING WORLD OF EDUCATION_Dean_ Mao_s Legacy.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the 1950's and 60's, China mobilized higher education to produce physicists and rocket engineers capable of giving the Communist Party leadership the ultimate in international prestige: a thermonuclear weapon deliverable by intercontinental ballistic missile. 
It was an enormous achievement for a nation of peasant farmers led by rough-hewn revolutionaries.
But Mao Zedong, the Communist Party chairman, then decided to tear it all down in the name of permanent revolution and class struggle, and higher education was suspended during the years of the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution.
When it recovered in the late 1970's, higher education was still permeated by the tradition of excellence in hard sciences. 
Today, after a wave of Chinese immigration to the West following the reform policies of Deng Xiaoping, the discipline and excellence of Chinese students have made significant contributions to Western universities.
But at home, higher education remains hobbled. 
Chronic, crippling fiscal limitations coupled with Draconian political repression on campuses are eroding any prospects for serious education reform. 
As a result, China's stated goal of developing 100 universities of "international repute" by the 21st century is little more than official sloganeering.
SINCE THE late 1970's, when higher education began rebuilding, both the number of colleges and total enrollment have more than doubled. 
But state funding in real terms has made only small gains.
The result: bleak dormitories with six to eight students crammed to a room; teaching material typed by hand and run off on archaic mimeograph machines, and libraries pathetically short of up-to-date books and periodicals.
Professors live on subsistence salaries, and an alarming percentage of them are leaving their posts to sell their talents in China's burgeoning private sector. 
"The more you teach, the thinner you get," goes the ditty that is a play on the Chinese characters that stand for "professor."
Life is little better for students, who are under increasing financial pressure to pay a greater share of their education costs. 
Fees and other expenses now have risen beyond the income of an average public-sector worker.
The number of "self-paid" students has grown to nearly 15 percent of enrollment, and some professors bemoan the loosening of admission criteria that is evident for the children of China's new wealthy.
The commercialization of Chinese universities has not loosened the ideological grip on history, the humanities, social and political sciences.
Textbooks are highly selective, and sensitive subjects like Tibet and the 1989 protest movement are banned from classrooms.
But mandatory military training and manual labor for students have been eased. 
Last summer, one class of sophomores was shepherded out of Beijing to "engage in agricultural labor" for 10 days in a peasant village. 
Upon returning, they confided: All they had had to do was watch.Â Â Â PATRICK TYLER

file: Internet-Fluent M.I.T. Students Teach Basics in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
DAN DWYER, a sophomore at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, knew that spending last summer hooking up a high school in Beijing to its first Internet connection was not going to be easy. 
But his biggest obstacle was not tussling with the Chinese bureaucracy or outmaneuvering Government restrictions on Internet access. 
It was the telephone.
When he tried to call the high school's computer director at home one evening, "the person who answered the phone said, 'You'll have to call right back,' " Mr. Dwyer said. 
"It was one phone line that was shared by two families living in adjacent apartments."
Sharing the wonders of the Internet with the rest of the world is a noble pursuit, but bringing thousands of dollars' worth of equipment and all that cutting-edge knowledge to a country where phones are still party lines, computers are scarce and few have even heard of the World Wide Web might seem laughable.
Not to the students who volunteer for the China Educational Technology Initiative (web.mit.edu/mit-ceti/www), an M.I.T. program that sends college students overseas to teach high school students about the Internet. 
Two years ago, two graduate students, Jake Seid and Ron Cao, not only persuaded M.I.T. to let them go, basically unsupervised, to set up the first Web site at a high school in China, but they also later persuaded the school to talk big-name companies into sponsoring them. 
Last summer, the program sent 13 students.
This summer, 24 new interns have traveled to 9 high schools. 
They go in teams of two or three, including at least one student who speaks either Cantonese or Mandarin and at least one who speaks the more exotic languages of Java and HTML. 
Together they set up a server and teach the students to create Web sites.
Mr. Seid and Mr. Cao (pronounced sow) came up with the idea as an alternative to the typical graduate-student project.
"Why is it important that two M.I.T. students write a report on telecommunications that nobody is going to read?" said Mr. Seid (pronounced sayd). 
"It really made us think, what do we want to accomplish?"
And where?
News articles they read in 1996 described China as extremely cautious in its exploration of the Internet. 
Those who did have Internet accounts had to register with the police, and those who applied for accounts had to sign an agreement to abide by Chinese law and not endanger state security. 
The M.I.T. students soon learned, however, that they could set up sites on the Chinese Educational Research Network, which connects all the universities.
True, some schools are hesitant to encourage access to sites outside China, not because of censorship but because most are charged for every such site they call up.
"Two years ago there were a lot of questions about who should be hooked up to the Internet," Mr. Seid said. 
"I think they took a chance on us."
Some of the student-built Web sites are written in both English and Chinese. 
The Fudan High School site (highschool.fudan .edu.cn) has pictures of the school, names of award-winning students, even a photo of Cao Tianren, the headmaster. 
Another school's site offers a practice test for the college entrance exam.
"It's more than just connecting the wires or getting a computer into the school," said Robert Yung, Sun Microsystems' director for technology in Asia and a project mentor. 
"This is about how do we teach, how do we show people how to use the technology?"
So far, Sun Microsystems and other companies have donated more than $250,000 worth of hardware and software. 
Each team has to figure out a strategy for its project, from getting the hardware shipped to figuring out how to teach Java programming to 40 ninth graders in six weeks, a commitment that impressed Mr. Yung, who discussed the teams in a recent interview.
"I'm amazed at their energy level," he said. 
"It was finals week at M.I.T. this week, and I still get E-mail from them at 3 in the morning. 
I look at them and say, 'Why don't I take care of this problem?
You go and study.'
"
The months before the trip are filled with incessant E-mails, faxes and phone calls. 
(The translators have the worst of it, they agree, because they have to deal with the 12-hour time difference.) Another first -- setting up a wireless Internet connection to a Chinese high school -- took days.
The five-floor high school building did not have telephone wires, so the volunteers used antennae to connect it to a university, and its dedicated line, about a half-mile away.
"We never even saw the buildings -- it was all through E-mail," said Roger Hu, who went to Shanghai as a freshman. 
"We needed to see what buildings were in the way, if they would interfere with the line of sight. 
They would go up and on the roof and say, 'Oh, yeah, I can see the building from there.'
"
The students' Chinese hosts were eager to help. 
Some of the schools updated their computers or bought new ones. 
So many people were interested in their progress that last summer the American students held a conference about the Web in education that drew chief executives, school principals and Chinese Government officials.
The China Education Technology Initiative inspired another M.I.T. student, Ameet Ranadive, to start a similar program in India last year. 
The population there is approaching one billion, but only 100,000 have Internet access. 
Mr. Ranadive, who will be a graduate student in the fall, said he planned to have the Indian students start pen-pal relationships with the Chinese students using E-mail.
"If you start with small steps like that, at least it's promoting connections with the two sides," he said.
The interns have concerns about nuclear testing in India, human rights violations in China and civil war in Africa, where yet another M.I.T. student is looking to start a similar program. 
But they keep their corner of cyberspace apolitical.
"What I heard about China was all very negative things," Mr. Seid said. 
"You'd hear about issues like Taiwan, you hear about the Dalai Lama and Tibet, you hear about Tiananmen. 
Then you hear about the people. 
It's a very different perspective than what you hear about the Government."

text:
ï»¿
WARREN B. BAILEY is no J. Mark Mobius, the guru of emerging markets at the Franklin Templeton mutual funds.
But for the last seven years Mr. Bailey, an assistant professor of finance at the Samuel Curtis Johnson Graduate School of Management at Cornell, has taken his own money to the front lines in Asian emerging markets. 
While most Americans who dare to invest in these places do so by popping a check into the corner mailbox, Mr. Bailey, 38, is often in Asia -- checking out a fast-food company's wares in Manila, for example, or buying stock in Tsingtao, the Chinese brewer, on its first day of trading in Hong Kong.
In this interview, Mr. Bailey maps out his approach to Asian emerging markets, appraises the recent turbulence there and describes some of his successes and failures. 
His basic advice to wannabe emerging-markets investors: "Have a strong stomach and no ego."
Mr. Bailey had an initial stake of $24,000 in the market, added a few thousand dollars each year and says the holdings are now worth $70,000 to $80,000.
But now he gets a chance to start anew: for personal reasons that have nothing to do with the recent tumult in Asia, he plans to liquidate the portfolio shortly. 
However, he will resume his do-it-yourself investing style in Asia's developing lands soon.
Q. Tell us a little about yourself and your experience in investing.
A. I was born in Brooklyn, went to Cornell, got an M.B.A. at McGill and a doctorate at U.C.L.A. 
My first teaching job was at Ohio State in 1986. 
I've been at Cornell since 1991, and was tenured three years ago.
I collected and dealt in coins as a kid, but I didn't buy my first stock until after the 1987 crash and after I had read Peter Lynch's book, "One Up on Wall Street."
Then I invested in a few domestic stocks.
Q. Do you own any American stocks now?
A. I have about $40,000 to $50,000 in consumer stocks like McDonald's and Pepsi and a strong interest in oil companies, particularly those that produce in secure areas.
Q. How did you get interested in Asia?
A. I made my first trip to Thailand in 1984 when I was a grad student, and I was amazed at how industrious the people were. 
And then, about seven years ago, I recognized that certain academic problems, like political and currency risk, were best studied with data from nontraditional markets.
At about the same time, I left Ohio State and found myself with about $24,000 in pension money. 
I could have rolled it over into another pension fund or taken it out and started a brokerage account.
I chose to be adventurous instead. 
Most of these Asian countries have laid the groundwork for good, safe, long-term investing, while also offering the opportunities that exist in places that are not fully developed.
The timing of the move was great, because Saddam Hussein was getting comfortable in Kuwait about then. 
It was a time of great pessimistic sentiment, and I bought four blue-chip stocks in Singapore, one in Malaysia and one in Hong Kong and said let's start with this.
Since then my teaching and investing activities in Asia have proceeded in parallel.
Q. Do you use an American broker?
A. No, I use a foreign broker, except for the Asian stocks that trade here as A.D.R.'s. 
But anyone with a sizable portfolio, say $500,000 or more, can get their American broker to do it, and some American firms will do these trades for smaller accounts.
When I first decided to invest the money myself, I sent faxes to brokerages in Singapore and Jakarta, asking them what I needed to do. 
I got a lot of funny, handwritten notes and unintelligible responses. 
I got one from a brokerage in Jakarta that said to wire them the money and they will fill out the forms later. 
Yeah, right.
Some time later I was at a conference talking about my situation with an Indonesian official involved in securities regulation. 
He pulled out a card and said: "This is my uncle's business card. 
He is a broker -- why don't you call him?"
I took the card, said thank you and walked away real fast.
Anyway, I ended up going with a Singaporean broker attached to a respected bank as my main broker in the region.
Q. Have you had a problem getting orders filled at the prices you wanted?
A. Brokers in former British colonies operate under strict rules, and you are not likely to get ripped off. 
The only place I ever had a problem was in Jakarta, when I was trading very thinly traded stocks in very small amounts. 
But it wasn't clear if I was being ripped off or if I was merely paying for the liquidity that was being supplied.
Q. What is your investment strategy?
A. It is based on two principles. 
The first, my Peter Lynch principle, is to find a company that seems to have a sensible product, seems to do a good job and could benefit from economic growth.
Second, most professional managers have built-in impatience. 
If you ask a fund manager today if he thinks Thailand is going to stink forever, he will say "of course not," but he is going to be evaluated on performance three months from now.
I try to combine those principles: find things that make sense and buy them when others will not or cannot. 
And I have had some successes and some failures.
I found a good company when I went to Manila in 1995. 
I was told that Jollibee Foods, a Philippine fast-food company, is even more popular than McDonald's with the locals. 
It is a combination of McDonald's and Kentucky Fried Chicken and it follows an aggressive "value pricing" strategy.
I took a look at the restaurants and bought some shares in nominee or street name, because foreigners can't buy Philippine shares. 
That is a big game in Asia. 
You can pretty much avoid ownership restrictions if you are willing to trust your broker.
Q. What about failures?
A. So far my approach has not worked well in China. 
In 1993 I bought shares in Tsingtao, the beer company, on the first day it was offered on the Hong Kong exchange. 
I read the prospectus and it did not seem grossly overpriced. 
But I did not find out until later that even though they have a good product, the company hasn't built good distribution networks. 
The stock has been on a roller-coaster ride ever since I bought it.
Lack of information has also hurt me with Brilliance China Automotive, a mini-bus maker and the first Chinese company listed on the New York Stock Exchange.
The stock did well to begin with, because people were looking at the vehicle market in China. 
But the vehicles they turn out are not any good, and no one is pressuring them to do better. 
The stock went public at $16 and went as high as about $34. 
I bought at $26, thinking I was clever. 
The stock fell as low as $5, and is now $9.75.
When people ask me what I like in China, I tell them I would like to buy a 30-year call option -- something that pays off if the underlying instrument goes up -- on China's gross national product. 
At the moment, there is no equivalent of 3M, Intel or McDonald's to buy there that represents an honest piece of that economy.
Q. How do you get your ideas?
A. I spend two to four weeks in Asia every six to nine months. 
I do research and am surrounded by students who want to hear about it. 
I get phone calls and E-mails from former students who are living in the region. 
And I read The Economist and The Far Eastern Economic Review every week.
Q. What are your thoughts about the recent turbulence in Asian emerging markets?
A. These are not situations where whole societies and economies are collapsing. 
In Asia there are a lot of very solid economies with basically well-run governments that are just screwing up right now.
There has been an unfortunate spillover, too, with Malaysia getting painted with the Thai brush, but that is how markets work. 
People who are imperfectly informed rationally overreact to protect themselves. 
It is almost ridiculous for the Malaysian ringgit to be so cheap, because it implies so many bargains in stocks, real estate, vacations. 
I am going to be spending a lot of money next summer, or perhaps over the winter, in the region.
Q. Any tips for neophytes on picking stocks?
A. I would ask which industry typifies the country's promise. 
And then I would try and identify a solid company in that industry. 
In Singapore, look for financial services and shipping companies, for example. 
In Indonesia, look for natural resources companies.
Q. What advice would you give to people who are thinking about investing on their own in Asia, or in emerging markets generally?
A. Have patience, a sense of humor and a trustworthy broker. 
Buy safe, big companies that make sense, hold them for a long time and buy them when everyone else is afraid. 
Have a strong stomach, and no ego.
And travel to the region. 
When I went to China for the first time in 1992, I crossed by land from Hong Kong, and found that it was like going into Mexico from Tijuana. 
There were no threatening soldiers; if anything, it was extremely friendly. 
And it punctured any notion I had of a highly authoritarian state. 
Had I not done that in person I would not be comfortable investing there.

file: It_s Mostly Business as Usual For the Taiwanese in Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
This week at the Great Hall of the People, Chinese leaders threatened military action against Taiwan, warning that China "would not sit idly by" if the island it claims as its own moved toward formal independence.
But it was business as usual here at the Purple Vine, an elegant Taiwan-style teahouse run by a businessman from Taipei that is snuggled between the Great Hall and China's leadership compound -- and counts many mainland officials as loyal customers.
"The political tension hasn't had the slightest impact on me," said Zha Fuhua, the owner, as he carefully choreographed the preparation of oolong tea, a Taiwanese favorite.
"Sure there's been lots of angry talk," he said, "but I think it's just mouthing off. 
I'm not the least bit worried. 
I don't think war is possible, because there's too much to lose. 
The essence of the relationship between China and Taiwan is economic development, not battle."
It might be easy to imagine that Beijing's tens of thousands of residents from Taiwan live a bizarre existence, members of a divided family in the heart of the enemy camp. 
There are occasional vexations: enduring an occasional cabbie's harangue about the need to bomb Taiwan into submission, and wondering how to respond when a teenage son is invited to join the Communist Youth League.
But most Taiwanese here say they are happy and feel at home in China, living with a language and culture that they for the most part understand. 
They are mostly small-business people, and they blend in well with Beijing's increasingly affluent middle class. 
They have Chinese neighbors and Chinese business partners, and they often send their children to Chinese schools.
And so with only days to go before the Taiwan presidential election, which has prompted Beijing's most recent saber rattling, Taiwanese here seem largely oblivious to the arrows flying above them in political space, convinced that business interests and brotherhood will somehow ensure the peace.
"We're all used to this kind of talk by now, and it's not something that impacts us greatly," said Lin Yen-hung, the manager of a cooking oil company on the outskirts of Beijing, who has lived here for eight years.
Taiwan's government relaxed its ban on citizens' contacts with the mainland in 1987, and an estimated 60,000 Taiwan companies now operate directly or indirectly in China, according to the Beijing Association of Taiwanese Entrepreneurs.
At least several hundred thousand people from Taiwan now live in the People's Republic, the overwhelming number of them business people drawn by the opportunities of its fast-growing market.
In Beijing they are sprinkled throughout the city and integrated into the community.
"We express our views in an appropriate way, but in general we avoid the topic of reunification," said Chen Kuo-yuen, who owns a cafe and a leather goods factory. 
"Business is business and politics is politics. 
But our relationship with the mainland community is extremely close."
He pointed to his cafe, filled with Chinese business people having power lunches on glass-topped tables enclosing seaside dioramas evocative of Taiwan. 
"My customers are Beijingers," he said. 
"My partner's from here too. 
If I tried to do it myself I'd be quickly shut down."
The many business relationships that have evolved in recent years have various roots. 
Taiwan business people want to make money. 
The Chinese partners have benefited from the managerial and technical skills the Taiwanese bring. 
And the Chinese government, which has established special concessions for Taiwanese businesses, believes that such ties will help reel the island, separated from the mainland since 1949, into the fold.
Although Taiwan and mainland figures differ, by both accounts Taiwanese trade and investment here are growing fast. 
Bilateral trade amounted to $14.045 billion in the first seven months of 1999, a 9 percent increase over the comparable period in 1998, according to Taiwan's figures. 
In 1998 there was nearly $3 billion in direct investment from Taiwan to the mainland, according to the China Statistical Yearbook.
But that probably vastly underestimates the magnitude of Taiwanese involvement, Mr. Chen said, since many Taiwanese invest in China through a third region, like Hong Kong. 
And he said there was also a good deal of "invisible" investment, including his own cafe, in which money is invested in the name of a mainland partner, since, strictly speaking, it is illegal for a foreigner to own that type of business in China.
Taiwanese here say the advantages of doing business in a familiar culture and language far outweigh the somewhat daunting prospect of dealing with a Communist bureaucracy, one that spends vast amounts of time and effort maligning the leaders of their island home.
"When I first came to the mainland in 1992, I felt some terror toward the Communist Party," said Mr. Lin, of the Tongyi Edible Oil Company. 
"But I easily became accustomed to how things work here, and I think it's because we share many habits and customs."
And so in the last few years, Taiwanese have continued to rush in.
People were far more nervous in 1996, when China fired missiles near Taiwan during the last presidential election campaign, the Taiwanese here say. 
Then, tens of billions of dollars left Taiwan in one week and many Taiwanese, including Mr. Zha, the teahouse owner, started making preparations for their families to emigrate to the West.
But today the atmosphere is far more relaxed, they say, in part because of increasing communication and familiarity between the two sides. 
Last year tourists from Taiwan made more than 2.5 million visits to the mainland, up from about 500,000 a decade before.
"Three years ago if you got in a taxi and revealed you were from Taiwan, the driver would start ranting," said Mr. Zha, who moved to coastal China to start a seaweed business in 1987. 
"But there are so many Taiwanese here now that there's more contact and communication, so there's also more understanding."
"Generally people don't bring it up," he said. 
"And anyway, if people ask, 'Where are you from?'
I say, 'Jiangxi,' " the southern Chinese province where his ancestors lived.
In general it is easy for Taiwanese to live a life of "strategic ambiguity" by avoiding political discussions -- an easy maneuver in a country where the ruling Communist Party now has little obvious direct influence on everyday life. 
Still, there are times when they feel forced to show their colors. 
Mr. Lin said his teenage son grappled this year with whether to accept an invitation to join the Communist Youth League, a group that most teenagers join as much for its social as its political function. 
(He didn't.)
And on the first day of school, Mr. Lin's 6-year-old son found himself onstage being introduced by the principal, who proceeded to lecture the students about the inevitability of Taiwan's return to the motherland.
Mr. Zha said his in-laws visiting from Taiwan in the mid-1990's were horrified when his son, then 5 years old, spoke fondly of Mao Zedong, referring to him as "Uncle Mao."
The boy now lives in Taiwan with his mother, but mostly because life in Beijing is "too hard" compared with Taiwan, Mr. Zha said.
Taiwanese cannot cast ballots from the mainland, but those in Beijing appear split among the three leading presidential candidates, just like Taiwanese voters at home.
And on the question of Taiwan independence, most seem to favor the status quo, something resembling independence without a formal declaration. 
Some predict reunification with the mainland at some point in the distant future, and all reject a quick bid for independence as too damaging for business.
The Chinese government, "from top to bottom," has guaranteed Taiwan businessmen here that "Taiwanese business wouldn't be affected by political tension, that there can be no threats or personal threats to business people here," said Mr. Chen, the cafe owner and general secretary of the Beijing Association of Taiwanese Entrepreneurs, which frequently meets with local and national leaders.
Still, he said, the question of reunification is difficult for people like him, whose loyalties are split.
"The vast majority of business people here would oppose any move to independence," he said, "because it would immediately bring threats from the mainland. 
But at the same time, they also oppose pressure from the mainland."
Then he added, with an apologetic look, "I know that's a cautious answer, but under the circumstances it's the best I can give."
