file: P.&G. to Increase Stake in China Venture.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Procter & Gamble Company is planning to increase its stake in a Chinese joint venture with Hutchison Whampoa Ltd. to 80 percent from 69 percent for $650 million.
The agreement gives Procter & Gamble's management control of the venture, which makes and sells Tide detergent and other P.& G. products, and permits the company to increase its stake to 100 percent by 2017 for an undisclosed price.
While the weakening of currencies in Southeast Asia has hurt the earnings of American companies that do business there, the strong dollar gave P.& G. added buying power in its transaction with Hutchison, the company said.
P.&G.'s sales in Asia total about $3.5 billion a year, though only 3 percent of that comes from Southeast Asian nations where currencies have been sliding for months. 
It sells about $1 billion in goods annually in China.
Under the agreement, P.& G. will pay Hutchison $650 million between now and early 1998. 
Hutchison will realize a gain of $186 million this year and $434 million during 1998.
The venture -- called P.& G.-Hutchison -- said it had the biggest share of China's market in skin- and hair-care products, soap detergents, dental care and paper products.

file: Paper Tiger_Asian Money,_ American Fears.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN the 1980's, the Asian money that fueled scores of conspiracy theories in America was all Japanese. 
The sale of giant American icons -- Rockefeller Center and Columbia Pictures, the Seattle Mariners and much of downtown Los Angeles -- gave rise to dark warnings that decisions about the country's economic future would be made in Tokyo, not New York or Washington.
Exactly how this power would be exercised was always left a bit vague. 
Would executives at Sony kill movie scripts about the Emperor's role in World War II or about the dark side of corporate life in Japan?
And would Nintendo, the new owner of the Mariners, ship home-run hitters back to Osaka, where power-hitting is in scarce supply?
In the short retrospect of seven years, the questions now sound even more paranoid than they did then. 
The Japanese took a multibillion-dollar bath on most of their investments. 
If anything, they exerted too little control over their acquisitions, especially in Hollywood, and it cost them dearly.
It seems almost laughable these days to think of the United States as an imminent "techno-colony" of Tokyo, a phrase slung around with great abandon in Silicon Valley until Japan plunged into recession.
Â 
Â 
Â 
The New Bogeyman
Yet the underlying fear that struck such a chord in late 80's, a fear that Asian economic powerhouses were using their great wealth to buy power and influence in America, has cropped up anew. 
Now, the money is largely from ethnic Chinese, but -- and the distinction is important -- not from China itself.
The conduit for most of the money was John Huang, a Democratic National Committee fund-raiser who helped conceive and execute a carefully drawn plan to tap a rich vein: the Asian-American community. 
Mr. Huang appealed to the aspirations of a group eager to have a political voice equal to its accomplishments in American society, and he focused his efforts on those he knew best: the prosperous Chinese-Americans living in the suburbs of Los Angeles and New York.
As long as the donors were citizens or legal residents, those contributions were perfectly legal. 
But in racing to reach an ambitious $7 million fund-raising goal, he quickly raked in more than $1 million in clearly illegal donations from the wealthy precincts of Taipei, Bangkok, Jakarta and other outposts of the Chinese diaspora.
Now, in the public mind, the legal and the illegal have melded under the imprecise rubric of "Asian money."
Just as Japan's investments touched a nerve about American economic impotence, the ethnic Chinese money has fed into today's anxiety that Greater China poses the next great challenge to America, economically and militarily.
This shift in fear from Japan to China is nothing new -- that pendulum has swung many times in the American mind, back to the late 19th century. 
John W. Dower, a historian at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, noted that "as a nation we can handle only one Asian bogeyman at a time, and these days Japan is down and China is up as the country with the greatest potential and the greatest potential menace."
Â 
Â 
Â 
Murky Motives
But sometimes the smoke can mask some real fire, and the Democrats' problems clearly have elements of both. 
"In one sense, we've seen this cycle before," said Representative Robert T. Matsui, Democrat of California, who was 6 months old when he and his parents were placed in a World War II detention camp for Japanese-Americans, during an era when many Asians on the West Coast wore signs that said "I'm Chinese" for fear of being caught on the wrong side of the pendulum. 
"But this is a particularly difficult case, because there are legitimate issues to be debated here and a lot of questions no one has answered. 
And still, you'd be deaf if you didn't also hear the tone of racism that's running through a lot of this."
The key question, of course, is what kind of return on investment Mr. Clinton's biggest campaign donors -- who were usually the foreign contributors whose money has since been returned -- were expecting. 
So far, there is no evidence of a single policy or trade dispute that changed course after one of Mr. Clinton's now-famous kaffeeklatsches with Asia's rich and famous, though every new disclosure of a meeting sends investigators and journalists scurrying to figure out what Mr. Clinton's visitors really wanted.
For example, no one yet understands the real motives of the Riady family, the ethnic Chinese owners of the Indonesia-based Lippo Group, who gave Mr. Huang a $700,000 goodbye present when he left Lippo in 1994 to take a mid-level job in the Clinton Commerce Department. 
Did they seek intelligence about American Asian policy?
Influence from a bureaucrat with regular access to the President?
Or, as many suspect, were they simply using their many pictures with the President and their connections in Washington to create an image back home that could be exploited to profitable advantage?
Â 
Â 
Â 
Double Standards
There are also a host of subsidiary mysteries, including whether it was greed or ignorance that led the White House, on the recommendation of a Chinese-American restaurateur-turned-entrepreneur from Little Rock, Ark., named Charles Yah Lin Trie, to allow the head of China's state-owned arms manufacturer into a campaign-organized meeting with Mr. Clinton about Asia policy. 
The White House says it had no idea then that the businessman ran the arms operation, or that he held a senior political post in the Chinese Government (a denial that does not instill great confidence in the vetting of Presidential visitors).
There is little doubt that some of the frenzy surrounding Mr. Clinton's meetings with big donors and their Asian business-leader friends has been fueled by the fact that many of the White House visitors have hard-to-pronounce names and run conglomerates few in America have heard about. 
It's hard to imagine the Washington press corps getting too excited about a White House dinner invitation to the chief of Airbus Industrie, even though the European consortium's profitability -- like the Lippo Group's -- hinges on major issues of trade policy (including China policy) that are decided in the Oval Office. 
But bring in the Thai-Chinese chief of Ban Chang, the huge Thai conglomerate and one of the largest investors in China, and suddenly accusations fly.
In the last few weeks, though, even some Asian-American business leaders admit to wondering whether they -- with the Democratic National Committee's direct encouragement -- raised the flag of "Asia bashing" too quickly. 
"No one in the Asian-American community can say this publicly, but in private a lot of the talk you hear is that there are some real problems with the way access was being sold," said one Asian-American banker, who insisted, of course, that he couldn't talk publicly.
But questions of prejudice aside, Americans and Asians clearly hold radically different views about where global power lies. 
American suspicions of "Asian money" these days are partly rooted in the sense that American jobs are still flowing across the Pacific. 
Very few people in America may have heard of the rich entrepreneurs whom the President was entertaining at election time, but many share a gut sense that somehow these Asians are pulling the strings of the world economy, building plants in Southern China using family connections (and bribery) that American firms could never match.
The soaring American trade deficit with China, which is quickly overtaking that with Japan, is often cited as proof that this is a battle the United States is losing. 
In this view, the Asian money flowing into the nation's political system is intended to spread that web of influence -- much like the Japanese investment in the 80's.
But Asian executives at the summit meeting President Clinton attended in Manila last November hardly flaunted their power. 
They worry about the future of Hong Kong when it reverts to China on July 1, wonder if China and Indonesia will descend into political chaos after their current leaders die, and maintain that America is in command of the world economic system. 
They talk about the hidden goals of Washington's trade policies in the same tones that some in Washington talk about Lippo's hidden goals in China. 
And if Washington gets into a prolonged spat with Beijing over human rights, arms proliferation or the pirating of American movies and videos, China's unfettered access to its biggest market, the United States, could be cut off. 
And that would crush ereryone's plans to export from their new base in China.
So if it costs an Asian company a few hundred thousand dollars to keep lines of communication to Washington open, well, that's fine. 
After all, that's a fraction of what is regularly paid to keep a provincial governor happy in southern China, or to keep friendly politicians in office in South Korea.
In America, however, it is unclear whether they are getting their money's worth. 
Perhaps, like the Japanese in the 80's, they will soon decide this is a bad investment. 
The reality of life in Washington is that many of the policies sought by Asian business executives -- including separating China's human-rights record from trade -- are generally also sought by American global giants like Boeing, I.B.M. and Bechtel.
Of course, American and Asian corporate interests often diverge. 
But for now, it's still hard to figure out exactly what the Asian executives are buying, beyond intelligence, some nice pictures for the office wall and a lot of publicity they now wish they didn't have.

file: Papers Show White House Staff Favored a China Satellite Permit.txt
text:
ï»¿
The White House released a trove of internal documents today showing that President Clinton approved the Chinese launching of an American satellite last February after his top staff advised him that the economic and diplomatic advantages outweighed the opposition of Federal prosecutors.
The prosecutors had warned that the approval would jeopardize their investigation into the satellite maker's earlier, unauthorized help to China's rocket program, the President was told in the memorandums.
The documents, demanded by Congress, were made available to the news media today by the White House, which argued that they showed that the President, while aware of the risks, approved the launching on the basis of policy debate and not because the chairman of the satellite company, the Democratic Party's largest personal contributor, was pressing hard for a decision.
"I think the decision was the correct one," Mr. Clinton said in remarks in the White House Rose Garden, where he came to talk about the highway bill that passed Congress today, but was clearly prepared for questions on China. 
It "was based on what I thought was in the national interest and supportive of our national security," he said.
The President said the Justice Department's concerns were evaluated and balanced against the views of all the other participating departments, who "concluded that, on balance, we should go forward."
But Republicans questioned the President's decision and promised further inquiries. 
They said a preliminary review of the 394 documents the White House released raised troubling questions about Mr. Clinton's decision to overrule Justice Department objections to a Presidential waiver to allow the launching.
"There's no question there were plenty of red flags at the time," said Representative Christopher Cox, the California Republican who will head a House select committee examining the China issues.
The documents paint a fascinating portrait of the intense struggles surrounding Mr. Clinton last February as he weighed whether to allow the satellite launching and ignore the pleas of prosecutors and the probable outrage from some in Congress.
A top State Department official had warned White House staff members that the satellite company, Loral Space and Communications, engaged in "unlawful" and "criminal" activity by providing valuable help to the Chinese rocket program.
And the chairman of the company, Bernard L. Schwartz, combed a White House dinner on Feb. 
5, looking for Samuel R. Berger, the national security adviser, to plead for a decision on the satellite launching, a decision worth tens of millions of dollars to the company.
As it all played out, with the company arguing it needed an immediate decision, the senior White House staff were concluding that the President's broader strategy of engaging China should not be endangered by blocking the launching.
"We believe that the advantages of this project outweigh this risk, and that we can effectively rebut criticism of the waiver," said the memorandum to Mr. Clinton, dated Feb. 
12, 1998, and signed by Mr. Berger, Larry Stein, the Congressional liaison, and Daniel K. Tarullo, assistant to the President for international economic policy.
"The project is in the national interest," the memorandum said, "because the development of China's civil communications infrastructure will promote access by Chinese citizens in remote areas to people and ideas in democratic societies."
In addition, it said, "the current project also will help maintain the competitiveness of U.S. satellite exporters in a most important satellite market."
The President's top advisers warned him in the memorandum that his approval might be seen as letting Loral's space subsidiary "off the hook on criminal charges for its unauthorized assistance to China's ballistic missile program."
But they also said it would be unfair to "penalize" Loral by denying a license "before they have even been charged with any crime."
On Feb. 
13, Loral's lobbyist, Tom Ross, pleaded with Mr. Berger for a "prompt decision" and mentioned how Mr. Schwartz "had intended to raise this issue with you" a week earlier at the dinner for Prime Minister Tony Blair of Britain "but missed you in the crowd."
White House spokesmen noted that Mr. Ross's letter was dated the day after the staff memorandum to the President recommending approval of the launching.
On Feb. 
18, the President approved the deal.
Mr. Schwartz was the largest personal contributor to the Democrats last year and has donated almost $1 million since 1995. 
His name is not in the memorandums sent to the President for his approval.
Mr. Ross, Loral's vice president of government relations, said today that he "considered it perfectly proper for me to make an inquiry on the timing of the issue."
He said it would also have been proper for Mr. Schwartz to have asked for a prompt decision because "there is a distinction between that and demanding a favorable decision."
The documents were made available to the House International Relations Committee on the eve of a long holiday weekend. 
The committee requested them on May 7 after a story in The New York Times disclosed the President's decision despite the objections of Justice Department officials. 
A week later, it was also disclosed that a China aerospace executive funnelled almost $100,000 from the Chinese military to the Democratic Party in 1996, according to an account by a Democrat fund-raiser, Johnny Chung, who is cooperating with investigators after pleading guilty to campaign-related bank and tax fraud charges.
The chairman of the House committee, Representative Benjamin A. Gilman, Republican of New York, said today that the documents raised "some troubling questions that will have to be pursued," and that the committee was awaiting further documents from the White House and other agencies.
The Justice Department is also weighing whether to investigate the President's approval for Loral, and if so, whether it should be done by its own campaign finance task force or an independent counsel, law-enforcement officials said.
The new documents complicate that decision because two senior Justice officials have played dual roles: advising the White House against Mr. Clinton's approval for Loral and deciding now whether to investigate that approval.
Today's release of documents comes as Mr. Clinton's policy on Chinese satellite launches is caught up in a cross current of diplomatic, legal and political issues.
In a month, the President is going to China, where he hopes to improve space cooperation with Beijing. 
But the House of Representatives this week may have upset his summit plans by overwhelmingly adopting amendments that ban future exports of American satellites to China.
Republicans said such exports may jeopardize national security by giving China the ability to learn space technology that can improve its ballistic missile capabilities.
The Clinton Administration argues that stringent safeguards insure that national security is protected and that American satellite companies need to maintain their competitiveness in an important global market, points made in the memorandum to Mr. Clinton. China, which offered low-cost services, launches about 10 percent of American satellites.
At the center of the debate is the criminal case that prompted prosecutors to express their concerns to the White House. 
In the spring of 1996, Loral officials helped the Chinese investigate why a rocket carrying a Loral satellite exploded. 
The company acknowledged that it turned information over to the Chinese without telling the Government.
The President was told by his advisers that Loral "acknowledges that an unauthorized transfer of technical information took place but Justice has not decided whether it will take criminal action against" the company.
"Justice believes that a jury would not convict once it learned that the President had found" the latest Loral satellite launching "to be in the national interest," the memorandum stated.
As a result of sanctions imposed after the killings at Tiananmen Square in 1989, satellites can be exported to China only through a Presidential waiver demonstrating that the launch is in the national interest.
Loral maintains its officials did nothing wrong. 
A Loral fact sheet released this week said that all its scientists did was an analysis that confirmed the findings of Chinese scientists.
But the State Department's top defense trade regulator, Will Lowell, told a White House lawyer that Loral "went beyond analysis to telling cause of failure and how to prevent," according to the lawyer's notes of the conversation.
Mr. Lowell also told the lawyer that he thought Loral's behavior was "criminal" and "unlawful," but he added that even though the company was "likely to be indicted," it was "hard to pull the plug" on a license without an indictment.
The cost of delaying approval for Loral -- which might have cleared up the question of whether the company would be indicted -- was estimated by White House aides at $4-6 million, the documents show.
In the end, the concerns of regulators like Mr. Lowell and Justice Department prosecutors from the criminal division were given less weight than the views of top-ranking political appointees and the diplomatic and commercial imperatives.
On Feb. 
13, White House counsel Charles F.C. 
Ruff wrote a memorandum to Mr. Berger, the National Security Adviser, noting the failure of the highest officials at the Justice Department to weigh in on the satellite decision. 
And curiously, the documents released today contained no written communications from anyone at the Justice Department.
"The department had every opportunity to weigh in against the waiver at the highest levels and elected not to do so," Mr. Ruff wrote, adding that Mr. Berger could himself balance "the national security and criminal justice interests."
Mr. Berger already had. 
A day earlier he and other top advisers recommended that the President go forward with his approval.
Meanwhile, the Justice Department, despite its earlier concerns, is proceeding with the investigation, officials said.

file: Paris Journal_An Old Prediction Speeds France_s Annual Exodus.txt
text:
ï»¿
Summertime, with all France ready to head off on vacation in le grand depart -- but will anybody be around for la rentree in September?
Ominous signs are everywhere. 
It's the end of the second millennium; the moon is about to blot out the sun all across a swatch of northern Europe on Aug. 
11, and apocalyptic traffic jams are about to make the French sorry they all insist on starting their five-week annual vacations on July 14, the Gallic Fourth of July.
But France is also the birthplace of Michel de Nostre-Dame, better known as Nostradamus, and he had dire predictions for 1999.
Nostradamus had dire predictions for just about every year since his death in 1566, at least for those who find ways of reading them into his sometimes Delphic verse -- people like Paco Rabanne, the fashion designer.
"From mid-July to after the 11th of August," Mr. Rabanne told Le Figaro's weekly magazine last month, "I am recommending to all my friends to stay at least 60 kilometers from the capital."
Nostradamus, by Mr. Rabanne's reading, had foreseen space travel and predicted that the battered Mir space station would crash down onto Paris and leave much of it looking like Hiroshima in 1945.
In a country where book publishers seem willing to slap out any paperback at all as long as a celebrity's name is on the cover, that was enough to make Mr. Rabanne a best-selling author this year, with a book called "1999, Fire From the Heavens," published by Editions Michel Lafon.
Since the book was written, though, Russia has decided to keep Mir up in the heavens, at least through next January, so perhaps it will be the fire next time. 
But with at least 10 books on Nostradamus still on the shelves, Mr. Rabanne's has plenty of company this summer.
What makes this year especially portentous, and sent Mr. Rabanne into Chicken Little mode, is a Nostradamus quatrain that could be translated from 16th-century French this way:
In thousand nine-hundred ninety-nine, seven months,
A king of terror will come from heaven
To revive the great King of Angouleme,
Setting Mars to reign before and then.
According to Jean-Charles de Fontbrune, a Nostradamus scholar, the King of Angouleme originally meant Attila the Hun, whose advance into Gaul in 451 was supposedly stopped near the city of Angouleme in west-central France.
Nowadays, as Mr. de Fontbrune sees it, the phrase must refer to China, and Mars, the god of war, was much in evidence in Iraq and later Kosovo through the first six months of 1999.
A horrified frisson went through Paris in May, therefore, when a United States plane mistakenly bombed the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade, an act that threatened to bring China into NATO's war against Yugoslavia -- real Armageddon.
"Nostradamus predicted it!" a wealthy real-estate speculator in the tony 16th arrondissement exclaimed in horror, before heading off as Mr. Rabanne recommended to his country house a safe distance from Paris.
"If by the 30th of June, 'seven months,' President Clinton has not stopped hostilities in Yugoslavia," Mr. de Fontbrune warned, "the Chinese and the Russians are going to intervene."
As it happened, Russia's diplomatic intervention helped persuade President Slobodan Milosevic of Yugoslavia to accept NATO's conditions -- perhaps Mr. Milosevic knew that Attila the Hun had also razed Belgrade -- and the bombing stopped before "seven months" arrived.
As for whether Mars will reign after this month, you don't have to be Nostradamus to predict that Kosovo will not be humanity's last war. 
Scholars who take Nostradamus seriously as the historian and poet he was say he sometimes had to write in elliptical terms, because the Renaissance was a capricious and dangerous time. 
In France people were being massacred by the thousands in religious wars for what was considered blasphemy.
Seen in this light, the verse about 1999 takes on a quite different meaning. 
Louis Schlosser, author of a biography of Nostradamus, thought he was referring to 1559, not 1999, and to the death of King Henry II of France that July.
Roger Prevost, a French scholar, explains it differently. 
The king of terror in the first two verses, he says, is a French pun on Geoffrey (Geoffroi rhymes with effroi, literary French for fear or terror), a reference to Geoffroi or Godefroi de Bouillon, a Crusader who conquered Jerusalem in July 1099.
The great King of Angouleme, then, is simply Francis I of France, known as Francis of Angouleme and King of France from 1515 to 1547. 
Nostradamus, the King's loyal subject, was just paying tribute.
In Mr. Prevost's book on the subject, "Nostradamus, Myth and Reality: A Historian in the Time of Astrologers," published this year by Editions Robert Laffont, he suggested reading all these verses not as prophecies but as fascinating glimpses into a bygone era and milieu.
As far as July 1999 is concerned he wrote, "when this book appears we'll be about to find out."

file: Party Paper in China Makes Rare Mention of _89 Protests.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Communist Party's flagship newspaper made a rare reference today to the 1989 democracy movement in Tiananmen Square, calling the violent crushing of those demonstrations essential to the protection of national stabilityI and economic progress.
The editorial in People's Daily, "Unswervingly Maintaining Social StabilityI," cited the NATO attack on the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade last month as evidence that "hostile forces in the West have never abandoned their scheme to ruin China."
History has demonstrated, the editorial added, that the "firm and resolute suppression of the political turmoil in Beijing" in 1989 protected "national independence, dignity, security and stabilityI and insured the sustained, healthy development of economic reforms and opening to the outside world."
"China must steadfastly avoid letting a disturbance created by outside forces spark internal chaos," said the editorial, the latest installment in a campaign mounted after the embassy bombing, to paint Western human rights concerns as a plot to undermine China's progress.
Oddly, the English-language version of the editorial distributed by the official New China News Agency omitted the direct references to the demonstrations in 1989.
On the surface, life goes on as normal here and elsewhere in China. 
But there are many signs of official nervousness as the June 4 anniversary of the crackdown on the student-led demonstrations approaches.
Some 80 democracy advocates around the country have been detained, at least temporarily, by the police in the last month, and 28 remained in custody today, according to the Information Center of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China, a small watchdog group in Hong Kong. 
The detainees included seven people in the southern city of Hangzhou who had planned to commemorate the 1989 demonstrations and were held today, the information center said.
In Beijing, in luxury hotels and some private compounds housing foreigners, CNN service on cable television has been temporarily cut off, apparently because the channel is transmitting numerous programs on the legacy of the demonstrations and their suppression. 
But almost no Chinese have access to CNN, anyway.
In another action that largely affects foreign visitors, Hong Kong and foreign newspapers delivered to hotels here and in Shanghai have been arriving with articles about China cut out by Government censors. 
But journalists and diplomats with subscriptions received complete nonexcised copies, as usual.
One popular Chinese-language Internet chatroom, at www.sohu.com, announced that it was shutting down for 10 days, ostensibly to "improve the system," but possibly under pressure to avoid discussions about the 1989 crackdown in which army troops killed hundreds of civilians.
Tiananmen Square itself, where hundreds of thousands of students and others chanted and camped, has been closed at least through the month, officially for renovations in preparation for the 50th-anniversary celebrations in October of the Communist victory. 
But extra police officers are in the streets, and hundreds of people involved with the 1989 movement have in recent weeks received visits or calls to warn them not to speak with foreign journalists or to engage in disruptive activities.

file: PERSONAL HEALTH_Tea_ The Latest Health Food (but Hold the Clotted Cream).txt
text:
ï»¿
Coffee lovers, take heed. 
For the sake of your health, you might consider switching at least some of those daily cups of java for tea. 
Not herbal tea but "real" tea -- green tea, black tea, Chinese tea, fruit-flavored tea, with or without caffeine, lemon, milk or sugar.
As long as the leaves come from the plant Camellia sinensis, tea will contain potent antioxidant chemicals that have been linked to protection against major diseases like cancer and heart disease. 
Even the caffeine in tea may be somewhat beneficial, emerging evidence suggests.
The popularity of tea in Japan and China may partly explain why heart disease rates are so much lower in the Far East than in Western countries.
Â 
The Truths of Tea
There are three types of real tea: green, black and oolong. 
Green tea, which is most popular in Japan and China, has in recent years found a small but growing following here as word about its potential health benefits has leaked out. 
It is the least processed of all the teas, made by quickly steaming or heating the leaves of Camellia sinensis.
Black tea, by far the most popular in Western countries and India, is prepared by exposing tea leaves to air. 
That exposure causes oxidation, which turns them a deep brown and intensifies their flavor. 
The leaves are then crushed. 
According to Dr. Gary Beecher, food chemist with the United States Department of Agriculture, black tea contains as much of the protective chemicals as green tea, though the form may differ.
Oolong is between the two: more processed than green tea but less so than black tea. 
It is exposed to heat, light and crushing for less time than black tea.
Herbal teas, on the other hand, come from a wide variety of plants other than the tea plant and may include roots and flowers as well as leaves. 
Most herbal teas do not possess the antioxidant properties of real tea, although they may contain certain other biologically active compounds. 
A few also contain caffeine.
Contrary to common belief, green tea has as much caffeine as black tea, though all teas have less caffeine than drip-brewed coffee. 
A typical eight-ounce cup of tea prepared from one tea bag brewed for three to five minutes contains 40 milligrams of caffeine, compared with 100 milligrams in a cup of brewed coffee.
The caffeine content of tea can range from 20 to 90 milligrams a cup, depending on the blend of tea leaves, method of preparation and length of brewing time, whereas a cup of coffee may contain from 60 to 180 milligrams of caffeine. 
Decaffeinated tea, like decaffeinated coffee, has about 4 milligrams of caffeine per cup.
Instant teas and prepared iced teas, which can be purchased with or without caffeine, may be too highly processed to contain much of the protective chemicals.
Throughout the 1990's researchers exploring the health effects of tea have gradually accumulated highly suggestive, though not definitive, evidence for tea's ability to prevent or ameliorate several common serious diseases.
Â 
Making It Healthy
Most of the presumed health effects are related to polyphenols, chemicals that act as antioxidants, preventing cell damage caused by highly reactive molecules called free radicals. 
The polyphenols in tea, especially green tea, are more potent antioxidants than well-known antioxidants like vitamins C and E, experts say.
The bulk of evidence for tea's health benefits comes from studies in animals that were treated with amounts of tea polyphenols equivalent to what might be consumed by a regular tea drinker.
For example, in a study published in April, a research team from Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine added green tea polyphenols to the drinking water of 18 mice and none to the water of 18 other mice. 
All the animals were then injected with a substance that causes a condition like rheumatoid arthritis in people. 
Of the group that got the polyphenols, only eight developed arthritis; in the group that got plain water, all but one developed arthritis.
With regard to cancer, several dozen animal studies indicate that the polyphenols and related compounds in tea are protective, especially against cancers of the oral cavity and digestive tract. 
Tea chemicals are believed to act by preventing damage to DNA that could result in a loss of control over cell growth.
According to cancer researchers at Rutgers University College of Pharmacy, "Tea is one of the few agents that can inhibit carcinogenesis at the initiation, promotion and progression stages."
However, they added, it is not yet known how effective tea can be in preventing human cancer, what dose is most effective or what is the best way to administer the active compounds.
Studies in people have yielded inconsistent results, in part because in some studies other factors may have entered into the picture to distort the findings, like the heat of the tea and the use of tobacco or alcohol. 
In one well-designed study conducted in Beijing, China, among 59 patients with precancerous mouth lesions, those treated for six months with capsules of oxidized green tea polyphenols experienced a decrease in the size of the lesions; in the untreated group, the lesions got larger.
A study of more than 35,000 postmenopausal women in Iowa suggested that women who drank two or more cups of tea daily were less likely to develop cancers of the digestive tract and urinary tract. 
However, no protection was found against other cancers.
Likewise, a study in the Netherlands among 58,000 men and 62,000 women found no link between tea drinking and a reduced risk of cancers of the lung, breast or colon. 
However, in a study in laboratory mice and rats, Dr. Fung-Lung Chung of the American Health Foundation found that both green and black tea and caffeine given in drinking water protected the animals against lung cancer caused by a major carcinogen in tobacco.
Another study in mice showed that both green and black tea inhibited the growth of both malignant and nonmalignant skin tumors. 
And a study in rats conducted by Dr. Roderick H. Dashwood of Oregon State University showed that both green and black tea inhibited the formation of precancerous lesions in the colon.
With regard to heart disease and stroke, a study of 1,330 Chinese men found a significantly lower level of serum cholesterol and triglycerides among those who drank more than 10 cups of green tea a day.
Some studies in Western countries have indicated that tea drinkers may be less likely to develop heart disease and stroke.
A Harvard study by Dr. Howard Sesso indicated that people who drank one or more cups of black tea a day were half as likely to suffer a heart attack as those who did not drink tea, regardless of other risk factors for heart disease.
However, much more research is needed to sort out the effects of tea on blood vessel diseases as well as cancer. 
For example, in a study of 880 Japanese men, researchers found that heavy tea drinkers were also likely to eat more fruits and vegetables, which may account for or contribute to their lower risk of heart disease and cancer.
Still, the evidence to date is sufficiently suggestive to prompt the National Cancer Institute to conduct studies of the capacity of the biologically active chemicals in green and black tea to curb the development of cancer in people at high risk for developing cancers of the colon, lung, esophagus and skin.
And Japanese researchers have suggested that the ability of green tea and its chemicals to inhibit a substance called tumor necrosis factor-alpha may make it useful in treating a wide range of health problems that include Crohn's disease, multiple sclerosis, malaria and sepsis as well as rheumatoid arthritis.

file: PERSPECTIVES_Priming the Pump for New Middle-Income Housing.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE tenants living in a year-old apartment building called the Bristol in the Flushing section of Queens include a 26-year-old registered nurse free from the parental nest for the first time, a 45-year-old teacher who left her husband as well as her apartment when she moved to the Bristol with her two young children, and a Chinese astrologer.
The astrologer is Yung Yuan Lai, 63, who moved into a fifth-floor, two-bedroom apartment with his wife, Mei Chu, and two children in their 20's. 
Astrology is an honored profession in China, Mr. Lai noted, although 30 percent of his clients are Americans or other non-Asians.
Those proportions are close to those of the demographics at the Bristol itself, a 60-unit building at 138-49 Barclay Avenue, near Main Street. 
The Bluestone Organization, the builder-owner, says that 60 percent of the tenants are Asian, mainly of Chinese descent.
The more important tenant characteristic from a housing perspective is that 80 percent of the tenants are middle-income. 
As a 1990's housing product in New York City, the Bristol is a rare specimen -- a new rental apartment house outside Manhattan. 
It was built with tax-exempt bond financing, a method typically used only in Manhattan, where market-rate rents are high enough to permit the project to support low-income occupancy. 
Twenty percent of the tenants must be low income under this "80-20" program.
But now New York City has come forward with a new housing loan program, which, if successful, should generate about a dozen new middle-income apartment buildings outside prime Manhattan locations. 
Unlike the 80-20 program, it has no requirement for partial low-income occupancy. 
From the reaction of builders and lenders it could provide the impetus for construction in such locations as Flushing and Forest Hills in Queens, Park Slope and Carroll Gardens in Brooklyn, and Manhattan Valley and East Harlem in Manhattan.
The program is run by the city's Housing Development Corporation, a state-chartered public benefit corporation that provides financing for multifamily housing within the city. 
It was announced in late October, just before the mayoral election. 
Richard T. Roberts, who is chairman of the board of the corporation as well as Commissioner of the Department of Housing Preservation and Development, called the program a model for future city assistance to new multifamily construction.
The financing, which will come from long-term taxable bonds, will not impinge on the capacity of city agencies to promote economic development through tax-exempt borrowings. 
And, since H.D.C. bonds have an AA rating from Standard and Poor's, the housing will get the benefit of interest rates somewhat lower than current conventional mortgage rates.
In addition, the development corporation is prepared to offer a direct low-interest loan for each apartment built to further help make the apartments affordable. 
This subsidy is expected to average $15,000 an apartment and be offered at 1 to 3 percent interest over the term of the loan, which may be as long as 35 years. 
The amount will vary depending on the location of the project and the rent-generating capacity of the market in that area.
Eligible projects will be those with at least 20 apartments, produced either through new construction, the substantial rehabilitation of an existing residential building or the conversion, on an as-of-right basis, of an existing nonresidential building. 
In Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx or Staten Island, the property can be in any location where multifamily development is permissible. 
In Manhattan the site must be north of 110th Street in the case of new construction, or north of 96th Street in a rehabilitation.
The income limits on renters -- or buyers if the project is done as a limited-equity co-op -- are the same as those that apply to Mitchell-Lama middle-income housing, last produced in the late 70's. 
In households of one or two persons, annual income can be as high as seven times the annual rent, or as much as eight times the annual rent for larger families, up to a maximum of 250 percent of median income in New York City, or $118,500 for a family of four at present.
There are also rent or carrying-charge limits -- $800 for a studio, $1,050 for a 1-bedroom, $1,350 for a 2-bedroom and $1,750 for a 3-bedroom. 
A family earning as little of $40,000 a year might be able to afford a $1,000-a-month 1-bedroom apartment, paying 30 percent of annual income as rent. 
But the income limit for eligibility would be much higher, $84,000 a year. 
Because of the sites that are likely to developed, most tenants will probably be at an income level well below the maximum theoretically allowed.
TO get the program started, the Housing Development Corporation has set aside $15 million, which at an average of $15,000 a unit would finance about 1,000 new middle-income housing units. 
The money comes from the corporation's reserves built up from housing-finance operations, said Barbara Udell, president of the Housing Development Corporation, and if they are used successfully a second phase will follow.
Charles A. Brass, the corporation's vice president for development, said that preliminary responses from builders who have worked with city programs in the past has been positive. 
"We're basically looking for housing for families earning from $35,000 to $75,000 a year," Mr. Brass said.
The challenge for builders, several of them said in interviews, will be to find sites at low enough prices that are capable of attracting tenants who can pay, say, $1,300 a month for a 2-bedroom apartment. 
Most hopeful are those situations where builders already hold the property and are close to feasibility already.
"It's geared toward places where the market is at $1,300 to $1,600 a month and not many neighborhoods have that," said Ronald Moelis, a partner in in L & M Equity Ltd., a developer based in Larchmont, N.Y., that has participated in various city-assisted housing programs.
"If you can find a renovation project you might have a better shot at making the numbers work than in new construction," said Barry Zelikson, director of development at Sparrow Construction Company in the Bronx, another builder.
Michael D. Lappin, president of the Community Preservation Corporation, a major citywide construction lender, predicted the program would provide an opportunity for smaller, efficient builder-owners. 
"This could produce some affordable housing," he said.
For multifamily housing, that would be progress. 
Private multifamily housing production outside Manhattan has been nil in the 90's, said Frank P. Braconi, executive director of the Citizens Housing and Planning Council, although 20,000 units were created by city-assisted rehabilitations of vacant buildings, typically for low-income occupancy. 
The council's figures are compiled from city agencies. 
The Department of City Planning, which also reports on housing completions, has not yet released any data for the post-1995 period.
For builders generally, the biggest problem will be finding sites at a low enough cost in neighborhoods capable of attracting people able to pay $1,200 to $1,500 a month in rent. 
Typically, even when such sites exist owners tend to raise the asking price for land once a new subsidy program becomes available, again throwing feasibility into question. 
But sometimes builders already own the land. 
"We've had a site in Park Slope for 12 years where we could do 50 units as of right," said David Gaunt, a principal in Premiere Management and Development Company, based in Manhattan. 
"It's hard to pencil out a rental project. 
We're doing an evaluation now to see if this new program will work for us."
One likely user is the Bluestone Organization, the builder-owner of the Bristol in Flushing and nine other rentals in Queens and Great Neck, L.I., over the last 30 years. 
"We have a site in Forest Hills where we think it will work," said Harold Bluestone, a principal in the organization. 
"I can't disclose the location yet."

file: Photographic Evidence.txt
text:
ï»¿
AN EMPIRE OF WOMEN
By Karen Shepard.
262 pp. 
New York:
G. P. Putnam's Sons. 
$24.95.
What should a mother do or be?
How much does an artist owe her family?
Given that every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way, would such households flourish or deteriorate if men were removed from the picture?
These are among the inconvenient questions raised by "An Empire of Women," Karen Shepard's delicate yet searing first novel. 
As it opens, Cameron Arneaux is driving from Manhattan to rural Virginia with her mother, Sumin, and a 6-year-old Chinese girl called Alice. 
Alice's mother is Cameron's best friend from graduate school. 
She has since lost her visa and returned to China, but still wants her daughter to be raised in America. 
The only solution is to grant Cameron temporary guardianship of Alice until the visa problem can be worked out.
Cameron's destination is the cabin where she was photographed as a child by her French-Chinese grandmother, Celine, in a notorious series of portraits. 
Celine's reputation rests on three books of photographs: of Cam at ages 1, 6 and 12. 
Like Sally Mann's work (which Shepard has acknowledged as an inspiration), Celine's family portraits are sexually provocative. 
"A 12-year-old in heavy makeup wears a traditional Chinese silk dress. 
It is several sizes too large. 
She holds the excess fabric bunched at her hip. 
Beneath the dress, she is naked."
In another, she touches herself. 
The images also have a political edge. 
In one photograph, 6-year-old Cam, wearing only the jacket from a Red Guard's uniform, has been asked by Celine to spread her legs. 
To further incriminate political torturers, Celine photographs her naked daughter cruelly bound to a tree: "She looks over her shoulder . . . almost to the camera. 
The rope goes around her wrists and forearms in X's, like the straps on Roman sandals."
Sumin is the result of Celine's affair with a Chinese painter, a disposable male never told of the pregnancy. 
Cam has likewise been deprived of contact with (or even much knowledge of) her father, a Japanese man who briefly served as her grandmother's assistant. 
Alice's father, too, is "nowhere to be found."
Though fatherless, Cam has been spoiled, relying on her looks and Celine's checkbook to make her way in the world. 
"Every so often, it bothered her that she depended on that money. 
It didn't bother her enough to make her do anything about it," perhaps because of all the time she spends "looking like she had spent no time at all thinking about how she looked."
While Cam is a striking example of young, bitchy cool, in Celine the author
has created a cryogenic empress of self-absorption, and the reader cannot take his eyes off her. 
Not since the seven-foot-tall hairless Judge Holden in Cormac McCarthy's "Blood Meridian" have we met a figure of such magisterial narcissism. 
"You are not a mother," Celine tells her granddaughter. 
"I did not raise you to be a mother. 
You're a model; the vessel of viewers' feelings, not the caretaker of those feelings."
When her daughter threatens to expose a mortifying secret, Celine chides her: "Don't pursue this. 
It's ugly. 
It's pointless. 
And it's beneath even you."
How did this woman acquire the touch of dry ice?
Shepard provides several hints. 
"Her pregnancy had been trouble-free, but her labor and delivery so agonized that she still hadn't fully forgiven her daughter."
Celine is given to wondering how photographers like Julia Cameron (for whom she named Cam) accomplished what they did with "all those children" around them. 
As for herself: "First and foremost, I was un imagier. 
Maternity found time when it had to."
For her daughter, "there would never be the knowledge of what it was to be desperate over an image. 
There was no passion, no unadulterated dedication. 
. . . Her passivity filled me with contempt."
Cameron, Celine's pet, has become a painter -- or at least obtained an M.F.A. 
-- but what she's focused on now, at the age of 24, is a child. 
Because of her physical beauty, "men thought that going out with her would be more magical than it actually turned out to be."
And without a man with whom to conceive a child, she becomes so neurotically attached to her new maternal role that she schemes to keep Alice and her mother on separate continents. 
All three Arneaux women, in fact, prove almost psychotically ruthless in their need to be loved by this child, regardless of what might be in Alice's best interests.
Because of Celine's stature as an artist and her kowtowing to the Chinese government after the Tiananmen Square bloodbath, she has the leverage to determine whether Alice's mother gets her visa renewed, as well as the money to finance whatever makeshift family might be forced into being. 
To enhance the suspense, Shepard front-loads her novel with a dossier on each of the women, followed by neutral third-person accounts of their week at the cabin and italicized descriptions of Celine's photographs.
Celine's sections are told in a frosty first person, allowing her to reflect on her girlhood in China and Paris. 
She recalls in graphic detail Chiang Kai-shek's massacre of Communist-led union members in 1927 and, more intimately, her mother's bound feet, with their broken toes folded "under the sole."
She reports overhearing her French grandmother speak to her father about the distress caused by mixed-blood offspring. 
"You must not," she demands, "have any more children."
Certainly not girls, is the clear implication. 
When her father fails to protest, Celine decides her life's course: "I would make them both crumble under the iron evidence that I was someone who could belong anywhere."
At the dinner to celebrate Celine's 75th birthday, Cam asks her mother and grandmother, "Did you want sons?"
Celine avoids the question. 
And she refuses to answer at all when Sumin asks rhetorically, "What do you call those people so absorbed by one thing that everything else is up for sacrifice?"
Un imagier, we are left to conclude.
In a tautly condensed narrative encompassing disparate time periods, the author's lapidary prose is tainted now and then by an overuse of the pluperfect tense, and the sheer number of feminine pronouns leaves a few referents unclear. 
Yet Shepard (who is herself Chinese-American, and the granddaughter of the writer Han Suyin) has ably portrayed how obsession with female beauty can disfigure not only families and individuals but cultures and governments. 
Drawing on the weight of mixed blood, of Celine's battle against being the wrong class and sex, Shepard delineates the pathology of movements like the Cultural Revolution as well as the mind-bending challenges facing those who would balance parenthood with the making of art.
The novel's brief final chapter is shocking but feels inevitable, as the story makes ironically tangible the disappointment felt in many Chinese families when a daughter arrives, not to mention the seething resentment of those unwanted girls. 
When Celine presents Alice with a gift of carved jade, to confer upon her "the strength, the good fortune, the luck that our ancestors wished only for boys," we begin to understand how they feel.

file: Ping-Pong Diplomacy Revisited_Players Big and Small Recall the China Opening of _71.txt
text:
ï»¿
On the salmon-colored carpet of the delegates' lounge of the United Nations, beneath the enormous tapestry of the Great Wall that the Chinese Government sent as a gift in 1974, the Ping-Pong table seemed a little incongruous. 
So did the pairs of middle-aged men and women in shorts or sweatsuits doing paddle-to-paddle combat, engaging in forehand slams and backhand chops to the applause of well-dressed onlookers. 
So, against that backdrop, did Henry Kissinger.
But to those who gathered there Thursday evening to celebrate one of the more remarkable chapters in diplomatic history, the scene was a perfectly apt reminder that in 1971, an American table-tennis team visited China and thawed relations between two stubborn superpowers that had been frozen in rigid enmity for more than 20 years.
The American visit (which the Chinese reciprocated by coming here a year later), brought two cultures face to face for the first time in a generation, and not without mutual astonishment. 
But more important, it initiated the era of what became known as "Ping-Pong diplomacy."
Three months after the 15 American table-tennis players and officials returned home, Mr. Kissinger, then President Richard M. Nixon's national security adviser, traveled to Beijing (the city formerly known as Peking) for talks with the Chinese Prime Minister, Zhou Enlai. 
That October, the Communist Government of the mainland took China's seat in the United Nations from the Nationalist Government on Taiwan; the following year, President Nixon made his own celebrated trip to China, meeting with Zhou and the Communist Party chairman, Mao Zedong.
At the United Nations Thursday night, Mr. Kissinger, speaking in his signature deadpan rumble, recounted for the 200 or so guests -- who included several table-tennis luminaries and Tricia Nixon Cox, one of the former President's daughters -- a little of the history in which he played so central a role.
By the time the Chinese invited the American team, he said, he and President Nixon were already involved in back-channel negotiations to hold talks between the two nations.
Indeed, Zhou had already extended the invitation for an American emissary to visit Beijing, but the Americans had been dilatory in responding. 
The Chinese, he suggested, must have thought the Americans needed prodding, so they took advantage of the fact that the American table-tennis team was playing in a tournament in nearby Japan to send a signal.
"I think Zhou Enlai thought Westerners were slower than the Chinese in mental perception, and didn't think we had understood the message," Mr. Kissinger said. 
"So just as we were drafting a response to the message we had received, we heard he had invited the Ping-Pong team."
Beyond the history being celebrated, Thursday's event, which was organized by the National Committee on United States-China relations, was an occasion for laughter and reminiscing, if not exactly nostalgia; it was more like amazement at what can transpire in a mere quarter-century.
"Everything was different from anything I'd ever seen," said Tim Boggan, an American player, recalling his arrival in Beijing. 
After a wine reception and a few speeches, Mr. Boggan had changed from a jacket and tie into a sweatsuit, and was jogging in place in anticipation of playing a mixed-doubles exhibition. 
"The streets were different," he said. 
"The food was different. 
The people, of course, were different. 
The bicycles were different."
Connie Sweeris, an American who also played in an exhibition Thursday, was 23 when she went to China in 1971; she said she had been basically unaware of the significance of the visit until it was over.
"When we came out, it was news all over the world," she said. 
Ms. Sweeris, who now runs a preschool in Grand Rapids, Mich., still remembers that at dinner one night, out of politeness more than inclination, she drank a toast with a beverage apparently popular in China.
"After I drank, they poured some out of the glass, and lit it up," she said. 
"That was interesting."
To this day, she has no idea what she had been drinking.
The Chinese, more than the Americans, remembered apprehensions.
"I knew they would be unlike any other games I'd ever played," said Zheng Minzhi, 51, speaking through an interpreter. 
"I knew their significance and my responsibilities. 
I knew I was not only there to play, but more important, to achieve what cannot be achieved through proper diplomatic channels."
She had also been nervous. 
"I knew nothing about the country or the people," said Ms. Zheng, who now runs a cultural exchange program in Shanghai. 
"What would I say to them?
What would they say to me?
But all these concerns vanished as soon as we met."
It was in late March 1971, when both the American and Chinese teams were playing in the world championships in Nagoya, Japan, that the Chinese extended their surprise invitation. 
Barely two weeks later, the nine American players, four officials and two spouses were in Beijing. 
It seems today like an unremarkable gesture, but it was a landmark moment. 
Relations between the two nations had been nearly stone silent since 1949, when Mao and his Communists drove the Nationalist followers of Chiang Kai-shek from the Chinese mainland.
"As I told the U.S. 
Table Tennis association officials at the time," said Bill Cunningham, who in 1971 was serving in the American Embassy in Tokyo as a "China watcher," " 'the number of people who are going with you to China is greater than the aggregate number of Americans who have been to China since 1950.'
"
The visit was not without its political and cultural clashes. 
One member of the American team, who had been born in South Korea, decided, out of loyalty to his homeland and family, not to make the trip. 
John Tannehill, a 19-year-old from Ohio, declared, much to the embarrassment of the United States, that Mao was "the greatest moral and intellectual leader in the world."
And Glenn Cowan, a long-haired Californian, also 19, who walked China's streets in tie-dyed blue jeans, asked Zhou what he thought of American hippies.
"Youth wants to seek out the truth, and out of this search various forms of change are bound to come," Zhou replied.
But there was little to clash over on Thursday. 
And indeed, Mr. Kissinger, a longtime advocate of American trade with China, declared during his remarks that "all we need now is a Ping-Pong team to give the enterprise a human touch and break down the encrusted debate."
Of course, the Chinese, still the world's best players, have never been much at risk at the Ping-Pong table with the Americans. 
Most of those who visited China in 1971 admitted that even though they lost their matches -- which were against local teams, not the national team -- they felt the Chinese had taken it easy on them, letting them win a few games.
Thursday night, after several good-humored exhibition matches between the older rivals, four members of the current Chinese national team, including Deng Yaping, the women's world champion, and Liu Guoliang, the 1996 men's Olympic champion, stepped up to the Ping-Pong table. 
The speed and power of the play was ratcheted up by several orders of magnitude.
The oohs and aahhs became more audible, just as they had been in 1972, when the Chinese team made its return visit to the United States and played Ping-Pong at the United Nations. 
The New York Times covered the event then, saying "the most sustained applause and loudest shouts of admiration were during the games the Chinese played against one another."
Some things don't change.

file: Playing the China Card_One Company_s Decision, and the Employees Left Behind.txt
text:
ï»¿
American business is rushing into China, and Marilyn C. Grant, 56, who drives a forklift for a fishing reel company, is being left behind.
The Zebco Corporation, Ms. Grant's employer, began moving much of its fishing reel production to China at the end of June. 
Though the company has been under pressure for a long time, the move came just a few weeks after the House passed a measure that would end cold war restrictions on trade with China. 
Most of Zebco's 240 workers will eventually lose their jobs, and Ms. Grant, who has worked at the company's stone headquarters plant in Tulsa for 25 years, expects to be one of them.
"I thought this only happened to other people, and now it's about to happen to me," Ms. Grant said. 
"We're just another company moving over there."
In promoting permanent normal trade relations with China, which the House approved in late May and the Senate is expected to vote on in late July, President Clinton predicted an "almost incalculable" increase in exports of American goods to China. 
But critics say the move also seems likely to encourage exports of some American jobs.
China agreed to open its markets to join the World Trade Organization and to get permanent trading rights in the United States. 
That should make it easier to sell American-made products there. 
But as China modernizes and loosens controls, its lure as a manufacturing base, which has been growing since the early 1980's, is also proving irresistible to many multinationals.
International trade is not a zero-sum "you win, I lose" game, and most economists say that even if some people lose their jobs, the United States reaps big advantages from trade and foreign investment -- like greater productivity, higher corporate profits and cheaper spincast reels. 
But while those substantial benefits are diffused among a vast number of people, the recipients are not celebrating as much as Zebco's workers are seething.
"Our government just handed our jobs to a Communist country," said Brenda McCoy, 50, a Zebco assembly-line veteran who wore a T-shirt to work that bears an image of two Chinese police officers choking a Chinese labor activist. 
"It just makes you feel angry and helpless."
The Chinese claim to have invented the modern fishing device more than a millennium ago by spooling line onto wicker reels. 
But it was the Zero Hour Bomb Company of Tulsa that invented and patented the spincast reel 50 years ago, with line spinning off the end of a stationary spool and remaining, famously, backlash free.
Now called Zebco, the company is a classic American success story. 
Its nearly fool-proof reels helped make fishing perhaps the nation's most popular leisure activity. 
They carry a "Made in America With Pride" logo.
Even in the last decade, as it had to fight competitors that paid much lower hourly wages to workers in Asia, Zebco remained the dominant fishing tackle brand. 
Though Zebco once tested production in Mexico, it pulled back when its Tulsa workers proved they could produce more reels in less time with fewer defects.
The dike finally gave way this year, however. 
With most of Zebco's competitors having already set up fishing tackle plants in China, allowing them to undercut Zebco's prices at Wal-Marts everywhere, Zebco began a year ago to explore the possibility of moving its own lines to China. 
The company found that it could commission Chinese factories to produce and deliver reels to the United States for one-third less than it could make them at home, company officials said.
Zebco decided to make most of its low-end reels at factories in China. 
For now, it will continue to produce more expensive reels in Tulsa, though union officials say the company has put them on notice that it is searching for further ways to lower labor costs, including the possibility of shifting the remaining reels to China, too.
"We made valiant efforts to keep production in the United States," said Kathryn J. Chieger, vice president for corporate and investor relations at the Brunswick Corporation, Zebco's parent company, in Lake Forest, Ill. 
"We just had a flood of product coming from Asia at prices we could not meet."
Even so, the layoffs, which began on June 27, left Zebco's unionized workers, who are mostly women, perplexed and angry.
Sitting in a dimly lit Transport Union Workers hall, the air soured by cigarette smoke and the tables stacked with copies of protest literature that workers distributed at a recent anti-China trade demonstration, Kristie L. Cater said she had expected to retire in the job.
"They kept telling us we were members of the Zebco family," she said with angry sarcasm. 
"I guess they just forgot about that."
As assembly-line factory jobs go, Zebco offers ordinary pay but solid benefits, including Christmas gifts of stock certificates. 
Workers returned the loyalty. 
Turnover was low. 
Some workers also became avid anglers, showing off Zebco's reels at bass and crappie fishing tournaments.
For Linda Allen, 41, an assembly-line supervisor since 1976, work was literally a family affair: her mother and grandmother preceded her in the job.
Those ties started to unravel last year. 
When company executives visited Qingdao, a city in northeastern China, to inspect factories, word leaked out. 
Then, earlier this year, the company pushed assembly-line workers to raise their output by at least 10 percent a month, and China became a cattle prod.
"When we don't get quota, it is another day closer to China taking our jobs," read a Feb. 
3 memorandum from the company that was circulated among employees. 
"So today China won by 45 points."
Ms. Chieger of Brunswick said such memos were intended to show workers what they were up against in terms of competitors that had factories in China.
Still, the shop floor fell into stunned silence one March afternoon when the president of the company read a brief statement as first-shift workers finished their day. 
Zebco was moving some production to China. 
Many of those listening would lose their jobs. 
Zebco reels no longer commanded an "adequate profit," the statement said.
The explanation offended Ms. Grant, the Zebco forklift driver.
Ms. Grant has gray hair and delicate manners. 
As she speaks, her eyes dart about the living room of her A-frame house, which is decorated with porcelain figurines and homemade quilts. 
Only her strong shoulders reveal the heavy lifting she does each day as a Zebco receiver.
"They have never said they don't make a profit," she said. 
"It's that word 'adequate.'
They're going over to China because of greed."
Just a few years from retirement, she said she had begun looking for a new job. 
Tulsa's economy is relatively strong, and she found one prospect. 
But if she got the job -- she worries that a touch of arthritis might hurt her chances -- she would lose her quarter-century seniority and $1.50 of her current $10.63 hourly wage, she said, money she needs to make payments on her secondhand Jeep.
Ms. Cater, 37, a mother of two, said that after she learned of her layoff on the assembly line, she told her 17-year-old daughter to check out community colleges in Tulsa; the higher-priced Colorado school she had been considering was now out of reach.
"I had some savings put away, but that's going to disappear," she said.
At least in theory, the recent steps China has taken to open its markets should be good for American factory workers and farmers by making it easier for companies to export goods to that nation.
But as union leaders argued when they tried unsuccessfully to block the China trade bill in the House, many leading United States companies are like Zebco: they face competitive pressure to save money by producing in China -- often exporting back to the United States -- rather than making goods here to sell in China.
The United States has been losing manufacturing jobs for decades, of course, and dire warnings about the hollowing out of the economy seem a little hyperbolic during the longest expansion in the nation's history. 
Most economists believe that the trade boom of the last decade -- more exports, cheaper imports and the reallocation of jobs to more productive parts of the economy -- forms a central pillar of the 1990's expansion.
Moreover, although the Clinton administration often listed exports as the headline benefit of broadening trade with China, the real advantage for United States companies is probably enhanced rights of investment and ownership there. 
Phone, Internet, bank and insurance companies can buy larger stakes in Chinese counterparts and set up operations in more cities under the terms of China's entry to the World Trade Organization. 
Most companies try to crack the difficult China market by setting up local operations, often using those plants as export production bases as well.
That means that the push into China is not limited to low-wage assemblers. 
Cisco, Intel, Eastman Kodak and Motorola are among the multinational companies that have lobbied Congress to grant China permanent normal trade relations even as they have expanded their manufacturing operations in China, according to a survey by the United States Business and Industry Council, which has been critical of Clinton administration trade policies.
Over all, exports to China will probably grow. 
But the volume of imports is expected to grow even faster. 
The United States International Trade Commission, a government agency, predicts that American exports will increase 10 percent a year if China opens its markets as promised. 
But it also sees China's appeal as a manufacturing base rising fast, bolstering China's exports to the United States by 7 percent annually. 
Since imports from China already exceed exports to China by a wide margin, the gaping $62 billion trade deficit is likely to widen rather than contract.
The way many workers see it, America loses.
Asked whether the United States was better off with cheaper fishing reels or job security for Zebco workers, Ms. Grant reflected for a moment.
"People might like buying things cheaper," she said. 
"But there's a price. 
They're going to wake up one day and find that nothing's made here."
