file: Political Jargon, China_s Barometer, Shows Clear Skies for Art and Sex.txt
text:
ï»¿
Throughout the ideological and cultural worlds, Chinese are again testing the limits, and mostly getting away with it. 
Bold films, plays and books are appearing, newspapers are virtually becoming readable, China's foremost rock-and-roll star is back onstage, and sex and democracy (in that order) are again on the agenda.
The kind and gentle face of Communism, a young woman in a silk blouse who is the anchor for the evening news, has been opening the broadcast in recent weeks with a smile and a greeting that is startling in what it leaves out: "Good evening, viewers."
In one of those signals that the ideological winds have shifted, that the cultural world is opening up, she and the other news anchors have abandoned the previous greeting, "Viewers and comrades, good evening," which the hard-liners have insisted upon for three years.
"Comrades" is not just a word in China but a storm signal. 
Whenever it is hoisted, it is a warning that the cultural commissars are on patrol. 
When it is dropped, people know they can have fun again.
"The Government's lightening up," said a Chinese journalist who has been in political trouble for most of the last few years. 
"We can breathe again."
The novelty of having interesting or entertaining things to do has a political dimension as well. 
A few years ago, when the hard-liners were at the apex of their power, most ordinary workers and young people in towns around the country did not feel so much repressed by Communism as bored by it.
When pressed about the reasons for their alienation, they did not mention the lack of a vote so much as the lack of decent entertainment. 
The problem with the newspapers and television, in the minds of many people, was not so much that they lied but that they were so excruciatingly dull.
Â 
Soaps and Tractors
Now that is changing. 
Romantic soap operas appear on television to supplement the documentaries on fine tractor factories. 
At the cinemas, Hong Kong kung fu films have replaced propaganda movies about gallant Communist Party officials dying young.
Some of the new books and newspaper articles are about politics, including careful calls for more democracy, but the taboo that artists and audiences are breaking with the greatest zeal has to do with nudity and sex.
"Nudity" declared the Culture Ministry newspaper in a huge Chinese character superimposed over a photo of a Western woman's partly uncovered torso. 
The accompanying article was a sober discussion of the lack of nudity in Chinese films, but the photo could scarcely have been more out of place in a newspaper that until recently was a bastion of orthodoxy.
"We're now trying to reform the newspaper and push it onto the market system," said Zhang Zuomin, an editor. 
"Of course there may be a few problems here and there. 
But our direction is the right one."
Theaters in both Beijing and Shanghai have experimented with partial nudity on stage, but in Shanghai a couple simulated love-making behind a glass panel and in Beijing an actress wore flesh-colored underwear. 
In the southern city of Shunde, which has never been renowned for either culture or restraint, a floor show features a young woman disrobing under a strobe light for what purports to be an artistic shower scene.
Â 
Banned but Profitable
Pornography is banned in China and yet is hugely profitable, so publishers have been searching for excuses to peddle lurid material. 
A company in the central city of Wuhan seems to have hit the jackpot with a cheap booklet whose cover is a pastiche of tiny photos of naked buttocks and breasts.
"Selected Cases of Young Women Molested Around the Nation," the headline reads in bold red characters. 
A one-paragraph preface explains that the publisher's purpose is to alert women to the dangers of rape and sexual abuse. 
The next 75 pages provide examples.
"The cultural environment reflects the fact that the overall political atmosphere is more relaxed now, and the economy is doing well," said He Xin, a social critic who is identified with the hard-liners and now appears to be trying to refurbish his image. 
"Sure, the opening may generate some problems, but that's O.K. 
The scale of the problems is very small."
Controls over films have been eased, and Chinese viewers have finally been able to see the movies of Zhang Yimou, the Chinese director whose productions "Judou" and "Raise the Red Lantern" were banned at home while being nominated for Academy Awards in the United States.
Moreover, young film makers are learning that they can largely ignore the authorities. 
When a veteran Chinese actor returned recently to Beijing from an extended stay abroad, he marveled that young people were putting together rock-and-roll films without ever getting approval from anyone.
"That never used to be possible," he told them in awe.
Â 
Dancing in the Aisles
Cui Jian, China's best-known rock musician, was allowed to hold a large concert in Beijing at the end of December for the first time in several years. 
Every seat was taken, and the fans cheered and shouted and danced as the police watched stonily from their seats; just a couple of years ago, a man who tried to dance at a rock concert was dragged off by the police.
The authorities last month allowed Chinese to operate private ham radio stations for the first time, and discos and karaoke bars are sprouting throughout the country. 
Newspapers are starting weekend entertainment sections, and the afternoon tabloids in particular are writing about crime, scandals and pop stars.
Occasionally they even publish news. 
The Communist Party has had to warn the New People's Evening News in Shanghai three times in the last few months about its new-found enthusiasm for publishing scoops.
"Journalism is changing extremely rapidly," said a Chinese journalist who is reporting about changes in the newspaper industry. 
"Plenty of publications will lose their subsidies this year, so all of a sudden they're scrambling for readers. 
They'll never be the same."

file: Political Muscle_ The Only Good Enemy is a Strong_Weak Enemy_When Allies Are Fierce Competitors.txt
text:
ï»¿
LATE in the day on April 6, Energy Secretary Bill Richardson showed up at the White House with some bad news for President Clinton: The leakage of nuclear secrets from America's weapons labs was far worse than anyone thought. 
The Chinese -- whose Prime Minister was on his way to Washington -- may have obtained computer codes that are the key ingredient for simulating nuclear weapons explosions.
It was the kind of chilling discovery that would make for a good Washington thriller. 
But real life is more complex. 
In a speech the next morning, Mr. Clinton said Americans do indeed have reason to worry about China, but not only a muscular China with the latest weapons technology. 
Americans have as much to fear, he argued, from a weak China whose ailing banks and bankrupt enterprises could undermine the world economy.
"If we've learned anything in the last few years from Japan's long recession and Russia's current economic troubles, it is that the weaknesses of great nations can pose as big a challenge to America as their strengths," Mr. Clinton said. 
"So as we focus on the potential challenge that a strong China could present to the United States in the future, let us not forget the risk of a weak China, beset by internal conflicts, social dislocation and criminal activity, becoming a vast zone of instability in Asia."
It was the starkest moment yet in what has emerged as the central foreign policy conundrum in Washington: In an age when your military adversary can also rank among your biggest trading partners, and when your military allies double as your fiercest economic competitors, does America want weak global neighbors or strong ones?
That question is increasingly the subtext of daily debate here, fracturing the Democratic and Republican parties across unusual lines, trapping lawmakers and pundits in circular arguments about where America's true interests lie. 
It helps account for the crazy-quilt of American foreign policy. 
And the problem is made more complex by the fact that the world stage is crowded by weak states -- countries that are jockeying for global influence while struggling to keep from drowning in debt, self-doubt and rising unemployment.
The Japanese, once masters of the art of converting old-fashioned capital into political capital, have watched their global influence decline faster than the price of an office building in the Ginza. 
While Russia tries to flex old muscles in the Balkans, it is submitting to the humiliation of having the International Monetary Fund micro-manage its economy. 
(Last week, spurred by fears that Moscow is feeling dangerously alienated from the West, the I.M.F. finally committed to $4.5 billion in new loans for the nearly insolvent Government, just enough to stave off national default for another year or so.)
The Chinese spies who may be tinkering with the nuclear codes are probably thankful for the fact that, unlike millions of others who toil for the state, their jobs are going to be around for a while. 
And then there are the Europeans, who are slogging through a war in Yugoslavia just at the moment that their economies are slowing and their new currency, the Euro, has fallen 10 percent. 
This was supposed to be the year the continent focused on becoming the next great economic superpower, linked by a single currency and a huge market. 
Instead, one European finance minister visiting Washington last week moaned, "We're spending all our political energy on a 600-year-old problem."
"It's an extraordinary moment that perhaps we haven't seen since the '20's, or at least since the days of the Marshall Plan," said Kenneth Courtis, the chief Asian economist for Deutsche Bank. 
"You have the world economy flying on one engine -- the United States. 
And almost everyone else is dealing from a weak hand."
You would think this would leave Washington filled with joy, and often it does. 
After all, that single engine still has its afterburners lit: The Government reported Friday an astounding 4.5 percent annual growth rate in the first quarter, once again beating virtually every forecast. 
It's hard to imagine any country threatening America's sole-superpower status for decades. 
It's even harder to recall that only a decade ago Washington was still preoccupied with Japan's buying spree in Hollywood and on Wall Street, and wringing its hands about the successes of Asian-style capitalism. 
But the celebration of American supremacy sometimes obscures the far more complex risks of managing world affairs amid global economic and political fragility. 
And the truth is that Washington is still a lot more comfortable containing an easily identifiable enemy than managing a system where cracks on one side of the globe can radiate to the other.
Part of the problem is that weakness comes in many forms. 
There is Russian-style weakness, an inability of the state machinery to make the country function, to keep control. 
Whatever temporary pleasure Americans derived from watching the Russian military threat fall apart has been tempered by the fear that economic chaos has put its nuclear expertise up for sale. 
"During the cold war we knew that Russia's nukes were under strict control, but we were terrified of the people controlling them," said Michael Mandelbaum, a Johns Hopkins University professor who has written about the new challenges of managing a global system in which leaders are overwhelmed by the forces around them. 
"Now the fear about Russia is that nothing is under anyone's clear control -- not the taxation system and not the atomic-industrial complex."
And then there is Japanese-style weakness, a subject President Clinton will be carefully dancing around on Monday as Prime Minister Keizo Obuchi arrives for an official visit. 
In Tokyo the problem isn't a collapsing state; it's a chronic inability to get political consensus, whether the issue is bolstering security in Asia or remaking the world's second-largest economy.
Mr. Obuchi will be arriving with the news that the lower house of Parliament has finally passed legislation that would allow it, in theory, to act like a real ally of American forces should a military emergency break out in the Pacific. 
But the bill was stripped of several key elements, including one that would let Tokyo participate in enforcing international sanctions, and the Pentagon still fears that if North Korea lashes out, Japan may sit on its hands.
OF more immediate concern is whether Japan's seven-year recession is finally ending, as the Japanese insist. 
If not, Japan's troubles could choke off Asia's fragile recovery and force the United States to continue taking in a wildly disproportionate amount of the world's exports. 
Sooner or later, that will cost American jobs, which is why Treasury Secretary Robert E. Rubin warned again last week that America's soaring trade deficits are "not politically sustainable."
But in Japan's case, as in Russia's, Washington has few levers to pull.
In fact, Washington is never quite sure with whom it should be negotiating. 
Mr. Obuchi has scant control over the pace of Japanese reforms. 
That power is in the hands of the country's scared corporate heads, its much-criticized bureaucrats and its workers, who are terrified by the rising unemployment rate and know that they have few options if they lose their job.
If Boris N. Yeltsin was once committed to reforming the Russian economy, he has given it up. 
It is notable that ever since Russia's currency devaluation and default on some of its debt last August, the Clinton Administration has cut back on providing free advice about the wonders of making the transition to a market economy. 
"It would only stoke their resentments further," one senior State Department official said. 
"We're wiser to shut up about reform."
But at least there is some agreement in Washington that a stronger Japan and an economically stable Russia are in the country's interests. 
Raise the subject of China, and it's a different story. 
On Capitol Hill these days, China is once again a power to be contained.
The revelations of nuclear espionage bolster the arguments of conservatives who say the Clinton Administration has been blinded by big business and big donors, and that it buried the evidence of transgressions at Los Alamos because they threatened the policy of engagement. 
Add their voices to those of human rights groups who are horrified by China's recent crackdowns, unions that fear trade deals, and Taiwan supporters who want more protection from the mainland's missiles.
At the other end of the spectrum are Mr. Clinton and many of America's China experts, who see 100 million jobless wandering the Chinese countryside, failing state-owned enterprises and insolvent banks that -- at the Government's insistence -- keep those enterprises afloat. 
And there are Russia-like symptoms: arms proliferation, the rising power of organized crime, a military in business for itself.
The theory of integrating China into the World Trade Organization -- the deal President Clinton walked away from earlier this month -- is that it would help the Chinese pull off the feat that the Russians couldn't. 
It would force China to deal in a Western legal system, to open up, to let a billion Web users bloom.
A nice theory, but the reality is that Washington wants China, like Russia, to be strong on Washington's terms. 
Washington wants to encourage Chinese economic strength and discourage military strength; it wants nations to independently find their own way to a market economy -- as long as it runs strictly according to Western rules. 
In short, Washington wants strong economies run by leaders who will shrink their military power and act weakly beyond their borders. 
But Washington is not likely to get what it wants.

file: POLITICS_ THE CONDUIT_Fund-Raiser for Democrats Now Faces Harsh Spotlight.txt
text:
ï»¿
In 1986, when John Huang arrived in Los Angeles as the chief representative of one of Indonesia's wealthiest families, he brought Asian-American business leaders some advice: with skillful organization and well-targeted campaign contributions, they could gain influence to match their new wealth.
Early this year, after an undistinguished career in banking and a brief, frustrating stint as a Commerce Department official, Mr. Huang returned to California and heeded his own counsel. 
He became one of the most successful fund-raisers for the Democratic National Committee, tapping Asian-American sources neither party had called on.
And now Mr. Huang, 51, has found himself, and his cause, at the focal point of far more attention than he ever imagined. 
He is at the center of Republican attacks over foreign contributions to the Democrats -- including an illegal $250,000 donation from a South Korean company that was later returned -- and his own party has suspended him from any further fund raising until an investigation is completed.
Interviews with Mr. Huang's colleagues and competitors in recent days suggest that in each phase of his career he has been a man with two missions: to increase the political influence of Asian-Americans and to aid his patrons, the Riady family of Indonesia, which controls the Lippo Group, a major financial powerhouse in Southeast Asia. 
What is being questioned now is where the one role ended and the other began, and who this highly regarded member of the Chinese-American community has really been serving by cultivating influence in Washington. 
Republicans have called loudly for an independent counsel. 
Some Asian-Americans have been quietly asking whether Mr. Huang's activities, no different in many respects from those of any other political fund-raiser, are being regarded suspiciously because he is Asian-American.
The Republican Presidential candidate, Bob Dole, is arguing that Mr. Huang -- who was naturalized as an American citizen 20 years ago -- was an agent of foreign influence. 
"We cannot allow the political influence of any American to be outweighed by foreign money," Mr. Dole said. 
But the picture of Mr. Huang's career that emerges from the interviews is more complex. 
At the Commerce Department he sat in on none of the important strategy meetings about Asia -- but he did show up in the Oval Office for private meetings between President Clinton and James Riady. 
So far there is little sign that any Government policy -- affecting Indonesia or the Riadys' far-flung business interests -- was changed because of Mr. Huang. But there is evidence that in his drive for donations, Mr. Huang at a minimum skirted the legal limitations on fund raising and ignored the cardinal rule of campaign finance: Know the real source of your contributions.
Mr. Huang himself has remained out of view and the Democratic National Committee has deflected all requests for interviews with him. 
Appearing on CBS' "Face the Nation" yesterday, the chairman of the D.N.C., Senator Christopher J. Dodd of Connecticut, was pressed on when Mr. Huang would answer questions in public. 
"I'm certain that it will be done," Mr. Dodd said, but later seemed to hedge a bit, saying, "We'll try and make him available to you."
Mr. Huang was born in China, but raised in Taiwan, where he served in the air force before attending the University of Connecticut in 1969. 
In 1972 he started working in banking, first in Washington, then in Louisville, Ky., and Memphis. 
He moved to Hong Kong, and soon jumped to the banking operations run there by the Lippo Group, the Riadys' business empire. 
Then he joined the Worthen Bank of Little Rock, Ark., in which the Riady family held a large stake, before he was moved to Los Angeles in 1986 to help run the Lippo Bank, a small institution owned by James Riady, who had worked in Little Rock, where he became friendly with Bill Clinton. 
Mr. Huang quickly established himself in Los Angeles -- in part by using the Lippo Group's name and money -- as a prominent member of the Asian-American community and a member of numerous civic organizations.
"He always had this vision that the Chinese-American community had not been active enough in politics and that our interests were being ignored," said Charles Woo, the chief executive of P. C. Woo, which produces Megatoys. 
"He always said that with donations of money the political establishment would pay attention to us. 
I admire him a lot for that, and so did a lot of other people."
Among the issues Mr. Huang concentrated on were immigrants' rights and helping Asian-American businessmen build networks that would increase their influence.
Mr. Huang's career at Lippo Bank, which has four branches in California, was conspicuously less successful than his efforts in politics. 
The bank has had run-ins with regulators for poor management, bad loans and discriminatory lending practices. 
And its performance has been desultory at best. 
Lippo Bank lost $3 million last year, and in its best year, 1993, it earned just $1 million.
"If James were here they would have grown substantially," said Len Rushfield, the executive vice president of a consulting company in Los Angeles and a friend of James Riady, the son of the Lippo Group's chairman and its No. 2 official. 
"John's focus was different. 
It was not so much on making the bank a bank, it was representing the Lippo Group here."
Â 
At Commerce: Quiet and Frustrated
In its early days, the Clinton Administration, already critical of Indonesia's treatment of dissidents in East Timor, threatened to terminate Jakarta's special trade preferences unless it improved its record. 
The Riadys saw a role for themselves as intermediaries between the Administration and the Indonesian Government. 
By late 1993, working through Mr. Huang, Administration officials said, James Riady was pressing to meet the key members of the Cabinet who had a voice in the decision, including United States Trade Representative Mickey Kantor and Commerce Secretary Ronald H. Brown. Lower-level trade officials had already seen Mr. Riady in Jakarta; Mr. Kantor said last week that he and his deputy, Charlene Barshefsky, refused, as did Mr. Brown.
Soon thereafter Mr. Huang decided to seek a job at Commerce; some Riady family associates say he was "placed" there, but none of his colleagues can recall who proposed him as deputy assistant secretary for international economic policy.
The one official who does recall pressing senior Commerce officials to hire Mr. Huang is Maria Haley, a friend of President Clinton's and of Mr. Huang's from Arkansas, who helped place several Asian-Americans in the Clinton Administration. 
"You help the people who bring you to power," Ms. Haley, now a director of the Export-Import Bank, said in an interview last week.
Mr. Huang's handwritten financial disclosure report shows that the pain of taking a pay cut for a Government job was eased by a farewell gift from the Riady family: $788,750 in "salary, bonus and severance" from Hip Hing Holdings, a Riady-family property firm in Los Angeles.
At the Commerce Department Mr. Huang recused himself from issues affecting Indonesia and his former employer. 
But if he had hoped to delve into the major initiative of the department -- a focus on the "Big Emerging Markets" of China and the rest of Southeast Asia -- he was soon disappointed. 
His office was not involved.
By all accounts, most of Mr. Huang's tasks were administrative -- personnel issues, budgets, preparing Congressional testimony for senior officials. 
"He was incredibly quiet," one of his superiors recalled last week. 
"This is a guy who never asked to go to a meeting, never overtly sought to involve himself in policy."
The exception to that rule was dealing with Taiwan: Mr. Huang's office was asked to take up the problems of American companies seeking to get a piece of a major nuclear project there, chiefly because China would react badly if the same officials dealing with Beijing were also visiting Taipei. 
He visited Taipei twice.
Mr. Huang held a "Top Secret" security clearance, but appears not to have had access to truly sensitive material about China, the role of corruption in major deals, and intelligence analysis of foreign governments and companies.
But at least once during his tenure at Commerce Mr. Huang found himself in the Oval Office -- on Sept. 
13, 1995, with James Riady. 
Bruce Lindsey, the deputy White House counsel, who also attended the meeting, called it a "social visit."
Soon thereafter Mr. Huang asked Mr. Lindsey for help getting a job at the Democratic National Committee. 
By early December he was packing his desk at the Commerce Department.
"The man was frustrated by his lack of involvement in matters he thought were in his purview and the best use of his background," said one senior official, recalling Mr. Huang's comments as he left the department.
Â 
The Fund-Raiser: Busy in California
By early January, now a vice-chairman of the D.N.C. for finance, Mr. Huang was back in California, holding meetings in San Francisco's Chinatown and telling supporters he wanted to raise more than $3 million in Asian-American contributions for the Presidential campaign. 
"We have to bring ourselves into the political arena and let the rest of the country as a whole understand the role Asian-American communities are playing and will be playing in the coming century," he said at one meeting on Jan. 
8, according to local press reports at the time.
To reach that goal, Mr. Huang appears to have violated election law on at least one occasion. 
He brought in a $250,000 contribution from the United States' subsidiary of a South Korean company called Cheong Am, a maker of electronic display boards. 
But its American subsidiary has generated no revenue, and taking money from a foreign company -- even if it is funneled through an American unit -- is illegal. 
When The Los Angeles Times reported the contribution, it was given back. 
The company's Los Angeles office has since been cleared out and its chief, John Lee, who met Mr. Clinton briefly at a fund raiser after making his contribution, has not been seen for some time.
Mr. Huang and Maria Hsia, a prominent Los Angeles immigration consultant with whom he had worked on Democratic events in the 1980's, put together other major California projects: a big fund raiser this summer in Century City, attended by Mr. Clinton, and another fund raiser attended by Vice President Al Gore at a large, Chinese Buddhist Temple in Los Angeles on April 29.
The event at the temple has raised a number of questions. 
The temple is tax-exempt, and that status makes it legally questionable for political fund raisers. 
After recent press reports the Democratic Party announced that it would reimburse the temple for the $15,000 the event cost.
Moreover, a lawyer for the temple, Peter Kelly, a former chairman of the California Democratic Party, confirmed that a nun from an affiliated temple in Texas reported last week that she had been handed $5,000 in cash and then asked to write a check to the party to conceal the real donor's identity, a clear campaign finance law violation. 
The temple is investigating, he added.
Officials at the Hsi Lai Temple also confirmed that some monks and nuns made donations, but said they possessed the means to do so from teaching and lecturing. 
The temple has also been popular with other Democratic politicians, including Representative Patrick J. Kennedy of Rhode Island, the son of Senator Edward M. Kennedy. Representative Kennedy visited twice this year in what the temple says were nonpolitical meetings.
The Riady family has not contributed to the D.N.C. for several years, records show; James Riady is no longer living here, and thus is barred from contributing.
One question facing the Federal Election Commission now is whether the Riadys' acted through proxies. 
Arief Wiriadinata is often referred to by Republicans as a "gardener" -- he appears to be a landscape architect -- and his wife, Soraya, is the daughter of a now-deceased founder of the Lippo Group with close ties to President Suharto of Indonesia. 
They contributed more than $400,000, in a series of gifts, earlier this year, including nearly $300,000, that were apparently made after they left Virginia and returned to Jakarta. 
The legality of that contribution is now one of several under investigation.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: POLITICS_ THE CONGRESS_Republicans Are Rushing to Widen Investigations of Fund Raising by the Democr.txt
text:
ï»¿
Racing to expand a growing investigation, Congressional Republicans have filed more than 77 requests seeking information from an assortment of Federal agencies, the Democratic National Committee and the White House regarding questionable fund raising by the Democratic Party.
The requests have mushroomed into one of the most sprawling Congressional investigations in recent times and could spill into next year. 
The Republicans have already asked for information ranging from the Administration's conduct of foreign policy in Asia and control of sensitive intelligence information to the regulation of the Lippo Bank, the California bank run by John Huang, the Democratic National Committee official at the center of the inquiry, and his Indonesian associates.
The Congressional investigators have gone to every agency they think could have been helpful to the business and political interests of Mr. Huang and his Indonesian and American associates. 
The committees seek thousands of Government records, like telephone logs, office diaries, immigration records about the Indonesians and Secret Service records of White House visits.
But the Republicans say that most of their requests have gone unanswered.
Although the investigations will continue beyond Tuesday's elections no matter who retains control of Congress, the direction and the scope of the investigations could change if the Republicans hold onto Congress. 
Should the Democrats retake Congress and retain the Presidency, Congressional Republicans would have much less power to get executive branch information.
"Lippo Bank needs to be hoping that the Democrats capture control of the House and Senate," said Senator Christopher S. Bond, a Republican from Missouri who has been actively seeking information from a variety of Federal agencies.
Michael D. McCurry, the White House spokesman, acknowledged that some legitimate issues had been raised that needed to be explored by Congress. 
But he said the Republicans had demonstrated an excessive zeal over the last year, turning reasonable avenues of inquiry into personal attacks on President Clinton.
"There has been a calculated effort by Speaker Newt Gingrich and the Republicans to use the investigative apparatus of Congress to undermine the executive branch," Mr. McCurry said.
But Senator John McCain, Republican of Arizona, said the issues raised by the various investigations were vitally important because they included the possible influence of campaign money in setting foreign policy. 
Mr. McCain said he "doubted very seriously" that these issues would be thoroughly explored if the Democrats controlled Congress.
No matter who controls Congress next year, Mr. Huang and the Democrats will face two more narrowly focused reviews of fund-raising activities that have begun in recent months at the Justice Department. 
Attorney General Janet Reno announced on Thursday that she had begun the process of deciding whether to appoint an independent counsel to investigate some fund-raising issues. 
In June, the Justice Department began to examine whether the United States liaison in Taiwan was involved in soliciting campaign gifts from foreign businessmen.
What has made so many different Republican-controlled committees interested in Mr. Huang is the unusual path his career has taken. 
Mr. Huang, 51, was born in China and educated in Taiwan and the United States. 
He has been an executive of Riady family banks in Asia, Arkansas, New York and California.
With the help of the Riadys, a family controlling a $12 billion empire that centers on holdings in Indonesia, Hong Kong and China, Mr. Huang landed a job at the Commerce Department in 1994.
He left his Government post early this year and joined the Democratic National Committee. 
As a vice chairman earning $60,000 a year, he has raised millions of dollars for the party, much of it from Asian-Americans, and $425,000 from an Indonesian couple associated with the Riadys who lived briefly in the United States.
Many House committees are seeking information from the Clinton Administration. 
The main inquiries from the Senate have come from members of the Banking Committee.
On Friday, Senator Lauch Faircloth, Republican of North Carolina and a member of the Banking Committee, wrote to Treasury Secretary Robert E. Rubin. Mr. Faircloth asked for Government records of a Federal investigation in the early 1990's about "money laundering at Lippo Bank."
The letter did not spell out the details of the Federal investigation, but officials who have seen some records and insisted on anonymity said investigators had found evidence of 900 separate transactions in 1989 and 1990 in which $7 million was transferred from Lippo to the Hong Kong Chinese Bank, another institution controlled by the Riadys.
The records were said to contain evidence that no Federal currency reports, required for cash transactions of more than $10,000, had been filed on the hundreds of cash transfers from Lippo to 13 Hong Kong accounts held in fictitious names.
Mr. Huang was a senior executive of Lippo Bank in 1990, and in the mid-1980's, he served as a vice president of the Hong Kong Chinese Bank.
No prosecution ever resulted from the investigation, and top executives at the two banks said in recent interviews that they had no knowledge of any illegal activity.
Investigators are also interested in two telephone message slips found in Mr. Huang's office at the Commerce Department from Ken Quincy, the chief of the compliance and enforcement section of the Division of Compliance and Consumer Affairs at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. 
During the early 1990's, Mr. Quincy was a senior regulator who reviewed a number of Federal examinations of the Lippo Bank.
The messages were left for Mr. Huang on the eve of an important F.D.I.C. examination of the bank in 1995. 
Mr. Quincy said he had no recollection of ever leaving the messages or of having any conversations with Mr. Huang.

file: Pope Offers the Chinese a Deal on the Church_s Role.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a radio message beamed to China on Saturday, Pope John Paul II offered a hard-nosed bargain to Beijing: recognize papal authority over China's Catholics in return for the Vatican's acknowledgement of the country's officially sponsored church.
If accepted, the Pope's offer would represent a major departure for the Chinese authorities, who have long resisted any foreign intrusion into their affairs and who maintain rigorous controls on the country's millions of Catholics.
The Pope's challenge to China was made on the eve of a huge open-air mass today marking World Youth Day that attracted so many people -- Philippine estimates ran to four million -- that the Pope himself found his way to the Mass site in Luneta Park here blocked.
Vatican officials said the crowds thronging the streets were so huge -- even by the standards of papal Masses -- that the Pope had been unable to leave the Papal Nuncio's residence, where he is staying
Philippine authorities finally used a helicopter to transport the Pope, who seemed unfatigued and rosy-cheeked as he began the Mass after an 80-minute delay. 
The size of the crowd was apparently a record in the 17-year history of this Papacy.
"This is an excess of success," said the Papal spokesman, Joaquin Navarro-Valls.
Another spokesman, Archbishop John Foley, said he has attended papal Masses dating to to John Paul's first in Poland 1979 and "I have never seen anything to match the numbers" of the Mass today.
The Pope's radio message to China involved Vatican policy toward the officially run Chinese Patriotic Catholic Association, which does not permit Catholics to recognize the spiritual supremacy of the Pope and rejects the Vatican's right, exercised in most other countries, to appoint bishops.
For its part, the Vatican does not acknowledge the Patriotic Association, which it calls schismatic, and supports clandestine worshipers among China's often-persecuted Catholics who recognize papal authority.
The issue may come to a climax at the Mass today. 
Five priests from the Patriotic Association have asked to join the Pope to celebrate the Mass with him -- a move that would imply Vatican recognition of the official Chinese church.
But in a message to China sent by the church's Manila-based Radio Veritas on Saturday, the Pope insisted on what he called "sincere acceptance of the unchanging principles laid down by Christ for his church."
"Particularly important among these principles is the effective communion of all the parts of the church with her visible foundation: Peter the Rock," he said, evoking Roman Catholic belief in the Pope as the successor of St. Peter.
Dr. Navarro-Valls told reporters that local church authorities here would insist "where necessary" that priests co-celebrating the Mass with the Pope declare allegiance to him.
It was not clear Saturday whether the representatives of the Patriotic Association had agreed to the demand.
The Vatican's aim is to open the way for a new relationship with Beijing on its own terms to permit Catholic missionaries to evangelize in the huge nation. 
At present only 3 percent of Asians profess Catholicism, most of them in the heavily Catholic Philippines. 
The Pope has made impassioned pleas here for a broader effort to gather souls.
Chinese Christians registered with the Beijing authorities number some eight million, three million of them Catholics, according to Chinese estimates. 
The Vatican says it is aware of three million to five million Chinese Catholics but says the number could rise dramatically if restrictions on worship are removed.
For several years, the Vatican has been training what it calls a task force of more than 40 missionary priests to evangelize in China if they are allowed to do so. 
The Pope is to visit them here today.
Dr. Navarro-Valls said Saturday that two groups of Catholics from clandestine churches recognizing papal authority had arrived in Manila from China to join the World Youth Day celebration.
The Pope's visit to Manila, which started Thursday, is part of an 11-day tour that will take him on to Papua New Guinea, Australia and Sri Lanka. 
It is by far his most arduous voyage since a broken leg last April forced him to cancel trips to Belgium and the United States. 
His slow recovery from hip replacement surgery has obliged him to walk with a cane.
While his schedule has been reduced compared with earlier papal voyages, the Pope put in a busy working day Saturday, holding a long open-air Mass in the morning before meeting with Filipino bishops, visiting Radio Veritas and going on to a three-hour prayer vigil with some 450,000 young people.
As they sang, he swayed in rhythm with them, and waved a large candle in tune with the songs, seeming unfatigued and in good spirits. 
But he slumped heavily as he returned to a papal throne after embracing youthful delegates.
"Very good young people," he told the crowd Saturday night as the ceremonies drew to a close. 
"Incredible, but it is true. 
Very good young people."
And, taking his walking cane, he used it to wave to the crowd before him.

file: POSTINGS_ Hotel Expanding Into Old Chinese Mission_100 Rooms On W. 66th St.txt
text:
ï»¿
Millennium Partners has taken control of the building on West 66th Street formerly occupied by the Chinese Mission to the United Nations, which has moved to First Avenue between 34th and 35th Streets in a swap arranged by Millennium.
The arrangement, in negotiations for over four years, permits Millennium to expand the adjacent Phillips Club, its extended-stay hotel, by incorporating the old mission building into the real estate development company's Lincoln Square complex. 
The remodeled building will add 100 units and 25,000 square feet of retail space between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenue, more than doubling the number of rooms.
The new Chinese mission on First Avenue, developed by Millennium, is in two buildings containing 125,000 square feet of headquarters space and 88,000 square feet of residential and recreational space.
"This landmark deal was an education and an experience of a lifetime," Christopher M. Jeffries, a founder of Millennium, said of the negotiations, which were conducted in New York, Washington and Beijing. 
According to Millennium, it was the first real estate transaction in the United States between a private American company and the government of China. 
The existing Phillips Club, which Mr. Jeffries said has an occupancy rate of well over 90 percent, has 96 rooms in the Grand Millennium building at Broadway and 66th Street. 
The expansion is to be completed in a year.

file: Power Array Pushes the China Trade Bill.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two former presidents and an array of senior officials from Democratic and Republican administrations rallied today with President Clinton and Vice President Al Gore at the White House to urge Congress to approve a landmark China trade bill.
Speaking at a ceremony in the ornate East Room, Mr. Clinton intensified his lobbying in advance of the House vote, now likely on May 24 or May 25, to grant China permanent normal trading privileges.
"If the Congress votes against it, they'll be kicking themselves in the rear 10 years from now, because America will be paying the price," Mr. Clinton told scores of invited dignitaries.
Statesmen, scholars and military chiefs, including former Secretaries of State Henry A. Kissinger and James A. Baker 3d, whose public service spanned nearly 50 years in some cases, stood with Mr. Clinton in warning of the consequences of defeat.
"A negative vote in the House or Senate would be catastrophic to American agriculture, electronics, telecommunications, autos and countless other products and services," said former President Gerald R. Ford.
Critics of the measure, which would allow American companies to benefit fully from a market-opening agreement that would pave the way for China to enter the World Trade Organization, say it would sacrifice lawmakers' influence over Beijing's record on human rights and religious freedoms.
Former President Jimmy Carter acknowledged that China had fallen short in those areas, but cautioned against rejecting the measure. 
"There's no doubt in my mind," Mr. Carter said, "that a negative vote on this issue in the Congress will be a serious setback and impediment for the further democratization, freedom and human rights in China."
Sandwiched between Mr. Clinton and the former presidents in turns at the microphone, Mr. Gore, the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, appeared reluctant to give his full-throated endorsement. 
His words sounded like support. 
But his subdued tone suggested the pains that Mr. Gore has taken to avoid alienating a pivotal ally, organized labor, which opposes the accord.
"It is right for American jobs, it is right for the cause of reform in China, and I believe it will move us closer to the strong and stable world community that we all seek to create," Mr. Gore said.
With just two weeks left before the vote, the White House and its allies on Capitol Hill say they are still 10 to 15 votes shy of the 218 needed for passage. 
About 30 Democrats and roughly as many Republicans remained officially undecided, and the presentation today was aimed at pulling both camps down off the fence.
Mr. Clinton said opponents -- an unlikely coalition of liberal Democrats and conservative Republicans -- were unwittingly doing the bidding of the measure's foes in China, the owners of state-owned enterprises and reactionary military leaders.

file: PRESIDENT IMPOSES TRADE SANCTIONS ON CHINESE GOODS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Clinton Administration imposed punitive tariffs today on more than $1 billion of Chinese goods, the largest trade sanctions in American history, and warned of further action if the Communist Government continued to refuse to crack down on rampant piracy of American software, movies and music.
The decision to impose 100 percent punitive tariffs on goods ranging from silk blouses to cellular telephones was met almost immediately by an angry Chinese announcement of tariffs against American goods.
The confrontation comes at a particularly delicate moment in Chinese-American relations, with disagreements brewing on human rights and arms control, and with China's 90-year-old paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, reported to be seriously ill.
But after several meetings at the White House in recent days on the deteriorating relations, Administration officials decided that despite the delicate transition of power presumed to be under way, they could not justify delaying the sanctions any longer. 
Through the first 11 months of 1994, the United States imported $36 billion of products from China while exporting $8.5 billion of goods there.
Each country said its penalties would take effect on Feb. 
26. The delay, a common practice in cases of trade sanctions, is intended to assure that goods shipped before the retaliatory tariffs were announced would not be affected.
The delay also provides a chance for further talks; last February, the Chinese struck a deal in a textile dispute on the day when previously announced sanctions were to take effect. 
But some trade officials speculate that the unsettled state of the Chinese leadership makes such last-minute bargaining less likely.
American consumers will be among the first victims of the trade dispute, as they are any time the Government decides to set a tariff to harm the sales of another country's goods. 
Under the rules published today, for example, the United States Customs Service would be required to put a $100 tax on every $100 Chinese-made bicycle imported to the United States.
Over the last five weeks, however, American officials have been pruning the list of products selected for retaliation, homing in on goods produced in several other nations as well, so that American consumers could choose, for example, a Japanese or British-made bicycle that is not subject to the tariffs.
They have also avoided products on which tariffs would be likely to hurt American business, including two of China's biggest exports to the United States, toys and electronic goods.
Today's action was the culmination of a dispute between the United States and China that has bubbled along for nearly two years, a period in which the Administration said it would no longer link human rights issues to preferential trade status.
The current dispute has begun to eclipse Washington's long-running trade arguments with Japan. 
Last year the American trade deficit with China climbed to $30 billion -- roughly half the size of the deficit with Japan -- and United States businesses say that piracy of American "intellectual property," particularly copyrighted material like movies and music, has contributed to the trade imbalance.
The United States has repeatedly demanded, for example, that China close 29 factories -- many of them state-owned -- that are producing 70 million compact disks and videodisks every year, from illegal copies of Whitney Houston's hit soundtrack from "The Bodyguard" to movies like "True Lies" and "Clear and Present Danger."
Those goods can be found all over Asia, from the streets of Hong Kong to many stores in Tokyo.
At a news conference here today, Mickey Kantor, the United States trade representative, held up bootleg products purchased around Asia, including knockoffs of the latest version of the Microsoft Corporation's personal computer operating system and canned foods bearing the label "Del Monte."
Mr. Kantor said that after 21 negotiating sessions in the last two years, China still refused to crack down on the production and distribution of such products.
"The Chinese know what they have to do," he said. 
"They are the third-largest economy in the world, and they can stop this if they want."
Mr. Kantor said the sanctions were approved by President Clinton.
China also said today that it would suspend negotiations with American auto makers over the establishment of joint ventures in China to build mini-vans and passenger cars. 
Getting American car makers into China, as both German and Japanese manufacturers are expanding their presence there, has been an important economic priority of the Clinton Administration.
Even so, business support for a tough stand has spread in the last month, in contrast to trade sanctions in the past, which have often divided business leaders. 
The chairman of the Ford Motor Company, Alexander J. Trotman, said last week at an economic conference in Davos, Switzerland, that if the company was caught in the middle of a Washington-Beijing trade war, "so be it."
He added, "I think it's a very important question that needs to be addressed."
Mr. Kantor made it clear, however, that the list of affected goods had been shaped with the aim of minimizing the impact on American businesses.
"We have also tried to pick products that are produced by China's state-owned enterprises," Mr. Kantor said. 
While he declined to go into the reasoning behind singling out those businesses, many of those enterprises are owned by the People's Liberation Army and other Government agencies, and their profits have frequently enriched China's leaders and their families.
The decision not to include toys and electronics came after hearings in recent weeks convinced Mr. Kantor's aides that so many toys are now produced exclusively in China that doubling the tariff would harm American retailers and anger consumers. 
"It didn't take a political genius to see that we would be blamed for taking toys out of the hands of little kids," one Administration official said Friday as the final list was being prepared.
In fact, because of a quirk in trade laws, the United States actually ended all tariffs on toys as of Jan. 
1, under the new General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade approved by Congress in November. 
While China is not a signer of the agreement, President Clinton's decision last year to extend preferential trade status to China mandated that it, too, would benefit from the elimination of toy tariffs.
American officials said today that they did not know how much those tariffs would total, but outside experts said they could compensate for the penalties imposed today and perhaps exceed them.
Administration officials said they excluded most electronic components from the sanctions after American computer makers were told that China was the main supplier of a large variety of cables and circuit boards used in personal computers.
Imposing sanctions on those goods, Mr. Kantor concluded, would only work to the advantage of foreign computer makers. 
But his aides said other items could be added to the list if China refused to reach a satisfactory agreement.
Mr. Kantor acted today under the "special 301" provisions of the 1974 Trade Act, which covers intellectual property. 
The law requires that after an investigation, the trade representative can declare a country's trade practices unreasonable. 
He made that declaration in December, two years after a previous dispute with China on the same subject resulted in an agreement with Beijing to write laws protecting copyrights and patents.
"They passed the laws, and they are well written," Mr. Kantor said in an interview in his office on Friday. 
"They have just refused to enforce them."
Lengthy negotiations were held in Beijing in January that yielded some progress, including an agreement by the Chinese to place a distinctive identifier code on compact disks produced in its factories, so that they can be traced to their point of manufacture. 
But the talks stalled when it came to taking tougher action, and China declined an invitation to continue talking in Washington last week, during the celebration of the lunar New Year.
Administration officials have a variety of theories as to why this dispute is proving so intractable.
The most popular centers on the transition in power in Beijing. 
Several State Department officials say they think the intense focus on Mr. Deng's health has distracted the Chinese leadership. 
They also speculate that some top leaders, mindful of the price they paid during the Cultural Revolution, do not want to be identified as internationalists -- seeking accommodation with the United States -- until it is clear who will dominate China's leadership.
The current dispute is linked to a broader argument between China and the West: whether Beijing is ready for admission to the new World Trade Organization, the successor to the GATT organization in Geneva that has presided over world trade since the end of World War II.
Entry to the World Trade Organization, with the trade benefits that implies, has been a central objective of China's leadership. 
But the United States has stood in the way, saying that until China respects intellectual property and opens its markets, it is not suited for membership.
"We must stand firm," said Representative Philip M. Crane, an Illinois Republican and chairman of the trade subcommittee of the House Ways and Means Committee. 
"If China wishes to become a member of the World Trade Organization, it must show that it is complying with the rules of the multilateral trade regime."
China's restrictions on American imports are legion, and many go beyond Japan's most protectionist policies. 
Only 10 American films, for example, are permitted to be shown in China each year, a quota that has both political and commercial roots. 
But that restriction has created an enormous demand for bootleg copies of American video cassettes and videodisks, the large, CD-like platters that can store an entire movie.
While the focus of the dispute has been on movies and music, the bigger money may lie in computer software. 
Copies of the most popular American software are available in shops from Beijing through the new economic zones in Southern China at a fraction of their retail prices in the United States.
"One of our negotiators paid $100 for a CD-ROM that had $10,000 worth of American software on it," Mr. Kantor said Friday. 
"And the Chinese told us this was out of their control."

file: President Views Success of China Trade Bill as His Foreign Policy Legacy.txt
text:
ï»¿
For seven years now, very little has gone as planned in Bill Clinton's effort to shape a new relationship with China. 
Now, amid increasing confidence among White House officials this weekend that they will prevail in one of the most crucial Congressional votes in a decade, the president who came to office knowing little about China may leave claiming he fundamentally altered Washington's relations with Beijing.
For Mr. Clinton, the problem has not been a lack of vision. 
Once in office, he quickly cast away his campaign attacks on President Bush for "coddling dictators" in Beijing. 
And since 1994, he has steadily built on his theme that the Internet and China's growing economic ties to the West would ultimately create pressures for political openness that Beijing will not be able to control.
The problem has been one of execution. 
The Chinese have hardly cooperated, jailing more dissidents even as Mr. Clinton argued that economic freedom would eventually produce political freedom. 
Nor has there been much help from the president's fellow Democrats, most of whom have fought his trade and China policies at every turn.
But in recent weeks, Mr. Clinton has sworn to close friends and colleagues that he will not let himself repeat the same mistake he now blames himself for making at least twice before -- letting the politics of the moment, or even the prospect of a war within his own political party, pull him back from a step he is convinced is the best hope of keeping China from becoming an adversary.
"He knows he blew it in 1995 and again last year," said one of Mr. Clinton's foreign policy advisers, referring to Mr. Clinton's decision to grant a visa to Taiwan's president in 1995 to visit the United States, and then to walk away last year from a sweeping trade deal with China's reform-minded prime minister, Zhu Rongji.
So with the passion of a convert, Mr. Clinton is spending hours each day arguing the merits of a strategic vision he took years to adopt. 
In small gatherings in the Yellow Oval Room of the White House residence and even aboard Air Force One as he took New York Democrats to his wife's formal nomination for the Senate race, he has offered lectures about competing scenarios of what America's dealings with China may look like in 2025.
In public, his aides say the vote, scheduled for Wednesday, is still too close to call. 
"We don't have the 218 to pass it, and the opposition do not have 218 at this point, in my opinion, to stop it," Commerce Secretary William Daley, who is leading the administration's lobbying drive, said today on CBS' "Face the Nation."
In private, however, many of Mr. Clinton's advisers suspect the bill to give China permanent trade status -- thus ending an annual Congressional review -- will pass by a margin of 10 votes or more, chiefly because of the support of Republicans. 
The Republican whip in the House, Representative Tom DeLay of Texas, said today that "we're moving toward that magic number of 218," giving much of the credit to lobbying by the president.
For Mr. Clinton, the vote may be the last hope of making a deep imprint on foreign affairs in his second term. 
With time running out for a Mideast peace accord or a new arms deal with Russia, the outcome of the vote has taken on huge importance in the president's mind.
"He hates the word, but it's the legacy thing, in a big way," said one cabinet member.
But even if Mr. Clinton wins, the victory may feel incomplete.
Mr. Clinton acknowledges that for all his talk about the benefits for America of economic globalization -- how it opens new markets for American exports and innovation -- fewer Democrats are with him on this than on the1993 passage of the North American Free Trade Agreement. 
He told a colleague not long ago, "I'm doing this despite my party, not with it."
Even allies say that is because his commitment to rebuilding the China relationship and pursuing a trade policy for a new era of globalized commerce has waxed and waned.
"As in so many things," said Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a leading advocate of the trade bill, "he too often let the politics of last month or next month affect decisions toward China that go to half-century strategic issues."
Only in recent times, he added, "has the president begun to see this in historic terms."
So far, the White House strategy has been fairly straightforward. 
Mr. Clinton has largely let others argue the economic benefits, and avoided direct engagement with the labor unions that fear that any gains from an increase in exports to China will be outweighed by the movement of American jobs there.
Instead, the president has focused his arguments on national security, saying the real point of letting China into the World Trade Organization is to further economic engagement to give a boost to China's reformers and prevent the two nations from drifting into adversarial roles.
But with the coalition in Congress so fragile, Mr. Clinton's staff has carefully shielded him from much public engagement about the deal. 
They canceled a television address to the nation this evening, for fear it would anger undecided Democrats. 
After lengthy discussions, they declined to make him available for an interview on his seven years of dealings with China, again out of concern he might say something that could cost a few needed votes.
To the enormous frustration of the White House, the Chinese are hardly aiding Mr. Clinton's cause. 
In past years, when Congress was gearing up for a vote on the annual renewal of trading status, Beijing usually released a few long-imprisoned dissidents.
But this time, as Mr. Daley said recently, "the Chinese certainly aren't making it any easier."
While they moderated their reaction to the inauguration this weekend of a new Taiwanese president, Chinese authorities have continued to arrest members of the Falun Gong religious group, and recently sentenced a leader of the fledgling Democracy Party to a long term in prison. 
Mr. Clinton, curiously, has made no recent public comments about those arrests.
Mr. Clinton and his team have tried to turn China's continued crackdowns to their advantage, arguing that the trade deal, by ushering in Western technology, legal systems and ideas, will ultimately undercut the ability of the Chinese government to repress dissent.
At the United States Coast Guard Academy on Wednesday, the president took this argument further than he ever has before, making the case that "when over 100 million people in China can get on the Net, it will be impossible to maintain a closed political and economic society."
"He's right, but it will take a generation," said Sandra Kristoff, who headed the Asian operations of the National Security Council in Mr. Clinton's first term. 
President Jiang Zemin of China is taking the other side of that bet, hoping that -- like Singapore -- he can reap the benefits of an open economic system while suppressing, or at least managing, true political opposition.
Mr. Clinton will likely be deep into retirement before historians can assess whether he or Mr. Jiang have guessed right. 
But it is already clear that Mr. Clinton's journey to his strategic vision of dealing with China was a long road with many unintended detours.
His first 18 months in office were spent digging his way out of his own campaign rhetoric. 
His comments had inflamed the Chinese, and Sen. Max Baucus, a Montana Democrat, said, "I remember telling him one day that the first step was that he had to treat China with respect."
Mr. Clinton, he said, "seemed surprised."
By the end of 1993, and a disastrous trip to China by Secretary of State Warren Christopher, it was clear that the president's effort to link China's trading rights to its performance on human rights and arms proliferation was collapsing. 
It was a short intellectual leap to granting permanent trade status.
"There was no evidence that we ever gained any leverage over the Chinese with annual renewal," said Charlene Barshefsky, Mr. Clinton's trade representative. 
"It was an empty threat. 
We knew it, and the Chinese knew it."
Mr. Clinton reversed course, saying he could make more progress with China through engagement than with threats -- the conclusion his predecessors had reached.
Then in 1995, with his re-election looming, Mr. Clinton allowed Lee Tung-hui, Taiwan's president, to make a private visit to Cornell University for a college reunion, over the objections of many advisers. 
Mr. Clinton feared that denying the visa would prompt Congress to rewrite the Taiwan Security Act, worsening relations with Beijing. 
But he underestimated the outrage in Beijing.
Mr. Clinton now views that as a mistake. 
"There were two stages to his learning about China," said one former adviser, who dealt with China policy daily. 
"After the campaign he learned that China was a lot more complex than he believed. 
And now he's learned the second part -- that dealing with China means putting the security interests first, and not letting politics get in the way."
If that was the lesson, it was forgotten again in April 1999. 
By that time Mr. Clinton and Mr. Jiang had exchanged visits to China and the United States, and gotten to the final stages of the 13-year-long negotiations for China's entry into the World Trade Organization. 
Mr. Zhu, the prime minister who has come to personify China's economic reform movement, arrived in Washington ready to end the wrangling with an offer of a huge range of openings.
Many advised Mr. Clinton to take it; but he listened to Treasury Secretary Robert E. Rubin and Gene Sperling, the head of the National Economic Council, who feared that if a deal were struck, Congress was in no mood to pass it.
Mr. Clinton realized almost immediately he had made a mistake, but it was too late. 
Once the United States accidentally bombed the Chinese embassy in Belgrade during the air war over Kosovo just a few weeks later, talks froze. 
They were not resumed until marathon negotiations in November, and then some of the terms had changed -- for better, and for worse.
"The previous deal couldn't have passed,"' Mr. Sperling said recently, referring both to the details of the pact and the Congressional climate. 
"This one can."

file: PRIVATE SECTOR_An Empire Built on China Chic.txt
text:
ï»¿
VVIVIENNE Tam has not lived here in her home town for 18 years an eternity in the turbocharged life of this Asian metropolis. 
But as she worked the room at the Luk Yu Tea House the other day, putting even the notoriously surly waiters in line, Ms. Tam looked every inch the hardened Hong Konger.
Perhaps that is because she resides in New York City, which is not all that different from home when it comes to brusqueness and type-A personalities.
"Hong Kong is the New York of Asia," Ms. Tam said. 
"I love the speed of Hong Kong people, the way they talk, the mix of two languages. 
Hong Kong is a different kind of China because it's a mix, East meets West."
Ms. Tam, 43, has parlayed the fusion of Asian and Western styles into a successful career as a fashion designer. 
She rented the teahouse on a recent visit here to promote her new book, "China Chic" (Regan Books, 2000), a coffee-table volume of her musings on Chinese style, from the Ming dynasty to Mao.
The book is not little, but with its red cover and reverent discussion of Mao Zedong as a pop-culture icon, "China Chic" seems like a manifesto. 
Indeed, Ms. Tam is laying the theoretical foundation for an expansion beyond her business of designing stretchy gowns for celebrities like Julia Roberts.
Ms. Tam says her style could lend itself to a broad range of merchandise, including cosmetics, skin-care products and home furnishings. 
They could be sold under her name in department stores or in her boutiques.
Is Vivenne Tam out to become a Chinese Martha Stewart?
"When I was writing the book, I wasn't conscious of trying to do that," she replied without missing a beat. 
"But towards the end, people began talking about it. 
It's interesting when you have a label, and other things start coming to you. 
It's the other things that make it interesting."
Ms. Tam is not the first to try to peddle more than clothes with a Chinese motif. 
Yue-Sai Kan, a former television personality who lives in New York and Shanghai, has a line of cosmetics. 
She recently introduced a Barbie-like doll, with Chinese features and her signature red lipstick.
David Tang, the flamboyant Hong Kong merchant, sells umbrellas, wine coasters and picture frames, as well as Mao T-shirts, sweaters and cheongsams, which are form-fitting, traditional Chinese dresses, in his Shanghai Tang boutiques.
Shanghai Tang does a brisk tourist trade in Hong Kong, but New York has been bumpy. 
Its first store -- a 12,500-square-foot glass palace on Madison Avenue and 61st Street -- closed after 20 months because of poor sales. 
A more humble store opened this year three blocks north.
Recalling his troubles, Mr. Tang offered a glimpse of the challenges Ms. Tam may face.
"When I did the Shanghai Tang shop initially, I jumped on the Mao idea, Communist chic, all that stuff, and people didn't understand it," he said. 
"They hardly knew where the Great Wall was."
Ms. Tam's book, written with Martha Huang, a Chinese literature scholar, contains meditations on Buddhism, the aesthetics of the Ming and Qing dynasties and the child's role in Chinese society.
But "China Chic" most comes to life when it discusses the kitsch appeal of Mao and the Communist Party. 
Ms. Tam recounts how in 1994, she and a Chinese artist, Zhang Hongtu, subverted Mao's image by putting a bee on his nose or adding pigtails. 
Ms. Tam stamped the images on T-shirts, jackets and dresses.
"I loved the twist of it," she said. 
"You're not supposed to be wearing it, but you are wearing it. 
That makes it edgy."
The clothing hit a nerve in politically sensitive Hong Kong, where angry pedestrians rapped on the windows of stores that carried it. 
But in New York, Ms. Tam was celebrated as hipper-than-thou. 
"If I had stayed in China," she writes in the book, "I probably would have been a Red Guard."
As it happens, Ms. Tam's family fled the Communists, migrating from the southern city of Guangzhou to Hong Kong a few years after the 1949 revolution. 
Ms. Tam was born in Guangzhou, and initially stayed behind with her grandparents. 
She was later reunited with her parents in Hong Kong, where she enrolled in a Catholic school and dropped her Chinese name, Yin Yok, in favor of Vivienne.
Ms. Tam moved to New York in 1982 after discovering that Hong Kong offered little to a fledgling couturier. 
She sold her first designs out of a duffel bag to Henri Bendel and a handful of Manhattan boutiques.
Now, Ms. Tam said her label generates retail sales of $62 million a year in New York, Hong Kong and several Japanese cities. 
She has no backers and is the sole owner of her company, East Wind Code, which has annual revenue of $30 million. 
Ms. Tam said she would probably announce a distribution deal with a European partner next year, which could add $10 million in annual revenue.
Building even a small fashion empire is all-consuming, but Ms. Tam said "China Chic" was a labor of love for which she had made time. 
The book includes interviews that she conducted with people like Tsui Hark, the Hong Kong filmmaker, and Chan Do Ping, a laborer who erects bamboo scaffolding on skyscrapers.
STILL, Ms. Tam is nothing if not a shrewd businesswoman. 
To sell more than $98 T-shirts and $1,315 gowns, she must broaden her appeal beyond the Madison Avenue set.
When General Motors invited her to design the interior of a 1999 Oldsmobile Alero as part of a special promotion, she jumped at the chance. 
She was also thrilled that the book party in Hong Kong drew filmmakers, writers, and Cantonese pop stars, as well as fashion people.
"People think this book is about my fashion, but it's not," Ms. Tam said. 
"It's about all the things I love: furniture, gardens, spirituality, the body, health, city life. 
I had to cut a lot."

Dennis Byrd, walking with a slight limp, the result of his spinal-cord injury almost six years ago, visited his old Jets team today. 
And then he went over to the nearby Nassau County Medical Center in East Meadow and spent an hour and a half talking to the paralyzed Chinese gymnast, Sang Lan.
She suffered her injury last Tuesday night while warming up for her specialty, the vault, in the Goodwill Games. 
Byrd spoke to her at bedside through an interpreter. 
Her condition remains critical, but stable, according to a hospital spokeswoman, and she will undergo extensive vertebrae surgery on Saturday, hours before her parents are scheduled to arrive from China.
It was not an uncommon moment for Byrd, whose ability to walk again after being completely paralyzed following a hit in a game has attracted the attention of many people similarly injured. 
He said he writes hundreds of letters a year to those who have neck and spinal-cord injuries. 
But he asked the Jets to arrange a personal visit with Sang.
"She loves Beanie Babies," Byrd said after seeing the 17-year-old. 
"When you go to visit her, she's a doll and she'll break your heart."
In a late-season game against the Chiefs in 1992, Byrd, the club's best pass rusher, was trying to get to the quarterback. 
With his head down, he inadvertently dug his helmet into the chest of a teammate, Scott Mersereau. 
Byrd immediately knew he had been paralyzed, but the Jets' medical staff quickly began a series of procedures on the field, including huge doses of steroids to stem the swelling around the spinal cord. 
Two and a half months later Byrd was able to walk into a news conference and talk about the experience.
"It's an emotional time any time you visit people who have undergone something so traumatic," Byrd said about his talk with Sang.
Byrd had not been around the Jets for more than a year. 
But he wanted to visit the team and its coach, Bill Parcells.
Asked how he would have done under Parcells, Byrd said: "I thought about that quite a bit. 
I would have loved it. 
I always enjoyed playing for someone who is very goal-driven."
Byrd currently works with a foundation he created for children with life-threatening diseases, at P.O. 
Box 90, Owasso, Okla. 
74055.

Visit Jets, See the World
