file: Profile_Yang Jiaxing_Pushing the Limits In Chinese Banking.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN a nation where courtesy is often regarded as a sign of weakness, the most startling thing about China's first private bank is that its tellers are polite. 
They smile. 
They say thank you. 
They don't take impromptu tea breaks at their desks while waiting customers look on murderously. 
In another innovation that has people here shaking their heads in wonderment, the bank lends money based on creditworthiness.
"At state banks, it's the state's money, so if you have good connections or if you send the loan officers a gift, then you can get a loan even if your credit isn't so good," said Yang Jiaxing, the private bank's 47-year-old manager and founder, sitting in his small office above his bank. 
"Here it's much stricter. 
We don't have buddy loans, the way they do. 
If you don't meet our requirements, then I won't make you a loan even if you are my friend."
Mr. Yang, an affable man whose name is pronounced Yahng Gee-ya-shing, has lived most of his life at the frontiers of the economically permissible, exploring and mapping the nether world between Communism and capitalism.
For six years now, he has been the thin edge of a wedge, prying open China's byzantine banking system to outsiders. 
Now, a growing number of unofficial banks and financial institutions are emerging -- 45 in this bustling coastal city alone. 
And there are signs that selected foreign banks may eventually be allowed in the domestic banking market.
If the state-run behemoths notorious for their sloth, obliviousness to market principles and discourtesy are shouldered aside, this could be a hugely profitable business.
CHINA'S 1.2 billion inhabitants save an average of 38 percent of their incomes, one of the highest levels in the world. 
The per-capita totals may look low to a Westerner, but the total is enough to make any banker salivate: Government statistics show the Chinese have squirreled away the equivalent of $187 billion -- a figure that is rising by 25 percent a year. 
On top of that, there are unknown sums in underground banks and savings in foreign currency. 
Industrial output soared 20 percent in 1992, meaning demand for loans is huge.
In the West, the modern banking system has been developing since the late Middle Ages, when Florentine merchants began financing the international wool trade -- and helped support the Renaissance.
But in China, the economic revolution of the last dozen years has been achieved in spite of the nation's banking system. 
While economic growth rates are among the highest in the world -- China's gross national product was up 12 percent last year -- the dynamo has been small privately and collectively owned companies that often are unable to borrow money.
That is why Mr. Yang's bank, the Wenzhou-Lucheng Credit Cooperative, was born.
In and of itself, the bank is insignificant, for it has less than $7 million in assets, compared with $100 billion and more for the biggest banks in Japan and the West. 
Yet Mr. Yang serves as a reminder not only of the possibilities that China offers but also of the risks: his experience illustrates the ways in which state-owned companies can try to stifle competitors who nibble at their turf.
Mr. Yang, a former factory worker with only a junior high school education, had always been inclined toward private business. 
Indeed, he founded his first factory, making electrical parts, in early 1976 when the Maoist Gang of Four was calling on all Chinese to "beat back the deviationist wind from the right."
Private factories were just what the Gang of Four had in mind, but Mr. Yang was sheltered to some extent because he lived here in Wenzhou, perhaps the most entrepreneurial place in China. 
Local officials have made a specialty of preaching Communist sermons as their congregations practice something perilously close to capitalism.
Wenzhou's private merchants, frozen out of the official banking system, turned to underground lenders that in some cases were run by criminals. 
In the mid-1980's, a huge Ponzi scheme gathered nearly $100 million in Wen zhou before it collapsed, sending shockwaves through the community. 
More than 100 people either committed suicide in the aftermath or were killed by others who thought they were to blame.
That was when Mr. Yang decided it would be an appropriate time to open a private bank, catering to the merchants. 
There was no legal basis for private banks in China, but the local Communist authorities -- shaken by the tumult caused by the Ponzi scheme -- decided that an above-ground private bank would at least be easier to monitor than the underground variety. 
With $86,000 in capital, some his own and some from two friends, Mr. Yang opened shop in November 1986.
To attract deposits, Mr. Yang paid interest rates one-fifth higher than those state banks offered. 
He also offered late hours, seven-day-a-week banking, courteous service and occasional deliveries of cash to important customers.
"Service is much better at the credit cooperatives," said Cai Yanjiong, an economic planner in Wen zhou. 
"If it's just before closing, the girl at the state bank may tell you to come back tomorrow and wave you away. 
But at the credit cooperatives, they're more patient."
Borrowers too were easy to find, even though Mr. Yang charged rates a bit higher than what was available at state banks. 
He supplies loans to private merchants and small factories that the big banks have ignored, and to reduce the risks, he lends only when real estate is available as collateral, and only up to 60 percent of the value of the property.
He also typically lends money for only four months at a time -- often financing trade or purchases of raw materials that are quickly turned into finished merchandise -- although these loans are often rolled over.
Mr. Yang enjoys a nice interest rate spread: his average payment on deposits is now 7.8 percent annually, while his loans bear an average rate of 15.4 percent.
IT is a chilly January morning, and his warm breath hangs in the frosty air like puffs of smoke. 
Of course, there is smoke as well, for Mr. Yang has a voracious appetite for Zhonghua cigarettes. 
He does not acknowledge the chill, even though he is wearing no outer coat, just a white shirt, red-striped tie and a green-gray suit with the label still sewn on the sleeve -- to insure that customers realize what a fine suit it is.
Irrational loans are perhaps the worst problem at state banks; they have huge portfolios that will never be paid back. 
The best way to get a loan, as Mr. Yang suggests, is to cultivate good guanxi -- connections -- with Communist Party officials. 
Second best is to give the bank managers merchandise "samples," like color televisions, or at least to invite them to lavish banquets with shark's fin soup and mao tai liquor.
"Now clients don't even offer 'gifts' to our lending officers any more," Mr. Yang said. 
"They figured out that a gift doesn't make any difference."
Because state banks are already chock full of bad loans that are rolled over whenever they become due, no one is ever disciplined for adding one more irrational loan to the pile. 
Mr. Yang, on the other hand, docks the salary of his loan officers if they approve a loan that is not repaid.
Mr. Yang and his imitators have attracted a combined $100 million in deposits. 
That caught the attention of the state-owned banks, which used their political influence to try to smother the private institutions in red tape. 
In 1988, for example, the state banks pushed through a regulation banning the private institutions from paying higher interest on deposits. 
The private banks are also banned from opening branches -- even from expanding. 
Mr. Yang's bank is now forbidden to lend more than a total of about $5.5 million. 
So there is no point in attracting additional deposits; there is nothing to do with the money.
On top of that, taxes are virtually confiscatory. 
In addition to a 55 percent tax rate there is a 15 percent levy for transportation and energy, along with various other fees and restrictions on use of earnings. 
In sum, the owners of the bank can pocket only 7.2 percent of the profits.
Mr. Yang said that he was optimistic that rules on private banking would gradually be relaxed and that China's economic revolution would continue to gather steam.
Prodded, he acknowledged the one uncertainty that most Chinese entrepreneurs feel: apprehension about what will happen after the death of Deng Xiaoping, the 88-year-old senior leader under whom the capitalist experiments got under way.
"Everybody feels that nervousness," Mr. Yang said. 
"Things have changed so much in the last few years that I don't think there would be a big problem. 
But we know that there will be change after him, and no one knows what kind."

Â 
INCHING TOWARD INDEPENDENCE
THE first thing to know about Chinese bankers is that they are glorified plumbers. 
Their task is to respond to orders from Communist Party officials and open or close the spigots of credit to state-owned factories.
This usually is antithetical to creditworthiness: if a factory is in long-term decline, manufacturing kerosene lamps or pink sofas that nobody wants, then that is all the more reason to extend a loan so that the factory can meet its payroll. 
It does not matter whether the factory will pay back the loan; the important thing is avoiding labor unrest.
Since the mid-1980's, however, China's handful of state-owned banks has been joined by a growing number of other institutions. 
The Bank of Communications in Shanghai was reactivated in 1986 and at about the same time the Citic (China International Trust and Investment Corporation) Industrial Bank began operating in Beijing. 
Both are controlled by the state, but have a deal of autonomy.
A few regional banks have sprung up, and the Capital Steel Corporation was allowed last year -- on the orders of Deng Xiaoping, the senior leader -- to start its own bank. 
Now every big company in the country dreams of doing the same thing. 
Credit cooperatives have also become ubiquitous, with an estimated 60,000 branches around the country.
Foreign banks have until now been restricted to hard currency transactions, but Citibank and other foreign institutions are thriving in Hong Kong, and are expected to win a large share of the mainland market if they are allowed to attract local deposits.

text:

For the mob of mainland Chinese immigrants who massed in the 13th-floor lobby of Hong Kong's immigration tower on Wednesday afternoon, the time for filling out forms or even howling in protest had passed.
After having been turned away yet again by immigration officers in their quest for residency permits, the immigrants doused the lobby floor with a flammable liquid and ignited it. 
The fire raced through the offices. 
By the time a sprinkler system extinguished it, 50 people had suffered burns, several serious. 
Six immigrants were listed in critical condition today.
The eruption of violence flabbergasted people in this normally tranquil city. 
Most had stopped paying attention to the lonely struggle of 6,000 mainland Chinese for the right to settle in the former British colony.
Rebuffed repeatedly by local courts and facing deportation to the mainland, the immigrants were a sad reminder of the awkward ties between China and Hong Kong.
Although Hong Kong reverted to Chinese sovereignty under an agreement with Britain in July 1997, the former colony retained much of its autonomy under China's "one country, two systems" formula. 
That included control over immigration, which means Chinese mainland citizens here must have residency permits or they will be sent back home.
As the mainlanders have run out of options, they have grown frustrated and angry. 
On Wednesday, the anger mutated into a desperate attack.
"It's very difficult to control our emotions," said a mainland woman who gave her name as Ngai. 
"We've been here so long. 
We can't work. 
We can't earn a living. 
Even our families in China are now against us."
Ms. Ngai, 26, from Guangdong Province, was not involved in the attack. 
She deplored the actions of her fellow immigrants, which she said did not reflect the vast majority of the immigrants. 
And she fears that the attack will lead to a backlash against mainland Chinese here.
Indeed, the Hong Kong government moved swiftly today to crack down. 
It announced that it would immediately deport 1,000 mainland Chinese who are not involved in legal cases. 
Until now, Hong Kong has treated the mainlanders gingerly, partly for political reasons and partly to guard its reputation for the rule of law.
The police arrested 15 immigrants in connection with the blaze, and Hong Kong's leaders condemned the attack in unusually blunt terms. 
Tung Chee-hwa, the territory's chief executive, called it "brutal behavior, irrational behavior that is unacceptable to all of us."
The showdown between the mainlanders and the Hong Kong government had been brewing for more than a year. 
In December, 50 protesters clashed with the police outside Mr. Tung's office, hurling bamboo sticks and flower pots. 
Last week, 10 mainlanders scuffled with guards and threatened to commit suicide after immigration officers had refused to meet them.
Their frustration stems from a ruling by Hong Kong's high court early last year that granted residency to mainland-born children with at least one Hong Kong parent. 
The ruling opened the door to tens of thousands of mainland Chinese who are the products of cross-border marriages or relationships. 
And it terrified the local government, which said Hong Kong would be inundated by 1.6 million people.
Six months later, at the behest of the government, China's Parliament, the National People's Congress, overturned the ruling by rewriting the parts of Hong Kong's Constitution on which it was based. 
That closed the door to all but 6,000 immigrants, who had already entered the territory.
Hong Kong allowed those people to remain in the territory to fight their cases. 
But the high court recently reaffirmed China's right to overturn its ruling. 
And a series of lower courts have hewed to that line, ruling against the immigrants or refusing to hear their cases.
Officials here said they had been tolerant of the mainlanders, letting them camp for weeks in front of the government offices and protest almost daily at the immigration tower. 
But the rampage could poison the attitude of Hong Kongers toward their mainland cousins.

file: Protests Flare as Hong Kong_s Highest Court Upholds China_s Limits on Residency.txt
text:

In what amounts to a legal genuflection to Beijing, Hong Kong's highest court ruled today that the Chinese government had the right to overturn its landmark decision earlier this year that granted residency to more than a million people from mainland China.
Today's decision, which involved 17 Chinese who were seeking the right to stay in Hong Kong, ignited outraged protests by hundreds of mainland Chinese, who massed in front of the government headquarters. 
The protesters tried to storm the building, pelted the police with bamboo sticks and plastic bottles, and brought out 200 riot police in this usually orderly city.
The protesters were angry because the court rejected the appeal of the 17 Chinese, who claimed they were entitled to live here because they had at least one parent who was a legal resident of Hong Kong. 
In February, the court granted that right, but the decision was nullified four months later when China's legislature reinterpreted provisions of the Hong Kong Constitution on which it was based.
Today's ruling resolves any lingering doubt that Hong Kong's British-style legal system is firmly subordinate to the Chinese system. 
Legal experts and pro-democracy leaders expressed fear that the government could appeal to Beijing to overturn other decisions that went against it.
"My concern is that the Hong Kong government can now do what it likes, provided that the Chinese government backs it up," said Margaret Ng, a lawyer who represented the 17 mainland Chinese.
Government officials welcomed the ruling, though they insisted that Hong Kong would appeal to Beijing only in extraordinary cases. 
They said the immigration case demanded such action because the original court ruling would have thrown open Hong Kong's doors to an estimated 1.6 million people -- straining the resources of one of the world's most densely populated cities.
"The whole world is watching, and China is aware that if it interferes, there will be serious political fallout," said Robert Allcock, Hong Kong's acting solicitor-general.
Other experts, however, said that the reversal of the immigration ruling had already eroded the authority of its highest court. 
Other powerful members of Hong Kong society might seize on the precedent to appeal unfavorable rulings to Beijing.
Several hundred mainland Chinese held a sit-in demonstration at the government headquarters here throughout the case. 
As word of the ruling filtered out this morning, their frustration turned into rage. 
The police said eight people were injured in a melee that started when the protesters tried to enter the offices of Hong Kong's chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa.
The police repelled the demonstrators, but not before deploying a wall of riot troops to ring the building. 
Public disorder is so rare in this city here that the riot shields still bore the initials of the Royal Hong Kong Police, a remnant of the British colonial past.

file: PUBLIC LIVES_A Witness to a Smear_ _Who Lost China__.txt
text:
ï»¿
ARTHUR W. HUMMEL JR. is far from China these days, but it is never far from his mind. 
The living room walls of his modest red-brick house in Chevy Chase, Md., are covered with the delicate screens and placid clay figurines he collected in China first as a child, then as a teacher, then as an unlikely soldier and finally as United States ambassador from 1981 to 1985.
The hum of nearby traffic is muffled by a thick stand of bamboo he planted alongside his driveway, and he is hard at work translating into English the memoirs of a Nationalist Chinese guerrilla leader.
With the death this month of John S. Service -- the first of the so-called "China hands" falsely accused of being Communist sympathizers and driven from the State Department in the 1950's -- Mr. Hummel, 79, took an afternoon last week to recall an era when his long career as a China specialist was just beginning and he watched paranoia and demagoguery prematurely end the careers of so many others.
It was a fate that struck closer to home for Mr. Hummel than for many of his young colleagues. 
His life before coming to the State Department closely mirrored that of Mr. Service and a handful of other China experts whose careers were destroyed. 
Though about a decade younger, he too was born in China, the child of missionary parents, with a knowledge of the language and culture much deeper than that of his superiors in Washington.
Mr. Hummel joined the State Department in 1950, the year that North Korea invaded South Korea. 
It was also the year that Senator Joseph McCarthy stood up in Wheeling, W.Va., and first announced that he had a list of 205 people "known to the Secretary of State as being members of the Communist Party and still working and shaping the policy of the State Department."
The climate at Foggy Bottom then was one of circled wagons, but a growing sense of bewilderment and anger, he recalled. 
"There was very little paranoia among those you worked with because everyone felt like it was us against them," he said. 
In fact, one of Mr. Hummel's first jobs was helping Oliver Edmund Clubb, another of the accused China hands, compile documents for his defense.
"But we all discussed it a lot," Mr. Hummel said. 
"Where is it going to go next?
What kind of idiocy can right-wingers be perpetrating next -- maybe domestically, and not just foreign affairs?'
"
Personally, Mr. Hummel had little to worry about. 
He had an anti-Communist credential that even McCarthy would have had trouble tarnishing: during World War II, for 15 months, he had actually fought against both the Chinese Communists and the Japanese with a column of Nationalist Chinese guerrillas.
In his low, gravelly voice, Mr. Hummel does his best to play down any heroic Hemingway plot lines. 
At that point in his life, during his early 20's, he said, he was simply trying to find anything to occupy his time and "get my parents off my back."
He had been born in Shanxi province, west of Beijing, where his father -- a noted Sinologist and later head of the Oriental book division of the Library of Congress -- was then a Congregationalist minister. 
The family returned to the United States when Mr. Hummel was 8, and he struggled for a sense of belonging. 
He said he was kicked out of two prep schools and dropped out ("well, actually, flunked out") of Antioch College. 
He then lived as a self-described "early hippy," working a series of odd jobs -- including factory worker and detective -- before agreeing to go back to China in 1940 to help his father on a book-buying trip.
But his father ended up not going, and on the day the Japanese invaded Pearl Harbor, Mr. Hummel was rounded up and locked in an internment camp along with about 2,000 other foreigners.
"There was no way," he explained, "to ask the Japanese kindly, 'Would you let me go home?'
" So he and a British friend engineered an escape with the help of Nationalist guerrillas concealed nearby. 
He crawled over barbed-wire and walked most of the night and the next day.
HE was 20 and had no military training. 
But he was handed a small Belgian pistol, and he had little choice but to stay and help, harassing Japanese patrols by night and trying to defend a small patch of plains against Communist takeover.
"I don't know why, but I really cannot remember being scared," he said. 
"It all seemed like great fun."
Later, after McCarthy's fall, Mr. Hummel said he liked to joke that he "was too small a fish for him to be interested in, but if he had ever hauled me up for a hearing, I would have said, 'I was fighting Chinese Communist troops in 1944. 
Where were you, Mr. Senator?'
" Through his experience, though, he learned of the corruption of the Nationalist leadership, which later became the refrain of Mr. Service and his colleagues.
Looking back now, Mr. Hummel said perhaps the only shortcoming of many of those drummed out of the State Department was a lack of political sophistication. 
Mr. Clubb, for example, read from his diary during a hearing. 
Senator McCarthy then subpoenaed the whole diary and "went through it with a red paintbrush" to make it appear that Mr. Clubb was disloyal.
As senators only a few miles away wrapped up the impeachment trial of a President, Mr. Hummel recalled those earlier years as a crisis in government still unlike any he has known. 
"We worried not merely about these people," he said, "but about the whole apparatus of government. 
It was a feeling of, 'What the hell is happening?' and 'Thank God,' when it was over."

text:
ï»¿
SANDER M. LEVIN hardly fits the classic free-trade profile. 
He is a liberal Democratic congressman from the Detroit suburbs who proudly owns a 94 percent career voting record with organized labor.
Yet with thousands of protesters in town to demonstrate against the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and what they view as the evils of globalization, Representative Levin will be lucky if he isn't hanged in effigy.
The 68-year-old legislator is fine-tuning a plan that could give wavering House Democrats the political cover they want to vote yes on the biggest trade deal in years, an accord with China. 
If Mr. Levin succeeds, Congress will help hand Beijing a diplomatic coup while opening new markets for American goods but will still keep leverage over China's behavior on human rights, religious tolerance and the environment.
"Members are searching for a way to both keep the heat on China and get the benefits of what we negotiated," Mr. Levin said in his Capitol Hill office, where photographs of Thomas P. O'Neill and Robert F. Kennedy adorn the wall. 
"We have to strive to combine active engagement with constructive confrontation."
For 20 years Congress has gone through the motions of an annual debate and vote to grant China the same trading privileges that Washington gives almost every other country. 
Congress has never refused to provide this plum.
But now China is on the verge of joining the World Trade Organization, and as part of a deal negotiated last fall, President Clinton promised to try to lift the annual review and grant Beijing permanent trading status.
The House will vote just before Memorial Day, but the outcome is too close to call. 
The fate of the agreement rests with about two dozen uncommitted Democrats. 
Passage in the pro-business Senate is considered certain.
Enter Mr. Levin, a senior member of the House Ways and Means Committee, who is one of the fence-sitters and has long wrestled with trade issues. 
He voted against the North American Free Trade Agreement in 1993 and opposed giving President Clinton fast-track authority to negotiate trade pacts. 
He has voted both for and against granting China normal trading status.
"I'm an activist internationalist who's worked on both sides: expanded trade and expanded issues of trade," said Mr. Levin, who banged on Japan's doors in the 1980's to pry open its market to American automobiles.
Mr. Levin came away from a 10-day trip to China in January convinced that this trade agreement would influence the future of U.S.-China relations for years to come.
"I came back feeling that changes in China are irreversible, but that the direction is not inevitable," said Mr. Levin, who talked to students, artists and intellectuals about how free trade could open up China's repressive society. 
"You have to shape globalization."
Mr. Levin sees himself as an organizer and a problem solver, and set out to steer all sides to a middle ground. 
He has drawn up a plan to monitor China once it joins the W.T.O., and to react swiftly to any violations. 
The proposal sets up a Congressional-executive branch commission to monitor China's behavior on human rights and trade -- the biggest concern of opponents to giving up the yearly review -- and arms it with a quiver of rewards and penalties.
THE plan would also write into law promises China made to the United States to avoid surges of Chinese exports into the American market.
At first, no one on Capitol Hill paid much attention to Mr. Levin's plan. 
But by the time lawmakers headed home last week for a recess and the administration anxiously sought to nail down undecided votes, the idea was catching on. 
Backers say Mr. Levin's plan could swing 10 to 15 votes.
Mr. Levin is not flashy, nor is the low-key, details approach he has used in shopping his plan to about 40 undecided Democrats and Republicans. 
A Democratic colleague once described him as "a pit bull with manners."
"What Sandy is doing is extremely helpful because he's trying to get some accountability over time," said Representative Tom Allen, a Maine Democrat whose vote is up for grabs.
The China trade wars have catapulted Mr. Levin into the limelight somewhat to the chagrin of his party's leaders. 
Representative Richard A. Gephardt of Missouri, the House Democratic leader who is strategically neutral on the vote, has been dismissive of Mr. Levin's efforts, choosing to broker his own third way with the White House.
The No. 2 Democrat in the House, David E. Bonior of Michigan, is leading the charge against the deal, and has called Mr. Levin's plan toothless.
In a rare flash of pique, Mr. Levin bristles at that criticism: "It has a lot of teeth in it, and I hope they're sharp and will bite when they need to."
Sander Martin Levin, the grandson of Russian and Polish Jews, was born and raised in Detroit. 
After earning degrees from the University of Chicago, Columbia University and Harvard Law School, he threw himself into the political arena.
Mr. Levin served in the Michigan State Senate for five years, but after two failed attempts to become governor in the 1970's, he thought he was washed up in politics. 
He was assistant administrator of the Agency for International Development during the Carter administration.
But in 1982, Michigan's 12th Congressional District opened up, and Mr. Levin has occupied it ever since, forming the lesser-known half of the Levin brother act in Congress. 
(Mr. Levin's younger brother, Carl, is the senior senator from Michigan and ranking Democrat on the Armed Services Committee.) Mr. Levin and his wife, Vicki, have four grown children.
For Mr. Levin, who worked one summer at a Dodge auto assembly plant, the China pact brings his trade career full circle: "My feeling on trade is that it's more than the humdrum of tariffs. 
A key part of economic life is rolling up your sleeves on a daily basis to work it out and to avoid the extremes."

text:
ï»¿
THE faced down the rampaging mobs in the streets of Beijing last spring. 
But it took a lesser adversary to incapacitate James R. Sasser, the former Democratic Senator from Tennessee who has just returned home after three and a half tumultuous years as the American Ambassador to China.
"I had survived thousands of Chinese screaming for my head," Mr. Sasser explained. 
"And then about two days after I get home to Washington, I'm walking down the steps to my house and I step on the cat that my daughter had brought home from China. 
And I tumbled head over heels down a flight full of steps."
Mr. Sasser broke his left arm in the fall. 
It has been only a few days since the cast came off. 
As he takes a seat at a small corner table in a Washington coffee shop, he has to lift his still weak left arm into place with his right hand. 
"It's getting better," he said.
The healing is also under way, he hopes, in the relationship between the United States and China, scarred by the mistaken American bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade, accusations of Chinese espionage and tensions over Taiwan.
Mr. Sasser, a courtly 62-year-old politician-turned-diplomat, insists that the violent anti-American demonstrations that trapped him in the embassy in Beijing for four days last May were an aberration. 
The demonstrations were a result of the missile strike in Belgrade, which killed three Chinese journalists.
Mr. Sasser knows that the most striking visual image of his tenure in China may be the widely reprinted photograph of him staring somberly through the jagged remains of a window in the battered United States Embassy compound. 
"I think that is unfortunate," he said. 
"We can't quite forget what happened in May," he said of the embassy siege in Beijing, "but it ought to be put in context."
In the months since the demonstrations, Mr. Sasser said, he has become convinced that senior leaders of the Chinese Government did not encourage the violence and that they were unaware that the police had lost control of the mob outside the embassy.
"They did not know the extent of it," he said. 
"What they were seeing on television -- Chinese television -- were peaceful student demonstrations. 
They weren't seeing the rocks being thrown, the Molotov cocktails."
When a junior Foreign Ministry official finally drove to the embassy, "he got out of his car, and he saw what had happened and his jaw just sort of fell," Mr. Sasser said. 
"The Foreign Ministry just didn't have any idea, I don't think, of what was going on."
The situation became so dangerous that Mr. Sasser ordered that all sensitive papers in the embassy be destroyed, including his private journals, which would have been the raw material for the book he is now thinking of writing. 
"The Marine guards came in and destroyed them, and I couldn't tell them not to," he said.
About a quarter of a mile from the embassy, his wife, Mary, and their 29-year-old son, Gray, were trapped in the Ambassador's residence, facing their own rock-throwing demonstrators. 
It took a frantic call by Ambassador Sasser to his Chinese counterpart in Washington to have the Beijing police protect his family.
Mrs. Sasser, he said, was jarred. 
The Chinese have a saying, he said, "that if you do something they disapprove of, that you've hurt the feelings of 1.3 billion Chinese. 
Well, Mary says that 1.3 billion Chinese hurt her feelings."
Mr. Sasser said he never received a formal apology for the attacks. 
But at a rare private dinner in the home of President Jiang Zemin in the week before he left China, Mr. Sasser said, "He said to me that 'things happened that we did not intend to happen and should not have happened.'
" It was, Mr. Sasser said, "the closest anyone ever came" to an apology.
Despite the recent strains, Mr. Sasser said he was convinced that the Chinese leaders and most of the Chinese people were eager for a good relationship with the United States.
"I came back from China with a very optimistic view about our long-term relationship, and I say that because there were a lot of pro-American feelings there within the leadership," said Mr. Sasser, who is considering joining an international law firm that could use his expertise on China.
"As far as the Chinese were concerned, the Americans were the people they liked the best," he said. 
The bombing "may have a chilling effect on that," he added, but it won't last.
THE road to Beijing began for Mr. Sasser in the back roads of Memphis, where he was the first child born to a Federal agricultural official and his homemaker wife. 
Two daughters followed. 
After Vanderbilt University, the younger Mr. Sasser settled on a career in law and then in Democratic politics. 
He was elected to the Senate in 1976.
Mr. Sasser had been chairman of the Senate Budget Committee and seemed poised to become his party's Senate leader, but he was forced into political retirement when defeated in the Republican avalanche of 1994. 
He does not hide the pain of the defeat. 
"My feelings were hurt," he said.
"The President called me as I was leaving the Senate and asked me if I wanted another job in Government and I said absolutely not," he said. 
"I was tired of being in Government, tired of trying to live on a Government salary. 
And he said, 'Well, how about an ambassadorship?'
And I said, I'm not interested -- except maybe China.'
" The Beijing offer came about 10 days later.
"As soon as I got to China, it felt as if my batteries had been recharged," Mr. Sasser said. 
Despite persistent human rights abuses, he said, China is a much freer, more prosperous nation than many Americans imagine.
"The Chinese are now able to make their own decisions about what kind of job they want, where they want to work, where they want to live," he said. 
"They can travel abroad, they can go into business. 
None of these things were possible in the China of the 1950's or 1960's or even the early 1970's."
"And the Chinese do criticize their Government -- in private," he said. 
"What you can't do is stand out on a street corner and do it."

file: PUBLIC LIVES_Witness to the Atrocity Behind the Medicine.txt
text:
ï»¿
EVERY atrocity spits out a few, the ones who make it through and cannot forget, who are oppressed with the need to bear witness. 
Close your eyes and Harry Wu, the human rights advocate, might be Elie Wiesel. 
Just a few details of time and geography are different.
Mr. Wu was 23 when one of Mao's crackdowns caught up with him, in 1960. 
His father had been a banker in Shanghai; Mr. Wu had been educated by Jesuits. 
Mr. Wu's crime: being a counterrevolutionary rightist. 
He spent 19 years in prison camps.
"They broke my back, they broke my neck, they broke my arm, they broke my leg," Mr. Wu says, in heavily accented English. 
"I was put in solitary confinement, in cement, a case made from cement. 
Six feet long, three feet wide, three feet high. 
A coffin. 
I was 28."
Now Mr. Wu is 61. 
He has been out of the prison camps for 20 years and still the Chinese Government obsesses him. 
He has written three books on his experiences with the Government, the third of which is titled "Troublemaker."
He has made four undercover trips to China to research and document human-rights abuses.
Earlier this month, Mr. Wu posed as a doctor, meeting with two Chinese citizens who reportedly offered to sell him kidneys from prisoners who had been executed in China. 
That meeting, which Mr. Wu videotaped, led to the arrest of the two men by the Federal Bureau of Investigation earlier this week. 
One might argue that it was foolhardy for a man who has been featured on television to do this work, that it might have jeopardized the investigation, but that would be missing the point. 
The point is, Mr. Wu's life was stolen and he wants to do something about it. 
The point is, it's personal with Mr. Wu.
"There are Chinese doctors who say, 'I am sorry about those criminals, but I care about my patients,' " Mr. Wu says, enraged. 
" 'The criminals, they're shot, they die, it's a waste if we don't use them. 
Anyway, they're dead, they don't have rights.'
"
What about the argument that if the organs are used, others may live?
"I'm going to donate," Mr. Wu says. 
"I carry the card in my wallet. 
I think donation is a good thing. 
But look at the law. 
The constitutional code has 16 crimes which carry the death penalty; 9 are so-called political crimes. 
There is no justice, no real attorney system, even today. 
I never had a lawyer, no trial."
MR. WU is also suspicious of the guidelines he says the Chinese claim to follow. 
Their criminal code, Mr. Wu says, gives the Government the right to extract body parts when the condemned give their consent or when their bodies are "uncollected."
" 'Uncollected dead bodies,' what that means?"
Mr. Wu asks, angrily. 
"Take myself. 
When I was labeled as counterrevolutionary rightist, all my family separate from me. 
My mother commits suicide. 
In 19 years, I have one visitor. 
My older brother comes to visit me, first month, that's it. 
They have to separate."
A man in desperate conditions will consent or confess to anything, Mr. Wu says. 
He confessed to crimes he did not commit when he was arrested during the Cultural Revolution -- his captors showed him a room of the dead and bleeding. 
The Jews in the concentration camps sometimes also consented. 
He went to Auschwitz himself, in 1994. 
He saw the evidence.
"The Nazi doctors, they try to find out how save lives if the German U-boat is sinking in the cold water," Mr. Wu says. 
"They use a dog, they use a rat, then the Nazi doctors say, 'Oh, every day, couple hundred Jewish walk into the gas chamber, this is a waste,' O.K.?
Then the Nazi doctor presents himself in front of the Jewish prisoners. 
'Hey, are you willing to come into my lab?
This is a paper. 
Sign it. 
I am not guaranteeing your life, but there is a chance. 
For two weeks, you will have good food. 
Otherwise you will go to the gas chamber.'
"
Mr. Wu came to the United States in 1985 and became a citizen in 1994. 
He still wishes to be buried in China. 
He is married and lives in California, but he is rarely home. 
Last year he had 200 speaking engagements. 
His investigative trips, often carried out alone, have been dangerous. 
On Mr. Wu's last trip to China, in 1995, he was arrested at the border, charged with spying and deported. 
Mr. Wu insists he would have preferred to stay.
"I wanted justice," he says. 
"If they keep me, that means people are aware there is an injustice system."
The Chinese people might not be informed.
"Yeah, there is a chance, the Chinese, maybe only a very small group would know," Mr. Wu says. 
He recites the chant of the ones who are doomed to bear witness. 
"But anyway, if I don't go, who else to go?"
Perhaps Mr. Wu wanted to die?
"I want alive, I want alive much as anyone. 
I lost my life. 
If God say to me, 'Harry, I know you suffered, I wanted to give you a favor, what do you want?'
I want 20 years back. 
It's not possible. 
That's why today I work very hard. 
I am 61 years old. 
I know the time for me is very short."
He snatches up a document in Chinese regarding the use of organs from condemned criminals, so passionate now that his speech becomes rushed, harder to understand. 
He is asked to repeat himself.
"Uncollected body is possible Harry Wu's body," he says, almost shouting. 
"Do you want buy this kidney?
From executed prisoners. 
Who is the executed prisoners?
Maybe is Harry Wu. 
So you want this one?
You don't care?
You just want a kidney?
A part, body parts for yourself?
Explain to me what is so-called uncollected body. 
Explain to me how prisoner have a consent."

text:

President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia arrived in Beijing tonight on the first stop of an Asian tour intended to revive his country's faded diplomatic role in the region and build what could become a Chinese-Russian axis to counter American influence.
Mr. Putin is expected to sign at least six accords with Chinese leaders on Tuesday, including a joint statement with President Jiang Zemin condemning American proposals for missile defense systems over North America and Asia. 
Opposition to the American plan has accelerated a relationship that Russia and China describe as a "strategic partnership" intended to counter American power.
"The partnership is an effort to oppose hegemony and supremacy, and one single country dominating the world," said Zhao Huasheng, director of the Russian Studies department at the Shanghai Institute for International Studies.
On Wednesday, Mr. Putin travels to North Korea, where he is expected to ask that country's leader, Kim Jong Il, to forgo its missile development program. 
The United States has told Russia and China that the proposed American missile defense system is intended to counter threats posed by smaller, missile-armed states like North Korea.
Mr. Putin then stops in Blagoveshchensk, in eastern Russia, for a conference on a region that is experiencing increased immigration from China. 
He ends his tour on the Japanese island of Okinawa, where he is due to arrive late Friday for the annual gathering of leading industrial countries.
China is by far Mr. Putin's most important stop. 
It will be his first visit there since he was elected president in March. 
And it follows eight visits by his predecessor, Boris N. Yeltsin, who agreed with President Jiang in 1996 to establish the strategic partnership to build a "multi-polar world," a euphemism to describe opposition to America's status as the world's sole superpower.
"Russia shares a strategic partnership with China and puts relations with Beijing among the highest priorities of its foreign policy," Mr. Putin said in an interview with China's state television last week.
While it is not yet clear how warmly Mr. Putin will embrace the Chinese worldview, Western analysts say the rapprochement between the countries is taking on an increasingly anti-American cast.
"On one level, this is classic realpolitik balance-of-power, but on another it has the appearance of a united front against the United States," said David Shambaugh, a China specialist at George Washington University and the Brookings Institution in Washington.
Mr. Jiang and Mr. Yeltsin had pledged to increase economic cooperation between the two countries to bolster that partnership, but bilateral trade has fallen far short of the targeted $20 billion a year, stagnating at around $6 billion. 
Russian arms sales to China account for much of that.
Mr. Putin hopes to change that, though it will not happen overnight. 
Russia's troubled economy presents a far less attractive export market for China than the United States, Europe and Japan, and Russian goods cannot compete in China against domestically manufactured products or high technology imports from Japan and the West. 
About the only things Russia can offer China besides arms are commodities like natural gas.
Among the agreements Mr. Putin is expected to sign in Beijing is one calling for a feasibility study for a gas pipeline from Russia's Irkutsk region to China. 
That project has been talked about for years with little progress, partly because China does not really need more natural gas.
Another deal on the table during Mr. Putin's visit is Russia's sale of a second pair of nuclear reactors for the Tianwan nuclear power plant in eastern China. 
An initial two Russian reactors are currently being built at the plant.
Still, weapons are likely to remain the strongest bond in the two countries' economic relationship. 
China wants weapons to modernize its military and Russia's overdeveloped arms industry is begging for customers with cash. 
Already, China has bought advanced fighter aircraft, submarines and Russian guided-missile destroyers.
Russia has become even more important to China since Israel bowed to American pressure earlier this month and canceled the sale to Beijing of an early-warning radar system mounted atop a Russian jet. 
Russia could supply China with similar technology.
Mr. Putin's large delegation includes Defense Minister Igor Sergeyev and the director of Russia's arms exporter Rosvooruzheniye, Alexei Ogarev. 
And China is expected to place additional weapons orders during Mr. Putin's visit.
China remains decades from developing a military force sufficient to challenge the United States, but it is intent on building a credible threat to Taiwan, over which Beijing claims sovereignty. 
Though China has repeatedly threatened to recover control of the island by force, it does not currently have the military capability to do so.
That military build-up is just one of the many areas in which China and Russia's economic and political interests converge. 
Russia not only offers China the hardware necessary to achieve its goals in the Taiwan Strait, it also acts as a potential diplomatic counterbalance to any intervention by the United States, which supports Taiwan.
China, for its part, has stood by Russia in opposition to the 1999 NATO bombing of Yugoslavia and in Moscow's brutal war against separatists in Chechnya. 
Beijing sees parallels between those cases and separatist movements in its own regions of Tibet and Xinjiang, where it fears Western condemnation or even intervention if conditions deteriorate.
In fact, Mr. Putin first met Mr. Jiang earlier this month in Tajikistan, bordering Xinjiang, where they signed an agreement to fight ethnic separatism and terrorism in the region.
Still, those areas of common interest pale in comparison to the American missile defense proposal, which both countries see as a means of securing the United States military dominance in the world.
"Of course, since this will affect both international security, the security of Russia and China, I can tell you I expect that we will have to have more consultations and discussions to find out ways and means to eliminate or at least reduce this kind of security threat," Sha Zukang, head of the Foreign Ministry's Department of Arms Control and Disarmament, said last week.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: PUTTING DREAMS TO THE TEST_ A special report_Elite High School Is a Grueling Exam Away.txt
text:
ï»¿
Few New York City spectacles radiate as much anxiety as the annual surge of eighth graders outside Stuyvesant High School, the educational Valhalla on the Hudson, for a one-shot, grueling entrance exam that many believe will determine the rest of their lives. 
The most recent test one icy winter day -- with scores released just last month -- was, as usual, full of held-back tears, stomachaches and dreams.
More than 1,000 students, from recent Chinese immigrants to girls from the exclusive Brearley School, huddled behind police barricades this past December as teachers with bullhorns told parents to "kiss your loved ones goodbye."
Then they retreated to wait and worry.
Everyone knew that Stuyvesant, although bitterly criticized by minorities for a test they say benefits students from districts with white majorities, remains a nonnegotiable meritocracy. 
Connections, money or a dazzling interview will not help a student get in. 
The sole criterion for admission is still the two-and-a-half-hour entrance exam that Adam Robinson, the co-founder of the Princeton Review test-preparation service, considers more difficult than the Scholastic Assessment Test taken in 11th grade. 
The average college-educated adult, he said, could not be admitted to Stuyvesant without preparation.
What follows is the story of three talented eighth-graders, from different backgrounds, who took the Stuyvesant test in December for admission as freshmen this fall. 
Their stories show how Stuyvesant, a free public school in lower Manhattan, has been seen for nearly a century as an Ivy League dream-ticket for the poor, the rich and especially the immigrant. 
In some years, Stuyvesant sends more students to Harvard than any other public or private school in the nation. 
(Last year 21 of 700 seniors were admitted to Harvard, 20 to Yale, 47 to Columbia and 103 to Cornell.)
Jing Wang, 12, lives on the Lower East Side. 
She is shy, talkative once you get to know her, and academically relentless. 
She started studying for the Stuyvesant test on her own in sixth grade. 
She came to the United States from China when she was 4, and excels at Dr. Sun Yat-sen Intermediate School 131 in Chinatown, which in 1996 was shut out of Stuyvesant -- no one from the school passed the test. 
Jing's father was a radiologist in China but is now unemployed.
Heather McLeod, 14, lives in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn. 
She is sunny, enthusiastic and determined, and has wanted to go to Stuyvesant since she was in fifth grade. 
She has a 94 grade-point average at Mark Twain Intermediate School for the Gifted and Talented, a magnet school in Coney Island that is one of the best public junior highs in the city. 
It is also one of Stuyvesant's biggest feeder schools. 
Heather's parents are separated, and her father lives in Jamaica. 
Her mother, a medical clerk, makes $27,000 a year.
Adam Bloch, 13, lives on the Upper West Side. 
He is, already, something of a wry intellectual, who can discuss Henryk Sienkiewicz, the Polish novelist, as easily as "The Simpsons," one of his favorite shows. 
He is a top student at the private Bank Street School on West 112th Street. 
He also applied for ninth grade to three private schools: Horace Mann, Fieldston and Dalton. 
His father owns a graphic design firm. 
His mother, who has stayed home, will soon start graduate school in social work.
For Jing, Heather, Adam and anyone else, getting into Stuyvesant is harder than ever. 
This year, 11,397 eighth graders competed for 850 spots, meaning fewer than one in 13 got in. 
In 1991, it was more than one in 12, when 6,675 eighth graders competed for 580 spots. 
Jinx Cozzi-Perullo, Stuyvesant's principal, says the applicant increase is largely a result of the luxurious, $150 million building that opened in 1992. 
(Statistically, getting into Stuyvesant is harder than admission to Harvard, which this month will accept 2,073 students from 16,818 applicants, or one in 8.)
Jing, Heather and Adam were recommended by their schools and interviewed before they received their test results. 
Their teachers said each had an excellent chance of getting in. 
But only two did.
Â 
Jing Wang
Excellence At English, Too
"I want to go to Harvard," said Jing Wang. 
"But then, a lot of people want to go to Harvard."
Jing was talking after school in her fourth-floor walk-up on East Second Street, in a cramped two-bedroom apartment with a big television set and stacks of Chinese videotapes. 
She was apprehensive at first, then pleased to be asked questions about herself and her views, and generally tolerant of her 5-year-old sister, who hovered around wanting to be interviewed, too.
Her teachers say Jing is one of the brightest students in a school that is 80 percent Asian, and where even those born in America have difficulty with English because they don't speak it at home, in Chinatown or with their friends at school. 
Jing's English is idiomatic, and rapid. 
"I have an idea I'm at the top of the class," she said matter-of-factly. 
She wants to be a pediatrician, or maybe a lawyer.
Jing's father, An Yin Wang, came to the United States in 1987 from northwest China, studied radiology at Mount Sinai Hospital, and worked as a sonographer at North General and then at a Chinese-run clinic on the Lower East Side. 
He was laid off from that job last fall, he said, because the manager hired cheaper Chinese help. 
His wife had joined him in New York in 1988, but Jing remained in China until her parents were able to send for her in January 1990. 
She cried with fear when she first saw them at the airport in New York. 
"They were like total strangers," she said. 
"I wanted to go back to China with my grandmother."
Jing does two to four hours of homework a night -- only then does she watch TV -- but last fall was also in a self-created total immersion course as she counted down to the Stuyvesant test. 
On Saturdays she took a test preparation course at I. S. 131, offered free to the best 30 students based on previous test scores. 
On Sundays she took a private preparation class given by the Kaplan testing service, at $700, which her father paid for before he was laid off. 
She also studied S.A.T. preparation books that she checked out of the library. 
To relax, she read horror fiction for young adults.
The Stuyvesant test is officially called the "Examination for the Specialized Science High Schools" -- Stuyvesant, the Bronx High School of Science and Brooklyn Technical High School. 
The same test is given for admission to all three, and students simply list their first, second and third choice. 
Since a majority of students list Stuyvesant first -- 11,397 out of 18,524 eighth graders who took the most recent test -- the cutoff for admission to Stuyvesant is higher. 
This year students had to score 559 or better for Stuyvesant's admission, or get about 85 of the 100 questions right.
The test is divided into English and math sections, just like the S.A.T., and is prepared and graded by American Guidance Service, an educational publishing company outside Minneapolis-St. 
Paul. To make the test more fair to immigrants whose English lags, sections on sentence completion and word synonyms, antonyms and analogies have been eliminated. 
The English part of the Stuyvesant test emphasizes "logical reasoning," which educators say makes the test more difficult.
"It's an indication of a more sophisticated learner," said Carolyn West, an I. S. 131 teacher who helped prepare Jing for the test.
A sample question for the "logical reasoning" section goes like this:
Five students are in line according to height, from tallest to shortest. 
Liz is taller than Mickey but shorter than Fred. 
Mickey is shorter than Noah but taller than Judy. 
Noah is shorter than Fred. 
In which position is Noah?
A. first B. second C. third D. fourth E. cannot be determined from the information given.
To get the answer, Ms. West said, a student has to be able to think enough to draw a diagram for help, from tallest to shortest. 
But after plotting out the information in each sentence, all a student can learn of Noah is that he goes somewhere between Mickey and Fred. 
A student still doesn't know how Noah compares with Liz. 
The answer is E.
Jing headed off to Stuyvesant at 7 A.M. on Dec. 
6, nervous. 
A week later, she talked to a reporter, whom her father later escorted to the neighborhood subway stop.
"I cannot make big money," he said quietly as he walked, describing the difficulties of a China-trained doctor in the United States. 
"But for my daughter, the future is important. 
After many years, she can be a specialist."
Â 
Heather McLeod
'I Want to Go To Harvard'
Heather McLeod was not nervous about the Stuyvesant test until her friend Justin told her that his life depended on passing it. 
"He said, 'If I don't make it to Stuyvesant, I can't get into a good college, and I can't make a lot of money and I'll live on the street,' " she recalled.
Heather laughed, but she had her heart set on Stuyvesant, too. 
"I want to go to Harvard, I really do," she said. 
"So many people from Harvard get someplace."
She and her mother, Sylvia, were talking the night before the test in their living room in the Jackie Robinson Apartments, a complex built over Ebbets Field. 
Lots of families like the McLeods live there, but Heather feels different. 
"The kids say, 'Come out and play,' and I'll say, 'I have a book report due.'
And they'll say, 'You're a nerd.'
"
Heather's parents -- her father worked in a boiler room, her mother has a high school education -- came from Jamaica 28 years ago. 
"Our children are going to do well in this country," Mrs. McLeod said firmly. 
She is pleased so far. 
Heather's two older brothers went to parochial schools, then Georgetown and Fordham. 
One is now a mid-level manager at the Federal Aviation Administration, the other a manager at a Marriott Hotel. 
Neither passed the Stuyvesant test, but Mrs. McLeod has always had bigger hopes for Heather. 
"She thought farther ahead than her brothers did," she said.
Heather gives her mother all the credit. 
"She read to me every night when I was little," she said later in the evening, her eyes growing moist, when her mother had left the room. 
"Golden Books, Cinderella, children's Bible stories. 
I don't know how she did it, but she made me want to excel."
Heather started studying for the Stuyvesant test last summer and by fall was spending her school lunch hours in a test prep course offered free by the Mark Twain School. 
"They drilled it into you," she said. 
She was well aware of how few black students pass the test, but said she was not going to think about that.
Blacks account for 4.1 percent of Stuyvesant's student body, Latinos 3.7 percent. 
(The rest of the student body is 47.7 percent Asian and 45.5 percent white.) The numbers outrage community advocacy groups like Acorn, which in 1997 released a report, "Secret Apartheid II," showing that private and parochial schools plus three public school districts provided more than half the students at Stuyvesant and Bronx Science.
The report found that the five districts that sent the most students to the schools were predominately white, and the five that sent the fewest were predominately black and Latino. 
The report also said schools in those districts offered few of the advanced courses that help in passing the test.
Acorn recommended suspending the test altogether, an idea rejected by Schools Chancellor Rudy Crew. 
But the Board of Education now has an 18-month prep course, the Math/Science Institute, housed at Stuyvesant, for 400 mostly minority students. 
Students are selected based on standardized test scores and principals' recommendations, and then by lottery. 
The institute is financed by the Board of Education at a cost of $1.2 million a year. 
Of the first Math/Science group, which started after sixth grade in the summer of 1995, 304 took the test and 45 got in -- 10 of them black and 11 Latino. 
"It has to start somewhere," said Bruce Ravage, the institute's director. 
The institute has just added three new sites in other boroughs, for 700 more spots.
Â 
Adam Bloch
Outsmarted By His Cleverness
Adam Bloch vividly remembers the last math question on his Stuyvesant test: i is a 28-consecutive number set. 
What is the maximum number of multiples of seven that can be in i?
"Four times seven is 28 -- you immediately think that," Adam said. 
He decided the answer was obviously four.
And yet, it seemed a little too obvious. 
His test-preparation teachers had told him to think, and this answer didn't seem worthy of the Stuyvesant test. 
Adam decided it must be a trick.
He skipped up to seven through 35, calculating that since seven plus 28 is 35, it was another 28-consecutive number set. 
And that got him the multiples of 7, 14, 21, 28 and 35. 
The answer, he decided, was 5.
After the test he saw his mistake. 
Seven through 35 is in fact a 29-consecutive number set. 
The right answer, all along, was 4. 
"Looks like it's a double-trick," Adam said. 
"They try to trick you into thinking when you shouldn't think."
Adam talked easily at the dining table in his high-rise apartment, decorated with his parents' collection of Judaica, as his mother, Ofra, wandered in and out. 
She once worked in an art gallery in Tel Aviv, and came to the United States in 1980. 
Adam's father came from Poland in 1972.
Adam seemed amused to be interviewed, and offered many opinions about books, movies and history. 
Talking to him was a lot like talking to an adult, if the average adult had his discipline.
He said that when he arrives home after school, "I've always had this tradition: I say hi to my mother, and I rush into my room."
There he always does his homework -- before a snack, before phone calls.
Adam loved studying Greek mythology and Minoan Crete at Bank Street last fall -- he read the Iliad and the Odyssey -- and the Middle Ages in the sixth grade. 
He said he is currently reading "American Sphinx: The Character of Thomas Jefferson" by Joseph J. Ellis. "It's not a book I would dive into and read for several hours a day," he admitted. 
"But it's interesting."
For 10 weeks last fall, Adam took a private test preparation course, GRF, costing about $500, and was one of 26 students at Bank Street -- which goes only through eighth grade -- who applied to Stuyvesant. 
Adam's older brother goes to Stuyvesant. 
When he was taking the test, Mrs. Bloch said, money was a concern.
Adam said he thought private school tuition was $17,500 a year.
"No, it's 18 and a half," his mother told him gently. 
Then she sighed. 
"It's a stretch, of course it is."
Â 
The Results
'I Didn't Cry Or Anything'
The results came in the first week of March, delivered to the three by their schools: Adam and Jing got in, Heather did not.
"I didn't cry or anything," Heather said. 
"But I was disappointed."
She scored 483, meaning she got about 70 of 100 questions right. 
Jing got a 584, or about 88 right. 
Adam got 625 and about 93 right, ranking 118 out of the more than 18,000 who took the test.
Jing, who was speechless when she got the news -- "I was like really, really happy" -- will go to Stuyvesant. 
Adam, who thinks his test-preparation course may have added 50 points to his score, was one of six students from Bank Street who made the Stuyvesant cutoff. 
Adam also got into his three private schools. 
After thinking it over, he decided that Stuyvesant, with its 3,000 students, was too big. 
He'll go to Dalton.
Heather did qualify for Brooklyn Tech, but next year will go to Bishop Ford Catholic Central High School in the Bay Ridge section of Brooklyn, as her brothers did. 
"She'll do fine no matter where she goes," said Gary Goldstein, Heather's principal. 
"She'll be an exemplary student."

text:

Pretty Poison
Q. What is cinnabar?
A. True cinnabar is a mineral, HgS, or red mercuric sulfide, the only important ore of mercury. 
Cinnabar is also known under names like cinnabarite, native vermilion, Chinese vermilion and quicksilver vermilion. 
It has been used since ancient times as a pigment, but the familiar rust-red "cinnabar" carved beads and boxes from China may or may not be colored with it, as cinnabar is now relatively expensive, as well as poisonous.
Red mercuric sulfide is formed when the black version of the same mineral, called black mercury or black mercuric sulfide, is heated. 
The two kinds have different crystal structures; cinnabar forms hexagonal or rhombohedral crystals, which are sometimes large and jewel-like in their luster.
Some notable examples of large cinnabar crystals have been found in China. 
However, most deposits are red or brown earthy or granular masses, and are found near recently formed volcanic rocks and hot springs. 
Besides China, historical producing areas for cinnabar have included Spain, Yugoslavia, Italy, Peru, the Soviet Union, Mexico and California.
When heated to 835 degrees Fahrenheit, cinnabar sublimes, that is, vaporizes and separates into its components. 
Oxygen then combines with the sulfur vapor, which passes off as SO2 , sulfur dioxide, leaving the pure mercury behind.
Cinnabar is insoluble in water or organic solvents, making it valuable as a protectant. 
The vermilion used in paints to protect iron and steel was formerly obtained by grinding pure cinnabar. 
It is too expensive for large-scale use as a paint pigment, so now vermilion is either highly adulterated or produced artificially, or is actually an imitation vermilion made with red lead.
Genuine cinnabar has a romantic history. 
In ancient times, it was used as a preservative in Chinese tombs. 
The highly prized Chinese cinnabar lacquer is made with the refined sap of the lac tree, Rhus verniciflua, a relative of poison ivy, which is also highly irritating or poisonous to humans. 
The sap is mixed with the cinnabar or built up in layers over a base of cinnabar, then carved.Â Â Â C. 
CLAIBORNE RAY

file: Race to Lead Hong Kong Stokes Fear of the Future.txt
text:
ï»¿
There have been no balloons, no bunting and no brass bands. 
No babies have been bussed, no handshakes at the rope line, and no rallies have jarred Hong Kong's single-minded pursuit of wealth.
Yet four men -- two tycoons and two former judges -- have declared that they want to be the first to lead Hong Kong under Chinese rule, which is to resume next July after 150 years of British control.
Sometime before the end of this year, China will decide who will be Hong Kong's first Chief Executive under Communist rule. 
But to lend the selection the semblance of a horse race, Beijing has encouraged prominent Hong Kongers to step forward and announce their interest in succeeding Britain's last colonial Governor, Chris Patten.
It is, however, not much of a contest. 
Hong Kong's people will have no voice in selecting their new ruler. 
Instead, an electoral college of Hong Kong's elite, hand-picked by China, will ordain whomever Beijing chooses to be the territory's first Chief Executive, as the post will be known.
The new executive will oversee one of Asia's most muscular financial centers, the region's unrivaled port, and the international gateway to the vast markets and resources of China. 
At the same time, he will, under the territory's new constitution drafted by Chinese and Hong Kong representatives, be charged with defining and defending the autonomy promised Hong Kong.
With the transition only eight months away, the Hong Kong stock market is at new highs and property prices have begun surging after a sharp slowdown last year. 
Despite assurances from Beijing that Hong Kong will remain "substantially" unchanged for the next 50 years, many people here have grave doubts about Beijing's promises. 
Indeed, earlier this month China renewed its threats against some long-held freedoms, including freedom of assembly and of the press.
Further souring the local mood, the candidates have avoided any hint of criticism of Beijing and have refrained from making audible commitments to democratic processes.
"The more secretive the process," said Christine Loh, an independent member of Hong Kong's legislature, "the more hesitant the candidates. 
And the more the Preparatory Committee" -- the Beijing-appointed body that is overseeing the transition to Chinese rule -- "ignores the public dimensions of the selection process, the less confidence Hong Kong as a whole will feel."
Of the four candidates, the odds-on favorite is a shipping magnate who has now admitted that he was bailed out of financial oblivion in the 1980's by $120 million of secret financing from China.
Tung Chee Hwa, like all but one of his rivals, was born in Shanghai and fled Communism with his family, relocating first to Taiwan and later here, where his father built Orient Overseas (International) Ltd., one of Hong Kong's two large shipping companies. 
After inheriting the concern in the 1980's at a time when global shipping shrank dramatically, Mr. Tung used money secretly invested from China to save the company.
He also served as a member of Mr. Patten's cabinet, a position from which he resigned in June.
Another prominent businessman, Peter Kwong-ching Woo, a former Chase Manhattan banker in New York and the enormously successful chairman of a property and shipping conglomerate founded by his father-in-law, has also declared his interest in leading Hong Kong under Chinese rule. 
At 50, he is the youngest aspirant for the job, but his chairmanship of the local hospital authority has given him experience in public administration that none of the other candidates possess.
The other two candidates are former Justices on the Supreme Court. 
Sir Ti Liang Yang, 67, whose resignation as Chief Justice took effect today, was also born in Shanghai and studied law there before Mao's troops entered the city in 1949. 
He was very much an innocuous fixture in Hong Kong until last year, when he suggested that the Bill of Rights Ordinance, a series of laws intended to codify basic civil rights, should be weakened.
The second judge, Simon F. S. Li, entered the race last week. 
The 74-year-old Mr. Li, the only native Hong Konger, is unapologetically pro-China, even resorting to familiar Communist jargon to describe Hong Kong's relationship with China as "similar to lips and teeth."
But his candidacy is not helped by the fact that his daughter, Gladys Li, is the chairwoman of the Bar Association, a body that has forcefully dissented from China's plans for Hong Kong, or that a son, Simon Li, is the foreign editor of the Los Angeles Times.
Despite rounds of news conferences, meetings with business groups, and consultations with delegations of the civil services by each of the four men, Hong Kong seems resigned to the fact that there is no real race for the job. 
But some argue that popular sentiment will be taken into account.
From a democratic perspective, the selection process is "totally dictated by China," said Peter Cheung, a political scientist at Hong Kong University. 
"But this creates a dilemma for China," he added. 
"It doesn't want things to get out of control; on the other hand it cannot send its trusted officials to rule. 
So China would like to see a candidate acceptable to the Hong Kong people."
Still, the jockeying has clearly done little to bolster faith in the future. 
A survey by the Hong Kong Transition Project, a multi-university research effort begun in 1993, found Hong Kongers still skittish about China's impending takeover, still identifying themselves as distinctly Hong Kongers as opposed to Chinese, profoundly unhappy with Beijing's dealings with Hong Kong and deeply worried about a rise in corruption and threats to personal freedom.
"There is yet to be a majority of people who want to join China," said Michael DeGolyer, the director of the project, and a professor of political science at Hong Kong Baptist University. 
"We've been expecting this number to increase but it's been increasing very, very, very slowly."
Since 1993, when 42 percent of those polled said they wanted unification, today only 48 percent desire unification; the rest are split among other choices, including independence and remaining a colony. 
The poll found that 44 percent of Hong Kong's 6.2 million people would try to leave if the situation under Chinese rule deteriorated significantly.Â Â Â Â Â Â

On the other hand, there was no limit to how many films the studios could simply sell to Chinese distributors. 
In recent years, 40 to 50 films made outside China, mostly small independent ones, have been sold for flat fees there.
