text:
ï»¿
Ordinarily, it takes at least a little courage to wear pajamas outside in the middle of the day.
But if you live in a city where plenty of other people are doing it, why even hesitate?
Striped, spotted and floral-patterned pajamas are plainly visible on the streets of Shanghai this summer, worn by a growing number of residents who appear to favor comfort over style. 
Morning shoppers, afternoon strollers, even casual cyclists: so many people sport their pajamas in public that they almost seem to be members of a cult.
"Comfort, No. 1," said Shi Lingmen, counting off the reasons for his pajama-wearing like tenets of a religious belief. 
"Convenience, No. 2. Looks, No. 3."
To Mr. Shi, wearing his blue-and-white pj's at his place of work -- an outdoor stall selling turtles, shrimp and crabs at a market on Yongkang Street -- does not really mean neglecting his appearance. 
On the contrary, he acts as though there were something distinctly hip about wearing pajamas.
"What do you think?" he asked, tugging on one of his short sleeves, inviting -- and clearly expecting -- approval.
In another city, like New York, a mobster like Vincent Gigante could try to use his pajama-wearing in public as evidence that he was mentally unfit to stand trial. 
That defense would probably have been laughed at in Shanghai, where such behavior is now so common.
For those who strain to interpret fast-changing trends in China, Shanghai's pajama game is more than just a fad, or a way to beat the summer heat. 
It may be seen as a sign that this city has achieved a certain stage of development, like Hong Kong and Taiwan in the 1960's, when pajamas appeared in public there, too.
In Shanghai, few people could afford the luxury of pajamas until recently, generally sleeping in underclothes. 
Besides, the political fanaticism that engulfed Shanghai in the 1960's and 70's discouraged wearing anything as bourgeois as clothing reserved for bedtime.
But since Western things are again in fashion, and ordinary people have pocket money and more, new spending habits are finding their way all the way into the bedroom.
And back out onto the street again. 
For even if simple laziness is what keeps many people in pajamas all day, wearing them in public is also a way to show off to the neighbors, and to show them you don't care what they think.
"It's not so much convenience as feeling relaxed," said Xu Xing, wearing a frilly but skimpy white nightgown to buy some groceries one recent morning. 
"My whole attitude is different when I'm dressed like this."
Ms. Xu said that, yes, she feels a touch of camaraderie with neighbors she sees wearing nightclothes on the street, partly because she guesses that many are unemployed. 
But she also seemed eager to compare her own upscale nightgown with less fancy versions, pointing to a woman in a relatively plain version to ask, with barely disguised disdain, "What do you think of that style?"
As in so much of China, semi-hidden class distinctions persist, even when it comes to pajamas. 
Several people in nightwear agreed that only working-class people would dress as they did in public, while Shanghai's more sophisticated folk -- who generally own many more clothes -- consider such behavior declasse.
Not that you can judge someone by their pajamas. 
But the well heeled, if caught wearing them on the street, may blush.
"I am a professional woman, so it's not very civilized of me to be dressed like this in public," said a morning shopper in her cotton nightgown, before scurrying off in evident embarrassment. 
"Excuse me."
In other Chinese cities, the summer heat reduces many people to shorts and T-shirts, with men often tucking their shirts up to bare a midriff, or going topless altogether. 
Pajama sightings have been made in a few other southern cities, like Guangzhou and Xiamen, but Shanghai clearly leads the pack.
"About 2 percent of the people wear pajamas out during the day," said Zhang Qianghua, a retired postal worker who asserted that his long experience delivering mail gave him a keen sense of street phenomena.
Out of 14 million residents, who make Shanghai the largest city in China, even Mr. Zhang's rather unscientific estimate would mean roughly 280,000 people.
Pajama-wearing has come back into vogue in the past few years, Mr. Zhang said, like the other Western-style clothes that were made popular by the foreign powers that divided and ruled Shanghai before Communist forces chased them out in 1949.
"I remember the way people wore pajamas before Liberation," Mr. Zhang said, using the Communist Party term for the revolution, and seemingly amazed at the relentless passage of time. 
"Now they're back."
Hu Zhonghua wears a nightgown as she wanders through a street market each morning, but her intention is not comfort so much as sales. 
Laid off by her factory two years ago, she now sews her own nightgowns and sells them for $2.50 apiece, or about half the typical store price.
"It's comfortable," she said. 
"Here, buy one for your girlfriend and let her try it."
Many Shanghainese, wearing the studied nonchalance of a big city, say pajama-wearing is no big deal.
"In China, people wear pajamas in public the way Americans wear bikinis," said a man selling eggs on the street. 
"It's not strange. 
If we saw a woman wearing a bikini on the street, that would be very strange."

file: Shanghai Journal_In 75 Years, a Party_s Long March to Irrelevance.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a small brick home on a leafy side street in this city, a dozen idealistic young men gathered around a scuffed wooden table 75 years ago today to launch China's Communist Party, or so the history books say.
One of the participants, Mao Zedong, then just 27, later rose to lead the Communist Party through civil war to make it the ruling power of the land. 
For decades, Mao directed efforts to install the party's authority in every office, factory and school, creating a juggernaut that could spread the party's word to every household and monitor the daily activities of every worker or student.
Today, the old building is a museum to a lost ideal. 
Virtually no one believes in Communism anymore.
As economic growth eats away at old systems and habits, the Communist Party's influence in daily life has receded sharply in the past few years, particularly among young urban dwellers -- the kind, in their 20's, who might be setting up a political party if they lived in a different era. 
In the most modern sectors of Chinese society, such as securities firms, trading companies, banks and real estate dealers, the once-omnipresent party has almost no presence at all.
The party still has an iron grip on the national levers of political power. 
Yet its ground-level organization seems to be falling farther and farther out of touch with the work and life styles of the men and women who increasingly drive China's bustling economy.
"No one with any ability joins the party today," said Yang Jun, a 26-year-old computer salesman who likes gold-rimmed glasses and polo shirts. 
"My company has 80 employees, but there's no party organization. 
If there are any party members, I don't think any of them would admit it."
Not long ago, a college graduate like Mr. Yang would be assigned a job by one party official and supervised in a new workplace by another. 
If he wanted to get married, his choice of spouse would also have to be approved by a superior. 
A neighborhood committee would keep an eye on his home, noting who came and went.
In contrast, today Mr. Yang lives relatively free from party interference. 
He chose his own job and home -- he shares a two-bedroom apartment in downtown Shanghai with a co-worker -- and doesn't worry about who approves of his girlfriend, or when she stays over. 
"I haven't introduced her to my parents yet," he said, a little sheepishly.
Party officials do not seem overly concerned with individualistic computer jocks like Mr. Yang, though their indifference would disappear in a flash if he organized any anti-Government activity. 
But they concede that they are having difficulty setting up party cells in free-market sectors of the economy.
"New companies are being set up faster than we can keep track of," acknowledged Zhou Heling, who as deputy director of the organization department in Shanghai's Communist Party oversees the establishment of new party units. 
"We are encountering a lot of problems with these new economic entitites.
"Joint ventures are very complicated," Mr. Zhou added, referring to companies with both domestic and foreign investment. 
"Sometimes they register but don't operate; sometimes they operate without registering. 
It's hard to keep up with them."
Paradoxically, as party organizations lose touch with China's young professionals, they are aggressively enrolling more new young members than ever before. 
Perhaps it is to co-opt as many young people as possible; perhaps it is simply to pad the fiction that the party is getting ever stronger.
"Young people are the key," Mr. Zhou said. 
"Last year, 54 percent of our new members were under 35.
In addition to the 19,600 35-and-unders who joined the party in Shanghai last year, Mr. Zhou said proudly, 110,000 more people applied, up 20,000 from the previous year. 
Altogether, there are 1.14 million members of the Communist Party in Shanghai, a city of 14 million, and 57 million nationwide.
But numbers can be deceiving.
A 35-year-old currency trader at a leading Chinese investment firm recalled how a manager at his company recently pressed him to apply for party membership, simply because an order had come down to step up recruitment.
"But I don't want to have to pay the party fees," the trader protested, as he remembered it later, because he would owe 3 percent of his $3,000 monthly salary in fees.
"You don't have to join, just apply. 
We need to raise our numbers," pleaded the manager. 
"Help me out."
The trader agreed, on the condition that the manager made sure his application would be rejected. 
But then the trader had trouble finding any colleagues to write him a recommendation, because none were familiar with the party line that needs to be regurgitated in an application, and eventually gave up.
The implications of this sometimes-comical attitude toward party enrollment, like the political future of China itself, are anyone's guess. 
One of the puzzles of modern China is whether the Communist Party, if it remains in power, will simply decide to shed its outdated name.
Even a leading party organizer like Mr. Zhou does not sound much like a Communist when he discusses the establishment of party cells in a company.
"Our primary concern is money-making ability," he said. 
"Setting up a party organization should be done in parallel with business functions. 
We will not get in the way."
Outside the museum where the Communist Party's first meeting was held, Wu Xiaoyong, a 40-year-old party member who arrived with a busload of colleagues, pondered the future of the organization.
"Not too clear," he said. 
"Young people have a lot more choices today than we did."

text:
ï»¿
Upstairs at the Hujiang Beauty Salon, as hairdressers fussed over eight women seated regally before the mirrors and bright lights, two dozen other women waited anxiously on a long puffy sofa, in a various stages of preparation for the big day.
Every one a bride or a bridesmaid, many looked like princesses-in-the-making. 
Turban-towels floated on the heads of some, and cheesecloth adorned the faces of others, with holes cut out at the eyes, dark with mascara, and at the mouth, shiny red with lipstick.
Wan Jingjing, delayed between shampoo and blow dry, twirled a finger through the wet, stringy hair that fell limply around her shoulders as she considered the question: why did she, like all the other women in the salon, and like innumerable thousands of women in Shanghai, choose to wed on this particular day, May 18?
"Everyone knows what today is!"
Miss Wan, 24, shouted, her tiny frame shifting stiffly in a glittering silver dress with see-through black sleeves, a warm-up for the three outfits she planned to wear at a banquet that evening. 
"I will get rich!"
"Five-one-eight," or "wu yao ba," as the Chinese call the 18th day of the fifth month, sounds close enough to "wo yao fa," or "I will get rich," that it is considered as good as an omen can be. 
Sure as "I will get rich" is a motto for contemporary Shanghai, May 18 has become the city's most popular day of the year to marry.
To plan a wedding the traditional way, consulting an ancient Chinese almanac that marks lucky and unlucky days each year, is still socially acceptable. 
But many young couples are eager, without negating the old way, to add a modern twist by actually articulating their hope for riches.
In most societies, a wedding day is a time of celebration for a family and of nervous exhaustion for bride and groom. 
Yet the full flavor of a wedding day -- in traditional China it was sometimes the first time a bride and groom laid eyes on each other -- virtually disappeared during recent decades of austere Communist rule, when a trip to the local registrar and a small banquet at home were the norm.
In China today, as money-making takes ever fuller force, a showy side is bound to spill out in grander and more extravagant ways, particularly in Shanghai, the nation's financial capital.
On May 18, it was spill, spill, spill. 
Before noon, Cadillac and Lexus limousines with red roses taped across the hood and tinsel-like streamers in tow cruised Huaihai Road, Shanghai's major shopping thoroughfare, as if to celebrate an unbridled enthusiasm for the day's activities. 
Beauty salons like the Hujiang were packed, most of them booked solid weeks beforehand.
"You can't really have a decent wedding today for less than 150,000 renminbi," or about $18,000, said Li Jun, a clothing store manager who helped pay for his nephew's banquet, even though he makes $350 a month. 
When Mr. Li was married in 1981, he said, it cost about $800. 
"And that was considered fancy."
In Shanghai, many couples now follow elaborate customs, many of them adopted from Hong Kong and Taiwan: Western-style wedding gowns and suits, a set of photos taken weeks beforehand so that copies can be shown on the wedding day, four hours of hairdressing in the morning, a limousine escort in the afternoon, a multi-course banquet at a restaurant in the evening, and a final party at home with bawdy party games.
The Communist authorities, while no longer banning such extravagance, seem uncomfortable with it. 
An editorial in The Liberation Daily of Shanghai warned against putting too much store on May 18.
"Fixing May 18 as an auspicious day is groundless," the newspaper declared. 
"Let us advocate a civilized, healthy and scientific way of life, and oppose bad, stupid and backward customs and habits."
With no actual wedding ceremony before or after a banquet, most couples are legally married when they register a few days beforehand at a government office.
A spokesman for the Ministry of Civil Affairs said the number of marriages performed in Shanghai is an official secret, but a handful of beauty salon and restaurant managers agreed that May 18 is the undisputed favorite.
At Meilongzhen, an elegant restaurant on Nanjing Road with traditional Chinese decor that makes it a favorite for wedding parties, 150 friends and relatives crowded the main dining room as a groom dutifully went around to each table to toast each guest with a sip of beer. 
By the 10th table, he was having trouble standing.
His bride, dressed in a red, floor-length moire gown, was trying to light a cigarette for each male guest, most of whom reacted as expected by blowing out the match several times to enjoy her company a few moments longer.
Although the idea of getting married on May 18 is that the bride and groom will lock in a shot at getting rich, Shanghai's big-spending ways are actually making the owners of hair salons, restaurants, florists and cake shops the ones most likely to profit from that day, in part because they can charge inflated prices.
"We're full today," said Cai Jirong, manager at the Hujiang Beauty salon. 
"I like May 18."

text:
ï»¿
"It's so much fun," squealed Yue-Sai Kan as she stripped a tiny jacket off the pale, thin arms of a plastic doll in her antique-filled Shanghai apartment. 
The doll, an idealized version of her younger self, is Ms. Kan's latest effort to close the gap between the country of her birth and her Sutton Place home in Manhattan.
Ms. Kan became an instant star here in the mid-1980's when she was host of a television program called "One World," which introduced knowledge-hungry Chinese to the outside world with short documentaries about just about everywhere from Egypt to England. 
Almost every television set in China tuned in.
She later started a make-up line under her name, and her signature bob and bright red lips are still seen in cosmetics advertisements all over China. 
Her book of etiquette, which counsels men against spitting and women against sitting with legs splayed, was also an immediate best seller.
Now Ms. Kan, 51, has taken her one-woman cultural revolution to China's children with a Barbie-like doll that she wants to represent the Chinese ideal of beauty. 
Like her American cousin, the Yue-Sai doll comes freighted with the politics of consumerism, body image and gender stereotypes.
It is, perhaps, a reflection of the times: padded bras, plastic surgery and chronic dieting are increasingly common in the generation of urban Chinese women now coming of age.
Nearly 40 years ago, Mao warned his comrades that enemies of the Cultural Revolution would arrive to try to change China through "peaceful evolution," nudging third-generation cadres back toward the comfortable middle class values dominant in the West. 
Ms. Kan, a Chinese-American, maintains homes in both New York and Shanghai.
Of course, he was right. 
Like clockwork, agents of the bourgeoisie are back in droves, and nobody among them is more prominent or more persistent than Ms. Kan, whose face is almost as well known in China's cities as Mao's own.
In an auditorium here recently, she held a fashion show of lanky, leggy models baring their midriffs in life-size versions of her doll's extensive wardrobe. 
There Ms. Kan answered well-rehearsed questions from ruddy cheeked, red kerchiefed Young Pioneers, prepubescent members of the feeder organization for the Communist Party Youth League.
"Auntie Yue-Sai, before I could only find foreign dolls, so when I saw a black-haired doll it touched my heart," said a pudgy 11-year-old girl wearing a red photojournalist vest and lugging an expensive camera. 
"Why did you decide to make the Yue-Sai doll?"
The doll idea was born, Ms. Kan told the children and assembled guests, when an American friend in New York asked her to bring back a Chinese doll for the friend's 6-year-old daughter. 
To her dismay, she could not find any Chinese dolls in China other than a series representing the country's 56 minority groups. 
The brochure she handed out at the fashion show said: "Yes, I did find some ugly Chinese 'minority' dolls but nothing really modern and beautiful, nothing representing us!"
(There is no strong tradition of playing with dolls in Chinese culture.)
"All of a sudden," Ms. Kan said, "I realized this is one of the reasons why so many Asians don't find themselves beautiful!"
So she set out to create her own doll, working with the best doll makers in Hong Kong, who had previously just made Western dolls. 
And after 12 head molds and a lot of tinkering with eyebrows, she finally had "a doll that we can be proud of as Chinese."
She is unabashed about promoting the doll as an educational toy, quoting Deng Xiaoping, who used the Chinese word for childhood -- which also means doll -- when he said, "everything starts from childhood."
"It is hoped that the doll will inspire young Asian women to examine who they are and to appreciate their own unique beauty and heritage," her press release says. 
So far, that includes dressing as a Disco Girl or a Birthday Princess and playing with accessories like a make-up table, a beauty salon and a dining room set. 
The dolls will sell for $7 to $35 each, depending on the accessories.
She is sharply critical of the current fad among Asian women who bleach their hair blond or dye it reddish brown, and she criticizes the Japanese for starting the trend. 
She also says she is troubled by Asia's fascination with Caucasian models, which are used to sell everything from cigarettes to underwear.
"There's a sociological phenomenon here of feeling that we are inferior," she said.
Still, Ms. Kan's doll suggests that equally complex emotions were at work when she designed her doll, which despite its name has a distinctly non-Chinese feel. 
Dolls of this type, whether with Asian features or not, are known generally as "Western dolls" in Chinese, and their foreignness is one of the things that attracts Chinese children to them.
Her doll's face is squarer than a Barbie, she explained while sorting through a plastic bag of doll heads a few days before her fashion show. 
And while most Barbies are sold with blond hair and blue eyes, Yue-Sai dolls are sold with black or brown hair and dark brown eyes, as well as bright red lipstick that matches her own.
"One of the biggest problems I encountered was that almost everyone who paints dolls makes them Western, with really round eyes," she said. 
"I cannot tell you how hard it is to explain to the technical people that we have almond eyes."
But her doll's eye shape is barely distinguishable from Barbie's except for the absence of a painted eyelid fold above the lashes. 
And while her doll's waist is half a centimeter broader -- about an eighth of an inch -- than America's most popular doll, the other measurements are basically the same. 
Both Barbie and Yue-Sai have a four and seven-eighths inch bust, for example, though Yue-Sai's torso is slightly thicker and so her breasts have a little less loft.
"We found that if we make them too flat chested or the waistline thicker, the clothes don't look as good," said Ms. Kan. She said she extended the legs for the same reason, so the doll is as tall as a Barbie with the same tapered feet.
The persona that Ms. Kan has created for her doll, meanwhile, belies a fascination with the West: she's a 16-year-old Chinese-American girl who stars in a comic strip that will be published in children's newspapers and magazines in China.
Ms. Kan hired a Japanese artist to draw the strip, whose characters have the big round eyes characteristic of Japanese comics.

text:

After a final round of negotiations failed to yield a workable compromise, Shanghai's Bureau of Culture refused tonight to let a classic Chinese opera be staged as scheduled next month at the Lincoln Center Festival in New York.
Nigel Redden, director of the festival, said late tonight that Shanghai officials maintained that the production of the opera, "The Peony Pavilion," would have to be extensively revised to better reflect Chinese tradition before it would be allowed to travel to the festival. 
Although Mr. Redden was willing to accept a staging with minor changes, the officials insisted on a new set of rehearsals that would make it impossible for the opera, a 20-hour production that was to have been presented in several segments, to open on July 7 as planned.
"They have effectively canceled the project," said Mr. Redden, who flew to China on Monday to try to negotiate a way out of the impasse. 
"This is a tremendous loss for us, but it's even worse for people in the company, who worked day and night for so long to pull this together."
Mr. Redden said he planned to leave Shanghai on Thursday night. 
Yet he still expressed the hope that President Bill Clinton or Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who are to arrive in China that evening, would intervene and persuade Shanghai officials to reverse their decision.
Ma Bomin, the director of Shanghai's Bureau of Culture, said she blocked "The Peony Pavilion" because it was a national treasure that needed to be protected from unorthodox interpretations like the one Lincoln Center wanted to perform.
"This is a precious piece of Chinese culture," Ms. Ma, a former opera singer, said in an interview. 
"If we are going to show it to the world, it must be presented in line with Chinese tradition."
Speaking publicly about "The Peony Pavilion" for the first time since its staging was suddenly thrown into doubt last week, Ms. Ma defended her bureau's right to be the arbiter of what is consistent with Chinese tradition. 
Her comments reflected the doggedness with which opera buffs in China can try to guard their turf.
"We have the power to decide how an opera is performed," Ms. Ma said. 
"You must understand, our standards for Kunqu Opera and Peking Opera are not the same as for other arts. 
I am an artist, and I have a responsibility to see it done properly."
At Lincoln Center, Beverly Sills, the chairman, and Nathan Leventhal, the president, issued a statement saying that the Bureau of Culture's position "makes it physically impossible for Lincoln Center to receive the production in time to mount and present it as scheduled."
They praised "the superb artistry of the Shanghai Kunqu Opera Company," which was to have performed the work, and congratulated the director of the production, Chen Shi-Zheng, "for his brilliant and evocative conception."
Lincoln Center will explore legal steps, Mr. Leventhal said. 
"We own the production," he said, referring to Lincoln Center and its partners in the commissioning consortium. 
"They don't."
Ms. Ma brushed aside arguments that the opera be judged by Lincoln Center, which is financing the production with co-producers in France, Australia and Hong Kong, where the opera is also scheduled to appear. 
She also discounted the importance of a contract that she approved last year granting Mr. Chen full artistic freedom in its staging.
"We agreed to the contract, and we thought the production was a good idea," Ms. Ma said. 
"But now we find that it includes elements that cannot be allowed, unhealthy elements that violate China's cultural exchange regulations."
With President Clinton arriving for a nine-day visit to China on Thursday, Mr. Redden expressed hope that Chinese and United States officials would be eager to resolve a dispute involving a cultural exchange, especially since Shanghai is now trying to present itself as a vibrant financial and cultural center.
Unless some senior official intervenes, Ms. Ma is having her way. 
"I don't see what this has to do with President Clinton's visit," she said. 
"This is about art, and the debate should remain about art."
Ms. Ma cites three artistic objections to the modern staging of "The Peony Pavilion": that the production violates the spirit of the author Tang Xianzu, who wrote the opera in 1598; it violates the specific rules of Kunqu Opera, one of China's most refined and classic strands of traditional opera; and it introduces what she called "unhealthy elements," which she defines as "feudal," "superstitious" and "pornographic."
Yet as Ms. Ma spoke, it became clear that her biggest problem was with Mr. Chen, a native of China who moved to the United States in 1987 and became an American citizen.
Mr. Chen's innovative staging of the opera uses an elaborate set -- complete with a duck pond, water wheel and singing birds -- in what he described as an effort to recreate the atmosphere of daily life in China for ordinary people in the Ming Dynasty.
Ms. Ma and other elders of Shanghai's culture bureaucracy, accustomed to simple staging and more stylized acting, are also apparently accustomed to getting the changes they demand when they preview a piece of theater. 
Ms. Ma expressed surprise and some resentment when Mr. Chen resisted some changes she sought after seeing a dress rehearsal this month.
"We understand the director has the right to interpret the opera, but the spirit must be true to the original," Ms. Ma said. 
"When we made suggestions, he said he would accept some, but not others."
Wrinkling her nose in disgust, she delivered what seemed to be the most serious criticism she could make about a fellow artist of classic opera: "He lacks knowledge."
A director like Mr. Chen -- with new ideas, a healthy American budget and a firm artistic vision -- is almost inevitably going to raise hackles or induce professional jealousy in a country like China.
"He has his own ideas and he is very stubborn," Ms. Ma said. 
Asked why her bureau's objections to "The Peony Pavilion" were raised only after the production had rehearsed in Shanghai for eight months, she said concerns had been raised indirectly all year long. 
Only after Mr. Chen staged the dress rehearsal, Ms. Ma said, did she have a chance to fully explain what was wrong.
When Mr. Chen wanted to go over the script with her, to ask which points she specifically objected to, Ms. Ma seemed to rely on a tactic common to Communist Party censors, insisting that he make the changes himself and then let her judge the finished product.
"I told him: 'You're the director,' " Ms. Ma said. 
"You have to make the changes, and then let us see the rehearsal as it will be performed. 
Then we will decide."

file: Shuttle Found Lost Sections of Great Wall in _94.txt
text:
ï»¿
Segments of the Great Wall of China that have been lost in centuries of desert sand were discovered in radar images taken from the space shuttle Endeavour in April 1994, says a scientist with the space agency.
The images show that two parallel sections of wall were built centuries apart, said the scientist, Diane Evans of the space-imaging project at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, an arm of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration in Pasadena.
The Great Wall findings and the wider archaeological potential of space-based radar were the subject of a University of Florida symposium on Thursday in Gainesville, organized by the World Monuments Fund, the Royal Angkor Foundation and the university.
The shuttle captured images of two generations of the wall along a 47-mile remote stretch in north-central China, 430 miles west of Beijing.
"In the images we can recognize two different dynasties that built the Great Wall," said Guo Huadong, a member of the Institute of Remote Sensing Applications at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing, and of the space radar-imaging team. 
"One was built in the Ming Dynasty and is about 600 years old. 
The other was built during the Sui Dynasty and is more than 1,000 years old."
From the ground, the low crumbling sections do not look much like images associated with the 1,500-mile wall, first begun in the third century B.C. to fend off invaders.
"One's usual image of the Great Wall is Nixon walking along with Chairman Mao," said Jeffrey J. Plaut of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. 
"That part around Beijing has always been maintained, whereas out in the countryside, the more typical condition of the wall is just kind of crumbling. 
In this area, they didn't use rock to build it. 
They used mud and soil."
Ms. Evans said space-based radar could penetrate vegetation and even loose sand to reveal structures beneath. 
It has been used to study the heavily overgrown ruins of Angkor in Cambodia and to search for stretches of the Silk Road in the northwestern desert in China.
Around the Great Wall, the radar penetrated about 3 feet, but in very dry sand, it can penetrate 16 to 20 feet, Ms. Evans said. 
Searching for the wall was a sideline of radar-imaging studies of geological and climate changes in northwestern China, she added.

file: SMUGGLED TO NEW YORK_ The Homeland_High Hopes, and Stakes, For China_s Boat People.txt
text:
ï»¿
The desperate risks that Chinese boat people take to get to the United States, even jumping into the ocean to swim to shore, reflect the burden of the trust that has been placed in them by friends and family.
Very few Chinese can afford the thousands of dollars demanded by the "snakeheads," or smugglers. 
So those who yearn for a better life in the United States borrow from relatives, friends and even neighbors.
They may carry with them an entire village's hopes for a better future, for if the migrant prospers in the United States he will send back money and help others migrate as well. 
On the other hand, if he is caught and sent back, he has not only humiliated himself but wasted the savings of those who bet their money on him.
Why do they go?
Some want more political or religious freedom, or to escape from the tyranny of the village Communist Party secretary, but the most powerful force usually appears to be the yearning for a better life.
Many of the boat people are peasants, especially young men. 
The per capita income for peasants in China is only about $125 a year, and land is so scarce that most can look forward to farming only a fraction of an acre.
Most of the migrants come from Fujian province, a hilly coastal region opposite Taiwan. 
The boldest people of Fujian have been emigrating since the 17th century, when the first waves began sailing for Taiwan and Southeast Asia.
Even today, Fujianese dialects are common in Singapore and Hong Kong, and the southern Fujianese dialect is dominant in Taiwan. 
President Lee Teng-hui of Taiwan and Corazon Aquino, the former president of the Philippines, are among the many overseas Chinese who traces their roots to Fujian.
Today Fujian is richer than many other parts of China, but it is still clear to any Fujianese peasant that those who migrate do better than those who stay behind.
Â 
Unrealistic Expectations
The yearning to flee is compounded by unrealistic expectations about what life abroad can offer. 
The snakeheads tell prospective migrants that ship conditions will be comfortable and the journey easy, that it is simple to make a fortune in Meiguo, "the beautiful country," as the United States is called in Chinese.
The phenomenon of the boat people is a consequence of the economic liberalization in China, and of the Communist Party's diminishing control over the population.
Private boats used to be rare, wealth was difficult to hide, and peasants were stuck in their own villages. 
But these days, the economic boom and loosening of Government policies have resulted in a profusion of private boats and far greater mobility for peasants.
No one notices or complains if a peasant disappears from his village, or if a worker resigns from his factory job. 
And the Fujian coastline is dotted with boats that since the early 1980's have done a thriving business in smuggling goods from Taiwan and Hong Kong.
Â 
Boom in Smuggling
Smuggling takes place on a huge scale -- more than 90 percent of the videocassette recorders sold in China are smuggled in -- and has resulted in growing corruption among the police. 
It has also led to the emergence of Mafia-style criminal gangs that have contacts in Taiwan and in Chinatowns in the United States and Hong Kong.
Starting in the late 1980's, the snakeheads began to smuggle Fujianese peasants into Taiwan, and that business is still going strong. 
But in the last few years, the boom has been in the smuggling of Fujian peasants to the United States. 
Taiwanese ships are usually used, partly because individual mainlanders still have mostly fishing boats rather than ocean-going cargo ships.

file: So Friendly_ Chinese and Christopher.txt
text:

What a difference eight months make.
On his last trip to Asia, in March, Secretary of State Warren Christopher verbally battled the Chinese over their human rights record every day of his visit.
But that was before the Clinton Administration ended its policy of linking trade benefits to human rights and before a parade of Cabinet secretaries marched into Beijing armed with business contracts and pledges of better relations.
Today Mr. Christopher and the Chinese Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, looked downright comfortable together as they met on the fringes of a meeting of foreign ministers of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, shaking hands vigorously for the cameras and accentuating the positive.
Their meeting was a prelude to President Clinton's meeting with the Chinese President next week.
In a brief exchange with reporters, Mr. Christopher praised China for what he called its constructive role in the negotiations that led to the nuclear deal between the United States and North Korea, and announced that China would have an important role in carrying it out. 
He noted that the Chinese had signed a pledge not to export missiles or technology controlled under an international nonproliferation accord.
He also said China had taken some positive steps on human rights, but did not mention the widespread belief within the Administration that the situation has deteriorated in recent months.
"This broad engagement is producing progress on various fronts," Mr. Christopher said.
Perhaps to reassure Mr. Qian of American constancy, Mr. Christopher brushed aside a question that the Administration might find it more difficult to execute its policy of engagement with a Republican-dominated Congress.
When asked about the election, Mr. Qian, whose Government has accused the American Congress of meddling in China's affairs in the past, politely deferred to Mr. Christopher. "I believe the election of the U.S. 
Congress is the entitlement of the United States," he said. 
"Therefore, I consider that question directed to Mr. Christopher."
But in their private meeting, Mr. Qian stepped out of character. 
He told Mr. Christopher that he appreciated his words about continuity in foreign policy during his formal speech to the forum. 
"We're interested and concerned to know how the election affects us," a senior State Department official quoted Mr. Qian as saying.
In a way the remark was not surprising. 
The two foreign policy committees in Congress will be headed by men who are sworn enemies of Beijing: Senator Jesse Helms, who favors independence for Taiwan and demonizes the Chinese military, and Representative Benjamin A. Gilman, who considers himself a close friend of the Dalai Lama of Tibet.
The cozy atmosphere between Mr. Christopher and Mr. Qian did not mean that there were no issues dividing them. 
Mr. Christopher raised the matter of China's refusal to accept revisions and updates of an international accord controlling missile exports or to disclose what missile technology it shipped abroad before it agreed to abide by the accord. 
He also told Mr. Qian that the United States would like China to make more progress in improving its human rights record.
Human rights in Indonesia was one of the themes discussed today by Mickey Kantor, the United States Trade Representative. 
He announced an agreement with Indonesia on the rights of workers, a source of tension between Washington and Jakarta. 
Among the accord's provisions are vague pledges by Indonesia to amend its labor laws and regulations and to make the Government-run All Independent Worker Union more independent.
Early last year, Mr. Kantor suspended a formal review of whether Indonesia deserved certain trade benefits despite its poor record on workers' rights.
In analyzing Indonesia's human rights record at the time, Mr. Kantor noted the overwhelming role of the military and the absence of free association in the workplace.
But neither of these issues was addressed in today's accord. 
Mike Jendrzejczyk, the Washington director of the human rights organizationAsia Watch, said: "For any labor accord to be meaningful, it would have to allow truly independent labor organizations to emerge and curb the pervasive role of the military."
Mr. Kantor acknowledged that the agreement had its limitations, telling reporters even as he touted it that it was only "a step in the proper direction."

file: SOCCER_A Narrow Victory Leaves Questions for U.S. Women.txt
text:

With the women's World Cup approaching in June, the United States appeared to have lost its scoring touch and any certainty that it was still head and shoulders above every other team in the tournament.
But after missing numerous opportunities tonight, the Americans rescued a 2-1 exhibition victory over China two minutes into extra time on a rebound shot by Tisha Venturini.
Mia Hamm fired a low cross from the right side that Han Wenxia, the Chinese goalkeeper, poked away. 
Venturini, who had entered in the 90th minute as a substitute, pounced on the ricochet and punched the ball into the net from seven yards out, awakening a quiet crowd of 15,257 at Hersheypark Stadium.
"I hit it as hard as I could across the goal and Tisha made this unbelievable run from midfield," Hamm said.
Venturini said, "You know Mia is going to get there, so I just kept running."
Tonight's friendly was seen by many as a potential preview of the World Cup final, scheduled for July 10 at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, Calif. 
The teams will meet again Sunday in an exhibition at Giants Stadium.
The Americans, who lost by 2-1 to China in Portugal's Algarve Cup last month, dominated play in the first half but continued to struggle with putting the ball into the net. 
Cindy Parlow pounded a shot off the post in the seventh minute, then failed to lift a chip shot over Han.
In the 12th minute, Hamm made a brilliant feint to her left, moved to her right around a Chinese defender but shot the ball just wide left from 17 yards out.
Hamm is considered the world's best player, and with 104 career goals, she is only 3 shy of the women's career record. 
But it has now been six games since she has scored a goal.

Wen Lirong had no choice but to drag Hamm down in the penalty area.
Michelle Akers took the penalty kick and drilled the ball low and to the left.

file: SOFTWARE_Professor Higgins Would Be Pleased.txt
text:
ï»¿
From the computer's speakers came a well-modulated American male voice with perfect diction, delivering "model utterances" to a Chinese student. 
The phrases were nothing like those in a Berlitz course for tourists or in a high school language textbook; these were designed for college professors, doctors, executives and other professionals.
"Your college transcripts are absolutely confidential," the voice said. 
It continued with other sentences: "She has office hours in the morning. 
Specifically, do you know which algorithms are causing problems?
We have no doubts that the software is pirated."
And, "Sign these checks."
The program, developed by Arthur H. Schwartz, a speech pathologist, is an advanced example of a growing effort on campuses and in businesses nationwide to teach not English, but English pronunciation.
Learning to speak any language exactly like a native becomes impossible for most people after the age of 12, and thus nearly everyone who learns English as an adult lacks the ability to pronounce some of its consonants. 
But according to Dr. Schwartz and others, Asians generally find English harder than Europeans do, because most Asian languages lack the patterns of stress and intonation that impart much of the meaning in spoken English.
Another reason for the Asian emphasis is that what used to be called the "brain drain" is still operating, drawing a torrent of professionals to the United States -- more and more of them from Taiwan, Korea, Japan and China. 
Programs that work on pronunciation have sprung up in places ranging from Honolulu to Stillwater, Okla., as well as Cincinnati, Boston, Syracuse and traditional centers of immigration like the New York City area. 
According to the United States Census Bureau, more than 200,000 people arrive in the United States from Asia and the Pacific Islands every year.
An example is Oliver Wong, the student seated at Dr. Schwartz's computer. 
A physician at the Cleveland Clinic, Dr. Wong, 35, arrived from Hong Kong six years ago with both an M.D. and a Ph.D. in nuclear medicine. 
Staring intently at the computer's screen, he tried saying, "Sign these checks."
What he saw on the monitor was a voiceprint of the "model," showing the pitch and volume of each sound. 
Below it was a print of his own effort.
Dr. Wong did well with the "n" in "sign," which is often a problem for Chinese students, who tend to drop final consonants. 
He also pronounced the "th" in "these" correctly, another tricky area, because Chinese students sometimes produce the sound without using their vocal cords, so it resembles the whispery "th" in "think."
But Dr. Wong, who is one of Dr. Schwartz's most advanced students, found the real value of the computer-based system in the last word, "checks."
For Dr. Wong, it had come out "chess."
Dr. Schwartz pointed at the voiceprint of the sample utterance and the print of Dr. Wong's effort. 
"Did you have a match for the word ending?" he asked, indicating the thin squiggle, which represented the "s" sound, at the end of the print.
Yes," said Dr. Wong, but he frowned at the screen. 
Something else was wrong, he knew, but like many students, he was having trouble identifying his error.
"Was it the 'ch' sound?" he asked. 
But no, that was fine. 
Then he looked near the end of the voiceprint. 
In the model there was a tiny gap, representing silence, between the main body of the word and the ending "s," but in the print of his voice, there was no such gap.
"There's a 'k' sound; I missed the 'k' sound," he said.
Then Dr. Wong moved on to the sentence about college transcripts. 
Dr. Schwartz congratulated him on correctly producing the last vowel sound in "confidential," and the "ts" in transcripts. 
Getting those correct made his whole sentence easy to understand, even though he missed the "p" in "transcripts."
Dr. Wong, who was born in Fujian Province and thus speaks two Chinese dialects in addition to English, said: "In Chinese, when you're done with one vowel, you're done with that particular word. 
We don't depend on consonants that much."
But in English, he said, "you need to master several vowels and consonants in one word."
Dr. Schwartz is a professor of speech and hearing at Cleveland State University, where several faculty members had referred graduate students to him for remedial work. 
That prompted him to found a small company, Accent Services, USA, and begin teaching students on the side, like Dr. Wong. His goal, he said, is not to produce students who sound just like Americans, but to help people make enough of the sounds that the listener expects so that their speech will be clear, or at least intelligible. 
As an example, he gave the word "parallel."
An Asian-born speaker trying to produce the word "parallel" might miss one sound, and say something like "pawallel," but that would still be intelligible, Dr. Schwartz said. 
Missing a second sound might still work, he said. 
"The listener is willing to work to fill in one, or to struggle for two," he said. 
But if the speaker missed a third sound, a native-born American would say, "the hell with it," Dr. Schwartz said.
SOME academic institutions have found that out the hard way. 
Syracuse University, for example, now runs a course in English pronunciation for foreign-born teaching assistants. 
Jeanette D. Macero, who teaches the course, said the genesis was complaints from parents that they were paying tuition for instructors whom their children could not understand.
Now, she said, "We have rankings, one to four."
One is near-native speaking; two is very good; three is someone who needs help, and four is "needs a great deal of help," she said.
"In order to teach, everybody needs to be a two," she said. 
"Eighty-five percent of all students become a two by the end of the second semester, and most of the remainder are a two by third semester."
In addition to English pronunciation, the course also teaches instructors that if they do not understand a question raised by an undergraduate, they should ask to have the question repeated. 
Female teachers from countries in which women do not raise their voices are taught to speak more firmly, and teachers of both sexes are taught a mixture of rhythm, intonation and melody (called prosody) that is characteristic of English. 
In Chinese, for example, tones give meanings to individual words but not to whole sentences. 
In English, tone differentiates a question from a declarative statement and also shows emphasis.
Foreign students at Syracuse and other colleges are given carefully graded tests of spoken English. 
The Educational Testing Service, in Princeton, N.J., developed a Test of Spoken English in 1981, and last year, nearly 20,000 people registered to take it; the number is still growing, according to Anthony P. Ostrander, associate director of the service. 
Tens of thousands more take a SPEAK test, or Speaking Proficiency English Assessment Kit, which is sold by the service to colleges and universities to administer to their foreign graduate students.
On many campuses the pronunciation programs originated in a speech pathology center, even though there is nothing wrong with these students; they simply grew up speaking another language.
At the Queens, N.Y., campus of St. John's University, Dr. Donna Geffner, director of the Speech and Hearing Center, also teaches graduate students and faculty members whose native tongue is not English. 
She encourages them to bring in their textbooks for help with certain words.
"If it's a teacher in the College of Pharmacy and Allied Health Professions," she said, "if he doesn't put the stress on the right syllable in the name of the chemical, the students don't have a clue about what he's talking about."
That is a problem not only for the listeners, but for the speakers, too. 
Adelina Samuels, who came to New York from Tashkent, Russia, six years ago, said: "You have no idea how frustrating it is. 
I didn't speak to people for a year and a half after I came to this country, even though in a year I knew some English already. 
Understanding what harm I do to language when I speak, I was afraid to communicate."
Ms. Samuels, who was a speech pathologist in Russia and now works with mentally handicapped Russian children in Queens, helping them speak, has developed her own multimedia computer program to help with pronunciation. 
Unlike Dr. Schwartz's, hers combines sounds with pictures of a mouth making the sounds.
Ms. Samuels herself speaks with less than perfect grammar, but her pronunciation is clear and, with her linguist's ear, she can produce on request a credible imitation of a native saying "Lawn Gyland," where she now lives.
Dr. Schwartz's program and Ms. Samuels's, which is not yet commercial, are two of several that use a personal computer. 
Computers with microphones and speakers are now almost universally available. 
Virginia Brogan, a speech pathologist who is a partner with Dr. Schwartz at Accent Services, contrasted this equipment with earlier tools.
"Tape recorders were a major step forward for grammar and vocabulary, and for someone who has a good ear," she said. 
"For a visual learner, it's a problem."
The computer, on the other hand, can give visual input to someone working on an aural task.
But the computer is only a tool, and Dr. Schwartz has found that the software, which was developed in part with a grant from the United States Department of Education, is most useful with an instructor to run it. 
And a speech professional's time tends to cost more than a piano teacher's or even a plumber's: Accent Services charges about $125 an hour, and students usually take an hour or two a week. 
Most are professional people, like doctors or engineers.
It also takes repeated sessions for the lessons to sink in, instructors say. 
But, said Ms. Brogan, "At 18 to 25 hours, it all gels."

file: Sold China _Spirit Tree_ May Have Been Stolen.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese officials charged with protecting relics are investigating the possibility that a spectacular ancient bronze candelabra recently sold in New York for a reported $2.5 million may have been illegally unearthed last year in south-central China and smuggled out of the country.
Last fall stories began circulating among Chinese archeologists and officials that a rare bronze funerary candelabra, known as a spirit tree, had been secretly unearthed from a tomb along the Yangtze River, in the region to be inundated by the Three Gorges Dam, and sold to a smuggler. 
The theft was never verified, although officials acknowledge that looting of artifacts in the dam area and nearby construction sites is a problem.
In late March a spirit tree, four feet high with dozens of branches and a blue patina, was offered for sale at the International Asian Art Fair, held at the Seventh Regiment Armory in New York City. 
It was sold to Leon D. Black, a trustee of the Museum of Modern Art in New York, for at least $2.5 million. 
Mr. Black is the founder and president of Apollo Advisers, a New York investment firm that owns stakes in many corporations, including Vail Resorts in Colorado; Samsonite, the luggage maker; Converse, the shoe manufacturer, and Telemundo, the Spanish-language television network.
Only two other intact spirit trees have been described in professional literature, according to Elizabeth Childs-Johnson, an art historian at New York University and expert on archeology in the region of the dam, in Sichuan and Hubei Provinces. 
Like the other examples, it almost certainly originated in the Three Gorges region, she said, and dates from the Eastern Han dynasty, of the first to third centuries A.D.
The possibility that the item sold in New York had recently been smuggled out of China has been publicized by international opponents of the Three Gorges Dam. 
In a press release on Thursday, the California-based International Rivers Network cited as evidence an Oct. 
7, 1997, article in a Chinese newspaper, Southern Weekend.
That article quoted Yao Jiong, head of the Cultural Relics Unit in Fengjie County, Sichuan, as saying that an intact spirit tree had been unearthed and sold on the black market for about $25,000.
But Mr. Yao, in a telephone interview today, said only that he had heard rumors that a spirit tree had been found in neighboring Wushan County and sold illegally. 
Government regulations, only spottily enforced, forbid export of older and significant artifacts.
Yu Weichao, the Beijing-based director of the Government's program to protect cultural relics in the Three Gorges area, is in the region investigating the charges.
Reached by telephone in the town of Zongxian, Mr. Yu said he had heard stories of a smuggled spirit tree last fall, and, after becoming aware of the sale in New York, decided to pursue the matter with local officials. 
Until recently Mr. Yu was also director of the National Museum of Chinese History in Beijing.
The sale in New York was arranged by a Belgian art dealer, Giselle Croes. 
Ms. Croes's office said today that she was traveling and could not be reached.
A spokesman for Mr. Black, Steven Anreder, said today that according to Mr. Black the seller was a reputable Hong Kong dealer and that the item came with all the proper papers. 
No one has suggested that Mr. Black did anything illegal or improper in buying the object in New York.
Mr. Black came into public view in the 1980's as co-head of corporate finance at Drexel Burnham Lambert, the defunct Wall Street firm that was dominated by Michael R. Milken, the junk-bond king. 
Now, besides his investment activities, Mr. Black is a well-known collector of Chinese bronzes and works by such 19th- and 20th-century European masters as Picasso, Cezanne, Degas and Bonnard. 
He also sits on the board of the Jewish Museum and the Mount Sinai Hospital, and recently endowed a Shakespeare Studies chair at Dartmouth College, his alma mater.
His firm is said to be considering bids for Polygram, the record company, and Simon & Schuster.
The narrow canyons above the Three Gorges Dam are sprinkled with subsurface and standing tombs, temples and other historical sites. 
Chinese historians have openly lamented the shortage of money and time to assess what will be lost when the dam is closed and waters start rising five years from now. 
They warn that a crucial, little-studied aspect of early Chinese history as well as the entire record of at least one ancient culture will be lost forever.
Another problem has emerged just above the future water line, where bulldozers are erecting new towns for the displaced populations and have little time for "salvage archeology."
What the machines do not destroy is taken by local people for sale to antique dealers.
Since the dam construction began in 1992, according to an article last January in the Three Gorges Public Security Newspaper, "antique traders converged on Wushan from different parts of the country and from Southeast Asia," and local looters shifted from trailing bulldozers to actively prospecting for artifacts. 
In May 1997 the police in Wushan County formed a special task force to deal with looting and smuggling, some by organized gangs.
Reached by telephone today, Luo Zhihong, Director of Cultural Relics for Wushan County, said that because of the lack of resources, "a lot of relics have been sold to private dealers."
He said his entire 1997 budget for protection was only about $3,600, while he had to offer that amount to entice local farmers to turn in even a single valuable relic they found.

file: Some Suspects In Spying Not Prosecuted.txt
text:
ï»¿
A federal court today made public affidavits filed by lawyers for the former Los Alamos scientist Wen Ho Lee in which two former intelligence officials said they were aware of instances in which government employees had been caught in serious cases of espionage but not prosecuted.
The defense has introduced the statements in its efforts to prove that Dr. Lee, who has been indicted on charges that he illegally downloaded a wealth of nuclear weapons secrets with the intent of helping a foreign country, was unfairly singled out for prosecution because of his race. 
Dr. Lee, 60, a naturalized American citizen, was born in Taiwan and, although he is not accused of spying, he was initially investigated on suspicions he had passed secrets to China.
The defense has previously released statements in which government intelligence officials said that Dr. Lee had been unfairly targeted because of concerns that because he was of Chinese descent he might be inclined to commit espionage for China. 
The fact that Dr. Lee was born in Taiwan, a strident enemy of the People's Republic of China, had been ignored, they said.
The affidavits released today go further, though, by providing details of serious espionage cases in which admitted spies apparently escaped criminal prosecution altogether.
Robert Vrooman, the former head of counterintelligence at the Los Alamos National Laboratory, where Dr. Lee worked, provided one affidavit. 
Mr. Vrooman, who has since retired from Los Alamos and who was reprimanded for not pursuing Dr. Lee more vigorously, disclosed for the first time an intelligence investigation code-named "Buffalo Slaughter."
In this investigation, he wrote, sometime in the late 1980's a person working at an Energy Department laboratory was caught after having passed secrets to a foreign country. 
"That individual was granted full immunity in return for agreeing to a full debriefing on the information that he passed," Mr. Vrooman said. 
That person, he added, was not of Chinese origin.
The second affidavit unsealed today was by Charles E. Washington, the former acting head of counterintelligence at the Department of Energy. 
Mr. Washington, who still works at the department as an international policy analyst, said that while he was head of counterintelligence he read an administrative report on the investigation of Dr. Lee and believed it "was wholly lacking in any support to identify Dr. Lee as a suspect."
Mr. Washington said that he knew of a number of department employees who were not prosecuted "for committing offenses that are much more serious than the 'security infractions' alleged to have been committed by Dr. Lee."
"I am personally aware of a D.O.E. employee who committed a most egregious case of espionage that cost our nation billions of dollars and drastically impacted our national defense," he said. 
"That D.O.E. employee was not prosecuted."
No further details were provided.
"The department aggressively pursues all such allegations," said Natalie Wymer, an Energy Department spokeswoman, but she would not comment on the specific cases mentioned.
These affidavits, unsealed today in Federal District Court in Albuquerque, follow by several days an order by the federal judge in Dr. Lee's case, James A. Parker, in which he gave the government two weeks to hand over thousands of pages of classified internal documents to determine if there is evidence that Dr. Lee was a victim of selective prosecution. 
If the judge finds that that was the case, the charges against him could be dropped.
In previous statements, Mr. Vrooman had disputed F.B.I. assertions that Dr. Lee had been singled out for investigation because he fit the description of a spy they were searching for. 
Mr. Vrooman said again in today's affidavit that dozens of people who also met the criteria, but who were not ethnically Chinese, were not pursued. 
The intelligence official said that even though he had investigated Dr. Lee for years, he considered him "naive," but not a spy.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: Sourly, Christopher_s Talks in Beijing Come to an End.txt
text:
ï»¿
Three days of talks between Secretary of State Warren Christopher and China's leaders ended today with only token gestures by Beijing on human rights. 
China's Foreign Minister blamed the United States for the lack of progress.
The two sides were so far apart that plans to hold a joint news conference after the meeting between Mr. Christopher and the Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, were canceled and the two men conducted separate, simultaneous briefings.
"The United States should be held accountable for all the consequences" of the talks, Mr. Qian told reporters after the meeting with Mr. Christopher, their second in three days.
Mr. Qian said that Washington's main "mistake" was that John Shattuck, the Assistant Secretary of State for Human Rights, met in secret late last month with Wei Jingsheng, China's most prominent dissident.
Mr. Qian again accused Mr. Shattuck of breaking China's laws and interfering in China's internal affairs by meeting with Mr. Wei, who has been described by Chinese officials as "a criminal on parole."
Â 
Meeting Called 'Appropriate'
At his news conference, Mr. Christopher called the meeting with Mr. Wei "appropriate," adding that the Chinese criticism of it was unjustified.
Mr. Christopher is the most senior American official to visit Beijing since President Clinton took office, and the trip had been planned as the high point of the Administration's six-month strategy of intensive engagement with the Chinese.
But by sending home Mr. Christopher with little to show for his trip, the Chinese instead have complicated their chances of retaining trade privileges with the United States.
Under President Clinton's executive order last year, China must make "significant, overall progress" in human rights by June to win extension of the so-called "most favored nation" trade benefits, which allow Chinese goods to enter the United States with virtually no tariffs.
"I came to China to try to insure that the Chinese side understands the importance of human rights to the United States in connection with the most-favored-nation treatment," Mr. Christopher said. 
"I doubt we would have achieved such clarity, at least at the highest levels, without the advantage of this visit."
President Clinton, while traveling in Detroit today, said he was not happy with the Chinese response on trade, but said American policy on the issue remained firm.
"I was disappointed at the results of the meeting with the Secretary of State. 
Our policy is the same. 
We'll just have to wait and see what happens between now and June. 
I'll make a judgment at the appropriate time."
Â 
Rancor Is Lacking
Mr. Christopher sought to portray his three days of talks in a positive light, and his statements at the news conference today lacked the rancor and critical tone of remarks made during his first two days here, when he also met with President Jiang Zemin and Prime Minister Li Peng.
"In an overall sense I find the differences between the United States and China are narrowing somewhat," Mr. Christopher said. 
But, he added, "more work clearly needs to be done."
Mr. Christopher noted "developments" undertaken by the Chinese on a number of fronts during his trip, but provided no assessment of whether he believed any were significant.
On the sensitive issue of accounting for and releasing political prisoners, Mr. Christopher said that his team had received "a great deal of information" on the 235 specific cases first presented to the Chinese last fall. 
And for the first time, the Chinese have pledged to provide detailed information about 106 Tibetan political prisoners, he said.
Assessing the importance of the information on the Chinese prisoners, Mr. Shattuck said afterward that the Clinton Administration would have to evaluate it carefully, but that at first blush it appeared to be "definitely more than we had before."
Â 
Inquiry on Jamming Promised
The two sides also codified, as expected, an oral agreement reached in principle with Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen in Beijing in January to reopen Chinese prisons to American customs officers to insure that prison factories are not making products for export to the United States.
Finally, the Chinese told Mr. Christopher they would investigate reports of the jamming of Voice of America broadcasts into China and within a few weeks would begin technical talks with representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross on how to open Chinese prisons to outside inspection.
But contrary to expectations, the Chinese did not give Mr. Christopher a concrete agreement to end the jamming of Voice of America.
They did not release ailing prisoners for medical treatment as has been requested repeatedly by the Clinton Administration and again by Mr. Christopher on this trip. 
They did not formally state their intention to enter into an agreement with the International Committee of the Red Cross to allow inspections of Chinese prisons.
Mr. Shattuck had asked for all of these concessions during his visit to China early this month.
But the fact that the Chinese were willing to make even largely symbolic moves indicates that they have not yet abandoned the effort to retain their trading privileges.
In an unusual departure from Chinese hospitality, the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters on Saturday that the Chinese had suggested that Mr. Christopher postpone his trip because it coincided with the opening of the National People's Congress, but that when the Americans said they could not change their arrangements, "in the end we have accommodated the Secretary."
Â 
Trip in Jeopardy
Aides to Mr. Christopher said that he came very close to canceling his visit at the last moment because of detentions of Chinese dissidents surrounding the trip. 
But he decided to go ahead because he felt it was absolutely necessary for him to deliver a clear, unambiguous message in person to the Chinese about what they had to do to win renewal of their trade benefits.
In addition, he was locked into going to Australia for a regularly scheduled meeting and may not have wanted to make another long trip to the Pacific at a different time.

file: South Koreans Sign Petitions To Aid North.txt
text:
ï»¿
Putting new pressure on the South Korean Government, religious groups here handed officials a huge stack of petitions today calling for increased food aid to North Korea.
The organizers said the petitions contained 1.1 million signatures, a remarkable number in a nation of 45 million people. 
The success of the petition drive underscores the growing discomfort in South Korea with the images filtering out of the North of emaciated children with vacant stares, and an increasing sense that some aid is necessary to avert a famine in North Korea.
South Korea has been ambivalent about assistance in the last few years. 
Many South Koreans feel a strong emotional tie with North Koreans, but they are also resentful of Pyongyang's failure to show gratitude for past aid and are alarmed about the risk that the food will go to bolster the North Korean Army.
The theme of today's rally by religious leaders was that North Korea's politics may be repugnant but that the most important thing is that Korean people are starving.
The sense of crisis was underscored by a video, titled "How Many More Must Die?" which was shown at the rally and which presented images of excruciatingly thin children and of bodies washed ashore on the Chinese side of the Yalu River, which marks China's border with North Korea. 
The narrator said the bodies were of North Koreans who had tried to flee to China because of the famine, but had drowned because they were too weak to swim.
The petition drive was strongly backed by Christian and Buddhist organizations, which have been gathering contributions for private assistance as well as calling on the South Korean Government to do more. 
The aid groups also emphasized that North Korea should allow more monitoring to insure that the food is actually given to people who need it and is not diverted to North Korean soldiers.
North Korea is one of the most isolated countries in the world, and some experts and visitors have said they saw few signs of hunger there and have suggested that the talk of famine there is exaggerated. 
But others have reported seeing bodies and have taken photos showing children suffering from malnutrition.

Falun Gong followers in Hong Kong and the United States are squabbling over assertions by a woman in the southern Chinese territory that she is the "true master" of the spiritual movement, having taken over from its founder, Li Hongzhi, who has dropped from view.
The power struggle is a potentially important one for Falun Gong, which drew millions of adherents in the late 1990's, because most of its followers are on the Chinese mainland, across the border from Hong Kong.

The assertion that the woman, Belinda Pang, 37, is the "Lord of Buddhas" has led to more of a cat fight than catharsis for the movement, which went underground on the mainland after Beijing banned the group a year ago.

The dispute began on May 11 -- celebrated as Buddha's birthday and, Mr. Li says, his birthday, too, though birth records in his hometown in China show otherwise. 
Ms. Pang, a tireless organizer in the Hong Kong chapter, organized a march through the city. 
Although only 24 people turned up, along the way most of them said they had experienced a vision of Ms. Pang seated in outer space while angels flew around her plucking flowers and dropping them to Earth. 
The flowers turned into raindrops when they hit the skin, said Mary Qian, one of those who said they saw the image.
