text:
ï»¿
President Clinton yesterday urged China's president, Jiang Zemin, to open a dialogue with the new government of Taiwan and put a stop to China's missile exports to Pakistan.
But in what had already been a week of diplomatic frustration for Mr. Clinton, Mr. Jiang offered little more than good wishes for the president's retirement in four months and thanks for supporting China's bid to join the World Trade Organization.
While Mr. Clinton's aides described the session as cordial, it was not expected to produce any breakthroughs -- and it did not.
It came on a day that Mr. Clinton's efforts to restart the peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians made such little headway that the president was overheard by photographers telling the Irish prime minister, Bertie Ahern, "This Middle East thing -- it's maddening."
He was not the only leader unhappy at the diplomatic gridlock as the summit talks here ended. 
A senior Japanese official said Israel's prime minister, Ehud Barak, had vented his unhappiness to his Japanese counterpart, Yoshiro Mori. 
At a meeting yesterday, he complained that the Palestinian leader, Yasir Arafat, "has not responded" to several new proposals on the status of Jerusalem, and questioned whether "Arafat has the political courage to make the move."
Mr. Clinton's aides had played down the prospect of any major progress on Chinese missile exports, Tibet or Taiwan during Mr. Clinton's last months in office. 
But they had hoped that the expected Senate approval this month of permanent normal trade relations with China -- which the United States promised as part of the accord with China that ushers it into the World Trade Organization -- would be rewarded. 
They hoped to claim political progress on issues that have bedeviled Washington's relations with Beijing since the two first met in 1993.
In a measure of the two leaders' continuing communications problems after seven years of interchanges, a senior administration official said yesterday that the meeting was "designed to get these two men on the same wavelength a little more."
But Mr. Jiang was eager to show his American hosts that he could talk the talk of a high-tech nation, even while offering up familiar lectures about respecting China's sovereignty. 
Immediately after his hour-and-a-half meeting with Mr. Clinton, he used a luncheon meeting with America's top business executives to declare that China is plugging into the world.
"We now have over 16 million netizens," he said in a speech delivered entirely in English, "more than 27,000 World Wide Web sites, over 70,000 Chinese domain names and 61 million mobile phones in China."
But he did not mention China's recent efforts to crack down on the use of the Internet for the spread of dissenting opinions in China, and Mr. Clinton, aides said, never broached the subject.
When Mr. Jiang was done reciting China's technological advances to the executives, though, he wove back to familiar territory. 
He argued that China was a place of religious tolerance, saying, "The languages, religions and customs of ethnic minorities in China, including the Tibetans, are protected and respected, and their cultural traditions have been carried forward and developed."
Pro-Tibet groups argue that China has done all it can to stamp out the Tibetan culture, and they succeeded in killing a World Bank project this summer that some feared would relocate ethnic Tibetan farmers and further dilute Tibetan culture.
Mr. Jiang also called the Falun Gong religious group, whose members have been arrested in large numbers in recent months, a cult and said any government would crack down on "those who have done severe harm to the people."
As he spoke, members of the group performed silent exercises across Park Avenue, under the watchful eye of the police.
James Lilley, a former American ambassador to Beijing who was at the luncheon, said Mr. Jiang's arguments amounted to "an effort to grab the religious issues by the throat and say, 'We have religious tolerance, but not your kind,' " adding, "He just wants to sail right by the issue."
The conversation on China's missile exports to Pakistan came after Mr. Clinton, earlier this summer, sent a delegation to China to try to cut off the supply. 
The administration worries that any new missile technology would heighten Pakistan's ability to strike India.
But Mr. Jiang, by all accounts, has paid little attention to the issue. 
"This is going to take a while," an aide to Mr. Clinton said.
Nor did the Chinese leader indicate that he was ready to open talks with Taiwan's newly elected leader, Chen Shui-bian. 
The aide said "they spent a long time on Taiwan, but Jiang took much of that describing China's historical claims" to the island.
That also seemed out of place for what will probably be the second-to-last meeting between the two leaders; Mr. Clinton, by now, has heard China's claims to Taiwan many, many times.

file: Surprise for Indonesia_s Chinese_ Peaceful Election.txt
text:
ï»¿
This time, Enin Supriyanto is ready. 
Like other ethnic Chinese here, he has his escape plan, his emergency telephone numbers and his extra rations.
On Saturday night, surrounded by the music of frogs and the sweet scent of clove cigarettes, he took his turn on neighborhood watch, sitting by a barbed-wire barricade at the gated entrance of his housing complex until well past midnight.
One year after a paroxysm of rioting in which ethnic Chinese were the targets of widespread vandalism, arson and rape, Chinese all across the country have been preparing for new attacks before the general election next Monday.
Some bought guns. 
Some are paying military units to guard commercial areas. 
Many of those who can afford to have left the country.
But something utterly unexpected has happened. 
The election campaign, in most parts of the country, has so far been mainly peaceful.
The threatening telephone calls to Chinese residents and the anonymous leaflets and rumors of attacks that have circulated in Chinese communities have not reappeared.
Sitting by their barbed-wire barricade, Mr. Enin and a dozen of his neighbors strummed a guitar, played cards and discussed their tennis strokes over late-night snacks and glasses of hot Ovaltine.
"We are playing cards, we are eating noodles, we are talking nonsense," Mr. Enin said, happily relieved.
Although Indonesia's Chinese people know that they can become targets of violence at any time, as they have been periodically over the decades, there is an emerging hope here that something fundamental may be starting to change.
The cautiously upbeat mood among the residents here in the western suburbs of Jakarta is repeated among political analysts -- both Chinese and non-Chinese -- as they survey the national scene.
After the shock of the riots and the forced resignation of President Suharto last year, the analysts say, Indonesia's Chinese may be inching toward the mainstream of society.
Adapting a pattern set by centuries of Dutch colonization, Mr. Suharto created what one analyst called a "golden cage" for the Chinese. 
They were offered economic opportunity in exchange for their support and their exclusion from the country's political and cultural life.
They constitute less than 4 percent of the population in this country of more than 200 million, but they control the bulk of its private commerce -- ranging from small rice merchants to billionaire tycoons.
Mr. Suharto's departure after 32 years of rule opened the way for a reorganization of all aspects of society, from freeing the press to forming political parties to redefining the role of Indonesians of Chinese ancestry.
Led by a better-educated, better-integrated younger generation, many of the Chinese have begun to seek a new, more active place in society.
"They had been convinced for about 30 years that everything was fine," said Daniel S. Lev, an expert on Indonesia at the University of Washington. 
"They were isolated in a sense -- they were denied any right to participate politically, but there was, at the higher levels, a payoff: you got rich.
"But for many, what happened last May came as a really brutal shock, because the part of the deal they forgot was that if things got serious they would have to serve as scapegoats."
Hari Tjan, a political analyst with the independent Center for Strategic and International Studies, who is an ethnic Chinese, said of the riots, "The cost was very high, but it is a learning process that has been started."
For the moment, he said, there has also been a change in the attitudes of indigenous political leaders, who he said "don't want to play this Chinese card anymore."
"I am amazed that their conscience as human beings has revived," Mr. Tjan said, "and it is a wonderful, encouraging development. 
Nearly all the parties are now embracing the Chinese and telling them, 'You are one of us. 
Please work together for the country.'
"
In a country where Chinese schools, newspapers, signboards and public ceremonies were banned by Mr. Suharto, it has been an extraordinary sight at some political rallies to see, among the crowds, traditional Chinese lion and dragon dances.
As they feel freer to redefine their role, Chinese here have begun a debate over whether to assert their cultural separateness or to try to blend into the broader national identity.
Some Chinese have banded together to form a culturally based political party. 
Others have chosen not to emphasize their separateness and have joined some of the 47 other parties engaged in the campaign.
Some responded to the riots by reaching out in solidarity to the overseas Chinese in other nations, said Anugerah Pekerti, an Indonesian Chinese who is chairman of World Vision Indonesia, an aid organization.
Others, like Mr. Pekerti himself, advocate a process he calls "Indonesianization," in which the country's scores of disparate ethnic groups will draw closer together in a common identity.
The debate illustrates an essential and wide-ranging change from Mr. Suharto's father-knows-best era: Indonesians are reconstructing their nation on their own terms.
And the basic lesson the Chinese seem to be applying, in the often-quoted words of the Indonesian Chinese political analyst Arief Budiman, is: "If you remain timid, you will forever be trampled on."

file: Survival of the Prudent.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Middle Heart
By Bette Bao Lord.
370 pp. 
New York:
Alfred A. Knopf. $25.
The historian W. J. F. Jenner has said that China is caught in a prison of history. 
He suggests that there is no escape from the past, that even the Chinese language -- which can describe a situation today, last year and 2,000 years ago in identical linguistic forms -- traps the culture and people in the stagnant, and often violent, ways of the past. 
Mr. Jenner posits that this adherence to the old led inevitably to the events at Tiananmen Square in the spring of 1989.
Bette Bao Lord, the Chinese-born wife of a former United States Ambassador to China, has carved out an interesting career by bringing China and the lives of the Chinese to American readers in a variety of forms. 
She wrote "In the Year of the Boar and Jackie Robinson," a fictionalized account of her childhood as an immigrant in Brooklyn, as a children's book. 
She told the story of her younger sister, who was left behind with an aunt in China because she was too young to travel, and became separated from the rest of the family when the bamboo curtain came down, in the biography "Eighth Moon."
Her popular novel "Spring Moon" appealed to lovers of historical fiction, telling a story that spanned five generations. 
"Legacies" was a series of essays and first-person narratives on the events leading up to the Tiananmen Square massacre. 
Her new novel, "The Middle Heart," draws on her facility with all these genres -- it is a compelling and admirably accurate history of China over the last 75 years, lightly disguised as a conventional multigenerational love story.
In 1932, the year of the Japanese conquest of Manchuria, Steel Hope, the spoiled son of the patriarch of the House of Li, and Mountain Pine, a physically lame but academically brilliant servant, befriend Firecrackers, a wild orphan girl masquerading as a boy. 
They become blood brothers, pledging to die in defense of their country. 
Over the next 50 years, the three companions are separated, thrown into disgrace and left for dead, fall in love with the wrong people and spend a decade here and there in solitary confinement. 
They also survive the invasion by the Japanese, the civil war, attacks on rightists, the madness of the Cultural Revolution and, finally, the tragedy of Tiananmen Square.
At times, "The Middle Heart" seems hopelessly obvious. 
In 1940, in the Nationalist wartime capital of Chongqing, Steel Hope and Mountain Pine -- the former now an engineering student, the latter an aspiring writer -- go to the opera to see a beautiful actress, Summer Wishes. 
She turns out to be none other than Firecrackers. 
After the revolution, when the Communist Party man arrives in the old ancestral village where Summer Wishes and Mountain Pine are happily married, guess who that turns out to be.
To some readers these coincidences will seem implausible, but they should reconsider. 
In times of turmoil, which China has certainly had its share of during the last three-quarters of a century, doesn't it make sense that the same groups of people (the elite, intellectuals, artists) would repeatedly run into one another -- struggling to return to their homes, seeking solace in exile, languishing in labor camps?
Ultimately, it is this dramatic aspect of "The Middle Heart" that makes it so readable. 
In fact, Mrs. Lord has given her fictional story a good deal of authenticity by using small details -- telling nuggets of fact -- from her interviews for "Legacies."
In "The Middle Heart," Steel Hope, released from 10 years in solitary confinement, is able to pace only four steps in one direction and back again. 
This anecdote comes directly from the opening page of "Legacies," where Mrs. Lord tells the story of a former prisoner she met in Beijing. 
Mountain Pine, after years of forced labor, loses his temper when someone wastes half a glass of water. 
Mrs. Lord found this detail when she asked some Chinese children how prison had changed their mother. 
When another character in this novel is tied into the "takeoff position" -- arms twisted and tied up and back to a board as a means of humiliation and pain during the Cultural Revolution -- Mrs. Lord is using an experience she has elsewhere described as happening to her own aunt.
As each of Mrs. Lord's characters is forced to renounce loved ones, political beliefs, even his or her own morals to survive, it is important to remember that few people in China reached the 1990's without making some similar sacrifices.
In the late 1950's, Mountain Pine, declared a rightist, encourages his wife to divorce him so that their son will not be disgraced. 
"Once I'm sent away," he tells Summer Wishes, "no one must ever speak of me again, so that Little Panda will learn not to talk about his father. 
Since my existence can only harm him, I must cease to exist."
During the Cultural Revolution, in the 1960's, Summer Wishes, now married to Steel Hope, must beat her husband before hundreds of people. 
As he whispers encouragement, she addresses the crowd: "I know this filthy Revisionist better than anyone."
These scenes may seem melodramatic to American readers, but they were played out again and again in real life by people who were just trying to outlast the latest political upheaval.
At the end, a granddaughter, North Star, goes to take part in the demonstration at Tiananmen Square. 
She recalls the words Summer Wishes kept repeating at her death -- "I wanted to be a human being."
Bette Bao Lord has taken the modern history of a quarter of the world's population and turned it into the story of human beings surviving against tremendous adversity. 
"The Middle Heart" is a moving tribute to the Chinese people and their capacity to endure and, despite all, hope.

file: Suspect in Loss of Nuclear Secrets Unlikely to Face Spying Charges.txt
text:
ï»¿
Three months ago, a research mathematician was dismissed from his job at the Los Alamos nuclear weapons laboratory for security violations. 
Today Federal authorities say it is most unlikely that the mathematician, who is at the center of the uproar over the suspected theft of nuclear secrets by China, will ever face criminal charges of espionage.
Moreover, the officials are unsure whether the scientist, Wen Ho Lee, will be accused of any wrongdoing, even though investigators found in March that he had downloaded thousands of secret codes used in the design of the most sophisticated American nuclear weapons.
The uncertain status of the case has infuriated some Government officials and lawmakers, primarily Republicans, who say Mr. Lee may be responsible for the most damaging espionage of the post-cold-war era. 
That conclusion was reinforced last month, when a Congressional panel found that China had used nuclear secrets stolen from American labs to develop advanced miniature warheads and a mobile ballistic missile.
Mr. Lee's lawyer, Mark Holscher, said his client was an innocent scientist who had been branded as a spy even though he had not even been charged with any crime. 
"Mr. Lee has been unfairly injected into a politically charged debate over America-China relations and has been subject to improper leaks in violation of Federal law," Mr. Holscher said.
The extent and nature of evidence against Mr. Lee remains obscure. 
But interviews with officials about the still classified evidence -- including details about Mr. Lee's work, his meetings with Chinese scientists and his overseas travel -- help explain why after three years of investigation law-enforcement officials acknowledge that they will probably never learn the truth.
Over all, officials said, the evidence is a mosaic of fact and conclusions that suggests why counterintelligence cases are frustrating and often fail to result in prosecutions. 
These are some of the points:
*There are no witnesses who saw Mr. Lee engage in espionage.
*There is no evidence of a motive in the form of unexplained income or a change in his style of life.
*Nor are there indications that Mr. Lee, a naturalized American who was born on Taiwan, was ideologically allied with Beijing.
*Even the evidence that a theft occurred is circumstantial.
Still, counterintelligence officials said, they strongly suspect that China stole the important information data in the mid-80's. 
The loss was apparently not found at the time, when an investigation might have had the greatest chance of success. 
Authorities did not realize that the information had been stolen until 1995, when suspicions were aroused at the lab in New Mexico by an analysis of Chinese nuclear tests and when the Central Intelligence Agency obtained a document with esoteric computations indicating that Beijing had acquired nuclear secrets.
Mr. Lee emerged as a suspect because he was one of the few researchers in the area that is thought to have been compromised, computational fluid dynamics. 
Many people at the Energy Department were aware of the information. 
But officials said Mr. Lee was the sole scientist with full access who had also visited Chinese counterparts in Beijing.
From there the evidentiary trail followed a meandering course. 
Investigators pieced together an account of Mr. Lee's contacts with Chinese over the years, producing an outline of circumstantial information. 
Some of it seemed to raise questions about Mr. Lee. Some of it seemed too speculative to shed significant light on his activities. 
And none of it was solid enough to form the basis for an indictment, Government officials said.
One crucial component is missing. 
There is no direct evidence that Mr. Lee ever passed or tried to pass on to China any classified national security information.
Although the evidence is apparently insufficient to prosecute Mr. Lee, the Federal Bureau of Investigation thought that the case against him was compelling enough to ask the Justice Department in 1997 for permission to eavesdrop on Mr. Lee under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act. 
The law lets the Government monitor subjects electronically, not to assemble evidence of a crime, but to gather intelligence in national security cases.
The still classified F.B.I. application cited questions about Mr. Lee dating from the early 80's, when he contacted a scientist who had been ousted from a weapons lab in California after an inquiry into the theft of secrets about the neutron bomb.
The application, made up of drafts of documents exchanged between the F.B.I. and the Justice Department, described how Chinese intelligence differed from espionage by the United States' traditional adversaries. 
The Chinese, the document said, usually seek information from overseas Chinese who are traveling in China through scientist-to-scientist contacts, a more elusive form of espionage because it does not rely on identifiable intelligence officers.
The F.B.I. request said Mr. Lee had failed to disclose the identities of all the scientists whom he contacted in China on visits in 1986 and 1988. 
The Energy Department had approved the trips and authorized his meetings and discussions of nonclassified matters with Chinese officials. 
After the trips, Mr. Lee and his wife met American security officials and identified a number of Chinese scientists whom they had met.
But counterintelligence officials apparently suspected that Mr. Lee might have held back some pertinent information about his activities during vacations taken after each trip. 
On the vacations, the officials said, Mr. Lee had undisclosed contacts with scientists, including one identified as Side Hu, a top official at an institute of engineering physics involved in nuclear weapons research. 
Other officials said the omissions might have been inadvertent, in light of the numerous contacts that Mr. Lee did report.
In 1992, Mr. Hu led a delegation of Chinese officials on a tour of Los Alamos that the Energy Department had authorized, documents show. 
On the visit, Mr. Hu spoke privately with Mr. Lee and embraced him in a congratulatory manner.
Later, counterintelligence agents surreptitiously analyzed Mr. Lee's spending and found what they thought might be another puzzle piece. 
They found two charges on a credit card at a travel agency while Mr. Lee was in Hong Kong in 1994. 
One charge was for $100, the other for $700, enough to pay for what officials said might have been an airline ticket to China.
Republican Senators like Fred Thompson of Tennessee and at least one Democrat, Robert G. Torricelli of New Jersey, have expressed outrage that the Justice Department blocked the F.B.I. request for a warrant to eavesdrop on Mr. Lee, a step that they suggest would have accelerated the investigation at a critical time, before Mr. Lee realized that he was under suspicion.
In mid-1997, the Office of Intelligence Policy Review at the Justice Department found that the evidence was so nebulous and dated that it refused the F.B.I. request for electronic monitoring. 
After a bureau official questioned the decision, Attorney General Janet Reno ordered a second review by the Justice Department, which also found that the bureau had failed to produce enough evidence to justify the request.
Ms. Reno has said bureau officials dropped the issue. 
For her part, she said recently, "I assumed that since I did not hear from the F.B.I. that the matter had been resolved to their satisfaction."
Instead, bureau officials said investigators decided to pursue other avenues. 
An agent who was posing as a Chinese intelligence officer approached Mr. Lee. The scientist rebuffed an invitation to spy for Beijing, Government officials said, but he did not tell authorities about the contact until they had approached him to explain it.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: SWIMMING_New Accusations Aimed at Chinese Swimmers.txt
text:
ï»¿
Luggage belonging to a Chinese swimmer was seized yesterday by Australian custom officials who said it contained a substance labeled as human growth hormone. 
If the label is correct, the incident would reinforce the widely held belief that China's female swimmers have been using banned bodybuilding drugs.
Yuan Yuan, a breast-stroke swimmer who won a silver medal at the 1994 world championships, was part of a 29-person Chinese group flying from Beijing to Sydney to Perth for the world championships. 
The Australian customs service said a routine search of luggage in Sydney uncovered 13 vials packed in ice in a thermos flask. 
It said there were 13 more vials of a diluting fluid.
The spokesman said the vials, which were not declared, were clearly labeled in English as human somatropin, a human growth hormone that athletes have been known to use in place of anabolic steroids. 
All those drugs are banned by the International Olympic Committee and the international federations governing each Olympic sport, but there are no effective tests to detect the use of human growth hormone.
Athletes use the drugs to train more intensively, with a quicker recovery time. 
Used in conjunction with weight lifting and a high-protein diet, the drugs also promote muscle growth.
A laboratory analysis of the substance seized at the airport may be available today. 
The International Swimming Federation, known by its French initials as FINA, said it would have no comment until the vials had been analyzed. 
It also said it could not take action without proof that athletes had used illegal drugs.
It was unclear exactly who the vials belonged to, and there has been no official comment on the incident from Yuan or the Chinese swimming federation. 
Yuan told customs officers that the vials belonged to her coach. 
John Hawksworth, an Australian customs official, said a team coach said he packed the bag. 
A Chinese team official said Yuan was bringing in the substance for a friend in Australia.
Deryk Snelling, the national performance director for British swimming, said FINA should consider banning China from the championships, which began earlier this week. 
"It'll penalize a lot of people," he said, "but it's the only way they'll get the message."
Western swimming officials have insisted that despite denials by the Chinese, the rise of China's female swimmers in the 1990's is a result of illegal drug use. 
The reaction to the seizure in Australia was one of vindication.
"This time, they've been caught with their hands in the cookie jar," said Don Talbot, the Australian national coach.
"We dream of such moments," said Mark Schubert, an assistant coach of the United States team.
In last October's Chinese national championships, two world records were set and the women swam the year's fastest time in eight events, fueling suspicions that the Chinese were using banned substances. 
In 1994, the swimmers won 12 of the 16 gold medals in the world championships in Rome. 
Two months later, at the Asian Games in Hiroshima, Japan, seven Chinese female swimmers tested positive for the use of anabolic steroids.
In all, 23 Chinese swimmers have tested positive since 1990 for using steroids. 
Officials from other nations demanded that FINA establish out-of-competition testing, which it did. 
Shi Tianshu, the leader of the Chinese team at Perth, said his federation had conducted more than 100 out-of-competition tests in the last two months, more than 650 in the last year, with no positive results.
On Tuesday, Shi said his country was clean on the drug issue. 
"We compare with any nation in the fight against drugs," he said.
Hawksworth said the confiscated material was found by accident. 
He said one passenger on the plane fit a narcotics profile. 
That person's baggage was inspected and nothing turned up. 
Yuan's bags were on the same trolley, and, Hawksworth said, "We found the stuff."
A journalist from Hong Kong Star Television identified Yuan's coach as Zhou Ming and said he remained in Sydney after the vials were discovered. 
After questioning, the others went on to Perth, where they learned that 12 teammates who arrived two days before had been tested for drugs after practice that morning.
It was a bad day all around for FINA. 
It had lifted the world-championship accreditation of Winfried Leopold, the German coach, after he admitted he had given banned drugs to athletes in East Germany. 
Yesterday, an Australian court ordered the credential restored.
And in an interview to be published today in the German newspaper Chemnitz Morgenpost, Petra Kind-Schneider, a 1980 Olympic swimming champion for East Germany, said she had heart and liver problems as a result of years of drug use. 
She said she started taking drugs just after her 14th birthday and was told to take blue pills four times a day, but that no one told her they contained anabolic steroids.

file: SWIMMING_Thompson_s Two Golds Cap Fine U.S. Showing.txt
text:
ï»¿
The United States won three of four events today on the final day of the Pan Pacific swimming championships and emerged as the top team in the first major test of the "fast" pool where Olympic events will be swum next year.
Twelve world records were set during the 8-day, 12-nation meet at the Sydney International Aquatic Center.
The American team -- led by the sprinter Jenny Thompson and the backstrokers Lenny Krayzelburg and Brooke Bennett, who among them won 11 medals -- edged out the host nation in medals, 35-32, and in points, 391-372.
However, the Australians, led by Ian Thorpe, Michael Klim and Susie O'Neill, matched the American gold medal tally of 13. 
The last time Australia bested the United States in total medals at a swimming competition was in 1956, at the Olympics in Melbourne.
Today, for the first time in these championships, no world records were set. 
Thompson earned her fifth and sixth gold medals of the meet, winning the 50-meter freestyle and swimming the butterfly leg in the women's medley relay. 
The American men's medley relay also won.
In the men's 1,500 freestyle, 19-year-old Grant Hackett of Australia won in 14 minutes 45.60 seconds, the second-fastest time ever.
The brightest star of the championships was Penny Heyns, the 24-year-old South African breast-stroke specialist who lives in Canada. 
Heyns set four world records at distances from 50 to 200 meters, bringing her haul of world records to eight in the last six weeks.
Swimming's oldest record survived the onslaught. 
Mary T. Meagher's 2:05.96 in the 200 butterfly, set in 1981, withstood a strong challenge last Thursday by O'Neill, the defending Olympic champion. 
O'Neill, 26, fell 0.64 of a second short.
However, the second butterfly record Meagher set in 1981 was finally broken. 
Thompson, 26, clipped five-hundredths of a second off Meagher's 18-year-old record in the 100 butterfly.
Meagher, now 34, said: "I knew this day would come. 
This now means that a part of my journey in swimming is over. 
There is a new record holder, and someone can go after Jenny."
The Chinese team was conspicuous for being almost invisible. 
Chinese swimmers qualified for only one final and finished last in that.
China originally named 20 swimmers for the meet, but sent only five. 
The reason given by Chinese authorities was the "conflicting domestic schedule" of the All-China Games in October.
The coach of the United States women's team, Richard Quick, and Australia's national coach, Don Talbot, were among officials here who expressed suspicions of the Chinese explanation. 
A series of Chinese female swimmers have been suspended for using performance-enhancing drugs in recent years.
However, the president of the Australian Swimming Federation, Terry Gathercole, said he was encouraged by the fact that in the last year Chinese officials had reported 10 instances of the use of banned substances by their own swimmers. 
"This indicates that China is trying" to act on the problem, he said.

file: SWIMMING_U.S. Ban of Chinese Swimmers Criticized.txt
text:
ï»¿
Officials of swimming's world governing body yesterday criticized the United States, Canada and Australia for banning China from a pre-Olympic meet this summer in Atlanta.
In light of seven recent positive drug tests among Chinese swimmers, including two world champions, the three aquatic powers voted on Sunday in Honolulu to prohibit China from swimming in the Pan Pacific Championships in August. 
The Pan Pacs, as they are known, will serve as a test event for the 1996 Summer Games in Atlanta. 
Japan cast the lone dissenting vote among Pan-Pac charter members.
Yesterday, two officials of FINA, the sport's governing body, said it was premature to ban China from the meet. 
Last week, FINA announced plans to control the drug problem in Chinese swimming.
First, it will send a commission to China in March to investigate the involvement of swimmers, coaches, doctors and team officials in the use of banned substances. 
Second, FINA will substantially increase the number of out-of-competition drug tests administered in 1995. 
Third, a special congress will be convened in Rio de Janeiro in December to impose stricter penalties for doping.
United States swimming officials have called for greater vigilance since the Chinese women won 12 of 16 gold medals at the world championships in Rome last September. 
While they applaud the latest steps taken by FINA, American officials said, the ban was necessary because harsher penalties for drug use would not be implemented in time for the Pan Pacific Championships.
"We believe that this is not premature; it is based on substantial evidence that there is some kind of structured or organized doping for sports in the People's Republic of China," said Ray Essick, the executive director of the United States Swimming Federation. 
"Until we are given absolute proof that this will no longer take place, or until appropriate rules or sanctions are in place from FINA to deal with it, we're not interested in having our athletes compete in an unfair competition."
Gunnar Werner, the honorary secretary of FINA, called the ban of Chinese athletes from the Pan Pacs "regrettable."
Cornel Marculescu, the director of FINA, said in a telephone interview: "Perhaps this is not the best way to solve these problems. 
FINA has already taken strong actions against doping."
Officials from FINA and the International Olympic Committee also made it clear yesterday that they have no intention of banning all Chinese swimmers from the 1996 Summer Games. 
The seven Chinese swimmers suspended after the Asian Games in Japan last fall will be ineligible, however, including the world champions Lu Bin and Yang Aihua. 
All seven tested positive for the anabolic steroid dihydrotestosterone, commonly known as DHT.
"Excluding a whole nation or a delegation because some athletes, or some in their entourage, break rules, I don't think would be an appropriate measure," Francois Carrard, director general of the I.O.C., said in a telephone interview from Lausanne, Switzerland.

file: SYDNEY 2000_ GYMNASTICS_After 40 Years of Expectation, Mighty Chinese Come Through.txt
text:
ï»¿
The last event of the night was unfolding when the usually stoic Chinese gymnasts tilted their heads to the rafters like dust bowl survivors welcoming the first raindrop.
Suddenly, there was relief. 
Revealing untraditional emotion, they jumped around in a huddle on the side of the podium once they realized the 40-year spell that had left their mighty teams with nothing but Olympic consolation prizes had come to an end.
Tonight, the team gold medal in men's gymnastics belonged to China for the first time. 
Almost giddy, the Chinese gymnasts floated onto the podium at the Dome and saluted the collection of fans waving their country's flag in the seats. 
A moment later, several of the gymnasts glanced down at their priceless medallions, stared at every detail and held them in their palms, not wanting to let go.
"We have worked hard for several generations," Coach Huang Yubin said through a translator. 
"We have fought for this for 40 years. 
We think we should taste the fruits of the Champagne."
In every pocket of China, there was cause for celebration. 
After five world championships, but three Olympic silver medals since 1984, China could go home having conquered all the heavy expectations. 
Instead of buckling under the Olympic pressure as they had in the past, the Chinese thrived on the challenge, finishing a dominant 1.613 points ahead of the silver medalists from Ukraine and 2.062 points in front of the bronze medal winners from Russia.
"We were under some pressure," Huang acknowledged, "but this was our best chance today."

This was their moment to separate themselves from their position as background scenery to the popular United States women's program, and grab their first medal since their 1984 gold medal heyday. 
After their fourth-place position in the preliminaries, the Americans had a bronze medal on their minds.
But at the same time the Chinese began their celebration on one side of the arena, a snapshot of the United States' collapsible performance was developing on the horizontal bar. 
In need of a miracle as they entered the event, languishing in fifth position after five of the six apparatus, the Americans watched with horror as their top two gymnasts crashed to the mat during their routines.
The 17-year-old Paul Hamm blew his usually calm cover and fell twice on a difficult release move. 
Then, the team's star, Blaine Wilson, swung into his release move but could only swipe at the bar with his fingertips as he fell into the padding.

Wilson, the five-time national champion, wasn't up to it.

Although he scored a 9.7 on the vault and a 9.775 on the parallel bars, the Americans needed Wilson to be spectacular in every area. 
The horizontal bar, and his score of 9.050, only punctuated a disappointing night for him.
"We wouldn't be where we are without Blaine; he has carried us for a long time," said the three-time Olympian John Roethlisberger, who finished his gymnastics career with a 9.7 on the horizontal bar.

Wilson left his teammates to speak for him. 
He exited after the competition without answering questions.

"Obviously, my coaching just wasn't good enough.

In the end, the catastrophes on the horizontal bar didn't doom them. 
The flurry of deductions along the way did.
This wasn't the way Kormann wanted to go out as coach of the team. 
Kormann said he is set to retire Oct. 
1, and does not know who his successor will be. 
If he could recommend someone, it would be the 30-year-old Roethlisberger, who gathered the group for an emotional team meeting after the competition.

The United Nations Charter offers membership to all "peace-loving states" that are judged willing to carry out the Charter's obligations.

"All we are asking at this moment is the option of a study committee," Mr. Hu said.
The agenda item that China defeated proposed that Taiwan's "exceptional situation" be considered by the General Assembly "in accordance with the established model of parallel representation of divided countries at the United Nations."
This alluded to West Germany and East Germany, which had separate seats before Germany's unification, and to North Korea and South Korea, which are both members.

"Only after the reunification is accomplished can the Taiwan compatriots, together with other Chinese people of all ethnic groups, truly and fully enjoy the dignity and honor attained by their great motherland in the world," Mr. Qin said.
