text:
ï»¿
Chinese Pavilion Featured
Workers from Westchester's sister city Jingzhou in China completed construction of a traditional pavilion and garden in May at Lasdon Park and Arboretum in Somers, a property of the county's Department of Parks, Recreation and Conservation.
Called the Chinese Friendship Pavilion, it was built by Chinese artisans sent to Westchester along with all the construction and finishing materials they would need. 
The building, dedicated on June 2, will be featured on a free tour of the park today at 2 P.M. Typically Chinese in its architectural style, it is the sort of structure one would have seen in the gardens of royalty. 
Painted orange, turquoise and red, it has a tile roof and is open on all sides, the better to contemplate the surrounding landscape and a pond. 
The interior ceiling and overhang are painted with 108 dragons flying among clouds.
Also on the tour are the arboretum's many species of trees, shrubs and perennials and a native American chestnut tree grove where the American Chestnut Foundation does research.
In 1991 the 180-acre preserve established a continuing project called the Famous and Historic Tree Grove, where seeds taken from trees at significant locations or dating from centuries ago are planted.
Some of them are from the homes of American Presidents. 
Among them are an Overcup Oak from Abraham Lincoln's home and seeds from trees at the homes of George Washington and Franklin D. Roosevelt. A yellowwood seedling was obtained from John F. Kennedy's grave site at Arlington Cemetery, and a water oak seed was taken from the grounds of the Brown African Methodist Episcopal Chapel in Alabama, where the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke at the start of the march to Montgomery.
Battles also figure in the collection of seeds. 
A Saratoga red oak represents a 1777 victory for the American Revolutionary forces at that site, and a northern white cedar seed was taken from Fort Ticonderoga, commemorating a 1759 battle in which the British took the fort from the French. 
A seed from the rare Franklinia Tree, prized for its fragrant white flowers, which bloom in July and August, is a descendant of the original, planted in the 1600's by John Bartram, an American botanist.
Admission to the tour is $3. 
Call 232-9147 for more information.
Â 
'The Waking Dream'
Teun Hocks's painted photograph "Untitled," exemplifies the theme of an exhibition opening Tuesday and remaining through Oct. 
25 at the Castle Gallery of the College of New Rochelle. 
"The Waking Dream: Psychological Realism in Contemporary Art" tries to explore the lighter and darker sides of life as expressed enigmatically by 21 artists. 
Viewers will read whatever they wish into the results.
D. Dominick Lombardi and Steven Lowey were the guest curators, and they will give free gallery talks at a reception on Sept. 
20 from 1:30 to 4 P.M. The artists' names would not be familiar to most people, but they are all professionals. 
They include Mike Cockrill, Julie Harvey, Antonio Petracca, Steven Skollar and Lisa Zwerling.
The college is at 39 Castle Place, and the gallery is open Tuesdays through Fridays from 10 A.M. to 5 P.M. and Saturdays and Sundays from noon to 4 P.M. It will be closed for the Labor Day weekend from Saturday through Monday. 
Admission is free. 
Call 654-5235 for more information.
Â 
Candid Shots in China
Forty-four color photographs of people in some of China's major cities will be on display in the Somers Public Library from Tuesday through Sept. 
29. They were taken by C. Richard Donahue, a clinical social worker who recently traveled through Hong Kong, Beijing, Xian, Guilin and Guangzhou with a group of colleagues.
"I'm a people person, and most of the pictures are of people I would see from the time they went to work at 6 in the morning through the rest of the day," he said.He photographed many fathers tending their children, which surprised him. 
"They are very family oriented," he said. 
"And they are doing simple, unusual entrepreneurial things that they would have been arrested for 20 years ago."
He recalled a man who had set up a little business by the side of a road well traveled by people on bicycles -- the most prevalent mode of transportation. 
"He had a canvas spread on the ground, with a complete set of bike repair tools."
Struck by the unexpected freedom that the Chinese have to travel, he said, "They were streaming into Hong Kong and experiencing unprecedented growth and expansion."
Unframed prints of the photographs may be bought for $25 each. 
An indication of their content is in the titles: "Haircut on the Street in Beijing," "Mother and Child at the Market in Guangzhou," "Life on the Li River in Guilin," "Young Girl in a Newsstand in Beijing," "Art Student at the Children's Palace in Xian," "Women Waiting for a Bus in Guilin" and shots of families in the temple, an old woman begging, a woman hanging wash and a customer in a butcher shop.
Call the library at 232-5717 for visiting hours.
Â 
The Flag as Chronicle
An unusual exhibition of antique American flags can be seen at the Darien Library through Sept. 
14. Ken Reiss, curator of the show, is co-owner with his wife, Catherine, of many of the flags on view. 
"It has often been said," he said, "that the American flag is unique in providing an ongoing chronicle of the growth of the nation it represents."
Upholding that premise are flags tracking 10 changes in design from 1861 to 1912. 
Different patterns of stars in rows or circles reflected individuals and manufacturers' concepts, sometimes to the point of adding new stars in anticipation of new states. 
The flags and related materials, some from the Darien Historical Society collection, mostly date from the half century after the start of the Civil War.
The exhibition can be seen on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays from 9 A.M. to 6 P.M., Tuesdays and Thursdays from 9 A.M. to 9 P.M. and Saturdays from 9 A.M. to 1 P.M. The library is on Leroy Avenue, off Route 1. 
Call the historical society at (203) 655-9233 for more information, or call the library at (203) 655-2568 for directions.Â Â Â ELEANOR CHARLES

text:
ï»¿
A day after President Jiang Zemin of China said the people of Tibet were "living and working in happiness and contentment," Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright appointed a new special coordinator today to focus attention on China's suppression of Tibet's cultural and religious traditions.
The creation of the position became a diplomatic problem for the Clinton Administration this week. 
Ms. Albright had promised Congress that she would make an appointment by Nov. 
1, a deadline that left Administration officials worried about offending Mr. Jiang during his three days in Washington.
Ms. Albright waited until the last moment -- after Mr. Jiang had left Washington on Thursday to continue his weeklong tour of the United States in Philadelphia and in New York and New Jersey today.
Ms. Albright appointed Gregory B. Craig, who is now director of the State Department's office of policy planning, which is devoted to strategic planning and long-range issues. 
Mr. Craig is one of Ms. Albright's close aides, and as Special Coordinator for Tibetan Affairs, he will report directly to the Secretary. 
He will continue in his current post.
China has long bristled at international criticism of its treatment of Tibet, the remote, mountainous region that has sought greater autonomy since Chinese troops violently established Communist rule starting in 1950. 
In the weeks leading up to this week's sessions between President Clinton and Mr. Jiang, Chinese officials repeatedly objected to the creation of a post devoted to Tibetan affairs.
In a speech in Washington on Thursday, Mr. Jiang brushed aside criticism of China's rule over Tibet. 
He even compared the Communist Government's crushing of a Tibetan rebellion in 1959 to the emancipation of slaves in the United States. 
"With the support of the central Government and the rest of the country, today's Tibet is developing prosperity," he said.
Reflecting the sensitivity of the appointment, Ms. Albright informed Foreign Minister Qian Qichen of her decision in a meeting on Thursday before making the announcement today.
Mr. Craig, 52, has been director of policy planning since June. 
A lawyer, he was an adviser to Senator Edward M. Kennedy, Democrat of Massachusetts, from 1984 to 1988. 
He also served as chairman of the International Human Rights Law Group.
The United States considers Tibet a part of China and does not support its independence, as do many Tibetans in exile. 
The State Department's spokesman, James P. Rubin, said one central aspect of the new post would be to promote talks between China and representatives of Tibet's exiled leader, the Dalai Lama.
Since the new position does not carry the rank of ambassador, Mr. Craig's appointment does not require Senate confirmation. 
But the appointment drew praise in Congress, where Democrats and Republicans had pressed the Administration to create the post and to raise the profile of Tibet in American foreign policy toward China.
Senator Jesse Helms of North Carolina, the Republican chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, said through a spokesman that he was pleased with the appointment of an official with so high a rank in the department's bureaucracy.
Representative Benjamin A. Gilman of New York, chairman of the House International Relations Committee, said he would hold a hearing next week on Tibet and ask Mr. Craig to testify.
"The destruction of Tibet's religion and culture must end," Mr. Gilman said, "and hopefully the Special Coordinator will play a leading role in the effort to seek greater recognition of Tibet."

file: THE JIANG VISIT_ THE OVERVIEW_CHINA_S PRESIDENT DRAWS APPLAUSE AT HARVARD TALK.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Jiang Zemin of China, a permanent smile on his face, basked today in the prestige of Harvard University, where the White House, fearing large protests, had urged him not to go.
But Mr. Jiang, ignoring silent protests in the church-like lecture hall where he spoke and much louder demonstrations outside, deflected questions about human rights, Tibet and the protesters themselves with humor, earning applause from some of the Chinese-Americans and American China scholars in the hall. 
Excerpts, page 14.
"Although I am already 71 years old, my ears still work very well," Mr. Jiang said when asked about the protesters outside in the blustery rain. 
"As I spoke, I did hear the sound of loudspeakers from outside, but I believed my only approach was to speak even louder."
He said that having been to Harvard as a young bureaucrat 40 years ago, he already understood "the general concept of democracy."
Then he added, "During my current trip to the United States, starting from Hawaii, I felt more specific understanding of the American democracy -- more specific than I learned from books."
That gentle allusion to the protests that have followed him everywhere produced laughter and applause, even as he steadily ignored a man who stood with his back to the stage in a T-shirt reading: "Taiwan not part of China. 
One Taiwan. 
Free Tibet. 
One China. 
Human Rights Now."
The demonstrators, pro-Jiang and anti-Jiang, numbered about 5,000, the Cambridge police said, making this the largest street gathering at Harvard since the Vietnam War.
Mr. Jiang's speech was a kind of summary of his weeklong state visit to the United States, and he stressed both China's new pride and its peaceful intentions. 
He called for deeper understanding and friendship between China and the United States, and he praised Harvard for being among the first American universities to accept Chinese students in the mid-1800's.
Reading roughly half his speech in English, Mr. Jiang vowed that China would work with the United States to "shoulder common responsibility on many important questions crucial to human survival and development, such as maintaining world peace and security, preventing the spread of weapons of mass destruction, protecting the environment and combating international crime."
In their talks last week, he and President Clinton agreed to work together, Mr. Jiang said, "to build a constructive strategic partnership" that "will mark a new stage of development in China-U.S. relations."
But "to promote the development of China-U.S. relations," he said both politely and pointedly, "China needs to know the United States better, and vice versa."
He asked for a fuller American understanding of the deep roots of Chinese civilization, and also of its century and a half of "frequent bullying and humiliation by imperialist powers."
"However," he continued, "after a hundred years' struggle of the entire Chinese nation, China has stood up again as a giant."
To American critics of Mr. Clinton's policy of "constructive engagement" with China, that is precisely the problem, because they fear that Beijing's interests will inevitably clash with Washington's, and that a rising China will seek to shape the global order to suit its own priorities.
But during this visit, Mr. Jiang and Mr. Clinton have worked hard to try "to improve the relationship from a position of fragile public support in the United States," said Richard Solomon, a China specialist who directs the United States Institute of Peace in Washington. 
"They're trying to build a broader constituency in the American political mainstream for the relationship itself."
Mr. Jiang compared nations to sunlight, which he said is composed of seven colors. 
"We should respect and learn from each other and draw upon others' strong points to offset one's own deficiencies for achieving common progress," he said.
And in a clear riposte to Mr. Clinton, who said China's policy of repressing political dissent cut against "the current of history," Mr. Jiang said today that China's policy choices "are all based on both the reality and history."
"Therefore," he continued, "they are not only in conformity with the trend of the historical development of mankind and that of the times, but also reflect the characteristics of the Chinese nation."
A country of 1.2 billion people values stabilityI and security, he said, and China's choices "serve not only the fundamental interests of the Chinese people, but also world peace, stabilityI, prosperity and progress; this is the key to an understanding of the present China and its future."
Mr. Jiang, who goes from here to Los Angeles today for his last stop before returning to Beijing on Monday, has tried to do his part to give post-Tiananmen China a human and unthreatening face, as he paid tribute both to colonial Williamsburg and the shrines of American technology, like I.B.M. and Lucent.
For Mr. Jiang, clearly, Harvard is as much a shrine of American achievement as Wall Street, and he praised the late Harvard historian, John King Fairbank, for his work in understanding China.
Mr. Jiang said he would present Harvard's Fairbank Center for East Asian Research a set of the newly published "Twenty-Four Histories with Mao Zedong's Comments," which Mr. Jiang called "a rich heritage of philosophy, in understanding and drawing useful lessons from China's history."
In his responses to questions, Mr. Jiang denied that he had no dialogue with the Chinese people, citing his many visits as President "to grass-roots units in the countryside and the cities."
Denying widespread dissent, he said that "the people are very satisfied with the achievements we have scored under our program of modernization and opening up," and that the Government, despite its shortcomings, was simply trying to give the people what they want.
In what could have been an oblique reference to the crushing of protesters in Tiananmen Square, raised in a question, Mr. Jiang said: "It goes without saying that, naturally, we may have shortcomings and even make some mistakes in our work. 
However, we have been working on a constant basis to further improve our work."
Having defended the actions at Tiananmen Square in Washington on Wednesday, it is unlikely that Mr. Jaing would have changed the verdict of his party only three days later in answer to an extemporaneous question.
He also repeated that he would not meet with the Dalai Lama, the spiritual leader of Tibet, because, "to my regret, the 14th Dalai Lama has not yet given up his efforts to split the country."
The questions Mr. Jiang answered had been chosen by a committee of four Harvard scholars led by Ezra Vogel, the director of the Fairbank Center, and Bill Kovach, the curator of the Nieman Foundation for Journalism. 
The Chinese had insisted that there be no questions from the floor during the 15 minutes they allotted to them, to reduce the possibility of a demonstration or speechifying, and Mr. Vogel decided to solicit questions from the Harvard community by mail and electronic mail.
The committee picked five questions it thought best represented key concerns, but did not forewarn Mr. Jiang of their content.
In the end, Mr. Jiang answered two of them and then called for a question from the floor. 
A protester in a T-shirt tried to ask a question, but Mr. Jiang said he wanted a question "from an American," and Mr. Vogel shouted the protester down, in the end calling on a Newsweek reporter.
Mr. Kovach said in an interview that all the questions were given afterward to the Chinese delegation, and that copies of all of them would be made available to the public.
After his lecture, Mr. Jiang went to a lunch in Boston with some 200 business executives that was sponsored by the John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Company. 
The United States is pressing China to open up its markets in services, too, including insurance.

file: THE JIANG VISIT_Exercise in Democracy_ Engaging in Dialogue Leads to Some Hostile Questions.txt
text:
ï»¿
Following are excerpts from a question-and-answer session after a speech at Harvard today by President Jiang Zemin of China.
Q. Jiang Zemin asked the West not to engage in confrontation but dialogue. 
However, why does he refuse dialogue with his own people?
Why did the Chinese Government order tanks in Tiananmen Square on June 4, 1989, and confront the Chinese people?
A. In China there are various channels for us to learn about people's views. 
For instance, when I was the Mayor of Shanghai, I had frequent contact with the People's Deputies there. 
And after I went to work with the Party's Central Committee, I visited almost all the 30 provinces, municipalities, and autonomous regions of China.
China is a large country, with different levels of development in different parts of the country, and there are some places in China that I have visited even more than three times.
I have been to many grass roots units in China's countryside, in the cities, and in the factories, and have had extensive contacts with people from different walks of life, and therefore, the people are very satisfied with achievements we have scored under the reform and opening-up program of China, and the policy of the Government is to serve the people.
Therefore, we have to reflect on the people's requests and do everything that will meet the people's requests. 
And also, as a result of our effort along that line, we have enjoyed the support of our people.
It goes without saying that, naturally, we may have shortcomings and even make some mistakes in our work. 
However, we have been working on a constant basis to further improve our work.
Q. You said before you would not meet with the Dalai Lama if independence was addressed. 
Given that the Dalai Lama has now said he is willing to meet you without discussing independence, why, therefore, do you still refuse to meet with him?
A. Our policy toward the 14th Dalai Lama is a very clear-cut one, and you also referred to part of it in raising your question. 
That is, he must recognize publicly that Tibet is an inalienable part of the People's Republic of China; that he must state publicly his willingness to give up Tibet independence, and that he must stop all activities aimed at splitting the motherland.
However, much to my regret, up until this date, the 14th Dalai Lama has not stopped his separatist activities.
Q. (In a question that was mostly inaudible, President Jiang was asked about his reaction to the protest occurring outside the hall.)
A. I do have my understanding about the general concept of democracy. 
However, during my current trip to the United States, starting from Hawaii, I felt more specific understanding of the American democracy, more specific than I learned from books.
Although I am already 71 years old, my ears still work very well, so when I was delivering my speech, I did hear the sound from the loudspeakers outside. 
However, I believe the only approach for me is to speak even louder than it.

file: THE LOS ALAMOS SECRETS CASE_ THE OVERVIEW_Nuclear Weapons Engineer Indicted in Removal of Data.txt
text:
ï»¿
A federal grand jury in New Mexico indicted a nuclear weapons engineer today on 59 counts of illegally removing highly classified design, construction and testing data from the Los Alamos weapons laboratory where he was employed.
The indictment charged that the engineer, Wen Ho Lee, had violated the Atomic Energy Act and Foreign Espionage Act, assembling collections of 19 computer files that contained some of the country's most closely held nuclear weapons secrets.
Dr. Lee, who has been under scrutiny for more than five years, was arrested this afternoon at his home outside of Los Alamos by agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.
He made an initial appearance at the federal courthouse in Albuquerque and, after prosecutors described him as a flight risk, a federal magistrate ordered him held without bail pending a detention hearing on Monday.
The indictment accused Dr. Lee of transferring classified information into unclassified computer files at the Los Alamos laboratory and downloading other material onto portable tapes. 
The indictment said that seven of the tapes that Dr. Lee had made, containing critical nuclear secrets, could not be found.
The most serious offenses in the indictment, removing classified nuclear weapons data, are punishable by a maximum of a life sentence in prison.
The indictment accused Dr. Lee of mishandling nuclear data but did not accuse him of spying or of any espionage offenses related to a foreign government. 
Nevertheless the case has been one of the most notably sensitive issues in recent United States relations with China, as well as internal American debates over policy.
Separately, officials said they were aware that the government would be criticized for singling Dr. Lee out for prosecution and would be prepared to show at his trial that unlike any other scientist or laboratory employee who mishandled secrets, Dr. Lee had selectively stripped the Los Alamos files of every conceivable secret related to nuclear weapons development over the last 50 years, an incalculable loss of research that in the wrong hands could alter the global balance of nuclear arms. 
Page A17.
Today, Dr. Lee's lawyer, Mark Holscher of Los Angeles, issued a statement saying that the charges against Dr. Lee were groundless and that federal prosecutors were "wholly unjustified in suggesting that Dr. Lee is a flight risk."
Mr. Holscher said that Dr. Lee had been unfairly singled out because of he is a Chinese-American and that "prosecutive decisions in this case have been influenced by other branches of government."
His complaint was an apparent reference to accusations by Dr. Lee's supporters that the scientist had been turned into a scapegoat by law enforcement and energy officials who had been criticized by Republicans in Congress for security lapses at the country's nuclear weapons laboratories.
Mr. Holscher specifically denied any accusations of wrongdoing in connection with the tapes in a letter dated today to the federal prosecutor in New Mexico, John J. Kelly. He offered to make Dr. Lee available for a polygraph test "to verify our repeated written representations that at no time did he mishandle those tapes in question and to confirm that he did not provide the tapes to any third party."
It is unlikely that prosecutors will accept Dr. Lee's offer. 
In the past Dr. Lee has voluntarily taken government polygraph examinations, law enforcement officials said, and has given some answers about his activities that appeared to be deceptive. 
The results of polygraph examinations are not admissible as evidence.
The indictment did not allege that Dr. Lee gave the material to any unauthorized person or government, but it did charge that he removed classified nuclear weapons data "with the intent to injure the United States and with the intent to secure an advantage for a foreign power."
The indictment did not explain how the government would prove Dr. Lee's intent, and at a news conference in Albuquerque, Mr. Kelly declined to discuss what evidence the government had obtained that would demonstrate Dr. Lee's motives.
At the federal courthouse in Albuquerque, the intense drama involving Dr. Lee, which has seemed at times to threaten the nation's relationship with China, was reduced to a brief and routine procedural hearing.
Dr. Lee sat calmly in the sparsely filled courtroom wearing a brown leather jacket over a pink, open-collared shirt. 
He sat at the defense table across from Mr. Kelly, the United States attorney, and three assistants.
The magistrate, Donald Svet, asked Dr. Lee whether he had read the charges against him.
"Yes," he answered quietly, "I read them in the last couple of hours."
The magistrate asked, "Are you aware of the penalties," and Dr. Lee shook his head, no.
After the counts were summarized, the magistrate asked again, "Do you understand?"
Dr. Lee answered, "What is the total number of years, I don't understand."
Neither the judge nor the prosecutors fully answered Dr. Lee's query before the hearing ended and he was placed in the custody of a United State marshal and escorted to jail until the detention hearing on Monday.
For months, Dr. Lee's case has been the focal point of a furious debate within the cloistered worlds of counterintelligence, law enforcement and nuclear science. 
And today's charges are unlikely to quell that controversy, particularly within scientific circles.
Since Dr. Lee was fired from his job in March, some scientists have said he was selectively punished because other researchers had sometimes removed classified information without being severely punished.
But Dr. Lee was charged with 29 counts of removing and tampering with restricted data, 10 counts of retaining restricted data, 10 counts of gathering national defense information and 10 counts of unlawful retention of national defense information under the Federal Espionage Act.
With its lengthy list of serious felony charges the government left little doubt that prosecutors had concluded that Mr. Lee was responsible for what some counterintelligence officials regarded as the most serious breach in security at the weapons laboratories in recent decades.
But in the politically charged debate over American-Chinese relations, the indictment seemed certain to further stir emotions about Dr. Lee's case and whether he could be blamed for what government officials said was the loss of a vast store of secret data sufficient to alter the world's strategic balance of power.
But after a security investigation dating back to late 1994, investigators have been unable to uncover concrete evidence that Dr. Lee passed any nuclear secrets to China or any other government.
Mr. Lee, 59, is a naturalized American citizen born in Taiwan who has worked in United States weapons labs for 20 years. 
He had been under suspicion in an inquiry into Beijing's suspected theft of technology known as W-88, the design for the United States' most advanced miniaturized nuclear warhead.
Investigators were unable to determine who was responsible for the W-88 loss or even whether Chinese scientist might have acquired the technology on their own. 
But counterintelligence authorities continued to investigate Dr. Lee on circumstantial grounds that he had access to some of the information and had traveled to China on scientific exchange visits.
Dr. Lee's lawyers have portrayed these trips as innocent and said that they were approved by the government in advance.
Investigators eager to step up their inquiry into Dr. Lee had long sought permission from Attorney General Janet Reno to begin covert electronic surveillance of him. 
While that effort was blocked by Ms. Reno's intelligence aides, the point became moot earlier this year when Dr. Lee agreed to a voluntary search of his office and home.
Agents said that in the search they uncovered evidence that he transferred weapons data to nonsecure computers -- the first indication of the extensive removal of information that came to be the central point of today's indictment.

file: THE MARKET TURMOIL_ THE OUTPOST_It_s a Dark and Stormy Night . . . and Here_s Hong Kong Trying to Li.txt
text:
ï»¿
Amid the battering of stock markets around the world this week, Hong Kong has seemed strangely stable -- an oasis of calm at the eye of the storm. 
But appearances are deceiving.
In a climax to an unprecedented two-week-long direct intervention in the stock market, Hong Kong's government spent at least $8 billion today on a buying spree to prop up shares and foil speculators it accuses of manipulating its market.
On Thursday, an earlier round of intervention had managed to push the Hong Kong stock market up while every other market around the globe was down. 
Today, for all the money spent, the benchmark Hang Seng index still declined 93.23 points, or 1.2 percent, to 7,829.74.
Hong Kong has always been unusual in Asia, a rare outpost of free markets in a region of state-managed capitalism. 
The government, while committed to a fixed exchange rate with the United States dollar and prepared to support the property market the way South Africa's DeBeers regulates the price of diamonds, historically has gone to great lengths to avoid meddling in its markets.
So, in a city where tracking the Hang Seng is a favorite parlor game, today's wild ride -- by far the market's biggest trading volume ever -- left people slack-jawed. 
At moments during the morning trading session, the Hong Kong Stock Exchange seemed less a market than a giant clearance sale, with the government buying everything in sight.
"They did this at a time when there is gloom around the world," said Glenn Lesko, the director of regional sales and trading at ABN Amro Securities in Hong Kong. 
"I think they ran into far more sellers than they expected."
Government officials, however, claimed victory. 
They said the intervention had stabilized the Hang Seng, even as markets across Asia, Europe and the United States were plummeting because of fears about the financial turmoil in Russia and other emerging markets. 
That stymied traders who had taken short positions on shares and futures contracts on the bet that the Hong Kong market would tumble.
For Hong Kong, today's action was the boldest step yet in a costly effort to erect a wall between itself and the financial typhoon raging around it. 
Although Hong Kong has already been whipsawed by the Asian crisis, the territory's leaders are determined not to be sucked into an even more calamitous vortex of currency attacks followed by a stock market collapse.
Traders estimate that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has spent at least $12 billion since it began buying shares and futures contracts on Aug. 
14. Nonetheless, Sir Donald Tsang, Hong Kong's financial secretary, said the government was ready to continue intervening. 
Hong Kong has already spent more than 10 percent of its $100 billion in foreign reserves on the effort.
Tung Chee-hwa, the chief executive of Hong Kong, held open the possibility that China might support Hong Kong's campaign, with its $140 billion worth of reserves. 
"The central Government has said many, many times openly that they are very willing to support us if there is a need to do so," he said.
In fact, Hong Kong seems determined to drive out the currency traders, even if it means intervening indefinitely. 
It is unclear, however, whether the government has an end-game strategy. 
And at today's rate of buying, it will run out of reserves in about 13 trading sessions.
Hong Kong's tough stance came in the wake of more bad economic news. 
The government released data confirming that Hong Kong had slipped into a recession in the second quarter, as the economy contracted 5 percent. 
It also projected that the economy would shrink 4 percent in 1998 -- the first full year of contraction since Hong Kong began keeping records in 1961.
But it was the government's intervention that had analysts rattled. 
Several said the stock market would plummet as soon as the government stopped supporting it. 
And some argued that Hong Kong was squandering both its reserves and its reputation as the freest market in Asia.
"In the short run, if you pour billions of dollars into stocks, you can pump up the market," said Steve H. Hanke, a professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University. 
"But in the long run, this is doomed to fail because it convinces speculators that Hong Kong can't take the pain."
Indeed, no less prominent a currency trader than George Soros seems to view Hong Kong's intervention as a quixotic effort. 
Stanley Druckenmiller, the manager of Mr. Soros's Quantum Fund, said in an interview on Thursday with CNBC: "No matter what they do in their market, when they wake up on Monday morning, they're still going to be in a depression."
Hong Kong may not stop at simple intervention. 
Sir Donald announced that the government was considering measures to curb "manipulative practices."
These could include restrictions on the short-selling of stocks and increased disclosure requirements in the trading of index futures.
Hong Kong would not be the first Asian market to place restrictions on certain kinds of trading. 
Japan, Korea and Malaysia all do it, just as they intervene in their markets. 
But Hong Kong has long prided itself as the New York of Asia -- a market where Wall Street openness meets Chinese entrepreneurialism.
As it happens, some analysts believe the government has been forced to act by Hong Kong's most prominent entrepreneurs -- the property tycoons -- who have seen their share holdings decline in value by 50 percent since last year. 
Two months ago, the government announced it would suspend sales of land, in an effort to halt the downward spiral of property prices.
"The irony is that the government is taking the people's money and using it to bail out the property developers," said Marc Faber, an investment adviser and managing director of his own brokerage firm.
Sir Donald dismissed the suggestion that the government was putting Hong Kong's reserves at risk. 
He noted that the Hang Seng index has risen 1,200 points since the intervention began, which means that the government's owns more in shares than it did in cash before it began buying.
Still, the government's buying spree has put it in the uncharacteristic -- and potentially awkward -- position of being a major shareholder in many blue-chip Hong Kong companies.
Sir Donald said he was not concerned about owning large stakes in Hong Kong companies, nor about the potential negative effect of dumping those positions on the open market once the intervention was over.
Hong Kong's battle with the currency traders has mutated from a guerrilla skirmish into a full-scale war of attrition. 
Several traders said the government had recruited an unidentified expert to help it plot moves to thwart even the shrewdest of hedge funds. 
Beyond buying blue-chip shares like HSBC Holdings and Hong Kong Telecom, the government has taken a complex set of long and short positions on August and September index futures contracts.
Beyond the mechanics of the market, Hong Kong's intervention has rekindled a debate about how much governments can -- and should -- intervene to protect themselves from the vagaries of the global marketplace.
Ronnie Chan, a prominent Hong Kong property developer, said the government had an obligation to protect its citizens from a wave of speculation that was threatening to swamp the stock market and the local economy.
"The total annual output of Hong Kong is dwarfed by the daily capital flow of the markets," Mr. Chan said. 
"At will, the market can destroy an economy overnight. 
Is Hong Kong being destroyed?
No. But is it suffering hugely?
You bet."
In Hong Kong's case, however, the debate is complicated by the fact that it has set itself up as a mecca for global capital. 
Last year, the Hang Seng index rocketed to 16,000 points as foreign investors poured money into shares of "red chips" -- Chinese companies with publicly listed Hong Kong subsidiaries.
The Hong Kong dollar is another example of the territory's supposed openness to the global economy. 
The currency is pegged to the United States dollar at a fixed rate. 
The price for preserving that link at a time when most Asian countries devalued their currencies has been a spike in interest rates, which drove down property prices and the stock market.
Until this summer, Hong Kong had seemed ready to absorb those blows. 
But then in June, the government announced it would stop selling land. 
And two weeks ago, it waded into the stock market. 
After today, some market experts began talking about the "nationalization" of Hong Kong.

file: THE MARKETS_ CURRENCIES_Yen Continues Its Slide, Threatening Other Asian Markets.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Japanese yen weakened to 140 to the dollar for the first time in seven years yesterday, extending a yearlong decline that is now threatening the economic recovery of the emerging markets in Asia that were battered by their currency devaluations last year.
Despite the fallout from the weakening yen, many currency traders and strategists expect its value to decline further because the Japanese Government has not come up with a convincing program to stimulate the economy. 
Many economists have already said Japan is in a recession, which could be confirmed Friday when Tokyo is expected to report its second consecutive quarterly decline in growth.
Economists and analysts said the falling yen was hurting Asia's recovery in two ways: One, the decline is a reflection of a weakening Japanese economy that means Japan will not be a big buyer of products from the troubled countries of South Korea, Thailand and Indonesia.
The weakening yen also means South Korean, Thai and other Asian manufacturers will have a harder time competing against Japanese goods sold elsewhere, especially in the United States.
A weakening currency makes that country's products less expensive abroad. 
But the advantage that South Korea and other Asian countries gained with their devaluations has been reduced by the 18 percent fall in the yen since last July, when the Asian crisis began.
"The competitive edge that South Korea has obtained is minimal," said Desmond Lachman, the head of emerging-markets research at Salomon Smith Barney. 
And, he said, "If the yen slides toward 150 we can be sure we are going to have real regional currency turmoil."
He said that one important unknown was how the Chinese would react to the yen's weakness. 
The Chinese said they would not devalue in the wake of the Asian devaluations. 
But Mr. Lachman said that he believed China's restraint was based on the assumption that the yen would remain relatively stable and not damage China's competitiveness. 
A Chinese devaluation now could set off another round of devaluations.
The yen's latest decline came after Koji Tanami, Japan's Vice Finance Minister, indicated that finance ministers in the Group of Seven industrialized nations were not going to discuss the yen's problems in Paris today and tomorrow. 
In addition, Mr. Tanami said it was unlikely that the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada would take action to support the yen.
"The main topic of the meeting will be Russia," he said.
In late trading in New York, the dollar cost 140.71 yen, up from 139.75 Friday. 
The dollar also rallied against the German mark, rising to 1.7794 marks from 1.7745.
In contrast to its strength against the yen, the dollar had been falling in value against the mark since April.
"There is not a whole lot the G-7 can do for the yen without the Japanese Government providing the policy for support," Mr. Lachman said. 
Even a surprising round of central bank intervention to support the yen after these comments would only have a temporary impact if Japan's policies are not changed.
Despite a succession of fiscal stimulus programs, the Japanese Government has not yet done enough to stimulate the economy or to deal with the mountain of bad loans that is undermining its banking system, said Jeremy Fand, senior foreign exchange strategist at BankBoston.
"Fundamentally, there is no reason why the yen should strengthen," said Mr. Fand, who is forecasting that the dollar could strengthen to 180 yen in the next 12 months. 
But he also said that the yen had fallen so much recently that it might be in line for a sharp rebound in the near term before resuming its decline.
The impact of the dollar's strength was also highlighted yesterday in a report by the Bank for International Settlements, which coordinates the activities of the world's central banks. 
The bank said the dollar was overvalued by 33 percent against the yen and 21 percent against the mark, which makes American exports less competitive and increases the likelihood that the American trade deficit will keep growing.

file: THE MARKETS_ Market Place_As Yen Slides, U.S. Renews Pressure on Japan.txt
text:
ï»¿
A week after the Clinton Administration signed off on a multibillion-dollar intervention in the currency markets to support the Japanese yen, American authorities stepped up pressure on the Japanese Government today to make good on its promises of economic reform and avoid another decline in the yen's value.
"The steps we can take -- currency intervention -- can have an effect, but they can have an effect primarily through what they signal," Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence H. Summers told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee today, hours after returning from a trip to Japan and Indonesia. 
"What is crucial is the pace of action," he said.
So far, investors seem to have been unimpressed with the speed of Japan's efforts to clean up $600 billion in bad bank debts, spur the economy and accelerate the deregulation of its financial markets. 
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told President Clinton last week that he would accelerate those efforts, a promise that led to the joint intervention in the currency markets last Wednesday. 
That sent the yen's value up sharply, though briefly -- it lingered at a rate around 136 to the dollar for a day or so.
But the yen has slipped ever since, as Japanese leaders reverted to talking about the difficulties inherent in moving quickly. 
Late today, the yen settled in New York trading at 141.25 to the dollar, compared with 139.15 on Tuesday, and not far below the level when the United States agreed to step in.
Investors appeared to interpret Mr. Summers's comments as suggesting that Washington would not intervene again any time soon. 
But they have been burned once before: When Mr. Summers's boss, Secretary of the Treasury Robert E. Rubin, told Congress earlier this month that interventions only worked temporarily, traders saw that as a green light to bet against the Japanese currency. 
Their rush to sell yen at that time gave Mr. Rubin an opportunity to take the markets by surprise.
Today, Mr. Summers also told the Senate committee he had received additional assurances from Chinese officials that they were "committed to maintain exchange-rate stabilityI," despite growing pressure to devalue their currency, the yuan.
United States officials fear that a devaluation, while intended to keep Chinese exports competitively priced with the goods of other Asian nations, would greatly worsen the Asian financial crisis -- setting off another round of currency devaluations.
President Clinton is expected to raise these matters directly when he meets with Chinese leaders in Beijing this weekend. 
But already the Administration is praising China for its restraint, and the Chinese are hoping to parlay their resolve not to devalue into some kind of diplomatic advantage.
Mr. Summers said further today that the International Monetary Fund was on the verge of another economic agreement with Indonesia -- its fourth, but the first since President Suharto's resignation. 
While details of the accord are skimpy, it will enable the I.M.F. to resume aid to Jakarta at a time when economic projections for the country are growing considerably more dire.
The country is suffering what United States officials call a food crisis, with increasing reports of malnutrition in outlying islands, after years in which Indonesia boasted of self-sufficiency in food production. 
The number of Indonesians living below the poverty line may increase by almost 80 million this year, or nearly 40 percent of the population, the World Bank warned several days ago.
American officials fear that such distress would worsen attacks on ethnic Chinese in Indonesia.
Mr. Summers made an oblique reference to such attacks today. 
He said that when he met with Indonesia's new President, B. J. Habibie, in Jakarta on Monday, he told him "it is essential that all of Indonesia's people, rich and poor alike, enjoy a sense of security that their homes, their businesses and their futures in the country are secure."
The focus of Mr. Summers's testimony today, though, was on Japan, and he repeated the theme that the Japanese had only a brief "window of opportunity" to act.
But in private, many at the Treasury and the White House are skeptical about how much Japanese leaders will be able to deliver before Prime Minister Hashimoto visits Washington on July 22 -- a visit that is intended in part to keep pressure on Japan and in part to appease it after Mr. Clinton's extended visit to China, which begins in Xian on Thursday.
"The situation in Japan is a source of very considerable concern," Mr. Summers said today. 
"Growth has turned negative; the banking system is increasingly stressed. 
While the passage last week of a significant stimulus package is a welcome step, we remain very concerned about Japan's economic and financial situation."
"This is a pivotal moment for Asia and the global economy," he added. 
The weakness in Japan is now having a clear impact on the other troubled economies in Asia."

file: THE MARKETS_ Market Place_By anyother name, could China.com be so confident_.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN the helium-filled world of Internet investing, a lot can ride on a new company's name. 
When that name is China.com, you might reasonably assume its stock would float on gossamer wings.
After all, the China.com Corporation combines two of the decade's hottest investment concepts -- China and the Internet -- in a single stock offering. 
While both have lost a bit of their luster among investors in recent weeks, China.com seems convinced that putting them together will prove irresistible.
The company, based in Hong Kong, plans to raise $56.3 million through an initial public offering on the Nasdaq stock market in two weeks. 
It began its road show for investors, at a lavish lunch here yesterday, with a familiar mixture of intoxicating predictions and fuzzy details.
"We believe we have presented one of the most exciting investment opportunities in Asia," said Peter Yip, the vice chairman and chief executive of China.com. 
"No other company has our integrated approach."
He noted that the number of Internet users in China was projected to rise from 2.4 million in 1998 to 16.1 million in 2003, a compound annual growth rate of 46 percent. 
As the first public company to tap that vast market, Mr. Yip believes, China.com will be one of the cyberheavyweights of Asia.
It is a tantalizing prospect -- one that lured America Online to buy 10 percent of China.com for $25 million earlier this month.
Executives at China.com's investment bank, Lehman Brothers, said the offering was already oversubscribed. 
And analysts predicted that China.com would take off like a rocket after the shares begin trading.
"The company has a great name," said Kaushik Shridharani, a media analyst at Salomon Smith Barney here. 
"That will drive investor enthusiasm for the stock, because most investors don't delve into the details."
The details in China.com's case are eye-opening. 
Despite its all-encompassing name, China.com does most of its business in Hong Kong, where it operates an Internet portal service called hongkong.com, an Internet advertising service and a Web design and consulting business.
China.com's Hong Kong portal -- and a similar one on Taiwan -- offer a menu of services, from English- and Chinese-language news and information to E-mail, search engines and message boards. 
The company does operate a portal called china.com, which is aimed at users in mainland China, but technology executives said it generated little traffic. 
In a recent ranking of Web sites conducted by the Chinese Government, it placed 17th, behind destinations like Sinanet and Sohu.
"Given all the P.R. they've created, they really should be generating more traffic," said Hanson Cheah, the executive director of Asia Tech Ventures, a venture capital firm here that specializes in Internet companies.
Kenneth Farrall, an expert on the Internet in China who runs a consulting firm in New York, said: "China.com has never been a factor in the Internet business in China. 
It doesn't register on the radar screen."
China.com said yesterday that it had 400,000 registered users of its three main portals. 
The company said it recorded one million "page views" a day, and would double that by year's end.
Peter Hamilton, the chief operating officer of China.com, acknowledged in an interview that the number of users "doesn't satisfy our internal objectives."
But he added, "We're satisfied with the growth rate."
Mr. Hamilton said the company's critics were placing too much emphasis on its relatively low traffic. 
He said the company could expand its reach through its regional advertising service, 24/ 7, which places ads on Web sites in 11 Asian and Pacific Rim countries, from Japan to Australia.
"If you build a business based solely on China, you're going to have a long and hungry wait for ad revenue," he said.
Like most fledgling Internet companies, China.com has never made money. 
In 1998, it reported losses of $11 million on revenue of $3.4 million. 
More than three-quarters of its sales come from its Web consulting business. 
And China.com said it would not turn a profit until 2001.
Despite its meager revenues, China.com has been able to attract an impressive array of United States technology companies as partners. 
They include Netscape Communications, Bay Networks, Sun Microsystems, Pointcast, and most recently, America Online. 
But the critics note that most of these partnerships have fizzled.
"Have any of China.com's ventures become real businesses?"
Mr. Cheah asked. 
"As far as I can tell, none."
Perhaps China.com's most sensitive relationship is with Xinhua, China's official news agency. 
Xinhua is one of the original investors and still owns a 13.6 percent stake. 
In addition to supplying China.com with mainland news, Xinhua edits news from Reuters and Agence France-Presse that is distributed on the company's Chinese site -- deleting references to Taiwan and Tibet.
Mr. Yip said it was an honor to work with Xinhua, adding, "As we all know, the Internet business in China is highly regulated."
For all the questions about its business, China.com has a couple of likely advantages. 
It is the first China-focused Internet company to go public, and it is doing so at a time when analysts say investors in the United States are becoming jaded by the constant stream of Silicon Valley start-ups. 
Moreover, it is entering the market at a time when other high-profile Chinese companies are stepping out. 
The China National Petroleum Corporation, the country's biggest oil company, and China Unicom, a rival to the dominant China Telecom, are both planning major share offerings.
With potential investors overflowing a hotel ballroom in Hong Kong yesterday, the buzz surrounding China.com was unmistakable. 
Mr. Shridharani said such interest was bound to result in disappointment.
"To the extent that expectations are shaped by what's going on in the States, investors are going to be disappointed," he said. 
"This company is going to grow fast, but not on a scale that will excite investors."Â Â Â Â Â Â

text:

THE fever over Asian Internet stocks came close to delirium here yesterday as tens of thousands of Hong Kong residents besieged local banks to buy shares in the stock offering of Tom.com, a one-month-old Chinese-language Internet service.
By the time the offering expired at midday, it had been oversubscribed more than 1,000 times, putting Tom .com on track to be the most sought-after initial public offering in Hong Kong history. 
The last such stock mania occurred in May 1997 when Beijing Enterprises, a mainland Chinese company known as a red chip, issued shares amid a wave of euphoria over the return of Hong Kong to China.
A tiny Internet start-up and a sprawling state-controlled conglomerate would seem to have little in common. 
But market watchers here were struck by the parallels.
"It's very reminiscent of the red chip craze in 1997," said David Webb, the editor of Webb-site.com, a site that tracks stock offerings. 
"We've got a huge speculative frenzy in a single category of stocks."
At a branch of HSBC in Kowloon, nearly 50,000 people lined up after dawn to submit forms. 
As the noon deadline approached, the crowd became restive and 100 police officers were summoned to keep order.
Tom.com and Beijing Enterprises have something else in common: Investors are less interested in their business than in the perceived value of their political connections. 
Beijing Enterprises is controlled by the Beijing municipal government; Tom .com is majority owned by the two flagship companies of Li Ka-shing, a Hong Kong billionaire who is almost as well known for his ties to Beijing as for his business acumen.
Among the minority investors in Tom.com is Pacific Century Cyberworks, an Internet firm controlled by Mr. Li's son, Richard Li. 
Pacific Century is negotiating to take over Hong Kong's main telephone company, Cable and Wireless HKT, and its shares have also rocketed in recent weeks.
"I bought the stock only because of Li Ka-shing; I believe in the Li dynasty," said C. M. Law, 37, a homemaker who is one of the more than a million applicants. 
"I don't really know what kind of business they're in. 
I know it is some sort of technology company, like Amazon.com."
Tom.com is not an online bookseller like Amazon.com. 
But that may be one of the few businesses it does not plan to enter, judging from the company's 200-page prospectus, printed in Chinese and English. 
It aims to be "the leading multilingual China-related new-media mega-portal," with Web sites in cities with big Chinese populations, like Singapore; San Francisco; Sydney, Australia, and Vancouver, British Columbia.
At the moment, though, Tom.com operates a single Web site that broadcasts programming from a Hong Kong radio station. 
For 1999, the company reported losses of $10.3 million on sales of $6.7 million. 
The company only acquired its catchy three-letter domain name in December, buying it from a Nevada company, Vortexx, for $2.5 million and stock options.
"There's not very much there, frankly," Mr. Webb said. 
"They seem to be promoting 'push' technology, which I thought went out with Pointcast."
Still, its operations seem beside the point. 
After slogging through more than two years of economic misery, Hong Kong residents have recovered their appetite for speculation. 
That coincides with the emergence of Internet start-ups like Tom.com and Pacific Century Cyberworks. 
Analysts said the speculative surge could just as well have been set off by a rally in property prices.
"Hong Kong adjusts instantly to any change in the market," said William H. Overholt, the head of Asian research at Nomura International. 
"This is a population that has survived by being fast on its feet."
The overwhelming response will allow Tom.com to price its stock at the high end of its offering range, though still only 23 cents a share. 
The company will issue 428 million shares, plus a possible extra allotment of 64.2 million shares, so it could raise a total of about $113 million. 
The stock is to begin trading on Hong Kong's new technology exchange on March 1, and analysts expect it to rise tenfold the first day.
In an interview with Dow Jones Newswires, the chief executive of Tom.com, Carl Chang, said, "We're going to build the Time Warner of China, only using the Internet as a starting point."

text:

MAYBE it depends which side of the Pacific you're on.
In the days since China and the United States signed a deal that may lead to Chinese admission into the World Trade Organization, the Chinese stock market has made small gains, with indexes of mainland stocks up about 1 percent. 
Hong Kong stocks did better, with the leading index of such shares up 3.6 percent since Friday.
But most of the relatively small number of Chinese stocks traded on major American stock markets have risen sharply. 
In some cases they have gone absolutely berserk. 
Suddenly, any stock with China in its name seems to have willing buyers.
The biggest gains have gone to stocks that previously had been of little interest to American investors. 
By contrast, China Telecom (Hong Kong), which provides cellular telephone services in China and has been an institutional favorite in America, rose on Monday and Tuesday but fell $5.9375, to $86.5625, yesterday, and is up just 2 percent for the week.
But such languid performance is more than offset by other stocks that have skyrocketed. 
A list of nine stocks -- all traded on the New York Stock Exchange or Nasdaq and all with the word "China" in their names -- shows increases of at least 60 percent for six of the nine since Friday. 
Investors who put an equal amount of money into each of the stocks on Friday -- the last trading day before the W.T.O. agreement was announced -- would have more than quadrupled their money by yesterday's close.
The most amazing move came in the shares of China Prosperity International Holdings, a company that does property renovations in China -- but that has also been talking about doing something related to the Internet.
China Prosperity was once something of a hot stock, moving as high as $37 a share in Nasdaq trading in 1996 -- adjusted for a later reverse split. 
But it had fallen out of investors favor, and by Monday was trading at $1 a share.
Then on Tuesday, the stock leaped to $11.06, trading as high as $14, and volume rose to 521,100 shares, or more than had traded in the previous year. 
That however, was just the prelude. 
Yesterday, volume totaled 4.4 million shares, or more than the total volume in this country since the company went public in 1995. 
The price leaped as high as $80, then began to slide before ending at $32.0625.
There was no announcement from the company, but the same could not be said for another suddenly highflier. 
China Resources Development, a distributor of natural rubber, reported that its losses were growing. 
It added that it had no explanation for the stock's movement in Nasdaq small-cap trading.
That stock jumped $19, to $25 a share, in trading yesterday, on volume of 906,800 shares. 
That volume is nearly twice the total number of shares outstanding.
Another amazing performance was turned in by the Dransfield China Paper Corporation, which rarely trades on Nasdaq. 
During October, there were only two days when shares in the company, which distributes paper products and is building pulp mills in China, were traded. 
The price then was $1 a share. 
It fell to 43.75 cents on Monday, and then did not trade Tuesday.
But yesterday, with anything named China looking hot, 1.3 million shares were traded -- more than triple the total volume traded since the company was listed on Nasdaq in 1997 -- and the price rose as high as $29 before closing at $12.
China.com, a company based in Hong Kong that provides a portal for Chinese users of the Internet, leaped from $58 on Friday to a close of $105 yesterday, trading as high as $137. 
It had gone public, at $20 a share, in July.
Even China Tire, a company that makes car and truck tires, got in on the action. 
Since Friday, it is up 77 percent, to $10.625.
It is not easy to explain such moves based on expectations of what will happen if China is successful in entering the World Trade Organization, something that could yet be derailed by Congressional opposition. 
Changes in the Chinese economy will arrive over a period of years, and the opening of the economy to competition from foreign companies may damage some Chinese businesses even as others are helped.
But there seems to have been little in the way of such analysis regarding many of the stocks that were moving yesterday. 
Instead, Internet chat rooms were full of comments about how certain stocks were sure to keep moving because there were relatively few shares available for trading. 
Traders were chasing performance, and in the process they were creating it.
