file: THE MEDIA BUSINESS_ ADVERTISING_China_s Censor Is Customer No. 1.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Saatchi & Saatchi set out to create a Chinese television commercial for Daktarin, an athlete's foot medication made by a unit of Johnson & Johnson, the advertising firm faced a predicament. 
Chinese government regulations prohibit advertisements from showing patients or symptoms -- critical elements for a pharmaceutical commercial.
Saatchi & Saatchi eventually resolved the problem by using weeds as a visual analogy for a foot fungus. 
That satisfied the regulators, but frustrated the ad agency.
"Creatively, we could be 10 times better than now if it wasn't for the regulations," lamented Philip Li, executive creative director for Saatchi & Saatchi's Beijing office.
Rigid government control, however, is the price to enter one of the world's fastest-growing advertising markets. 
Mr. Li said he had often had to rework commercials to address the objections of Chinese censors -- or to avoid running afoul of them in the first place. 
"The regulations are always in the back of your mind," he said.
Advertising is just as problematic for the government. 
In China's march from a centrally planned economy to a market economy, officials have promoted advertising as an accelerator of economic development and welcomed it as a way to supplant government subsidies for many television stations and periodicals. 
On the other hand, the government has also criticized advertising as a conduit for both fraud and unwelcome foreign ideas.
"They will try to be as lenient as possible, but whenever anything touches cultural values or political stabilityI, it is something they have to crush right away," said Louisa Ha, president of Dr. Ad Marketing International, a consulting firm based in the United States that focuses on China.
Coca-Cola, for example, recently withdrew a multimillion-dollar campaign for its Sprite soda because the ads featured a popular Taiwanese singer, A-Mei, who had sung Taiwan's national anthem at the inauguration of President Chen Shui-bian of Taiwan. 
China regards Taiwan as a renegade province.
"If they allowed her to be on the commercial, they would be allowing dissidence," Dr. Ha said. 
"Politics is above everything else in this country's agenda, whatever economic interests are sacrificed."
Those interests are not insignificant. 
In the 21 years since a Shanghai station showed China's first television commercial, for a Chinese tonic wine, advertising spending in China has soared from zero to more than $7 billion, and by some estimates is as high as $12 billion. 
The range results from discrepancies between published rates and discounted rates that advertisers are actually charged, coupled with the weakness of China's accounting system.
While that is a fraction of the $165 billion spent on advertising in the United States last year, China is one of the world's fastest-growing markets. 
It has surpassed South Korea to become Asia's second-largest market behind Japan.
As advertising has mushroomed, so has the government's determination to keep it under control. 
In a country where the media are monitored carefully for their political and social influence, advertising is considered a privilege bestowed by the government and not a commercial extension of the right of free speech.
In adjusting this privilege, the government has updated its advertising rules more than 30 times in the last six years.
The guidelines range from vague principles, like insisting that advertisements not "jeopardize the social order," to specific prohibitions, like those that forbid the use of state symbols like the flag or national anthem. 
Companies are also not allowed to use superlative terms like "best" or compare their products with those of competitors.
The prohibitions have scuttled ads for such products as the Bristol-Myers Squibb painkiller Bufferin, which claimed to be "the best," and Colgate's diamond-headed toothbrush, which the company asserted was superior to traditional rectangular toothbrushes. 
However, Budweiser's slogan that it is "America's favorite beer" was allowed after its brewer, St. Louis-based Anheuser-Busch, provided statistical evidence to support the claim.
While the regulations may seem severe, the government considers them a necessary consumer-protection measure in a country where soaps have claimed to help people lose weight and tonics have promised to make people smarter. 
In the United States, consumer sophistication backed by government regulations has convinced most advertisers that it is in their own best interest to shun exaggerated claims and outright falsehoods in advertising.
"Self-regulation is the hallmark of maturity in an advertising industry," said Hong Cheng, a professor of communications at Bradley University in Peoria, Ill. 
"This kind of system is still in the making in China. 
That is why the government has to act as a Big Brother."
Since the regulations went into effect, the government said it had found 160,000 examples of false or misleading advertisements and had imposed penalties of more than $54 million. 
The number of "advertising malpractice" cases handled by the authorities rose 36 percent last year, led by ads for drugs, medical services and food.
These included products called Jiannan Capsules (which translates as Healthy Male Capsules) and Alaska Shengmin Lixiong Platinum (Alaska Life Strength Chest Platinum). 
Several of the cited products trade on the Chinese translation of Viagra, the impotence treatment, which is not trademarked in China. 
The government did not identify the manufacturers.
"The shadow of the regulations hangs over the advertising creative process from beginning to end," said Louis Wong, president of Beijing-based Megacom Advertising, who estimates that half of his commercials have to be modified during the approval process. 
"It is annoying, but this is reality."
Television commercials, which receive the greatest scrutiny because of their wide viewership, must be submitted to each regional office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce before being shown. 
Many companies submit their storyboards and script before filming just as a precaution.
The approval process is subjective and fragmented, with some regional offices approving commercials that other offices reject. 
A shampoo commercial that showed a glimpse of a bather's shoulder was accepted in cosmopolitan Shanghai, for example, but banned in a conservative neighboring province. 
Other commercials that received storyboard approval were rejected after the final edit. 
Some commercials are censored after they go on the air.
Commercials that violate standards can sometimes be salvaged by rewriting the script or making other adjustments, but some are banned.
"Most of our problems are pharmaceuticals and things related to underwear," Mr. Wong said. 
"The problem is often over-exaggeration of a product, or that it goes against the general moral standards of the Chinese population."
Pharmaceuticals face the strictest regulations. 
That industry, the largest spender in advertising, faces reviews by public health officials as well as advertising regulators. 
And, because of a history of exaggerated claims for medicines, advertisers in China are not allowed to show patients, children or symptoms. 
Nor can they associate products with the names of doctors or hospitals.
Sexual modesty is also emphasized by the government. 
Models must be covered at least 15 centimeters (5.9 inches) down from their necks and 15 centimeters up from their knees, which can be inconvenient for companies trying to sell shampoo or underwear.
"If you are the marketer for the underwear, you want to demonstrate that a piece of underwear fits well," said Mr. Wong, whose firm is working on an account for Embroform, a Hong Kong underwear company. 
"But if you just featured a face of a woman up to the shoulders, then what is the point of an underwear commercial?"
His firm is looking into using computer animation for the commercial, hoping in that way to avoid the fate of a previous ad that was censored because authorities thought a model's miniskirt was too short.
Foreign manufacturers are not the only advertisers who have run into trouble. 
The government itself has on occasion run afoul of the censors. 
A commercial advocating condom use to avoid AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases was pulled late last year, two days after it first appeared, when the State Administration for Industry and Commerce decided it was too risque
Regulations not only restrict the content of advertisements, but the structure of the industry. 
China has 50,000 advertising firms employing almost half a million people, an average of just under 10 people a company. 
To protect domestic agencies from foreign competition and to limit foreign cultural influence, multinational advertising agencies are required to set up joint ventures and are limited in their equity. 
Foreign advertising executives said they expect China to relax or eliminate that requirement if the country is admitted to the World Trade Organization.
While China's advertising market is experiencing surging revenue growth, creative growth is unremarkable as a consequence of all the restrictions.
"If you look at all the award-winning commercials in the Cannes festivals, I can bet 80 percent could not be in China because of the content," Mr. Wong said. 
It's frustrating, he said, but he and others knew to expect it when they walked into China.
"If you want fun and creative," Mr. Li concurred, "that's not China."

file: The Nation_ Agony of Victory_America Finds It_s Lonely At the Top.txt
text:
ï»¿
IT is impossible to pinpoint the moment when America's successes in the 1990's moved from a topic of grudging admiration around the world to a constant source of annoyance at Washington's triumphalism to a rationale for mistrust and resistance.
Perhaps the clincher was envy over the Dow's dramatic ascent from a little over 2,000 at the start of the decade to a little over 11,000 this year. 
Maybe it was the dawning realization that people around the globe are all flicking on the same Windows operating system in the morning, on their way to navigating an Internet dominated by American innovations and businesses and driven by Intel inside everything. 
Maybe it was when the United States, in the wake of the Asian economic crisis, began offering tutorials on American-style capitalism, and insisting that the world's financial architecture be rebuilt to American building codes.
But surely the capstone was Kosovo. 
Whether Washington intended this outcome or not, the war demonstrated to allies and potential adversaries alike how much more formidable American military technology has become since the Persian Gulf war. 
Europeans got a rude awakening when they learned that the gap between the United States' capability and their own had so widened that they now have to rethink their we'll-build-it-on-the-Continent mentality.
And nothing sent a greater chill through the Kremlin and the Chinese leaders' compound next to the Forbidden City than the image of those B-2 bombers lazily lifting into the air over Missouri at midday, flying an 11,000-mile, 32-hour mission to drop laser-guided weapons over Belgrade -- and getting back in time for dinner the next evening. 
Feeling the need to stake out some ground, Moscow hastily flew a ragtag force into Kosovo, and Beijing boasted last week that it had the neutron bomb -- don't-mess-with-us messages that undercut the Clinton Administration's talk of strategic partnerships with old cold war adversaries.
Of course, the world looks very different to Americans, who have already moved beyond the Kosovo war. 
In the national self-image, America's pillars of global power -- unparalleled financial clout, unmatched technological prowess and unchallenged military reach -- are separate entities, bits of a far more fragile mosaic. 
Sure, times are good, but Americans don't feel particularly powerful now, even with the Russians broke, the Chinese consumed with unemployment and slowing growth, and the Japanese unable to get their breath back.
But talk to Thai politicians stewingover what they view as an American conspiracy to keep their candidate from running the World Trade Organization, or scan the People's Daily, or listen to talk radio in Toronto, and it becomes clear that America's triple threat -- the dollar, the Pentium III chip and the B-2 -- is now also its biggest diplomatic challenge. 
It may be a case of being too powerful for one's own good.
OR as Michael Mandelbaum, a professor at Johns Hopkins University, puts it, "If you are the 800-pound gorilla, you're concentrating on your bananas and everyone else is concentrating on you."
Of course, the reactions differ dramatically when America talks to friends like the Western Europeans and to potentially hostile powers. 
Nonetheless, officials at the State Department, the Treasury and the Pentagon, who agree on precious little, all say fear of America's widening lead has become the subtext of nearly every major conversation they hold around the world.
It underlies Europe's near-panic over the precipitous fall of the euro, the new currency meant to represent a more economically powerful Europe. 
And it underlies Russia's perpetual negotiations to avoid national default, in which Moscow fights every step of the way as the International Monetary Fund -- synonymous with Washington in the Russian view -- demands economic reforms in return for aid.
"What we need is a policy of strategic reassurance," a Clinton Administration official lamented, "a way of demonstrating that not only is this power benign, but that it isn't a zero-sum game."
BUT turning that desire into policy isn't easy. 
The new Treasury Secretary, Lawrence H. Summers, warns against trying to fix the world, noting that "we cannot want prosperity and reform in any country more than its people do."
"It's our challenge," he says, "to succeed as the first outward-looking, non-imperialist, continental superpower."
The unspoken comparison is with the old Soviet Union, which was continental but expansionist and the continental but inward-looking China.
From other capitals, though, Washington doesn't look so benign. 
Its push for more open markets around the world is often viewed as nice ideological justification for speeding the pace at which more efficient American companies can drive their foreign competition into the ground. 
Meanwhile, the White House jumps when American companies complain that low-cost imports are hurting American workers: In the past two weeks alone, Washington has announced restrictions on cheap steel from Russia and Brazil and cheap lamb from Australia and New Zealand. 
No matter how it defends such moves as legal responses to "dumping," from overseas it looks more like protectionism.
On top of that is puzzlement over the deliberately vague "Clinton Doctrine."
It doesn't get much press in the United States, but everywhere else there is speculation over how far the Americans might extend the principles of Kosovo, intervening inside other nations' borders to enforce "international values" of humanitarian treatment or human rights. 
Russia looks at Kosovo and worries about Chechnya; China looks at it and worries about Tibet and Taiwan.
An intense decade of global competition and technological innovation has only heightened the contrast between America's view of its power and the very different view held by the rest of the world.
Europeans struggling with 12 percent unemployment and Japanese trying to emerge from a lost decade look at America's surging markets and employment rolls and see a train speeding by so fast that it looks uncatchable. 
When Americans look at the same facts, many get as queasy as Alan Greenspan, wondering how long the boom can last. 
(That insecurity, some economists think, has actually helped spur America's growth, sustaining the pressure for cost-cutting and productivity gains.)
When foreign companies look at the pace of American technological development, they see a gap far greater than a decade ago. 
But American corporate executives look over their shoulders and worry. 
"You sense quite the opposite of triumphalism from c.e.o.'s," said Jeffrey Garten, the dean of the Yale School of Management. 
"They feel they are in a brutally competitive world, and they think they are in a race for their lives."
The developing world holds a similar fear. 
The United Nations Development Program issued a report last week arguing that the digital divide is widening faster than ever. 
Twenty-six percent of Americans use the World Wide Web, it said, compared to 3 percent of Russians and a tiny fraction of a percent of the population of South Asia. 
The United States has more computers than the rest of the world combined. 
In other words, the faster rich nations log on, the further they pull ahead of countries that aren't even plugged in. 
But the closest the report came to advocating a solution was a 1-cent tax on long E-mails, with the revenue earmarked for connecting up the rest of the world.
The perception gap grows whenever the subject turns to the lessons of Kosovo and American military power. 
Washington looks back at the events of the spring and wipes its brow, relieved that it got through with negligible casualties and no ground troops. 
It sees a truly multinational mission: After all, there was Prime Minister Tony Blair, feeling his oats, arguing for ground troops.
The European allies emerged with a different view: The war was won with American air power that homegrown military technology cannot match. 
Meeting last week in Washington to review the war, European defense contractors and officials concluded that trans-Atlantic mergers of defense contractors -- something both Europe and America have long resisted -- are now inevitable.
The Chinese saw Kosovo through another lens. 
When Thomas R. Pickering, the Under Secretary of State, went to Beijing last month to explain the series of mistakes that led to the accidental bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade, a senior Chinese official said China believed that the United States was involved in Kosovo simply to test its latest armaments, according to American officials who have reviewed transcripts of the conversation.
"I don't think that we appreciate how this integration of financial, military and technological power looks from the outside," said Gerrit Gong, the director of Asian studies at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. 
"It makes random, unconnected events seem like part of a plan for America to hog the road."
THIS may be a problem without a solution. 
Perhaps it could be eased with a little less talk of America as the "indispensable nation" -- Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright's phrase -- and a little more attention to sharing technology and the wealth it creates.
That, however, is not exactly the mood that Congress is in. 
Nor is the Administration so inclined; it is trying to get through its last 18 months with no more ethnic wars, no more economic collapses around the globe and no abrupt end to the age of prosperity.
"Economic progress is a Faustian bargain," concludes Mr. Mandelbaum. "You gain a lot, you pay a price. 
That's what international politics is all about."

text:
ï»¿
WHEN investigators were trying to find out who might have given sensitive weapons secrets to China, they paid special attention to Wen Ho Lee in part because of his Chinese ancestry. 
But last week, when the Taiwanese-born American scientist pleaded guilty only to downloading sensitive information onto an insecure computer and prosecutors conceded they had no further case to make against him in open court, the quick association of Mr. Lee's ethnic origins with suspicions about his loyalty seemed mostly an embarrassment for the government.
Accusations of "racial profiling" in Mr. Lee's case didn't just offer a new example of the historic tension in America between concerns about national security and civil liberties principles. 
There were also practical arguments, offered by experts on counterintelligence, against zeroing in early on an espionage suspect primarily on the basis of ethnicity.
To be sure, some Justice Department investigators felt last week that they were the ones who had been treated unfairly. 
To them, it was thoroughly legitimate to consider Mr. Lee's ethnic background, among several other factors, in forming suspicions that he might have helped Beijing. 
It was especially logical, they said, because the Chinese government has a well-documented history of using ethnic Chinese in other countries to help gather intelligence.
Those investigators said they are obliged to make their best effort to narrow the list of suspects when trying to determine the source of a leak of information and should not be hampered by notions that to do so might offend some group.
But many experts are now saying that such an approach is not only inherently offensive but also potentially counterproductive.
Experts on espionage have long accepted that using factors like ethnicity carries a risk of reprising historically corrosive assertions that some Americans have a dual loyalty based on their heritage.
For many years, it was fear of that very accusation that lay behind an Israeli government policy of not using American Jews to gather intelligence in the United States. 
When Jonathan Pollard, an American Jew and civilian analyst for the Navy, was arrested in 1987 on charges of spying for Israel, the shock was all the greater for that reason, and the Israeli government made a point of insisting that the intelligence unit that recruited Mr. Pollard had been a renegade outfit.
Phillip B. Heymann, a Harvard law professor who served as the deputy attorney general in the early Clinton years, said that using a suspect's heritage is not only offensive to concepts of civil rights but is also often a lazy form of stereotyping that can do more to hamper a counterintelligence investigation than help it. 
"At the early stage of an investigation, you have to identify a relatively limited number of suspects and do so in a relatively inexpensive way," he said in an interview. 
"And then you can work harder on that smaller group."
Mr. Heymann, who oversaw the Justice Department's counterintelligence operations, said that the most important factor in narrowing a list of suspects is determining who had access to the information and motive to provide it to a foreign power.
"Motivation and opportunity are the two things you look for," he said. 
"You might look at who had unusual debts, who is bitter and angry, who has the opportunity to make contact with the country that received the material."
Ethnicity, he said, can serve as a misleading surrogate for those factors. 
"What you're getting out of knowing that Wen Ho Lee is Chinese is an extremely crude estimate of the larger list of factors about motive and opportunity. 
It comes very cheap but it isn't nearly as probative as the others.
"Ethnicity turns out to be a very difficult factor to use properly," he said. 
"There are so many steps between the initial observation of someone's ethnicity and making an intelligent use of it that it's really not worth using. 
And if you use it to focus too quickly on a narrow category of people, you're giving a pass to other people in other categories."
John L. Martin, who supervised the Justice Department's investigation and prosecution of espionage cases for 26 years until 1997, said in an interview that "what should lead a good investigator are the facts and not necessarily the ethnicity of anybody in the pool of suspects."
Mr. Martin now heads the Washington office of the OSO Group Ltd., an international investigative company. 
He said that most spies of recent vintage were mercenaries, people who chose to help foreign governments for money. 
"You would be wasting your resources if you pursued a potential suspect largely on the basis of ethnicity and not all the underlying facts," he said.
In the case of Mr. Lee, he said, it seemed that his Chinese heritage had increased suspicion of him because he had traveled to China and had met with Chinese government scientists in the United States. 
"But it appears a flaw in the Wen Ho Lee case was that there were non-Chinese scientists who made some of the same trips and had some of the same contacts" but were not investigated as closely, he said.
Another feature of the Lee case that strongly suggests that investigators were too quick to rely on Mr. Lee's ethnic heritage was that in the end they weren't sure which foreign country he might have been motivated to help. 
Some investigators suspected China, but because Mr. Lee had been born in Taiwan, others thought it might have been that country, which is the People's Republic of China's most resolute foe.
It may never be fully clear to the public just how much Mr. Lee's ethnicity was a factor in singling him out because the plea agreement that ended the case also halted an inquiry on that matter by the federal judge hearing the case. 
But the issue has already had other consequences. 
Last week, lawyers for several Muslims charged in connection with the plot to bomb two United States embassies in Africa in 1998 said they would use the Lee case to argue that the prosecutors had unfairly singled out their clients on the basis of their religion.
And just as the "racial profiling" of minorities for special suspicion of involvement in crime can backfire on law enforcement by arousing a whole community's resentment, there was evidence that the Wen Ho Lee case may have actually cost American security research some valuable talent. 
Chinese-American civil rights groups said that Chinese-Americans are now greatly reluctant to take government positions at the national laboratories.

file: The Nonproliferation Treaty Bares Its Toothlessness.txt
text:
ï»¿
ONLY a few months ago North Korea seemed like a pathbreaking example of how the world's great powers can set aside other differences to make sure that fanatical leaders and nuclear bombs are kept apart. 
Faced with overwhelming evidence that the hard-line Communist regime of Kim Il Sung was building a bomb, the United States harnessed the West, and then Russia and China, to stop the project from turning into a nightmare. 
For most of last year, it looked like the strategy was working.
Beneath his usual cloud of defiant oratory, the 80-year old Mr. Kim finally agreed to live up to his obligations under the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty. 
He allowed international inspectors to visit the mysterious nuclear site called Yongbyon. 
His motives seemed clear. 
He sought the trade and investment he desperately needs, especially now that there are reports of food riots and troops stand on rail-side coal piles to keep the residents from stealing enough to heat their homes.
On Friday, though, it was Washington's seeming success that turned to coal -- and along with it, much of the world's confidence in the workability of the treaty that 153 nations have signed. 
In an unnerving and perhaps self-destructive act of defiance, North Korea became the first nation ever to renounce the treaty, barring the door completely to international inspectors who were on the scent of a secret cache of plutonium. 
Vice Foreign Minister Kang Sok Ju declared that the North had signed the accord in 1985 to reduce what he termed a nuclear threat from South Korea and the United States, and said "We are now withdrawing from it because it is being abused to destroy our republic."
Surprised and more than a little scared, Japan and South Korea denounced the action as destabilizing and dangerous. 
At the same time, though, there were second thoughts about whether the safeguards designed 25 years ago, in an age of superpower patrons for countries like North Korea, still have any teeth.
Â 
Something Fishy
What use is a treaty that allowed a country to develop nuclear weapons for seven years while it barred inspectors -- and that is renounced as soon as the first inspectors in the door smell something fishy?
Is the International Atomic Energy Agency, a United Nations affiliate with no enforcement powers, the right institution to keep countries like North Korea in line?
And even if the issue goes to the Security Council, what can you take away from a country that has nothing?
"The treaty is no longer quite so sacrosanct today," said Leonard Spector, head of a project on nuclear proliferation on the Korean Peninsula at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. 
"Now that one country has pulled out, others obviously can begin to think about it."
In many ways the North Korean experience is significantly different from the challenges the West has faced in dealing with nonsignatories -- including India, Pakistan, Israel and Algeria -- and even with countries that have signed and dodged, like Iraq. 
First, by all accounts, Saddam Hussein seems much farther from realizing his dreams than Kim Il Sung is. 
Estimates vary widely, but more and more analysts in the United States Government seem to agree that North Korea already has the raw material for at least one bomb, and a few think some crude, still-untested devices may have already been built. 
Second, North Korea has turned weaponry into its only successful export business; it ships home-grown missiles to the Middle East, and presumably would have few qualms about shipping nuclear weapons.
But perhaps most important, rather than play an Iraq-style game of hide-and-seek with the inspectors, the North has used the access to its nuclear facilities guaranteed by the treaty itself as a bargaining chip. 
In its statement Friday it said it would only return to the regime if "the United States stops its nuclear threats against the North" -- which was interpreted as a reference to the annual "Team Spirit" military exercises now under way between South Korea and the United States -- and if the atomic energy agency "returns to its principle of independence and impartiality."
In short, Mr. Kim turned a situation in which it held no cards -- he was trying to hold off a "special inspection" of two sites that American spy satellites have identified as waste dumps that would probably show how much plutonium he has produced -- into a situation in which he now holds at least one: re-entry into the treaty. 
In fact, once a three-month waiting period to exit the treaty expires, his bomb-development work will become legal.
"From the start it was always assumed that if a country did withdraw from the treaty, it would be a signal that they had decided to make a bomb," Gary Milhollin, the head of the Wisconsin Project on Nuclear Arms Control, said recently. 
"If not, why take the political heat?"
What got everyone to this point is a 25-year-old system that acknowledges the right of every nation to use nuclear materials for peaceful purposes, even if those same materials, especially plutonium, are relatively simple to rework into weapons. 
It is the "safeguards" system of inspection that is supposed to assure that materials intended for civilian plants stay in civilian use.
The biggest advocates of that system are countries like Japan, which is already extracting plutonium from nuclear waste, much as North Korea is trying to do, as part of its aggressive civilian nuclear power program. 
These days the Japanese find themselves in the diplomatically embarrassing position of arguing that they have every right to do so because the world recognizes them as a solid international citizen, while at the same time arguing that their North Korean neighbors must be denied the right because they have an attitude problem.
Â 
Plutonium Politics
The North Koreans, naturally, say that their intentions are benign and that the I.A.E.A. is "tacitly approving" moves by Japan and South Korea to secretly arm themselves.
"We are seeing the breakdown of a regime that believed that plutonium and bomb-grade material are O.K. as long as they are under safeguard," said Paul L. Leventhal, president of the Nuclear Control Institute and a harsh critic of the precedent set by Japan's plutonium effort.
Officials in Japan and South Korea, naturally, say they have no interest in nuclear arms. 
The Japanese have long renounced them, and South Korea stopped developing them after the United States got wind of its project in the late 1970's. 
But preventing such an arms race has always depended on Seoul and Tokyo remaining unshakably confident that the United States' support, and its nuclear umbrella, extends over them.
Though few will say it publicly, that is what the Team Spirit exercise, which was suspended last year when the North looked like it was beginning to cooperate, is all about. 
This year the United States brought the B-1B bomber and other nuclear-capable equipment to South Korea for the exercises, presumably to make a point. 
And it was exactly that which sent the North into a frenzy, declaring early last week that they were going on a "semi-war footing" because invasion was imminent.
Now Washington is in the position of having few attractive options. 
Some officials, including many in Japan and a few members of the two-week old South Korean Government, argue that going ahead with the 125,000-troop Team Spirit exercise this year is an unnecessary provocation. 
But it is too late to back down. 
Though the American military has endless scenarios for eradicating Yongbyon, everyone acknowledges they are of little use: If the North retaliated on Seoul, only 35 miles from the border, or on South Korean civilian nuclear plants, it would be disastrous.
Economic sanctions are likely to have little effect on a country that is already isolated from virtually all of its neighbors except China. 
Getting the Chinese to seal off that border, and with it food and fuel, is unlikely.
"It may not be over yet," said Mr. Spector. "We are about to see an intense diplomatic effort to get this turned around."
But it may be, he said, that the world has little cause to be optimistic: Perhaps the North Koreans knew that they were about to get caught, he said, and the only solution was to jettison the one treaty that could betray them.
