file: Tibet Crisis Centers on 6-Year-Old Living Buddha.txt
text:
ï»¿
On a terraced hillside overlooking the gilded temples of the remote Taer Monastery here in western China, a young monk implored a visitor: "Would you please send me a photograph of the Dalai Lama?
We are always waiting for him."
As he spoke, dozens of artisans were putting the finishing touches on an ornate guest residence for the Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama, who serve as political and spiritual leaders for the Tibetan people.
The problem is that no one can say when these living Buddhas might ever get the opportunity to visit here.
The 14th Dalai Lama has lived in exile since 1959, and the latest reincarnation of the Panchen Lama, the 6-year-old son of a herder, has not been "approved" by the Communist Party leadership in Beijing.
For anyone traveling in western China, it takes little time to discover the depth of support here for the Dalai Lama in secular and religious matters relating to the six million Tibetans who populate the sweeping Qinghai-Tibetan landscape.
"Because the Dalai Lama is the highest figure of authority for our Yellow Hat Sect, all of the believers and we monks worship him," said one of the monks who moments before had been chanting from ancient scriptures in the Temple of Longevity, one of the many sacred halls among the labyrinth of courtyards and buildings that can be seen from the terraced hills. 
"Whatever is decided needs to have his approval."
The monk then rose and moved nimbly around a tiny altar, on which he prepared an offering of lamb, yak butter and candy wrapped in colored foil to the memory of a 17th-century peasant named Luo Qi, who saved the life of the Panchen Lama by carrying him piggyback through the flood waters of the Yellow River.
Perhaps the most urgent matter for Tibetans now is the political standoff with Beijing over the reincarnation of the 11th Panchen Lama. 
The 10th Panchen Lama died in January 1989, and according to the tenets of Tibetan Buddhism, his soul has migrated to a new host.
In May the Dalai Lama announced from exile in India that after six years of searching, the 11th coming of the Panchen Lama had been found incarnate in the body of the boy, Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, in the Tibetan village of Nagqu.
Recognition of the reincarnation "is a religious matter and not political," the Dalai Lama said, adding, "It is my hope that the Chinese Government will extend its understanding, cooperation and assistance."
The proclamation was denounced by the authorities in Beijing, who for the first time since 1949 have an opportunity to select the Panchen Lama and control his upbringing and education. 
They have attacked the Dalai Lama's "split-ist" behavior and "illegal and invalid" act -- accusing him of seeking to wreck the unity of the motherland and calling him every name secular leaders dare call a living Buddha without offending the Tibetan masses who worship him as a god-king.
But they have yet to challenge the religious verity of the Dalai Lama's choice: the boy with frost-reddened cheeks and an impish gaze who faces an uncertain future.
The struggle between the Communists and the Dalai Lama over who has the right to name the Panchen Lama is not just an arcane religious struggle; it is part of the collision of interests over who rules Tibet.
Since fleeing Tibet in 1959, when China crushed the most recent independence uprising, the Dalai Lama, 60, has built a worldwide campaign for return and for greater autonomy.
The Taer lamasery is in a valley 15 miles southwest of Xining, the capital of Qinghai Province, which was once part of Tibet. 
The lamasery was founded here in 1560 and today supports 560 monks and 11 living Buddhas, ranging in age from 7 to 80.
The 10th Panchen Lama visited the lamasery in 1987, and though he was greeted warmly, he was regarded as a collaborator by some Tibetans because he stayed after Chinese troops marched into Lhasa in 1959. 
He gave legitimacy to the Chinese occupation even as the Dalai Lama fled and fought for Tibet in exile.
But he also struggled for Tibetan interests, petitioning the Government to end torture, preserve Tibetan culture and stop the immigration of ethnic Chinese to Tibet. 
For his efforts, he spent a decade in prison in the Cultural Revolution of 1966-76.
The monks here want any new Panchen Lama to avoid political entanglement with the Chinese Government. 
Politics, another monk said, should be left to the Dalai Lama.
"The Panchen Lama should be a purely religious man and not a political figure," the monk said. 
"If the new Panchen Lama devotes himself solely to religion, then we would fully support him. 
But if he also concerns himself with politics, then we would be concerned."
The struggle over naming the reincarnation of the Panchen Lama, if not a crisis yet, could still become one, as Beijing has yet to reveal how it will orchestrate the official steps to recognition.
After the 10th Panchen Lama's death at the age of 50, the search for his reincarnation began. 
Monks from the Tashilhunpo Monastery, the traditional seat of the Panchen Lama in Xigaze, scoured the countryside for six years, examining candidates and seeking omens.
It now seems likely that as the abbots narrowed the list, word leaked out to the Dalai Lama's exile home in Dharamsala, India. 
There, his proclamation and recognition of the boy pre-empted China's secular recognition by the State Council under Prime Minister Li Peng.
"If the Panchen Lama would have been enthroned only with the blessing of the State Council, that would have been a disaster," said Lodi Gyari, the Dalai Lama's representative in Washington.
A number of Western experts say they believe that the Dalai Lama's strategy is not to foment a crisis. 
Rather, they say, he seems to be building a negotiating position for a possible compromise over authority in Tibet after the death of Deng Xiaoping, the ailing Chinese paramount leader.

file: Tiger Tales_Why Africa Can Thrive Like Asia.txt
text:
ï»¿
ONE of the great paradoxes of Africa is that its people are for the most part desperately poor while its land is extraordinarily rich. 
East Asia is the opposite: a region mostly poor in resources that over the last few decades has enjoyed the greatest economic boom in human history.
The area around this river port city in eastern Congo, the former Zaire, is a case in point: it is dilapidated and impoverished yet studded with diamonds, like a billionaire on Skid Row. 
Back in the 1950's, when this country and several others in Africa were at the same income level as South Korea while blessed with far more natural resources, it might have seemed reasonable that Africa would soon leave Asia in the dust.
Now South Korea has a per capita income of about $10,000 a year, and Congo stands at $150 per person. 
Narrowing the gap is a fundamental challenge for Congo's new leaders as they try to rebuild their country after the overthrow this month of the longtime Zairian dictator, Mobutu Sese Seko. 
And a vital first step, not only for this country but for others across Africa -- and for big aid donors like the United States -- is understanding why such yawning disparities have occurred.
A wave of new research into the contrast between Africa and East Asia is producing some surprising findings. 
The most striking and reassuring conclusion is that although East Asia enjoyed some significant cultural and historical advantages, its economic boom relied on factors that probably can be replicated elsewhere.
In a nutshell, the formula was an outward-oriented, market-based economic policy coupled with an emphasis on education and health care. 
Countries in other regions like Chile have followed the strategy with great success. 
Several African countries, led by Congo's neighbor Uganda, are trying to learn from the Asian experience and are enjoying their own Asian-style boom.
Â 
Encouraging Signs
Uganda, a beautiful, vividly green nation on the banks of Lake Victoria in East Africa, with vast herds of antelope that graze beside modern highways, now has one of the fastest-growing economies in the world. 
Yet it is simply at the crest of a wave of African countries experimenting with privatization and stock markets -- there are 16 so far in Africa -- and trying to prove that rapid economic growth is not a prerogative of East Asia alone.
"This is still in the early days, and we're not euphoric and jumping up and down, but we think that parts of Africa are moving in the right direction," said Alan H. Gelb, chief economist for Africa at the World Bank. 
"I think there are grounds for optimism."
At last count, four countries -- Uganda, Angola, Lesotho and Malawi -- were enjoying growth rates of 10 percent. 
That is about as fast as the peak growth rates for the Asian "tigers," Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore and South Korea.
"There's an emerging consensus that Africa is not hopeless, and that in fact there is an emerging renaissance going on in Africa," said Salih Booker, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.
But to travel the back roads here and in Asia is to be reminded how many opportunities Africa missed over the last few decades, and how much it continues to mortgage its future by giving short shrift to education and health care. 
The new research suggests that a central feature of the successful East Asian model was a high level of education and public health -- a level partly inherited from past centuries and partly nurtured in recent decades. 
Despite its own ancient educational traditions, Africa lags far behind in building this "human capital."
In the little village of Lalia, in eastern Congo, the principal of the mud-brick elementary school throws up his hands at the challenges he faces educating the barefoot children who swarm around him.
"We have no notebooks and no teaching materials, and some teachers don't come because we cannot pay salaries," said the principal, Bibi Masakama, an energetic 32-year-old, as he showed a visitor around the school. 
The mud walls leaned ominously, and light came from holes in the walls that functioned as windows. 
Lizards ran about on the walls and on the rough wooden planks that served as desks and benches.
"None of these kids has ever been vaccinated against any disease," Mr. Masakama added. 
"None has ever had a medical examination."
Many reasons have been cited over the years for the different economic trajectories of Africa and East Asia. 
Some said that the colonial burden on Africa was much heavier, or that Africa was troubled more by artificial boundaries and disparate tribes and languages. 
Others, including some Africans, pointed to climate or culture.
"In Africa the climate is such that there's always fruit around, in back of the house, and you just reach up and pick it when you're hungry," said Alauwa Lobela, the mayor of Kisangani. 
"But in Europe and Asia, the climate forced people to get food, to protect themselves from the cold in the winter, to develop a spirit of battle."
Such climate-based explanations are common, and analysts have found that the economies of tropical countries do indeed grow a bit more slowly than those of temperate countries, all other things being equal. 
But the statistical relationship is slight, and one study suggested that climate explains only one-twentieth of the difference in economic performance between Africa and East Asia since 1965.
Of course, East Asia includes North Korea, healthy and well-educated but an economic disaster area facing famine, while Africa includes countries like Botswana that have prospered over the years. 
But regionally per capita incomes grew about 11 times faster in East Asia than in sub-Saharan Africa in the years since 1965.
Â 
Educated and Healthy
Why?
Economists point to a conjunction of factors associated with rapid growth: places like Japan, China, Taiwan and South Korea underwent land redistribution after World War II and became relatively egalitarian societies; they were relatively well-educated and healthy, and they experienced a sharp drop in birth rates. 
On top of that, economic policies were ideal: the East Asian countries sooner or later adopted relatively open, market-oriented policies emphasizing exports.
East Asian countries pursued various economic models, but there was also a common economic strategy, which countries like Uganda are now emulating. 
The strategy emphasizes fiscal prudence and avoiding inflation while vigorously promoting exports and keeping the currency undervalued. 
In the past, African countries often tolerated soaring inflation and overvalued their currencies, keeping exports uncompetitive on world markets.
Â 
The Socialist Path
A central issue was politics: many African countries flirted with socialism and an anti-capitalist brand of nationalism that was in fashion during the cold war. 
In East Asia, the most successful countries avoided socialism and, in the case of South Korea and Taiwan, flirted with fascism. 
Even China since 1980 has arguably been closer to fascism than Communism, not so much Marxist-Leninist as market-Leninist.
Another critical factor has been savings, which are needed to finance new factories and other investments that stimulate economic growth. 
Partly because of market incentives and government dictates, national savings rates have been much higher in Asia (more than 30 percent of gross domestic product) than in Africa (about 12 percent).
"Our problem is that we don't save," lamented Samuel Ndomba, a British-educated professor at the University of Kisangani in Congo. 
"When people get a bit of money, they just spend it to buy a beer."
That might change, though, were there more incentives for investment. 
There is nothing intrinsically Asian about high savings, for Japan had very low savings rates in the 19th century. 
They soared in part because of Government campaigns and the spread of deposit-taking institutions, and eventually financed Japan's industrial revolution.
One major reason not to save and invest in Africa has been inflation and instability: when people save money, it often ends up being confiscated. 
Victoria Baenongandi, for example, lasted just two weeks as an entrepreneur in eastern Congo. 
She bought a pile of merchandise to resell, but everything was seized by soldiers. 
So she returned home and gave up on business -- and put her savings into beer.
Economic policy aside, East Asia enjoyed another crucial advantage over Africa, one that may be harder to replicate. 
Countries like South Korea or even China started the development process with citizens who were more literate and more healthy than those in other nations at their income levels, and they continued to improve. 
For all of China's persistent poverty, a child born in Shanghai in the early 1990's was more likely to learn to read and more likely to survive childhood than a baby born in New York City.
Some experts argue that East Asia's success in education derives not from Government programs -- Asian governments actually spend a smaller share of G.N.P. on education than do African governments. 
Rather, literacy and other education achievements in Asia may have been helped greatly by a culture of parental concern that supports enormous private spending on education, arising from a Confucian reverence for scholarship.
Because of Confucianism, China has had national exams and the rough equivalent of university graduates for 2,000 years. 
In contrast, Tanzania is said to have had only 13 university graduates at independence in 1961.
Their histories also meant that most Asian countries slipped fairly easily into the form of the modern nation-state, for they had a sense of nationhood that in some cases went back for millenniums. 
On the other hand, some African countries -- a hodgepodge of ethnic groups within borders drawn arbitrarily by colonial rulers -- are still struggling to adjust to modern nationhood. 
Such instability has always been fatal to economic development, whether in Cambodia or in Mozambique.
Health problems have also been a greater economic burden on Africa than is often realized. 
Most Africans, for example, have stomach worms, and as a result millions of people cannot study or work energetically, and some children have their intelligence permanently impaired because of anemia caused by the parasites.
"From the age of two, most people here have worms," shrugged Bakondagama Barandala, a 24-year-old nurse at a shabby clinic in Mambasa, in northeastern Congo. 
The clinic is a metaphor for public health in Congo: it is the only clinic in the region, yet it has no doctor, no electricity, no drinking water, no instruments and no medicines.
Â 
The Graft Factor
For all the importance of education and health care, the cultivation of human capital seems to be effective only in tandem with the right economic policies. 
China was healthy and literate for its income level in the early 1960's when under Mao it underwent one of the worst economic contractions and famines in world history, one in which 30 million people died. 
Likewise, Tanzania for many years vigorously promoted education and health, but it stagnated because of catastrophic economic policies inspired by a quasi-socialist ideology.
One reason for some optimism about Africa now is its parallels with Asian countries earlier this century. 
Much like Asia was before its boom, Africa is relatively egalitarian in wealth, partly because land is not concentrated in the hands of a small elite (as in parts of Latin America). 
Similarly, in many African countries birth rates are dropping and literacy is rising.
Moreover, it's instructive to recall that Western pessimism over global basket cases was once directed at Asia too: it used to be fashionable to say that Chinese had no capacity for hard work and no feel for business, and that China was destined, as Samuel Taylor Coleridge put it, to "permanency without progression."
Among the most important studies of the lessons of East Asia are a 337-page report edited by two Harvard economists and just released by the Asian Development Bank, and another major report published by the World Bank in 1993. 
Those studies and related research point to other factors that go along with the nurturing of financial and human capital -- especially the effectiveness of Asian governments.
Asian governments have often been more effective than Africa's in part because they have been less corrupt. 
Asia has huge amounts of corruption by American standards, but for the most part graft there is just another cost of doing business; in Africa it often prevents business from being done at all. 
A joke heard in business circles makes the point:
An African visited an Asian friend, a Government official, and admired the official's spectacular home and opulent life style. 
The Asian explained his wealth with a wink toward his "cut": "You see that highway out there?
Fifteen percent!"
Then the Asian visited the African, also a Government official, and found that he was living just as lavishly. 
Asked how he had prospered, the African pointed outside, saying: "You see that highway out there?"
"No," the Asian said, peering helplessly out the window. 
"What highway?"
"That's just it. 
One hundred percent."

file: To Bolster Olympic Bid, China Eases Its Surveillance of Reporters.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese authorities appear to have stopped following foreign reporters, as part of an effort to spruce up their image and help their bid to become host of the Olympic Games in the year 2000.
The State Security Ministry and Foreign Ministry jointly issued an internal Government circular this month announcing an end to the following of foreign journalists, Chinese familiar with the document say. 
The circular said the step was necessary to improve Beijing's human rights image and therefore its chances of being awarded the Olympic Games.
Beijing is one of half a dozen cities competing to become host of the 2000 Summer Olympics. 
It is vigorously rebuilding roads and renovating its airport in the hopes of winning the Olympics, while also encouraging the use of English and taking other steps to improve its bid.
Considering how security-conscious the Chinese authorities are, the change suggests that they are extremely concerned with the Olympic bid, which is to be decided this fall. 
Diplomats say that China has generally managed its application well and that Beijing will be one of the stronger contenders to get the Olympics.
Â 
An Unusual Vigor
For several years, Government agents have followed certain foreign journalists with a diligence that rarely surfaces in other endeavors. 
While Government ministries often empty by late afternoon, and take days to answer the simplest questions, three carloads of security agents can miraculously appear at 10 on a rainy Saturday night to pursue a foreign reporter.
Reporters for The New York Times, who have apparently been followed more than reporters from any other news organization, were followed almost every time they left their residence in recent months. 
But that kind of surveillance stopped abruptly about 10 days ago, and other journalists said they too had not been followed recently.
Diplomats from the United States and other countries are followed much less frequently than reporters, perhaps because the authorities are less concerned with their secrets getting out than with the embarrassment of having them splashed across foreign newspapers.
The Foreign Ministry and State Council News Office declined today to confirm or deny that the following of reporters had been suspended.
A Foreign Ministry spokesman, asked for a comment, inquired who had told the reporter about the document. 
When the reporter declined to say, the spokesman added that it was difficult to make a comment without this information.
Â 
Harsh Punishment for Chinese
The Government is still extremely concerned with the flow of information to foreign journalists and diplomats, and it has severely punished Chinese accused of giving documents to foreigners. 
The Chinese in such cases are always punished far more harshly than the foreigner.
Wu Shichen, a mid-ranking editor at the official New China News Agency, was detained in October on charges of giving a Hong Kong reporter an advance copy of an important speech. 
Mr. Wu, who is accused of accepting money in exchange for the speech, was recently sentenced to 15 years in prison for revealing state secrets, a Beijing journalist said.
But that sentence seems unusually long and it cannot be confirmed. 
Officials have declined to comment.
The Hong Kong reporter who allegedly paid Mr. Wu for the document was detained for several days and then expelled from the country.
Bai Weiji, a former Foreign Ministry employee who was arrested in May for allegedly giving documents to The Washington Post, remains in custody but has not yet been tried. 
By some accounts, another Chinese who allegedly gave the documents to Mr. Bai may also be awaiting trial.
Chinese security agents searched the office of The Washington Post in May and confiscated what they said were secret documents -- apparently the ones that Mr. Bai is accused of supplying -- but did not expel or take other action against the newspaper's correspondent, Lena H. Sun.
Â 
Electronic Surveillance Goes On
While the following of foreign journalists may be suspended for now, surveillance will presumably continue in more subtle ways. 
Telephones are tapped, offices and homes are bugged, and Chinese are still asked to spy on their foreign acquaintances.
The problem for the security forces is that China has opened up so much in the last few years that surveillance has become more difficult: some Chinese cheerfully cooperate with State Security and then with equal cheerfulness discuss their cooperation with the foreign reporter. 
Others explain the workings of the telephone bugs to those who are being bugged.
Another problem is that State Security docks the salaries of its agents who allow a reporter to get away. 
For fear of losing wages, the agents therefore sometimes disobey orders and stay so close to the reporter that the following is very obvious.

file: To Pray in a Tibetan Temple, Buddhists Built One in California.txt
text:
ï»¿
For years when Judith Leeper drove a back road near here, she was mystified by glimpses, first, of copper domes and pagoda-like structures shining through the trees, then of a towering golden monument that glimmered in the California sun.
The mystery was cleared up on a recent Saturday when she joined 1,500 other visitors at an open house at Odiyan, a newly opened Tibetan Buddhist temple and study center in the mountains overlooking the Pacific about 100 miles north of San Francisco.
As more than 800 orange, yellow and red prayer flags, silk-screened with passages from sacred texts, snapped gloriously in the breezes, the visitors filed between walls of hundreds of prayer wheels, their copper cylinders, covered with mantras, encasing miles of tightly rolled prayer scrolls.
Odiyan's profusion of colors and images can astonish: a 108-foot-tall temple contains a central monument with 108,000 small gilded statues of Padmasambhava, a founding figure of Tibetan Buddhism revered as a second Buddha and believed to have been born miraculously, in an earlier incarnation, from a lotus blossom.
But no less striking is the fact that this repository of Tibetan sacred symbol, art and form was created almost entirely by several dozen American volunteers who, for two decades, learned both the spiritual discipline of Tibetan Buddhism and the practical skills of construction.
What is happening at Odiyan -- and at a growing number of other Buddhist centers around the country -- is part of a new chapter in the 2,500-year-old history of Buddhism, which spread from the tree in northern India where a young prince, Siddhartha Gautama, is believed by his followers to have attained perfect enlightenment.
Not only has the Buddhism that arrived on these shores with Chinese and Japanese immigrants been augmented by new waves of immigrants from Vietnam, Cambodia, Thailand and Korea, but the interest in Buddhism among non-Asian Americans, once largely focused on the meditation and riddles of Japanese Zen Buddhism, has been reinforced by a diaspora of Tibetan Buddhist leaders, including the Dalai Lama, revered by his people as the incarnation of a compassionate heavenly being.
Buddhists now number at least 800,000 in the United States, according to a 1991 survey by the City University of New York, and some Buddhist organizations say that figure should be doubled or tripled. 
The number of Buddhist centers and publications is increasing rapidly.
Bruce Smith is part of this new chapter. 
Two decades ago, he was a geophysicist doing research on earthquakes. 
His pursuit of Japanese martial arts led him to take a course in meditation from Tarthang Tulku, one of the first prominent Tibetan lamas, or holy men, in the United States and the spiritual leader and organizer of Odiyan.
Now 51 years old, he has spent the last 17 years living and working at Odiyan alongside other volunteers -- an experience that he says has transformed his life even more than the regular practice of meditation.
Tarthang Tulku said Odiyan was part of an effort to preserve a form of Buddhism ravaged in its homeland by Chinese Communist rule and to implant its wisdom in a new land.
For the Buddha -- or Enlightened One, as Prince Siddhartha came to be known -- wisdom involved the realization that life is an endless cycle of birth, death and suffering, from which one can escape by compassionate living and disciplined insight into the impermanence of reality.
Spreading, over a thousand years, from India to Southeast Asia and then to China, Korea and Japan, Buddhism developed a wide variety of spiritual practices, subtle philosophical schools and forms of monastic living. 
And once Tibet became thoroughly Buddhist, between the 7th and 11th centuries, the country's isolation in the Himalayas made it a treasure chest of ancient teachings and elaborate beliefs and practices.
That body of teaching and way of life was threatened with extinction after the Chinese Communists occupied Tibet in 1950 and suppressed a rebellion in 1959, destroying monasteries, books and religious objects and detaining, executing or driving into hiding numerous monks and scholars.
Tarthang Tulku went into exile in India, to which the Dalai Lama, revered as a living god by Tibetans, later escaped. 
Then, in 1968, he came to the United States. 
He organized projects to preserve, print and distribute in both the West and Tibet 755 volumes of sacred texts. 
He also helped rebuild his original monastery in Tibet. 
Carrying out these tasks were individuals drawn to the meditation centers and classes he established in Berkeley, Brazil, Germany and the Netherlands.
The lama, who is now 60, praises Americans and the nation's religious liberty. 
"Americans in some way are very religious, generous and ethical," he said sitting and sipping tea in Odiyan's central temple, "but at the same time they are more neurotic and chaotic in their heads," something that he believes the disciplines of Buddhism could repair.
Odiyan -- the name comes from Oddiyana, a mythical land of Padmasambhava's birth -- is not designed to become a traditional monastery for celibate monks who take vows but rather a center where 15 to 50 serious lay students of Buddhism can live and work for short retreats or even years.
The buildings preserve a kind of nonwritten sacred text: images and objects vital to Tibetan Buddhism.
Tarthang Tulku designed the area as a replica of Samye, Tibet's first Buddhist monastery, and as a "mandala," a symbolic representation of cosmic forces.
At Odiyan, a simple one-story structure of rooms and living areas runs around the edge of a square approximately 100 yards on each side, which is surrounded in turn by a moat-like lagoon with swans and edged with formal gardens.
At the center is an 80-foot-tall temple with a bright copper dome. 
Smaller temples stand over the east, west, north and south gates. 
At some distance is a shimmering gold-leafed stupa, a 113-foot-high multitiered monument.
Built in accordance with sacred specifications and arrayed with texts, symbols and works of art, the structures are meant to convey multiple levels of Buddhist teaching in thousands of details. 
All of the physical patterns, as well as the natural beauty of the flowers, darting swallows and jasmine-scented air, are meant to gradually transform a person's consciousness. 
The fluttering prayer flags and prayer wheels powered by electricity, an American innovation, are believed to radiate multitudes of blessings and healing energy to counter harmful natural forces and human designs.
This luxuriance of image, color and celestial beings put Tibetan Buddhism into sharp contrast with the austerity and simplicity of Zen Buddhism, the form of Buddhism familiar to Americans.
Tibetan Buddhists believe that enlightenment can be achieved in one lifetime rather than through the series of reincarnations in which adherents of some other forms of Buddhism believe. 
Tibetan Buddhists say this can be done by rigorous chanting, and praying, by participating in ceremonies and by visualizing sacred beings. 
These complicated techniques demand, more strongly than in many other strands of Buddhism, submission to the guidance of a guru or teacher.
The question of the teacher or master's authority is one area of tension with American culture, according to American Buddhist leaders.
Tarthang Tulku agreed. 
Americans believe that "if you follow someone, you are brainwashed," he said. 
"That's the negative side, but the positive side is that if there is a good teacher, someone who has compassion, there will be genuine respect."
Not all the visitors to Odiyan last weekend were equally impressed. 
Ms. Leeper, the visitor from Sea Ranch, a few miles to the north, praised the effort to preserve Tibetan Buddhism but felt that the center had a slightly inauthentic aura and "didn't quite fit the land."
But a friend, Rosemary McGinnis, quoted her son-in-law as saying, "I don't believe in God, but I felt I had walked into a prayer."

file: To the Party, Victor_s Exile Invalidates China Nobel.txt
text:
ï»¿
For decades, Chinese intellectuals have brooded over the lack of a Chinese Nobel laureate in literature, half blaming the outside world for its ignorance, half wondering if their artists are up to standards and always bemoaning the severe language barrier. 
Only this week, a popular newspaper here ran articles on what it called the "Nobel blues."
So for many in the literary elite, the news that the coveted prize had gone to a writer in exile, the experimental playwright and novelist Gao Xingjiang, had a bittersweet quality. 
Reactions ranged from elation to bewilderment to suspicion of the Nobel Committee's motives.
The Communist Party, which denounced Mr. Gao when he wrote a play about the 1989 killings of demonstrators at Tiananmen Square, had a simple response. 
This morning the official news media did not report on the award at all, though word had already spread fast among the literati via the Internet and telephone.
Then, this afternoon, the Foreign Ministry said in a statement that while "China has had an outpouring of outstanding literary works and literary giants," this Nobel Prize had been used for "ulterior political motives."
The evening news briefly noted that a politically motivated Nobel had been given to a "French-nationality Chinese writer."
In an interview this afternoon, Jin Jianfan, secretary of the official China Writers Association, repeated the political charge, adding for good measure that when Mr. Gao worked in the association back in the 1980's, "we all had the view that his work was very, very average."
Mr. Gao made a mark in the Beijing theater scene in the early 1980's with his absurdist plays, in the style of Becket and Ionesco, and courted controversy with an essay attacking socialist realism in art. 
But he tired of the official constrictions and in 1987 moved to France, where he has lived ever since, producing plays, novels and paintings.
His works have not been performed in China for many years, and he is better known in Europe.
But he does have admirers among intellectuals who are struggling to make the avant-garde more respectable in China, and this award seems bound to play into a simmering cultural battle.
Though Mr. Gao is in the official doghouse, a recent issue of the Beijing magazine Avant-Garde Today published an essay extolling his work as trying to "rewrite China's mythical-poetic history through folklore."
An editor of the magazine, Shi Jian, said today by telephone from Nanjing, where he was attending a book fair, that thousands had shown up at the fair this afternoon for a hastily organized celebration of the award.
"There was a good buzz around here," Mr. Shi said. 
"Everyone is happy with the news."
Mr. Shi said it was understandable that a writer like Mr. Gao would be better received overseas than in China. 
One reason is that his work, while often drawing on Chinese themes, employs complex, unfamiliar Western experimental forms.
A second reason, Mr. Shi said, "is the fact that the creative space for work like this is so confined in China."
"For drama like his, which has elements of experimental theater, traditional opera and drama, Noh and other influences," Mr. Shi added, "there is very little space to develop and stage it here."
Han Shaogang, editor of the literary magazine Horizon, shared the general surprise at the selection of Mr. Gao. Writers like Mo Yan, the author of "Red Sorghum" and a succession of other inventive novels, and the dissident poet Bei Dao, who lives abroad, had been higher on nearly everyone's list.
But Mr. Han, who has kept up a friendship with Mr. Gao, also called the award "great news" and said he hoped it would be "a boost for literary creativity" in China.
Experimental painters, writers, performance artists and filmmakers from China have often found it easier to live abroad, where they can escape official pressures and incomprehension, and also find a greater commercial market for their work.
In turn, Chinese-born artists who achieve high honors abroad are often viewed with suspicion or jealousy here, sometimes by artists who are trying to work in China's still-daunting artistic environment, sometimes by party culture officials.
The surprising news of Mr. Gao's award prompted lively debate on China's Internet bulletin boards, the country's freest forums these days.
"What's the point of getting excited?" one writer asked. 
"This is just a Frenchman with a Chinese name who won the prize."
But others pointedly asked why the official press had been muzzled.
"A Chinese won the prize," another writer said. 
"His country did not congratulate him. 
And countless people who know nothing about him have attacked him. 
What is wrong with our people?"

file: Top Court in Hong Kong Upholds Ban on Defacing Chinese Flag.txt
text:
ï»¿
Steering clear of another legal confrontation with the Chinese government, the top court in Hong Kong ruled today that defacing the Chinese flag is a crime. 
The decision was a victory for the local government and reversed a ruling by a lower court that said defacing the flag was a form of expression guaranteed by the constitution of this former British colony.
Striking down a Hong Kong law that protects the flag, legal experts said, could have led to a showdown with China. 
The new legislature adopted the law hours after the colony reverted to Chinese rule in 1997.
The flag decision was released a week after the court had said that Beijing had the right to overturn its landmark decision that granted residency to more than a million people from mainland China.
Taken together, the rulings prompted some critics here to contend that the Hong Kong judiciary had lost its independence.
"I'm afraid people will see this as a trend," the leader of the Hong Kong Democratic Party, Martin Lee, said. 
"It won't be long before Hong Kong goes down the same route as Singapore or mainland China, where the courts never rule against the government on sensitive cases."
Mr. Lee, a lawyer, refused to comment on the case itself.
Other legal experts noted that unlike the immigration case, where the court made a well-reasoned decision that Beijing overturned, the decision today involved a thorny issue that has bedeviled courts in the United States and Europe.
"I'm sure people will say the court is collapsing," the former solicitor general of Hong Kong, Daniel R. Fung, said. 
"But this ruling is not a knee-jerk response to executive pressure. 
On the contrary, the judges are looking at how other mature jurisdictions have approached this issue."
The case stemmed from a pro-democracy rally in January 1998 in which two men, Ng Kung-siu and Lee Kin-yun, carried heavily defaced Chinese and Hong Kong flags. 
Both flags were torn, smeared with black ink and had the Chinese word for "shame" scrawled on them.
Lawyers for the two argued that they had the right to express themselves, even by destroying the flags, under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which is enshrined in the Hong Kong Constitution. 
The government countered that the men had violated laws that protect national and regional flags. 
The defendants won their case on appeal.
In the 51-page ruling, Chief Justice Andrew Li acknowledged that the flag ordinance restricted civil liberties.
But Chief Justice Li said it did not stifle other forms of political expression, and he said it was justified because the Chinese flag symbolized Hong Kong's effort to integrate itself into the Chinese motherland.
"Protection of the national flag and the regional flag from desecration, having regard to their unique symbolism, will play an important part in the attainment of these goals," the judge declared.
In a concurring opinion, another justice, Kemal Bokhary, seemed eager to show that Hong Kong was squarely in the mainstream of international legal opinion. 
He noted that defacing the flag was a crime in Germany and Italy. 
The Portuguese colony of Macao, which returns to Chinese rule on Sunday, also recently banned the practice.
Judge Bokhary acknowledged that the ban was "just within the outer limits of constitutionality."

file: TRACK AND FIELD_Chinese Lead Millrose Women_s Pole-Vault Field.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was 1987, and Cai Weiyan was performing acrobatics at a Chinese sports school.
"A coach who was doing well with men in the pole vault asked me if I liked track and field and did I like pole-vaulting," she recalled yesterday. 
"I was 14. 
I didn't know anything about it. 
He said: 'Are you afraid?
Try it.'
I did. 
The first day, I couldn't clear the bar. 
By the end of the year, I did 3.15 meters" -- 10 feet 4 inches -- "and it was exciting."
In 1989, at another Chinese sports school, Sun Caiyun was playing many sports, including basketball.
"Before that," she said through the same translator, Zhou Xinmin, the manager of the Chinese track team now in New York, "I had no idea about the pole vault. 
A pole-vault coach saw I had a tall body. 
He asked me to try the pole vault. 
I tried it and liked it, but I lacked strength. 
The first time I cleared the bar, I did 2.80 meters," or 9-2 1/4.
Tomorrow night, in the 92d annual Chase Millrose Games at Madison Square Garden, Cai and Sun will compete in the women's pole vault. 
Last year, when America's leading indoor track meet introduced the event, it became one of the competitive highlights of the night. 
This year, with Cai, Sun and Daniela Bartova of the Czech Republic, there is great potential again.
In the 1998 world ranking by Track and Field News, Cai is third and Sun is eighth. 
They are the pioneers of a relatively new sport, which met wide resistance when it was introduced in the United States. 
Too unladylike, critics said.
"It was the same in China," Cai said. 
"When I start to vault, some teammates said this is a dangerous sport. 
I wasn't afraid."
Sun found the same reaction.
"Some friends said it wasn't an Olympic event," she said. 
"Some friends said this is a men's sport not fit for women. 
Now they think I made the right choice."
Good thinking. 
Sun became the first official world record-holder at 13-3 3/4, and five weeks later Cai raised the record to 13-4 1/4. 
In all, Sun has set world records 11 times indoors and 6 times outdoors. 
Their career bests are 14-3 1/4 for Cai and 14- 1/2 for Sun.
The world records are now held by Emma George of Australia -- 15- 3/4 outdoors and 14-11 indoors. 
The progress is amazing in an event for which world records were first recognized only five years ago and which has not yet been contested in a world outdoor championships or Olympics.
Women's pole-vaulting is still an esoteric sport. 
Cai said that perhaps 100 women in all of China are pole-vaulters. 
But last year alone, 17 women from 9 nations cleared 14 feet outdoors, led by George (15- 3/4), Bartova (14-9 1/2) and Stacy Dragila (14-8 1/4), the American record-holder and last year's Millrose winner. 
Dragila is injured now. 
Sun said that if men can clear 6 meters (19-8 1/4), which eight men have done in the last decade, then women can clear 5 meters (16-4 3/4).
But as the bar gets higher, the expectations do, too.
"It used to be a little easier," Cai said, "because China started the event. 
But now it's everywhere and it's high pressure, but it's also an encouragement for the sport."
Cai and Sun are the first Millrose athletes to come from mainland China. 
Li Tong ran in the men's hurdles at Millrose in the 1980's, but at the time he was a student at Washington State, where his name was Americanized to Tony Lee.
The Chinese pole-vaulters are a little Americanized, too. 
When Sun was asked if she knew she would be competing on the same floor where Michael Jordan had performed wonders, her eyes lighted, then saddened. 
"It's a pity,' she said, "that he is retiring from basketball."

file: Tracking the Web Across China_ From the _Wang Ba_ of the West.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE roads here are sometimes barely roads. 
Bathrooms are pits in the ground. 
Fur coats are a necessity, not fashion. 
In a nod to tradition, and for self-defense, some men travel with swords at their sides.
Yet, thanks to modem connections and the efforts of local entrepreneurs, the Internet is trickling into back alleys and basements of the most remote regions of western China. 
A nationwide system of local Internet service providers was completed last year; now the seven westernmost provinces -- half of China's land, with 20 percent of its population -- account for 5 percent of the country's Internet use.
So, in early January when I set out with my backpack and no itinerary for a seven-week trek through the mountains and deserts of western China, e-mail was the intercontinental umbilical cord that tethered me to my anxious mother 12,000 miles away in New York City. 
From Inner Mongolia to Kashgar to Lhasa, I hunted for the elusive wang ba, or "Net bar," to send reassuring updates.
(Some things are better left out of such dispatches: I did not tell my mother about the time my bus almost slipped off an icy mountain road, or about another bus that fell off a cliff outside Lhasa, killing 12 people.)
In the one-room Net bar in Kashgar, where eight personal computers were strung together with a tangle of wires, the coal-burning stove spewing black smoke was not enough to keep my fingers from becoming too cold to type. 
In the monastery town of Xiahe in the Gansu Province, Internet users look out the window at the mule-drawn carts and the nomadic herdsmen who trudge along the town's one main street, oblivious to the information revolution.
While the Internet may be a web of dreams, China is a country of stark realities. 
Like its roads and infrastructure, China's Internet is being sewn together piecemeal and unevenly, but it is coming together.
Depending on where you go and whom you ask, China is alternately prosperous or poor, cutting-edge modern or heartachingly backward. 
Multinational corporations salivate over magazine images of Levi-clad adolescents eating at the McDonald's in Shanghai and talking on their Nokia cell phones. 
But that slice of the demographic pie is very slim and very urban. 
More than two-thirds of China's 1.2 billion population is rural, and the overwhelming majority of that rural population is poor.
Forty-five percent of China's Internet users live in Shanghai, Beijing or in the affluent province of Guangdong, which account for just 8 percent of the country's total population. 
Eighty percent of users live in large cities; almost 80 percent are men and 85 percent are 18 to 35, according to a government-sponsored survey by the China Internet Network Information Center. 
Few rural residents can afford computers or the fees charged by their local Internet bars, the equivalent of $2.50 to $4 an hour. 
(Urban Internet bars are cheaper.)
The Internet presence reflects these disparities. 
A wang ba can be a sleek mirrored club where uniformed attendants bring tea to customers at their computers or a dirt-floor hovel where men huddle under dim lighting.
Beyond larger cities, wang ba customers are largely foreign tourists seeking quaint, traditional villages but demanding modern communications services. 
Many wang ba's use the names Hotmail and Yahoo as synonyms for Internet access on their store signs. 
These services' increasing presence is leading the way for infiltration of the Internet throughout the underdeveloped areas of China. 
Nonetheless, local residents who go to wang ba's seem more interested in the multiplayer video games than in the potential for revolutionizing commerce.
Tim Jin, who owns Tim's Internet Cafe in Dali in the Yunnan province, estimates that 95 percent of his customers are foreigners, 4 percent come from other parts of China and less than 1 percent are local residents.
As for e-commerce, Mr. Jin said, a number of the communities surrounding Dali still do their purchasing and bargaining at weekly outdoor markets.
"No way we can do an e-commerce site here," he said, citing the lack of infrastructure in Yunnan, the difficulty of transportation and the low population density.
"In big cities and through foreign mail-order companies, maybe. 
Locally, there's no way."
In the Tibetan capital of Lhasa, which is not connected to the rest of China by railroad, Tsering Tashi opened the Khang Li Internet Bar as soon as Tibet established an Internet service provider last year. 
He said it was the only Tibetan-owned Internet bar in Tibet. 
Within 10 months, he said, he recovered his original investment of almost $10,000. 
Still, nearly all of his customers are tourists.
"Tibetans almost never use high technology; they don't understand it," Mr. Tashi said. 
"They have heard of the Internet, but the Internet cafe is a wholly new concept to them."
In the off-season, October through February, he converts most of his Internet cafe into a clothing store.
Sluggish connections are a problem throughout China. 
In mid-February, Mr. Jin closed his cafe for two days because the Internet was too slow, particularly the e-mail provider Hotmail, which 80 percent of his customers use.
Of course, China is changing rapidly, and so is the Internet. 
Entrepreneurs say they are optimistic that logistical obstacles can be overcome. 
But corporate profits in China have historically been elusive. 
Ask any multinational corporation that has set up shop in China in the last decade, eager to tap into the billion-customer market.
A majority of companies is still waiting for the investments to pay off. 
Plagued by distribution difficulties, inflated estimates of demand and bureaucratic red tape, more businesses are leaving China, deciding that the market can wait.
Predictably, profits in e-commerce are elusive as well, though not just in China. 
E-business opportunities in China could therefore prove to be doubly difficult.
But low costs and tourists' cash, it turns out, can become a very workable, albeit modest, business plan. 
"Our fundamental goal is to make money," Mr. Tashi said. 
"So far, the Internet has been very good for making money."

text:

The nation's trade deficit narrowed markedly in June as exports rebounded to a new record and imports subsided for the first time this year, the Commerce Department reported today.
The decline in the deficit, to $8.2 billion from $9.54 billion in May, followed two sizable increases and reflected what analysts said was the faster growth of the American economy in the spring than had initially been estimated. 
Stocks rose and the dollar advanced against most leading currencies. 
Yields on Treasury bonds increased.
"This shows a lot of strength," said James F. O'Sullivan, an economist at J. P. Morgan & Company. 
"The trend in exports is booming," he added, despite the dollar's strength and the lackluster performance of various trading partners whose economies have only begun to revive.
Despite the decline in June, the most recent month for which figures are available, the trade deficit for the first half of 1997 was still about 6 percent larger than in the corresponding period of 1996, though below the level of the first half of 1995.
And while the deficits narrowed with Canada and Mexico, two of the country's biggest trade partners, imbalances with China and Japan increased significantly, prompting fresh expressions of displeasure by the Clinton Administration.
The trend toward widening deficits with Asian countries could increase, economists said, because of economic difficulty accompanying currency crises in several South and South Asian nations.
Nonetheless, the report provided further evidence of the American economy's recent strength, showing that demand for goods and services from overseas was helping to keep growth rolling along.
Indeed, combining the latest trade data with figures showing a larger buildup in inventories than had been thought, analysts now say that the economy probably grew at a rate upward of 3.5 percent in the April-June quarter, perhaps by as much as 4 percent.
That would be considerably above the 2.2 percent pace the Commerce Department estimated at the end of July. 
If borne out, it could undermine a widely held view that the economy had slowed substantially, as policy makers desired, from a first-quarter growth rate of 4.9 percent, which raised concerns about resurgent inflation.
And if consumer spending revives, as it shows signs of doing, analysts said the Federal Reserve could decide to cool the economy by raising interest rates. 
On Tuesday, the Fed made no change in rates, apparently preferring to sit tight without clearer evidence of inflation. 
The next policy meeting is scheduled for Sept. 
30.
Today's trade report showed a June deficit nearly $2 billion smaller than had been expected. 
In addition, the May deficit was revised downward by $700 million from an initial figure of more than $10 billion.
But despite the overall decline, the Clinton Administration continues to be stymied in its efforts to reduce the trade deficits with big Asian nations. 
"Our trade with China is problematic," Secretary of Commerce William M. Daley said at a briefing. 
He noted that exports so far this year had risen 3 percent while imports from China jumped 26 percent.
"There is no reason why our products cannot have a higher presence in the Chinese market, as they do in ours," said Mr. Daley, who plans to visit China in October.
June was only the fourth time that the American deficit with China surpassed the deficit with Japan. 
Major contributors to the China deficit, which was up $500 million to $4.3 billion, were imports of clothing, shoes and toys, the Commerce Department said.
With Japan, the American deficit swelled $500 million to $4.1 billion -- with the imbalance in auto trade, now about $2.5 billion, and in office machines accounting for much of the increase.
Mr. Daley urged Japan to be "more aggressive" in opening its economy and not rely on exports for growth. 
On Friday, the Administration sent a letter to the Japanese complaining about slow application of an agreement to open the Japanese market to American automotive products.
In contrast to the imbalances with Asians, the United States sold record exports to Mexico, reducing that deficit by $500 million in June, to $1.2 billion. 
The deficit with Canada, the other partner in the North American Free Trade Agreement, eased $100 million, to $1.4 billion.
Over all, exports climbed nine-tenths of 1 percent, to $78.4 billion, while imports eased seven-tenths of 1 percent from May's record, to $86.6 billion, the report showed.
Analysts were surprised by the lower imports because an earlier report showed a big jump in inventories held by wholesalers for the month. 
Imported goods tend to enter the country through these middlemen.
About two-thirds of the revision in the May deficit, to $9.5 billion from $10.2 billion, reflected stronger exports, the department's report also showed.
As usual, the June deficit would have been far bigger without surpluses in services and in advanced technology products, of $6.8 billion and $2.4 billion, respectively.

file: Trade Gap Grows, Complicating Visit By Gore to Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
America's global trade deficit soared to $12.7 billion in January, the largest gap between imports and exports since the Commerce Department adopted a new method of measuring international trade in 1992. 
The figures included a 36 percent increase in the deficit with China that will further complicate the politics of Vice President Al Gore's trip to Beijing next week.
Mr. Gore's aides have made clear that they want to steer away from economic issues during his visit, in large part because questions of trade policy have lurked just beneath the surface of the investigations into Asian donations to the Democratic Presidential campaign.
But the figures today showed a $3.7 billion trade deficit with China for the month, compared with $2.7 billion a year ago. 
The widening disparity continues a trend suggesting that the trade gap with China this year will rival the one with Japan. 
That puts further pressure on the Administration to force China into lowering a vast array of trade barriers in negotiations, now under way in Geneva, concerning China's entry into the World Trade Organization.
Mr. Gore had hoped to make only glancing references to that subject during his meeting with China's leaders next week. 
But as one senior Administration official said today, "This is not the time to appear soft on Chinese trade issues."
C. Fred Bergsten, the director of the Institute for International Economics, who has been deeply involved in Asian trade issues, noted today that "there's no question now that Gore will have to go harder on market access issues."
The pressure on the Administration also increased today because three leading Democrats, including Representative Richard A. Gephardt of Missouri, the House minority leader, introduced legislation that would require a Congressional vote before the Administration could agree to let China join the World Trade Organization.
White House officials have said in the past that they would "consult" Congress, but they want to avoid a lengthy debate that could link China's human rights record or arms proliferation to its membership in the club of trading nations.
"This is not a garden-variety entry into the W.T.O.," said Mr. Gephardt, who is widely considered a potential competitor with Mr. Gore for the Democratic Presidential nomination in three years. 
"There are enormous implications of how this is done, for every worker in America and every major company in America."
At the White House today, Mr. Gore's aides changed course on one element of the trip, saying that the Vice President would attend the signing of a deal to sell roughly $1 billion in Boeing aircraft to China, if the deal is sealed in time for his visit. 
Earlier this week, when the Chinese offer was first made known, Mr. Gore's office said he would "consider" attending the signing.
In the past, that would have been just the kind of event that Administration officials would have unhesitatingly jumped at to make the case that exports and economic engagement with China were sustaining high-paying jobs in the United States. 
But recently there has been a rethinking of how deeply President Clinton and Mr. Gore should involve themselves in individual transactions. 
In part, that is in response to the Administration's critics, who say that it has been too close to business executives with interests in China and too mercantilistic in relations with Beijing.
The figures released today contained other complications for Mr. Clinton. The deficit with Mexico was flat compared with January 1996 but rose sharply from the end of last year, just as the Administration is seeking approval from Congress to negotiate an extension of the North American Free Trade Agreement, to embrace Chile and, ultimately, other Latin American nations.
Reading too much into one month's trade figures is always risky, because a few major sales -- especially of aircraft or computers -- can send the monthly numbers sharply in one direction or another. 
Over all, the decline of six-tenths of a percent in exports, to $70.8 billion, reflected a drop in military shipments and a slowdown in aircraft deliveries. 
Imports of goods and services rose 2.2 percent to $83.5 billion, due in part to increased auto shipments from Canada as well as higher prices and greater demand for imported oil. 
Using the old method, the Commerce Department said January's deficit of $19 billion for goods alone was the largest ever.
The widening trade deficit also reflects broader trends, including the fact that America's economy is growing at a faster pace than most of its major trading partners, sucking in imports and drying up markets abroad. 
The rise in the value of the dollar in recent months also appears to be starting to cut into America's exports.

file: Trade Status With China_ Risky Vote Tomorrow.txt
text:
ï»¿
For the seventh time since he took office, President Clinton will ask Congress, on Thursday, to renew China's trading privileges with the United States. 
That has always been a dicey proposition, though one that Mr. Clinton -- with aggressive lobbying help from companies with interests in China -- has always won.
But this year the battle over what are now called "normal trade relations" promises to be more confused, more emotional and far trickier than any time since the military crackdown in Tiananmen Square, 10 years ago. 
Just a few months ago, Mr. Clinton and the Chinese had hoped to be asking Congress for far more, for permanent trade privileges, as part of a deal that would usher China into the World Trade Organization.
Mr. Clinton's aides say that on Thursday the President will hold open the possibility that the bigger and more permanent deal will soon be struck, presumably after the furor dies down here over accusations of Chinese spying and in Beijing over bombing the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade. 
But some of Mr. Clinton's advisers said privately they feared that the chances of having a trade deal signed with the Chinese and through an angry Congress were increasingly remote.
"What we are watching," an adviser said last week, "is a seven-year initiative with China crumble in our hands."
Once the White House called that initiative the development of a "strategic partnership" with China, a phrase stricken from all official references to that country. 
So has the term "commercial diplomacy," once used to describe how increased economic engagement with China would strengthen ties in other arenas.
Now the White House, and business leaders, are arguing the opposite, why national security issues should be divorced from trade.
The White House's seeming ambivalence about how to tackle the vote, which usually becomes a Congressional referendum on the state of Chinese-American relations, is mirrored by the Republicans' ambivalence. 
Roughly half the Republican Presidential hopefuls, including Gary Bauer, Patrick Buchanan and Steve Forbes, argue that the spy case underscores why the United States should suspend negotiations with China over entering the W.T.O.
The other half, including George W. Bush and John McCain, have carefully separated the issues, with Mr. McCain, chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, arguing: "We should make judgments on the basis of our trade interests. 
The scandal is not that they spied on us, but that we let them."
For many executives the debate on responding to the spying accusations echoes the debate that played out in the first two years of the Administration, over tying China's human rights record to its trade privileges. 
Mr. Clinton himself started out that way and reversed course, separating human rights issues from arguments over the annual renewal.
The chairman of Intel Corporation, Andrew Grove, said he saw the relationship in terms of parallel universes. 
"There is the political and geopolitical universe, where nations have problems and collaborations," Mr. Grove said. 
"There is the trade universe, and then there is a universe of technology issues. 
And what we have to deal with -- whether we want to tie those three together, so that if hits a brick wall they all stop making progress."
Mr. Grove's concern, one that he and other technology executives plan to voice here next week, is that Congress will link the trade vote to new restrictions on technology transfers.
"It's entirely possible that higher-end Pentium III's will not be salable in China," Mr. Grove said, referring to top-of-the-line Intel microprocessors. 
"Imagine that, a personal computer you will be able to buy for $1,200 at CompUSA by the end of the year could not be shipped to China."
Mr. Grove and other technology executives argue that such restrictions would not deny technology to China, but that they would rather force China to develop its own processes. 
"And then you have to ask are we better off in any of those universes -- the political one or the trade one or the technological one -- if we force them to build up their technological base on their own?"
In Congress, though, such subtleties have not been debated. 
After Tiananmen, Congress imposed trade and technology restrictions, many of which have since been lifted. 
There may be the same reaction this time.
But some experts on Capitol Hill say they believe that when passions cool, there will once again be momentum for a trade deal that opens China's markets.
"In the end," said Senator Max Baucus, the Montana Democrat who is pushing for permanent trade privileges, "people will come to realize that all the concessions in this trade agreement are on China's side."
