file: U.S. Intelligence Officials Pushed to Focus on China.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a sign of the new importance that Congress is placing on China's growing international power, lawmakers have taken several steps recently to insure that intelligence officials track the country, and particularly its military, more closely.
Not since the cold war, when the Soviet Union was subject to similar measures, have members of Congress pressed for such an extensive effort to keep tabs on a foreign power.
Last week the House passed a provision in the intelligence authorization act calling for a report to Congress within one year on Chinese intelligence and military activities that affect the United States.
Two weeks ago the House approved creation of a center, financed with $5 million from the Pentagon, to employ academics independent from policy makers to study Chinese military affairs. 
The center is needed, the act says, because of the "low priority accorded to the study of Chinese strategic and military affairs within the Government and within the academic community."
Representative Nancy Pelosi, the California Democrat who co-sponsored the provision for the intelligence reports, said, "I don't think we have enough counterintelligence activity going on concerning China, as well as straight intelligence gathering, especially for a country with so much military capability."
The Senate has not passed either measure, but Congressional aides said approval was likely, suggesting that both provisions might become law later this year.
The Senate Intelligence Committee is considering hearings on China soon, including an option for an open hearing, and the House Intelligence Committee has held several closed sessions on China in recent weeks, Congressional aides said.
These new steps come as Chinese efforts to influence American domestic politics are at the center of Senate hearings into campaign finance irregularities. 
Members of Congress have also begun pressing for ways to insure that sales of American technology to China, including supercomputers that can be used to make lighter and more efficient nuclear warheads, are subject to greater governmental scrutiny.
The Pentagon welcomed Congress's intent to set up a center at the National Defense University, a branch of the Defense Department, to study Chinese military affairs.
"We believe it's a positive step to help focus attention on an important country in the coming decades," said Charles Wells, a spokesman for the Defense Intelligence Agency, the intelligence arm of the Pentagon.
Other intelligence officials gave differing assessments of whether the intelligence community was doing a good job of evaluating China's strategic and military plans.
"There is a tremendous amount of analytical work on the Chinese military" being produced already, one official said. 
A senior intelligence official said the number of people studying China had increased and the quality of their work was "better than it has ever been."
But another official said the end of the cold war had not brought about a needed reallocation of resources.
"The proportion of dollars spent on studying China in a strategic context has stayed about the same since the end of the cold war, and hardly anyone is looking beyond 15 years," by which time China could become a significant power, another official said. 
All of the officials spoke on the condition that they not be identified.
Increasingly, Congress has pushed intelligence officials to file public reports on China. 
Last year's intelligence authorization act required a report twice a year by the Director of Central Intelligence on the spread of weapons of mass destruction.
The most recent report found that China was the biggest supplier of such weapons.
But most of the intelligence work on China is secret. 
And some of it is contracted out to experts.
In 1995 American intelligence officials hired outside consultants to analyze China's aerospace abilities, including the McDonnell Douglas Corporation, which has a long history of joint ventures with China, Government and industry officials said.
But now, China's dealings with McDonnell Douglas are the subject of a criminal investigation, adding to concerns by some officials about whether the Federal Government is looking in the right places in its efforts to understand China better.
McDonnell Douglas, the Central Intelligence Agency and the Science Applications International Corporation, the prime contractor responsible for the study of Chinese aerospace, have no comment, their spokesmen said.
In 1994 a Chinese state-owned company acquired aerospace machines from McDonnell Douglas, some of which were improperly diverted to a Chinese military plant in Nanchang, leading to the criminal inquiry. 
Part of the inquiry involves an attempt by McDonnell Douglas, while still working on the intelligence consultancy, to obtain sensitive American satellite photos of the Nanchang plant, American officials said.
The request for the photos was denied, and no one has been charged in the case, which is under investigation by a Federal grand jury here.

file: U.S. Is in a Quandary as Chinese Wait Off Shore.txt
text:
ï»¿
Ten days after the Coast Guard stopped three ships trying to smuggle 659 Chinese into California, senior officials in the Clinton Administration continued to argue over solutions -- none attractive -- to the increasingly difficult and embarrassing situation.
As the United States continued to press the Mexican Government to accept the refugees, the crowded, fetid ships remained about 100 miles southwest of San Diego, surrounded by Coast Guard cutters.
The ships represent the first test of the Clinton Administration's vow to crack down on illegal immigration, a vow made after another smuggler's ship, the Golden Venture, spilled nearly 300 illegal Chinese immigrants onto New York's shores last month.
Even as it wavered over action on the three ships, the Administration said today that it would back tough new legislation on asylum seekers.
Â 
Ejected the Same Day
The measure will allow quick and summary hearings for people who request asylum at airports and other ports of entry, and would stiffen penalties against alien smugglers.
Government officials and others familiar with the plan say it includes charging alien smugglers under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act. 
As a result it will allow Federal prosecutors to seize the assets of smugglers, including ships like the Golden Venture.
Under the bill, a corps of immigration officers will screen aliens caught trying to enter the country without proper documents to determine if their asylum claims are worthy to be heard by an immigration judge. 
Those whose claims are deemed frivolous could be placed on airplanes and sent back to their country of origin on the same day they arrived in the United States.
Under current immigration law, an alien's statement that he has a well-founded fear of persecution is generally sufficient to allow him to be scheduled for a hearing. 
The hearing process can take years, during which the applicant is generally allowed to stay in the United States.
Immigration experts say that in 1992 about 14,000 people tried to enter the country without documents or by using fraudulent documents and then claimed asylum. 
A sizeable percentage of them turned up at Kennedy International Airport in New York, the experts said.
Â 
Unpleasant Alternatives
The bill, which is to be announced when President Clinton returns to Washington, was drafted by Congressional staffs and an interagency task force made up of officials from the Justice Department, the State Department, the Office of Management and Budget and the White House.
For the last 10 days, senior officials of the Departments of State, Defense, Justice and Transportation and the Central Intelligence Agency have been struggling with the problem of the three ships off Mexico. 
The officials are considering these alternatives, immigration officials said:
*Allow the refugees into the United States and hear their pleas for political asylum. 
State Department and immigration service officials vow they will not let that happen.
*Dragoon the refugees onto a United States Navy vessel and ship them back to China. 
But the Navy wants no part of that plan, immigration officials said.
*Force the home nation of the freighters to take their human cargo. 
No one is sure of the ships' true flags; two of the ships claimed Taiwanese registry, an assertion the Government of Taiwan denies.
Â 
'U.S.A. I Love You'
The United States imposed a news blackout on the ships today, keeping the faces of the Chinese passengers waving signs -- "USA I Love You" and "Bread We Want, Freedom We Want" -- off television and out of the newspapers.
No responsible official would comment publicly on the stranded refugees, the so-far fruitless talks with the Mexican Government or the implications for the new policy of preventing boatloads of immigrants from applying for political asylum.
The State Department spokesman, Michael McCurry, said it was "obvious that this is a sensitive matter of diplomacy."
He also said it was "being addressed with urgency on the part of the officials here in the United States that are dealing with it," and added, "We remain in contact with the Mexican Government" on the issue of Mexico's accepting the refugees.
Such contacts were at best strained. 
Senior Mexican officials insisted that they would not take on the immigration problems of the United States, and expressed fury at the way the situation has been handled.
Â 
A Backlog of Applications
Simply put, the Administration wants to prevent the Chinese refugees aboard the ship from applying for political asylum in the United States. 
The system has due-process requirements and legal protections that can take months and years to fulfill. 
It is hard-pressed to handle its backlog of applications: 10,000 new requests a month, and 300,000 people on a waiting list.
The United States also wants to prevent a repeat of the June 6 wreck of the Golden Venture, in which 10 Chinese died trying to swim ashore. 
All but 14 of the 301 illegal immigrants who survived the beaching are still being detained in Immigration and Naturalization Service prisons in Pennsylvania and Louisiana, an I.N.S. spokeswoman said yesterday.
By intercepting the three ships at sea, the United States aims to send a signal that might stop tens of thousands of Chinese people from paying smugglers tens of thousands of dollars apiece to take them to the United States in the filthy holds of freighters.

file: U.S. IS TO MAINTAIN TRADE PRIVILEGES FOR CHINA_S GOODS_A Policy Reversal.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Clinton renewed China's favorable trade status today with virtually no conditions, and said he would abandon his effort to use trade as a lever to force Beijing to make progress on human rights.
While Mr. Clinton said there had been some improvement in human rights, he acknowledged that China's actions had fallen far short of the steps he set forth a year ago as conditions for renewing the trade privileges. 
But he said that as punishment he would do little more than prohibit imports of Chinese guns and ammunition.
Sounding anguished and defensive, the President said at a White House news conference that China's economic and strategic importance had grown so great that it would be unwise to impose the broad sanctions he had threatened.
"We have reached the end of the usefulness of that policy," Mr. Clinton said, "and it is time to take a new path toward the achievement of our common objectives."
[Excerpts, page A8.]
Many American corporations and consumers welcomed his decision. 
[Business Day, page D1.]
But Mr. Clinton's announcement came after weeks of agonizing at the highest levels of the Administration, where officials had to contend with shifting signals from the Chinese Government and a last-minute campaign from rights advocates. 
While his decision had been expected, Mr. Clinton had not been expected to offer so frank an argument that his own approach had been misguided.
Congress could still seek to impose sanctions on China, as it sought unsuccessfully to do during the Bush Administration. 
But Mr. Clinton's remarks amounted to a call for an end to a rite that since the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989 has caused annual battles linking China's trade status to its human rights conduct.
Thus Mr. Clinton cast aside the executive order issued last year, when he became the first President to tie China's trade benefits to progress in the treatment of dissidents and political prisoners. 
He also cast aside his 1992 campaign language, when he accused President Bush of "coddling" Chinese dictators by blocking legislation that would have punished China for its human rights record.
While saying that China continues to commit "very serious human rights abuses," Mr. Clinton noted that Beijing had made some progress toward meeting his demands.
But he made clear his belief that broad trade sanctions had become too heavy a club to wave at a time when commerce between the two countries has grown to billions of dollars and accounts for tens of thousands of American jobs.
As a single punitive act, Mr. Clinton ordered a ban on imports of Chinese guns and ammunition, which amount to $200 million a year. 
He also said he would maintain the few Bush Administration sanctions that remain in effect, including prohibitions on shipments of United States weapons and other goods to the Chinese military.
But those measures will affect only a tiny fraction of the $31 billion in goods that China sold to the United States last year. 
Thus Mr. Clinton has sided with those in Congress and his Administration who warned against jeopardizing relations with Beijing.
Members of Congress who had called for firmer action expressed anger and disappointment. 
Senator George J. Mitchell of Maine, the majority leader, said he planned to introduce legislation on trade sanctions that would "be more likely to encourage the Chinese Government to improve its practices on trade and human rights."
Human Rights Watch, which led the battle to block renewal of the trade benefits, voiced even greater disdain, accusing Mr. Clinton of "effectively removing all pressure on China to improve its human rights practices."
Â 
Business Groups Pleased
But the decision was applauded by business groups, including the United States Chamber of Congress, which likened the policy of tying human rights to trade to "using a blunt instrument for brain surgery."
The decision by Mr. Clinton leaves intact the Jackson-Vanik Amendment of two decades ago that ties trade benefits for Communist countries to their immigration policies. 
But since it first won the privilege in 1980, that barrier has never prevented China from winning renewal of its "most favored nation" trade status, which allows it to send its exports to the United States at the lowest applicable tariffs.
Instead, Mr. Clinton's approach becomes roughly comparable to Washington's strategy toward other nations -- using diplomatic pressure but not holding trade hostage in efforts to make progress on rights.
Today, Mr. Clinton mentioned China's importance in putting pressure on North Korea to abandon its nuclear weapons program as one of the reasons he believed it wise to tread softly. 
He also cited China's role as the most populous country, with 1.2 billion people, and the third-largest economy.
Â 
The Vanity of Pressure
But the fundamental reason he offered for the shift amounted to a repudiation of a year's worth of American pressure tactics. 
He said there would be "inevitably a reluctance" for China to act on rights issues "if it looks like every step that is taken, is taken under the pressure of the United States, some outside power making them do it."
Mr. Clinton's national security adviser, Anthony Lake, nevertheless suggested that the President's strong stance during the 1992 campaign and last year had "allowed us to achieve the progress that has been achieved this year" in focusing Beijing's attention on human rights.
Among the areas Mr. Clinton singled out as examples of progress were China's resolution of all emigration cases involving dissidents and its agreement to a plan to prevent goods produced with prison labor from being shipped to the United States.
But he used strong language to criticize China for its "arrest and detention of those who peacefully voice their opinions" and for its continued repression of religious and cultural traditions in Tibet.
Â 
A Round of Consultations
Before making his announcement, just after 5 P.M., Mr. Clinton spent much of the day on the phone with Congressional leaders and foreign policy experts to gauge their reactions to the steps he might take. 
He also met for 30 minutes with Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who urged the President to impose at least symbolic sanctions, Administration officials said.
Among those who welcomed Mr. Clinton's decision was Rep. Gary Ackerman, Democrat of New York and chairman of the House Foreign Affairs subcommittee on Asia and the Pacific. 
Mr. Ackerman said the separation of trade policy from China's human rights record "will promote American prosperity while enhancing our ability to advance American values and interests throughout the world."
But the minimal penalties Mr. Clinton imposed for what he described as China's "very serious human rights abuses" left labor leaders, human rights advocates and some Democratic lawmakers voicing scorn.

file: U.S. Lowers Goals on China After Glitches in Early Talks.txt
text:

When President Jiang Zemin meets President Clinton on Wednesday in the first state visit of a Chinese leader in a dozen years, there is likely to be a nuclear agreement and possibly one to provide American assistance to clear China's air pollution from its coal-fired power plants.
There will be talk of a new age of economic cooperation, greased by at least $4 billion or more in freshly signed deals, more than half with Boeing.
Naturally there will also be plenty of food and plenty of champagne. 
And the White House will declare, as its top officials have been saying for weeks now, that the main accomplishment of this summit meeting is that it is happening at all.
But that declaration is making a virtue of necessity, senior Administration officials privately admit, because the months of frenzied pre-summit negotiations between Chinese and American officials have produced significantly less than once hoped.
The agreement to get China to reduce its dangerous exports of nuclear expertise will be the substantive centerpiece of Wednesday's meeting, and it will clear the way for billions of dollars in sales of American nuclear power plants to a country whose economic ambitions outstrip its electrical capacity. 
China has also promised to stop selling anti-ship cruise missiles to Iran, reducing threats to American naval ships in the Persian Gulf and helping to mute Republican criticism of Mr. Jiang's visit.
But the once-feverish discussions about getting China to open its markets to foreign competition, especially with state-owned enterprises that are attempting a perilous transition to private ownership, have all but stalled -- and with it, China's hopes that this summit meeting would speed its entry into the World Trade Organization.
In other areas, progress will be at best incremental, senior officials say, and the main importance of this meeting is to provide a new beginning for what they concede has been the single most badly handled foreign policy of Mr. Clinton's Presidency.
In a speech on Friday, Mr. Clinton reiterated the need for broad engagement with China -- "expanding areas of cooperation, dealing forthrightly with our differences" in order to "advance fundamental American interests and values."
But his defense of this visit by Mr. Jiang seemed passionless, and his critics are bound to argue that Mr. Clinton will not get enough in return for ending America's diplomatic quarantine of China after the 1989 military crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square.
Representative Christopher H. Smith, a Republican of New Jersey, who will hold hearings on Tuesday on Chinese human-rights abuses, said the summit meeting itself "should never have happened without preconditions on human rights."
"We don't want nice-sounding words and sound-bites," he added. 
"We want meaningful action for the victims of this dictatorship, which understands only power."
There are already concerns about the 71-year-old Mr. Jiang's reaction to the sight of protesters. 
He says his host, Mr. Clinton, should "handle these events."
Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright said today on NBC's "Meet the Press" that demonstrations were an example of democracy at work, that the Chinese had dictated their own itinerary, and that Mr. Jiang should not expect "a totally fuzzy time."
The biggest accomplishment of this summit meeting is expected to be a written pledge from China to phase out its nuclear assistance to Iran, even though there is no international obligation to do so.
In return, Mr. Clinton will lift a 12-year American ban on sales to China of nuclear technology for civilian power, which Beijing wants to buy and Westinghouse and ABB Combustion Engineering Nuclear Systems desperately want to sell.
Samuel R. Berger, Mr. Clinton's national security adviser, insists that sales of power plants "are the cart, but assurances to end nuclear cooperation with Iran is the horse."
"This is not in the first instance about whether we sell civilian nuclear power to China," he said. 
"It's about nonproliferation."
But many in Congress question the Administration's willingness to crack down on China for the sale of dangerous materiel to Pakistan and Iran. 
The issue has become highly politicized; Republicans have accused Mr. Clinton of downplaying alleged Chinese violations of past pledges to stop dangerous exports.
So Mr. Clinton has made security issues like proliferation and restraining North Korea important justifications for deepening American "engagement" with China at the highest level, and for his refusal to allow American policy toward China to rise or fall on human rights.
For the American business community, however, the power plants are the horse. 
To them, the nuclear sanction is another example of how Washington drives China into the arms of French, Russian and Canadian businesses. 
America's allies long ago came to terms with post-Tiananmen China, noting that China has possessed nuclear weapons for three decades. 
And Westinghouse and ABB Combustion Engineering have spent months documenting to lawmakers how sanctions have already cost the United States $16 billion in lost sales.
"Clearly, the Chinese have the capability to build power reactors on their own and get help from others," said R. Ian Butterfield, director of government affairs at Westinghouse, which is ready to swoop as soon as Mr. Clinton signs the waiver. 
"What they are looking for now is advanced technology, and they are making it clear that they want to standardize on one nuclear-power technology for the country."
Far more business is at stake during this visit, he argues. 
If China's economy keeps expanding rapidly, the country will need $60 billion in new reactors over the next 15 years, and American companies think the vast majority of that business can be theirs.
But the cost will be high: China wants extensive nuclear power technology transfer, just as it has obtained knowledge from Boeing about building sophisticated aircraft. 
And it wants assurances that the United States will be a reliable supplier, no matter what the Congressional mood.
Early this year, Mr. Clinton's aides were betting that the meeting's centerpiece would be China's impending entry into the World Trade Organization, a sign of the country's economic arrival. 
The unspoken part of the deal was that Washington would end the annual Congressional debate over "most favored nation" trade status for China.
But months of negotiations have produced little but doubts over whether Mr. Jiang is truly willing to make the sacrifices to join the W.T.O. 
-- summit or no summit.
China has missed several deadlines to produce a timetable for dismantling layers of protection and subsidies for China's inefficient state enterprises, which employ nearly two-thirds of the urban population.
After his trip to China last month,Treasury Secretary Robert E. Rubin reported to President Clinton that Mr. Jiang has considered the political impact of the economic dislocations of joining the W.T.O. 
-- and was aware that opening markets too fast could worsen the pain. 
"He is quite realistic about the challenges of making this work," Mr. Rubin concluded.
The economic crisis unfolding in Asia may further slow that opening, especially if Mr. Jiang concludes that a battered Hong Kong will not prove to be a cash cow, helping to pay for the privatization of Chinese enterprises. 
The first stock offering in two of those companies, including the huge China National Aviation Corporation, were indefinitely postponed over the weekend.
China's rethinking of when to enter the W.T.O. is understandable. 
Investors poured $42 billion into the country last year, roughly 40 percent of global investment in developing nations. 
Its growth is double digit and even without Hong Kong, it now has foreign currency reserves of an astounding $130 billion. 
Because Congress has consistently extended "most-favored nation" status to China, the Chinese are enjoying all the biggest benefits of joining the W.T.O. 
-- low tariffs for exports -- without any of the responsibilties of membership.
"The Chinese know that they only get into the W.T.O. one way -- on commercially acceptable terms," said Charlene Barshefsky, the United States trade representative. 
But some experts wonder if the American position is shortsighted.
"I think the U.S. side made a mistake and should have recalibrated its approach," said Nicholas R. Lardy, a senior fellow at Brookings Institution, who argues that it is better to get China inside the tent, preventing it from backtracking on past liberalizations. 
"Unless there is a change in policy there is a risk that China stays out indefinitely."
At every meeting, the Americans ask that dissidents like Wang Dan and Wei Jingsheng be granted medical parole. 
They also want Red Cross visits to Chinese prisons and an institutionalized "dialogue" on human rights, an end to religious repression in Tibet and elsewhere, and continued freedoms in Hong Kong. 
The Chinese respond, almost ritually, that these are purely internal affairs.

text:

The Clinton Administration, in an effort to resolve the crisis in relations with China, has been quietly signaling Beijing that if it met Washington's minimum human rights demands, the United States would consider ending the annual threat of trade sanctions to change Chinese behavior.
Administration officials said today that there was already a consensus within President Clinton's economic team, which is now spreading to the White House and even parts of the State Department, that the annual rite of threatening China with a withdrawal of its beneficial trade status if it does not meet certain human rights conditions is outmoded and should be replaced.
That sentiment, which has been conveyed to China by the Administration, also seems to be taking hold on Capitol Hill, from which the pressure to link human rights and trade originally came.
Â 
Threat of Trade Sanctions
The United States has for years used the threat of trade sanctions to promote free immigration and human rights in Communist countries, from the former Soviet Union to China. 
Any move by the Administration and Congress now away from that approach would be a major policy shift, one that reflects the increasing importance of trade to the American economy.
"I think that today, the Congressional mainstream would still want to maintain some linkage between trade and human rights, but the drift is toward delinkage," said Representative Lee H. Hamilton, Democrat of Indiana, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. 
"It is impossible to improve the relationship if you have to go through this fight every year."
He added that there is "a very strong possibility that the Administration will recommend, and the Congress will adopt, the use of other tools" besides trade sanctions to promote American human rights concerns provided that China meets President Clinton's basic human rights demands laid out in an executive order last June.
Administration officials are increasingly arguing that the current policy is outmoded because, as the President has told aides and lawmakers in recent days, the last thing Mr. Clinton wants to do is withdraw China's trade benefits, which would costs thousands of American jobs and billions of dollars in contracts. 
So in some ways the policy rests on an empty threat.
It is also outmoded, other officials argue, because trade is now such an important instrument for opening up Chinese society, for promoting the rule of law and the freedom of movement there, and for encouraging the Chinese authorities to allow citizens to own everything from their own satellite dishes to foreign newspapers, that revoking it would be self-destructive for both sides.
Finally, American policy toward China is only effective if there is a united front, and that united front has broken down as more Americans do business in China and refuse to see their economic interests imperiled by making them a weapon for pressing human rights concerns.
Administration officials say that in dropping the threat of trade sanctions, they would continue to press China in other ways -- from diplomatic censure to holding up World Bank loans.
Â 
Conditions for China
Last May the President signed an order, which many in the Administration now regret, stipulating the precise steps that China must take to win renewal of its trade benefits, which allow it to send its imports to the United States at the lowest available tariff.
The President has told lawmakers and aides that while he would do all that he could to avoid having to withdraw trade benefits from Beijing, he feels politically, morally and legally bound to fulfill the basic terms of that executive order.
One senior official said, "We have told the Chinese, 'Get us over the executive order, and we will consider all kinds of alternatives.'
"
The Administration's intent, officials say, is both to offer an inducement for China to cooperate, but at the same time to signal hard-liners in the Chinese leadership that they cannot get by with just doing nothing.
Administration officials said that they believed last May that they had to adopt the executive order because Mr. Clinton, during the campaign, had strongly criticized President Bush for "coddling" China and he did not want to appear to be going back on another campaign promise. 
They also did it out of a fear that Congressional Democrats might otherwise have forced an even more stringent approach on them through legislation.
The order calls for China to begin putting into effect an agreement made two months ago to end its practice of using prison labor to make products exported to the United States, and to fully comply with American demands to allow a list of Chinese dissidents and their families to leave the country.
Â 
Visit to Prison
The Chinese have told the United States they are prepared to deal with most of the immigration cases and have already allowed one visit by a team of American inspectors to a suspected prison labor camp. 
The Administration feels that China is thus at least getting close to satisfying its demands on these points.
In addition, the President's order calls for "overall significant progress" in China's handling of and accounting for political prisoners, relations with Tibet, and the jamming of foreign radio programs. 
The Administration has always been prepared to interpret that progress loosely, but officials say that Beijing, while it has been inching in the right direction, has not yet given them even the bare minimum they need to convince Congress on these points.
Therefore, the Administration's China policy between now and June is to redouble efforts to persuade Beijing to take the last few steps. 
This is going to be done primarily through quiet diplomatic channels, and not high-profile visits -- in light of the confrontation that erupted during Secretary of State Warren Christopher's recent tour.
Â 
Views of Economic Official
There has been much wrangling over the Administration's China policy in recent days. 
At a White House meeting on Monday, members of the Clinton economic team -- particularly Secretary of the Treasury Lloyd Bentsen -- said they wanted to see more frequent meetings by all the principal policy makers on China to insure that the views of the economic officials of the Administration were being fully taken into account.
The economic aides said they were not troubled by Mr. Christopher pressing the human rights issue, but said that on his recent visit to China he or some of his aides seemed to be doing it in a confrontational manner that was encouraging Beijing to dig in its heels.
Secretary Christopher, backed by the President's National Security Adviser, Anthony Lake, asked that Mr. Clinton issue a public statement reaffirming his commitment to the executive order and the general approach to China being carried out by the Secretary of State.

text:

The United States appears to be heading for another clash with China, this time over a divisive World Bank development loan that would help Chinese authorities resettle tens of thousands of Chinese in regions traditionally inhabited by Tibetans and Mongolians.
The Clinton Administration seems to be getting ready to oppose the plan when it comes before the World Bank's executive board for a final approval next month, though White House officials say no final decision has yet been made.
Private pro-Tibetan groups are lobbying against the project, which would spend $160 million to resettle 60,000 poor farmers from eroded hillsides in China's western Qinghai province to better lands about 300 miles farther west.
China and the World Bank see the plan as part of a campaign to alleviate rural poverty in remote areas by offering farmers the chance to make a better living and relieving population pressures in vacated areas.
But critics argue that moving these farmers, who are mainly Han Chinese and members of the minority Hui, Tu and Salar ethnic groups, will further erode the position of the Tibetan inhabitants of Dulan County in Haixi Prefecture, where the farmers are to be resettled and which is a designated Tibetan and Mongolian Autonomous Area. 
Tibetans are already in a minority there.
Qinghai province is outside the borders of the Tibetan region China annexed in 1959, but has traditionally been strongly ethnically Tibetan and is the birthplace of the Dalai Lama, the Tibetan spiritual leader.
Although Qinghai has been a province of China since the 17th century, critics see the proposed resettlements as part of a broader campaign by the Chinese authorities to weaken Tibetan national identity.
Asked about the project during an appearance before the House Banking Committee last week, Treasury Secretary Robert E. Rubin said, "We are enormously concerned about it," adding that the United States is "inclined to oppose it."
John Ackerly of the International Campaign for Tibet, a Washington-based organization fighting for Tibetan rights, said: "This relocation, which the World Bank now proposes to help finance, is part of a larger Chinese policy which is now the greatest threat to the continued existence of the Tibetans as a distinct people and culture."
Critics say the plan violates World Bank guidelines, which state that indigenous ethnic minorities should "not suffer adverse effects from bank-financed projects and that they receive culturally compatible social and economic benefits."
"The proposed resettlement will make the indigenous Tibetans even more marginal than they are already," said Kate Saunders of the London-based Tibet Information Network, which first highlighted the dangers of the project.
Critics also argue that the scheme is part of a broader plan to establish the infrastructure needed to exploit the region's mineral resources, which would inevitably attract additional inflows of non-Tibetans.
For the moment, the World Bank is standing behind the project. 
In a briefing paper issued this week it defends the resettlement plan as an integral part of its efforts to reduce poverty in China, which has cut the number of rural poor from 280 million to 80 million over a decade.
The farmers to be resettled, it argues, are "among the poorest people in the world, with incomes of about $60 a year."
But it admits that the resettlement would weaken the position of indigenous Tibetans and Mongolians in the area.
In Haixi Prefecture, the Tibetan percentage of the population would fall from 11.1 percent to 10.3 percent, while in Dulan County it would decline from 22.7 percent to 14 percent. 
For Mongolians the declines are from 7.6 percent to 6.5 percent and from 14.1 percent to 6.7 percent.
The number of Han Chinese in Haixi Prefecture would rise from 236,918 to 261,375 and in Dulan County from 27,977 to 52,434.

file: U.S. Puts Sanctions On Taiwan.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Clinton Administration said today that it was imposing trade sanctions on Taiwan for refusing to halt the sale of tiger bones and rhinoceros horns, the first time that Washington has deployed trade sanctions to protect the environment.
While trade sanctions have often been used by the United States as a lever to promote human rights or to lower trade barriers imposed by other countries, they have never been used to protect endangered wildlife.
"I am delighted that the U.S. has taken the lead in this worldwide battle to save the rhinoceros and tiger before it is too late," Diana E. McMeekin, head of the African Wildlife Foundation, said. 
"It is as if the governor has issued a last-minute stay of execution for those magnificent creatures on the edge of extinction."
The sanctions on Taiwan will involve a ban on all Taiwan wildlife-product exports to the United States, which amount to about $25 million a year in coral and mollusk-shell jewelry and in snake, lizard and crocodile skin shoes and other leather products, the White House said.
This is a fraction of Taiwan's trade with the United States, which last year involved $25.1 billion in exports to the United States and $16.25 billion in American exports to Taiwan.
Â 
Â 
Underground Trade
Tiger and rhinoceros parts are used by people in Taiwan and many other Asian nations for medicinal purposes, and because many people consider them sexual stimulants. 
Their use has become so widespread that an underground trade has developed and populations of both animals have been decimated.
"This is the first time any country has acted on the international call for trade sanctions to protect endangered species, but if the illegal trade in rhinos and tigers is not eliminated, these species could be extinct in five years," President Clinton said in a statement. 
"The world must know that the United States will take strong actions to protect the earth's natural heritage."
[In a statement released Tuesday in Taipei, Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed "deep regret and dissatisfaction over the U.S. 
Government's obviously unfair and unjust sanction."
Asked if Taiwan planned reprisals, a Government spokesman, Eric Chiang, said, "We haven't discussed any counteractions."]
The American move underscores the fact that as trade grows more global and as barriers between countries come down, the environmental consequences can be enormous. 
When advances in hunting techniques are combined with lower trade barriers and rapidly growing populations that demand medicines made from exotic wildlife, a species can be wiped out in one generation.
Tigers, commonplace in circuses and zoos around the world, will shortly be extinct in the wild if this trade is not stopped. 
At the turn of the century, the world tiger population was estimated at about 100,000; today, there are fewer than 6,000.
In 1970, there were more than 65,000 African black rhinos and today there are fewer than 1,800, according to the African Wildlife Foundation. 
There are only about 10,000 rhinos of all species left in the world.
It is a common practice in Asia to grind the bones of both animals for medicines and aphrodisiacs. 
Tiger and rhino parts are prescribed by doctors in Taiwan, China and Korea for fevers, arthritis and impotence.
The Administration's Interagency Rhino/Tiger Task Force, which recommended sanctions to the President last week, had been considering imposing sanctions on China as well. 
At the last minute it decided to act only against Taiwan, saying China had taken some limited steps to curb the sale of exotic-animal parts.
At a time when Chinese-American tensions are running high over human rights issues and Washington is considering revoking Beijing's preferential trade status, the Administration probably did not want to open a new front with the Chinese on wildlife -- even though the Chinese are considered by experts to be among the worst offenders.
Still, the move against Taiwan, argued the United States trade representative, Mickey Kantor, constitutes "a major step forward."
"Other administrations have threatened these kinds of measures to protect the environment before, but none has ever acted," he said.
The United States had warned Taiwan and China in November that it might impose trade sanctions if they did not demonstrate by March 30 "measurable, verifiable and substantial progress" in curbing illicit trade in tiger and rhino parts.
China took some steps, the most notable a public burning of tiger and rhino medicines, and made an effort to register stocks of those medicines and to educate people against their use. 
But Taiwan did little to satisfy American demands to safeguard rhinos and tigers, which are protected under the Convention on International Trade and Endangered Species.

But that company was a dummy corporation set up as part of a sting operation by the Customs Service.
Federal officials are trying to determine whether Mr. Yao, who was arrested while attending a conference on fiber optics in San Diego, was working as an entrepreneur or as a purchaser for the Chinese military. 
During the transaction, Mr. Yao said he was representing a Beijing firm called Lions Photonics and insisted that the gyroscopes were destined for a Chinese university that was working on a railroad project.
While such gyroscopes can be used in railroad projects, Federal officials are skeptical, because an associate of Mr. Yao's said they also were seeking infrared sensors, which are commonly used in missiles to detect heat-generating targets.
One Federal official said using this kind of gyroscope for a railroad project "would be like flying an F-14 to the grocery store."
The arrest of Mr. Yao, who is believed to be 33, came only hours after the Clinton Administration, in an unrelated case, decided to prevent Hughes Electronics from exporting to China a $450 million communications satellite ordered by a Singapore consortium with links to officers of the Chinese Army. 
The State and Defense Departments said they feared that the satellite and the technology to launch it into a precise orbit could further improve the accuracy of Chinese missiles.
And as Mr. Yao was being escorted into Federal court in San Diego on Friday for a hearing at which he agreed to be transferred to Boston to face charges, the Pentagon delivered a report to Congress detailing China's buildup of tactical missiles on its coast facing Taiwan.
The report concluded that China was "still decades" away from being able to project military force far beyond its borders but that its cruise and ballistic missiles "will give Beijing the 'credible intimidation' needed to accomplish political and military goals without having to rely on overwhelming force-on-force superiority."
In the gyroscope case, a man identified by authorities as an associate of Mr. Yao, a Canadian citizen of Chinese origin, Collin Xu, was arrested two weeks ago in Boston. 
The authorities charge that he took delivery of the fiber-optic gyroscopes, all but one of which was a dummy, and he is being held without bail.
Mr. Xu pleaded not guilty. 
His lawyer, Richard M. Egbert, declined to discuss the case on Friday, saying, "The facts will come out when we develop them."
An affidavit filed in Boston by a customs agent, Timothy N. Gildea, asserts that Lions Photonics first sought to buy four advanced gyroscopes in December 1997 from a Massachusetts company that is not identified in the complaint.
Officials familiar with the case say the company was Fibersense Technology Corporation of Canton, Mass., which makes fiber-optic gyroscopes for the military, chiefly for missiles, aircraft and space vehicles.
The complaint says the company told Mr. Yao and Mr. Xu, who said the gyroscopes would be used for a "superspeed train navigation system," that they would need permission from the State Department because the gyroscopes were on the State Department's munitions list, a compilation of technologies that can be exported only with a license.
Two such applications were filed in May 1998, one listing the end user as Zhejiang University, and another listing the final user as Changsha Rail University, both in China.
The applications were immediately denied by the State Department, which noted that China was a "prohibited destination" for the gyroscopes.
In August a new order was received by the Massachusetts company for nearly identical equipment, listing a new company as the purchaser: Micro Techland in Montreal. 
An exemption to the State Department licensing rules permits the shipment of some types of equipment without a license to Canadian companies for use in Canada.
Their suspicions aroused, officials at the military manufacturer alerted the Customs Service, which soon began its sting operation. 
Mr. Yao was referred to officers of the agency's dummy company.
The undercover operation soon received an identical order for the gyroscopes. 
An expert on military gyroscopes, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the type the Chinese were trying to purchase were "tactical" gyroscopes used on missiles, on the gun turrets of tanks and sometimes on railroads.
For months the undercover company negotiated with its Chinese customers by E-mail, arguing over price, specificiations and even warranty conditions.
The final order amounted to about $70,000, and at one point, according to partial transcripts of the conversations included in the criminal complaint, Mr. Xu asked, "Do you also do infrared sensors?"
Mr. Xu ultimately picked up the gyroscopes in the Boston area, Federal officials say, and was arrested on his way to a Federal Express office. 
On Feb. 
19, Mr. Yao entered the United States, and he was arrested on Monday night in San Diego.

file: U.S. Says Ties With China Are On the Mend.txt
text:

After two days of meetings with senior Chinese officials, an American government delegation left Beijing on a positive note today, with members characterizing the talks as helping to get the bilateral "relationship back on track."
Relations soured after NATO war planes bombed the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade last May, in what the United States has insisted was an accident. 
Beijing reacted to the bombing by suspending talks with the United States on military issues, arms proliferation and human rights.
This week's visit, by a delegation that included Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott and top officials from the State Department, Defense Department and the Joint Chiefs of Staff, was part of an effort to resume dialogue. 
But the meetings came just a month before Taiwan's presidential elections, and seemed in part an effort to avoid the ugly confrontations that preceded the last Taiwan presidential election, in 1996. 
At that time, China lobbed missiles into the waters near Taiwan and American aircraft carriers sailed into the region in response.
American officials said that this week they told their Chinese counterparts they thought "what happened in 1996 was counterproductive," although they said they were "unclear" if the Chinese shared that view.
"We said we should regard the period ahead as a period of opportunity but also a period by definition of some uncertainty, that requires the greatest possible degree of restraint, caution and prudence on everybody's part," one American official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
That such cordial meetings could take place now is considered an improvement.
Joseph Prueher, the recently arrived American ambassador to China who was commander of the United States Pacific Fleet in 1996, has complained that he had no one in the Chinese military he could confer with as his ships were moving towards Taiwan. 
At a recent news conference in Beijing, he advocated more "communication between military leaders so there are not miscalculations."
In addition to Taiwan, this week's meetings, which included a five-hour session with Deputy Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi, covered a broad array of foreign policy issues including North Korea, tensions between India and Pakistan and relations with Russia.
The Americans also met with Deputy Prime Minister Qian Qichen and Lt. Gen. Xiong Guangkai, deputy chief of the People's Liberation Army's general staff and its central figure for foreign policy.
The Chinese took the opportunity to express their displeasure with United States military assistance to Taiwan and the national and regional missile defense systems currently under study. 
The Chinese worry that these might be used against them in any conflict with Taiwan.
In turn, American officials said they expressed objections to the Chinese missile build-up in Fujian, the Chinese province closest to Taiwan. 
They said they also reminded the Chinese that military sales to Taiwan were a reaction to threats from China.
The United States sells arms to Taiwan "for defensive purposes, depending on its needs. 
And that doesn't exist in a vacuum," an American official said.
In recent weeks, top Chinese officials, including Mr. Qian, have restated their longstanding threat to use military force if Taiwan makes any formal moves towards independence.
Despite these warnings, the mood on the mainland in the run-up to the Taiwan elections this time is far calmer than it was four years ago, when large stretches of the Chinese coast across from Taiwan were turned into a military zone and civilian airports there were closed to commercial traffic.
The American officials said that the Chinese have been studying Taiwan politics closely and seemed to understand the complexities of the election, in which ambiguity has become a virtue when it comes to relations with the mainland.
All three of Taiwan's leading presidential candidates have declared that they will not pursue independence from the mainland.

text:

Despite their strained relations, the United States and China have embarked on a program of environmental cooperation to address problems like rapid urbanization, pollution from energy consumption and the changing agricultural patterns of an increasingly prosperous population.
White House officials said a three-day meeting of senior agency officials from both nations at the White House last week was especially noteworthy because it occurred at a time when Chinese-American relations have been strained by differences over Taiwan and other trade and security issues.
They said the talks were the kind of step that Secretary of State Warren Christopher has been calling for in an attempt to put more focus on global environmental concerns as a central element of foreign policy.
"It is significant that this is moving forward with high-level backing when there are so many things going wrong with the relationship," an Administration official said. 
"The environment is a priority that supersedes those problems."
The meetings involved dozens of fairly senior officials -- assistant secretaries and vice ministers -- from agencies involved in energy, agriculture, environment, urban affairs, disaster relief and other such technical and economic fields. 
Hui Yong-zheng, vice minister of the State Science and Technology Commission, led the Chinese delegation. 
Mr. Clinton's science advisor, Jack Gibbons, attended about half the three-day session, and Vice President Al Gore also took part briefly.
White House officials said Mr. Gore and Prime Minister Li Peng consider the talks a preliminary step toward a permanent, high-level relationship aimed at what specialists call "sustainable development."
That philosophy assumes that economic growth, especially in countries that are advancing rapidly, like China, must be carefully managed to ensure that such growth does not impose unacceptable costs in environmental degradation and depletion of resources.
The talks were not intended to be negotiating sessions over particular projects or decisions, such as whether the Export-Import Bank of the United States will subsidize loans to American companies for construction of the Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River, American officials said. 
That enormous project has been strongly criticized by environmentalists, and the Administration has recommended against the bank providing financing.
An American participant in the talks said he was impressed with the depth of understanding displayed by the Chinese over the complexities of balancing economic and environmental considerations, the potential for achieving both sets of objectives at once, and the importance of doing so. 
Chinese delegates emphasized that China's new five-year plan, the Government's central declaration of policies, is a turning point in its explicit and detailed commitments to sustainable development.
China, with its huge population, rapid economic growth and accelerating urbanization, has long been recognized both as a nation with serious environmental problems and as a major market for environmental technologies, an area in which the United States is a world leader.
Among the problems discussed at the meeting, according to American participants, were these:
*China's enormous demand for new electric-generating capacity, which is expected to be met primarily with coal-fired power plants. 
That causes two main kinds of problems: acid rain in China, and a big source of carbon dioxide, one of the greenhouse gases that threatens to cause global warming.
*China's agricultural needs, which are shifting as the population eats more meat, as China imports more grain, and as arable land is converted to industrial and urban uses.
*The difficulties of housing, transportation and pollution control in growing coastal cities, and whether they can be relieved by planning more growth in smaller cities.
"The Chinese appear virtually certain to emerge as one of the largest economies on earth in the next century," an American official said. 
"With growth of 10 percent a year, their environmental problems can accelerate rapidly, and that can have a profound impact."
Both nations, in different ways, are major players in deciding whether emissions of greenhouse gases can be controlled in the century ahead. 
The United States is by far the biggest emitter of carbon dioxide. 
It could be the leader in technologies to cut those emissions, but so far has failed to live up to its pledge to quickly cut its emissions, which continue to grow. 
China is the leading example of a fast-growing new contributor to the atmospheric burden of carbon dioxide.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: U.S. Studying Limited Penalties for Chinese Sale.txt
text:
ï»¿
Instead of issuing a blanket sanction against loans to companies doing business in China, American officials are drafting penalties against the Chinese company that sold $70,000 of ring magnets to Pakistan, a violation of an American law, Clinton Administration officials said today.
The penalties, which are being reviewed by Government legal experts, are a reflection of the Administration's judgment that it would be wrong to institute a general sanction that would penalize American companies doing business in China rather than the Chinese company that made the sale.
"A consensus has been reached that this is the most sensible approach and the legal people are working to check its consistency with the law," a senior American official said, while cautioning that a final decision, expected soon, has yet to be made by Secretary of State Warren Christopher and President Clinton.
American officials describe themselves as frustrated by the rigid nature of the 1994 Nuclear Nonproliferation Act, which is being applied for the first time, and by the Chinese refusal to admit any wrongdoing, at a time when the Americans are trying to manage a delicate relationship during a complicated political season in both countries.
Administration security, foreign policy and trade officials met for an hour on Tuesday, then broke up into subcommittees to decide what to do in the face of the law, which requires $10 billion to $11 billion in sanctions against American companies in response to the $70,000 Chinese sale.
The Chinese have refused to be helpful on the ring magnets. 
They say the magnets were not on any forbidden list of products and refuse to promise to refrain from such behavior in the future. 
They said the deal was not a central Government decision, but an open sale by a Government-owned company with a high degree of independence -- the China National Nuclear Corporation.
American officials admit that the ring magnets, which are akin to those used in huge stadium loudspeakers, are not on the American "trigger list" for the Nonproliferation Act. 
But the 5,000 magnets were designed to be used in a Pakistani centrifuge, in an unsafeguarded laboratory, to produce fissile material -- in the same way that Iraq made it, and the Americans themselves made it at Oak Ridge in World War II.
The act requires the Secretary of State to inform Congress and the Export-Import Bank if any country "has willfully aided or abetted any non-nuclear weapons state" to acquire unsafeguarded, special nuclear materials.
If so, the Bank must then halt Government loans or loan guarantees to American companies doing business in the offending state, in this case China, with between $10 billion to $11 billion outstanding. 
The President may waive the Export-Import Bank suspension on national security grounds, but then may, under separate authority, come up with other, more specific sanctions against the Chinese military or the China National Nuclear Corporation itself.
The Chinese corporation has a $150 million deal with Export-Import Bank support, the officials say, on Westinghouse technology for a reactor at Qinshan, near Shanghai. 
There is another, potential $500 million deal between the corporation and Bechtel.
In meetings this week, many officials judged the evidence of central Chinese Government knowledge of the sale to be unclear, raising questions about the "willful" quality of the proliferation. 
And the officials have always objected to the blanket Export-Import Bank suspension in the law. 
So the consensus emerged to declare sanctions against China but then waive the sanctions on national security grounds, and to penalize the corporation itself.
The Administration does not want increased tensions in the relationship, but needs to obey the law and remain credible, while also dealing with Chinese violations of an agreement to protect American intellectual property rights. 
And the Administration wants these issues resolved before May, when it will certify the Chinese as a most-favored nation for trade purposes.
The Congressional debate on that certification will be a way for legislators to register their fury with Beijing on issues from trade to human rights to nuclear exports, and both houses could reject it, forcing Mr. Clinton into an embarrassing veto during his re-election campaign. 
American officials say that Congress, where Mr. Clinton's rival Senator Robert Dole wields strong influence, wants China to be hit hard on the nuclear issue in return for an easier time on certification.

file: U.S. to Apply New Vigor in Policing Trade.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Clinton Administration plans to announce a broad initiative to enforce dozens of trade accords with China, Japan, Canada and other big trading partners, in a move that appears directed at protecting President Clinton from Republican accusations that his free trade agreements are costing jobs in the United States.
Administration officials said today that as part of the initiative, the United States trade representative, Mickey Kantor, would create an enforcement office, charged with forcing several nations to live up to their agreements.
But Mr. Kantor, who was President Clinton's campaign chairman in 1992, said that the effort to be announced on Friday would be much broader, involving the Commerce Department and other agencies.
"We're convinced that you've got to be willing to show the sword to get results," said Stuart E. Eizenstat, President Jimmy Carter's domestic-policy adviser, who was nominated by President Clinton this week to be under secretary of commerce for international trade. 
"We know that making the case for free trade also means showing that we are not going to tolerate violations of the agreements we have already reached."
Administration officials have frequently spoken of a more rigorous monitoring of trade accords. 
And to get those agreements, the Clinton White House has threatened sanctions against trading partners, including close allies, far more often than previous administrations.
But after grabbing considerable attention with its threats, especially during the protracted dispute with Japan last year over automobile trade, the Administration stopped short of invoking many of those sanctions, declaring that last-minute agreements made them unnecessary.
Until now, however, there has been no formal system for resuscitating agreements that are failing, whether with South Korea, Canada or others.
And while Administration officials say that they are simply carrying through on three-year-old promises to enforce American trade laws, the new and tougher tone seems prompted, at least in part, by fear that Patrick J. Buchanan, along with other Republican Presidential aspirants, is striking a chord in voters by arguing that the Administration has become a paper tiger on trade matters -- threatening, but rarely acting.
If a major showdown develops this election year, many trade experts and some Administration officials say, it will probably be with China.
So far, the Beijing authorities have done very little to enforce a significant agreement struck last February to crack down on the piracy of music, movies and computer software. 
American officials say that 29 Chinese factories churning out huge volumes of counterfeit compact disks are still running at top speed.
Mr. Kantor has set a deadline next month for China to change its ways and avoid a renewal of trade sanctions against exports to the United States.
The issue is also politically charged in Congress, where Republicans and Democrats both say that Beijing's continued repression of dissidents, combined with the soaring American trade deficit, has undermined the Administration's policy of "comprehensive engagement.". 
The term describes a strategy in which economic and commercial ties are used to attempt to influence countries' political behavior.
Publicly, the Clinton Administration continues to defend its China policy, arguing that it was right to stop linking the renewal of preferential trade status for the Chinese to their record on human rights. 
In private, though, there is increasing nervousness that Mr. Clinton is open to the same accusation that he leveled at George Bush in 1992: that the United States is coddling China's leaders to benefit American exports.
Assailing China's failure to comply with trade accords has the political advantage of getting tough without bringing human rights into the discussion.
"The pattern has been that the United States calls on China to remedy its trade sins, China agrees to do so, then China breaks its promise," Greg Mastel, a China expert at the Economic Strategy Institute, wrote recently. 
"The credibility of U.S. trade policy around the world will be severely undermined if such blatant disregard goes unanswered."
In a speech scheduled for Friday, Mr. Kantor is expected to steer clear of the matter of intellectual-property rights, another area in dispute with China, because negotiations are under way to resolve it without threatening to reimpose $1 billion in trade sanctions.
He is, though, expected to announce a series of enforcement actions involving other countries.
One of the first is with Canada, which recently placed an 80 percent tax on advertising carried in Canadian editions of Sports Illustrated, a Time Warner property. 
American officials view the tax as an effort to protect Canadian publications from competition, and argue that it violates both the North American Free Trade Agreement and the world trade accord signed last year.
Another early action expected would seek enforcement of Japanese obligations -- not those involving last year's agreement over autos and auto parts, which the Administration says is being faithfully observed -- but Japan's refusal to protect music recordings made between 1946 and 1971.
It may be the first time, Mr. Kantor conceded today, that he has come to the defense of Frank Sinatra, the Beatles and Bo Diddley -- artists whose early recordings have remained popular in Japan.
Another important American ally, South Korea, will also be a target: It reached an agreement last year to permit American meat to be sold in its grocery stores, but it has missed several deadlines to file the agreement with the World Trade Organization in Geneva.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: U.S. to China_ Be More Open On Arms Plan.txt
text:

In a rare address to Chinese military officers, Defense Secretary William J. Perry urged China's armed forces today to be more open about the budget and the planning in order to ease concerns abroad.
"Your capabilities in all areas, including the military areas, are growing by the day," Mr. Perry told 300 Chinese colonels and generals. 
"It would be helpful if your defense budget and strategic planning were more open and visible to the outside world."
China's efforts to strengthen its armed forces has led to worries that Beijing might use its military to bully its neighbors and support its territorial claims in the South China Sea. 
And those concerns have been aggravated by the military's penchant for secrecy.
Aides to Mr. Perry reported that the Chinese had agreed to send a team of defense officials to the Pentagon to outline their military plans until 2000, as part of a reciprocal information exchange.
But the officials said it was not clear just how forthcoming Beijing was prepared to be about the areas of concern cited today by Mr. Perry: China's actual level of military spending, its military strategy and its plans to upgrade its weaponry.
As the first American Defense Secretary to visit China since the Tiananmen Square crackdown in 1989, the simple fact that Mr. Perry was speaking to the officers was itself something of an event.
As he arrived at the National Defense University in Bejing, a military band in gleaming white uniforms struck up "America the Beautiful."
A large Red Star, the emblem of the People's Liberation Army, dominated the room as Mr. Perry spoke to a crowded room of officers dressed in green uniforms with yellow epaulets.
During the speech, a soft-spoken Mr. Perry made his case for closer ties between the American and Chinese militaries, saying that Washingon and Beijing have a special responsibility to insure stabilityI in the western Pacific.
Mr. Perry said China needed to do more to restrain its sale of missile and other military technologies. 
Alluding to Chinese arms deals with Pakistan, he warned that an arms race between Pakistan and India, two nuclear powers, could lead to a "catastrophic" war on China's southern border.
Mr. Perry also warned that a nuclear-armed North Korea would be a menace. 
And he said China and Vietnam needed to eschew inflammatory statements and military issues intended to reinforce their territorial claims in the South China Sea.
Mr. Perry's mention of human rights, however, was brief and somewhat indirect. 
He said the failure to make progress in this area would give ammunition to critics of ties between Washington and Beijing.
Then the Defense Secretary took questions for about an hour from the Chinese officers, most of whom appeared to be looking toward their superiors on the podium for a guide about how to react.
At the end of the event, Gen. Zhu Dunfa, the president of the defense university, said Mr. Perry had given a speech of "great significance," raised his hands and gave a hearty applause. 
The officers quickly followed suit.
Mr. Perry's speech was one of the highpoints of his three-day visit to China, in which he also met with top military and civilian leaders, including Premier Li Peng. 
Mr. Perry's visit ends on Wednesday, when he visits Wuhan and Chongqing, and meets with President Jiang Zemin.
The polite and occasionally warm reception Mr. Perry received from the Chinese military stood in marked contrast to his meeting this morning with American business representatives. 
At the meeting, sponsored by the American Chamber of Commerce, business officials expressed little interest in the military issues Mr. Perry said were important for the future of the region and complained that Washington was not doing enough to help American companies do business here.
But in Washington, Mr. Perry's military talks have attracted more interest, including some criticism from conservatives and human rights supporters.
Mr. Perry sought to deal with the critics today by underscoring the potential benefits for American security of dealing with the Chinese while playing down expectations for immediate results.
Describing the overall progress in the talks as "modest," Mr. Perry said the Chinese appeared sensitive to American concerns. 
But he added, "The value you can put on those steps needs to be seen yet."

file: U.S. to Pay China for Embassy Bombing.txt
text:
ï»¿
Ending more than two months of acrimony, the United States and China agreed here today that Washington would pay $4.5 million in compensation for the victims of NATO's bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Yugoslavia.
The agreement removes one of the biggest obstacles in relations between Washington and Beijing at a time when several sensitive issues -- Taiwan and trade, above all -- remain on the table as the two nations prepare for a meeting between Presidents Clinton and Jiang Zemin at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in New Zealand in September.
David Andrews, a State Department legal adviser who led the American side in the negotiations, said the agreement reflected "the critical importance of the U.S.-China relationship."
He said the money would be paid as soon as possible.
The agreement does not resolve several other issues, including compensation for damage done both to China's Embassy in Belgrade on May 7 and to the American Embassy and consulates in China in days of violent protest after the bombing. 
Talks on property damage will begin in late August.
Mr. Andrews said the Chinese Government would decide how the compensation will be divided among the families of the 3 people who were killed and 27 who were wounded and will distribute the money.
An Administration official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said in Washington that the agreement was an "important step in putting this issue behind us and mending the relationship with Beijing."
"obviously it's very significant."
The bombing was viewed by Beijing and ordinary Chinese alike as an affront to national dignity, sparked violent anti-American demonstrations and prompted China to adopt a stern line in all contacts with the United States. 
Meetings on human rights, security issues and China's effort to join the World Trade Organization were all postponed.
China demanded a full apology, a detailed accounting of how the bombing occurred and punishment for those responsible as conditions for restoring normal ties. 
To date, Beijing's official position is that Washington's explanation that the bombing was caused by faulty planning and intelligence is insufficient.
But American officials say they have detected recent efforts by Chinese officials to find a way past their more confrontational demands. 
China's state media gave wide coverage to telephone calls that Mr. Clinton made to Mr. Jiang. The two Presidents spoke when teams from the two countries played each other in the Women's World Cup Final on July 10.
They conferred again last week after Taiwan's President, Lee Teng-hui, infuriated Beijing with remarks interpreted as nudging Taiwan closer to formal independence -- something China has vowed to block with military force if necessary.
Earlier this week, the Chinese played host to an American Under Secretary of Commerce, David L. Aaron, for a day of talks that appeared to be breaking the ice for something more substantive.
Previously, China had been unwilling to discuss compensation for damage to the American Embassy and consulates in China, arguing that it was caused by student demonstrators, as opposed to the four NATO-launched missiles that hit the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade.
Mr. Andrews said today that Yin Yubiao, the Chinese Foreign Ministry's director general for treaties and law, had agreed to proceed at the same time on discussions about damage to each side's embassy.
Mr. Andrews went out of his way to say the compensation was voluntary and not an admission of American liability. 
Washington has insisted that the bombing was an accident.
"This payment will not create any precedents," Mr. Andrews said, apparently trying to quell concern about possible claims against the United States in the future that arise from other military action.
Perhaps the most pressing issue in American-Chinese relations in the coming months will be China's desire to enter the World Trade Organization. 
With limited time in a complex schedule of hurdles that have to be crossed to win United States support for China's entry, American officials said the talks would have to restart before the September meeting between Mr. Clinton and Mr. Jiang.
So far, China has been unwilling to resume negotiations. 
The compensation talks had been considered the primary obstacle, but United States officials say they will not know until they actually sit down again at a negotiating table.
The official New China News Agency today reiterated China's position that the bombing was indefensible.
"The Chinese side stressed that the U.S. bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Yugoslavia caused serious personnel casualties and property losses and grossly violated the international law and the norms governing international relations," the agency said. 
"The U.S. side must bear all the responsibility for this and make immediate, adequate and effective compensations for all the losses occurred to the Chinese side."

Robert E. Rubin, director of the National Economic Council, says he would like the Clinton Administration to ultimately adopt a China policy that ended the link between trade and human rights.
